<!-- tutorial/15-transactions-and-accounting.md -->

# 15. Transactions and accounting

- Category: Tutorial

## What you will learn

- Keep users (register and login) and money (accounts and a ledger) in KarelaDB.
- Stop bad data with **CHECK constraints** (for example: no balance below zero).
- Move money with a **transaction**: all steps are saved, or none.
- Get a new id back with **RETURNING**.
- Keep a transaction open over **many requests** (kareladb shell, HTTP, PostgreSQL protocol).
- What happens when many programs write at the same time, and what the **timeouts** do.
- What happens on an **error** and after a **crash**.

The examples use a new, empty database `market`. Each example is a file in `examples/15-transactions-and-accounting/`. The results are real.

## The rules in short

| Rule | What it means for you |
|---|---|
| One writer per table | While one transaction is open, other changes of its tables **wait**; changes of other tables go on. Two transfers never mix. |
| Reads do not wait | A `SELECT` of another program sees the data **as it was before** the open transaction. It never sees half of a transfer. |
| All or nothing | `COMMIT` saves all changes of the transaction in one log write. An error saves nothing. |
| Crash safe | After a crash or power cut, every transaction that got `COMMIT` OK is there. A transaction without `COMMIT` is not there at all. |
| CHECK | A row that breaks a `CHECK` is never written. |

## The tables

```sql
-- Users who can log in, their accounts, and every movement of money.
CREATE TABLE users (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO,
  email STRING NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  password_hash STRING NOT NULL,
  created TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO,
  user_id INT NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  balance DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (balance >= 0)
);

CREATE TABLE ledger (
  id LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO,
  from_account INT NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),
  to_account INT NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),
  amount DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL,
  created TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now(),
  CONSTRAINT positive_amount CHECK (amount > 0),
  CONSTRAINT two_accounts CHECK (from_account != to_account)
);
```

```text
table 'users' created

table 'accounts' created

table 'ledger' created
```

Some choices here are important for money:

- **`DECIMAL(2)`** for money, never `DOUBLE`. A `DECIMAL` is exact: `0.10 + 0.20` is `0.30`.
- **`NOT NULL`** on every money column. A `CHECK` lets `NULL` pass, so use both.
- The **ledger** keeps every movement. Never update or delete ledger rows. To undo a transfer, write a new transfer back.

## Register and login

KarelaDB has the functions `password_hash(password)` and `password_verify(password, hash)`. They keep only a salted, slow hash of the password, never the password itself.

```sql
-- Register two users. RETURNING gives the new AUTO id back.
INSERT INTO users (email, password_hash) VALUES ('ram@example.com', password_hash('ram-secret-1')) RETURNING id, email;
INSERT INTO users (email, password_hash) VALUES ('sita@example.com', password_hash('sita-secret-2')) RETURNING id, email;
```

```text
id | email
---+----------------
 1 | ram@example.com
(1 row, 0.9 ms)
1 row(s) inserted

id | email
---+-----------------
 2 | sita@example.com
(1 row, 0.4 ms)
1 row(s) inserted
```

`UNIQUE` refuses a second user with the same email:

```sql
-- The same email again: UNIQUE refuses it.
INSERT INTO users (email, password_hash) VALUES ('ram@example.com', password_hash('other')) RETURNING id;
```

```text
error: column 'email' must be unique: 'ram@example.com' is already used
```

Login: find the user by email and check the password.

```sql
-- Login: find the user by email, check the password against the saved hash.
SELECT id, password_verify('ram-secret-1', password_hash) AS password_ok
FROM users WHERE email = 'ram@example.com';

SELECT id, password_verify('wrong password', password_hash) AS password_ok
FROM users WHERE email = 'ram@example.com';
```

```text
id | password_ok
---+------------
 1 | true
(1 row, 53.8 ms)

id | password_ok
---+------------
 1 | false
(1 row, 50.7 ms)
```

`password_verify` is slow **on purpose** (about 50 ms), so an attacker cannot try many passwords fast. In your app, give the same message for "no such email" and "wrong password".

In a real app, send the email and the password as **parameters** (`$1`, `$2` in the PostgreSQL protocol), never glued into the SQL text.

## RETURNING: get the new id

`INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` can end with `RETURNING` and a list of columns or expressions. You get the rows back like from a `SELECT`:

```sql
-- One account for each user. Ram starts with 1000.00.
INSERT INTO accounts (user_id, balance) VALUES (1, 1000), (2, 0) RETURNING id, user_id, balance;
```

```text
id | user_id | balance
---+---------+--------
 1 |       1 | 1000.00
 2 |       2 |    0.00
(2 rows, 2.0 ms)
2 row(s) inserted
```

| Statement | `RETURNING` gives |
|---|---|
| `INSERT` | the new rows, with `AUTO` ids and `DEFAULT` values filled in |
| `UPDATE` | the rows after the change |
| `DELETE` | the deleted rows |

`RETURNING *` gives all columns. If the `RETURNING` list has an error (an unknown column), nothing is written.

## CHECK constraints

A `CHECK` is a rule for every row. KarelaDB checks it on `INSERT`, `INSERT OR REPLACE`, `UPDATE`, `InsertRows` and the line protocol. A row that makes the condition **false** is not written, and the statement fails:

```sql
-- A balance below zero breaks the CHECK constraint: nothing is written.
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 5000 WHERE id = 1;
```

```text
error: CHECK constraint 'accounts_balance_check' of table 'accounts' failed: balance >= 0 is false for the row id='1', balance='-4000.00'
```

The message names the **constraint**, the **table** and the **row** (its key and the columns the rule uses).

Two ways to write a `CHECK`:

```sql
balance DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0)              -- after a column
CONSTRAINT positive_amount CHECK (amount > 0)                 -- after the columns, with a name
```

Without a name, KarelaDB makes one: `table_column_check` (for a column) or `table_check`. `SHOW CREATE TABLE` shows every `CHECK` with its name:

```sql
SHOW CREATE TABLE accounts;
```

```text
create_sql
"CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO,
  user_id INT NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  balance DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  CONSTRAINT accounts_balance_check CHECK (balance >= 0)
)"
```

Add or remove a rule later:

```sql
ALTER TABLE accounts ADD CONSTRAINT max_balance CHECK (balance <= 10000000);
ALTER TABLE accounts DROP CONSTRAINT max_balance;
```

`ADD` first reads every row of the table. If a row already breaks the rule, the rule is refused, and the message names that row.

| CHECK rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| NULL | `NULL` passes (the result is not false). Add `NOT NULL` when the value must be there. |
| What it can use | The columns of the same row, operators, `CASE`, built-in functions (`length(email) > 3`, `amount BETWEEN 1 AND 100000`). |
| What it cannot use | Other rows, subqueries, aggregates (`sum`), window functions, saved functions, computed columns. |
| Columns | A column used by a `CHECK` cannot be dropped. `RENAME COLUMN` also renames it inside the `CHECK`. |

## A transfer

Moving money needs **four** changes: take money from one account, give it to the other, write the ledger row, and save. They must happen together.

```sql
-- Move 250.50 from account 1 to account 2: all steps together, or none.
BEGIN;
SELECT id, balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN (1, 2) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 250.50 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 250.50 WHERE id = 2;
INSERT INTO ledger (from_account, to_account, amount) VALUES (1, 2, 250.50) RETURNING id;
COMMIT;

SELECT id, balance FROM accounts ORDER BY id;
```

```text
transaction started

id | balance
---+--------
 1 | 1000.00
 2 |    0.00
(2 rows, 0.2 ms)

1 row(s) updated

1 row(s) updated

id
--
 1
(1 row, 0.0 ms)
1 row(s) inserted

transaction committed: 3 change(s) saved

id | balance
---+--------
 1 |  749.50
 2 |  250.50
(2 rows, 0.0 ms)
```

Why each part is there:

| Part | Why |
|---|---|
| `BEGIN` | Starts the transaction. Every table it changes (or reads with `FOR UPDATE`) is locked from then on until `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`: no other program can change those tables meanwhile. |
| `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` | Reads the balances. Your app can check them (for example, show "not enough money" before trying). `FOR UPDATE` tells the reader: these rows are read to be changed. In KarelaDB it locks the table `accounts` at once, so the balances you just read cannot change before your `UPDATE`. Other databases need it too: write it, and your SQL stays correct everywhere. |
| `balance = balance - 250.50` | Let the database do the math, in one statement. **Do not** read the balance in your app, subtract there, and write the result back (`SET balance = 749.50`) outside a transaction: two programs could both read 1000.00. |
| `CHECK (balance >= 0)` | Even if your app forgets to check, the database refuses a negative balance. |
| `RETURNING id` | The ledger id, for the receipt. |
| `COMMIT` | Saves all changes with one log write. |

## When something goes wrong

Ram has 749.50 now. He tries to send 900.00:

```sql
-- Ram has 749.50. A transfer of 900.00 fails at the first UPDATE.
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 900 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 900 WHERE id = 2;
INSERT INTO ledger (from_account, to_account, amount) VALUES (1, 2, 900) RETURNING id;
COMMIT;
```

```text
transaction started
error: CHECK constraint 'accounts_balance_check' of table 'accounts' failed: balance >= 0 is false for the row id='1', balance='-150.50' (the transaction was rolled back)
```

The first `UPDATE` fails. The whole transaction is **rolled back**: nothing of it is saved. The books are the same as before:

```sql
-- Nothing of the failed transfer was saved. Check the books.
SELECT id, balance FROM accounts ORDER BY id;

SELECT sum(balance) AS total_money FROM accounts;

SELECT from_account, to_account, count(*) AS transfers, sum(amount) AS moved
FROM ledger GROUP BY from_account, to_account ORDER BY from_account;
```

```text
id | balance
---+--------
 1 |  749.50
 2 |  250.50
(2 rows, 0.2 ms)

total_money
-----------
    1000.00
(1 row, 0.1 ms)

from_account | to_account | transfers | moved
-------------+------------+-----------+-------
           1 |          2 |         1 | 250.50
(1 row, 0.1 ms)
```

Run queries like these every night. The total must not change (except for money that comes in from outside), and every balance must match its ledger rows.

| What happens | Result |
|---|---|
| A statement fails (CHECK, REFERENCES, UNIQUE, a typing error, ...) | The transaction is rolled back. Nothing is saved. |
| Your app sends `ROLLBACK` | Nothing is saved. |
| The client disconnects before `COMMIT` | Rolled back. |
| No statement for 30 seconds | Rolled back (see [Timeouts](#timeouts)). |
| KarelaDB crashes or the power goes off before `COMMIT` returns | Nothing is saved. |
| `COMMIT` returned OK | Saved, also after a crash or power cut. |
| The disk is full at `COMMIT` | `COMMIT` returns an error, and nothing is saved. |

## A transaction over many requests

A transaction can go over many requests when the program keeps a **session**:

- **kareladb shell**: one session for the whole shell.
- **HTTP**: `POST /session`, then the header `X-KDB-Session` on every `/exec`.
- **PostgreSQL protocol** (psql, and drivers for Python, Go, Node, Java, .NET): every connection is a session. Use `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` as usual.

Inside a session there is one more rule: **after an error, the session accepts only `ROLLBACK`**. Your next statements do not run by mistake outside the transaction:

```powershell
# In kareladb shell, a transaction goes over many lines. After an error, only ROLLBACK is accepted.
@"
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 2;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10000 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1 WHERE id = 2;
ROLLBACK;
SELECT id, balance FROM accounts ORDER BY id;
.exit
"@ | kareladb shell market
```

```text
KarelaDB 0.2.0-dev shell on market
End statements with ';'. Type .help for commands, .exit to quit.
kareladb> transaction started
kareladb> 1 row(s) updated
kareladb> error: CHECK constraint 'accounts_balance_check' of table 'accounts' failed: balance >= 0 is false for the row id='1', balance='-9250.50' (the transaction was rolled back; send ROLLBACK to end it)
kareladb> error: the transaction of this session was rolled back (a statement in it failed); nothing of it was saved. Send ROLLBACK to end it, then start again
kareladb> transaction rolled back (it was already rolled back: a statement in it failed)
kareladb> id | balance
---+--------
 1 |  749.50
 2 |  250.50
(2 rows, 0.1 ms)
kareladb>
```

The third line (`+ 1` for account 2) was **not** run: it would have given money without taking it anywhere. `COMMIT` in this state also fails (`COMMIT saved nothing: ...`), so your app cannot think the transfer was saved.

### Over HTTP

```text
POST   /session                 -> {"session": "<id>", "idle_timeout_ms": 600000}
POST   /exec  (header X-KDB-Session: <id>)   BEGIN, UPDATE, ..., COMMIT
DELETE /session/<id>            -> {"session": "<id>", "closed": true}   an open transaction is rolled back
```

PowerShell:

```powershell
$url = "http://127.0.0.1:9900"
$s = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post "$url/session"
$h = @{ "X-KDB-Session" = $s.session }
$r = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post "$url/exec" -Headers $h -Body "BEGIN"
$r.results[0].message
$r = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post "$url/exec" -Headers $h -Body "UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1 RETURNING balance"
"balance inside the transaction: " + $r.dataset[0][0]
$r = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post "$url/exec" -Body "SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1"
"balance seen by another request: " + $r.dataset[0][0]
$r = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post "$url/exec" -Headers $h -Body "UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2; INSERT INTO ledger (from_account, to_account, amount) VALUES (1, 2, 100) RETURNING id"
"ledger id: " + $r.results[1].dataset[0][0]
$r = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post "$url/exec" -Headers $h -Body "COMMIT"
$r.results[0].message
$r = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post "$url/exec" -Body "SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1"
"balance after COMMIT: " + $r.dataset[0][0]
$r = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Delete "$url/session/$($s.session)"
"session closed: " + $r.closed
```

```text
transaction started
balance inside the transaction: 649.50
balance seen by another request: 749.50
ledger id: 2
transaction committed: 3 change(s) saved
balance after COMMIT: 649.50
session closed: True
```

The request **without** the session header saw 749.50: the open transaction was not committed yet.

| HTTP session rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| Id | Random and long, so nobody can guess another client's session. Keep it secret like a password. |
| Unused | A session without a request for 10 minutes is closed (its open transaction was already rolled back after 30 seconds). |
| Unknown or closed id | `/exec` answers `404` with `session '...' does not exist`. |
| Busy | `table 'x' is busy`, `database is busy` and `deadlock` are answered with `503`: try again a moment later. |

## Many programs at the same time

KarelaDB locks **tables**, not the whole database. A writer locks every table it uses until its statement ends; inside `BEGIN` ... `COMMIT` it keeps them until the transaction ends. Two transfers can never mix, and every transaction sees the data exactly as the one before it left it (this is called *serializable*).

- **Writers of the same table wait.** While session A has an open transaction that changed `accounts`, session B's `UPDATE`, `INSERT`, `DELETE` or `CALL` on `accounts` **waits** until A ends. Writers wait in a queue: the one that came first goes first. Line-protocol writes and `InsertRows` into that table wait too.
- **Writers of other tables do not wait.** A price feed into `live_data` goes on while a transfer holds `accounts` and `ledger`.
- **What is locked:** the tables a statement changes and reads, and what it sets off: tables its triggers and procedures use, and tables linked to it by `REFERENCES`.
- **Deadlock:** when A waits for a table B holds, and B then needs a table A holds, one of them gets `deadlock: ...` at once and is rolled back. Run it again. Use the tables in the same order in every transaction (`accounts`, then `ledger`), and it cannot happen.
- **Schema changes** (`CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`) lock every table. They wait until no transaction is open.
- **Readers do not wait for an open transaction.** Session B's `SELECT` runs at once and sees the data **without** A's changes. Inside A, a `SELECT` sees A's own changes.
- A normal statement without `BEGIN` is its own small transaction, so it also waits for an open transaction that holds its table.
- **Commits share the disk.** Writers that commit at the same moment share one wait for the disk (group commit). Each one is still told "committed" only when its changes are on the disk.

A read can still wait for a writer's **running** statement, usually a millisecond. A long `CALL` or a slow trigger body can make reads wait for seconds. `kareladb serve --reader-yield on` (in Docker: `KARELADB_READER_YIELD=on`) lets reads in between the statements of such a writer: they read the last committed rows at once.

A transfer takes about a millisecond, so waiting is short. It becomes a problem only when a transaction stays open for a long time. **Never** keep a transaction open while you wait for a person (a click, a form, an SMS code). Read first, ask the person, then do `BEGIN ... COMMIT` quickly.

## Timeouts

| Option (`DatabaseOptions`) | Default | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| `lock_timeout_ms` | 5000 (5 s) | A writer that waited this long for a table gets the error `table 'x' is busy: another transaction has held it for N ms; waited 5000 ms ...` (a schema change: `database is busy: ...`). Nothing of its statement was done. Try again. |
| `idle_transaction_timeout_ms` | 30000 (30 s) | A transaction with no statement for this long is rolled back. Its session's next statement gets `the transaction of this session was rolled back (it was open without a statement for ...)`. Send `ROLLBACK` and start again. |

In your app:

- On `table 'x' is busy`, `database is busy` or `deadlock`: wait a little (for example 100 ms) and run the **whole** transaction again.
- On any error inside a transaction: send `ROLLBACK`, then show an error or try the whole transaction again. Never continue with the next statement.

## After a crash

Changes of a transaction are written to the log only at `COMMIT`, in one write, and KarelaDB waits until the disk has them. So:

- a transaction that got `COMMIT` OK is there after a crash or a power cut;
- a transaction without `COMMIT` leaves **no trace**, not even half of a transfer.

KarelaDB tests this all the time. `test_accounting` runs 8 threads doing 2,000 random transfers (with errors, rollbacks and clients that go away) while readers check the total at every moment, and copies the database folder in the middle of open transactions and opens the copies. `crash_test` kills a program doing transfers more than 200 times at random moments and checks every time: the total is the same, no balance is negative, the ledger matches the balances, and every confirmed transfer is there.

## Checklist for an accounting app

1. Money columns: `DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL`, with `CHECK` rules for what must never happen (`balance >= 0`, `amount > 0`).
2. Keep a ledger. Never update or delete its rows; correct a mistake with a new row.
3. Every transfer: `BEGIN`, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, `UPDATE ... SET balance = balance ± amount`, `INSERT INTO ledger ... RETURNING id`, `COMMIT`.
4. On any error: `ROLLBACK`. On `table 'x' is busy`, `database is busy` or `deadlock`: try the whole transaction again.
5. Keep transactions short. No waiting for people inside a transaction.
6. Use parameters (`$1`), not SQL glued together from user input.
7. Store `password_hash(...)`, check with `password_verify(...)`.
8. Check the books every night (total, and balances against the ledger), and make a backup (chapter 9).

## Try it yourself

1. Add a rule so that one transfer can move at most 50,000.00.
2. Ram sends 100.00 to himself (account 1 to account 1). What happens?
3. Your app does: `SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1` (749.50), then without `BEGIN`: `UPDATE accounts SET balance = 649.50 WHERE id = 1`. Why is this wrong, even with the `CHECK`?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. `ALTER TABLE ledger ADD CONSTRAINT max_amount CHECK (amount <= 50000);`
2. The ledger `INSERT` breaks `CHECK (from_account != to_account)` (`two_accounts`). The transaction is rolled back, so the two `UPDATE`s before it are undone too.
3. Between the `SELECT` and the `UPDATE`, another program can change the balance (for example, a transfer in or out). Your `UPDATE` then writes an old number and the other change is lost. Use `balance = balance - 100` inside `BEGIN ... COMMIT`.

</details>

# 16. Users, passwords and security

- Category: Tutorial

## What you will learn

- **Part A.** How your app lets people register and log in, with KarelaDB as the database: a users table, `password_hash`, `password_verify`, session tokens.
- **Part B.** Database users: who may use the KarelaDB server itself, and what each one may do (roles).
- **Part C.** A checklist for a small VPS on the internet.

Chapter 15 uses the same register and login in a small accounting example. Part A is about the people who use **your app** (customers, staff). Part B is about the **programs and people that connect to KarelaDB** (your app's backend, you in the web console, a report script). They are two different things. Most apps need both.

---

## Part A: users of your app

### Never store plain passwords

Do not put the password itself in a table. If somebody gets a copy of the database (a stolen backup, a bug, an old disk), they get every password. Many people use the same password for email and bank. So a leak hurts them far beyond your app.

Store a **password hash** instead:

- A hash is made from the password, but the password cannot be made back from the hash.
- KarelaDB's `password_hash()` is **slow on purpose** (about 0.05 to 0.4 seconds). One login is still fast. But an attacker who stole the hashes can only try a few guesses per second, not billions.
- Each hash has a **random salt**. Two users with the same password get different hashes.

| Do | Do not |
|---|---|
| `password_hash('the password')` when the user registers | store the password, or `sha256(password)` (far too fast to guess) |
| `password_verify('typed password', password_hash)` when the user logs in | compare hashes with `=` (every hash has its own salt, so it never matches) |
| give the user a random session token after login | send the password again with every request |

### The tables

```sql
CREATE TABLE app_users (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO,
  email STRING NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  password_hash STRING NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE TABLE app_sessions (
  token_hash STRING PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INT NOT NULL REFERENCES app_users(id),
  expires_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);
```

- `email ... UNIQUE`: the same email cannot register twice.
- `app_sessions` keeps the **SHA-256 of the token**, not the token. Then a leaked copy of this table cannot be used to log in either.

### Register

Your backend receives the email and the password (over HTTPS). It runs:

```sql
INSERT INTO app_users (email, password_hash) VALUES ('sita@example.com', password_hash('correct horse battery'));
SELECT id, email, password_hash FROM app_users;
```

```text
1 row(s) inserted
id | email            | password_hash
---+------------------+-------------------------------------------------
 1 | sita@example.com | $pbkdf2-sha256$i=600000$TJZOjybZUId98CTZjROu0...
(1 row, 0.1 ms)
```

The hash looks like `$pbkdf2-sha256$i=600000$<salt>$<hash>`. It says how it was made (PBKDF2 with SHA-256, 600,000 rounds, as OWASP advises), so KarelaDB can check it later, even if the default changes.

KarelaDB hashes the password **before** the `INSERT` locks the table, so other writers of `users` do not wait for the slow hash. The statement KarelaDB shows back has the hash, not the password, and the console's history saves `password_hash('***')`.

If the email is already used, the `INSERT` fails because of `UNIQUE`. Tell the user "this email is already registered".

### Log in

```sql
SELECT id FROM app_users
WHERE email = 'sita@example.com' AND password_verify('correct horse battery', password_hash);
```

```text
id
--
 1
(1 row, 53.5 ms)
```

With a wrong password there is no row:

```sql
SELECT id FROM app_users
WHERE email = 'sita@example.com' AND password_verify('wrong guess', password_hash);
```

```text
id
--
(0 rows, 52.2 ms)
```

Rules for the login:

- Call `password_verify` **once** per login. It is slow on purpose (see the time above).
- Show the same message for "no such email" and "wrong password", for example "wrong email or password". Then nobody can find out which emails are registered.
- Count failed logins in your app (per email and per IP address) and wait longer after each failure. KarelaDB does this for its own logins (Part B), but not for your app's table.
- `password_verify` gives `false` for a damaged hash. It never gives an error. `NULL` in gives `NULL` out.

### Sessions: stay logged in

After a good login, make a random token and keep its hash:

```sql
SELECT random_token() AS token;
```

```text
token
-------------------------------------------
gag86m0anriIibqzs8qzIZSay4l6JKe8vUOI1WqeyJ8
(1 row, 0.0 ms)
```

`random_token()` gives 32 random bytes from the operating system as URL-safe text (43 characters). Your backend sends it to the browser as a cookie (`HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` or `Strict`) and saves its hash with an expiry time:

```sql
INSERT INTO app_sessions VALUES (sha256('mR3v7yJ2nqKx0Qe8i4uX1t9LZbF5cH6aWgD2sP0oVkE'), 1, dateadd('d', 7, now()));
```

On **every request**, your backend finds the user of the token:

```sql
SELECT u.id, u.email
FROM app_sessions s JOIN app_users u ON u.id = s.user_id
WHERE s.token_hash = sha256('mR3v7yJ2nqKx0Qe8i4uX1t9LZbF5cH6aWgD2sP0oVkE') AND s.expires_at > now();
```

```text
id | email
---+-----------------
 1 | sita@example.com
(1 row, 0.1 ms)
```

This is fast: `sha256()` is not slow like `password_hash()`.

Log out:

```sql
DELETE FROM app_sessions WHERE token_hash = sha256('mR3v7yJ2nqKx0Qe8i4uX1t9LZbF5cH6aWgD2sP0oVkE');
```

Delete old sessions now and then: `DELETE FROM app_sessions WHERE expires_at < now();`

### Change a password, reset a password

- **Change** (the user knows the old one): check the old one with `password_verify`, then `UPDATE app_users SET password_hash = password_hash('new password') WHERE id = 1;` and delete the user's other sessions.
- **Reset** ("forgot password"): make a `random_token()`, save `sha256(token)` with a short expiry (for example 30 minutes) in a table like `app_sessions`, and email a link with the token. When the link is used, check it like a session, set the new password, and delete the reset row.

### Always use parameters

Never build SQL by gluing user text into it: `"... WHERE email = '" + email + "'"` lets a user write SQL (SQL injection). Use your driver's parameters (`$1`, `$2` with the PostgreSQL protocol), or put the text through a function that doubles every `'`.

### The functions

| Function | Gives | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `password_hash(text)` | `'$pbkdf2-sha256$i=600000$...'` | store a password (slow on purpose) |
| `password_hash(text, iterations)` | the same with 1,000 to 10,000,000 rounds | more rounds are slower and safer |
| `password_verify(text, hash)` | `true` / `false` | check a password; `false` for a damaged hash |
| `sha256(text)` | 64 hex characters | hash a token, a file name, ... (fast) |
| `hmac_sha256(key, text)` | 64 hex characters | sign a message with a secret key (webhooks) |
| `random_bytes(n)` | n random bytes as hex (n = 1 to 1024) | secrets, codes |
| `random_token()`, `random_token(n)` | n random bytes (default 32) as URL-safe base64 | session tokens, reset links, API keys |
| `gen_random_uuid()` | `'0465d47f-8194-4c94-a372-eda3b70504a0'` | random ids (UUID version 4) |

```sql
SELECT sha256('abc') AS hex, hmac_sha256('key', 'message') AS mac, gen_random_uuid() AS id, random_bytes(8) AS bytes;
```

```text
hex                                              | mac                                              | id                                   | bytes
-------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------+-----------------
ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177... | 6e9ef29b75fffc5b7abae527d58fdadb2fe42e7219011... | 0465d47f-8194-4c94-a372-eda3b70504a0 | 6614740117d2ce39
(1 row, 0.0 ms)
```

(`kareladb sql` cuts long text in table output; the full values are there.)

The random functions give a new value for every row and every call. `DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()` gives each new row its own id.

**How slow is `password_hash`?** On a PC with SHA instructions in the CPU (most PCs and servers since about 2018) 600,000 rounds take about 0.05 to 0.1 seconds. Without them, about 0.4 seconds. KarelaDB prints nothing about this; `test_crypto` shows the time on your computer. A small VPS with 1 CPU can do about 10 logins per second. That is fine for a normal app.

---

## Part B: database users and roles

### When does KarelaDB ask for a login?

| Server | Login needed? |
|---|---|
| `kareladb serve` on `127.0.0.1` (the default), no `--token`, no users | **No.** Only programs on the same computer can connect. This is how KarelaDB worked before. |
| a data folder that has **users** | **Yes**, for every request (except `/health`, `/api/login` and the console page itself). |
| started with `--token <secret>` | **Yes**. The token works like an admin. With users, the token and the users both work. |
| `--bind 0.0.0.0` (or any address that is not 127.x) without `--token` and without users | **Refused**: `kareladb serve` does not start (see below). |

`kareladb shell` and `kareladb sql` open the database files directly. They never ask for a login: whoever can read the data folder can do everything. Protect the folder with the file permissions of the operating system.

### Create the first user

Users belong to the **data folder** (they are kept in a hidden database `_system` in it). A server that opened one database folder by its path (`kareladb serve D:\kdb\market`) has no users; use `--data-dir` for users.

The first user must have `ROLE admin`. With the server **stopped**:

```sh
kareladb user add admin --role admin --data-dir /srv/kareladb/data
```

KarelaDB asks for the password twice (the typed text is not shown). From a script, pipe it in: `echo "the password" | kareladb user add admin --role admin`. Never put a password on the command line: other users of the computer can see command lines.

Or with SQL, in `kareladb shell` or in the console of a server that has no users yet:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER shop_app WITH PASSWORD 'Another-long-secret-42';
GRANT write ON DATABASE shop TO shop_app;
CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD 'Reports-only-secret-7' ROLE read;
SHOW USERS;
```

```text
user 'admin' created with role admin
user 'shop_app' created with role none
user 'shop_app' has role write on database 'shop'
user 'report' created with role read
name     | role  | grants     | created                  | changed
---------+-------+------------+--------------------------+-------------------------
admin    | admin | NULL       | 2026-09-11T16:49:06.180Z | 2026-09-11T16:49:06.180Z
report   | read  | NULL       | 2026-09-11T16:49:06.284Z | 2026-09-11T16:49:06.284Z
shop_app | none  | shop=write | 2026-09-11T16:49:06.229Z | 2026-09-11T16:49:06.232Z
(3 rows, 0.0 ms)
```

As soon as the first user exists, a running server asks for a login.

`SHOW USERS` never shows passwords or hashes. A user who is not an admin sees only their own row.

### Roles

| Role | May do |
|---|---|
| `none` | nothing (until a `GRANT`) |
| `read` | `SELECT`, `SHOW`, `EXPLAIN`, CSV export, cursors, `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`/`ROLLBACK`, `/api/info`, list backups |
| `write` | everything of `read`, and `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `CALL`, line protocol (`/write`) |
| `admin` | everything of `write`, and `CREATE`/`ALTER`/`DROP` of tables, views, functions, procedures and triggers, `BACKUP`, `CHECK` |

- The **ROLE** of a user (`CREATE USER ... ROLE read`) is for **every** database.
- A **GRANT** is for **one** database: `GRANT write ON DATABASE shop TO shop_app`.
- KarelaDB uses the stronger of the two.
- Only a user whose own ROLE is `admin` may create and drop databases and manage users (`CREATE USER`, `GRANT`, ...). `GRANT admin ON DATABASE shop` gives all rights inside `shop`, but not these.
- Every user may change their own password: `ALTER USER report WITH PASSWORD '...'`.

A refused statement gets an error that says what is missing, and nothing of it runs:

```text
{"error":"INSERT needs role write on database 'shop'; user 'report' has read"}   (HTTP 403)
```

Give each program only what it needs. Your app's backend: `write` on its own database (plus `admin` only when it must create tables). A report script: `read`. Keep `admin` for yourself.

### All user statements

```sql
CREATE USER [IF NOT EXISTS] name [WITH] PASSWORD 'secret' [ROLE admin|write|read|none];
ALTER USER name [WITH] PASSWORD 'new secret';
ALTER USER name ROLE read;
DROP USER [IF EXISTS] name;
SHOW USERS;
GRANT read|write|admin|ALL ON DATABASE db TO name;     -- ALL = admin
REVOKE [read|write|admin|ALL] ON DATABASE db FROM name;  -- removes the grant on that database
GRANT SELECT|INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE|ALL|DEFAULT ON TABLE t TO name;   -- chapter 21
REVOKE SELECT|INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE|ALL ON TABLE t FROM name;       -- chapter 21
ALTER USER name ENABLE TOTP;   -- two-factor login, chapter 21
```

| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| Names | letters, digits, `_` and `-`, 1 to 63 characters. `Bob` and `bob` are the same user. |
| Passwords | at least 12 characters, not the user name, at most 1024 bytes. Write `''` for a `'` inside. Older passwords keep working. |
| `REVOKE read` | takes away only a `read` grant. A `write` or `admin` grant stays (KarelaDB says so); use `REVOKE ALL` to take away any grant. |
| Last admin | the last user with `ROLE admin` cannot be dropped or lose that role while other users exist. |
| New password | ends every login (session) of that user at once. |
| `DROP DATABASE` | also removes every `GRANT` on that database. |

The same with the `kareladb` tool, when the server is stopped:

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `kareladb user add <name> [--role admin\|write\|read\|none]` | add a user (the first one is admin) |
| `kareladb user passwd <name>` | set a new password |
| `kareladb user role <name> <role>` | change the role |
| `kareladb user list` | names, roles and grants |
| `kareladb user remove <name>` | remove a user |
| `kareladb user reset-2fa <name>` | turn two-factor login off (a lost phone) |

All of them take `--data-dir <folder>`. While `kareladb serve` runs, they refuse (the server has the users open); use SQL in the console then.

### Logging in

**Web console.** It shows a login form. After the login, the top bar shows the user and a **Log out** button. The login is kept in a cookie that scripts in the page cannot read (`HttpOnly`) and that other web sites cannot use (`SameSite=Strict`). It ends after 12 hours, at **Log out**, when the server restarts, or when the password changes.

**Programs: HTTP Basic.** Send the user name and password with each request. KarelaDB remembers a good password for 10 minutes, so this is not slow:

```sh
curl -s -u report:Reports-only-secret-7 "http://127.0.0.1:9900/exec?db=shop&compat=0&query=SELECT%20id,%20email%20FROM%20app_users"
```

```text
{"query":"SELECT id, email FROM app_users","results":[{"statement":"SELECT id, email FROM app_users","columns":[{"name":"id","type":"INT"},{"name":"email","type":"STRING"}],"dataset":[[1,"sita@example.com"]],"count":1,"truncated":false,"rows_affected":0,"message":"","timings":{"parse_us":21,"execute_us":172}}],"timings":{"parse_us":21,"execute_us":172}}
```

**Programs: log in once.** `POST /api/login` gives a token. Send it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`:

```sh
curl -s -i -H "Content-Type: application/json" --data '{"user":"shop_app","password":"Another-long-secret-42"}' http://127.0.0.1:9900/api/login
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Set-Cookie: kdb_login=472axoBncSsNLsieeFTU2Vz8Nomiuun3fYBWjd80u5E; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Max-Age=43200
{"user":"shop_app","role":"none","grants":{"shop":"write"},"expires_ms":1789188565554,"token":"472axoBncSsNLsieeFTU2Vz8Nomiuun3fYBWjd80u5E"}
```

**The `--token`** still works as before, and can do everything.

**PostgreSQL clients** (port 8832) log in with the same users (SCRAM-SHA-256). See the PostgreSQL chapter.

### Failed logins

Every failed login is written to the server's output, with the user name and the address (never the password):

```text
2026-09-11 22:34:25  login failed: user 'admin' from 127.0.0.1 (wrong password; 1 failure in a row)
2026-09-11 22:34:26  login failed: user 'admin' from 127.0.0.1 (wrong password; 5 failures in a row); next try allowed in 1 s
```

After 5 failures for one user from one address (or 20 from one address for any users), that address must wait before the next try: 1 second, then 2, 4, 8, ... up to 15 minutes. Meanwhile the answer is HTTP 429:

```text
{"error":"wrong user name or password","login":true}   (HTTP 401)
{"error":"too many failed logins; try again in 1 s","login":true}   (HTTP 429)
```

A good login ends the waiting for that user. Behind a reverse proxy every request comes from `127.0.0.1`, so the waiting is shared by everyone who tries the same user name.

`kareladb serve --data-dir` also writes every login, failed login and lockout to the audit log (`SHOW AUDIT`, chapter 21). Every login gets a new token: a login request that still carries an old token ends that old login. For people, turn on two-factor login (`ALTER USER admin ENABLE TOTP`, chapter 21).

### How KarelaDB keeps passwords

- A PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 hash with 600,000 rounds and a random salt (the same as `password_hash`).
- A SCRAM-SHA-256 secret (salt, StoredKey, ServerKey, 4096 rounds, like PostgreSQL). The PostgreSQL protocol uses it, so the password never crosses the network.
- Login tokens are random (256 bits). KarelaDB keeps only their SHA-256, and only in memory.
- Passwords and tokens are compared in constant time.

Because the SCRAM secret has only 4,096 rounds (the PostgreSQL default), use **long random passwords** for database users, for example 20 or more characters from a password manager. People never type them often: programs keep them in their settings.

---

## Part C: VPS checklist

A small Linux VPS (1-2 CPU, 1-2 GB memory) with your app and KarelaDB on the same machine.

### 1. Run KarelaDB as its own user

```sh
sudo useradd --system --home /srv/kareladb --shell /usr/sbin/nologin kdb
sudo mkdir -p /srv/kareladb/data /srv/kareladb/backups
sudo ./install.sh --system          # from the unpacked Linux package (chapter 1)
sudo chown -R kdb:kdb /srv/kareladb
sudo chmod 700 /srv/kareladb/data /srv/kareladb/backups
```

Only the `kareladb` user (and root) can read the data and the backups.

`install.sh --system` puts the program in `/usr/local/bin/kareladb` and its folders `web/`, `help/` and `skill/` in `/usr/local/share/kareladb`, where `kareladb` finds them by itself. Copying only the program works too, but then the server has no web console and no help pages.

### 2. Create users before the first start

```sh
sudo -u kdb kareladb user add admin --role admin --data-dir /srv/kareladb/data
sudo -u kdb kareladb user add shop_app --role none --data-dir /srv/kareladb/data
```

Then give `shop_app` its rights in SQL (`GRANT write ON DATABASE shop TO shop_app`) from the console, or run the app's `CREATE TABLE` statements as `admin` first.

### 3. Keep KarelaDB on 127.0.0.1

```sh
kareladb serve --data-dir /srv/kareladb/data --backups /srv/kareladb/backups
```

The default `--bind 127.0.0.1` means only programs on the VPS can connect. Your app's backend runs on the same VPS, so it can. Do **not** use `--bind 0.0.0.0` unless you really need it. Without a token and without users KarelaDB refuses it anyway:

```text
error: --bind 0.0.0.0 without --token and without users would let anyone who can reach this computer
read, change and delete every database. Do one of these first:
  1. create an admin user:   kareladb user add <name> --role admin
  2. or start with a secret:  --token <long random text>
  3. or keep --bind 127.0.0.1 and put a web server with HTTPS in front of KarelaDB
See docs/tutorial/16-users-passwords-security.md
```

KarelaDB has no HTTPS. Over plain HTTP, passwords and tokens can be read by anyone on the network path.

### 4. If you need the console from home: HTTPS in front

Use a web server that gets a free certificate by itself, for example Caddy. `/etc/caddy/Caddyfile`:

```text
kdb.example.com {
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:9900
}
```

Caddy sends `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`; KarelaDB then marks its login cookie `Secure`. KarelaDB still asks for the login. Even better: do not open the console to the internet at all, and use an SSH tunnel from home:

```sh
ssh -L 9900:127.0.0.1:9900 you@your-vps
```

Then open <http://127.0.0.1:9900> on your own PC.

### 5. Firewall

Open only SSH and the web ports. Keep 9900 (HTTP API) and 8832 (PostgreSQL) closed:

```sh
sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status
```

Also use SSH keys instead of SSH passwords, and keep the system updated (`sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade`).

### 6. Start KarelaDB with the system

`/etc/systemd/system/kdb.service`:

```ini
[Unit]
Description=KarelaDB database
After=network.target

[Service]
User=kdb
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/kareladb serve --data-dir /srv/kareladb/data --backups /srv/kareladb/backups
Restart=on-failure
KillSignal=SIGINT
TimeoutStopSec=60

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

```sh
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now kareladb
journalctl -u kareladb -f          # the server's output, with "login failed" lines
```

For more protection in the same `ExecStart` line (statement timeouts, scheduled backups, `--safe-updates`), see [chapter 21](21-protection.md).

### 7. Backups, and a copy somewhere else

The easiest way: let the server do it, with a checked copy on a second disk ([chapter 21, Part C](21-protection.md#part-c-backups-on-a-schedule)):

```sh
kareladb serve --data-dir /srv/kareladb/data --backups /srv/kareladb/backups --backup-schedule "daily 10:15" --backup-copy /mnt/backup/kdb
```

Or make a verified backup every night through the running server from a script (as a user with `admin` on that database):

```sh
curl -s -u admin:'the admin password' -X POST "http://127.0.0.1:9900/api/backup?db=shop"
```

Put that in a small script that reads the password from a file only root can read, and run it from `cron`. Then **copy the backups to another place** (another server, cloud storage): a backup on the same VPS is lost with the VPS. Test a restore now and then (chapter 9). Backups hold the password hashes of your app's users and the `_system` database: keep them as private as the data.

### 8. Short checklist

| Check | Done |
|---|---|
| KarelaDB runs as its own user; data and backups are `chmod 700` | |
| `--bind 127.0.0.1` (the default); ports 9900 and 8832 closed in the firewall | |
| an `admin` user with a long random password; apps have their own users with the smallest role | |
| HTTPS (Caddy or nginx) or an SSH tunnel for the console | |
| app passwords stored with `password_hash`, checked with `password_verify` | |
| session tokens are random (`random_token`) and stored as `sha256` with an expiry | |
| nightly backup, copied off the VPS, restore tested | |
| `journalctl -u kareladb` checked for `login failed` now and then (or `SHOW AUDIT WHERE event = 'login_failed'`) | |
| the protections of [chapter 21](21-protection.md#vps-checklist): timeouts, audit, scheduled backups, two-factor login for admins | |

---

## Limits

- Logins (sessions) are kept in memory: a restart logs everyone out.
- No HTTPS inside KarelaDB; use a reverse proxy.
- Rights are per database, and per table with `GRANT ... ON TABLE` (chapter 21). No column or row rights.
- `kareladb shell` and `kareladb sql` do not ask for a login. Protect the data folder with file permissions.
- Old KarelaDB versions do not know users. Never start an older `kareladb` on a data folder that has users: it would serve it **without** a login.

---

Next: [Known limitations](known-limitations.md)

# 17. Indexes and search

- Category: Tutorial

## What you will learn

- Why a query can be slow, and how an index makes it fast.
- `CREATE INDEX`, `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX`, `DROP INDEX`, `SHOW INDEXES`.
- A forum: pages of a thread, replies, and fast "next page" links.
- News: full-text search in English, Nepali or any other language with `MATCH`, `search_rank` and `highlight`.
- How to see if a query uses an index (`EXPLAIN`).
- How fast it is, and the limits.

All examples are in examples/17-indexes-and-search/. The output under each example is real.

## Why indexes

Every table has a **storage key**: the `PRIMARY KEY`, or `SORT BY` / `DEDUP KEY` of a time-series table (chapter 3). Rows are kept in the order of this key. So `WHERE id = 5` finds the row at once.

A condition on another column is different. `WHERE thread_id = 7` must read **every row** of the table and check each one. With 10 rows this is fast. With 1 million forum posts it is slow.

An **index** is a second, sorted list of one or more columns. Each entry points to its row. With an index on `thread_id`, KarelaDB jumps to the posts of thread 7 and reads only those.

| Without index | With index |
|---|---|
| Reads every row | Reads only the rows it needs |
| 1 million posts: tens of milliseconds, more with long text | 1 million posts: about 0.05 ms |
| Writes are a little faster | Every write also changes the index |

Create an index for the columns your app uses in `WHERE` and `ORDER BY` again and again. Do not create indexes you do not use.

## Where the index lives

An index is kept **in memory**. KarelaDB does not write it to disk:

- When the database opens, `kareladb serve` **builds every index at once**, on a background thread. The first query then finds it ready. Building takes about 0.2 seconds per million rows (a full-text index: about 2 seconds for 200,000 news articles). Queries and writes go on while it builds.
- A query that needs an index before the build is done builds it itself, as before. `kareladb sql` and `kareladb shell` do not build at open: there the **first query that needs an index builds it**. `kareladb serve --warm-indexes off` (or `KARELADB_WARM_INDEXES=off`) makes the server do the same.
- After that, every change (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `InsertRows`, line protocol, `ROLLBACK`) also changes the index.
- After a crash or a power cut, the index is built again from the rows. It can never be old or broken. `kareladb check`, `kareladb repair` and backups have nothing extra to do.
- Only the **definition** (`CREATE INDEX ...`) is saved, with the table.
- A slow query that a page asks again and again (a dashboard, a front page) can be **pinned**: the server keeps its result ready in the result cache and makes it again after a write. See the help topic **Pinned queries** (`/api/pins`).

## Step 1: the forum tables

01-forum-schema.sql:

```sql
CREATE TABLE threads (
  id LONG PRIMARY KEY,
  title STRING NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE posts (
  id LONG PRIMARY KEY,
  thread_id LONG NOT NULL REFERENCES threads(id),
  parent_id LONG,
  author STRING NOT NULL,
  body STRING NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);

-- Pages of a thread, newest first.
CREATE INDEX posts_thread_time ON posts (thread_id, created_at, id);
-- The replies of a post.
CREATE INDEX posts_parent ON posts (parent_id);
-- Posts of one author.
CREATE INDEX posts_author ON posts (author);
```

```text
table 'threads' created

table 'posts' created

index 'posts_thread_time' created on table 'posts' (0 rows)

index 'posts_parent' created on table 'posts' (0 rows)

index 'posts_author' created on table 'posts' (0 rows)
```

- A reply has the `id` of the post it answers in `parent_id`. A post that starts a discussion has `parent_id` NULL.
- `posts_thread_time` has **three columns**. The order matters: first `thread_id`, then `created_at`, then `id`. It helps `WHERE thread_id = ...`, and also `WHERE thread_id = ... ORDER BY created_at`. It does **not** help `WHERE created_at > ...` alone, because `created_at` is not the first column.
- You can create an index on a table that already has rows. KarelaDB builds it at once.

The syntax:

```sql
CREATE [UNIQUE | FULLTEXT] INDEX [IF NOT EXISTS] name ON table (column, ...);
DROP INDEX [IF EXISTS] name;
SHOW INDEXES [FROM table];
```

Index names are unique in the whole database. A good habit: `table_columns`, for example `posts_thread_time`.

Then some posts: 02-forum-data.sql.

## Step 2: pages of a thread

A forum shows a thread in pages of 20 posts, newest first. Here the pages have 3 posts, so the example stays short.

03-thread-pages.sql:

```sql
-- Page 1 of thread 1: the 3 newest posts.
SELECT id, author, created_at FROM posts
WHERE thread_id = 1
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 3;

-- Page 2: the 3 posts older than the last row of page 1 (created_at and id of post 4).
SELECT id, author, created_at FROM posts
WHERE thread_id = 1 AND (created_at, id) < ('2026-09-01T11:00:00+05:45', 4)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 3;
```

```text
id | author | created_at
---+--------+-------------------------
 6 | sita   | 2026-09-01T06:15:00.000Z
 5 | ram    | 2026-09-01T05:45:00.000Z
 4 | gita   | 2026-09-01T05:15:00.000Z
(3 rows, 0.4 ms)

id | author | created_at
---+--------+-------------------------
 3 | hari   | 2026-09-01T04:35:00.000Z
 2 | sita   | 2026-09-01T04:20:00.000Z
 1 | ram    | 2026-09-01T04:15:00.000Z
(3 rows, 0.1 ms)
```

How it works:

1. The index `(thread_id, created_at, id)` already has the posts of thread 1 sorted by time. KarelaDB reads them from the newest end and **stops after 3 rows**. It does not read the other posts, not even the other posts of the thread.
2. For the next page, the app remembers `created_at` and `id` of the **last row** it showed (post 4). The **row comparison** `(created_at, id) < ('...', 4)` means: older than post 4, or the same time and a smaller id. KarelaDB starts reading the index right there.

This is called **keyset pagination**. Page 1000 is as fast as page 1.

Why not `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20000`? `OFFSET` must still count the 20,000 rows before the page. It gets slower on every page. Use `OFFSET` only for small tables.

Why `id` in the index and in `ORDER BY`? Two posts can have the same `created_at`. `id` makes the order exact, so no post is shown twice or skipped between pages.

## Step 3: replies and authors

04-replies.sql:

```sql
-- Posts that start a discussion (not replies) in thread 1.
SELECT id, author, body FROM posts WHERE thread_id = 1 AND parent_id IS NULL ORDER BY created_at;

-- The replies to post 1.
SELECT id, author, body FROM posts WHERE parent_id = 1 ORDER BY created_at;

-- How many posts each author wrote in thread 1.
SELECT author, count(*) AS posts FROM posts WHERE thread_id = 1 GROUP BY author ORDER BY author;
```

```text
id | author | body
---+--------+------------------------------------
 1 | ram    | CITY dividend looks good this year.
 4 | gita   | What about the bonus shares?
 6 | sita   | सिटी बैंकको नाफा राम्रो छ।
(3 rows, 0.4 ms)

id | author | body
---+--------+-----------------------------------
 2 | sita   | I agree, the profit grew 18%.
 3 | hari   | Price is high now. Wait for a dip.
(2 rows, 0.1 ms)

author | posts
-------+------
gita   |     1
hari   |     1
ram    |     2
sita   |     2
(4 rows, 0.1 ms)
```

- `parent_id IS NULL` can also use an index.
- Aggregates (`count`, `sum`, `GROUP BY`) read only the rows the index finds.

## Step 4: does my query use an index?

Put `EXPLAIN` before the query. 05-explain.sql (CSV output, so the lines are not cut):

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM posts WHERE thread_id = 1 ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM posts WHERE parent_id = 1;
-- No index on body: the table is read.
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM posts WHERE body = 'Which ones?';
```

```text
plan
"scan table posts (1 of 1 partitions, about 8 rows)"
"use index posts_thread_time (thread_id = value, rows in ORDER BY order, stops after 20 row(s))"
"build 3 of 6 stored column(s) per row: id, thread_id, created_at"
filter while scanning: 1 condition(s)
sort by 2 key(s)
limit 20
plan
"scan table posts (1 of 1 partitions, about 8 rows)"
use index posts_parent (parent_id = value)
"build 2 of 6 stored column(s) per row: id, parent_id"
filter while scanning: 1 condition(s)
plan
"scan table posts (1 of 1 partitions, about 8 rows)"
"build 2 of 6 stored column(s) per row: id, body"
filter while scanning: 1 condition(s)
```

The line `use index <name>` says which index is used. No such line: every row is read.
The line `build 3 of 6 stored column(s)` says that KarelaDB reads only the columns the query needs, not the long `body` text of every post.

**When KarelaDB uses an index** (plain index, columns `(a, b, c)`):

| Your query | Uses the index |
|---|---|
| `a = 5`, `a IN (1, 2, 3)`, `a IS NULL` | yes |
| `a = 5 AND b = 7` | yes, both columns |
| `a = 5 AND b > 100`, `b BETWEEN ...`, `b LIKE 'abc%'` | yes: `a` exactly, then a range of `b` |
| `a = 5 ORDER BY b DESC LIMIT 20` | yes, and it stops after 20 rows |
| `a = 5 AND (b, c) < (x, y) ORDER BY b DESC, c DESC LIMIT 20` | yes: keyset pagination |
| `b = 7` alone | no: `b` is not the first column |
| `a = 5 OR b = 7` | no: `OR` |
| `lower(a) = 'x'`, `a + 1 = 6` | only with an expression index on exactly that expression: `CREATE INDEX ix ON t (lower(a))` |
| `a != 5`, `a NOT IN (...)`, `a LIKE '%abc'` | no |

Other rules:

- `UPDATE ... WHERE` and `DELETE ... WHERE` use indexes too.
- In a `JOIN`, only the first table (after `FROM`) uses an index.
- When an index would find more than a quarter of the table (for example `status = 'active'` on most rows), reading the whole table is faster, and KarelaDB does that.
- The result is always the same, with or without an index. Only the speed changes.

## Step 5: UNIQUE indexes

A `UNIQUE` index makes sure no two rows have the same values. Use it for email addresses, user names, or "one row per company per quarter".

06-unique.sql:

```sql
-- One account per email address.
CREATE TABLE users (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, email STRING NOT NULL, name STRING);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email ON users (email);
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'ram@example.com', 'Ram'), (2, 'sita@example.com', 'Sita');
INSERT INTO users VALUES (3, 'ram@example.com', 'Another Ram');
```

```text
table 'users' created

index 'users_email' created on table 'users' (0 rows)

2 row(s) inserted
error: duplicate value violates unique index 'users_email' on table 'users': a row with email='ram@example.com' already exists
[exit code 1]
```

- The error names the index and the value. Your app can look for the word `unique` in the message and show "this email is already used".
- The check covers every way of writing: `INSERT`, `INSERT OR REPLACE`, `UPDATE`, `InsertRows`, transactions. Nothing is written when the check fails.
- Two rows may swap their values in one `UPDATE`.
- `NULL` values never clash: many rows may have a NULL email.
- `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` on a table that already has two equal values fails, and names the value. Fix the rows first.
- A `UNIQUE` index can have several columns: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX votes_one_per_user ON votes (user_id, post_id)` (chapter 18 uses this).

## Step 6: news and full-text search

`LIKE '%bank%'` reads every row and checks every letter. For thousands of news articles that is slow. A **FULLTEXT index** keeps a list of words: for each word, the articles that have it.

07-news-schema.sql:

```sql
CREATE TABLE news (
  id LONG PRIMARY KEY,
  symbol STRING,
  published_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  title STRING NOT NULL,
  body STRING
);

-- Search in the title and the body together.
CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX news_text ON news (title, body);
-- The newest news of a company.
CREATE INDEX news_symbol_time ON news (symbol, published_at);

INSERT INTO news VALUES
  (1, 'CITY', '2026-08-01T11:00:00+05:45', 'City Bank profit rises 18%',
      'City Bank reported a net profit of 3.27 billion dollars. The bank will pay a 12.5% dividend.'),
  (2, 'CITY', '2026-08-01T11:30:00+05:45', 'सिटी बैंकको नाफा बढ्यो',
      'सिटी बैंकले चौथो त्रैमासिकमा ३ अर्ब २७ करोड नाफा कमाएको छ। लाभांश १२.५ प्रतिशत।'),
  (3, 'VOLT', '2026-08-15T10:00:00+05:45', 'Hydropower company plans IPO',
      'Volt River Hydropower will sell new shares. The IPO opens next month.'),
  (4, NULL,    '2026-09-01T08:00:00+05:45', 'Market index closes at 2,840',
      'Banks and hydropower shares moved up. City Bank led the gainers.'),
  (5, 'COAST',  '2026-09-02T09:00:00+05:45', 'Coastal bank merger talks',
      'Coastal Bank is in talks about a merger. No loan changes are planned.');
```

```text
table 'news' created

index 'news_text' created on table 'news' (0 rows)

index 'news_symbol_time' created on table 'news' (0 rows)

5 row(s) inserted
```

A FULLTEXT index works on STRING (and SYMBOL, JSON) columns. With several columns, they are searched together as one text.

### How text is cut into words

| Rule | Example |
|---|---|
| Letters and digits of any language make words | `सिटी बैंकको नाफा` is 3 words |
| English letters: case does not matter | `Bank` = `bank` = `BANK` |
| Punctuation separates words, also `।` and `॥` | `छ।` is the word `छ` |
| A number keeps its dot; a comma inside a number is dropped | `12.5` is one word; `1,234.5` is `1234.5` |
| Devanagari digits are the same as 0-9 | `१२.५` = `12.5` |
| Words must be the same; there is no stemming | `bank` does not find `banks`; `बैंक` does not find `बैंकले` (use `बैंक*`) |

### Searching

08-search.sql:

```sql
-- Every word must be there (English letters: any case).
SELECT id, title FROM news WHERE MATCH(title, body, 'city bank') ORDER BY id;

-- The best matches first.
SELECT id, title, round(search_rank(title, body, 'bank'), 3) AS rank
FROM news
WHERE MATCH(title, body, 'bank')
ORDER BY rank DESC
LIMIT 3;

-- Nepali words; a number with a dot is one word (१२.५ is the same as 12.5).
SELECT id, title FROM news WHERE MATCH(title, body, 'नाफा') ORDER BY id;
SELECT id FROM news WHERE MATCH(title, body, '12.5') ORDER BY id;

-- An exact phrase, a prefix, and a word that must not be there.
SELECT id FROM news WHERE MATCH(title, body, '"net profit"');
SELECT id FROM news WHERE MATCH(title, body, 'hydro*') ORDER BY id;
SELECT id FROM news WHERE MATCH(title, body, 'bank -merger') ORDER BY id;

-- Full-text search together with other conditions.
SELECT id, title FROM news WHERE MATCH(title, body, 'bank') AND published_at >= '2026-09-01' ORDER BY id;
```

```text
id | title
---+-----------------------------
 1 | City Bank profit rises 18%
 4 | Market index closes at 2,840
(2 rows, 0.4 ms)

id | title                        | rank
---+------------------------------+------
 1 | City Bank profit rises 18%   | 0.806
 5 | Coastal bank merger talks    | 0.751
 4 | Market index closes at 2,840 | 0.562
(3 rows, 0.1 ms)

id | title
---+-----------------------
 2 | सिटी बैंकको नाफा बढ्यो
(1 row, 0.0 ms)

id
--
 1
 2
(2 rows, 0.0 ms)

id
--
 1
(1 row, 0.0 ms)

id
--
 3
 4
(2 rows, 0.0 ms)

id
--
 1
 4
(2 rows, 0.0 ms)

id | title
---+-----------------------------
 4 | Market index closes at 2,840
 5 | Coastal bank merger talks
(2 rows, 0.0 ms)
```

The search text:

| You write | It finds rows that |
|---|---|
| `city bank` | have both words, anywhere |
| `"net profit"` | have these words next to each other, in this order (not across title and body). The index keeps the place of every word, so a phrase is found in the index too. |
| `hydro*` | have a word that starts with `hydro` (`hydropower`) |
| `bank -merger` | have `bank` but not `merger` |

A search needs at least one word without `-`.

**`search_rank(columns..., 'words')`** says how well a row matches: higher is better, 0 when the row does not match. It uses the BM25 formula: a word that is rare in the table counts more than a common word, a word that is there many times counts more, and a long text counts a little less. Use the same columns and words as in `MATCH`.

`ORDER BY search_rank(...) DESC LIMIT 20` together with `MATCH(...)` is the fastest form: KarelaDB takes the 20 best rows straight from the index and reads only those rows.

`MATCH` and `search_rank` also work **without** a FULLTEXT index. Then KarelaDB reads every row.

### Highlight the words

`highlight(columns..., 'words')` returns the text with the found words inside `<b>` and `</b>`, for a search result page.

09-highlight.sql:

```sql
SELECT id, highlight(title, 'bank') AS title FROM news WHERE MATCH(title, body, 'bank') ORDER BY id;
```

```text
id,title
1,City <b>Bank</b> profit rises 18%
4,"Market index closes at 2,840"
5,Coastal <b>bank</b> merger talks
```

Row 4 matched because its **body** has `Bank`; the highlighted column here is only the title.

`highlight` does not change any other character. If users can type `<` or `&` (in a forum they can), do not put the result into a web page as it is: escape the text in your app first.

### Changes

10-news-changes.sql:

```sql
UPDATE news SET body = 'Coastal Bank and Harbor Bank signed the merger.' WHERE id = 5;
SELECT id FROM news WHERE MATCH(title, body, 'harbor');
DELETE FROM news WHERE id = 4;
SELECT id FROM news WHERE MATCH(title, body, 'gainers');
```

```text
1 row(s) updated

id
--
 5
(1 row, 0.2 ms)

1 row(s) deleted

id
--
(0 rows, 0.0 ms)
```

11-news-explain.sql:

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM news WHERE MATCH(title, body, 'bank') ORDER BY search_rank(title, body, 'bank') DESC LIMIT 20;
EXPLAIN SELECT id, title FROM news WHERE symbol = 'CITY' ORDER BY published_at DESC LIMIT 10;
```

```text

"use index news_text (full-text search, best 20 row(s) by search_rank)"
"build 3 of 5 stored column(s) per row: id, title, body"

"use index news_symbol_time (symbol = value, rows in ORDER BY order, stops after 10 row(s))"
"build 4 of 5 stored column(s) per row: id, symbol, published_at, title"
filter while scanning: 1 condition(s)
sort by 1 key(s)
limit 10
```

## Step 7: see and remove indexes

12-show-indexes.sql:

```sql
-- kareladb sql opens the database again, so no index is in memory yet. The first query builds one.
SHOW INDEXES FROM posts;
SELECT count(*) AS posts FROM posts WHERE thread_id = 1;
SHOW INDEXES FROM posts;
SHOW CREATE TABLE users;
```

```text
name,table,kind,columns,built,rows,memory_bytes,create_sql,building
posts_thread_time,posts,INDEX,"thread_id, created_at, id",false,,,"CREATE INDEX posts_thread_time ON posts (thread_id, created_at, id)",false
posts_parent,posts,INDEX,parent_id,false,,,CREATE INDEX posts_parent ON posts (parent_id),false
posts_author,posts,INDEX,author,false,,,CREATE INDEX posts_author ON posts (author),false
posts
6
name,table,kind,columns,built,rows,memory_bytes,create_sql,building
posts_thread_time,posts,INDEX,"thread_id, created_at, id",true,8,400,"CREATE INDEX posts_thread_time ON posts (thread_id, created_at, id)",false
posts_parent,posts,INDEX,parent_id,false,,,CREATE INDEX posts_parent ON posts (parent_id),false
posts_author,posts,INDEX,author,false,,,CREATE INDEX posts_author ON posts (author),false
create_sql
"CREATE TABLE users (
  id LONG PRIMARY KEY,
  email STRING NOT NULL,
  name STRING
)"
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email ON users (email)
```

- `built` is `true` when the index is in memory now; `rows` and `memory_bytes` show its size.
- `building` is `true` while the server's background thread builds it right after the database opened. `kareladb sql` never builds at open, so here it is always `false`.
- `SHOW CREATE TABLE` gives the table and then one `CREATE INDEX` line per index. Run them in this order to make the same table again.

13-drop-index.sql:

```sql
DROP INDEX posts_author;
DROP INDEX IF EXISTS posts_author;
ALTER TABLE posts DROP COLUMN parent_id;
```

```text
index 'posts_author' dropped

index 'posts_author' does not exist
error: cannot drop column 'parent_id' from table 'posts': index 'posts_parent' uses it; DROP INDEX posts_parent first
[exit code 1]
```

- A column that an index uses cannot be dropped. `RENAME COLUMN` and `RENAME TABLE` keep the index working.
- `DROP TABLE` also drops the table's indexes.
- `CREATE INDEX` and `DROP INDEX` cannot run inside `BEGIN ... COMMIT`.

## How fast

Measured with `kdb_bench_indexes` (bench/bench_indexes.cpp) on the test PC (Windows, 16 threads for KarelaDB, release build). Query times are the middle value of many runs and include parsing the SQL.

| What | Rows | Time |
|---|---|---|
| `CREATE INDEX posts_thread ON posts (thread_id, created_at, id)` | 1,000,000 posts | 170 ms |
| Build of that index when the database opens (`kareladb sql`: by the first query) | 1,000,000 posts | 150-320 ms, once |
| `SELECT * FROM posts WHERE author = 'user123'` (10 rows) | 1,000,000 posts | 0.03-0.04 ms |
| Forum page: `WHERE thread_id = x ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20` | 1,000,000 posts | 0.05-0.06 ms |
| Keyset page: `... AND (created_at, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20` | 1,000,000 posts | 0.06-0.07 ms |
| `INSERT` of one post (two indexes kept up to date, log saved to disk) | 1,000,000 posts | 0.3-1.8 ms (mostly the disk) |
| `CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX news_text ON news (title, body)` | 200,000 articles, 216 MB of text | 1.0-1.1 s |
| Build of that index when the database opens (`kareladb sql`: by the first search) | 200,000 articles | 1.6 s, once |
| Top 20 by `search_rank` for common words | 200,000 articles (23,000 to 199,000 matches) | 6-15 ms |
| `UPDATE` of one article (full-text index kept up to date) | 200,000 articles | 0.4-2 ms |
| Memory: `posts_thread` / `posts_author` / `news_text` | | 50 MB / 35 MB / 102 MB |

Run it yourself: `.\build\bin\kdb_bench_indexes.exe 1000000 200000`.

## Tips

- An index on `(a, b)` also serves queries on `a` alone. You do not need a second index on `(a)`.
- Put the column you compare with `=` first, and the column you sort or compare with `<` / `>` next.
- For "latest N rows of X" add the time column after X: `(symbol, published_at)`, `(thread_id, created_at, id)`.
- Time-series tables already sort by `SORT BY`. Indexes help them for other columns, like `broker` in a trade log table.
- Every index costs memory (about the size of its column values plus 20-30 bytes per row) and makes writes a little slower. Big line-protocol imports into a table with indexes are slower; create the indexes after a big first import.
- The limits are listed in [known limitations](known-limitations.md).

## What you learned

- An index is a sorted list of columns that points to rows. It lives in memory. `kareladb serve` builds it from the rows right after the database opens; `kareladb sql` builds it when first needed.
- `CREATE INDEX` makes `=`, `IN`, ranges and `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` fast. `EXPLAIN` shows `use index`.
- Keyset pagination with a row comparison `(created_at, id) < (?, ?)` keeps every page fast.
- `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` refuses duplicates.
- `CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX` with `MATCH`, `search_rank` and `highlight` searches text in English, Nepali and other languages.
