# 22. PostgreSQL schema compatibility

- Category: Tutorial

## What you will learn

The NChartPro app creates its PostgreSQL tables itself when it starts (`pgdb.CreateAllTables()`). This chapter shows what KarelaDB does with those statements:

- **Part A.** PostgreSQL type names (`SERIAL`, `VARCHAR(n)`, `NUMERIC(p,s)`, `UUID`, `TEXT[]`, ...).
- **Part B.** `CREATE TABLE` forms: constraints, composite keys, `CREATE TABLE ... AS`, `TEMP` tables.
- **Part C.** Foreign keys with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, `SET NULL`, `SET DEFAULT`, `RESTRICT`.
- **Part D.** `ALTER TABLE` forms.
- **Part E.** PostgreSQL index forms: partial and expression indexes.
- **Part F.** Sequences: `nextval`, `currval`, `setval`.
- **Part G.** `CREATE SCHEMA`, `CREATE EXTENSION`, `COMMENT ON`, `DO $$ ... $$` blocks.
- **Part H.** `information_schema` and `pg_catalog` views.
- **Part I.** plpgsql trigger functions and `FOR EACH ROW` triggers: what KarelaDB runs.
- **Part J.** Times: local time and UTC when you move data.
- What is **different** from PostgreSQL, what **older KarelaDB** programs do, and **speed**.

Chapter 14 explains how to connect with the PostgreSQL protocol. This chapter is about the schema (tables, keys, indexes); chapter 23 is about queries and data changes (`ON CONFLICT`, `WITH`, subqueries, arrays). The output under each example is real.

## The short version

| PostgreSQL | KarelaDB |
|---|---|
| `SERIAL`, `BIGSERIAL`, `GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY` | Works for a single-column `PRIMARY KEY` (`AUTO` id). |
| `VARCHAR(n)`, `CHAR(n)`, `NUMERIC(p,s)` | Works. Lengths, precision and scale are checked. |
| `UUID`, `TIME`, `INTERVAL`, `TEXT[]`, `JSONB`, `INET` | Works, with a KarelaDB type underneath (Part A). |
| `PRIMARY KEY (a, b)`, `UNIQUE (a, b)`, `FOREIGN KEY (a, b)` | Works. |
| `ON DELETE CASCADE / SET NULL / SET DEFAULT / RESTRICT`, `ON UPDATE CASCADE` | Works, also inside `BEGIN ... COMMIT`. |
| `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE / SET DEFAULT / SET NOT NULL`, `ADD CONSTRAINT` | Works. Rows are checked, or written again. |
| `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... (lower(email))`, `... WHERE cond` | Works. |
| `CREATE SEQUENCE`, `nextval('s')` | Works. A number is never given twice, also after a crash. |
| `information_schema.tables / columns / table_constraints`, `pg_indexes`, `pg_constraint`, ... | Read-only views. |
| `DO $$ BEGIN IF ... THEN ...; END IF; END $$` | Works for `IF`, `RAISE` and SQL statements. |
| `CREATE EXTENSION`, `CREATE SCHEMA`, `COMMENT ON` | Accepted. Nothing changes. |
| `CREATE FUNCTION ... RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql` with a `BEFORE UPDATE ... FOR EACH ROW` trigger | Works for `IF`, `RAISE EXCEPTION`, `NEW.col := ...` and `RETURN NEW` (Part I). Other plpgsql is refused with a clear message. |

When the app's PostgreSQL startup DDL runs on KarelaDB, **802 of 809** statements work (99%). Before this work it was 198 of 809. The 7 others are listed at the end of the chapter.

---

## Part A: Types

Write the PostgreSQL name. KarelaDB keeps the name (so `SHOW CREATE TABLE` and `information_schema.columns` show it) and stores the value in a KarelaDB type.

| PostgreSQL | KarelaDB stores as | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `SMALLINT`, `INT2` | `SHORT` | |
| `INTEGER`, `INT`, `INT4` | `INT` | |
| `BIGINT`, `INT8` | `LONG` | |
| `SMALLSERIAL`, `SERIAL`, `BIGSERIAL` | `SHORT` / `INT` / `LONG` `PRIMARY KEY AUTO` | Only as the single-column `PRIMARY KEY`. See below. |
| `GENERATED {ALWAYS \| BY DEFAULT} AS IDENTITY` | same as `SERIAL` | |
| `REAL`, `FLOAT4`, `FLOAT(1..24)` | `FLOAT` | |
| `DOUBLE PRECISION`, `FLOAT8`, `FLOAT(25..53)` | `DOUBLE` | `FLOAT` alone is KarelaDB's 4-byte `FLOAT` (in PostgreSQL it is 8 bytes). |
| `NUMERIC(p,s)`, `DECIMAL(p,s)`, `NUMERIC(p)` | `DECIMAL(s)` | Rounded to `s` places (half away from zero). More than `p` digits → error `numeric field overflow`. `s` at most 18. |
| `NUMERIC` (no precision) | `DOUBLE` | About 15 exact digits. |
| `DECIMAL(s)` (one number) | `DECIMAL(s)` | KarelaDB meaning: `s` is the **scale** (chapter 11). |
| `MONEY` | `DECIMAL(2)` | Rounded to 2 places. |
| `VARCHAR(n)`, `CHARACTER VARYING(n)` | `STRING` | At most `n` **characters** (letters of any language, such as Nepali, count as characters). |
| `CHAR(n)`, `BPCHAR` | `STRING` | At most `n` characters. Not padded with spaces. |
| `TEXT`, `VARCHAR`, `CITEXT`, `NAME` | `STRING` | `CITEXT` is not case-insensitive: use `lower(col)` (and a `lower(col)` index). |
| `BOOLEAN` | `BOOL` | |
| `DATE` | `DATE` | |
| `TIMESTAMP`, `TIMESTAMPTZ`, `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` | `TIMESTAMP` | Milliseconds, UTC. Text with an offset (`+05:45`) is converted. See Part J. |
| `TIME`, `TIMETZ` | `STRING` | Checked and written as `HH:MM:SS[.fff][zone]`: `'9:30'` becomes `'09:30:00'`. |
| `INTERVAL` | `LONG` | Milliseconds. `'7 days'` is `604800000`. A month counts as 30 days. |
| `UUID` | `STRING` | Checked. Written in lower case with dashes. |
| `JSON`, `JSONB` | `JSON` | Chapter 18. `jsonb` operators like `@>` are not there. |
| `BYTEA` | `BYTES` | |
| `INET`, `CIDR`, `MACADDR`, `XML` | `STRING` | Not checked. |
| `type[]` (`TEXT[]`, `INT[]`, ...) | `JSON` array | `'{a,"b c",NULL}'` becomes `["a","b c",null]`. Numbers and booleans are checked. |

```sql
CREATE TABLE ev (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, at_time TIME, took INTERVAL, at TIMESTAMPTZ);
INSERT INTO ev (at_time, took, at) VALUES ('9:30', '1 day 02:00:00', '2026-09-11 10:00:00+05:45')
  RETURNING at_time, took, at;
```

```text
table 'ev' created

at_time  | took     | at
---------+----------+-------------------------
09:30:00 | 93600000 | 2026-09-11T04:15:00.000Z
(1 row, 8.6 ms)
1 row(s) inserted
```

Errors use the PostgreSQL words, so the app's error checks still work. Over the PostgreSQL protocol they have the PostgreSQL error codes:

| Message | Code |
|---|---|
| `value too long for type VARCHAR(40) (48 characters, at most 40)` | `22001` |
| `numeric field overflow: ...` | `22003` |
| `invalid input syntax for type uuid: 'not-a-uuid'` | `22P02` |

### SERIAL must be the primary key

KarelaDB gives `AUTO` ids only to the `PRIMARY KEY`. A `SERIAL` column that is not the primary key is refused, with the fix in the message:

```text
error: line 1, column 24: column 'code' is SERIAL (or IDENTITY) but not the PRIMARY KEY; in KarelaDB such a column must be the table's single-column PRIMARY KEY (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY). For other columns use a sequence: code INT NOT NULL DEFAULT nextval('t_serial_code_seq')
```

`AUTO` ids work like a sequence: a failed or rolled back insert also uses up an id, so there can be gaps.

---

## Part B: CREATE TABLE

A small forum, written as PostgreSQL:

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgcrypto;
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS public.forum_users (
  user_id    SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  email      VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name       VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
  balance    NUMERIC(12,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (balance >= 0),
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS forum_posts (
  post_id   BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id   INTEGER REFERENCES forum_users(user_id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  parent_id BIGINT REFERENCES forum_posts(post_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  title     TEXT NOT NULL,
  tags      TEXT[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  public_id UUID NOT NULL DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()
);
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS post_likes (
  post_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  user_id INT NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT post_likes_pkey PRIMARY KEY (post_id, user_id),
  CONSTRAINT post_likes_post_fk FOREIGN KEY (post_id) REFERENCES forum_posts(post_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  CONSTRAINT post_likes_user_fk FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES forum_users(user_id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);
COMMENT ON TABLE post_likes IS 'one row per like';
```

```text
extension 'pgcrypto' accepted: its common functions are built in or not needed

table 'forum_users' created

table 'forum_posts' created

table 'post_likes' created

comment accepted (KarelaDB does not keep comments)
```

```sql
INSERT INTO forum_users (email, name) VALUES ('ram@example.com', 'Ram'), ('sita@example.com', 'Sita')
  RETURNING user_id, balance, created_at;
INSERT INTO forum_posts (user_id, title, tags) VALUES (1, 'CITY results', '{bank,"q1 2083"}') RETURNING post_id, tags;
```

```text
user_id | balance | created_at
--------+---------+-------------------------
      1 |    0.00 | 2026-09-11T19:01:54.203Z
      2 |    0.00 | 2026-09-11T19:01:54.203Z
(2 rows, 2.1 ms)
2 row(s) inserted

post_id | tags
--------+-------------------
      1 | ["bank","q1 2083"]
(1 row, 2.1 ms)
1 row(s) inserted
```

The rules are checked for every written row:

```text
INSERT INTO forum_users (email, name, balance) VALUES ('hari@example.com', 'Hari', 12.345) RETURNING user_id, balance;
user_id | balance
--------+--------
      3 |   12.35

INSERT INTO forum_users (email, name) VALUES ('ram@example.com', 'Ram again');
error: column 'email' must be unique: 'ram@example.com' is already used

INSERT INTO forum_posts (user_id, title) VALUES (99, 'Nobody');
error: column 'user_id' = '99' has no matching row in forum_users(user_id)

INSERT INTO forum_users (email, name, balance) VALUES ('gita@example.com', 'Gita', -5);
error: CHECK constraint 'forum_users_balance_check' of table 'forum_users' failed: balance >= 0 is false for the row user_id='5', balance='-5.00'
```

### What CREATE TABLE accepts

| Form | What KarelaDB does |
|---|---|
| `IF NOT EXISTS`, `public.name` | As in PostgreSQL. `public.` and `pg_catalog.` are removed from names. |
| `NOT NULL`, `NULL`, `DEFAULT expr`, `CHECK (...)`, `UNIQUE`, `PRIMARY KEY` | As in PostgreSQL. |
| `REFERENCES t` (no column) | Refers to the primary key of `t`. |
| `CONSTRAINT name ...` | The name is kept. It is used in errors, `DROP CONSTRAINT` and the catalog views. |
| `PRIMARY KEY (a, b)` | Rows are stored by the key. `INSERT OR REPLACE` uses it. |
| `UNIQUE (a, b)` | A unique index named like PostgreSQL (`table_a_b_key`). |
| `FOREIGN KEY (a, b) REFERENCES t (x, y)` | Checked when any part is not NULL (`MATCH SIMPLE`). |
| `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expr) STORED` | A KarelaDB computed column (worked out when read, not stored). |
| `CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT ...` `[WITH NO DATA]` | Types come from the query. Table and rows are written together. |
| `CREATE TEMP` / `TEMPORARY` / `UNLOGGED TABLE` | A normal table (it stays after the session). |
| `WITH (fillfactor = 70)`, `WITHOUT OIDS`, `TABLESPACE x` | Accepted and ignored. |
| `INHERITS (...)`, `PARTITION BY RANGE (...)` | Refused. Use KarelaDB `TIMESERIES` tables (chapter 3). |
| `DEFERRABLE` | Refused. KarelaDB checks keys at every statement. |

Table constraints (`PRIMARY KEY (...)`, `CONSTRAINT ... CHECK`) must come **after** the columns.

---

## Part C: Foreign key actions

`forum_posts.parent_id` has `ON DELETE CASCADE`, and `post_likes` has `ON DELETE CASCADE` to both tables. Add replies and likes, then delete post 1:

```sql
INSERT INTO forum_posts (user_id, parent_id, title) VALUES (2, 1, 'Good numbers'), (1, 2, 'Agree');
INSERT INTO post_likes VALUES (1, 2), (2, 1), (3, 2);
DELETE FROM forum_posts WHERE post_id = 1;
SELECT post_id, user_id, parent_id, title FROM forum_posts ORDER BY post_id;
SELECT * FROM post_likes ORDER BY post_id;
```

```text
2 row(s) inserted

3 row(s) inserted

1 row(s) deleted

post_id | user_id | parent_id | title
--------+---------+-----------+------
(0 rows, 0.1 ms)

post_id | user_id
--------+--------
(0 rows, 0.1 ms)
```

Post 1 took its reply (2), the reply's reply (3) and all three likes with it. `forum_posts.user_id` has `ON DELETE SET NULL`:

```sql
INSERT INTO forum_posts (user_id, title) VALUES (2, 'Sita post');
DELETE FROM forum_users WHERE user_id = 2;
SELECT post_id, user_id, title FROM forum_posts ORDER BY post_id;
```

```text
1 row(s) inserted

1 row(s) deleted

post_id | user_id | title
--------+---------+----------
      5 |    NULL | Sita post
(1 row, 0.3 ms)
```

| Action | What happens to the rows that refer to the deleted (or changed) row |
|---|---|
| `NO ACTION` (default), `RESTRICT` | The statement is refused: `cannot remove forum_users(user_id) = '1': table 'forum_posts' column 'user_id' still refers to it (foreign key 'forum_posts_user_id_fkey')`. |
| `CASCADE` | `ON DELETE`: they are deleted too (and their children, at most 32 levels). `ON UPDATE`: they get the new key. |
| `SET NULL` | Their column becomes NULL. Refused if the column is `NOT NULL`. |
| `SET DEFAULT` | Their column gets its `DEFAULT`. The default must exist in the parent. |

The rules:

- All changes of one statement, with every cascade, are **one transaction**. If one part fails (a `CHECK`, a `NOT NULL`, a `RESTRICT` deeper down), nothing changes.
- Inside `BEGIN ... COMMIT` it works the same. `ROLLBACK` brings back the parent and all children.
- After a crash, the log has the whole change or none of it.
- KarelaDB finds the child rows with the child's key or an index when there is one. Without one, it reads the child table. For big child tables, add an index on the foreign key column (`CREATE INDEX ... ON child (parent_id)`), as in PostgreSQL.
- A table that another table refers to cannot be dropped (`DROP TABLE ... CASCADE` is not supported).
- In one `INSERT` with many rows, a row can refer to a row **before** it in the same statement (a tree). PostgreSQL also allows a row that comes later.

---

## Part D: ALTER TABLE

```sql
ALTER TABLE forum_users ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS phone VARCHAR(15), ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS is_admin BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE;
ALTER TABLE forum_users ALTER COLUMN name TYPE VARCHAR(80), ALTER COLUMN balance SET DEFAULT 100;
ALTER TABLE forum_users ALTER COLUMN phone SET NOT NULL;
```

```text
table 'forum_users' altered
table 'forum_users' altered
error: column 'phone' of table 'forum_users' contains NULL values; set them first (UPDATE ... SET phone = ... WHERE phone IS NULL)
```

| Form | What KarelaDB does |
|---|---|
| `ADD [COLUMN] [IF NOT EXISTS] col type [rules]` | Old rows get the `DEFAULT`. |
| `DROP [COLUMN] [IF EXISTS] col [CASCADE]` | Refused while an index, `CHECK` or multi-column key uses the column; `CASCADE` drops them. |
| `ALTER [COLUMN] col SET DEFAULT expr` / `DROP DEFAULT` | Only new rows. |
| `ALTER [COLUMN] col SET NOT NULL` / `DROP NOT NULL` | `SET NOT NULL` checks all rows first. |
| `ALTER [COLUMN] col [SET DATA] TYPE type [USING expr]` | Every row is converted and written again, in the same transaction as the change. A value that does not fit stops it and nothing changes. |
| `RENAME [COLUMN] a TO b`, `RENAME TO new_name` | As in PostgreSQL. |
| `ADD [CONSTRAINT name] UNIQUE (...)` / `PRIMARY KEY (...)` / `FOREIGN KEY (...) REFERENCES ...` / `CHECK (...)` | Existing rows are checked. `ADD PRIMARY KEY` writes the rows again, stored by the new key. |
| `... NOT VALID` | For `CHECK` and `FOREIGN KEY`: old rows are not checked, new rows are. |
| `DROP CONSTRAINT [IF EXISTS] name` | Any named constraint, except the `PRIMARY KEY` (rows are stored by it). |
| Several actions with commas | All of them or none. |
| `ALTER TABLE IF EXISTS`, `ONLY`, `OWNER TO`, `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` | Accepted. |
| `ENABLE` / `DISABLE TRIGGER name` | KarelaDB triggers (chapter 13). |

`ALTER TABLE` and `CREATE INDEX` cannot be used between `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` (chapter 13). A `DO` block can use them, outside a transaction (Part G).

---

## Part E: Indexes

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS uq_forum_users_email_lower ON forum_users (lower(email));
INSERT INTO forum_users (email, name) VALUES ('RAM@example.com', 'Ram 2');
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS uq_one_admin ON forum_users (is_admin) WHERE is_admin;
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_posts_tags ON forum_posts USING gin (tags);
SELECT indexname FROM pg_indexes WHERE tablename = 'forum_users' ORDER BY indexname;
```

```text
index 'uq_forum_users_email_lower' created on table 'forum_users' (2 rows)
error: duplicate value violates unique index 'uq_forum_users_email_lower' on table 'forum_users': a row with the same (lower(email)) already exists
index 'uq_one_admin' created on table 'forum_users' (0 rows)
index 'idx_posts_tags' created on table 'forum_posts' (1 rows)

indexname
--------------------------
forum_users_email_key
forum_users_pkey
uq_forum_users_email_lower
uq_one_admin
(4 rows, 0.1 ms)
```

| Form | What KarelaDB does |
|---|---|
| `CREATE [UNIQUE] INDEX [CONCURRENTLY] [IF NOT EXISTS] [name] ON [ONLY] t [USING btree \| hash \| gin \| gist] (...)` | Accepted. Without a name, KarelaDB names it like PostgreSQL (`t_col_idx`). `USING` is only remembered. |
| `(col DESC NULLS LAST, col text_pattern_ops)` | Accepted. The order words are remembered; KarelaDB indexes work both ways. |
| `(lower(email))`, `(COALESCE(a, ''))` | An expression index. |
| `... WHERE condition` | A partial index: only rows where the condition is true. |
| `INCLUDE (...)`, `WITH (...)`, `TABLESPACE` | Accepted and ignored. |
| An index on a `GENERATED` column | Indexes the column's expression. |
| `DROP INDEX [CONCURRENTLY] [IF EXISTS] a, b [CASCADE]` | Drops them. The index of a `UNIQUE` constraint needs `ALTER TABLE ... DROP CONSTRAINT`. |

**Unique** expression and partial indexes are checked on every write (also inside transactions and after `ROLLBACK`). **Non-unique** ones are built and used too: `WHERE lower(email) = 'a@x.np'` uses `(lower(email))`, and a query whose `WHERE` has every part of a partial index's own `WHERE` uses that index. `EXPLAIN` shows it as `use index <name> (...)`. An expression key part works for `expr = constant` only (no ranges, no `IN (...)`, no `ORDER BY` on it); those queries scan.

---

## Part F: Sequences

```sql
CREATE SEQUENCE IF NOT EXISTS invoice_no START WITH 1000;
SELECT nextval('invoice_no') AS a, nextval('invoice_no') AS b;
SELECT setval('invoice_no', 5000);
CREATE TABLE invoices (invoice_no BIGINT PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT nextval('invoice_no'), amount NUMERIC(12,2));
INSERT INTO invoices (amount) VALUES (10), (20) RETURNING invoice_no;
```

```text
sequence 'invoice_no' created

a    | b
-----+-----
1000 | 1001
(1 row, 2.8 ms)

setval('invoice_no', 5000)
--------------------------
                      5000
(1 row, 2.0 ms)

table 'invoices' created

invoice_no
----------
      5001
      5002
(2 rows, 3.9 ms)
2 row(s) inserted
```

| Form | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `CREATE SEQUENCE [IF NOT EXISTS] s [AS type] [INCREMENT [BY] n] [MINVALUE n] [MAXVALUE n] [START [WITH] n] [CACHE n] [[NO] CYCLE] [OWNED BY t.c]` | A new sequence. |
| `ALTER SEQUENCE s RESTART [WITH n]` / `INCREMENT BY n` / ... | Changes it. |
| `DROP SEQUENCE [IF EXISTS] s, ...` | Removes it. |
| `nextval('s')` | The next number. |
| `currval('s')` | The last `nextval` of **this session**. Before that: an error, as in PostgreSQL. |
| `setval('s', n [, is_called])` | The next `nextval` gives `n + 1` (or `n` with `false`). |
| `lastval()` | The last `nextval` of this session, of any sequence. |

**A number is never given twice.** Not after a rollback, not after a restart, not after a crash. KarelaDB writes a mark to the log before it gives out the next 32 numbers. After a crash, the sequence starts after the mark, so a few numbers can be skipped (as in PostgreSQL).

Over HTTP every request is a new session, so `currval` works only inside one request (`SELECT nextval('s'); SELECT currval('s')`). Over the PostgreSQL protocol, the session is the connection.

---

## Part G: Other statements

| Statement | What KarelaDB does |
|---|---|
| `CREATE SCHEMA [IF NOT EXISTS] name` | Accepted: `schema 'reporting' accepted: KarelaDB has no schemas; use a separate database for its tables`. |
| `CREATE EXTENSION [IF NOT EXISTS] pgcrypto` | Accepted for `pgcrypto`, `uuid-ossp`, `citext`, `plpgsql`, `pg_trgm`, `btree_gin`, `btree_gist`, `unaccent`. Other names are refused. |
| `COMMENT ON TABLE / COLUMN / INDEX ... IS '...'` | Accepted. The comment is not kept. |
| `CREATE TEMP TABLE t AS SELECT ...` | A normal table with the rows (`table 'tmp_ids' created with 1 row(s)`). |

### DO blocks

The app uses `DO $$ ... $$` blocks to change the schema only once:

```sql
DO $$ BEGIN
  IF to_regclass('public.forum_posts') IS NOT NULL
     AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'forum_posts' AND column_name = 'views') THEN
    ALTER TABLE forum_posts ADD COLUMN views INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;
    RAISE NOTICE 'column views added';
  END IF;
END $$;
```

```text
table 'forum_posts' altered; NOTICE: column views added
```

A DO block may use:

- SQL statements (`SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `ALTER TABLE`, `CREATE INDEX`, `DROP INDEX`, ...), each ending with `;`.
- `IF ... THEN ... [ELSIF ... THEN ...] [ELSE ...] END IF;` The condition can use `EXISTS (SELECT ...)`, `(SELECT count(*) ...)`, `to_regclass('name')`, `information_schema` and `pg_catalog` views.
- `RAISE NOTICE / WARNING / INFO 'text %', value;` adds a line to the message. `RAISE EXCEPTION 'text %', value;` stops with an error.
- `NULL;`

`DECLARE`, `PERFORM`, `EXECUTE`, loops, `RETURN` and `EXCEPTION` handlers are refused with a message. Write a KarelaDB procedure (chapter 13), or do the work in the Go code.

**A DO block is not one transaction.** Each statement is saved when it runs. If a later statement fails, the earlier ones stay. The app's blocks are written to run again safely (they check first), so this is fine for them.

Of the app's 23 DO blocks, 19 work. Two fail only because the test tool joins the lines of the Go source and a `--` comment then hides the rest of the block (in the app they work). One is built by Go code at run time. One (`actionsimport`) compares `count(*)` with a value the tool cannot fill in.

---

## Part H: Catalog views

These read-only views describe the current database. They are made when a query reads them and kept until the schema changes.

| `information_schema` | `pg_catalog` |
|---|---|
| `tables`, `columns`, `views`, `schemata`, `sequences` | `pg_namespace`, `pg_class`, `pg_attribute`, `pg_type`, `pg_database` |
| `table_constraints`, `key_column_usage`, `constraint_column_usage` | `pg_index`, `pg_indexes`, `pg_constraint` |
| `referential_constraints`, `check_constraints` | `pg_tables`, `pg_views`, `pg_sequences` |

Every table is in the schema `public`.

```sql
SELECT column_name, data_type, character_maximum_length AS len, numeric_precision AS p, numeric_scale AS s, is_nullable, column_default
FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'forum_users' ORDER BY ordinal_position;
```

```text
column_name | data_type                | len  | p    | s    | is_nullable | column_default
------------+--------------------------+------+------+------+-------------+---------------------------------------------
user_id     | integer                  | NULL |   32 |    0 | NO          | nextval('forum_users_user_id_seq'::regclass)
email       | character varying        |  120 | NULL | NULL | NO          | NULL
name        | character varying        |   80 | NULL | NULL | NO          | NULL
balance     | numeric                  | NULL |   12 |    2 | NO          | 100
created_at  | timestamp with time zone | NULL | NULL | NULL | NO          | now()
mobile      | character varying        |   15 | NULL | NULL | YES         | NULL
is_admin    | boolean                  | NULL | NULL | NULL | NO          | FALSE
(7 rows, 0.3 ms)
```

```sql
SELECT constraint_name, constraint_type FROM information_schema.table_constraints WHERE table_name = 'post_likes' ORDER BY 1;
```

```text
constraint_name    | constraint_type
-------------------+----------------
post_likes_pkey    | PRIMARY KEY
post_likes_post_fk | FOREIGN KEY
post_likes_user_fk | FOREIGN KEY
(3 rows, 0.1 ms)
```

The views have the columns apps and tools use most. They are not complete copies of PostgreSQL's views: `psql`'s `\d` and some ORMs ask for more and may still fail.

## Part I: plpgsql functions and triggers

KarelaDB runs a small part of plpgsql: a **trigger function** (`RETURNS trigger ... LANGUAGE plpgsql`) with a `BEFORE UPDATE ... FOR EACH ROW` trigger. This is the form of the app's two trigger functions. KarelaDB runs the body for every changed row.

The body may use:

- `IF ... THEN ... [ELSIF ...] [ELSE ...] END IF`
- `RAISE EXCEPTION 'text with % places', value, ...`
- `NEW.col := value` (change the new row)
- `NEW.col` and `OLD.col` in conditions and values
- `RETURN NEW`

**1. Refuse a change** (`user_register_block_identity_update`):

```sql
CREATE TABLE user_register (user_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(200), referral_code VARCHAR(20));
INSERT INTO user_register (email, referral_code) VALUES ('ram@example.com', 'R1'), ('sita@example.com', 'S1');

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION user_register_block_identity_update() RETURNS trigger AS $fn$
BEGIN
  IF OLD.email IS NOT NULL AND OLD.email <> '' AND NEW.email IS DISTINCT FROM OLD.email THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'user_register.email is write-once (user %)', OLD.user_id;
  END IF;
  RETURN NEW;
END;
$fn$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER trg_user_register_immutable BEFORE UPDATE ON user_register
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION user_register_block_identity_update();

UPDATE user_register SET referral_code = 'R2' WHERE user_id = 1;
UPDATE user_register SET email = 'new@example.com' WHERE user_id = 2;
```

```text
trigger function 'user_register_block_identity_update' created (plpgsql, run by KarelaDB for every row a BEFORE UPDATE trigger sees)

row trigger 'trg_user_register_immutable' created on table 'user_register': it runs 'user_register_block_identity_update' for every row of a BEFORE UPDATE

1 row(s) updated
error: trigger 'trg_user_register_immutable' on table 'user_register' stopped the change: user_register.email is write-once (user 2)
```

The `%` is filled in from the row's own `OLD.user_id`. Nothing of the refused `UPDATE` is written.

**2. Change the new row** (`ticker_alias_reset_confirmation`):

```sql
CREATE TABLE ticker_alias (alias_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, swap_ratio NUMERIC(10,4), confirmed BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE, notes TEXT);
INSERT INTO ticker_alias (swap_ratio, confirmed) VALUES (1.5, TRUE);

CREATE FUNCTION ticker_alias_reset_confirmation() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  IF OLD.confirmed AND NEW.swap_ratio IS DISTINCT FROM OLD.swap_ratio THEN
    NEW.confirmed := FALSE;
    NEW.notes := COALESCE(NEW.notes || ' | ', '') || 'confirmation reset';
  END IF;
  RETURN NEW;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER trg_ticker_alias_reset_confirmation BEFORE UPDATE ON ticker_alias
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION ticker_alias_reset_confirmation();

UPDATE ticker_alias SET swap_ratio = 1.6 WHERE alias_id = 1;
SELECT alias_id, swap_ratio, confirmed, notes FROM ticker_alias;
```

```text
alias_id | swap_ratio | confirmed | notes
---------+------------+-----------+-------------------
       1 |     1.6000 | false     | confirmation reset
(1 row, 0.2 ms)
```

What KarelaDB refuses, with a clear message when you create it (nothing is accepted and then quietly not run):

| You write | KarelaDB says |
|---|---|
| `AFTER UPDATE ... FOR EACH ROW` | `AFTER ... FOR EACH ROW triggers are not supported by KarelaDB; a plpgsql row trigger must be BEFORE (...)` |
| `BEFORE INSERT` or `BEFORE DELETE ... FOR EACH ROW` | `only BEFORE UPDATE ... FOR EACH ROW plpgsql triggers are supported by KarelaDB; INSERT row triggers are not (...)` |
| `DECLARE`, `PERFORM`, loops or SQL statements in the body | the name of the part that is not supported, and what the body may use |
| A function that does not `RETURNS trigger` (`LANGUAGE sql`, for example) | a `WARNING`: the function is recorded but **not run**. Write a KarelaDB function or procedure for it (chapter 13). |

For other work, write a **KarelaDB trigger** (chapter 13). It runs once per statement and sees all changed rows in the tables `OLD` and `NEW`. A KarelaDB trigger and a plpgsql row trigger can be on the same table.

The PostgreSQL function of the app lets a person skip the check with `SET LOCAL nchartpro.allow_identity_update = 'on'`. In KarelaDB, an admin runs `ALTER TABLE user_register DISABLE TRIGGER trg_user_register_immutable`, makes the fix, and runs `ENABLE TRIGGER` again.

---

## Part J: Times (local time and UTC)

KarelaDB stores every `TIMESTAMP` in **UTC** (chapter 4). The NChartPro PostgreSQL server runs with `TZ=Asia/Kathmandu` (Nepal time, +05:45). That matters when you move data:

| PostgreSQL column | What it holds | When you move it to KarelaDB |
|---|---|---|
| `TIMESTAMPTZ` | An exact moment. | Export it **with** its offset (`2026-08-25 10:08:38+05:45`). KarelaDB converts it to UTC. Nothing else to do. |
| `TIMESTAMP` (no time zone) | **Local wall-clock time** (for this app, Nepal time). `DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` and `now()` wrote local time. | **Subtract the zone offset** (5 hours 45 minutes here), or add `+05:45` to the text before you insert it. |
| `DATE` | A calendar day. | Keep it as it is. |
| `TIME` | A clock time ("show at 10:00"). | Keep it as it is. It stays local clock time. |

```sql
SELECT ('2026-08-25 10:08:38' || '+05:45')::TIMESTAMP AS utc;
SELECT '2026-08-25 10:08:38'::timestamp - INTERVAL '5 hours 45 minutes' AS utc;
```

```text
utc
------------------------
2026-08-25T04:23:38.000Z
(1 row, 0.1 ms)

utc
------------------------
2026-08-25T04:23:38.000Z
(1 row, 0.1 ms)
```

After the move:

- `now()` and `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` in KarelaDB are **UTC**. `WHERE expires_at > now()` is right when both sides are UTC.
- To show local time, add the zone offset (here 5 hours 45 minutes, `20700000` ms): `to_char(blocked_at + 20700000, 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS')`.
- To compare a `TIME` column with the local clock, use the local time: `to_char(now() + 20700000, 'HH24:MI:SS')`.
- Over the PostgreSQL protocol, start `kareladb serve` with `--pg-timestamptz` so Go gets the exact moment (chapter 14).

**Never mix** local times and UTC times in one column. Move all rows of a table the same way.

---

## What is different from PostgreSQL

- `SERIAL` and `IDENTITY` only for the single-column primary key.
- `NUMERIC` without precision is a `DOUBLE`. `NUMERIC(p,s)` allows at most 18 decimal places, and the value times 10^s must fit a 64-bit number (about 18 digits).
- `FLOAT` alone is 4 bytes. `CHAR(n)` is not padded. `CITEXT` is not case-insensitive.
- `INTERVAL` is a number of milliseconds; a month is 30 days.
- `TIMESTAMPTZ` and `TIMESTAMP` are the same KarelaDB type (UTC).
- `GENERATED ... STORED` columns are worked out when read, not stored.
- A `DO` block is not one transaction.
- Expression index keys work for `expr = constant` only; ranges, `IN (...)` and `ORDER BY` on them scan.
- The `PRIMARY KEY` of a table cannot be dropped. `DROP TABLE ... CASCADE`, `DEFERRABLE` constraints, `INHERITS` and declarative partitions are not supported.
- Table constraints must come after the columns.
- `CREATE`, `ALTER` and `DROP` are not allowed inside `BEGIN ... COMMIT`.
- Schemas other than `public` do not exist.

## The app's startup DDL on KarelaDB

`node tests/app_compat/run_compat.mjs` replays the app's startup statements: 809 for PostgreSQL and 39 for QuestDB. 802 PostgreSQL statements work (checked on 2026-09-23). The 7 that do not are faults of the test tool, not of KarelaDB:

| Count | What | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 2 DO blocks and 1 plpgsql function with a `--` comment inside | The test tool joins the lines of the Go source, so the comment hides the rest (the function then has no `END`). With the app's real text, with its line breaks, they work. |
| 1 | The trigger of that function | It fails because its function failed. |
| 1 | The other plpgsql trigger | The test schema still has an old hand-written KarelaDB trigger with the same name. |
| 2 | DO blocks built by Go code at run time (`{{...}}` parts) | The test tool cannot fill in the parts. |

Over the whole app (2,143 statements: reads, writes and startup DDL, PostgreSQL and QuestDB), **1,971 work (92%)** on the same day.

The QuestDB statements (`SYMBOL INDEX`, `TIMESTAMP(ts)`, `DEDUP UPSERT KEYS`, `DROP PARTITION LIST`) are not PostgreSQL. KarelaDB has its own `TIMESERIES` form for them (chapter 10).

## Older KarelaDB programs

A database is written in a way older KarelaDB programs understand, **until** you use a new feature:

| New feature | Stored as | An older KarelaDB program |
|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL types, named `UNIQUE`, `PRIMARY KEY (a, b)`, `FOREIGN KEY (a, b)`, partial or expression indexes | New parts of the table description (`T`, `K`, `F`, `X`) | Refuses to open the database: `needs a newer KDB` (its name then). Nothing is damaged. |
| Sequences | A new file `sequences` and log records | Refuses to open the database: `needs a newer KDB`. |
| plpgsql trigger functions and row triggers | New kinds in the file `routines` (feature `plpgsql_triggers`) | Refuses to open the database: `needs a newer KDB`. |
| `ALTER COLUMN TYPE`, `ADD PRIMARY KEY` | Rows written again, in one transaction with the change | Normal rows. |

Tables that use none of this stay in the old format. **Update every `kareladb` program before you run the app's PostgreSQL schema on a database.**

## Speed

- Plain KarelaDB tables pay nothing: the new checks run only for columns with a PostgreSQL rule.
- A `UNIQUE` column uses an index in memory, so an insert does not read the table.
- Foreign key actions look up the child rows with keys and indexes. A child table without an index on the foreign key column is read in full for each deleted parent.
- The catalog views are made once per schema change.
- A `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE` or `CREATE INDEX` that changes something takes about 20 ms on the test PC (it saves the table descriptions). An `IF NOT EXISTS` that changes nothing is faster. The whole app check (3,024 requests, with all startup DDL) took 15 seconds.
- `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE` and `ADD PRIMARY KEY` write every row again: slow for very big tables.

# 23. PostgreSQL queries and data changes

- Category: Tutorial

## What you will learn

Chapter 22 is about the app's tables. This chapter is about the app's **queries and data changes**: the SQL a PostgreSQL app sends every day.

- **Part A.** Upserts: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`, `RETURNING`, `xmax`.
- **Part B.** `INSERT ... SELECT`, `UPDATE ... FROM`, `DELETE ... USING`, subqueries in data changes.
- **Part C.** `WITH` queries: plain, `RECURSIVE`, and `WITH x AS (UPDATE ...)`.
- **Part D.** Correlated subqueries, `EXISTS`, `LATERAL`, and why they stay fast.
- **Part E.** More query forms: `FILTER`, `DISTINCT ON`, `UNION` / `INTERSECT` / `EXCEPT`, `GROUP BY 1`.
- **Part F.** Casts, times and intervals.
- **Part G.** Arrays and JSON.
- **Part H.** Advisory locks.
- **Part I.** QuestDB apps: `ALTER DATABASE ... SET dialect`, `/imp`, `to_str`.
- What is **different** from PostgreSQL, and **speed**.

The output under each example is real (`kareladb sql`). Times print in KarelaDB's style (`2026-09-10T05:20:00.000Z`); over the PostgreSQL protocol they have PostgreSQL's style.

## The short version

| PostgreSQL | KarelaDB |
|---|---|
| `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING / DO UPDATE SET c = EXCLUDED.c` | Works, with `WHERE`, `ON CONSTRAINT` and `RETURNING (xmax = 0)`. |
| `INSERT ... SELECT`, `DEFAULT VALUES` | Works. |
| `UPDATE t SET ... FROM s WHERE ...`, `DELETE FROM t USING s WHERE ...` | Works. |
| Subqueries in `SET`, `WHERE` and `VALUES` | Works, correlated ones too. |
| `WITH`, `WITH RECURSIVE`, `WITH x AS (UPDATE ... RETURNING ...)` | Works. A statement with data-changing `WITH` queries is one transaction. |
| Correlated subqueries, `EXISTS`, `IN (SELECT ...)`, `LATERAL` | Works. The usual shapes become hash lookups. |
| `FILTER (WHERE ...)`, `agg(x ORDER BY y)`, `DISTINCT ON`, `GROUP BY 1`, `NULLS FIRST` | Works. |
| `UNION`, `INTERSECT`, `EXCEPT` (with or without `ALL`), `(VALUES ...) AS v(a, b)` | Works. |
| `x::type`, `CAST`, `DATE '...'`, `INTERVAL '...'`, `E'...'`, `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` | Works. Casts round numbers as PostgreSQL does. |
| `INTERVAL` arithmetic, `AT TIME ZONE`, `EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM interval)`, `make_interval` | Works (time zones: fixed offsets and zones without daylight saving, such as `Asia/Kathmandu`; see Part F). |
| `= ANY($1)` with Go slices, `ARRAY[...]`, `array_agg`, `unnest`, `TEXT[]` results | Works, in text and binary form. |
| `jsonb_build_object`, `json_agg`, `jsonb_set`, `->`, `->>`, `#>>` | Works. JSON sorts like `jsonb` (9 before 10). |
| `pg_advisory_lock`, `pg_try_advisory_xact_lock`, ... | Real locks between sessions. |

When all 2143 statements of the app run on KarelaDB, **1971** work over HTTP (92.0%) and **1952** over the PostgreSQL protocol (91.1%) (checked on 2026-09-23). Before this work (and the schema work of chapter 22) it was 950 and 930. Most of the rest come from the test data or from table definitions the test schema left out (see the end).

---

## Part A: Upserts

`ON CONFLICT` says what to do when a new row has the key of a row that is there.

```sql
CREATE TABLE page_hits (page TEXT PRIMARY KEY, hits BIGINT NOT NULL, last_at TIMESTAMP);
INSERT INTO page_hits VALUES ('/chart', 5, '2026-09-10T05:00:00Z');

INSERT INTO page_hits (page, hits, last_at)
VALUES ('/chart', 1, '2026-09-11T05:00:00Z'), ('/news', 1, '2026-09-11T05:00:00Z')
ON CONFLICT (page) DO UPDATE SET hits = page_hits.hits + EXCLUDED.hits, last_at = EXCLUDED.last_at
RETURNING page, hits, (xmax = 0) AS inserted;
```

```
page   | hits | inserted
-------+------+---------
/chart |    6 | false
/news  |    1 | true
1 row(s) inserted, 1 updated
```

- `EXCLUDED.column` is the value of the new row. `page_hits.column` is the value that is there now.
- Write the table name (or the alias of `INSERT INTO t AS a`) before a column. A plain name is ambiguous in PostgreSQL.
- `RETURNING` gives the rows that were inserted or updated. `xmax` is 0 for an inserted row and 1 for an updated one.
- `DO UPDATE ... WHERE cond`: rows that do not match stay as they are and are not returned.
- `DO NOTHING` skips the row. Without a key list it means "any unique key".

```sql
INSERT INTO page_hits (page, hits) VALUES ('/news', 100) ON CONFLICT (page) DO NOTHING RETURNING page;
```

```
(0 rows)
0 row(s) inserted, 1 skipped (already there)
```

**Which keys.** The key list must be the primary key, a `DEDUP KEY`, a `UNIQUE` column or constraint, or a `UNIQUE INDEX` with exactly those columns (a partial index needs `ON CONFLICT (cols) WHERE ...`). `ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT name` names it (`table_pkey` for the primary key). Another list is an error, as in PostgreSQL: "there is no unique key on (...)".

**Rules from PostgreSQL.**

- A key with a NULL never clashes.
- Two new rows with the same key in one `DO UPDATE` statement are an error ("cannot change the same row twice"). With `DO NOTHING` the first one wins.
- `SERIAL` numbers are used also for rows that end as updates (so ids can have gaps).

**Speed.** `DO NOTHING`, and `DO UPDATE SET` of every other column from `EXCLUDED`, on the table's own key, run as `INSERT OR IGNORE` / `INSERT OR REPLACE`: big batches go in without looking rows up one by one. Other forms look each row up by its key (or index).

## Part B: Copying and joined changes

`INSERT ... SELECT` copies the rows of a query. `DEFAULT VALUES` writes one row of defaults.

```sql
INSERT INTO ledger (user_id, amount, balance_after) SELECT user_id, 25, balance FROM wallets WHERE balance > 0;
INSERT INTO logs DEFAULT VALUES;
```

`UPDATE ... FROM` changes rows with values from other tables. `DELETE ... USING` deletes rows that have a match.

```sql
UPDATE wallets w SET balance = v.balance
FROM (VALUES (1, 10), (2, 20), (9, 90)) AS v(user_id, balance)
WHERE w.user_id = v.user_id
RETURNING w.user_id, w.balance;
```

```
user_id | balance
--------+--------
      1 |      10
      2 |      20
2 row(s) updated
```

```sql
DELETE FROM ledger l USING wallets w WHERE l.user_id = w.user_id AND w.balance < 15 RETURNING l.id;
```

- A row of the table changes once, also when it matches several rows of `FROM` (as in PostgreSQL, one of them is used).
- The join is a hash join: `WHERE w.user_id = v.user_id` does not compare every pair.
- Subqueries work in `SET`, `WHERE` and `VALUES`, also ones that use the row being changed:

```sql
UPDATE tickets t SET vote_count = (SELECT count(*) FROM votes v WHERE v.ticket_id = t.ticket_id);
DELETE FROM tickets WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM votes WHERE votes.ticket_id = tickets.ticket_id);
UPDATE ai_models SET is_default = TRUE WHERE (provider, model) = (SELECT provider, model FROM ai_models ORDER BY rank LIMIT 1);
```

## Part C: WITH queries

A `WITH` query names a result for the statement. KarelaDB runs it the first time the statement reads it, once, and keeps its rows for the statement.

`WITH RECURSIVE` runs its second part again on the rows found last, until no new rows come. `UNION` (without `ALL`) stops at rows it has seen, so a loop in the data ends.

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE upline(user_id, referred_by, lvl) AS (
  SELECT user_id, referred_by, 0 FROM referrals WHERE user_id = 4
  UNION ALL
  SELECT r.user_id, r.referred_by, u.lvl + 1 FROM referrals r JOIN upline u ON r.user_id = u.referred_by WHERE u.lvl < 20
)
SELECT user_id, lvl FROM upline ORDER BY lvl;
```

```
user_id | lvl
--------+----
      4 |   0
      3 |   1
      2 |   2
      1 |   3
```

A recursive query that never stops is stopped after 100,000 rounds or 10 million rows, with an error.

**WITH queries that change data.** The app's wallet top-up changes a row, writes a ledger row from the changed row, and returns it, in one statement:

```sql
WITH upd AS (UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance + 25 WHERE user_id = 1 RETURNING user_id, balance),
     led AS (INSERT INTO ledger (user_id, amount, balance_after) SELECT user_id, 25, balance FROM upd)
SELECT user_id, balance FROM upd;
```

```
user_id | balance
--------+--------
      1 |     125
```

- The data changes run first, in the order written. Then the main query runs.
- The statement is one transaction: when a part fails, nothing is written.
- Such a `SELECT` locks the tables it changes, as any writer does (chapter 15), and is never kept in the result cache.

## Part D: Correlated subqueries and LATERAL

A **correlated** subquery uses a column of the outer row.

```sql
SELECT t.ticket_id, t.title,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM votes v WHERE v.ticket_id = t.ticket_id) AS votes,
       EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM votes v WHERE v.ticket_id = t.ticket_id AND v.user_id = 8) AS i_voted
FROM tickets t ORDER BY t.ticket_id;
```

```
ticket_id | title           | votes | i_voted
----------+-----------------+-------+--------
        1 | Dark mode       |     2 | true
        2 | Faster charts   |     1 | false
        3 | Nepali calendar |     0 | false
```

**How KarelaDB keeps this fast.** It does not run the subquery once per outer row.

- When the subquery joins the outer row with `=` (`v.ticket_id = t.ticket_id`), KarelaDB runs it **once** for all keys (grouped by `ticket_id`), puts the answers in a hash table, and every outer row looks its answer up. The work is one pass over `votes` plus one lookup per ticket.
- `count(*)` of a key without rows is 0, and `sum` is NULL, as in PostgreSQL.
- `EXISTS`, `NOT EXISTS`, `IN (SELECT ...)` and `NOT IN (SELECT ...)` work the same way (a set of keys).
- Other shapes (`v.amount > t.limit`) run once per **different** outer value, and the answers are kept for the statement.
- A subquery that uses no outer column runs once, before the query.
- A value subquery that finds two rows is an error, as in PostgreSQL. Add `LIMIT 1` or an aggregate.

`LATERAL` lets a `FROM` subquery use the tables before it:

```sql
SELECT t.title, last_vote.user_id
FROM tickets t
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT user_id FROM votes v WHERE v.ticket_id = t.ticket_id ORDER BY user_id DESC LIMIT 1) last_vote ON TRUE
ORDER BY t.ticket_id;
```

```
title           | user_id
----------------+--------
Dark mode       |       8
Faster charts   |       7
Nepali calendar |    NULL
```

A `LATERAL` subquery with an aggregate becomes a hash join; one with `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` runs per outer row (answers are kept for rows with the same key).

## Part E: More query forms

```sql
SELECT symbol,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE qty >= 10) AS big_trades,
       string_agg(price::text, ' -> ' ORDER BY ts) AS path
FROM trades GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
```

```
symbol | big_trades | path
-------+------------+-----------
CITY   |          2 | 510 -> 512
COAST  |          0 | 900 -> 905
```

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT ON (symbol) symbol, ts, price FROM trades ORDER BY symbol, ts DESC;  -- the newest trade of each symbol
```

```
symbol | ts                       | price
-------+--------------------------+------
CITY   | 2026-09-10T05:20:00.000Z |   512
COAST  | 2026-09-10T05:30:00.000Z |   905
```

| Form | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `agg(x) FILTER (WHERE cond)` | The aggregate only sees rows where `cond` is true. |
| `array_agg(x ORDER BY y)`, `string_agg(x, ',' ORDER BY y)` | The rows come in that order. |
| `DISTINCT ON (a) ... ORDER BY a, b` | The first row of each `a` in `ORDER BY` order. |
| `GROUP BY 1`, `ORDER BY 2` | Position of a select column. An alias works too: `GROUP BY day`. |
| `ORDER BY sum(x)`, `HAVING count(*) > 1` | Aggregates that are not select columns. |
| `NULLS FIRST`, `NULLS LAST` | NULL counts as bigger than every value (first with `DESC`), as in PostgreSQL. |
| `LIMIT ALL`, `OFFSET n ROWS`, `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY` | Also QuestDB's `LIMIT lo, hi`. |
| `UNION`, `INTERSECT`, `EXCEPT` [`ALL`] | Without `ALL` the result has no copies. `INTERSECT` goes first. |
| `(VALUES (1, 'a'), (2, 'b')) AS v(n, s)` | A small table of values. |
| `(a, b) < (x, y)`, `(a, b) = (SELECT ...)` | Row comparisons. |
| `FROM (SELECT ...)` | The subquery needs no alias. |

## Part F: Casts, times and intervals

```sql
SELECT '12.5'::numeric(6,1) AS n, 2.5::int AS rounded, E'tab\there' AS e,
       (DATE '2026-01-31' + INTERVAL '1 month')::date AS next_month;
```

```
n    | rounded | e        | next_month
-----+---------+----------+-----------
12.5 |       3 | tab	here | 2026-02-28
```

- Every PostgreSQL type name works after `::` and in `CAST`: `int4`, `float8`, `numeric(10,2)`, `text`, `varchar(20)`, `timestamptz`, `interval`, `text[]`, `bigint[]`, ...
- A cast to a whole number or to `numeric(p,s)` rounds half away from zero. Other places (a value for an `INT` column, an argument of a saved function) still refuse `2.5`.
- `x::text` of a time gives PostgreSQL's text: `2026-09-10 12:00:00` (with `+00` for a `timestamptz`).
- A text constant next to a number is read as a number: `'1.50' + 1` is `2.50` (a numeric parameter sent as text works too). Text from a column or a function is not: `doc ->> 'n' + 1` is an error; write `(doc ->> 'n')::int + 1`.
- `md5(text)` and `initcap(text)` work as in PostgreSQL.
- `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, `CURRENT_DATE`, `LOCALTIMESTAMP`, `now()` are the time the statement started. KarelaDB times are UTC.
- `DATE - DATE` is a number of days. A month added to the 31st ends on the last day of the next month.

**Intervals** keep months, days and time apart, as in PostgreSQL:

```sql
SELECT INTERVAL '1 day' - INTERVAL '1 hour' AS i, EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM INTERVAL '1 month') AS month_seconds,
       make_interval(days => 3, hours => 2) AS m;
```

```
i               | month_seconds | m
----------------+---------------+----------------
1 day -01:00:00 |       2592000 | 3 days 02:00:00
```

`justify_hours`, `justify_days` and `justify_interval` move 24 hours into a day and 30 days into a month. For comparing, a month counts as 30 days.

**AT TIME ZONE** follows PostgreSQL:

- `timestamp AT TIME ZONE z` reads a clock time of zone `z` and gives the instant (a `timestamptz`).
- `timestamptz AT TIME ZONE z` shows an instant as the clock time of zone `z` (a `timestamp`).

```sql
SELECT (TIMESTAMP '2026-09-10 12:00:00' AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kathmandu')::text AS utc_instant,
       (TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-09-10 06:15:00+00' AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kathmandu')::text AS local_clock;
```

```
utc_instant            | local_clock
-----------------------+--------------------
2026-09-10 06:15:00+00 | 2026-09-10 12:00:00
```

A `TIMESTAMP` column holds UTC instants in KarelaDB, so KarelaDB treats `now()`, `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, `timestamptz` casts and `TIMESTAMPTZ` columns as instants, and other `TIMESTAMP` values as clock times. Zones are fixed offsets (`'+05:45'`, `'UTC'`, `'Asia/Kathmandu'`, ...); zones with daylight saving time are refused.

## Part G: Arrays and JSON

KarelaDB keeps an array as a JSON array. Over the PostgreSQL protocol it is a real array (`text[]` is type 1009, `bigint[]` 1016, ...) in text and binary form, so `pgx` scans it into a Go slice and sends Go slices as parameters.

```sql
CREATE TABLE feeds (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, tags TEXT[], roles JSONB);
INSERT INTO feeds VALUES (1, '{market,ipo}', '{"admin": "sita"}'), (2, ARRAY['hydro'], '{}');
SELECT id, unnest(tags) AS tag FROM feeds ORDER BY id, tag;
```

```
id | tag
---+-------
 1 | ipo
 1 | market
 2 | hydro
```

| Form | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `x = ANY($1)`, `x <> ALL($1)` | `$1` is an array (a Go slice, `'{1,2}'`, or `ARRAY[...]`). A constant array becomes an `IN` list, so indexes and key ranges still work. |
| `ARRAY[1, 2]`, `ARRAY(SELECT ...)`, `'{a,b}'::text[]` | Make an array. |
| `tags[1]`, `cardinality(tags)`, `array_length(tags, 1)`, `array_to_string`, `string_to_array`, `array_append`, `array_remove`, `array_position` | Read and change arrays (from 1, as in PostgreSQL). |
| `array_agg(x)`, `(array_agg(x ORDER BY y))[1]` | Collect values. |
| `unnest(array)` | In `SELECT`: one row per element. In `FROM`: a table (`FROM unnest($1::int[]) AS u(id)`). |
| `tags @> ARRAY['a']`, `&&`, `<@` | Contains, overlaps, is contained. |

JSON functions: `jsonb_build_object`, `jsonb_build_array`, `json_agg` / `jsonb_agg` (with `ORDER BY`), `to_jsonb`, `row_to_json(t)`, `jsonb_set(doc, path, value, create)`, `jsonb_typeof`, `jsonb_array_length`, `->`, `->>`, `#>`, `#>>`.

```sql
UPDATE feeds SET roles = jsonb_set(roles, ARRAY['editor'], to_jsonb('ram'::text), true) WHERE id = 1 RETURNING roles;
```

```
roles
-------------------------------
{"admin":"sita","editor":"ram"}
```

JSON values sort like PostgreSQL's `jsonb`: numbers by value (9 before 10), strings by text, and null < strings < numbers < booleans < arrays < objects.

## Part H: Advisory locks

Advisory locks are named by a number (or two). KarelaDB keeps them between sessions of one database.

| Function | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `pg_advisory_lock(key)` | Waits until no other session holds the key, then holds it until `pg_advisory_unlock` or the session ends. |
| `pg_try_advisory_lock(key)` | The same without waiting: `true` or `false`. |
| `pg_advisory_xact_lock(key)`, `pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(key)` | Held until `COMMIT` / `ROLLBACK` (or the end of the statement outside `BEGIN`). |
| `pg_advisory_unlock(key)`, `pg_advisory_unlock_all()` | Let it go. `unlock` returns `false` when the session did not hold it. |
| `..._shared` forms | Several sessions may share the key; an exclusive lock waits for all of them. |

- `(a, b)` with two `int` keys is another lock than one `bigint` key, as in PostgreSQL.
- A session may take its own lock again; it must unlock it as many times.
- Waiting ends after 30 seconds with an error (PostgreSQL waits forever).
- A statement alone outside a transaction waits without holding any table lock, so the session that holds the key can go on working. Inside `BEGIN ... COMMIT` it waits holding the locks of the tables the transaction used; keep such waits short.
- Over HTTP without a session, locks end with the request.

## Part I: QuestDB apps

**The dialect.** `ALTER DATABASE qdb SET dialect = 'questdb'` makes a database read SQL the QuestDB way:

- A plain `INSERT` into a table with a `DEDUP KEY` replaces the row with the same key (QuestDB's `DEDUP UPSERT KEYS`).
- `CAST(time AS LONG)` gives microseconds since 1970 (PostgreSQL mode: milliseconds).

`SET dialect = 'postgres'` goes back. The setting is kept in `_system` and applies every time the database opens (chapter 21 has the other `ALTER DATABASE` settings).

**CSV import.** `POST /imp` takes a CSV file the way QuestDB does (chapter 8 has the details):

```bash
curl -F "data=@Ochl_Day.csv" "http://127.0.0.1:9900/imp?name=Ochl_Day&timestamp=time&partitionBy=DAY&fmt=json"
```

**Functions.** `to_str(time, 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss')` formats a time with QuestDB's letters.

## What is different from PostgreSQL

- `WITH` queries that change data run before the main query and the main query sees their changes (PostgreSQL uses one snapshot). The app's statements give the same answers.
- A recursive `WITH` query stops with an error after 100,000 rounds or 10 million rows.
- Advisory locks wait at most 30 seconds.
- Time zones are fixed offsets; `AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London'` is refused.
- A plain column name in `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET` means the row that is there (PostgreSQL calls it ambiguous).
- Casting a whole number from `double precision` rounds half away from zero (PostgreSQL: to the nearest even number).
- Arrays have one dimension in binary form; nested arrays are sent as text.
- `refdata.companies` means the table `companies` of the **database** `refdata` on the same server (PostgreSQL would look for a schema `refdata`). You can read it in `SELECT`, joins, subqueries and `INSERT ... SELECT`. A statement changes only the database it runs in. `public.companies` is your own table. The help topic **Queries across databases** has the details.

## The app's queries on KarelaDB

`tests/app_compat/run_compat.mjs` runs all 2143 statements of the app against a fresh server with sample data.

| Statements | HTTP before | HTTP now | PostgreSQL protocol before | now |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| All 2143 | 950 (44.3%) | 1971 (92.0%) | 930 (43.4%) | 1952 (91.1%) |
| SELECT (786) | 549 | 734 | 548 | 734 |
| WITH (20) | 0 | 15 | 0 | 15 |
| INSERT (209) | 26 | 142 | 26 | 142 |
| UPDATE (164) | 81 | 156 | 79 | 155 |
| DELETE (72) | 55 | 56 | 55 | 55 |
| Schema statements (889, chapter 22) | 238 | 866 | 221 | 849 |

"Now" is the run of 2026-09-23. Over the PostgreSQL protocol a few QuestDB `ALTER` and `RENAME` statements of the test fail because the test tool replays them in another order (the column or table is already there), and a few test values (`'test'` for a number) are refused earlier, when the parameters are read.

Most of the statements that still fail are not about query support:

- 44 "no unique key" for `ON CONFLICT`: the test schema (`schema_kdb.sql`) was written for an older KarelaDB and left out composite keys. With the app's own `CREATE TABLE` they work.
- Sample values that do not fit (`'test'` for a number), and template parts the test cannot fill (`{{spec.conflict}}`).
- A few features of other chapters: QuestDB's `tables()` functions, and `COPY` sent over HTTP (over the PostgreSQL port `COPY` works, chapter 14).

## Speed

- A statement without the new forms runs the same code as before: the checks are a few flag tests.
- `ON CONFLICT` on the table's key with `DO NOTHING` or a full `DO UPDATE SET ... EXCLUDED` writes batches as fast as `INSERT OR REPLACE`.
- Correlated subqueries and `LATERAL` with `=` joins cost one pass over the inner table plus one hash lookup per outer row.
- A constant `= ANY(...)` becomes `IN (...)`: indexes, key ranges and the column engine still work.
- Queries with `FILTER` or `ORDER BY` inside an aggregate use the row engine.

# 24. Versions and upgrades

- Category: Tutorial

## What you will learn

KarelaDB gets new features all the time. Some of them change what KarelaDB writes on disk. This chapter explains what happens to your data when you update KarelaDB, and when you go back to an older KarelaDB:

- **Part A.** The rule: a new KarelaDB opens old data; an old KarelaDB refuses new data.
- **Part B.** `kareladb version` and `SHOW VERSION`: which features a database uses.
- **Part C.** A database from an older KarelaDB, and `kareladb upgrade`.
- **Part D.** What an older KarelaDB says, and what to do.
- **Part E.** How to update the KarelaDB programs on a server.

All examples are in examples/24-versions-and-upgrades/. The output under each example is real. The examples use the database `market` with the sample data.

## The short version

- Update **every** `kareladb` program (server, scripts, tools) at the same time, to the same build.
- A newer KarelaDB opens your old databases as they are. There is nothing to convert.
- Before you update a server, make a backup (you do that every day anyway, chapter 9). `kareladb upgrade <db>` does backup + feature list + check in one command, when you want it.
- If a `kareladb` command says `this database needs a newer KarelaDB` (exit code `3`): the data is **not damaged**. Use the newer KarelaDB. Do **not** run `kareladb repair` or `kareladb restore`.

---

## Part A: the rule

Each database keeps a **feature list** in its manifest (the file that lists the database's files, chapter 9). A feature is one change to what KarelaDB writes on disk. For example:

| Feature | The database has |
|---|---|
| `json` | a `JSON` column |
| `indexes` | a `CREATE INDEX` |
| `sequences` | a `CREATE SEQUENCE` |
| `audit` | a table with `SET AUDIT ON` |
| `runs` | rows written by the line protocol in the fast column form |
| `deferred_triggers` | a trigger made with `DEFERRED` (chapter 13) |
| `table_ttl` | a table with `TTL n DAYS` |

KarelaDB puts a feature into the list **before** it writes the first data that needs it. When a database opens, KarelaDB reads the list **first**, before it reads or changes anything else:

- Every name is known: the database opens.
- A name is not known: a newer KarelaDB wrote this database. KarelaDB stops with `this database needs a newer KarelaDB: it uses <name>` and changes nothing.

The same message comes for the other things only a newer KarelaDB writes: a newer file format number, a log record or catalog part KarelaDB does not know. KarelaDB never calls such data "damaged", and it never starts a repair.

Only schema statements (`CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`), the first use of a feature and checkpoints look at the list. Writing rows costs nothing extra: the write benchmark gave the same numbers before and after (see the report `reports/versioning.md`).

## Part B: which features does a database use?

### kareladb version

Without a database, `kareladb version` shows this KarelaDB and every feature it can read:

```powershell
kareladb version
```

```text
kareladb 0.2.0-dev (crc32c hardware: yes)

  views                0.2.0-dev (2026-09-10)   CREATE VIEW: the "views" file
  partition_format_2   0.2.0-dev (2026-09-11)   table partition files in format 2 (one raw block per column)
  block_stats          0.2.0-dev (2026-09-11)   column stats section in partition files (count, min, max, sum per column)
  runs                 0.2.0-dev (2026-09-11)   log record 'C': rows of a bulk upsert kept as columns
  auto_meta            0.2.0-dev (2026-09-11)   AUTO id counters in the manifest (auto.<table id>)
  json                 0.2.0-dev (2026-09-11)   JSON columns (type code 12)
  bytes                0.2.0-dev (2026-09-11)   BYTES columns (type code 13)
  check                0.2.0-dev (2026-09-11)   CHECK constraints (catalog format 2, part 'C')
  indexes              0.2.0-dev (2026-09-11)   CREATE INDEX, UNIQUE and FULLTEXT indexes (catalog part 'I')
  routines             0.2.0-dev (2026-09-11)   functions, procedures and triggers: the "routines" file
  users                0.2.0-dev (2026-09-11)   server users and roles (_system.users)

  table_grants         0.2.0-dev (2026-09-12)   GRANT ... ON TABLE (_system.users.table_grants)
  totp                 0.2.0-dev (2026-09-12)   two-factor logins (_system.users.totp)
  trash                0.2.0-dev (2026-09-12)   dropped tables kept as _dropped_<ms>_<name> for UNDROP TABLE
  database_settings    0.2.0-dev (2026-09-12)   ALTER DATABASE ... SET READ ONLY (_system.database_settings)
  dialects             0.2.0-dev (2026-09-12)   ALTER DATABASE ... SET dialect (_system.database_dialects)
  pg_catalog_parts     0.2.0-dev (2026-09-12)   PostgreSQL column types, multi-column keys, foreign keys, expression and partial indexes (catalog parts 'T', 'K', 'F', 'X')
  sequences            0.2.0-dev (2026-09-12)   CREATE SEQUENCE: the "sequences" file and its log records
  batched_log_sync     0.2.0-dev (2026-09-11)   --sync-commits batch: log segments with 16-byte commit records
  dedup_change         0.2.0-dev (2026-09-12)   ALTER TABLE ... DEDUP ENABLE / DISABLE: the DEDUP KEY of a table that already holds rows
  plpgsql_triggers     0.2.0-dev (2026-09-12)   PostgreSQL plpgsql trigger functions and FOR EACH ROW triggers in the "routines" file
  cached_views         0.2.0-dev (2026-09-13)   CREATE CACHED VIEW: which views are cached, and REFRESH ON COMMIT, in the "views" file
  deferred_triggers    0.2.0-dev (2026-09-13)   CREATE TRIGGER ... DEFERRED: job records in the log, and the "trigger_queue" and "q/<job>" files of queued jobs
  materialized_views   0.2.0-dev (2026-09-13)   CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW: catalog part 'M', REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW log records, mv_dirty.<id> in the manifest
  table_ttl            0.2.0-dev (2026-09-13)   TTL n DAYS on a table: catalog part 'L'

A database that uses a feature not in this list needs a newer KarelaDB (kareladb check exits with 3).
```

With a database, it shows the database's list. It reads only the manifest, so it also works while a server has the database open:

```powershell
kareladb version market
```

```text
kareladb 0.2.0-dev (crc32c hardware: yes)
database market
feature list (3):
  batched_log_sync     --sync-commits batch: log segments with 16-byte commit records
  block_stats          column stats section in partition files (count, min, max, sum per column)
  partition_format_2   table partition files in format 2 (one raw block per column)
```

The sample data has plain tables only, so its list is short. `batched_log_sync` is in every list today: writers that commit at the same moment share one wait for the disk (group commit, chapter 15), and the log keeps them in the same form as `--sync-commits batch`. Each commit is still on the disk before it is confirmed. So every database this build writes uses `batched_log_sync`, and a KarelaDB built before 2026-09-11 cannot open it.

### SHOW VERSION

In SQL (`kareladb sql`, `kareladb shell`, the web console, the PostgreSQL port), `SHOW VERSION` shows the same for the current database:

```sql
SHOW VERSION;
```

```text
item                    | value                                           
------------------------+-------------------------------------------------
kareladb version             | 0.2.0-dev                                       
database                | market                                          
features used           | batched_log_sync, block_stats, partition_form...
feature list            | saved: batched_log_sync, block_stats, partiti...
features this KarelaDB reads | 26: views, partition_format_2, block_stats, r...
(5 rows, 0.1 ms)
```

- `features used`: what the database uses right now.
- `feature list`: what is saved in the manifest. Normally the same.

## Part C: a database from an older KarelaDB

Databases made by KarelaDB programs **before 2026-09-12** have no feature list. KarelaDB opens them exactly as before. It works out their list from the tables, files and log, and saves it at the next checkpoint (for example when the database is closed).

The KarelaDB source has small databases made by the older programs, for the tests (`tests/fixtures`). This one was made by the `kareladb.exe` of 2026-09-11:

```powershell
# A database written by an older KarelaDB (2026-09-11, before feature lists)
Copy-Item "$env:KDB_EXAMPLES\..\..\..\tests\fixtures\sep11_clean" old-db -Recurse
kareladb version old-db
```

```text
kareladb 0.2.0-dev (crc32c hardware: yes)
database old-db
feature list: not saved yet (the database was written by a KarelaDB before feature lists).
It is saved at the next checkpoint of this KarelaDB, or now with: kareladb upgrade old-db
SHOW VERSION in kareladb sql or kareladb shell shows the features it uses.
```

### kareladb upgrade

`kareladb upgrade` does three things: a verified backup, then it saves the feature list, then `kareladb check`. The database must be closed (stop the server first).

```powershell
kareladb upgrade old-db --backups upgrade-backups
"exit code: $LASTEXITCODE"
kareladb version old-db
kareladb sql old-db "SELECT count(*) AS candles FROM ochl; SHOW VERSION"
```

```text
KarelaDB 0.2.0-dev, database old-db
saved feature list: none (written by a KarelaDB before feature lists)
1/3 verified backup into upgrade-backups ...
    upgrade-backups/20260923-121111-373 (7 files, 10.5 KB)
2/3 saving the feature list ...
    features used: batched_log_sync, block_stats, partition_format_2, views
    (no files need to be written again for this KarelaDB version)
3/3 check ...
checked 9 files (12.3 KB) and 2 log segments
OK: no damage found

Upgrade done. An older KarelaDB build that does not know one of these features now refuses this database with "needs a newer KarelaDB".
exit code: 0
kareladb 0.2.0-dev (crc32c hardware: yes)
database old-db
feature list (4):
  batched_log_sync     --sync-commits batch: log segments with 16-byte commit records
  block_stats          column stats section in partition files (count, min, max, sum per column)
  partition_format_2   table partition files in format 2 (one raw block per column)
  views                CREATE VIEW: the "views" file
candles
-------
    176
(1 row, 0.7 ms)

item                    | value                                           
------------------------+-------------------------------------------------
kareladb version             | 0.2.0-dev                                       
database                | old-db                                          
features used           | batched_log_sync, block_stats, partition_form...
feature list            | saved: batched_log_sync, block_stats, partiti...
features this KarelaDB reads | 26: views, partition_format_2, block_stats, r...
(5 rows, 0.1 ms)
```

- Without `--backups`, the backup goes into a folder next to the database: `old-db-backups` (for a database name in the data folder: `<data folder>-backups/<name>`). Older backups there are kept.
- You do not **have** to run `kareladb upgrade`. It is the safe way when you want a backup from just before, or before you move the folder to another computer.
- Exit codes: `0` done, `3` the database needs a newer KarelaDB (nothing done, no backup), `2` the check found damage (the backup is named), `1` could not run.

## Part D: when an older KarelaDB opens newer data

To show it here, the environment variable `KDB_TEST_HIDE_FEATURES` makes `kareladb` act like an older program that does not know `views`. It is **only for tests**; do not set it on a server.

```powershell
# Play an older KarelaDB that does not know "views" (KDB_TEST_HIDE_FEATURES is only for tests)
$env:KDB_TEST_HIDE_FEATURES = "views"
kareladb check old-db
"exit code: $LASTEXITCODE"
kareladb sql old-db "SELECT count(*) FROM ochl"
"exit code: $LASTEXITCODE"
$env:KDB_TEST_HIDE_FEATURES = ""
kareladb check old-db
"exit code: $LASTEXITCODE"
```

```text
error: this database needs a newer KarelaDB: it uses views (a stored-format feature this KarelaDB build does not know). Nothing was changed
This database was written by a newer KarelaDB. Open it with that KarelaDB or a newer one (kareladb version lists what this build can read). Do not run kareladb repair.
exit code: 3
error: this database needs a newer KarelaDB: it uses views (a stored-format feature this KarelaDB build does not know). Nothing was changed
This database was written by a newer KarelaDB. Open it with that KarelaDB or a newer one (kareladb version lists what this build can read). Do not run kareladb repair.
exit code: 3
checked 9 files (12.3 KB) and 2 log segments
OK: no damage found
exit code: 0
```

What to do when you see this message:

1. Do **not** repair or restore: the data is fine. `kareladb repair` would refuse too (exit code `3`).
2. Find the newer `kareladb` program that wrote the database, or build the newest one.
3. `kareladb version` on both programs shows which features each one reads.

Where you see it:

| Where | What you get |
|---|---|
| `kareladb check`, `kareladb repair`, `kareladb sql`, `kareladb shell`, `kareladb version <db>`, `kareladb upgrade` | the message and exit code `3` |
| `kareladb serve` | the database does not open; requests to it get HTTP status `500` with the message |
| PostgreSQL port | SQLSTATE `0A000` with the message |
| `kareladb restore` of a backup made by a newer KarelaDB | the message; nothing is copied |

In a nightly script:

```powershell
# In a script (not run here)
kareladb check D:\kdb\data\market | Out-Null
switch ($LASTEXITCODE) {
  0 { "check: OK" }
  2 { "check: DAMAGE FOUND - run kareladb repair" }
  3 { "check: this database needs a newer KarelaDB - update this kareladb, do not repair" }
  default { "check: could not run (exit code $LASTEXITCODE)" }
}
```

## Part E: updating KarelaDB on a server

1. Make a backup of every database (`BACKUP DATABASE`, or the scheduled backup of chapter 21), or run `kareladb upgrade` on each database while the server is stopped.
2. Stop the server. Replace **every** `kareladb` program on the machine (server, scheduled scripts) with the new build.
3. Start the server. Old databases open as they are; each gets its feature list at its next checkpoint.
4. `kareladb version <db>` or `SHOW VERSION` shows the lists.

Going back to an older KarelaDB:

- A database whose list has only features the older KarelaDB knows opens there.
- A database that uses a newer feature does not. Restore the backup from before the update with the **older** `kareladb restore` (changes made after that backup are then not in it).
- KarelaDB programs built **before 2026-09-12** do not read the feature list at all. They refuse most new data anyway, but not all of it. Never start such an old program on data of a newer KarelaDB.

## What you learned

- Every database has a feature list; KarelaDB records a feature before it writes data that needs it.
- A new KarelaDB opens old data; an old KarelaDB refuses new data with `needs a newer KarelaDB` and exit code `3`, never "damaged".
- `kareladb version`, `kareladb version <db>` and `SHOW VERSION` show the features; `kareladb upgrade` makes a backup, saves the list and checks the database.

More: the help topic **Versions and upgrades**, [known limitations](known-limitations.md#versions-and-upgrades-chapter-24), and `reports/versioning.md`.
