# Known limitations

- Category: Tutorial

This page lists what is missing, or works differently from QuestDB and PostgreSQL, in KarelaDB `0.2.0-dev` (checked against the program on 2026-10-24). Please check again after you update KarelaDB.

## Problems found while writing this tutorial (all fixed)

Writing and running this tutorial found 12 bugs. All of them are fixed, and each one has a test now.

| # | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `count()` without `*` crashed KarelaDB (and the whole server over HTTP). | `count()` is the same as `count(*)`. |
| 2 | `WITH OFFSET '00:15'` (no sign) failed when the query ran. | Works; it means `'+00:15'`. |
| 3 | `time IN '2026-09+05:45'` (a month or year with an offset) selected the wrong range. | Selects exactly that month or year in that time zone. |
| 4 | `ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT value`: rows already in the table got NULL. | They get the default value. |
| 5 | `kareladb check` right after a restore reported missing `(previous)` files. | A restored database checks clean. |
| 6 | After `kareladb repair --accept-log-loss`, `kareladb check` kept reporting the cut log forever. | The cut is reported once, by the repair. Later checks are clean. |
| 7 | On Windows, non-English text in command-line arguments became `?`. | Text in any language (for example Nepali) works in `kareladb sql market "..."`. |
| 8 | A DECIMAL written as a number with 15+ digits was refused with a wrong message. | Stored exactly up to about 15 digits; above that the message says to write it as text. |
| 9 | `PRIMARY KEY` on a time-series table was checked only inside one partition. | Refused when the table is created; use `DEDUP KEY (..., time)`. |
| 10 | Messages named port 9900 and "phase 3". | Messages point to the running server's console or HTTP API. |
| 11 | `kareladb info` looked like a full damage check. | `kareladb info` says it shows the recorded status and to run `kareladb check`. |
| 12 | `kareladb shell` ignored `.help` and other dot commands on the first line piped from PowerShell. | The byte order mark PowerShell adds is skipped. |

## Not available yet

### Connecting

- **PostgreSQL protocol** (port 8832, chapter 14) works for SQL and `COPY` (pgx `CopyFrom`, psql `\copy`), with TLS when `kareladb serve --tls-cert` is set (`sslmode=require`), but: only the common parts of the Postgres catalog (psql's `\l`, `\dt`, `\di` and `\d <table>` work; pgAdmin's own catalog queries do not, and ORMs that read the schema may not), no two-factor users. Most PostgreSQL SQL works (chapter 22); KarelaDB's own SQL adds time-series forms. A `TIMESTAMPTZ` column goes out as `timestamptz`, a plain `TIMESTAMP` as `timestamp` (start with `--pg-timestamptz` to send those as `timestamptz` too).
- **ILP** (InfluxDB line protocol) works over HTTP only (`POST /write`, like QuestDB's HTTP ILP). The separate TCP ILP port (QuestDB 9009) is not available.
- **`/imp` CSV upload**: works like QuestDB's (chapter 8). The `schema` part may only give column types (no date patterns).
- **One PostgreSQL port per machine.** Every `kareladb serve` opens port 8832 as well as its HTTP port. A second `kareladb serve` on the same machine stops with `port 8832 on 127.0.0.1 is already in use`; start it with `--pg-port 0` (off) or another port.
- **HTTPS**: `kareladb serve --tls-cert` (docs/help/topics/tls.md), or a reverse proxy. Certificates are read at start: restart after renewing one.
- **Users and roles** (chapter 16): rights per database (read, write, admin), per table (`GRANT SELECT ON TABLE`), per column (`GRANT SELECT (id, name) ON TABLE ...`) and per row (`CREATE POLICY`, row-level security): see the help topic `table-rights`. `CALL` and triggers ignore table rights. `kareladb shell` and `kareladb sql` do not check users.
- **CORS**: web pages on other sites cannot call KarelaDB. Call it from your backend.
- `kareladb.conf` holds the main server settings (data folder, log archive, result cache, file versions, trash, slow-query log, HTTP threads, PostgreSQL connections, the web, help and skill folders: help topic `cli-serve`). The rest are command-line options of `kareladb serve`.
- No Windows service mode (the Linux package has a systemd unit, `kdb.service`). Stop the server with Ctrl+C; killing it is safe but is an unclean shutdown.
- **Replies are not compressed.** Request bodies may be sent with `Content-Encoding: gzip` or `deflate`.
- `/exec` answers **10,000 rows** unless the request passes `limit`; a cut answer says `"truncated": true`.
- The HTTP server has one worker thread per CPU thread (at least 8, at most 64; `--http-threads N`). More slow statements than that at once make other requests wait for a free worker.
- **Other databases can be read, not written**: `SELECT ... FROM otherdb.t` works, `INSERT INTO otherdb.t` is refused. A transaction does not span databases.

### SQL statements

- `CREATE`, `DROP`, `ALTER` inside a transaction or a procedure.
- Row-level triggers (`FOR EACH ROW`), except a PostgreSQL `BEFORE UPDATE` trigger (chapter 22); `INSTEAD OF` triggers; triggers on views. KarelaDB triggers run once per statement and read all rows from `NEW` / `OLD`. Only `AFTER INSERT` triggers can be `DEFERRED`, and the queue of deferred jobs has no length limit yet.
- Exception handlers in procedures (`EXCEPTION WHEN ...`), `SAVEPOINT`, nested `BEGIN ... END` blocks, `LOOP`, `CASE` as a statement. An error always ends the `CALL` and undoes it.
- Functions that return tables, functions with statements (a saved function is one expression), aggregates written as saved functions.
- `OUT` parameters of procedures (use `SELECT` or `PRINT` to give results back).
- Changing `PARTITION BY` or `SORT BY` of an existing table. (A column's type can change with `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE`, chapter 22, but not the type of the time column or of a `SORT BY` / `DEDUP KEY` column. The dedup key itself changes with `ALTER TABLE ... DEDUP ENABLE UPSERT KEYS (...)`.)
- `NATURAL JOIN` (write `JOIN ... USING (columns)`). QuestDB's `ASOF JOIN ... TOLERANCE`.
- A recursive `WITH` query stops with an error after 100,000 rounds or 10 million rows. `WITH` queries that change data run before the main query, which sees their changes (chapter 23).
- Advisory locks wait at most 30 seconds (PostgreSQL waits forever); `SET statement_timeout` ends the wait sooner.
- Arrays are sent in binary form with one dimension only; nested arrays go as text.
- A series function inside another (`lag(sma(x, 3))`). Use a subquery. (A window function over `GROUP BY`, `SAMPLE BY` or aggregates works: `lag(sum(v)) OVER (ORDER BY time)`.)
- `DROP PARTITION LIST`, `LATEST BY`, `'2026-09-10;1d'` intervals (QuestDB forms). `DROP PARTITION OLDER THAN 6 MONTHS` works.
- JSON path wildcards (`$.items[*]`), the `jsonb` operator `?`. (JSON arrays and objects as SQL rows work: `json_each`, `json_array_elements`, `json_object_keys`.)
- Regular expression back references (`\1` inside a pattern) and look-around (`(?=...)`). `\1` works in the replacement text of `regexp_replace`.

### Behaviour to know

- A `WHERE` on a view goes into the view's query only for the parts that are safe to move; the rest is applied after the view's query has run.
- **FILL** uses one rule for all columns (for example, `FILL(PREV)` also copies the volume).
- Zones with summer time (`Europe/London`) work in `SET TIME ZONE` and `AT TIME ZONE`. `ROUND ... TIME ZONE`, `time IN ... TIME ZONE` and the zone argument of `date_trunc` / `to_char` take fixed offsets only (Nepal, +05:45, is fine).
- `hour()`, `day()`, `date_trunc()`, `is_trading_day()` and `::date` follow the session's clock (`SET TIME ZONE`, or the server's `--timezone`); without one they work in **UTC**.
- `is_trading_day()` does not know market holidays.
- `upper()`, `lower()` and `ILIKE` work for every letter that has a case (`'École' ILIKE 'é%'`); the regular expression flag `'i'` still folds English letters only. `length()` counts characters; `octet_length()` counts bytes.
- A STRING, JSON or BYTES value can be at most 16 MB. Keep PDF files and images outside the database; store their path or URL and a hash (chapter 18).
- JSON keeps the order of keys and the spelling of numbers (`1.0` stays `1.0`). Two JSON values are equal only when their text is equal (after spaces are removed), so `{"a":1,"b":2}` is not equal to `{"b":2,"a":1}`.
- Times and intervals are stored in **milliseconds**. Microseconds (PostgreSQL, QuestDB) are cut.
- Plain statements that change the same table run one after the other (reads run together, and writers of different tables run at the same time). Inside `BEGIN` ... `COMMIT`, an `UPDATE` or `DELETE` of rows by their primary key locks only those rows (below).
- Only **one program** can open a database. `kareladb backup` and `kareladb check` need the database closed, or the server's API.
- `kareladb sql` table format cuts text after 48 characters; use `--format csv`. With several SELECTs, CSV output has several header lines one after another.
- **Transactions** (`BEGIN` ... `COMMIT`, `CALL`, a statement with triggers) keep the old version of every changed row in memory until they end: at most 10 million changed rows. A statement that fails rolls back the whole transaction.
- **Row-level locks** (help topic `transactions`): inside `BEGIN`, an `UPDATE` or `DELETE` of rows of a table with a primary key locks those rows, and other transactions change other rows of the table meanwhile. An `INSERT`, a change of a table without a primary key, or of a table with a secondary `UNIQUE` or a `FOREIGN KEY`, still holds the whole table until `COMMIT`: other writers of it wait (the lock timeout, 5 s unless `SET lock_timeout`) and then get `table 'x' is busy`. Reads never wait for row locks. Keep transactions short.
- A transaction with no statement for 30 seconds (`idle_transaction_timeout_ms`) is rolled back. After an error or this timeout, the session must send `ROLLBACK` before anything else.
- While another session's transaction is open, a read takes that transaction's changes out of memory for a moment, and its next statement puts them back. For a transaction with very many changed rows (millions), this makes its statements slower when many reads come in between.
- `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on one table with a primary key locks the rows it returns; `SKIP LOCKED` skips rows others locked, so job-queue workers take different jobs at once. With a join, `GROUP BY` or a view it locks the tables. `FOR SHARE` and `FOR UPDATE OF t` work exactly as `FOR UPDATE`. Two transactions waiting for each other's rows get `40P01` at once.
- Isolation: `SERIALIZABLE` (the default) and `READ COMMITTED`; `REPEATABLE READ` runs as `SERIALIZABLE`. `SAVEPOINT`, `SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL` and `READ ONLY` transactions work. A transaction that read a row another one was changing, and then changes it, gets `40001` (run it again), so no update is lost. `CREATE`, `DROP` and `ALTER` are refused inside a transaction.
- `CHECK` constraints look at **one row**: no subqueries, aggregates, window functions, saved functions or computed columns in them. A `CHECK` cannot compare with other rows (for example "the sum of all balances"). A `NULL` value passes a `CHECK`; use `NOT NULL` too.
- `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CHECK` reads every row of the table once (slow for very big time-series tables).
- `AUTO` ids only go up, like a PostgreSQL sequence: the id of a deleted row, or of an insert that was rolled back, is **never used again**, so there can be gaps (1, 2, 4, ...). Do not use AUTO ids as a count of rows.
- `DECIMAL` / `NUMERIC(p,s)` arithmetic is exact (fixed point, up to 38 digits; `sum` adds exactly). A result that does not fit is refused with an error, never stored wrong. `NUMERIC` without precision is a `DOUBLE` unless `kdb.pg_compat` is on: give money columns a precision.
- `RETURNING` gives the rows as they are written (for `DELETE`: as they were). With `INSERT OR IGNORE`, skipped rows are not returned.
- In a procedure, a **column name wins over a variable** with the same name. Name variables so they are not column names.
- KarelaDB checks procedure and trigger bodies for syntax when they are created; unknown tables, columns and procedures are found only when they run. `DROP FUNCTION`, `DROP PROCEDURE` and `DROP VIEW` do not check who uses them.
- A table with triggers cannot be dropped or renamed; drop its triggers first.
- A table with an `INSERT` trigger that is not `DEFERRED` is loaded row by row (`InsertRows`, line protocol), with the trigger inside the write. Other tables of the database, and a table whose triggers are all `DEFERRED`, keep the fast way.
- A cursor keeps all its rows in memory (at most 10 million) until it is closed or unused for 10 minutes. At most 16 open cursors per database.
- A `WHILE` loop stops with an error after 10 million rounds.
- **Indexes live in memory** (chapter 17) and are built from the rows after every open: about 0.2 seconds per million rows for a plain index, about 1 second per 200 MB of text for a FULLTEXT index. `kareladb serve` builds them on a background thread right after the open (`--warm-indexes`, on by default); a query that comes first builds the index itself, and `kareladb sql` always builds on first use. A FULLTEXT index of a table with one partition makes writers of that table wait while it is built. A plain or FULLTEXT index bigger than `index_memory_bytes` (default 2 GB) is not built and queries read the table instead; `SHOW INDEXES` shows `built = false` then.
- Expression and partial indexes are built and used, but only in these shapes: an expression key part needs `expr = constant` with exactly the index's expression (no ranges, no `IN (...)`, no `ORDER BY` on it), and a partial index is used only when every part of its `WHERE` is also a condition of the query. `INCLUDE` columns are ignored.
- A join reads a joined table through its index when the join key has one (`EXPLAIN` shows `index lookup`). A query does not use an index for `OR`, `!=`, `NOT LIKE`, FLOAT columns, or text compared with a number. A function around the column (`lower(email) = ...`) needs an expression index on exactly that expression. When an index would read more than a quarter of the table, KarelaDB reads the table instead. Use `EXPLAIN` to see what happens.
- Tables with an index are slower to write in big line-protocol batches: every row looks up the row it replaces. A table with a `UNIQUE` index cannot use the fast column-wise path for `InsertRows` at all.
- **Full-text search** finds whole words. There is no stemming: `bank` does not find `banks`, and `बैंक` does not find `बैंकले`. Use a prefix (`bank*`, `बैंक*`). There are no stop words, no `OR` inside the search text, no fuzzy search, and no synonyms.
- `search_rank` on a table without a FULLTEXT index on the same columns reads the whole table once per query. (A phrase such as `'"city bank"'` is answered from the index since 2026-09-23: it keeps every word's positions.)
- The **statement timeout** of `kareladb serve` (chapter 21) is checked between rows (every 1,024 rows on the row path, once per batch in the column engine). One long step without rows in between (a huge sort, or one 16 MB value in a slow regular expression) finishes that step first. `kareladb sql`, `kareladb shell` and library apps have no timeout or memory limits.
- **A full disk**: a write gets HTTP 507 (`{"code":"disk full"}`) or SQLSTATE `53100`, and committed rows stay. With the default `--sync-commits always`, a full disk during the log flush **stops the whole database, reads too**, until it is reopened. An `INSERT` can get 507 although its rows were committed (the checkpoint after it failed): count before you send again.
- `DROP TABLE` of a table with named `UNIQUE`/`PRIMARY KEY` constraints skips the trash (no `UNDROP TABLE` for it). `UNDROP TABLE` does not bring back table rights.
- The web console's **Run** (Ctrl+Enter) finds a whole `CREATE PROCEDURE ... END` under the cursor, but a column or alias named `begin` right after `AS` confuses it; use **Run all** then.

### PostgreSQL schema (chapter 22)

- plpgsql runs only as a row trigger: `CREATE FUNCTION f() RETURNS trigger ... LANGUAGE plpgsql` used by a `BEFORE UPDATE ... FOR EACH ROW` trigger. `INSERT` and `AFTER` row triggers are refused. Any other plpgsql function is recorded with a warning and **never runs**. Write KarelaDB triggers and procedures (chapter 13).
- `DO $$ ... $$` blocks may use only `IF`, `RAISE`, `NULL` and SQL statements (no `DECLARE`, loops, `PERFORM`, `EXECUTE`, `EXCEPTION`). A DO block is **not one transaction**: statements before an error stay.
- `SERIAL` / `IDENTITY` only for the single-column `PRIMARY KEY`. Use a sequence for other columns.
- `NUMERIC` without precision is a `DOUBLE` (exact with `kdb.pg_compat = on`). `NUMERIC(p,s)`: up to 38 digits (more than 18 use 128 bits). `FLOAT` alone is 4 bytes. `CHAR(n)` is not padded. `CITEXT` is not case-insensitive. `INTERVAL` is milliseconds (a month is 30 days). `INET`, `CIDR`, `MACADDR`, `XML` are not checked.
- The `PRIMARY KEY` cannot be dropped. `DROP TABLE` is refused while a foreign key, view or materialized view uses the table; `DROP TABLE ... CASCADE` drops them too, as in PostgreSQL. `DEFERRABLE` constraints, `INHERITS`, `PARTITION BY RANGE`, `EXCLUDE` constraints and schemas other than `public` are not supported. Table constraints must come after the columns.
- In one `INSERT` of many rows, a row may refer (REFERENCES) only to rows before it, not to rows after it.
- A foreign key action reads the whole child table for each changed parent row when the child column has no key or index. Add an index on foreign key columns of big tables.
- `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE` and `ADD PRIMARY KEY` write every row again (slow for very big tables).
- The catalog views have the common columns only.
- Older KarelaDB programs refuse databases that use these features (`needs a newer KarelaDB`, or `needs a newer KDB` from a build before the name) or cannot replay their log (sequences). Update every `kareladb` program first.

### Analysis functions (chapter 19)

- The new aggregates (`corr`, `percentile_cont`, `mode`, `sharpe_ratio`, ...), window frames with `BETWEEN`, indicators and table functions run only in the **row engine**. A query that uses one of them never uses the fast column engine, so it is slower on very big tables.
- Aggregates that keep every value (`percentile_cont`, `percentile_disc`, `mode`, `mad`, `iqr`, `value_at_risk`, `expected_shortfall`, `string_agg`, `array_agg`) sort again for every row in a running `OVER (... ORDER BY ...)` window: slow for partitions of many thousand rows. Use `ROWS n PRECEDING`. `ROWS BETWEEN a PRECEDING AND b FOLLOWING` frames also add up every frame again.
- Window frames: no `GROUPS` frames, no `EXCLUDE`, no `RANGE` distances in months or years (use days), no named windows (`WINDOW w AS (...)`), no `IGNORE NULLS`.
- `WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY x DESC)` is not supported (use `1 - fraction`). `approx_count_distinct` counts exactly (there is no approximate method).
- A series function still cannot be inside another one (`macd(sma(close, 3))`), and an aggregate cannot hold a window function (`sum(lag(close))` gives "queries are nested too deeply"). A window over aggregates works (`sum(sum(qty)) OVER (ORDER BY time)` with GROUP BY or SAMPLE BY). Use one subquery per step for the rest, as in the chapter's cookbook.
- **Running indicators** (EMA-based ones, MACD, KAMA, ADX, SAR, OBV, MFI, SuperTrend, Heikin-Ashi) stop at the first NULL input: every later row of that partition is NULL. Filter NULL rows first.
- The older `rsi(x, n)` keeps its KarelaDB definition: a completely flat start gives 50 (TA-Lib gives 0), and a NULL price counts as no change. Otherwise it gives TA-Lib's values (tested within 1e-9). `stochrsi_k` uses TA-Lib's RSI.
- `macd` starts on row 34 (as TA-Lib); TradingView shows the MACD line from row 26. `supertrend_direction` gives 1 for an up trend, the opposite sign of TradingView's `direction`. `ichimoku_senkou_a/b` put the value computed `shift` rows before on each row (a table has no rows in the future); `ichimoku_chikou` reads rows in the future.
- `fiscal_year`, `fiscal_quarter` and `nepal_fiscal_year` use a fixed start day (July 17). They do not know the Bikram Sambat calendar: in a year where Shrawan 1 is July 16, that day is counted in the old fiscal year. There are no BS date conversions.
- `random()` and `setseed()` share one random generator for the whole server; with several query threads the numbers of a query can come in a different order.
- `generate_series` needs constant arguments (it cannot read columns of other tables) and makes at most 10 million rows. `PIVOT` needs the IN values written in the query (no dynamic pivot), and every column of the source that PIVOT does not use becomes a group key.

### Users, passwords and security

- Logins are kept across a server restart (only their hashes are stored, in `_system.login_sessions`).
- **HTTPS** inside KarelaDB needs `--tls-cert` (docs/help/topics/tls.md); otherwise use a reverse proxy (Caddy, nginx) or an SSH tunnel. Over plain HTTP, passwords and tokens can be read on the network.
- The failed-login limit counts per address. Behind a reverse proxy every client has the address `127.0.0.1`, so wrong passwords from one person also slow down others who log in as the **same** user.
- The **SCRAM-SHA-256** secret of a database user uses 4,096 rounds (like PostgreSQL); the password hash uses 600,000. Use long random passwords for database users.
- **Old KarelaDB versions do not know users.** A `kareladb` built before users existed would open a data folder with users and serve it **without** a login. Always update every `kareladb` program first, and never start an old one on that folder.
- `password_hash` in `UPDATE ... SET password_hash = password_hash('x')` gives every changed row the same hash (one salt). Change passwords one row at a time.
- `ADD COLUMN id STRING DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()` gives all **old** rows one and the same value; new rows get their own. Do not use random functions in computed columns (`AS (...)`): the value changes each time the row is read.
- The HTTP cursors (`/cursor/<id>`) are not tied to a user: another user with `read` on the same database who knows the id can read the rows. The id is long and random; do not share it.
- **The audit log** (chapter 21) writes security events every 200 ms: a crash can lose the events of that last moment (data-change audit rows are in the same transaction and are never lost). Its rows are hash-chained: `kareladb check` finds a changed or removed row. A server on one folder path (`kareladb serve D:\kdb\market`) has no security audit log.
- **Two-factor login** works only for HTTP logins (console, `POST /api/login`). HTTP Basic and the PostgreSQL port refuse users with two-factor login.
- Files can be encrypted at rest (help topic `encryption`); without it, protect the data folder with file permissions.
- Older KarelaDB programs refuse databases with audited tables and data folders with table rights or two-factor users (they would ignore them). Update every `kareladb` program first.
- User names and passwords go through `kareladb user add` from stdin or a prompt, never the command line. The console history masks `PASSWORD '...'`, but your own scripts and logs may still contain passwords you typed into SQL.

### Versions and upgrades (chapter 24)

- **KarelaDB programs built before 2026-09-12 do not read the feature list.** They still refuse most new data (new catalog parts, file formats), but not everything: for example they ignore sequences, table rights or the trash. Never open new data with an old program. Update every `kareladb` program first.
- **There is no downgrade.** Once a feature is in a database's list, an older KarelaDB that does not know it refuses the database, even after you drop the table that used it. Keep the backup that `kareladb upgrade` makes if you may need the older KarelaDB again.
- The list says *which* features a database uses, not *how much*. A database that used `JSON` once is refused by an older KarelaDB without JSON, for as long as it exists.
- `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` with a `JSON` or `BYTES` result column records that feature at the checkpoint right after the statement, not before it. A crash exactly between the two leaves the feature out of the list until the next checkpoint (the database itself is fine).
- `kareladb check` reads the catalog, file format numbers and log record types, but not every value inside every row of the log: a row value of an unknown type is found when the database opens (the same "needs a newer KarelaDB" message).
- `kareladb upgrade` rewrites no files in this version: nothing needs it.

## Parts of this tutorial that were not run

Everything else in the tutorial was run and the output was copied from the run (see `examples/verify.ps1`). These parts were **not** run:

| Part | Why |
|---|---|
| Build commands for Linux and macOS (chapter 1) | The tutorial was written on Windows. |
| C# client (chapter 8) | No .NET SDK on the test PC. |
| `Register-ScheduledTask` and `cron` lines (chapter 7) | They would change the test PC. The backup script itself was run. |
| QuestDB `/exp` export commands (chapter 10) | No QuestDB on the test PC. The sample CSV files were written by hand in QuestDB style. |
| `kareladb serve` banner with port 9900 (quick start, chapter 6) | Port 9900 was in use on the test PC; the banner was taken from a server on a test port, with only the port number changed. |
| Screen description of the web console (chapter 6) | Checked by using the console in a browser against a test server; screenshots are not included. |

# Databases and the data folder

> Where KarelaDB keeps databases, how to name them, and CREATE DATABASE, DROP DATABASE, SHOW DATABASES and USE.

- Category: Databases & folders
- Keywords: database, data folder, PURGE TRASH, PURGE TRASH ALL, data directory, --data-dir, KARELADB\_DATA\_DIR, default database, \_trash, trash, database name, folder path, CREATE DATABASE, IF NOT EXISTS, DROP DATABASE, IF EXISTS, SHOW DATABASES, USE, switch database, many databases, kdb.lock, wal\_archive, WAL\_ARCHIVE, old log, log archive, KARELADB\_WAL\_ARCHIVE\_MB, RESULT\_CACHE, result cache per database, MEMORY\_LIMIT, MEMORY\_RESERVED, memory per database, database\_memory, per-column loads, partial\_loads, BRANCH OF, branch, clone database
- See also: [Quick start](quick-start.md), [CREATE TABLE](create-table.md), [SHOW TABLES, COLUMNS, CREATE TABLE](show-tables.md), [Users and roles](users-and-roles.md), [Backup, check, repair and restore](backup-and-safety.md), [kareladb serve](cli-serve.md), [Queries across databases](cross-database-queries.md), [Time travel and branches: SELECT ... AS OF, CREATE DATABASE ... BRANCH OF](as-of-and-branches.md)

A **database** is one folder with its own tables, views, triggers and procedures. KarelaDB keeps many databases in one **data folder**: one sub-folder per database. `kareladb serve` without a database name serves all of them.

A real setup: one database for market prices, one for the accounting app, one for the forum.

**Example: Three databases for three apps**

```sql
CREATE DATABASE market;
CREATE DATABASE accounts;
CREATE DATABASE forum;
SHOW DATABASES;
```

Result:

`CREATE DATABASE market`

```text
database 'market' created
```

`CREATE DATABASE accounts`

```text
database 'accounts' created
```

`CREATE DATABASE forum`

```text
database 'forum' created
```

`SHOW DATABASES`

| name (STRING) | tables (LONG) | bytes (LONG) | current (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|---|
| accounts | 0 | 0 | false |
| demo | 0 | 0 | true |
| forum | 0 | 0 | false |
| market | 0 | 0 | false |

(4 rows)

<a id="data-folder"></a>

## The data folder

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb <command> --data-dir <folder> ...
KARELADB_DATA_DIR=<folder>
<folder of kareladb.exe>\data
```

KarelaDB looks for the data folder in this order. The first one that is set wins:

| # | Where | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | the option `--data-dir <folder>` | `kareladb serve --data-dir E:\kdb-data` |
| 2 | the environment variable `KARELADB_DATA_DIR` | `$env:KARELADB_DATA_DIR = "E:\kdb-data"` |
| 3 | the folder `data` next to the `kareladb` program | `D:\KarelaDB\build\bin\data` |

KarelaDB creates the folder when it is missing.

```text
E:\kdb-data\              <- the data folder
E:\kdb-data\default\      <- the database "default" (kareladb shell without a name uses it)
E:\kdb-data\market\        <- the database "market"
E:\kdb-data\_trash\       <- dropped databases (kept until PURGE TRASH ALL)
```

- **Notes:** use `KARELADB_DATA_DIR` when the data must be on another disk, or when `kareladb.exe` is in a folder where you cannot write (like `C:\Program Files`). To set it for good on Windows: `[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("KARELADB_DATA_DIR", "E:\kdb-data", "User")`, then open a new PowerShell window.
- **Notes:** never change files inside a database folder by hand. Only one program can open a database at a time (the file `kdb.lock` shows this).

**Command line: A shell on a data folder: make a database and list them**

```bash
kareladb shell --data-dir my-data
> CREATE DATABASE market;
> SHOW DATABASES;
```

Output:

```text
KarelaDB 0.2.0-dev shell on default (data folder my-data)
End statements with ';'. Type .help for commands, .exit to quit.
kareladb> database 'market' created
kareladb> name    | tables | bytes | current
--------+--------+-------+--------
default |      0 |     0 | true   
market  |      0 |     0 | false  
(2 rows, 0.1 ms)
kareladb>
```

<a id="names"></a>

## Database names and folder paths

Syntax:

```sql
name        letters, digits, _ and -   (1 to 64 characters)
.\folder    a path: always that folder
```

A database name has only letters `a-z A-Z`, digits, `_` and `-`, and is 1 to 64 characters long. Upper and lower case do not matter: `Market` and `market` are the same database. The folder keeps the spelling you used first.

| Not allowed | Why |
|---|---|
| `my shop`, `my.shop`, `नेपाल` | only letters a-z, digits, `_` and `-` |
| `_trash` | the folder for dropped databases |
| `_system` | the folder where KarelaDB keeps its users |
| `CON`, `PRN`, `AUX`, `NUL`, `COM0`-`COM9`, `LPT0`-`LPT9` | device names on Windows |

Commands like `kareladb sql` and `kareladb shell` take a **name** or a **path**:

| You write | KarelaDB uses |
|---|---|
| a name, and the data folder has that database | that database |
| a name, and the data folder does not have it | the folder with that name in the **current** folder (made when missing) |
| a path with `\`, `/`, `:` or `.` (`.\market`, `D:\kdb\market`) | always that folder |

- **Notes:** a command that opened a database by its **path** cannot create or drop databases. SQL names in quotes do not help: `CREATE DATABASE "my shop"` is still refused.

**Example: A name with a dot** (shows an error)

```sql
CREATE DATABASE my.shop;
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 19: unexpected '.' after CREATE DATABASE`

**Example: A reserved folder name** (shows an error)

```sql
CREATE DATABASE _trash;
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 17: bad database name '_trash': '_trash' is where dropped databases are kept`

**Command line: A name that is not in the data folder means a folder here**

```bash
kareladb sql shop "CREATE TABLE products (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING)"
kareladb sql .\shop "SHOW TABLES"
```

Output:

`> kareladb sql shop "CREATE TABLE products (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING)"`

```text
table 'products' created
```

`> kareladb sql .\shop "SHOW TABLES"`

```text
name     | kind       | partition | columns | rows
---------+------------+-----------+---------+-----
products | relational | NONE      |       2 |    0
(1 row, 0.0 ms)
```

<a id="create-database"></a>

## CREATE DATABASE

Syntax:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE [IF NOT EXISTS] name [WITH (pg_compat = on | off, encryption = on | off)]
```

Makes a new, empty database folder in the data folder. With `IF NOT EXISTS`, a database that is already there is not an error.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | database name | see [names](#names) |
| `pg_compat` | on / off | PostgreSQL 14's answers in this database ([PostgreSQL protocol](postgres-protocol.md)) |
| `encryption` | on / off | every file of the database is encrypted; needs the server's master key ([encryption at rest](encryption.md)). Default `off` |

- **Returns:** the message `database 'name' created` (`... created encrypted` with `encryption = on`), or `database 'name' already exists` with `IF NOT EXISTS`.
- **Notes:** `IF NOT EXISTS` never changes a database that is there: a plain one stays plain. Encryption is chosen only here; `ALTER DATABASE` cannot switch it.
- **Notes:** needs a data folder: it works in `kareladb shell`, in `kareladb sql` with a database name, and in `kareladb serve` started without a folder path. With users, only a user with `ROLE admin` may run it ([users and roles](users-and-roles.md)).
- **Notes:** an empty folder with that name becomes the database. A folder with other files in it is refused.
- **Notes:** `CREATE DATABASE test BRANCH OF live [AS OF ...]` makes a full, writable copy of another database in a moment, sharing its files ([branches](as-of-and-branches.md#branch)).

**Example: Safe to run again with IF NOT EXISTS**

```sql
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS accounts;
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS accounts;
SHOW DATABASES;
```

Result:

`CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS accounts`

```text
database 'accounts' created
```

`CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS accounts`

```text
database 'accounts' already exists
```

`SHOW DATABASES`

| name (STRING) | tables (LONG) | bytes (LONG) | current (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|---|
| accounts | 0 | 0 | false |
| demo | 0 | 0 | true |

(2 rows)

**Example: Upper and lower case are the same database** (shows an error)

```sql
CREATE DATABASE Forum;
CREATE DATABASE forum;
```

Result:

```text
database 'Forum' created
```

Error: `database 'Forum' already exists`

<a id="drop-database"></a>

## DROP DATABASE

Syntax:

```sql
DROP DATABASE [IF EXISTS] name
```

Closes the database and **moves** its folder to `<data folder>/_trash/<time in ms>-<name>`. KarelaDB never deletes the files. With `IF EXISTS`, a database that is not there is not an error.

- **Returns:** `database 'name' dropped; its folder was moved to ...`.
- **Notes:** refused while another request or shell uses the database, or while another program has it open. To get it back: stop the server and move the folder back from `_trash`. When you are sure you do not need it, [PURGE TRASH ALL](#purge-trash) frees the space.
- **Notes:** dropping the database you are using leaves you with **no** database: the next statement needs `USE` first.
- **Notes:** with users, the grants on that database are removed too, so a new database with the same name does not give old rights back.
- **Notes:** the database's [timers](timers.md) are deleted too, so they never run in a new database of the same name.

**Example: Drop an old test database; the second DROP is not an error**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE test_2025;
```

```sql
DROP DATABASE test_2025;
DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS test_2025;
SHOW DATABASES;
```

Result:

`DROP DATABASE test_2025`

```text
database 'test_2025' dropped; its folder was moved to kdb-data/_trash/1792822732452-test_2025
```

`DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS test_2025`

```text
database 'test_2025' does not exist
```

`SHOW DATABASES`

| name (STRING) | tables (LONG) | bytes (LONG) | current (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|---|
| demo | 0 | 0 | true |

(1 row)

**Example: Drop the database you are using** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE notes (id INT);
```

```sql
DROP DATABASE demo;
SHOW TABLES;
```

Result:

```text
database 'demo' dropped; its folder was moved to kdb-data/_trash/1792822732463-demo; no database is selected now (USE <name>)
```

Error: `no database is selected; choose one with USE <name>`

**Example: A database that is not there** (shows an error)

```sql
DROP DATABASE nothing;
```

Result:

Error: `database 'nothing' does not exist`

<a id="purge-trash"></a>

## PURGE TRASH

Syntax:

```sql
PURGE TRASH
PURGE TRASH ALL
```

Frees disk space. KarelaDB never deletes data on its own at once: it moves it to a `_trash` folder first. `PURGE TRASH` removes, for good, what is in the `_trash` folder of the **current database**. `PURGE TRASH ALL` does it for every `_trash` folder of the data folder, dropped databases too:

| Folder | What is in it | Emptied by | Without a purge |
|---|---|---|---|
| `<database>/_trash` | old copies of files after `TRUNCATE`, `DROP PARTITION`, `UPDATE`, checkpoints | `PURGE TRASH` in that database, or `PURGE TRASH ALL` | removed by itself after `trash_keep_hours` (1 hour): while the server runs, and when the database opens |
| `<data folder>/_trash` | dropped databases | `PURGE TRASH ALL` only | kept forever |

- **Returns:** `removed N folder(s) from the trash, freed 27.0 GB`.
- **Notes:** `PURGE TRASH` needs `ROLE admin` on the database. `PURGE TRASH ALL` needs the user's own `ROLE admin` (it acts on the whole server). Before 2026-09-25 plain `PURGE TRASH` emptied the whole server's trash.
- **Notes:** with no database selected (after dropping the one you used), `PURGE TRASH` is an error that points to `PURGE TRASH ALL`.
- **Notes:** tables and rows in use are not touched. Dropped **tables** stay: `UNDROP TABLE` still brings them back ([the trash](trash.md)). `PURGE TRASH ALL` does not open databases that are not open. A folder that is still in use is skipped and named in the message.
- **Notes:** a dropped database cannot be moved back from `_trash` after `PURGE TRASH ALL`.
- **Notes:** removing many gigabytes takes a while: minutes for a large trash, longer when the data folder is a Docker folder share on Windows. Only one `PURGE TRASH ALL` runs at a time; a second one meanwhile is refused with `PURGE TRASH is already running`.
- **Notes:** in the console: the **Tools** panel on the right, **Purge trash**, runs `PURGE TRASH ALL`. The dialog shows how long the purge has been running; it can be closed, and the result appears in the panel. **Save disk** on the Keep data page runs `PURGE TRASH` for one database.
- **Notes:** a database's own `_trash` (replaced files) also empties **by itself** while the server runs: every minute the database removes every folder older than `trash_keep_hours` (1 hour unless `kareladb.conf` or `KARELADB_TRASH_KEEP_HOURS` says otherwise), also while writes never stop. Beyond `trash_max_mb` (a quarter of the database's data, at least 256 MB, unless set; 0 = no limit) the oldest folders also go, whatever their age, until the trash fits. `PURGE TRASH` is for having the space back now.

**Example: Free this database's trash now**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ticks (time TIMESTAMP, price DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY;
INSERT INTO ticks VALUES ('2026-09-24T10:00:00Z', 1.5);
```

```sql
TRUNCATE TABLE ticks;
PURGE TRASH;
```

Result:

`TRUNCATE TABLE ticks`

```text
1 table(s) truncated (1 row(s) removed)
```

`PURGE TRASH`

```text
removed 1 folder(s) from the trash, freed 388 bytes
```

**Example: Drop a test database, then free its space**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE old_test;
```

```sql
DROP DATABASE old_test;
PURGE TRASH ALL;
```

Result:

`DROP DATABASE old_test`

```text
database 'old_test' dropped; its folder was moved to kdb-data/_trash/1792822732563-old_test
```

`PURGE TRASH ALL`

```text
removed 1 folder(s) from the trash, freed 680 bytes
```

<a id="purge-versions"></a>

## PURGE VERSIONS

Syntax:

```sql
PURGE VERSIONS [KEEP n]
```

Frees disk space in the current database by removing the **older versions** of its data files. Every checkpoint writes a data file anew and keeps the older versions (2 per file unless `keep_versions` in `kareladb.conf` or `KARELADB_KEEP_VERSIONS` says otherwise), so that a file found damaged can be repaired from one of them plus the log. On a table that is rewritten often they add up to more than the data itself. `PURGE VERSIONS` keeps `n` older versions per file (1 without `KEEP`, 0 to 10), moves the rest to the trash, and empties that trash at once.

- **Returns:** `N older file version(s) removed (3.9 GB), 1 kept per file; freed 3.9 GB from the trash`.
- **Notes:** needs `ROLE admin` on the database. The rows are untouched and the database stays consistent: the list of files is saved before anything moves. With `KEEP 0` a damaged file can only be repaired from a backup, so keep 1 unless space is short.
- **Notes:** in the console: the **Keep data** page, **Save disk** (runs `PURGE VERSIONS KEEP 1` and `PURGE TRASH`).

**Example: Keep one older copy of each file, free the rest**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ticks (time TIMESTAMP, price DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY;
INSERT INTO ticks VALUES ('2026-09-10T10:00:00Z', 1.5);
```

```sql
PURGE VERSIONS KEEP 1;
```

Result:

```text
0 older file version(s) removed (0 bytes), 1 kept per file; freed 0 bytes from the trash
```

<a id="truncate-all-tables"></a>

## TRUNCATE ALL TABLES

Syntax:

```sql
TRUNCATE ALL TABLES
```

Empties every table of the current database in one `TRUNCATE ... CASCADE`, then removes what that took out of use from the database's `_trash` at once, so the space is free right away. Meant for test databases.

- **Returns:** `N table(s) truncated (M row(s) removed); freed 1.2 GB from the trash`.
- **Notes:** needs `ROLE admin` on the database. The tables, columns, indexes, views, triggers and procedures stay. Materialized views are emptied with their tables. Dropped tables and `_audit_log` keep their rows. No row triggers run, as with `TRUNCATE`.
- **Notes:** it cannot be undone: the old rows are not kept in the trash. Make a backup first if you may need them.
- **Notes:** on a big database it takes as long as `TRUNCATE` of every table, and other writers wait meanwhile. In the console: **Tools**, **Delete all data**.

**Example: Empty a test database but keep its tables**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE customers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING);
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT, customer INT REFERENCES customers(id), total DOUBLE);
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1, 'Asha'), (2, 'Bikash');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10, 1, 99.5), (11, 2, 12.0);
```

```sql
TRUNCATE ALL TABLES;
SELECT count(*) FROM orders;
```

Result:

`TRUNCATE ALL TABLES`

```text
2 table(s) truncated (4 row(s) removed); freed 962 bytes from the trash
```

`SELECT count(*) FROM orders`

| count(*) (LONG) |
|---|
| 0 |

(1 row)

<a id="show-databases"></a>

## SHOW DATABASES

Syntax:

```sql
SHOW DATABASES
```

Lists the databases of the data folder.

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | `STRING` | database name |
| `tables` | `LONG` | number of tables |
| `bytes` | `LONG` | size of the data files |
| `current` | `BOOL` | `true` for the database your statements use now |

- **Notes:** with users, a user who is not an admin sees only the databases they may read. The web console has a **Database** list with the same data.

**Example: The size of each database**

Setup:

```sql
USE demo;
CREATE TABLE brokers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO brokers VALUES (58, 'Northgate Securities'), (45, 'Imperial Securities');
CREATE DATABASE forum;
```

```sql
SHOW DATABASES;
```

Result:

| name (STRING) | tables (LONG) | bytes (LONG) | current (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|---|
| demo | 1 | 674 | true |
| forum | NULL | 0 | false |

(2 rows)

<a id="use"></a>

## USE

Syntax:

```sql
USE name
```

The statements after `USE` run in that database.

| Where | How long `USE` lasts |
|---|---|
| `kareladb shell` | until the next `USE` |
| `kareladb sql` | until the end of the text you sent |
| HTTP `/exec` | until the end of that request; choose the database of a request with `db=<name>` |

- **Returns:** `using database 'name'`.
- **Notes:** `USE` of a database that does not exist is an error; `USE` does not create it. PostgreSQL has no `USE` (you connect to the other database); MySQL has the same statement.
- **Notes:** `USE` does not end an open `BEGIN ... COMMIT`. The transaction stays open in the first database until you go back there and `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`.

**Example: Make a table in another database**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE forum;
```

```sql
USE forum;
CREATE TABLE posts (id LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO, author STRING NOT NULL, body STRING NOT NULL);
SHOW DATABASES;
USE demo;
SHOW TABLES;
```

Result:

`USE forum`

```text
using database 'forum'
```

`CREATE TABLE posts (`

```text
table 'posts' created
```

`SHOW DATABASES`

| name (STRING) | tables (LONG) | bytes (LONG) | current (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|---|
| demo | 0 | 0 | false |
| forum | 1 | 270 | true |

(2 rows)

`USE demo`

```text
using database 'demo'
```

`SHOW TABLES`

| name (STRING) | kind (STRING) | partition (STRING) | columns (INT) | rows (LONG) |
|---|---|---|---|---|

(0 rows)

**Example: USE does not create a database** (shows an error)

```sql
USE shop;
```

Result:

Error: `database 'shop' does not exist; create it with CREATE DATABASE shop`

<a id="dialect"></a>

## ALTER DATABASE ... SET DIALECT

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER DATABASE <name> SET DIALECT = 'questdb'
ALTER DATABASE <name> SET DIALECT = 'postgres'
```

Says which SQL family this database should behave like when the two differ. The default is `'postgres'`. `'postgresql'`, `'kdb'` and `'default'` mean `'postgres'` too.

| Value | What changes |
|---|---|
| `'postgres'` (default) | `CAST(time AS LONG)` gives **milliseconds**; a plain `INSERT` of a row that is already there (by `DEDUP KEY`) is an error |
| `'questdb'` | `CAST(time AS LONG)` gives **microseconds**, as QuestDB does; a plain `INSERT` into a table with a `DEDUP KEY` **replaces** the old row, as QuestDB does |

- **Returns:** `database 'x' now reads SQL as ...`.
- **Notes:**
  - Needs a server admin. The setting is kept in the data folder (`_system`) and holds after a restart, so an app does not have to send it again.
  - It is **per database**, so a QuestDB app and a PostgreSQL app can share one server.
  - Set it before you move a QuestDB app over, so its `INSERT`s and its time maths keep the meaning they had.
  - A database that has this setting needs a KarelaDB that knows the `dialects` feature; an older KarelaDB refuses to open it (see [versions](versions.md)).

**Example: A QuestDB app: INSERT replaces a row with the same key**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE questdb_app;
USE questdb_app;
CREATE TABLE live_ticks (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, ltp DOUBLE)
  TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY DEDUP KEY (time, symbol);
```

```sql
ALTER DATABASE questdb_app SET DIALECT = 'questdb';
USE questdb_app;
INSERT INTO live_ticks VALUES ('2026-09-10T11:00:00Z', 'CITY', 512.5);
INSERT INTO live_ticks VALUES ('2026-09-10T11:00:00Z', 'CITY', 514.0);
SELECT * FROM live_ticks;
```

Result:

`ALTER DATABASE questdb_app SET dialect = 'questdb'`

```text
database 'questdb_app' now reads SQL as QuestDB does (plain INSERT replaces rows of a DEDUP KEY; CAST(time AS LONG) is microseconds)
```

`USE questdb_app`

```text
using database 'questdb_app'
```

`INSERT INTO live_ticks VALUES ('2026-09-10T11:00:00Z', 'CITY', 512.5)`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`INSERT INTO live_ticks VALUES ('2026-09-10T11:00:00Z', 'CITY', 514.0)`

```text
0 row(s) inserted, 1 replaced
```

`SELECT * FROM live_ticks`

| time (TIMESTAMP) | symbol (SYMBOL) | ltp (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-10T11:00:00.000Z | CITY | 514 |

(1 row)

**Example: Back to the PostgreSQL way**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE questdb_app;
```

```sql
ALTER DATABASE questdb_app SET DIALECT = 'questdb';
ALTER DATABASE questdb_app SET DIALECT = 'postgres';
```

Result:

`ALTER DATABASE questdb_app SET dialect = 'questdb'`

```text
database 'questdb_app' now reads SQL as QuestDB does (plain INSERT replaces rows of a DEDUP KEY; CAST(time AS LONG) is microseconds)
```

`ALTER DATABASE questdb_app SET dialect = 'postgres'`

```text
database 'questdb_app' now reads SQL as PostgreSQL does
```

**Example: Only those two names** (shows an error)

```sql
ALTER DATABASE demo SET DIALECT = 'mysql';
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 35: SET dialect needs 'questdb' or 'postgres'`

<a id="wal-archive"></a>

## ALTER DATABASE ... SET WAL_ARCHIVE

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER DATABASE <name> SET WAL_ARCHIVE = '<size>'
ALTER DATABASE <name> SET WAL_ARCHIVE = OFF
ALTER DATABASE <name> SET WAL_ARCHIVE = DEFAULT
```

Says how much **old log** a database keeps in its `wal_archive` folder. Old log is only used to repair a damaged file and by backups. Your tables do not need it: the data is in the data files and the current log.

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `'100MB'`, `'1GB'`, `'512 MB'`, `'1.5 GB'` | keep up to this much; the oldest files are removed beyond it |
| `250` (a number without a unit) | megabytes |
| `OFF` | keep no old log |
| `DEFAULT` | follow the server default again |

The server default is 1 GB. Change it on the console's [Settings page](console-settings.md#wal-archive), or with `wal_archive_mb` in `kareladb.conf` or `KARELADB_WAL_ARCHIVE_MB`.

- **Returns:** `database 'x' keeps at most 100 MB of old log in wal_archive`.
- **Notes:**
  - Needs a server admin. The setting is kept in the data folder (`_system`) and holds after a restart.
  - It works at once. A smaller size removes the oldest files now, not at the next checkpoint. Log that the current data files still need is never removed.
  - With `OFF`, a damaged data file can only be repaired from a **backup**. Keep it on if you have no backups.
  - A log file is 64 MB, so a size under 64 MB keeps few or no files.
  - In the console: the **Databases** panel, **Old log**. `/api/databases` shows each database's limit (`wal_archive_max_bytes`), where it comes from (`wal_archive_source`: `database` or `server`) and the size on disk now (`wal_archive_bytes`).

**Example: Keep only 100 MB of old log**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE prices;
```

```sql
ALTER DATABASE prices SET WAL_ARCHIVE = '100MB';
```

Result:

```text
database 'prices' keeps at most 100 MB of old log in wal_archive
```

**Example: No old log, then back to the server default**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE scratch;
```

```sql
ALTER DATABASE scratch SET WAL_ARCHIVE = OFF;
ALTER DATABASE scratch SET WAL_ARCHIVE = DEFAULT;
```

Result:

`ALTER DATABASE scratch SET WAL_ARCHIVE = OFF`

```text
database 'scratch' keeps no old log in wal_archive; a damaged file can now only be repaired from a backup
```

`ALTER DATABASE scratch SET WAL_ARCHIVE = DEFAULT`

```text
database 'scratch' keeps at most 1 GB of old log in wal_archive (the server default)
```

**Example: A size needs a unit KarelaDB knows** (shows an error)

```sql
ALTER DATABASE demo SET WAL_ARCHIVE = '100 XB';
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 39: SET WAL_ARCHIVE: unknown unit 'XB'; use KB, MB, GB or TB`

<a id="result-cache"></a>

## ALTER DATABASE ... SET RESULT_CACHE

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER DATABASE <name> SET RESULT_CACHE = '<size>'
ALTER DATABASE <name> SET RESULT_CACHE = OFF
ALTER DATABASE <name> SET RESULT_CACHE = DEFAULT
```

Gives a database a [result cache](performance-tips.md#result-cache) space of its **own**. Without it, all databases share the server's cache (`--cache-mb`, `cache_mb` in kareladb.conf, 256 MB by default), and a busy database's results can push out another's. Use it for the database behind a dashboard that must stay fast while other apps load data.

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `'512MB'`, `'1GB'`, `'1.5 GB'` | keep up to this much of this database's results, apart from the others |
| `128` (a number without a unit) | megabytes |
| `OFF` | keep no results of this database: every `SELECT` runs |
| `DEFAULT` | share the server's cache again |

- **Returns:** `database 'x' keeps up to 512 MB of query results in a space of its own; one result may use a quarter of it, a pinned one three quarters`.
- **Notes:**
  - Needs a server admin. The setting is kept in the data folder (`_system`) and holds after a restart.
  - It works at once. A smaller size drops the oldest results now.
  - `/api/databases` shows each database's size (`result_cache_bytes`) and where it comes from (`result_cache_source`: `database` or `server`). `/api/stats` shows `cache_own`.

**Example: A dashboard database with 512 MB of its own**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE board;
```

```sql
ALTER DATABASE board SET RESULT_CACHE = '512MB';
```

Result:

```text
database 'board' keeps up to 512 MB of query results in a space of its own; one result may use a quarter of it, a pinned one three quarters
```

**Example: No cached results, then back to the shared cache**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE loader;
```

```sql
ALTER DATABASE loader SET RESULT_CACHE = OFF;
ALTER DATABASE loader SET RESULT_CACHE = DEFAULT;
```

Result:

`ALTER DATABASE loader SET RESULT_CACHE = OFF`

```text
database 'loader' keeps no query results: every SELECT runs
```

`ALTER DATABASE loader SET RESULT_CACHE = DEFAULT`

```text
database 'loader' shares the server's result cache again (64 MB for all databases together)
```

<a id="memory"></a>

## ALTER DATABASE ... SET MEMORY_LIMIT and MEMORY_RESERVED

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER DATABASE <name> SET MEMORY_LIMIT = '<size>' | OFF | DEFAULT
ALTER DATABASE <name> SET MEMORY_RESERVED = '<size>' | OFF | DEFAULT
```

Gives a database its own part of the server's memory for table data ([`--memory`](performance-tips.md#memory)). Without them, all databases share it, and a big scan in one database can unload the tables another one reads all the time.

| Setting | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MEMORY_LIMIT` | the most loaded data this database holds. Over it, its **own** partitions are unloaded first, even when `--memory` has room. |
| `MEMORY_RESERVED` | loaded data of this database that nothing else can unload: not another database, not the [process memory limit](cli-serve.md#memory-limit). Its own trims still keep to its `MEMORY_LIMIT`. |
| `OFF` | none for this database, whatever kareladb.conf says |
| `DEFAULT` | the value in kareladb.conf `database_memory`, or none |

- **Returns:** `database 'x' holds at most 512 MB of loaded partitions; over it, its own partitions are unloaded first`.
- **Notes:**
  - Needs a server admin. The settings are kept in the data folder (`_system`) and hold after a restart. They work at once.
  - A reservation cannot be more than the database's limit, and all reservations together at most three quarters of `--memory`.
  - kareladb.conf can set start values per database: `"database_memory": {"sales": {"limit_mb": 512, "reserved_mb": 128}}`.
  - `GET /api/stats` shows `used_bytes`, `limit_bytes`, `reserved_bytes` and `resident_bytes` in each database's `memory`.
  - To keep one table loaded whatever happens, use [`ALTER TABLE t SET (resident = on)`](alter-table.md#resident).

**Example: A dashboard database keeps its data loaded while a loader scans**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE dash;
CREATE DATABASE loader;
```

```sql
ALTER DATABASE dash SET MEMORY_RESERVED = '32MB';
ALTER DATABASE loader SET MEMORY_LIMIT = '256MB';
```

Result:

`ALTER DATABASE dash SET MEMORY_RESERVED = '32 MB'`

```text
database 'dash' keeps 32 MB of its loaded partitions whatever other databases need
```

`ALTER DATABASE loader SET MEMORY_LIMIT = '256 MB'`

```text
database 'loader' holds at most 256 MB of loaded partitions; over it, its own partitions are unloaded first
```

**Example: Back to the shared budget**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE scratch;
ALTER DATABASE scratch SET MEMORY_LIMIT = '64MB';
```

```sql
ALTER DATABASE scratch SET MEMORY_LIMIT = DEFAULT;
```

Result:

```text
database 'scratch' has no memory limit of its own (kareladb.conf): it shares the server's budget
```

<a id="per-column-loads"></a>

### Per-column loads

A column-engine query (sums, counts, `GROUP BY` and the like) on a partition that is not in memory reads **only the columns it names** from the file, plus the time column and the key columns. A sum of one column of a 20-column table reads and keeps about a tenth of the bytes, so the same memory holds many more partitions and a repeated query does not read its files again.

| What | What happens |
|---|---|
| a later query names more columns | those columns are read and added |
| a write, a checkpoint or a row read (`SELECT *`) | the whole partition is read first, and replaces the columns read apart |
| a partition with changes not yet in its file | read whole, as before |
| memory runs short | the columns read apart are unloaded like any loaded partition |

`GET /api/stats` counts these reads in `partial_loads` (part of `partition_loads`). Nothing to set: it is always on.

<!-- docs/as-of-and-branches.md -->

# Time travel and branches: SELECT ... AS OF, CREATE DATABASE ... BRANCH OF

> Read a table as it was at an earlier time or commit, undo a bad change with one query, and make a full writable copy of a database in a moment, without copying its files.

- Category: Databases & folders
- Keywords: AS OF, AS OF TIMESTAMP, AS OF LSN, AS OF SYSTEM TIME, FOR SYSTEM\_TIME AS OF, time travel, flashback, read the past, table as it was, undo, undo a bad import, point in time, BRANCH OF, branch, clone, copy database, zero-copy, test copy, hard link, keep\_versions, KARELADB\_KEEP\_VERSIONS, no longer kept
- See also: [Databases and the data folder](databases.md), [Change stream and live subscriptions: changes('t'), GET /api/changes, GET /api/subscribe](change-stream.md), [Backup, check, repair and restore](backup-and-safety.md), [kareladb serve](cli-serve.md), [The trash - UNDROP TABLE](trash.md)

KarelaDB never changes a data file once it is written. Each checkpoint writes the changed files anew and keeps the older versions for a while. With those and the log, KarelaDB can show a table **as it was**, and make a new database from another one **without copying** its files.

| You want | Write |
|---|---|
| a table as it was at a time | `SELECT ... FROM t AS OF TIMESTAMP '2026-09-25 14:30'` (or `AS OF '2026-09-25 14:30'`) |
| a table as it was after a commit | `SELECT ... FROM t AS OF LSN 12345` |
| undo a bad change | `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO t SELECT * FROM t AS OF TIMESTAMP '...'` |
| a copy of a database to try things on | `CREATE DATABASE test BRANCH OF live` |
| a copy of a database as it was | `CREATE DATABASE before BRANCH OF live AS OF TIMESTAMP '...'` |

<a id="as-of"></a>

## SELECT ... AS OF

Syntax:

```sql
SELECT ... FROM <table> AS OF TIMESTAMP <time> [[AS] alias] ...
SELECT ... FROM <table> AS OF LSN <commit lsn> [[AS] alias] ...
SELECT ... FROM <table> AS OF SYSTEM TIME <time>        -- CockroachDB's spelling
SELECT ... FROM <table> FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF <time>    -- SQL:2011's spelling
```

- `AS OF TIMESTAMP <time>`: the table with every change committed **at or before** that time (to the millisecond). The time is any expression: `'2026-09-25 14:30'`, `now() - INTERVAL '10 minutes'`. A time without a zone is read like any other time of the session.
- `AS OF LSN <n>`: the table with every transaction committed at or before log position `n`. `changes('t')` shows the commit LSN of each change ([change stream](change-stream.md)).
- Each table in a query has its own `AS OF`. The others are read as they are now, so a query can compare then and now:

```sql
-- Which prices did the 14:30 import change?
SELECT now.sym, before.price AS was, now.price AS is_now
FROM prices now
JOIN prices AS OF TIMESTAMP '2026-09-25 14:29' before ON before.sym = now.sym
WHERE before.price <> now.price;
```

Undo a bad change with one statement:

```sql
INSERT OR REPLACE INTO prices SELECT * FROM prices AS OF TIMESTAMP '2026-09-25 14:29';
CREATE TABLE prices_before AS SELECT * FROM prices AS OF LSN 1200345;
```

Good to know:

| | |
|---|---|
| columns | the table's columns **as they were**: a column added since is not there |
| a renamed table | found by its name now |
| a table made after the point | `table 't' did not exist yet AS OF ...` |
| a view | refused: read the tables it reads AS OF instead |
| rights | the user's rights on the table **now** (a user who may not read it now may not read it AS OF either) |
| writes | none: the past is read only, from the files where they are |
| speed | the first read of a point opens the table's files of that time and replays the log from the checkpoint before it. That copy is kept a minute, so asking the same point again (a chart) is fast |

<a id="how-far-back"></a>

## How far back

A read AS OF needs, for each file of the table, a version older than the point, and the log after it. Both are kept only for a while:

| What limits it | Kept | Set with |
|---|---|---|
| older versions of each table file | 2 per file | `keep_versions` in `kareladb.conf`, `KARELADB_KEEP_VERSIONS` (0 to 10) |
| older versions of the catalog (the tables' definitions), views, routines, sequences | at least 16 | always (they are a few KB) |
| the old log | 1 GB | `ALTER DATABASE ... SET WAL_ARCHIVE`, `KARELADB_WAL_ARCHIVE_MB` |

So a table that changes often can be read back over its last few checkpoints, a table that rarely changes much further. A point that can no longer be rebuilt is **refused**, never answered with rows that were not there together. The error says why and the oldest point that still works:

```text
the data as of LSN 4 is no longer kept: an older version of its files was removed (keep_versions) ...
The oldest point it can be read at is LSN 14.
```

These also end a table's history, because their rows are in no file any more:

- a partition that became empty (all its rows deleted), `DROP PARTITION`, a TTL drop
- `TRUNCATE`, and `PURGE VERSIONS`
- a database last written by a KarelaDB from before AS OF, or restored from a backup: its history starts at its next open for writing

<a id="branch"></a>

## CREATE DATABASE ... BRANCH OF

Syntax:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE [IF NOT EXISTS] <new> BRANCH OF <database>
CREATE DATABASE <new> BRANCH OF <database> AS OF TIMESTAMP <time>
CREATE DATABASE <new> BRANCH OF <database> AS OF LSN <commit lsn>
```

A branch is a **full, writable database** with every table, view, routine, sequence and row of `<database>`, as it is now or as it was at the point. Try a repair, a migration or a new release on real data, compare, then drop the branch (or swap it in: `POST /api/databases/swap`).

```sql
CREATE DATABASE market_test BRANCH OF market;
-- database 'market_test' created as a branch of 'market' at LSN 1204551 in 120 ms (401 data files shared, 0 copied)
USE market_test;
UPDATE ochl_day SET close = close * 1.1 WHERE symbol = 'ACME';   -- market is not touched
DROP DATABASE market_test;
```

| | |
|---|---|
| speed | the data files are **hard links**: made in a moment whatever their size, and no extra disk until either side changes a file |
| no hard links | a file system without them (some network or Docker folders) gets copies: same result, slower |
| independent | each database writes its own new files; writes, checkpoints and `DROP DATABASE` of one never change the other |
| what goes with it | the tables, views, routines, sequences, triggers and waiting trigger jobs; its SQL dialect and `pg_compat` |
| what does not | users' rights, `READ ONLY`, timers and pinned queries: they belong to names. Grant them on the branch if needed |
| who | a server admin (as `CREATE DATABASE`) |
| safety | the branch is made in a hidden folder and gets its name last, so a crash never leaves half a database. The source keeps running meanwhile |

# Queries across databases

> Read a table of another database on the same server as database.table - in SELECT, JOIN, subqueries and INSERT ... SELECT.

- Category: Databases & folders
- Keywords: cross-database, cross database, other database, another database, database.table, db.table, otherdb.table, reference data, shared tables, copy a table between databases, join two databases, INSERT INTO ... SELECT from another database, dblink, linked server, three-part name, changes only the database it runs in
- See also: [Databases and the data folder](databases.md), [Joins](joins.md), [UNION and subqueries](union-subqueries.md), [Users and roles](users-and-roles.md), [Table rights - GRANT ON TABLE](table-rights.md), [The procedure language (execute)](procedure-language.md#execute)

One KarelaDB server holds many [databases](databases.md). A query can read a table of **another database** on the same server. Write the database name, a dot and the table name: `refdata.companies`.

A real setup: one database `refdata` holds the company list. Every app database reads it from there instead of keeping its own copy.

**Example: Company names from a shared reference database**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE refdata;
USE refdata;
CREATE TABLE companies (symbol STRING PRIMARY KEY, name STRING, sector STRING);
INSERT INTO companies VALUES ('CITY', 'City Bank', 'Bank'), ('HYDRO', 'River Hydro', 'Energy'), ('MART', 'Metro Mart', 'Retail');
```

```sql
CREATE TABLE trades (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, symbol STRING, qty LONG);
INSERT INTO trades VALUES (1, 'CITY', 100), (2, 'HYDRO', 40), (3, 'CITY', 25);
SELECT t.id, t.symbol, c.name, t.qty
FROM trades t JOIN refdata.companies c ON t.symbol = c.symbol
ORDER BY t.id;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE trades (`

```text
table 'trades' created
```

`INSERT INTO trades VALUES (1, 'CITY', 100), (2, 'HYDRO', 40), (3, 'CITY', 25)`

```text
3 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT t.id, t.symbol, c.name, t.qty FROM trades AS t JOIN refdata.companies AS c ON t.symbol = c.sy`

| id (LONG) | symbol (STRING) | name (STRING) | qty (LONG) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | CITY | City Bank | 100 |
| 2 | HYDRO | River Hydro | 40 |
| 3 | CITY | City Bank | 25 |

(3 rows)

<a id="names"></a>

## Name a table of another database

Syntax:

```sql
database.table
database.public.table
"database"."table"
```

| Written | Means |
|---|---|
| `companies` | the table in the database you are using |
| `refdata.companies` | the table `companies` of the database `refdata` |
| `refdata.public.companies` | the same; PostgreSQL apps write the schema `public` |
| `demo.companies`, when you use `demo` | your own database: the same as `companies` |

- **Notes:**
  - Database names ignore upper and lower case, like everywhere in KarelaDB.
  - With no alias, the table name is the alias: `SELECT companies.name FROM refdata.companies`.
  - It works over HTTP, the PostgreSQL port, `kareladb shell`, `kareladb sql --data-dir` and the web console. A `Database` opened on its own, without the server's databases, gives an error.

<a id="what-works"></a>

## What works

| Statement | Example |
|---|---|
| `SELECT` | `SELECT * FROM refdata.companies` |
| `JOIN`, `LEFT JOIN`, `CROSS JOIN`, `ASOF JOIN` | `FROM trades t JOIN refdata.companies c ON t.symbol = c.symbol` |
| subqueries: `IN`, `EXISTS`, a value, `FROM (SELECT ...)` | `WHERE symbol IN (SELECT symbol FROM refdata.companies)` |
| `WITH` | `WITH banks AS (SELECT * FROM refdata.companies WHERE sector = 'Bank') ...` |
| `INSERT INTO t SELECT ...` | copies rows from the other database into this one |
| `CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT ...` | makes a copy in this database |
| `UPDATE` / `DELETE` with a subquery | `DELETE FROM trades WHERE symbol NOT IN (SELECT symbol FROM refdata.companies)` |
| views, procedures, triggers, [EXECUTE](procedure-language.md#execute) | the other table is read each time they run |

**Example: Copy the banks into this database, and count trades of banks**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE refdata;
USE refdata;
CREATE TABLE companies (symbol STRING PRIMARY KEY, name STRING, sector STRING);
INSERT INTO companies VALUES ('CITY', 'City Bank', 'Bank'), ('HYDRO', 'River Hydro', 'Energy'), ('LAKE', 'Lake Bank', 'Bank');
```

```sql
CREATE TABLE trades (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, symbol STRING, qty LONG);
INSERT INTO trades VALUES (1, 'CITY', 100), (2, 'HYDRO', 40), (3, 'LAKE', 25);
CREATE TABLE banks (symbol STRING PRIMARY KEY, name STRING);
INSERT INTO banks SELECT symbol, name FROM refdata.companies WHERE sector = 'Bank';
SELECT count(*) AS bank_trades, sum(qty) AS bank_qty
FROM trades WHERE symbol IN (SELECT symbol FROM refdata.companies WHERE sector = 'Bank');
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE trades (`

```text
table 'trades' created
```

`INSERT INTO trades VALUES (1, 'CITY', 100), (2, 'HYDRO', 40), (3, 'LAKE', 25)`

```text
3 row(s) inserted
```

`CREATE TABLE banks (`

```text
table 'banks' created
```

`INSERT INTO banks SELECT symbol, name FROM refdata.companies WHERE sector = 'Bank'`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT count(*) AS bank_trades, sum(qty) AS bank_qty FROM trades WHERE symbol IN (SELECT symbol FROM`

| bank_trades (LONG) | bank_qty (LONG) |
|---|---|
| 2 | 125 |

(1 row)

<a id="writes"></a>

## Changes stay in your database

A statement changes only the database it runs in. `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` of `otherdb.table` are refused. To change the other database, run the statement there (`USE refdata`, or `db=refdata` over HTTP). From there, your database's tables can be read as `yourdb.table`.

**Example: Writing into another database is refused** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE refdata;
USE refdata;
CREATE TABLE companies (symbol STRING PRIMARY KEY, name STRING, sector STRING);
```

```sql
INSERT INTO refdata.companies VALUES ('NEW', 'New Company', 'Bank');
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 1: INSERT of table 'refdata.companies' is not allowed: a statement changes only the database it runs in ('demo'). Run it in database 'refdata' (USE refdata), where the tables of 'demo' can be read as demo.<table>`

**Example: A database that is not there** (shows an error)

```sql
SELECT * FROM nowhere.companies;
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 15: database 'nowhere' does not exist (SHOW DATABASES lists them) (in nowhere.companies)`

<a id="rights"></a>

## Rights

The other table is checked with **that** database's rights.

| To read `refdata.companies` a user needs | |
|---|---|
| role `read` on `refdata` | or `GRANT SELECT ON TABLE companies` made in `refdata` |
| no `REVOKE SELECT ON TABLE companies` in `refdata` | a revoke there wins over the role |
| role `admin` on `refdata` | only for `_audit_log` and dropped tables |

- **Notes:** the user also needs the usual rights in the database the statement runs in, for example `write` for an `INSERT ... SELECT`. See [users and roles](users-and-roles.md) and [table rights](table-rights.md).

<a id="speed"></a>

## Speed

A `SELECT` that reads only tables of **one** other database, and uses nothing of yours (no table, view, saved function or type of your database), is sent to that database whole. It runs there as if you had sent it yourself: `SELECT count(*) FROM market.prices` is answered from the saved row counts and copies no row, and a `GROUP BY` or `SAMPLE BY` over years runs next to the data. The answer is the same.

Any other statement reads the other table into your database first. Your conditions go with the read, so it skips partitions, uses the column engine and sends only the rows that match.

| Condition | Goes to the other database |
|---|---|
| `WHERE` of a query with only that table | yes |
| `WHERE p.time >= ...` in a join, written as `alias.column` | yes |
| a bare column name in a join (`WHERE time >= ...`) | no: it may belong to another table |
| `ON c.sector = 'Bank'` of a `JOIN` or `LEFT JOIN` | yes |
| `WHERE` on the right table of a `LEFT JOIN`, or of an `ASOF JOIN` | no: it would change the result |

- **Notes:**
  - When a statement also uses your database (a join with your table, for example), the matching rows come over to your database, then the join, `GROUP BY` and the rest run here.
  - In a join, write `alias.column` in `WHERE`, so a time range reaches the other table.
  - A change in the other database shows at once: a statement sent there whole is kept only in that database's [result cache](performance-tips.md), which a write there clears, and other results with its tables are never kept.

**Example: One day of prices from another database: only that day's partition is read**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE market;
USE market;
CREATE TABLE prices (time TIMESTAMP, symbol STRING, close DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY;
INSERT INTO prices VALUES ('2026-09-09T10:00:00Z', 'CITY', 510.0), ('2026-09-10T10:00:00Z', 'CITY', 512.5), ('2026-09-10T10:00:00Z', 'HYDRO', 88.2);
```

```sql
CREATE TABLE holdings (symbol STRING PRIMARY KEY, qty LONG);
INSERT INTO holdings VALUES ('CITY', 100), ('HYDRO', 50);
SELECT h.symbol, h.qty * p.close AS value
FROM holdings h JOIN market.prices p ON h.symbol = p.symbol
WHERE p.time >= '2026-09-10' AND p.time < '2026-09-11'
ORDER BY h.symbol;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE holdings (`

```text
table 'holdings' created
```

`INSERT INTO holdings VALUES ('CITY', 100), ('HYDRO', 50)`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT h.symbol, h.qty * p.close AS value FROM holdings AS h JOIN market.prices AS p ON h.symbol = p`

| symbol (STRING) | value (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|
| CITY | 51250 |
| HYDRO | 4410 |

(2 rows)

<a id="locks"></a>

## Locks

- A statement reads the other database's tables **before** it takes the lock of its own database. So a statement never waits for two databases at once, and two databases that read each other at the same time do not wait for each other.
- Reading is like any other reader of that database: it sees committed rows only, and an open `BEGIN ... COMMIT` there does not make it wait.
- Inside a procedure, trigger or `EXECUTE`, your database is already locked. Then the read waits at most `lock_timeout_ms` (5 seconds by default) for a long writer of the other database, and fails with `database is busy ... Try again`.
- The rows are read when the statement starts. Transactions do not span databases: a `ROLLBACK` here does not touch the other database.
