<!-- docs/create-table.md -->

# CREATE TABLE

> Make a relational or a time-series table, with partitions, sort order, a dedup key, rounded times and computed columns, or make one from a query with CREATE TABLE ... AS.

- Category: Tables
- Keywords: create table, new table, IF NOT EXISTS, TEMP TABLE, TEMPORARY, UNLOGGED, table options, relational table, time-series table, timeseries table, RECORDS, TIMESERIES, PARTITION BY, DAY, MONTH, YEAR, NONE, SYMBOL(col), SORT BY, DEDUP KEY, DEDUP UPSERT KEYS, TIMESTAMP(col), WAL, CREATE TABLE AS, CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT, AS SELECT, WITH NO DATA, copy a table, deduplication, ROUND, round time, computed column, generated column, GENERATED ALWAYS, STORED, stored generated column, virtual column, AS, schema, design, ttl\_column, row TTL, expire, EXPIRE, expires\_at, per-row TTL, key expiry, redis, session table, rate limit, max\_bytes, evict, durability, cache table, LRU, eviction, maxmemory, kv\_memory, volatile\_ttl
- See also: [Column types](column-types.md), [Constraints](constraints.md), [ALTER, RENAME and DROP TABLE](alter-table.md), [SHOW TABLES, COLUMNS, CREATE TABLE](show-tables.md), [INSERT](insert.md), [Partitions, SORT BY and DEDUP KEY](partitions-and-dedup.md), [Indexes](indexes.md)

`CREATE TABLE` makes a new table. KarelaDB has **two kinds** of tables:

| | Relational table | Time-series table |
|---|---|---|
| Holds | lists of things: users, accounts, brokers, posts | rows with a time: candles, trades, live prices |
| Written as | `CREATE TABLE t (...)` | `CREATE TABLE t (...) TIMESERIES(time_column)` |
| Duplicate check | `PRIMARY KEY`, `UNIQUE` | `DEDUP KEY (..., time)` |
| Split into files | no | `PARTITION BY DAY`, `MONTH`, `YEAR` or `NONE` |

Simple rule: **if every row has a time and many new rows come every day, use a time-series table.** You cannot change the kind, the partitions or the sort order later, so choose carefully before you load big data. The dedup key can be changed later, but that rewrites every row ([DEDUP ENABLE](alter-table.md#dedup-enable)).

**Example: Daily stock candles: a time-series table**

```sql
CREATE TABLE ochl_day (
  time   TIMESTAMP ROUND 1d,
  symbol SYMBOL,
  open   DOUBLE,
  high   DOUBLE,
  low    DOUBLE,
  close  DOUBLE,
  volume DOUBLE
) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY YEAR DEDUP KEY (symbol, time);
```

Result:

```text
table 'ochl_day' created
```

<a id="create-table"></a>

## CREATE TABLE

Syntax:

```sql
CREATE TABLE [IF NOT EXISTS] name (
  column TYPE [PRIMARY KEY [AUTO]] [NOT NULL] [UNIQUE] [DEFAULT expr]
              [REFERENCES table(column)] [ROUND interval] [AS (expr) | GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expr) STORED]
              [[CONSTRAINT name] CHECK (condition)],
  ...
  [, [CONSTRAINT name] CHECK (condition) ...]
)
[TIMESERIES(time_column)]
[PARTITION BY DAY | MONTH | YEAR | NONE [, SYMBOL(column)]]
[SORT BY (column, ...)]
[DEDUP KEY (column, ...)]
[TTL n HOURS | DAYS | WEEKS | MONTHS | YEARS]
[RECORDS]
[WITH (ttl_column = column)]
```

Makes a table with at least one column. The table options after `)` can come in any order, each at most once.

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `IF NOT EXISTS` | a table with this name is already there: do nothing, no error (the old table is **not** changed) |
| `name` | the table name; see [names](sql-basics.md#names) |
| `column TYPE` | a column and its [type](column-types.md) |
| column rules | `PRIMARY KEY`, `AUTO`, `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `DEFAULT`, `REFERENCES`, `CHECK`: see [constraints](constraints.md) |
| `TTL` | drop partitions older than this, by itself; see [SET TTL](alter-table.md#set-ttl) |
| `WITH (ttl_column = c)` | each row expires at the time in column `c`: see [rows that expire](#row-ttl) |
| `WITH (max_bytes = '64MB', evict = 'lru')` | a cache table: rows used longest ago go when it is full; see [cache tables](#cache-table) |
| `ROUND`, `AS (...)`, `GENERATED ... STORED` | see [ROUND](#round), [computed columns](#computed) and [stored generated columns](#generated) |
| table options | see the entries below |

- **Returns:** `table 'name' created`, or `table 'name' already exists` with `IF NOT EXISTS`.
- **Notes:** a view and a table cannot have the same name. `CREATE TABLE` cannot be used inside `BEGIN ... COMMIT`. To make a table from a query, see [CREATE TABLE ... AS](#create-table-as).
- **PostgreSQL:** `CREATE TEMP TABLE` makes a [temporary table](#temp-table). `CREATE UNLOGGED TABLE` is refused: every KarelaDB table is written to the log.
- **QuestDB:** `TIMESTAMP(col)` means `TIMESERIES(col)`, `DEDUP UPSERT KEYS (...)` means `DEDUP KEY (...)` with `dedup_insert = 'upsert'` (a plain `INSERT` replaces the row, as in QuestDB), and `WAL` / `BYPASS WAL` are read and ignored. `col SYMBOL INDEX [CAPACITY n]`, and `INDEX(col [CAPACITY n])` after the column list, make an [index](indexes.md) on the column. A SYMBOL's `CAPACITY n`, `CACHE` and `NOCACHE` are read and ignored: KarelaDB sizes its dictionaries itself.

**Example: App users: a relational table with keys and defaults**

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
  id            LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO,
  email         STRING NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  password_hash STRING NOT NULL,
  name          STRING,
  created       TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
SHOW COLUMNS FROM users;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE users (`

```text
table 'users' created
```

`SHOW COLUMNS FROM users`

| name (STRING) | type (STRING) | primary_key (BOOL) | not_null (BOOL) | computed (BOOL) | references (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| id | LONG | true | false | false | NULL |
| email | STRING | false | true | false | NULL |
| password_hash | STRING | false | true | false | NULL |
| name | STRING | false | false | false | NULL |
| created | TIMESTAMP | false | true | false | NULL |

(5 rows)

**Example: An install script that can run many times**

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS brokers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS brokers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING NOT NULL);
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS brokers (`

```text
table 'brokers' created
```

`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS brokers (`

```text
table 'brokers' already exists
```

**Example: The same name twice without IF NOT EXISTS** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE brokers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING NOT NULL);
```

```sql
CREATE TABLE brokers (id INT PRIMARY KEY);
```

Result:

Error: `table 'brokers' already exists; expected a new table name, or CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`

<a id="temp-table"></a>

## Temporary tables: CREATE TEMP TABLE

Syntax:

```sql
CREATE [GLOBAL | LOCAL] TEMP | TEMPORARY TABLE name (...) [table options]
CREATE TEMP TABLE name AS query
```

A **temporary table** belongs to one session, as in PostgreSQL:

| | |
|---|---|
| Who sees it | only the session that made it. For every other session the name does not exist |
| A table of the same name | is hidden in that session while the temporary one exists; `DROP TABLE` of the temporary one shows it again |
| When it goes | when the session ends (the PostgreSQL connection closes, or the HTTP [session](http-sessions-and-cursors.md) ends). Without a session, at the end of the request. A server that stopped with sessions open drops their tables when it starts |
| What it is | an ordinary table under the name `pg_temp_<session>_<name>`: indexes, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `TRUNCATE` and `ALTER TABLE` work as on any table |

- **Role:** `ddl`, like `CREATE TABLE`.
- **Notes:** `ON COMMIT DROP` and `ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS` are not supported; the table lives until the session ends.

**Example: A scratch table for one request: made, used, gone**

```sql
CREATE TEMP TABLE scratch (id INT, score DOUBLE);
INSERT INTO scratch VALUES (1, 0.5), (2, 0.9);
SELECT count(*) AS rows_now, max(score) AS best FROM scratch;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE pg_temp_4611686018427387904_scratch (`

```text
table 'pg_temp_4611686018427387904_scratch' created
```

`INSERT INTO pg_temp_4611686018427387904_scratch VALUES (1, 0.5), (2, 0.9)`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT count(*) AS rows_now, max(score) AS best FROM pg_temp_4611686018427387904_scratch`

| rows_now (LONG) | best (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|
| 2 | 0.9 |

(1 row)

**Example: After the request, the name is gone** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TEMP TABLE scratch2 (id INT);
```

```sql
SELECT * FROM scratch2;
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 15: table or view 'scratch2' does not exist`

**Example: UNLOGGED is refused** (shows an error)

```sql
CREATE UNLOGGED TABLE fast_scratch (id INT);
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 8: CREATE UNLOGGED TABLE is not supported: every KarelaDB table is written to the log and kept. Use CREATE TABLE`

<a id="create-table-as"></a>

## CREATE TABLE ... AS

Syntax:

```sql
CREATE TABLE [IF NOT EXISTS] name [(column, ...)] AS query
    [TIMESERIES(time_column)] [PARTITION BY DAY | MONTH | YEAR | NONE]
    [SORT BY (column, ...)] [DEDUP KEY (column, ...)] [RECORDS]
CREATE TABLE name AS query WITH NO DATA
```

Makes a new table from the result of a query, and copies the rows in. The columns get the names and types of the query's columns. The query may be in brackets: `AS (SELECT ...)`.

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `(column, ...)` | new names for the first columns, in order |
| table options | as for `CREATE TABLE`; without `TIMESERIES` the new table is a relational table |
| `WITH NO DATA` | make the empty table only |

- **Returns:** `table 'name' created with N row(s)`.
- **Notes:**
  - A `SYMBOL` column of the query stays `SYMBOL` (as QuestDB copies it). Keys, `NOT NULL`, defaults, `CHECK` rules and indexes are **not** copied.
  - A plain read (`SELECT ... FROM one_table [WHERE ...]`, no join, `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT`, window, `ORDER BY` or `LIMIT`) is copied in batches while the source is read, as `INSERT ... SELECT` writes, so a copy of millions of rows fits the memory limits (5M rows of 10 columns: about 2.4 GB at the peak instead of 9.7 GB, and twice as fast). Other queries keep their whole result first, under `max_result_memory`. Add them with [ALTER TABLE](alter-table.md) afterwards, or make the table first and `INSERT INTO t SELECT ...` (see [INSERT ... SELECT](insert.md#insert-select)).
  - `PARTITION BY ..., SYMBOL(col)` is not accepted here.
  - Two query columns with the same name are refused: name them with `AS`.

**Example: Copy one symbol's daily candles into a time-series table** (sample data: sample)

```sql
CREATE TABLE city_day AS
  SELECT time, close, volume FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = 'CITY'
  TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY YEAR DEDUP KEY (time);
SHOW CREATE TABLE city_day;
SELECT count(*) AS rows FROM city_day;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE city_day AS SELECT time, close, volume FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = 'CITY'`

```text
table 'city_day' created with 19 row(s)
```

`SHOW CREATE TABLE city_day`

| create_sql (STRING) |
|---|
| CREATE TABLE city_day (   time TIMESTAMP,   close DOUBLE,   volume DOUBLE ) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY YEAR SORT BY (time) DEDUP KEY (time) |

(1 row)

`SELECT count(*) AS rows FROM city_day`

| rows (LONG) |
|---|
| 19 |

(1 row)

**Example: A summary table with new column names**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE trades (symbol SYMBOL, qty LONG, rate DOUBLE);
INSERT INTO trades VALUES ('CITY', 10, 515.0), ('CITY', 20, 516.0), ('COAST', 5, 376.0);
```

```sql
CREATE TABLE turnover (symbol, amount) AS SELECT symbol, sum(qty * rate) FROM trades GROUP BY symbol;
SELECT * FROM turnover ORDER BY symbol;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE turnover (symbol, amount) AS SELECT symbol, sum(qty * rate) FROM trades GROUP BY symbol`

```text

```

`SELECT * FROM turnover ORDER BY symbol`

| symbol (SYMBOL) | amount (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|
| CITY | 15470 |
| COAST | 1880 |

(2 rows)

**Example: The same column name twice** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE trades (symbol SYMBOL, qty LONG);
```

```sql
CREATE TABLE bad AS SELECT symbol, qty, qty FROM trades;
```

Result:

Error: `the query of CREATE TABLE bad gives two columns named 'qty'; name them with AS`

<a id="relational"></a>

## Relational tables (RECORDS)

Syntax:

```sql
CREATE TABLE name (column TYPE [rules], ...) [RECORDS]
```

A table without `TIMESERIES` is a **relational** table. The word `RECORDS` says it explicitly; it changes nothing. Use relational tables for lists of things that you look up by a key and change often: users, accounts, the ledger, brokers, forum posts, news articles.

- Give it a `PRIMARY KEY`. Rows are kept in key order, so a lookup by key is fast.
- Without a key, every `INSERT` adds rows, also exact copies.
- For money, add rules like `CHECK (balance >= 0)`; see [CHECK](constraints.md#check).
- **Notes:** `PARTITION BY`, `SORT BY` and `DEDUP KEY` are only for time-series tables. `RECORDS` together with `TIMESERIES` is an error.

**Example: Accounting: accounts and a ledger with exact money**

```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id      INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO,
  owner   STRING NOT NULL,
  balance DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
) RECORDS;

CREATE TABLE ledger (
  id           LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO,
  from_account INT NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),
  to_account   INT NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),
  amount       DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL,
  created      TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now()
);
SHOW TABLES;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE accounts (`

```text
table 'accounts' created
```

`CREATE TABLE ledger (`

```text
table 'ledger' created
```

`SHOW TABLES`

| name (STRING) | kind (STRING) | partition (STRING) | columns (INT) | rows (LONG) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| accounts | relational | NONE | 3 | 0 |
| ledger | relational | NONE | 5 | 0 |

(2 rows)

**Example: Forum posts and news articles**

```sql
CREATE TABLE posts (
  id         LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO,
  thread_id  LONG NOT NULL,
  parent_id  LONG REFERENCES posts(id),
  author     STRING NOT NULL,
  body       STRING NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE news (
  id           LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO,
  symbol       STRING,
  published_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  lang         STRING NOT NULL DEFAULT 'en',
  title        STRING NOT NULL,
  body         STRING NOT NULL,
  source_url   STRING
);
SHOW TABLES;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE posts (`

```text
table 'posts' created
```

`CREATE TABLE news (`

```text

```

`SHOW TABLES`

| name (STRING) | kind (STRING) | partition (STRING) | columns (INT) | rows (LONG) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| news | relational | NONE | 7 | 0 |
| posts | relational | NONE | 6 | 0 |

(2 rows)

**Example: PARTITION BY on a relational table** (shows an error)

```sql

```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 56: PARTITION BY is only for time-series tables; expected TIMESERIES(<TIMESTAMP or DATE column>) on table 'users'`

<a id="timeseries"></a>

## TIMESERIES

Syntax:

```sql
CREATE TABLE name (...) TIMESERIES(time_column) [PARTITION BY ...] [SORT BY (...)] [DEDUP KEY (...)]
```

Makes a **time-series** table. `time_column` is its time column: a stored `TIMESTAMP` or `DATE` column. Time-series tables are made for many rows with a time: they are split into files by time ([PARTITION BY](#partition-by)), and they work with [SAMPLE BY](sample-by.md), [LATEST ON](latest-on.md), [ASOF JOIN](joins.md) and `WHERE time IN '2026-09'`.

- Every row needs a value in the time column.
- A time-series table cannot have a `PRIMARY KEY`. Use [DEDUP KEY](#dedup-key).
- **Notes:** partitions use the **UTC** date of the time column.

**Example: Minute candles and live prices**

```sql
CREATE TABLE ochl_minutes (
  time TIMESTAMP ROUND 1m, symbol SYMBOL,
  open DOUBLE, high DOUBLE, low DOUBLE, close DOUBLE, volume DOUBLE
) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY MONTH DEDUP KEY (symbol, time);

CREATE TABLE live_data (
  timestamp TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, ltp DOUBLE, pct_change DOUBLE, volume LONG
) TIMESERIES(timestamp) PARTITION BY DAY DEDUP KEY (timestamp, symbol);
SHOW TABLES;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE ochl_minutes (`

```text
table 'ochl_minutes' created
```

`CREATE TABLE live_data (`

```text
table 'live_data' created
```

`SHOW TABLES`

| name (STRING) | kind (STRING) | partition (STRING) | columns (INT) | rows (LONG) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| live_data | timeseries | DAY | 5 | 0 |
| ochl_minutes | timeseries | MONTH | 7 | 0 |

(2 rows)

**Example: A DATE time column: one row per company per trading day**

```sql
CREATE TABLE market_cap (day DATE, symbol SYMBOL, cap DECIMAL(2)) TIMESERIES(day) PARTITION BY YEAR DEDUP KEY (symbol, day);
INSERT INTO market_cap VALUES ('2026-09-10', 'CITY', 136637213200.00);
SELECT day, symbol, cap FROM market_cap;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE market_cap (`

```text
table 'market_cap' created
```

`INSERT INTO market_cap VALUES ('2026-09-10', 'CITY', 136637213200.00)`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT day, symbol, cap FROM market_cap`

| day (DATE) | symbol (SYMBOL) | cap (DECIMAL(2)) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-10 | CITY | 136637213200.00 |

(1 row)

**Example: The time column must be a TIMESTAMP or DATE** (shows an error)

```sql
CREATE TABLE trades (id LONG, price DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(id);
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 56: TIMESERIES column 'id' is LONG; expected a TIMESTAMP or DATE column`

**Example: A time-series table with a PRIMARY KEY** (shows an error)

```sql
CREATE TABLE trades (time TIMESTAMP, id LONG PRIMARY KEY, price DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time);
```

Result:

Error: `time-series tables cannot have a PRIMARY KEY ('id'); use DEDUP KEY (..., time) instead, or make it a relational table`

<a id="partition-by"></a>

## PARTITION BY

Syntax:

```sql
PARTITION BY DAY | MONTH | YEAR | NONE
```

A time-series table keeps its rows in one file (a **partition**) per day, month or year of the time column. The default is `DAY`.

| Value | Partition names | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| `DAY` | `'2026-09-10'` | trade log trades, live prices: many rows per day |
| `MONTH` | `'2026-09'` | minute candles |
| `YEAR` | `'2026'` | daily candles |
| `NONE` | one partition | very small time-series tables |

Add `, SYMBOL(column)` after `YEAR`, `MONTH` or `NONE` to split each partition again, one file per symbol: `PARTITION BY YEAR, SYMBOL(symbol)`. The rules are in [PARTITION BY ..., SYMBOL(col)](partitions-and-dedup.md#partition-by-symbol).

Why partitions help:

- `WHERE time IN '2026-09'` reads only the files of September 2026.
- `ALTER TABLE t DROP PARTITION '2025'` deletes a whole year at once ([DROP PARTITION](alter-table.md#drop-partition)).

- **Notes:** the choices are `DAY`, `MONTH`, `YEAR` and `NONE`; there are no weekly partitions, and `PARTITION BY WEEK` is an error. The partition is the **UTC** date. `2026-09-10T02:00:00+05:45` is 2026-09-09 20:15 UTC, so it goes into the partition `2026-09-09`. Too small partitions (DAY for a table with 50 rows a day) make many tiny files; too big ones (NONE for millions of rows) make writes slower. See [partitions and dedup](partitions-and-dedup.md).

**Example: Rows go to monthly partitions; drop one month**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ochl_minutes (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, close DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY MONTH;
INSERT INTO ochl_minutes VALUES
  ('2026-08-30T11:00:00+05:45', 'CITY', 508.1),
  ('2026-09-10T11:00:00+05:45', 'CITY', 504.6);
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE ochl_minutes DROP PARTITION '2026-08';
SELECT time, symbol, close FROM ochl_minutes;
```

Result:

`ALTER TABLE ochl_minutes DROP PARTITION '2026-08'`

```text
1 partition(s) of 'ochl_minutes' dropped
```

`SELECT time, symbol, close FROM ochl_minutes`

| time (TIMESTAMP) | symbol (SYMBOL) | close (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-10T05:15:00.000Z | CITY | 504.6 |

(1 row)

<a id="sort-by"></a>

## SORT BY

Syntax:

```sql
SORT BY (column, ...)
```

The order of the rows **inside** each partition file. Rows with the same first columns are stored close together, so a query for one symbol reads less.

- **Default:** the first `SYMBOL` column, then the time column: `SORT BY (symbol, time)`. Without a `SYMBOL` column: the time column only.
- Only stored columns (not computed ones), each once.
- **Notes:** you cannot change `SORT BY` later. Columns in `SORT BY` cannot be dropped. `SHOW CREATE TABLE` shows the sort order KarelaDB uses.

**Example: The default sort order is shown by SHOW CREATE TABLE**

```sql
CREATE TABLE trade_log (date TIMESTAMP, transaction_id LONG, symbol SYMBOL, quantity LONG, rate DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(date);
SHOW CREATE TABLE trade_log;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE trade_log (`

```text
table 'trade_log' created
```

`SHOW CREATE TABLE trade_log`

| create_sql (STRING) |
|---|
| CREATE TABLE trade_log (   date TIMESTAMP,   transaction_id LONG,   symbol SYMBOL,   quantity LONG,   rate DOUBLE ) TIMESERIES(date) PARTITION BY DAY SORT BY (symbol, date) |

(1 row)

**Example: Sort the trades of a day by transaction number**

```sql
CREATE TABLE trade_log (date TIMESTAMP ROUND 1d, transaction_id LONG, symbol SYMBOL, quantity LONG, rate DOUBLE)
  TIMESERIES(date) PARTITION BY DAY SORT BY (date, transaction_id) DEDUP KEY (date, transaction_id);
SHOW CREATE TABLE trade_log;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE trade_log (`

```text
table 'trade_log' created
```

`SHOW CREATE TABLE trade_log`

| create_sql (STRING) |
|---|
| CREATE TABLE trade_log (   date TIMESTAMP ROUND 1d,   transaction_id LONG,   symbol SYMBOL,   quantity LONG,   rate DOUBLE ) TIMESERIES(date) PARTITION BY DAY SORT BY (date, transaction_id) DEDUP K... |

(1 row)

<a id="dedup-key"></a>

## DEDUP KEY

Syntax:

```sql
DEDUP KEY (column, ..., time_column)
```

The columns that make two rows "the same row". It is the key of a time-series table, and it **must include the time column**.

| Statement | The key is new | The key is already there |
|---|---|---|
| `INSERT` | row added | **error**, nothing saved |
| `INSERT OR REPLACE` | row added | the old row is replaced |
| `INSERT OR IGNORE` | row added | the new row is skipped |

- Without a `DEDUP KEY`, KarelaDB keeps every row, also exact copies.
- `NULL` counts as a value here: two rows with the same time and `symbol` `NULL` are the same row.
- **Tip:** give every time-series table a `DEDUP KEY`. Then an import file can be loaded twice without double rows.
- **Notes:** QuestDB's `DEDUP UPSERT KEYS(...)` is read as `DEDUP KEY (...)` and, as in QuestDB, a plain `INSERT` of a key that is there then **replaces** the row ([dedup_insert](partitions-and-dedup.md#dedup-insert)). With KarelaDB's own `DEDUP KEY`, duplicates give an error unless you write `INSERT OR REPLACE`, the table has `dedup_insert = 'upsert'`, or the database uses the [QuestDB dialect](databases.md#dialect). See [INSERT](insert.md#duplicates).
- **Notes:** a load over the line protocol does less work when every `SORT BY` column is in the `DEDUP KEY` ([how loads find duplicates](partitions-and-dedup.md#load-dedup)).

**Example: One candle per symbol per day**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ochl_day (time TIMESTAMP ROUND 1d, symbol SYMBOL, close DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY YEAR DEDUP KEY (symbol, time);
INSERT INTO ochl_day VALUES ('2026-09-10', 'CITY', 504.9);
```

```sql
INSERT OR REPLACE INTO ochl_day VALUES ('2026-09-10', 'CITY', 505.2);
SELECT time, symbol, close FROM ochl_day;
```

Result:

`INSERT OR REPLACE INTO ochl_day VALUES ('2026-09-10', 'CITY', 505.2)`

```text
0 row(s) inserted, 1 replaced
```

`SELECT time, symbol, close FROM ochl_day`

| time (TIMESTAMP) | symbol (SYMBOL) | close (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z | CITY | 505.2 |

(1 row)

**Example: Without a DEDUP KEY, the same tick is stored twice**

```sql
CREATE TABLE ticks (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, price DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY;
INSERT INTO ticks VALUES ('2026-09-10T11:00:00+05:45', 'CITY', 510);
INSERT INTO ticks VALUES ('2026-09-10T11:00:00+05:45', 'CITY', 510);
SELECT time, symbol, price FROM ticks;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE ticks (`

```text
table 'ticks' created
```

`INSERT INTO ticks VALUES ('2026-09-10T11:00:00+05:45', 'CITY', 510)`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`INSERT INTO ticks VALUES ('2026-09-10T11:00:00+05:45', 'CITY', 510)`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT time, symbol, price FROM ticks`

| time (TIMESTAMP) | symbol (SYMBOL) | price (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-10T05:15:00.000Z | CITY | 510 |
| 2026-09-10T05:15:00.000Z | CITY | 510 |

(2 rows)

**Example: A DEDUP KEY without the time column** (shows an error)

```sql
CREATE TABLE live_data (timestamp TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, ltp DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(timestamp) DEDUP KEY (symbol);
```

Result:

Error: `DEDUP KEY must include the time column 'timestamp', e.g. DEDUP KEY (symbol, timestamp), or a column GENERATED ALWAYS AS (date_trunc('minute', timestamp)) STORED`

<a id="round"></a>

## ROUND

Syntax:

```sql
column TIMESTAMP ROUND interval
interval: number + ms | s | m | h | d | w      (1m, 5m, 15m, 1h, 1d)
```

Cuts every time **down** to the interval when a row is written. `ROUND 1m` turns `11:05:42` into `11:05:00`. Use it for candles, so that times are clean and the `DEDUP KEY` finds the same minute or day.

| Unit | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ms` | milliseconds |
| `s` | seconds |
| `m` | minutes (also `M`: `ROUND` has no months) |
| `h` | hours |
| `d` | days (UTC) |
| `w` | weeks of 7 days, counted from 1970-01-01 (a **Thursday**) |

- **NULL:** a `NULL` time stays `NULL`.
- **Notes:** only for `TIMESTAMP` columns. `ROUND 1d` rounds to the **UTC** day: `2026-09-10T02:00:00+05:45` becomes `2026-09-09T00:00:00Z`. For weeks that start on Sunday, use `ROUND 1d` and [SAMPLE BY 1w](sample-by.md) in queries instead of `ROUND 1w`.

**Example: Minute candles: 11:05:42 Nepal time is stored as 05:20:00 UTC**

```sql
CREATE TABLE ochl_minutes (time TIMESTAMP ROUND 1m, symbol SYMBOL, close DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY MONTH DEDUP KEY (symbol, time);
INSERT INTO ochl_minutes VALUES ('2026-09-10T11:05:42+05:45', 'CITY', 504.8);
SELECT time, symbol, close FROM ochl_minutes;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE ochl_minutes (`

```text
table 'ochl_minutes' created
```

<a id="computed"></a>

## Computed columns: AS (expr)

Syntax:

```sql
column TYPE AS (expression)
```

A **computed** column is not stored. KarelaDB works it out from the other columns of the same row each time you read it.

- The expression uses **stored** columns of the same row, operators and built-in functions.
- You cannot give it a value in `INSERT`, and `UPDATE` cannot set it. Change the columns it is made from.
- `INSERT INTO t VALUES (...)` without a column list skips computed columns.
- To keep the value on disk (for an index, `UNIQUE` or `NOT NULL`), use a [stored generated column](#generated).
- **Notes:** a computed column cannot also have `PRIMARY KEY`, `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `DEFAULT`, `REFERENCES` or `ROUND`, and cannot be in `SORT BY`, `DEDUP KEY`, a `CHECK` or an index. No subqueries, window functions or other computed columns inside. Do not use random functions (`gen_random_uuid()`) or `now()` in it: the value changes on every read.

**Example: Trade log amount and broker commission**

```sql
CREATE TABLE trade_log (
  date TIMESTAMP ROUND 1d, transaction_id LONG, symbol SYMBOL,
  quantity LONG, rate DOUBLE,
  amount DOUBLE AS (quantity * rate),
  commission DOUBLE AS (round(quantity * rate * 0.004, 2))
) TIMESERIES(date) PARTITION BY DAY DEDUP KEY (date, transaction_id);
INSERT INTO trade_log VALUES ('2026-09-10', 100010, 'CITY', 50, 517.0);
SELECT transaction_id, quantity, rate, amount, commission FROM trade_log;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE trade_log (`

```text
table 'trade_log' created
```

`INSERT INTO trade_log VALUES ('2026-09-10', 100010, 'CITY', 50, 517.0)`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT transaction_id, quantity, rate, amount, commission FROM trade_log`

| transaction_id (LONG) | quantity (LONG) | rate (DOUBLE) | amount (DOUBLE) | commission (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100010 | 50 | 517 | 25850 | 103.4 |

(1 row)

**Example: A computed column cannot be given a value** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE trade_log (quantity LONG, rate DOUBLE, amount DOUBLE AS (quantity * rate));
```

```sql
INSERT INTO trade_log (quantity, rate, amount) VALUES (100, 515.5, 51550);
```

Result:

Error: `column 'amount' is computed (AS ...) and cannot be given a value`

**Example: A computed column that uses a missing column** (shows an error)

```sql
CREATE TABLE trade_log (quantity LONG, amount DOUBLE AS (quantity * price));
```

Result:

Error: `column 'amount' of table 'trade_log' uses column 'price' in AS (...), which does not exist in table 'trade_log'`

<a id="generated"></a>

## Stored generated columns: GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expr) STORED

Syntax:

```sql
column TYPE GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expression) STORED
column TYPE GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expression) [VIRTUAL]
```

The PostgreSQL form. With `STORED`, KarelaDB works the value out **when the row is written** and keeps it like any other column. Without `STORED` (or with `VIRTUAL`) it is a [computed column](#computed), worked out when read.

| | `AS (expr)`, `VIRTUAL` | `STORED` |
|---|---|---|
| worked out | on every read | on every write |
| takes disk space | no | yes |
| an index, `UNIQUE`, `NOT NULL`, `CHECK`, `REFERENCES` | no | yes |

- Every write works it out again: `INSERT`, `UPDATE` of a column it reads, `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`, a foreign key `ON UPDATE CASCADE`, and API and line-protocol inserts.
- You cannot give it a value in `INSERT` or `UPDATE`, as in PostgreSQL. `INSERT INTO t VALUES (...)` without a column list skips it; `COPY` without a column list too.
- `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ... GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...) STORED` fills it in for the rows already in the table (the rows are written again).
- **Notes:** it cannot be the `PRIMARY KEY`, a time-series table's time column, or in `SORT BY`, and cannot have `DEFAULT`, `AUTO` or `ROUND`. It **can** be in a `DEDUP KEY`: `date_trunc('minute', time)` there makes seconds of one minute the same row ([a key on the minute](partitions-and-dedup.md#minute-key)). The expression uses stored columns that are not generated themselves, and built-in functions only. A column it uses cannot be dropped first.
- Tables made before 2026-09-24 with `STORED` keep a computed column (worked out when read). To store it, drop the column and add it again.

**Example: An order total you can index and search**

```sql
CREATE TABLE order_lines (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY, qty INT, price DECIMAL(2),
  total DECIMAL(2) GENERATED ALWAYS AS (qty * price) STORED
);
CREATE INDEX order_lines_total ON order_lines (total);
INSERT INTO order_lines (id, qty, price) VALUES (1, 2, 1.50), (2, 4, 2.00);
UPDATE order_lines SET qty = 3 WHERE id = 1;
SELECT id, qty, price, total FROM order_lines WHERE total > 4 ORDER BY id;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE order_lines (`

```text
table 'order_lines' created
```

`CREATE INDEX order_lines_total ON order_lines (total)`

```text
index 'order_lines_total' created on table 'order_lines' (0 rows)
```

`INSERT INTO order_lines (id, qty, price) VALUES (1, 2, 1.50), (2, 4, 2.00)`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`UPDATE order_lines SET qty = 3 WHERE id = 1`

```text
1 row(s) updated
```

`SELECT id, qty, price, total FROM order_lines WHERE total > 4 ORDER BY id`

| id (INT) | qty (INT) | price (DECIMAL(2)) | total (DECIMAL(2)) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3 | 1.50 | 4.50 |
| 2 | 4 | 2.00 | 8.00 |

(2 rows)

**Example: A stored generated column cannot be given a value** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql

```

```sql

```

Error: `column 'total' is GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...) STORED and cannot be set; KarelaDB works it out from the row`

<a id="row-ttl"></a>

## Rows that expire: WITH (ttl_column = ...)

Syntax:

```sql
CREATE TABLE name (..., expires_at TIMESTAMP, ...) WITH (ttl_column = expires_at)
```

Each row can have its own end of life, like a Redis key with `EXPIRE`. When the time in `expires_at` has come, the row is **gone at once** for every statement, and a background thread deletes it within about a second. Use it for login sessions, rate-limit counters, caches and short-lived tokens.

| `expires_at` is | the row is |
|---|---|
| later than now | there |
| now or earlier | gone: no `SELECT`, join, `UPDATE` or `DELETE` sees it |
| `NULL` | there for ever |

- An `INSERT` of an expired row's key is a new row, not an "already exists" error. `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` starts a fresh row, so a counter that expires counts from 1 again.
- To keep a row alive longer, `UPDATE` its `expires_at`.
- The deletes are ordinary deletes: they are in the log, and `DELETE` [triggers](triggers.md) see the rows.
- **Notes:** the column must be a stored `TIMESTAMP`. It cannot be dropped while the table has the option, and the option is set by `CREATE TABLE` only (`ALTER TABLE ... SET (ttl_column = ...)` is refused for now). A database with such a table needs KarelaDB 2026-09-25 or later ([versions](versions.md)).
- **Speed:** a read of such a table checks the time on each row and never comes from the [result cache](performance-tips.md#result-cache). The table's `TTL n DAYS` (whole partitions) is a different, older option: [SET TTL](alter-table.md#set-ttl).

**Example: Sessions that expire, and a counter that starts again**

```sql
CREATE TABLE sessions (
  token      STRING PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id    LONG,
  hits       LONG,
  expires_at TIMESTAMP
) WITH (ttl_column = expires_at);
INSERT INTO sessions VALUES ('old', 1, 5, '2020-01-01T00:00:00Z'), ('new', 2, 1, '2099-01-01T00:00:00Z'), ('api', 3, 0, NULL);
SELECT token, user_id FROM sessions ORDER BY token;
INSERT INTO sessions VALUES ('old', 1, 1, '2099-01-01T00:00:00Z')
  ON CONFLICT (token) DO UPDATE SET hits = sessions.hits + 1 RETURNING hits;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE sessions (`

```text
table 'sessions' created
```

`INSERT INTO sessions VALUES ('old', 1, 5, '2020-01-01T00:00:00Z'), ('new', 2, 1, '2099-01-01T00:00:0`

```text
3 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT token, user_id FROM sessions ORDER BY token`

| token (STRING) | user_id (LONG) |
|---|---|
| api | 3 |
| new | 2 |

(2 rows)

`INSERT INTO sessions VALUES ('old', 1, 1, '2099-01-01T00:00:00Z') ON CONFLICT (token) DO UPDATE SET `

| hits (LONG) |
|---|
| 1 |

(1 row)

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

<a id="cache-table"></a>

## Cache tables: WITH (max_bytes, evict, durability)

Syntax:

```sql
CREATE TABLE name (key ... PRIMARY KEY, ...)
  WITH (max_bytes = '64MB' [, evict = 'lru'] [, durability = 'none'])
ALTER TABLE name SET (max_bytes = '128MB')
ALTER TABLE name RESET (max_bytes)
```

A **cache table** has a memory cap, like Redis with `maxmemory`. When its rows take more than `max_bytes`, a background thread deletes rows until it fits again (within about a second), in the order `evict` says:

| `evict` | Rows that go first | Redis name |
|---|---|---|
| `'lru'` (the default with a cap) | the rows read or written longest ago | `allkeys-lru` |
| `'volatile_lru'` | the same, but only rows that expire | `volatile-lru` |
| `'random'` | any rows | `allkeys-random` |
| `'volatile_random'` | any rows that expire | `volatile-random` |
| `'volatile_ttl'` | the rows that [expire](#row-ttl) soonest | `volatile-ttl` |
| `'none'` | nothing (no cap) | `noeviction` |

| Option | Means |
|---|---|
| `max_bytes` | the cap: `'64MB'`, `'512KB'`, `'1GB'` or a number of bytes; `0` = no cap |
| `durability = 'none'` | the table is **emptied every time the database opens** (Redis `appendonly no`), for data you can rebuild |
| `durability = 'log'` | rows survive a restart (the default) |

- `SELECT kv_memory('name')` answers the bytes the table holds, as last measured. A row counts the bytes of its values (text by its length, numbers and times 8 bytes) plus 48 bytes.
- A row is "used" when a statement reads it row by row (a look-up by key, `SELECT ... WHERE`) or writes it. Aggregates over many rows (`count(*)`, `sum`) do not count as a use.
- **Needs:** a `PRIMARY KEY` for any `evict`; a [ttl_column](#row-ttl) for the `volatile_` ones. The evicting deletes are ordinary deletes: they are in the log and `DELETE` triggers see them.
- The key-value store has the same cap: `CONFIG SET maxmemory 64mb` ([kv](kv.md#kv-memory)).
- A database with a cache table needs KarelaDB 2026-10-02 or later ([versions](versions.md)).

**Example: A cache of 1 MB that keeps the rows in use**

```sql
CREATE TABLE page_cache (url STRING PRIMARY KEY, html STRING)
  WITH (max_bytes = '1MB', evict = 'lru');
INSERT INTO page_cache VALUES ('/', '<h1>home</h1>'), ('/about', '<h1>about</h1>');
SELECT html FROM page_cache WHERE url = '/';
ALTER TABLE page_cache SET (max_bytes = '4MB', durability = 'none');
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE page_cache (`

```text
table 'page_cache' created
```

`INSERT INTO page_cache VALUES ('/', '<h1>home</h1>'), ('/about', '<h1>about</h1>')`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT html FROM page_cache WHERE url = '/'`

| html (STRING) |
|---|
| <h1>home</h1> |

(1 row)

`ALTER TABLE page_cache SET (max_bytes = 4194304, durability = 'none')`

```text
table 'page_cache': max_bytes = 4194304, evict = 'lru', durability = 'none' (emptied every time the database opens)
```

# Column types

> Every column type, its range, how NULL is kept, and which values it accepts.

- Category: Tables
- Keywords: data type, type, types, column type, conversion, convert value, range, overflow, out of range, NULL storage, money, exact, precision, BOOL, BOOLEAN, BYTE, SHORT, INT, INTEGER, LONG, BIGINT, FLOAT, DOUBLE, DECIMAL, NUMERIC, DATE, TIMESTAMP, SYMBOL, STRING, VARCHAR, TEXT, JSON, JSONB, BYTES, BYTEA, BLOB, UUID, gen\_random\_uuid, ENUM, CREATE TYPE, ALTER TYPE, DROP TYPE, pg\_enum, label, hex, utf-8, time zone, +05:45, milliseconds
- See also: [CREATE TABLE](create-table.md), [INSERT](insert.md), [Conversion functions](functions-conversion.md), [Time and time zones](time-and-time-zones.md), [SQL basics](sql-basics.md)

Every column has a **type**. The type says what values the column holds, and how much space one value takes. When a row is written, KarelaDB **converts** each value to the column type, or refuses the row with a clear message.

| Type | Also written | Size | Values | Use it for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [`BOOL`](#bool) | `BOOLEAN` | 1 byte | `TRUE`, `FALSE` | yes/no flags |
| [`BYTE`](#byte) | | 1 byte | -127 to 127 | very small numbers |
| [`SHORT`](#short) | | 2 bytes | -32767 to 32767 | small numbers |
| [`INT`](#int) | `INTEGER` | 4 bytes | -2147483647 to 2147483647 | broker ids, counts |
| [`LONG`](#long) | `BIGINT` | 8 bytes | about ±9.2 × 10^18 | ids, share quantities |
| [`FLOAT`](#float) | | 4 bytes | about 7 digits | rarely needed |
| [`DOUBLE`](#double) | | 8 bytes | about 15 digits | prices, volumes, indicators |
| [`DECIMAL(s)`](#decimal) | | 8 bytes | exact, up to 18 digits, `s` after the point | **money** |
| [`NUMERIC(p, s)`](#decimal) | `DECIMAL(p, s)` | 8 or 16 bytes | exact, up to 38 digits | big money totals, TPoint |
| [`DATE`](#date) | | 4 bytes | a day | birthdays, report dates |
| [`TIMESTAMP`](#timestamp) | | 8 bytes | a moment in UTC, in milliseconds | candle and trade times |
| [`SYMBOL`](#symbol) | | 4 bytes | text that repeats a lot | stock symbols, sectors |
| [`STRING`](#string) | `VARCHAR`, `TEXT` | length + text | any text, up to 16 MB | names, posts, news |
| [`JSON`](#json) | `JSONB` | length + text | checked JSON, up to 16 MB | flexible extra data |
| [`BYTES`](#bytes) | `BYTEA`, `BLOB` | length + bytes | any bytes, up to 16 MB | hashes, keys, small files |
| [`UUID`](#uuid) | | 16 bytes | a UUID like `a0eebc99-9c0b-4ef8-bb6d-6bb9bd380a11` | ids made by apps, `gen_random_uuid()` |
| [an ENUM type](#enum) | made by `CREATE TYPE ... AS ENUM` | 4 bytes | one label of a fixed list | order status, moods, levels |

- Every type can hold `NULL`. For number types, the smallest value is used to keep `NULL`. That is why `BYTE` goes to -127, not -128.
- Type names do not care about case. `VARCHAR(100)` with a length is **not** accepted: write `STRING`.
- You cannot change the type of a column later ([ALTER TABLE](alter-table.md)).
- To convert in a query, use `CAST(x AS TYPE)` or `x::TYPE`; see [conversion functions](functions-conversion.md).

**Example: All basic types in one table**

```sql
CREATE TABLE type_demo (
  b BOOL, i8 BYTE, i16 SHORT, i32 INT, i64 LONG, f FLOAT, d DOUBLE, m DECIMAL(2),
  day DATE, ts TIMESTAMP, sym SYMBOL, txt STRING
);
INSERT INTO type_demo VALUES
  (TRUE, 127, 32767, 2147483647, 270578640, 1.5, 512.45, 1500.25,
   '2026-09-10', '2026-09-10T11:00:00+05:45', 'CITY', 'City Bank Limited'),
  (NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL);
SELECT * FROM type_demo;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE type_demo (`

```text
table 'type_demo' created
```

`INSERT INTO type_demo VALUES (TRUE, 127, 32767, 2147483647, 270578640, 1.5, 512.45, 1500.25, '2026-0`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT * FROM type_demo`

| b (BOOL) | i8 (BYTE) | i16 (SHORT) | i32 (INT) | i64 (LONG) | f (FLOAT) | d (DOUBLE) | m (DECIMAL(2)) | day (DATE) | ts (TIMESTAMP) | sym (SYMBOL) | txt (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| true | 127 | 32767 | 2147483647 | 270578640 | 1.5 | 512.45 | 1500.25 | 2026-09-10 | 2026-09-10T05:15:00.000Z | CITY | City Bank Limited |
| NULL | NULL | NULL | NULL | NULL | NULL | NULL | NULL | NULL | NULL | NULL | NULL |

(2 rows)

<a id="bool"></a>

## BOOL, BOOLEAN

Syntax:

```sql
column BOOL
column BOOLEAN
```

`TRUE` or `FALSE`.

| Value written | Stored as |
|---|---|
| `TRUE`, `FALSE` | itself |
| `1`, `0` | `TRUE`, `FALSE` |
| `'true'`, `'false'`, `'t'`, `'f'`, `'1'`, `'0'` (any case) | `TRUE`, `FALSE` |
| anything else (`2`, `1.0`, `'yes'`) | error |

- **NULL:** `NULL` is allowed unless the column is `NOT NULL`; it is kept as a special third value.
- **Notes:** in a query, a `BOOL` is not a number: `TRUE = 1` is an error.

**Example: Verified users, written in different ways**

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, verified BOOL, is_admin BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE);
INSERT INTO users (id, verified) VALUES (1, TRUE), (2, 0), (3, 'true'), (4, NULL);
SELECT id, verified, is_admin FROM users;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE users (`

```text
table 'users' created
```

`INSERT INTO users (id, verified) VALUES (1, TRUE), (2, 0), (3, 'true'), (4, NULL)`

```text
4 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT id, verified, is_admin FROM users`

| id (INT) | verified (BOOL) | is_admin (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | true | false |
| 2 | false | false |
| 3 | true | false |
| 4 | NULL | false |

(4 rows)

**Example: 'yes' is not a BOOL** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, verified BOOL);
```

```sql

```

Result:

Error: `column 'verified' (BOOL): 'yes' is not true or false`

## BYTE

Syntax:

```sql

```

- **NULL:** kept as -128, so -128 itself cannot be stored.
- Accepts the same values as [INT](#int).

**Example: Star rating of a forum post**


<a id="int"></a>

## INT, INTEGER

Syntax:

```sql
column INT
column INTEGER
```

A whole number from -2147483647 to 2147483647, in 4 bytes.

| Value written | Stored as |
|---|---|
| a whole number: `42`, `-7` | itself |
| a `DOUBLE` with no fraction: `5.0`, `1e3` | `5`, `1000` |
| a `DECIMAL` with no fraction: `12.00` | `12` |
| text with a whole number: `'42'` | `42` |
| `TRUE`, `FALSE` | `1`, `0` |
| `5.5`, `'5.0'`, `'abc'` | error: not a whole number |
| a number outside the range | error: out of range |

- **NULL:** kept as the smallest `INT` (-2147483648).
- **Notes:** use `LONG` when a number might grow past 2 billion (ids of a big table, share quantities, money in cents).

**Example: Broker ids written as numbers and as text**

```sql
CREATE TABLE brokers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING, branch_count INTEGER);
INSERT INTO brokers VALUES (58, 'Northgate Securities', 5), ('45', 'Imperial Securities', 2.0);
SELECT id, name, branch_count FROM brokers ORDER BY id;
```

Result:

|---|---|---|

<a id="long"></a>

## LONG, BIGINT

Syntax:

```sql
column LONG
column BIGINT
```

A whole number from -9223372036854775807 to 9223372036854775807, in 8 bytes.

- Accepts the same values as [INT](#int).
- **NULL:** kept as the smallest `LONG` (-9223372036854775808).
- **Notes:** a good type for `PRIMARY KEY AUTO` ids, transaction numbers and share quantities.

**Example: Transaction ids and quantities**

```sql
CREATE TABLE trades (transaction_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, quantity LONG);
INSERT INTO trades VALUES (2026091000012345, 270578640);
SELECT transaction_id, quantity FROM trades;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE trades (`


<a id="float"></a>

## FLOAT

Syntax:

```sql
column FLOAT
```

A number with a fraction, in 4 bytes. It keeps about **7** digits, so `512.45` comes back as `512.450012207031`.

- Accepts numbers and text like `'512.5'`. Bigger than about 3.4e38 is an error.
- **NULL:** kept as NaN (not a number).
- **Notes:** use `DOUBLE` for prices. `FLOAT` only saves space when you have very many rows and need few digits. Indexes are not used on `FLOAT` columns.

**Example: FLOAT keeps fewer digits than DOUBLE**

```sql
CREATE TABLE t (f FLOAT, d DOUBLE);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (512.45, 512.45);
SELECT f, d FROM t;
```


`INSERT INTO t VALUES (512.45, 512.45)`


| f (FLOAT) | d (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|
| 512.450012207031 | 512.45 |

(1 row)

<a id="double"></a>

## DOUBLE

Syntax:

```sql
column DOUBLE
```

A number with a fraction, in 8 bytes, with about **15** digits. Fast, and good for prices, volumes, percentages and indicators.

- Accepts numbers, `DECIMAL` values and text like `'512.5'` or `'1.5e3'`.
- **NULL:** kept as NaN.
- **Notes:** a `DOUBLE` is **not exact**: `0.1 + 0.2` is not exactly `0.3`. For money that must add up exactly, use [DECIMAL](#decimal). In a **relational table** a NaN is stored as NaN, as in PostgreSQL: the text `'NaN'`, a NaN an expression makes (`CAST('NaN' AS DOUBLE)`, `x * 'NaN'`) and a driver's NaN parameter. It is shown as `NaN` and is **not** `IS NULL`; write `NULL` for a missing value. (Before 2026-09-25 a NaN from an expression was stored as `NULL`.) The HTTP API writes NaN and infinities as JSON `null` unless you ask for `?nan=string` ([/exec](http-exec.md)).
- **NaN in a time-series table:** stored as `NULL`, as QuestDB does (since 2026-10-02). So `open IS NULL OR open <= 0`, the price guard written for QuestDB, also finds a bar whose price came in as NaN. A [CHECK](constraints.md#check) still sees the NaN first and refuses it, and a `NOT NULL` column refuses it too. Rows written before 2026-10-02 keep their NaN.
- **NaN in comparisons:** as in PostgreSQL, a NaN equals only another NaN and is **bigger than every number**, `Infinity` too: `100 = 'NaN'` is false, `'NaN' > 0` is true, `ORDER BY` puts NaN after every number, and `max()` of a column with a NaN is NaN. In `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT`, `count(DISTINCT x)`, `UNION` and `PARTITION BY` all NaNs make one group of their own, apart from the NULLs. A [CHECK](constraints.md#check) is stricter: there every comparison with a NaN is false, so `CHECK (price > 0)` keeps it out. Find NaN with [is_nan(x)](functions-math.md#is_nan) or `x = 'NaN'`.

**Example: Prices, and why DOUBLE is not for money**

```sql
CREATE TABLE prices (symbol SYMBOL, ltp DOUBLE, pct_change DOUBLE);
INSERT INTO prices VALUES ('CITY', 527.1, '2.71'), ('COAST', 401.9, 0.7);
SELECT symbol, ltp, pct_change FROM prices;
SELECT 0.1 + 0.2 AS sum, 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3 AS equal;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE prices (`

```text
table 'prices' created
```

`INSERT INTO prices VALUES ('CITY', 527.1, '2.71'), ('COAST', 401.9, 0.7)`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT symbol, ltp, pct_change FROM prices`

| symbol (SYMBOL) | ltp (DOUBLE) | pct_change (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| CITY | 527.1 | 2.71 |
| COAST | 401.9 | 0.7 |

(2 rows)

`SELECT 0.1 + 0.2 AS sum, 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3 AS equal`

<a id="decimal"></a>

## DECIMAL(s)

Syntax:

```sql
column DECIMAL(scale)
column NUMERIC(precision, scale)
```

An **exact** number with `scale` digits after the point. `DECIMAL(2)` is right for dollars and cents: `0.10 + 0.20` is exactly `0.30`.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `scale` | 0 to 18 (`DECIMAL(s)`), 0 to 38 (`NUMERIC(p, s)`) | digits after the point |
| `precision` | 1 to 38 | all digits. Up to 18 the value takes 8 bytes; more takes 16 |

| Value written | Stored as (`DECIMAL(2)`) |
|---|---|
| `1500.25`, `12`, `'99.5'`, `'1.500'` | `1500.25`, `12.00`, `99.50`, `1.50` |
| more digits after the point: `10.555` | **error**: KarelaDB never rounds money by itself |
| more than 18 digits: `123456789012345678.12` | error (`numeric value out of range`): use `NUMERIC(24,2)` |

- **NULL:** a `DECIMAL(s)` keeps it as the smallest `LONG`; a 16-byte `NUMERIC` keeps a flag.
- **Math is exact**, as in PostgreSQL. `DECIMAL` with `DECIMAL`, a whole number or a written decimal (`balance * 1.15`) gives a `DECIMAL`: `+` and `-` keep the larger scale, `*` adds the scales, `/` gives at least 16 significant digits (`10.00 / 3` is `3.3333333333333333`). A `DOUBLE` on either side gives a `DOUBLE`.
- **Notes:** `sum` is exact up to 38 digits, also past 64 bits. `avg` is exact too: `avg` of `1.50` and `2.50` is `2.0000000000000000`. `round(x, 2)` of a `DECIMAL` rounds half away from zero and stays `DECIMAL`.
- **Notes:** a result past 38 digits is an error (`numeric value out of range`, SQLSTATE `22003`), never a rounded number.
- **Notes:** a `NUMERIC(p, s)` column rounds extra places half away from zero (PostgreSQL does too), and refuses more than `p - s` digits before the point (`numeric field overflow`). `DECIMAL(s)` refuses extra places.
- **Notes:** a number written with more than 15 digits (`123456789012345678.12`) is read exactly, not as a `DOUBLE`.
- **Notes:** a table made from a query (`CREATE TABLE ... AS`, a materialized view) stores `avg` or a division of a `DECIMAL` as a `DOUBLE`: their places change with the values, so no one scale fits later rows. A `sum` is stored as `NUMERIC(38, s)`. Write `round(avg(x), 2)` or a cast to keep a `DECIMAL` of your own places.
- **Notes:** the line protocol writes a float field (`price=12.34`) exactly. A field with more places than the column (`1.2100000000000002`, as some clients print doubles) is rounded to the column's places when it is that close to them.
- **Notes:** a result written back to a `DECIMAL(2)` column (`UPDATE ... SET balance = balance * 1.015`) must fit its 2 places. Round it the way your rule says: `round(balance * 1.015, 2)`.

**Example: A wallet balance: exact money**

```sql
CREATE TABLE wallet (id INT PRIMARY KEY, balance DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO wallet VALUES (1, 1000.00), (2, '0.10');
UPDATE wallet SET balance = balance - 250.50 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE wallet SET balance = balance + 0.20 WHERE id = 2;
SELECT id, balance FROM wallet ORDER BY id;
SELECT sum(balance) AS total FROM wallet;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE wallet (`


```text

```

```text

```

`UPDATE wallet SET balance = balance + 0.20 WHERE id = 2`

```text
1 row(s) updated
```

| id (INT) | balance (DECIMAL(2)) |
|---|---|

<a id="date"></a>

## DATE

Syntax:

```sql
column DATE
```

A calendar day without a time, like `2026-09-10`, in 4 bytes (days since 1970-01-01).

| Value written | Stored as |
|---|---|
| `'2026-09-10'` | that day |
| a time as text: `'2026-09-10T20:00:00+05:45'` | the **UTC** date of that time (here 2026-09-10, because 20:00 Nepal time is 14:15 UTC) |
| a `TIMESTAMP` | its UTC date |
| a number, `'10/09/2026'`, `'2026-9-10'` | error |

- **NULL:** kept as the smallest `INT`.
- **Notes:** `date + 1` is the next day. Shown as `2026-09-10`. A `DATE` can be the time column of a time-series table.

**Example: Company listing dates and report dates**

```sql
CREATE TABLE companies (symbol STRING PRIMARY KEY, listed_on DATE, last_report DATE);
INSERT INTO companies VALUES ('CITY', '1985-07-12', '2026-07-16'), ('VOLT', '2019-01-21', NULL);
SELECT symbol, listed_on, last_report, last_report + 90 AS next_report_due FROM companies;
```

Result:

|---|---|---|---|
| CITY | 1985-07-12 | 2026-07-16 | 2026-10-14 |

<a id="timestamp"></a>

## TIMESTAMP

Syntax:

```sql
column TIMESTAMP [ROUND interval]
```

A moment in time, stored as milliseconds since 1970-01-01 **UTC**, in 8 bytes. KarelaDB always shows it in UTC with a `Z`: `2026-09-10T05:15:00.000Z`.

| Value written | Read as |
|---|---|
| `'2026-09-10T11:00:00+05:45'` (or `+0545`) | 11:00 Nepal time = 05:15 UTC |
| `'2026-09-10T07:00:00-04:00'` | 07:00 New York summer time = 11:00 UTC |
| `'2026-09-10 11:00:00'` (no zone) | 11:00 **UTC** (not local time!) |
| `'2026-09-10T11:00:00Z'` | 11:00 UTC |
| `'2026-09-10'` | 00:00 UTC |
| `'2026-09-10T05:15:00.250Z'` | with milliseconds; more than 3 digits are cut |
| `1789017300000` | milliseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC |
| a `DATE` | 00:00 UTC of that day |
| `'10/09/2026'`, `'2026-9-10'`, `'2026-02-30'`, `1.5`, `TRUE` | error |

- **NULL:** kept as the smallest `LONG`. A time-series table needs a value in its time column.
- **Notes:** **always add the zone offset to a local time**, for example `+05:45` for Nepal or `-04:00` for New York in summer. Without it, the time is read as UTC and is wrong by the offset. `ROUND` cuts times down when they are written; see [ROUND](create-table.md#round). More in [time and time zones](time-and-time-zones.md).

**Example: The same market open (11:00 in Nepal) written in different ways**

```sql
CREATE TABLE time_test (time TIMESTAMP, note STRING);
INSERT INTO time_test VALUES
  ('2026-09-10T11:00:00+05:45', 'Nepal time with +05:45'),
  ('2026-09-10T11:00:00+0545',  'Nepal time without the colon'),
  ('2026-09-10 05:15:00',       'no zone = UTC'),
  ('2026-09-10T05:15:00Z',      'Z = UTC'),
  (1789017300000,               'milliseconds since 1970'),
  ('2026-09-10T11:00:00',       'Nepal time WITHOUT +05:45: wrong');
SELECT time, note FROM time_test;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE time_test (`

```text
table 'time_test' created
```

`INSERT INTO time_test VALUES ('2026-09-10T11:00:00+05:45', 'Nepal time with +05:45'), ('2026-09-10T1`

```text
6 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT time, note FROM time_test`

| time (TIMESTAMP) | note (STRING) |
|---|---|
| 2026-09-10T05:15:00.000Z | Nepal time with +05:45 |
| 2026-09-10T05:15:00.000Z | Nepal time without the colon |
| 2026-09-10T05:15:00.000Z | no zone = UTC |
| 2026-09-10T05:15:00.000Z | Z = UTC |
| 2026-09-10T05:15:00.000Z | milliseconds since 1970 |
| 2026-09-10T11:00:00.000Z | Nepal time WITHOUT +05:45: wrong |

<a id="symbol"></a>

## SYMBOL

Syntax:

```sql
column SYMBOL
```

Text that repeats a lot, like stock symbols, sectors or order types. Each different text is kept once in a list; every row keeps only a 4-byte number that points into the list. So a `SYMBOL` column of millions of rows is small and fast to compare.

- Accepts anything; numbers, `BOOL` values and times are written as text.
- **NULL:** `NULL` is allowed; it is kept as a special number that is not in the list.
- **Notes:** in queries a `SYMBOL` works like text. A `REFERENCES` from a `SYMBOL` column may point to a `STRING` key. Use `STRING` for text that is different in almost every row (names, messages): the list would get as big as the table. The default [SORT BY](create-table.md#sort-by) of a time-series table starts with its first `SYMBOL` column.

**Example: Symbols and sectors**

```sql
CREATE TABLE securities (symbol SYMBOL PRIMARY KEY, name STRING NOT NULL, sector SYMBOL);
INSERT INTO securities VALUES ('CITY', 'City Bank Limited', 'Banking'), ('COAST', 'Coastal Bank Limited', 'Banking');
SELECT sector, count(*) AS companies FROM securities GROUP BY sector;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE securities (`

```text
table 'securities' created
```

`INSERT INTO securities VALUES ('CITY', 'City Bank Limited', 'Banking'), ('COAST', 'Coastal Bank Limi`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT sector, count(*) AS companies FROM securities GROUP BY sector`

| sector (SYMBOL) | companies (LONG) |
|---|---|
| Banking | 2 |

(1 row)

<a id="enum"></a>

## ENUM types (CREATE TYPE)

Syntax:

```sql
CREATE TYPE name AS ENUM ('label', 'label', ...)
ALTER TYPE name ADD VALUE [IF NOT EXISTS] 'label' [BEFORE | AFTER 'label']
DROP TYPE [IF EXISTS] name [, name ...]
column name
```

A fixed list of labels, as in PostgreSQL. You make the type once, then use its name as a column type. A column of the type takes **only** its labels. It is kept like a [`SYMBOL`](#symbol): 4 bytes a row.

| Rule | What happens |
|---|---|
| Value | must be one of the labels, exactly (case counts); anything else is refused with `invalid input value for enum ...` (Postgres code `22P02`) |
| Order | `ORDER BY`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `BETWEEN` follow the order the labels were listed in, not the alphabet. This works through a view, a subquery and a `WITH` query too. The other side is a label: `'paid'`, `'paid'::order_status` or `CAST('paid' AS order_status)`. Against another column or an expression, the text is compared |
| Cast | `'happy'::mood` and `CAST('happy' AS mood)` check the label too |
| New label | `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE` puts it at the end, or `BEFORE` / `AFTER` a label |
| Change type | `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN c TYPE other_type` checks every row: it is refused if a row holds a value that is not a label of the new type |
| Drop | `DROP TYPE` is refused while a column uses the type (code `2BP01`); drop or change the column first |

- **NULL:** `NULL` is allowed unless the column is `NOT NULL`.
- **Notes:** a label is 1 to 63 bytes. Labels cannot be renamed or removed: rows already hold them. `min()` and `max()` still compare the text. Arrays of an ENUM type are not supported (use `TEXT[]`). `pg_type` lists the type (`typtype` `'e'`) and `pg_enum` its labels; the Postgres port sends a column of the type as text, under the type's own oid ([types](postgres-protocol.md#types)).

**Example: Order status in the order the order moves**

```sql
CREATE TYPE order_status AS ENUM ('new', 'paid', 'shipped', 'delivered');
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, status order_status NOT NULL DEFAULT 'new');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'shipped'), (2, 'new'), (3, 'delivered'), (4, 'paid');
SELECT id, status FROM orders ORDER BY status;
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status >= 'shipped' ORDER BY id;
```

Result:

`CREATE TYPE order_status AS ENUM ('new', 'paid', 'shipped', 'delivered')`

```text
type 'order_status' created
```

`CREATE TABLE orders (`

```text
table 'orders' created
```

`INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'shipped'), (2, 'new'), (3, 'delivered'), (4, 'paid')`

```text
4 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT id, status FROM orders ORDER BY status`

| id (INT) | status (SYMBOL) |
|---|---|
| 2 | new |
| 4 | paid |
| 1 | shipped |
| 3 | delivered |

(4 rows)

`SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status >= 'shipped' ORDER BY id`

| id (INT) |
|---|
| 1 |
| 3 |

(2 rows)

**Example: Label order through a view, with a cast**

<a id="string"></a>

## STRING, VARCHAR, TEXT

Syntax:

```sql
column STRING
column VARCHAR
column TEXT
```

Any text in UTF-8 (any language: English, Nepali, Chinese, emoji), up to 16 MB per value. `VARCHAR` and `TEXT` are the same type.

- Accepts anything; a number, `BOOL` or time is written as its text (`12` becomes `'12'`, a time becomes `'2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z'`).
- **NULL:** `NULL` is allowed; it is kept as a special length. The empty text `''` is not `NULL`.
- **Notes:** KarelaDB has no length limit on text. `VARCHAR(255)` is **read and the number ignored**, so a PostgreSQL script runs; nothing is cut at 255. Keep PDF files and images outside the database, and store their path or URL.

**Example: A news article in two languages**

```sql
CREATE TABLE news (id LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO, lang STRING NOT NULL DEFAULT 'en', title VARCHAR NOT NULL, body TEXT NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO news (lang, title, body) VALUES
  ('en', 'City Bank profit rises 18%', 'City Bank reported a net profit of $3.27 billion.'),
  ('ne', 'सिटी बैंकको नाफा बढ्यो', 'सिटी बैंकले ३.२७ अर्ब नाफा कमायो।');
SELECT id, lang, title FROM news ORDER BY id;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE news (`

```text
table 'news' created
```

`INSERT INTO news (lang, title, body) VALUES ('en', 'City Bank profit rises 18%', 'City Bank reported`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT id, lang, title FROM news ORDER BY id`

| id (LONG) | lang (STRING) | title (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | en | City Bank profit rises 18% |
| 2 | ne | सिटी बैंकको नाफा बढ्यो |

(2 rows)

**Example: VARCHAR(255): the number is read and ignored**

Setup:


<a id="json"></a>

## JSON, JSONB

Syntax:

```sql
column JSON
column JSONB
```

A JSON document (objects, arrays, text, numbers, `true`, `false`, `null`), up to 16 MB. `JSONB` is the same type. KarelaDB checks that the text is valid JSON and removes the spaces between the parts.

| Value written | Stored as |
|---|---|
| JSON text: `'{ "a" : 1 }'` | `{"a":1}` (keys stay in their order; numbers keep their digits, `2.50` stays `2.50`) |
| a number or `TRUE`/`FALSE` | `5`, `true` |
| bad JSON: `'{"a": 1,}'`, `'hello'` | error with the character position |

- **NULL:** SQL `NULL` is allowed (kept as a special length). The JSON text `'null'` is a JSON value, not SQL `NULL`: `IS NULL` is false for it.
- **Notes:** read parts with `->`, `->>` and `json_value(...)`; change them with `json_set(...)`. See [chapter 18](../tutorial/18-content-data.md). Two JSON values are equal only when their text is equal, so `{"a":1,"b":2}` is not equal to `{"b":2,"a":1}`. The examples below show JSON with `CAST(... AS STRING)`, so you see the exact stored text.

**Example: Company profiles that differ per company**

```sql
CREATE TABLE companies (symbol STRING PRIMARY KEY, profile JSON DEFAULT '{}');
INSERT INTO companies VALUES
  ('CITY', '{ "head_office": "Kathmandu", "branches": 270 }'),
  ('VOLT', '{"capacity_mw": 456, "rivers": ["Volt River"]}');
INSERT INTO companies (symbol) VALUES ('COAST');
SELECT symbol, CAST(profile AS STRING) AS profile, profile ->> 'head_office' AS office FROM companies ORDER BY symbol;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE companies (`

```text
table 'companies' created
```

`INSERT INTO companies VALUES ('CITY', '{ "head_office": "Kathmandu", "branches": 270 }'), ('VOLT', '`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`INSERT INTO companies (symbol) VALUES ('COAST')`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT symbol, CAST(profile AS STRING) AS profile, profile ->> 'head_office' AS office FROM companie`

| symbol (STRING) | profile (STRING) | office (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| CITY | {"head_office":"Kathmandu","branches":270} | Kathmandu |
| COAST | {} | NULL |
| VOLT | {"capacity_mw":456,"rivers":["Volt River"]} | NULL |

(3 rows)

**Example: JSON of different kinds, and JSON null**

```sql

```

<a id="bytes"></a>

## BYTES, BYTEA, BLOB

Syntax:

```sql
column BYTES
column BYTEA
column BLOB
X'0A0B'    '\x0a0b'
```

Any bytes, also zero bytes, up to 16 MB. `BYTEA` and `BLOB` are the same type. Good for password salts, SHA-256 hashes, keys, signatures and small images.

| Value written | Stored as |
|---|---|
| `X'0A0B'` (hex, right after the `X`) | the bytes 0A 0B |
| `'\x0a0b'` (text that starts with `\x`) | the bytes 0A 0B |
| other text: `'hi'` | its UTF-8 bytes (68 69) |
| a number | error |

- **NULL:** `NULL` is allowed (kept as a special length). `X''` is zero bytes, not `NULL`.
- **Notes:** KarelaDB **shows** bytes as `\x` and hex (`\x0a0b`), in the shell, in CSV and in the HTTP API, like PostgreSQL. On `BYTES`, `length()` counts bytes. Functions: `hex()`, `unhex()`, `to_base64()`, `from_base64()`.

**Example: The SHA-256 hash of a report PDF**

```sql
CREATE TABLE reports (id LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO, pdf_url STRING, pdf_sha256 BYTES);
INSERT INTO reports (pdf_url, pdf_sha256) VALUES
  ('https://files.example.com/city/2082-83-q4.pdf', X'9F86D081884C7D659A2FEAA0C55AD015A3BF4F1B2B0B822CD15D6C15B0F00A08'),
  ('https://files.example.com/volt/2082-83-q4.pdf', NULL);
SELECT id, pdf_sha256, length(pdf_sha256) AS bytes FROM reports ORDER BY id;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE reports (`

```text
table 'reports' created
```

`INSERT INTO reports (pdf_url, pdf_sha256) VALUES ('https://files.example.com/city/2082-83-q4.pdf', u`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT id, pdf_sha256, length(pdf_sha256) AS bytes FROM reports ORDER BY id`

| id (LONG) | pdf_sha256 (BYTES) | bytes (LONG) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | \\x9f86d081884c7d659a2feaa0c55ad015a3bf4f1b2b0b822cd15d6c15b0f00a08 | 32 |
| 2 | NULL | NULL |

(2 rows)

<a id="uuid"></a>

## UUID

Syntax:

```sql
column UUID
'a0eebc99-9c0b-4ef8-bb6d-6bb9bd380a11'::uuid
```

A UUID, kept in **16 bytes** (as text it would take 36 characters and more). It reads back as text: 36 lower-case characters with dashes, as in PostgreSQL.

| Value written | Stored as |
|---|---|
| `'a0eebc99-9c0b-4ef8-bb6d-6bb9bd380a11'` | itself |
| upper case, `{...}` braces, or the 32 digits without dashes | the same UUID: `a0eebc99-9c0b-4ef8-bb6d-6bb9bd380a11` |
| `gen_random_uuid()` | a new random UUID (version 4) |
| text that is no UUID: `'abc'` | error `invalid input syntax for type uuid` (SQLSTATE 22P02) |

- **NULL:** `NULL` is allowed (kept in a flag, not in the 16 bytes).
- **Compare and find:** `id = 'A0EEBC99-...'` finds the row in any spelling. `ORDER BY` sorts like the text. A `PRIMARY KEY`, `DEDUP KEY` or index on a UUID column works like on text.
- **Convert:** `CAST(id AS TEXT)` or `id::text` gives the text; `'...'::uuid` reads any spelling and gives the lower-case text.
- **Older data:** a `UUID` column made before 2026-10-02 stays a text column with the UUID rule; it reads and compares the same. `ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c TYPE UUID` moves it to 16 bytes. A KarelaDB build before 2026-10-02 cannot open a table with a 16-byte `UUID` column ([versions](versions.md)).
- **From text:** `ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c TYPE UUID` also turns a `TEXT` column of UUIDs into a `UUID` column. Every value is checked first: if one is no UUID, the error names it and the column stays as it was.
- **Postgres port:** a UUID column, `x::uuid` and an older UUID text column go out as type `uuid` (OID 2950), in text or binary (16 bytes). Drivers like pgx, JDBC and psycopg read them as their own UUID type and can send a `uuid` parameter or `COPY ... (FORMAT binary)` the same way.
- **Loading:** `/imp` (CSV) and `POST /write` (line protocol: a tag or a string field) read any spelling into a UUID column. A value that is no UUID counts as a bad value, like any other. A new table made by `/imp` or `/write` keeps such a column as `STRING`; make the table first to get `UUID`.

**Example: Turn a text column of UUIDs into a UUID column**

```sql
CREATE TABLE devices (id TEXT, name STRING);
INSERT INTO devices VALUES ('A0EEBC99-9C0B-4EF8-BB6D-6BB9BD380A11', 'Gate'), ('{c0eebc999c0b4ef8bb6d6bb9bd380a13}', 'Pump');
ALTER TABLE devices ALTER COLUMN id TYPE UUID;
SELECT id, name FROM devices ORDER BY id;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE devices (`

```text
table 'devices' created
```

`INSERT INTO devices VALUES ('A0EEBC99-9C0B-4EF8-BB6D-6BB9BD380A11', 'Gate'), ('{c0eebc999c0b4ef8bb6d`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`ALTER TABLE devices ALTER COLUMN id TYPE UUID`

```text
table 'devices' altered (2 row change(s) written)
```

`SELECT id, name FROM devices ORDER BY id`

| id (UUID) | name (STRING) |
|---|---|
| a0eebc99-9c0b-4ef8-bb6d-6bb9bd380a11 | Gate |
| c0eebc99-9c0b-4ef8-bb6d-6bb9bd380a13 | Pump |

(2 rows)

<!-- docs/alter-table.md -->

# ALTER, RENAME and DROP TABLE

> Add, drop, rename and change columns, drop partitions, set a TTL, add and drop rules and keys, turn DEDUP on or off, rename and drop tables.

- Category: Tables
- Keywords: alter table, change table, add column, new column, drop column, remove column, rename column, COLUMN, TO, drop partition, delete old data, OLDER THAN, DROP PARTITION LIST, DROP PARTITION WHERE, add constraint, add check, drop constraint, rename table, drop table, delete table, remove table, IF EXISTS, IF NOT EXISTS, ALTER COLUMN, SET DATA TYPE, TYPE ... USING, USING, change column type, SET DEFAULT, DROP DEFAULT, SET NOT NULL, DROP NOT NULL, ADD UNIQUE, ADD FOREIGN KEY, FOREIGN KEY, NOT VALID, DEDUP ENABLE, DEDUP DISABLE, DEDUP ENABLE UPSERT KEYS, SET (dedup\_insert, RESET (dedup\_insert, SET (compression, RESET (compression, compression, SET (resident, RESET (resident, resident, keep in memory, ALTER TABLE RENAME TO, schema change, migration
- See also: [CREATE TABLE](create-table.md), [Constraints](constraints.md), [SHOW TABLES, COLUMNS, CREATE TABLE](show-tables.md), [UPDATE and DELETE](update-delete.md), [Triggers](triggers.md), [Indexes](indexes.md), [Partitions, SORT BY and DEDUP KEY](partitions-and-dedup.md), [Cold storage (S3, MinIO, R2, B2)](cold-storage.md)

Tables change when your app grows: a new column for the phone number, a better column name, old data to remove. Most of these statements change a table **without** copying its rows; changing a column's type and turning DEDUP on or off rewrite the rows.

| Statement | What it does |
|---|---|
| `ALTER TABLE t ADD [COLUMN] c TYPE [rules]` | adds a column at the end |
| `ALTER TABLE t DROP [COLUMN] c` | removes a column and its data |
| `ALTER TABLE t RENAME [COLUMN] a TO b` | renames a column |
| `ALTER TABLE t ALTER [COLUMN] c TYPE LONG` | changes a column's type; also `SET`/`DROP DEFAULT`, `SET`/`DROP NOT NULL` |
| `ALTER TABLE t DROP PARTITION 'key', ...` | deletes whole days, months or years of a time-series table |
| `ALTER TABLE t DROP PARTITION OLDER THAN 6 MONTHS` | deletes the partitions that ended more than 6 months ago, once, now |
| `ALTER TABLE t DROP PARTITION WHERE time < '2026-09-01'` | deletes the partitions whose whole time range matches (QuestDB's form) |
| `ALTER TABLE t SET TTL 90 DAYS` | drops partitions older than 90 days, by itself, from now on |
| `ALTER TABLE t ADD [CONSTRAINT name] CHECK (...)` | adds a rule for every row |
| `ALTER TABLE t ADD [CONSTRAINT name] UNIQUE (...)` or `FOREIGN KEY (...) REFERENCES ...` | adds a key |
| `ALTER TABLE t DROP CONSTRAINT name` | removes a rule or a key |
| `ALTER TABLE t DEDUP ENABLE UPSERT KEYS (...)` / `DEDUP DISABLE` | sets or removes the `DEDUP KEY` of a time-series table |
| `ALTER TABLE t SET (dedup_insert = 'upsert')` / `RESET (dedup_insert)` | a plain `INSERT` of a key that is there replaces the row, or fails again ([dedup_insert](partitions-and-dedup.md#dedup-insert)) |
| `ALTER TABLE t SET (compression = on)` / `SET (compression = off)` / `RESET (compression)` | stores the sealed partitions packed, about 5 times smaller on disk, or plain again ([compression](partitions-and-dedup.md#compression)) |
| `ALTER TABLE t SET (cold_storage = 'archive', cold_after = '90 days')` / `RESET (cold_storage)` | moves partitions older than 90 days to an S3-compatible object store, where queries still read them ([cold storage](cold-storage.md)) |
| `ALTER TABLE t MOVE PARTITION '2025-01' TO COLD` / `FROM COLD` | moves a partition to the table's cold store now, or brings it back as a local file ([cold storage](cold-storage.md#move-partition)) |
| `ALTER TABLE t SET (resident = on)` / `SET (resident = off)` / `RESET (resident)` | keeps the table's partitions in memory once read, whoever needs memory ([resident](#resident)) |
| `RENAME TABLE a TO b`, `ALTER TABLE a RENAME TO b` | renames a table |
| `DROP TABLE [IF EXISTS] t` | deletes a table and all its rows |

What you **cannot** change: `PARTITION BY`, `SORT BY`, the kind of table, and the type of the time column, of a `SORT BY` or `DEDUP KEY` column and of the `PRIMARY KEY`. To change those, make a new table with [CREATE TABLE ... AS](create-table.md#create-table-as) or `INSERT INTO new SELECT ... FROM old`, and drop the old table. `ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE TRIGGER` and `DISABLE TRIGGER` are explained in [triggers](triggers.md).

Several actions can go in one statement, with commas: `ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN a INT, DROP COLUMN b`. `DROP PARTITION` must be on its own. These statements cannot be used inside `BEGIN ... COMMIT`.

**Example: The users table of an app grows**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (id LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO, email STRING NOT NULL UNIQUE);
INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('ram@example.com'), ('sita@example.com');
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN phone STRING;
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN verified BOOL NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE;
ALTER TABLE users RENAME COLUMN email TO login_email;
SELECT id, login_email, phone, verified FROM users;
```

Result:

`ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN phone STRING`

```text
table 'users' altered
```

`ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN verified BOOL NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE`

```text
table 'users' altered
```

`ALTER TABLE users RENAME COLUMN email TO login_email`

```text
table 'users' altered
```

`SELECT id, login_email, phone, verified FROM users`

| id (LONG) | login_email (STRING) | phone (STRING) | verified (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ram@example.com | NULL | false |
| 2 | sita@example.com | NULL | false |

(2 rows)

<a id="add-column"></a>

## ADD COLUMN

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER TABLE table ADD [COLUMN] [IF NOT EXISTS] column TYPE [NOT NULL] [UNIQUE] [DEFAULT expr]
                                          [REFERENCES table(column)] [ROUND interval]
                                          [AS (expr) | GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expr) STORED]
                                          [[CONSTRAINT name] CHECK (condition)]
```

Adds a new column **at the end** of the table. The word `COLUMN` is optional.

- Rows already in the table get the `DEFAULT` value, or `NULL` when there is no default.
- A [stored generated column](create-table.md#generated) (`GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...) STORED`) is worked out for every row already in the table: the rows are written again, so this takes longer on a big table.
- **Returns:** `table 'name' altered`.
- **Notes:** a `NOT NULL` column needs a `DEFAULT` (old rows need a value). You cannot add a `PRIMARY KEY` column. With `IF NOT EXISTS`, a column that is already there is not an error. A default like `now()` or `gen_random_uuid()` is worked out **once** for all old rows, so they all get the same value; new rows get their own.
- **Notes:** `INSERT INTO t VALUES (...)` without a column list now needs a value for the new column too.

**Example: Add a phone number and a verified flag**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (id LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO, email STRING NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('ram@example.com');
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN phone STRING;
ALTER TABLE users ADD verified BOOL NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE;
INSERT INTO users (email, phone, verified) VALUES ('sita@example.com', '9800000000', TRUE);
SELECT id, email, phone, verified FROM users;
```

Result:

`ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN phone STRING`

```text
table 'users' altered
```

`ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN verified BOOL NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE`

```text
table 'users' altered
```

`INSERT INTO users (email, phone, verified) VALUES ('sita@example.com', '9800000000', TRUE)`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT id, email, phone, verified FROM users`

| id (LONG) | email (STRING) | phone (STRING) | verified (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ram@example.com | NULL | false |
| 2 | sita@example.com | 9800000000 | true |

(2 rows)

**Example: Add a sector link to securities (REFERENCES)**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE sectors (name STRING PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE securities (symbol SYMBOL PRIMARY KEY, name STRING NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO sectors VALUES ('Banking'), ('Energy');
INSERT INTO securities VALUES ('CITY', 'City Bank Limited');
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE securities ADD COLUMN sector STRING REFERENCES sectors(name);
UPDATE securities SET sector = 'Banking' WHERE symbol = 'CITY';
SELECT symbol, name, sector FROM securities;
```

Result:

`ALTER TABLE securities ADD COLUMN sector STRING REFERENCES sectors(name)`

```text

```

`UPDATE securities SET sector = 'Banking' WHERE symbol = 'CITY'`

```text

```

`SELECT symbol, name, sector FROM securities`

| symbol (SYMBOL) | name (STRING) | sector (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| CITY | City Bank Limited | Banking |

(1 row)

```sql
CREATE TABLE trade_log (date TIMESTAMP, transaction_id LONG, quantity LONG, rate DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(date) DEDUP KEY (date, transaction_id);
```

<a id="drop-column"></a>

## DROP COLUMN

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER TABLE table DROP [COLUMN] [IF EXISTS] column
```

Removes a column and all its values. The word `COLUMN` is optional.

These columns **cannot** be dropped:

| Column | Message says |
|---|---|
| the `TIMESERIES` column | `it is the TIMESERIES column` |
| a `SORT BY` or `DEDUP KEY` column | `it is part of SORT BY` / `DEDUP KEY` |
| the `PRIMARY KEY` | `it is the PRIMARY KEY` |
| a column that another table `REFERENCES` | `... REFERENCES it; drop that column first` |
| a column used by a computed column, a `CHECK` or an index | `... uses it` |
| the only column of the table | `drop the table instead` |

- **Returns:** `table 'name' altered`.
- **Notes:** there is no undo. Make a backup first when the data matters ([backup](backup-and-safety.md)). With `IF EXISTS`, a column that is not there is not an error.

**Example: Remove a column nobody uses**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE news (id LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO, title STRING NOT NULL, old_category STRING);
INSERT INTO news (title, old_category) VALUES ('City Bank profit rises 18%', 'banking');
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE news DROP COLUMN old_category;
SELECT * FROM news;
```

Result:

`ALTER TABLE news DROP COLUMN old_category`

```text
table 'news' altered
```

`SELECT * FROM news`

| id (LONG) | title (STRING) |
|---|---|
| 1 | City Bank profit rises 18% |

(1 row)

**Example: The symbol is part of the sort order** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ticks (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, price DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time);
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE ticks DROP COLUMN symbol;
```

Result:

Error: `cannot drop column 'symbol' from table 'ticks': it is part of SORT BY`

**Example: A computed column still uses it** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE trade_log (quantity LONG, rate DOUBLE, amount DOUBLE AS (quantity * rate));
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE trade_log DROP COLUMN rate;
```

Result:

Error: `cannot drop column 'rate' from table 'trade_log': computed column 'amount' uses it in AS (quantity * rate); drop 'amount' first`

<a id="rename-column"></a>

## RENAME COLUMN

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER TABLE table RENAME [COLUMN] old_name TO new_name
```

Gives a column a new name. The rows do not change. The word `COLUMN` is optional.

- KarelaDB also renames the column inside computed columns, `CHECK` rules, and `REFERENCES` of other tables.
- **Returns:** `table 'name' altered`.
- **Notes:** views, saved functions, procedures and triggers that use the old name are **not** changed; fix them yourself. Your app's SQL must use the new name too.

**Example: Rename price to ltp in a live prices table**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE live_prices (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, price DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time);
INSERT INTO live_prices VALUES ('2026-09-10T11:00:00+05:45', 'CITY', 513.0);
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE live_prices RENAME COLUMN price TO ltp;
SELECT time, symbol, ltp FROM live_prices;
```

Result:

`ALTER TABLE live_prices RENAME COLUMN price TO ltp`

```text
table 'live_prices' altered
```

`SELECT time, symbol, ltp FROM live_prices`

| time (TIMESTAMP) | symbol (SYMBOL) | ltp (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-10T05:15:00.000Z | CITY | 513 |

(1 row)

**Example: A REFERENCES of another table follows the new name**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE brokers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING);
CREATE TABLE trades (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, buyer INT REFERENCES brokers(id));
```

```sql

```

Result:

`ALTER TABLE brokers RENAME COLUMN id TO broker_no`

