
`SHOW COLUMNS FROM trades`

| name (STRING) | type (STRING) | primary_key (BOOL) | not_null (BOOL) | computed (BOOL) | references (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| id | LONG | true | false | false | NULL |
| buyer | INT | false | false | false | brokers(broker_no) |

(2 rows)


<a id="alter-column"></a>

## ALTER COLUMN

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER TABLE table ALTER [COLUMN] column [SET DATA] TYPE type [USING expression]
ALTER TABLE table ALTER [COLUMN] column SET DEFAULT expression
ALTER TABLE table ALTER [COLUMN] column DROP DEFAULT
ALTER TABLE table ALTER [COLUMN] column SET NOT NULL
ALTER TABLE table ALTER [COLUMN] column DROP NOT NULL
```

Changes one column. These are the PostgreSQL forms, so a PostgreSQL migration script runs.

| Form | What it does |
|---|---|
| `TYPE type` | converts every stored value to the new type, like `CAST`. It rewrites the rows |
| `TYPE type USING expression` | the new value of each row is `expression`, over the columns of that row |
| `SET DEFAULT` / `DROP DEFAULT` | the value new rows get when they do not give one; old rows keep theirs |
| `SET NOT NULL` | from now on the column needs a value. Refused while a row has `NULL` there |
| `DROP NOT NULL` | the column may be `NULL` again |

- **Returns:** `table 'name' altered`, with `(N row change(s) written)` when rows were rewritten, or `table 'name' not changed (already as asked)`.
- **Notes:**
  - When one stored value does not fit the new type, nothing changes and the message names the value: `12.7 is not a whole number`. Write a `USING` that fits, or fix the rows first.
  - The time column, a `SORT BY` column and a `DEDUP KEY` column cannot change type: the rows are stored by them, and KarelaDB refuses. A `PRIMARY KEY` column can: KarelaDB writes the whole table again in the new key order, in one commit (it takes as long as a copy of the table). A change that makes two keys equal, such as `TYPE INT USING round(id)`, is refused with "(duplicate)".
  - An index on the column is built again for the new type.
  - `COLLATE` after the type is read and ignored. Write `COLLATE` in the query instead ([ORDER BY](order-by-limit.md#collate)).

**Example: Ages were saved as text: make them numbers**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (id LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO, email STRING, age STRING);
INSERT INTO users (email, age) VALUES ('ram@example.com', '31'), ('sita@example.com', 'unknown');
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN age TYPE INT USING CASE WHEN age = 'unknown' THEN NULL ELSE CAST(age AS INT) END;
SELECT id, email, age FROM users ORDER BY id;
```

Result:

`ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN age TYPE INT USING CASE WHEN age = 'unknown' THEN NULL ELSE CAST(age `

```text
table 'users' altered (2 row change(s) written)
```

`SELECT id, email, age FROM users ORDER BY id`

| id (LONG) | email (STRING) | age (INT) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ram@example.com | 31 |
| 2 | sita@example.com | NULL |

(2 rows)

**Example: A default for new rows, then a NOT NULL rule**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE posts (id LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO, author STRING, lang STRING);
INSERT INTO posts (author, lang) VALUES ('ram', 'en');
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE posts ALTER COLUMN lang SET DEFAULT 'ne';
ALTER TABLE posts ALTER COLUMN author SET NOT NULL;
INSERT INTO posts (author) VALUES ('sita');
SELECT id, author, lang FROM posts ORDER BY id;
```

Result:

`ALTER TABLE posts ALTER COLUMN lang SET DEFAULT 'ne'`

```text
table 'posts' altered
```

`ALTER TABLE posts ALTER COLUMN author SET NOT NULL`

```text
table 'posts' altered
```

`INSERT INTO posts (author) VALUES ('sita')`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT id, author, lang FROM posts ORDER BY id`

| id (LONG) | author (STRING) | lang (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ram | en |
| 2 | sita | ne |

(2 rows)

**Example: A value that does not fit the new type** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql

INSERT INTO prices VALUES (1, 12.7);
```

```sql

```

Result:

Error: `cannot change column 'price' of table 'prices': a row already there does not fit (column 'price' (INT): 12.7 is not a whole number)`

**Example: SET NOT NULL while a row has NULL** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (id LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO, email STRING);
INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('ram@example.com'), (NULL);
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN email SET NOT NULL;
```

Result:

Error: `column 'email' of table 'users' contains NULL values; set them first (UPDATE ... SET email = ... WHERE email IS NULL)`

**Example: A SORT BY column keeps its type** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ticks (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, qty INT) TIMESERIES(time);
```

```sql

```

Result:

Error: `cannot alter column 'symbol' of table 'ticks': it is the TIMESERIES column or part of SORT BY / DEDUP KEY`

<a id="drop-partition"></a>

## DROP PARTITION

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER TABLE table DROP PARTITION [LIST] 'key' [, 'key' ...]
ALTER TABLE table DROP PARTITION OLDER THAN n HOURS | DAYS | WEEKS | MONTHS | YEARS
ALTER TABLE table DROP PARTITION WHERE time_column < '2026-09-01'
```

Deletes whole partitions of a time-series table: all rows of that day, month or year. It is much faster than `DELETE` for old data. `OLDER THAN` works out the keys itself, by the same rule as a [TTL](#set-ttl): a partition goes when its **last** moment is more than that long ago. It is the form for a [timer](timers.md) that cleans up on a set day, where a TTL cleans up by itself all the time.

`LIST` and `WHERE` are QuestDB's forms. `LIST 'a', 'b'` is the same as `'a', 'b'`. `WHERE` drops each partition whose **whole** time range matches the condition:

| `WHERE` | Partitions dropped |
|---|---|
| `time < '2026-09-22'` (a day boundary, DAY partitions) | every day before 2026-09-22 |
| `time < '2026-09-22T12:00'` (inside a day) | every day before 2026-09-22; the day 2026-09-22 is **kept** and named in the answer |
| `time IN '2026-08' OR time >= '2026-09-20'` | August, and every day from 2026-09-20 on |

- The condition may only compare the time column with fixed times: `=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `BETWEEN`, `IN (...)`, `IN '2026-09'`, joined by `AND`, `OR` and `NOT`. `now()` and `dateadd('d', -30, now())` count as fixed. Anything else (another column, a function of the time column) is an error, and nothing is dropped.
- A partition the condition cuts through is kept whole, because dropping it would delete rows the condition does not name. Delete those rows with [DELETE](update-delete.md#delete). QuestDB only tests a partition's first moment, so it would drop that partition too.
- **Returns (WHERE):** `N partition(s) of 'table' dropped`, then `; kept partition(s) only part of which matches: ...` when there are some; `no partition of 'table' matches as a whole` when nothing goes.
- The partitions it finds are written to the database log by name, so a restart or power cut repeats exactly the same drop.

| Table has | Partition keys look like |
|---|---|
| `PARTITION BY YEAR` | `'2025'` |
| `PARTITION BY MONTH` | `'2026-08'` |
| `PARTITION BY DAY` | `'2026-09-09'` |

- The keys are **UTC** dates, in single quotes.
- **Returns:** `N partition(s) of 'table' dropped`, or for `OLDER THAN` with nothing that old, `no partition of 'table' is older than 6 MONTHS`.
- **Notes:** a key that does not exist is an error, and the message lists the keys that do. A relational table and a table with `PARTITION BY NONE` have no partitions to drop; use [DELETE](update-delete.md#delete) or [TRUNCATE](update-delete.md#truncate).
- **Notes:** with [PARTITION BY YEAR, SYMBOL(col)](partitions-and-dedup.md#partition-by-symbol) the key is the time part: `'2025'` drops every symbol of 2025.
- **Notes:** it answers at once, even for hundreds of partitions on a busy database. The rows are gone for every query straight away; their files move to the database's `_trash` a moment later, in the background.

**Example: Remove the 2025 daily candles**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ochl_day (time TIMESTAMP ROUND 1d, symbol SYMBOL, close DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY YEAR DEDUP KEY (symbol, time);
INSERT INTO ochl_day VALUES ('2025-12-31', 'CITY', 542.4), ('2026-09-10', 'CITY', 504.9);
```

```sql
SELECT count(*) AS rows_2025 FROM ochl_day WHERE time IN '2025';
ALTER TABLE ochl_day DROP PARTITION '2025';
SELECT time, symbol, close FROM ochl_day;
```

Result:

`SELECT count(*) AS rows_2025 FROM ochl_day WHERE time IN '2025'`

| rows_2025 (LONG) |
|---|
| 1 |

(1 row)

`ALTER TABLE ochl_day DROP PARTITION '2025'`

```text
1 partition(s) of 'ochl_day' dropped
```

`SELECT time, symbol, close FROM ochl_day`

| time (TIMESTAMP) | symbol (SYMBOL) | close (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z | CITY | 504.9 |

(1 row)

**Example: Drop what ended more than a year ago (by hand, or from a monthly timer)**

Setup:

```sql
INSERT INTO trades_log VALUES ('2024-01-15', 'CITY', 100), ('2024-02-15', 'CITY', 200), ('2099-01-15', 'CITY', 300);
```

<a id="set-ttl"></a>

## SET TTL

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER TABLE table SET TTL n HOURS | DAYS | WEEKS | MONTHS | YEARS
ALTER TABLE table SET TTL NONE
CREATE TABLE ... TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY TTL 90 DAYS
```

A TTL (time to live) keeps a time-series table small. KarelaDB drops **whole partitions** whose time ended more than the TTL ago. It never deletes single rows.

- A background thread checks once a minute. It only runs when no statement is writing.
- A partition goes when its **last** moment is older than the TTL. With `TTL 3 DAYS` on 2026-09-10 12:00, the day `2026-09-06` goes and `2026-09-07` stays.
- `MONTHS` and `YEARS` are calendar months and years.
- **Returns:** `table 'name' drops partitions older than 90 DAYS`, or `table 'name' keeps its partitions (no TTL)` for `NONE`.
- **Notes:**
  - Only for time-series tables with `PARTITION BY DAY`, `MONTH` or `YEAR`.
  - `SHOW CREATE TABLE` shows the TTL.
  - Every drop is written to the audit log (event `ttl_drop`) and to the database log, like `DROP PARTITION`.
  - A [materialized view](views.md#materialized-view) keeps its rows when the TTL drops partitions of its table.
  - The TTL is checked every minute. It also runs on a busy database. It locks only a table that has a partition past its TTL, one table at a time, and waits only briefly for it. A table held by a long load or an open transaction is left for the next check, and writers of other tables never wait for it. Writers of the table being trimmed wait while the old partitions go, which is quick.

**Example: Keep 90 days of live prices**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE live_prices (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, ltp DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY;
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE live_prices SET TTL 90 DAYS;
SHOW CREATE TABLE live_prices;
```

Result:

`ALTER TABLE live_prices SET TTL 90 DAYS`

```text
table 'live_prices' drops partitions older than 90 DAYS
```

`SHOW CREATE TABLE live_prices`

| create_sql (STRING) |
|---|
| CREATE TABLE live_prices (   time TIMESTAMP,   symbol SYMBOL,   ltp DOUBLE ) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY SORT BY (symbol, time) TTL 90 DAYS |

(1 row)

**Example: TTL when the table is made, and taken off again**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE candles_1m (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, close DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY MONTH TTL 2 YEARS;
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE candles_1m SET TTL NONE;
SHOW CREATE TABLE candles_1m;
```

Result:

`ALTER TABLE candles_1m SET TTL NONE`

```text
table 'candles_1m' keeps its partitions (no TTL)
```

`SHOW CREATE TABLE candles_1m`

| create_sql (STRING) |
|---|
| CREATE TABLE candles_1m (   time TIMESTAMP,   symbol SYMBOL,   close DOUBLE ) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY MONTH SORT BY (symbol, time) |

(1 row)

**Example: A relational table has no partitions to drop** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE notes (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, body STRING);
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE notes SET TTL 30 DAYS;
```

Result:

Error: `TTL drops whole time partitions, so it needs a time-series table with PARTITION BY DAY, MONTH or YEAR; table 'notes' has none`

<a id="dedup-enable"></a>

## DEDUP ENABLE and DEDUP DISABLE

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER TABLE table DEDUP ENABLE UPSERT KEYS (column, ..., time_column)
ALTER TABLE table DEDUP DISABLE
```

Sets or removes the [DEDUP KEY](partitions-and-dedup.md#dedup-key) of a time-series table. It is QuestDB's statement; `UPSERT` may be left out.

- `DEDUP ENABLE` rewrites the rows by the new key. Rows that already share a key are **folded**: the newest of each key stays.
- `DEDUP DISABLE` takes the key off. From then on every row is kept, also exact copies.
- **Returns:** `table 't' now dedups on (time, symbol) (N row(s) rewritten, M duplicate row(s) folded: the newest row of each key was kept)`, or `table 't' no longer dedups (N row(s) rewritten)`.
- **Notes:**
  - The key must include the time column, as in `CREATE TABLE`. With [SYMBOL(col) partitions](partitions-and-dedup.md#partition-by-symbol) it must include that column too.
  - It reads and rewrites every row, so on a big table it takes a while. Folded rows cannot be brought back: make a backup first when they matter.
  - Only for time-series tables. A relational table uses a `PRIMARY KEY`.
  - This statement leaves the table's [dedup_insert](partitions-and-dedup.md#dedup-insert) as it was: on a table that did not have it, a plain `INSERT` of a key that is there still fails. To make it replace the row, as QuestDB does, add `ALTER TABLE t SET (dedup_insert = 'upsert')`. (A table made with `CREATE TABLE ... DEDUP UPSERT KEYS (...)` has it from the start.)

**Example: A tick table loaded twice: turn DEDUP on and the copies fold**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ticks (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, price DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY;
INSERT INTO ticks VALUES ('2026-09-10T11:00:00+05:45', 'CITY', 510), ('2026-09-10T11:01:00+05:45', 'CITY', 511);
INSERT INTO ticks VALUES ('2026-09-10T11:00:00+05:45', 'CITY', 510.5);
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE ticks DEDUP ENABLE UPSERT KEYS (time, symbol);
SELECT time, symbol, price FROM ticks;
```

Result:

`ALTER TABLE ticks DEDUP ENABLE UPSERT KEYS (time, symbol)`

```text
table 'ticks' now dedups on (time, symbol) (2 row(s) rewritten, 1 duplicate row(s) folded: the newest row of each key was kept)
```

`SELECT time, symbol, price FROM ticks`

| time (TIMESTAMP) | symbol (SYMBOL) | price (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-10T05:15:00.000Z | CITY | 510.5 |
| 2026-09-10T05:16:00.000Z | CITY | 511 |

(2 rows)

**Example: The key needs the time column** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ticks (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, price DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time);
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE ticks DEDUP ENABLE UPSERT KEYS (symbol);
```

Result:

Error: `DEDUP UPSERT KEYS must include the time column 'time' of table 'ticks', or a stored column GENERATED ALWAYS AS (date_trunc('minute', time)) STORED`

<a id="add-check"></a>

## ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER TABLE table ADD [CONSTRAINT name] CHECK (condition)
```

Adds a rule that every row must follow. KarelaDB first reads **every** row: if one row already breaks the rule, the rule is refused and the message names that row.

- Without `CONSTRAINT name`, KarelaDB makes the name `table_check` (or `table_check1`, ...).
- **Returns:** `table 'name' altered`.
- **Notes:** on a very big time-series table this reads all rows once, so it can take a while. The rules for the condition are in [CHECK](constraints.md#check).

**Example: No negative balances from now on: the rule stops a bad UPDATE** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO, owner STRING NOT NULL, balance DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0);
INSERT INTO accounts (owner, balance) VALUES ('Ram', 1000.00), ('Sita', 0);
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE accounts ADD CONSTRAINT balance_not_negative CHECK (balance >= 0);
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE owner = 'Sita';
```

Result:

```text
table 'accounts' altered
```

Error: `CHECK constraint 'balance_not_negative' of table 'accounts' failed: balance >= 0 is false for the row id='2', balance='-50.00'`

**Example: A row already breaks the rule** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO, owner STRING NOT NULL, balance DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0);
INSERT INTO accounts (owner, balance) VALUES ('Ram', -20.00);
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE accounts ADD CONSTRAINT balance_not_negative CHECK (balance >= 0);
```

Result:

Error: `cannot add the constraint: a row already in table 'accounts' breaks it (CHECK constraint 'balance_not_negative' of table 'accounts' failed: balance >= 0 is false for the row id='1', balance='-20.00'); fix or delete such rows first`

<a id="add-key"></a>

## ADD UNIQUE, ADD FOREIGN KEY

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER TABLE table ADD [CONSTRAINT name] UNIQUE (column [, column ...])
ALTER TABLE table ADD [CONSTRAINT name] FOREIGN KEY (column [, ...]) REFERENCES other (column [, ...])
                      [ON DELETE action] [ON UPDATE action] [NOT VALID]
```

Adds a key to a table that already has rows, the PostgreSQL way. KarelaDB first reads every row.

| Form | KarelaDB checks first | After it |
|---|---|---|
| `UNIQUE (...)` | no two rows have the same values | a new duplicate is refused |
| `FOREIGN KEY (...) REFERENCES other (...)` | every row has a matching row in `other` | a new row must point at a row that is there |
| `... NOT VALID` | nothing: rows already there are not checked | new rows are checked |

- **Returns:** `table 'name' altered`.
- **Notes:**
  - Without `CONSTRAINT name`, KarelaDB makes the name: `trades_ref_key`, `trades_buyer_fkey`. `SHOW CREATE TABLE` shows it, and [DROP CONSTRAINT](#drop-constraint) removes it.
  - A `FOREIGN KEY` must point at the `PRIMARY KEY` or a `UNIQUE` column of the other table, of the same kind of type. The `ON DELETE` actions are in [REFERENCES](constraints.md#references).
  - When a row breaks the rule, nothing changes and the message names the row.

**Example: Trades point at brokers from now on**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE brokers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE trades (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, buyer INT, qty LONG);
INSERT INTO brokers VALUES (1, 'Keystone Securities'), (45, 'Imperial Securities');
INSERT INTO trades VALUES (1, 1, 10), (2, 45, 20);
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE trades ADD CONSTRAINT trades_buyer_fk FOREIGN KEY (buyer) REFERENCES brokers(id);
ALTER TABLE brokers ADD CONSTRAINT brokers_name_key UNIQUE (name);
SHOW CREATE TABLE trades;
```

Result:

`ALTER TABLE trades ADD CONSTRAINT trades_buyer_fk FOREIGN KEY (buyer) REFERENCES brokers (id)`

```text
table 'trades' altered
```

`ALTER TABLE brokers ADD CONSTRAINT brokers_name_key UNIQUE (name)`

```text
table 'brokers' altered
```

`SHOW CREATE TABLE trades`

| create_sql (STRING) |
|---|
| CREATE TABLE trades (   id LONG PRIMARY KEY,   buyer INT CONSTRAINT trades_buyer_fk REFERENCES brokers(id),   qty LONG ) |

(1 row)

**Example: Old rows break the rule: NOT VALID checks only new rows** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE brokers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE trades (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, buyer INT);
INSERT INTO brokers VALUES (1, 'Keystone Securities');
INSERT INTO trades VALUES (1, 1), (2, 77);
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE trades ADD CONSTRAINT trades_buyer_fk FOREIGN KEY (buyer) REFERENCES brokers(id) NOT VALID;
INSERT INTO trades VALUES (3, 99);
```

Result:

```text
table 'trades' altered
```

Error: `column 'buyer' = '99' has no matching row in brokers(id)`

**Example: Two rows already have the same value** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, email STRING);
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'ram@example.com'), (2, 'ram@example.com');
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE users ADD UNIQUE (email);
```

Result:

Error: `cannot add constraint 'users_email_key': two rows of table 'users' have email='ram@example.com' (duplicate)`

<a id="drop-constraint"></a>

## DROP CONSTRAINT

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER TABLE table DROP CONSTRAINT name
```

Removes a `CHECK` rule, a `UNIQUE` key or a `FOREIGN KEY` by its name. `SHOW CREATE TABLE` shows the names, also the names KarelaDB made for you (like `accounts_balance_check`). The `PRIMARY KEY` cannot be dropped: the rows are stored by it.

- **Returns:** `table 'name' altered`.
- **Notes:** a name that does not exist is an error; the message lists the names the table has. A column called `constraint` is dropped with `ALTER TABLE t DROP constraint` (no name after it).

**Example: Remove a limit that is too strict**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ledger (id LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO, amount DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT max_amount CHECK (amount <= 100000));
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE ledger DROP CONSTRAINT max_amount;
INSERT INTO ledger (amount) VALUES (250000.00);
SELECT id, amount FROM ledger;
```

Result:

`ALTER TABLE ledger DROP CONSTRAINT max_amount`

```text
table 'ledger' altered
```

`INSERT INTO ledger (amount) VALUES (250000.00)`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT id, amount FROM ledger`

| id (LONG) | amount (DECIMAL(2)) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 250000.00 |

(1 row)

**Example: A wrong constraint name** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (id INT PRIMARY KEY, balance DECIMAL(2) CHECK (balance >= 0));
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE accounts DROP CONSTRAINT balance_check;
```

Result:

Error: `table 'accounts' has no constraint 'balance_check' (it has: accounts_pkey, accounts_balance_check)`

<a id="rename-table"></a>

## RENAME TABLE

Syntax:

```sql
RENAME TABLE old_name TO new_name
```

Gives a table a new name. `REFERENCES` in other tables follow the new name.

- **Returns:** `table 'old' renamed to 'new'`.
- **Notes:** refused when a table with the new name exists, and while the table has triggers (drop them first). Views, procedures and triggers that use the old name are not changed. The PostgreSQL form `ALTER TABLE a RENAME TO b` works the same.

**Example: Rename a table; the REFERENCES follows**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE brokers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING);
CREATE TABLE trades (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, buyer INT REFERENCES brokers(id));
```

```sql
RENAME TABLE brokers TO members;
SHOW COLUMNS FROM trades;
```

Result:

`RENAME TABLE brokers TO members`

```text
table 'brokers' renamed to 'members'
```

`SHOW COLUMNS FROM trades`

| name (STRING) | type (STRING) | primary_key (BOOL) | not_null (BOOL) | computed (BOOL) | references (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| id | LONG | true | false | false | NULL |
| buyer | INT | false | false | false | members(id) |

(2 rows)

**Example: The new name is taken** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE posts (id LONG PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE posts_old (id LONG PRIMARY KEY);
```

```sql
RENAME TABLE posts TO posts_old;
```

Result:

Error: `cannot rename table 'posts' to 'posts_old': a table named 'posts_old' already exists`

<a id="drop-table"></a>

## DROP TABLE

Syntax:

```sql
DROP TABLE [IF EXISTS] table [CASCADE | RESTRICT]
```

Deletes a table with all its rows and its indexes. With `IF EXISTS`, a table that is not there is not an error.

- **Returns:** `table 'name' dropped`, or `table 'name' does not exist` with `IF EXISTS`.
- **Notes:** the table goes to the [trash](trash.md) for some days, and `UNDROP TABLE` brings it back. It answers at once: it waits only for the statements running in the database at that moment, not for its files to be written or moved. Refused while anything uses it (another table's `REFERENCES`, a view, a materialized view; the error names each, SQLSTATE `2BP01`), and while it has triggers. To remove all rows and keep the table, use [TRUNCATE](update-delete.md#truncate).
- **CASCADE and RESTRICT:** as in PostgreSQL. `DROP TABLE t RESTRICT` (or no word) refuses while another table's foreign key, a view or a materialized view uses `t`. `DROP TABLE t CASCADE` drops what uses it first, then `t`:
  - the foreign keys of other tables that point at `t` (`ALTER TABLE other DROP CONSTRAINT ...`; the other tables and their rows stay),
  - the views and materialized views that read `t`.
  - The reply names them: `table 't' dropped; drop cascades to constraint orders_customer_fkey on table orders, view big_orders`.
  - A table with triggers is still refused before anything is dropped: `DROP TRIGGER` them first.
  - `DROP FUNCTION`, `DROP PROCEDURE` and `DROP TRIGGER` read both words and ignore them.

**Example: Remove a test table; safe to run twice**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE test_ticks (time TIMESTAMP, price DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time);
```

```sql
DROP TABLE test_ticks;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS test_ticks;
SHOW TABLES;
```

Result:

`DROP TABLE test_ticks`

```text
table 'test_ticks' dropped; UNDROP TABLE test_ticks brings it back within 7 days
```

`DROP TABLE IF EXISTS test_ticks`

```text
table 'test_ticks' does not exist
```

`SHOW TABLES`

| name (STRING) | kind (STRING) | partition (STRING) | columns (INT) | rows (LONG) |
|---|---|---|---|---|

(0 rows)

**Example: Brokers are still used by the trades** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE brokers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING);
CREATE TABLE trades (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, buyer INT REFERENCES brokers(id));
```

```sql
DROP TABLE brokers;
```

Result:

Error: `cannot drop table brokers because other objects depend on it: constraint trades_buyer_fkey on table trades. Drop them first, or use DROP TABLE brokers CASCADE to drop them too`

**Example: A table that is not there** (shows an error)

```sql
DROP TABLE nothing;
```

Result:

Error: `cannot drop table 'nothing': it does not exist`

**Example: CASCADE and RESTRICT on tables nothing uses**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE test_a (id INT PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE test_b (id INT PRIMARY KEY);
```

```sql
DROP TABLE test_a CASCADE;
DROP TABLE test_b RESTRICT;
SHOW TABLES;
```

Result:

`DROP TABLE test_a`

```text
table 'test_a' dropped; UNDROP TABLE test_a brings it back within 7 days
```

`DROP TABLE test_b`

```text
table 'test_b' dropped; UNDROP TABLE test_b brings it back within 7 days
```

`SHOW TABLES`

| name (STRING) | kind (STRING) | partition (STRING) | columns (INT) | rows (LONG) |
|---|---|---|---|---|

(0 rows)

**Example: CASCADE drops the view and the foreign key that use the table**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE test_prices (id INT PRIMARY KEY, symbol SYMBOL, price DOUBLE);
CREATE TABLE test_alerts (id INT PRIMARY KEY, price_id INT REFERENCES test_prices(id));
CREATE VIEW test_expensive AS SELECT symbol FROM test_prices WHERE price > 1000;
```

```sql
DROP TABLE test_prices CASCADE;
SHOW TABLES;
```

Result:

`DROP TABLE test_prices`

```text
table 'test_prices' dropped; UNDROP TABLE test_prices brings it back within 7 days; drop cascades to constraint test_alerts_price_id_fkey on table test_alerts, view test_expensive
```

`SHOW TABLES`

| name (STRING) | kind (STRING) | partition (STRING) | columns (INT) | rows (LONG) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| test_alerts | relational | NONE | 2 | 0 |

(1 row)

<a id="resident"></a>

## SET (resident = on): keep a table in memory

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER TABLE <t> SET (resident = on | off)
ALTER TABLE <t> RESET (resident)
CREATE TABLE <t> (...) WITH (resident = on)
```

A table an app reads on every request (sessions, users, symbols) should not be read from disk again because another query needed memory. With `resident = on`, its partitions are **never unloaded** once a read has loaded them: not for a big scan of the same database, not for another database, not for the [process memory limit](cli-serve.md#memory-limit).

- **Returns:** `table 't' stays in memory once loaded (resident = on); it counts against the database's MEMORY_LIMIT`.
- **Notes:**
  - It loads nothing by itself: the first read that needs the rows loads them.
  - What it holds still counts in `--memory` and in the database's [`MEMORY_LIMIT`](databases.md#memory), so keep it for small and medium tables.
  - `GET /api/stats` shows what resident tables hold as `resident_bytes` in each database's `memory`.
  - A database with a resident table needs KarelaDB 2026-10-02 or newer; `RESET (resident)` lets an older KarelaDB open it again.

**Example: The sessions table of an app stays loaded**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE sessions (token STRING PRIMARY KEY, user_id LONG);
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE sessions SET (resident = on);
```

Result:

```text
table 'sessions' stays in memory once loaded (resident = on); it counts against the database's MEMORY_LIMIT
```

# SHOW TABLES, COLUMNS, CREATE TABLE

> List the tables of a database, the columns of a table, its partitions, and the full CREATE TABLE statement - also with QuestDB's tables() and table_columns().

- Category: Tables
- Keywords: show tables, list tables, show columns, describe, describe table, table columns, schema, show create table, table definition, DDL, .tables, .schema, information\_schema, show partitions, partitions, QuestDB, tables(), table\_columns, table\_partitions, wal\_tables, upsertKey, designatedTimestamp
- See also: [CREATE TABLE](create-table.md), [ALTER, RENAME and DROP TABLE](alter-table.md), [Databases and the data folder](databases.md), [Views](views.md), [Indexes](indexes.md), [Saved functions](saved-functions.md), [Stored procedures](procedures.md), [Triggers](triggers.md), [Users and roles](users-and-roles.md)

These statements show what is **in** a database: which tables there are, which columns a table has, and how a table was made. They only read; they never change anything.

| Statement | Shows |
|---|---|
| `SHOW TABLES` | every table, its kind, partitions, columns and rows |
| `SHOW COLUMNS FROM t` | the columns of one table |
| `SHOW CREATE TABLE t` | the `CREATE TABLE` statement of one table |
| `SHOW PARTITIONS FROM t` | the partitions of one table: rows, time range, size |
| `tables()`, `table_columns('t')`, `wal_tables()` | the same facts with QuestDB's column names ([below](#questdb-meta)) |

Other `SHOW` statements: `SHOW DATABASES` ([databases](databases.md#show-databases)), `SHOW VIEWS` ([views](views.md)), `SHOW INDEXES` ([indexes](indexes.md)), `SHOW FUNCTIONS` ([saved functions](saved-functions.md)), `SHOW PROCEDURES` ([procedures](procedures.md)), `SHOW TRIGGERS` ([triggers](triggers.md)), `SHOW USERS` ([users and roles](users-and-roles.md)).

- **Notes:** KarelaDB has no `DESCRIBE`. `information_schema` and `pg_catalog` can be read like tables, and psql's `\d` works on the [PostgreSQL port](postgres-protocol.md#catalog). In `kareladb shell`, `.tables` is the same as `SHOW TABLES`, and `.schema t` shows `SHOW CREATE TABLE t`.

**Example: What is in the sample database** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SHOW TABLES;
SHOW COLUMNS FROM trade_log;
```

| ochl_day | timeseries | YEAR | 7 | 57 |
| ochl_minutes | timeseries | MONTH | 7 | 956 |
| securities | relational | NONE | 3 | 5 |
| trade_log | timeseries | DAY | 8 | 32 |

(6 rows)

<a id="show-tables"></a>

## SHOW TABLES

Syntax:

```sql
SHOW TABLES
```

Lists the tables of the current database, sorted by name. Views are not in this list (use `SHOW VIEWS`).

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | `STRING` | table name, spelled as in `CREATE TABLE` |
| `kind` | `STRING` | `relational` or `timeseries` |
| `partition` | `STRING` | `DAY`, `MONTH`, `YEAR`, or `NONE` (always `NONE` for relational tables) |
| `columns` | `LONG` | number of columns, computed columns included |
| `rows` | `LONG` | number of rows now |

- **Returns:** one row per table; `(0 rows)` for an empty database.
- **Notes:** the result can be used like any query result in scripts: `kareladb sql market "SHOW TABLES" --format csv`.

**Example: An app database with users, accounts and a ledger**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (id LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO, email STRING NOT NULL UNIQUE);
CREATE TABLE accounts (id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO, user_id LONG NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id), balance DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0);
CREATE TABLE ledger (time TIMESTAMP, account INT, amount DECIMAL(2)) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY MONTH;
INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('ram@example.com'), ('sita@example.com');
INSERT INTO accounts (user_id, balance) VALUES (1, 1000.00);
```

```sql
SHOW TABLES;
```

Result:

| name (STRING) | kind (STRING) | partition (STRING) | columns (INT) | rows (LONG) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| accounts | relational | NONE | 3 | 1 |
| ledger | timeseries | MONTH | 3 | 0 |
| users | relational | NONE | 2 | 2 |

(3 rows)

**Command line: The same list from the shell** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb shell market
> .tables
```

Output:

```text

End statements with ';'. Type .help for commands, .exit to quit.
kareladb> name         | kind       | partition | columns | rows
-------------+------------+-----------+---------+-----
brokers      | relational | NONE      |       2 |    5
live_data    | timeseries | DAY       |      12 |   12
ochl_day     | timeseries | YEAR      |       7 |   57
ochl_minutes | timeseries | MONTH     |       7 |  956
securities   | relational | NONE      |       3 |    5
trade_log    | timeseries | DAY       |       8 |   32
(6 rows, 0.0 ms)
kareladb>
```

<a id="show-columns"></a>

## SHOW COLUMNS FROM

Syntax:

```sql
SHOW COLUMNS FROM table
```

Lists the columns of one table, in table order.

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | `STRING` | column name |
| `type` | `STRING` | column type, like `LONG`, `DECIMAL(2)`, `TIMESTAMP` |
| `primary_key` | `BOOL` | `true` for the `PRIMARY KEY` column |
| `not_null` | `BOOL` | `true` when the column has `NOT NULL` |
| `computed` | `BOOL` | `true` for a computed column (`AS (...)`) |
| `references` | `STRING` | `table(column)` when the column has `REFERENCES`, else `NULL` |

- **Notes:** `not_null` is `false` for a `PRIMARY KEY` column without the words `NOT NULL`, even though a key can never be `NULL`. `UNIQUE`, `DEFAULT`, `ROUND`, `CHECK`, `SORT BY` and `DEDUP KEY` are not shown here: use `SHOW CREATE TABLE`. Works for tables only, not for views.

**Example: The trade_log table: references and a computed column** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SHOW COLUMNS FROM trade_log;
```

Result:

| name (STRING) | type (STRING) | primary_key (BOOL) | not_null (BOOL) | computed (BOOL) | references (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| date | TIMESTAMP | false | false | false | NULL |
| transaction_id | LONG | false | false | false | NULL |
| symbol | SYMBOL | false | false | false | NULL |
| buyer | INT | false | false | false | brokers(id) |
| seller | INT | false | false | false | brokers(id) |
| quantity | LONG | false | false | false | NULL |
| rate | DOUBLE | false | false | false | NULL |
| amount | DOUBLE | false | false | true | NULL |

(8 rows)

**Example: Forum posts that point to their parent post**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE posts (id LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO, parent_id LONG REFERENCES posts(id), author STRING NOT NULL, body STRING NOT NULL, words LONG AS (length(body)));
```

```sql
SHOW COLUMNS FROM posts;
```

Result:

| name (STRING) | type (STRING) | primary_key (BOOL) | not_null (BOOL) | computed (BOOL) | references (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| id | LONG | true | false | false | NULL |
| parent_id | LONG | false | false | false | posts(id) |
| author | STRING | false | true | false | NULL |
| body | STRING | false | true | false | NULL |
| words | LONG | false | false | true | NULL |

(5 rows)

**Example: A table that does not exist** (shows an error)

```sql
SHOW COLUMNS FROM userz;
```

Result:

Error: `table 'userz' does not exist`

**Example: FROM is needed** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (id LONG PRIMARY KEY);
```

```sql
SHOW COLUMNS users;
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 14: expected FROM after SHOW COLUMNS but found 'users'`

<a id="show-create-table"></a>

## SHOW CREATE TABLE

Syntax:

```sql
SHOW CREATE TABLE table
```

Gives the full `CREATE TABLE` statement of a table, with every rule KarelaDB keeps: types, keys, defaults, `ROUND`, computed columns, `REFERENCES`, `CHECK` rules with their names, and the table options with their **default values filled in** (like `PARTITION BY DAY` and `SORT BY (symbol, time)`).

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `create_sql` | `STRING` | the statement; newer KarelaDB versions add one more row for each index: `CREATE INDEX ...` |

- **Returns:** the text you can run in another database to make the same (empty) table.
- **Notes:** in `kareladb sql` and `kareladb shell` table format, long text is cut after 48 characters. Use `--format csv` (or `.format csv` in the shell) to see all of it.

**Example: The daily candles table of the sample data** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SHOW CREATE TABLE ochl_day;
```

Result:

| create_sql (STRING) |
|---|
| CREATE TABLE ochl_day (   time TIMESTAMP ROUND 1d,   symbol SYMBOL,   open DOUBLE,   high DOUBLE,   low DOUBLE,   close DOUBLE,   volume DOUBLE ) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY YEAR SORT BY (symbol,... |

(1 row)

**Example: Defaults filled in: PARTITION BY and SORT BY**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE live_data (timestamp TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, ltp DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(timestamp);
```

```sql
SHOW CREATE TABLE live_data;
```

Result:

| create_sql (STRING) |
|---|
| CREATE TABLE live_data (   timestamp TIMESTAMP,   symbol SYMBOL,   ltp DOUBLE ) TIMESERIES(timestamp) PARTITION BY DAY SORT BY (symbol, timestamp) |

(1 row)

**Example: An accounts table with a CHECK rule and an index**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO,
  email STRING NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  balance DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (balance >= 0)
);
CREATE INDEX accounts_balance ON accounts (balance);
```

```sql
SHOW CREATE TABLE accounts;
```

Result:

| create_sql (STRING) |
|---|
| CREATE TABLE accounts (   id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO,   email STRING NOT NULL UNIQUE,   balance DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,   CONSTRAINT accounts_balance_check CHECK (balance >= 0) ) |
| CREATE INDEX accounts_balance ON accounts (balance) |

(2 rows)

**Command line: See the whole text in CSV format** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb sql market "SHOW CREATE TABLE trade_log" --format csv
```

Output:

```text
create_sql
"CREATE TABLE trade_log (
  date TIMESTAMP ROUND 1d,
  transaction_id LONG,
  symbol SYMBOL,
  buyer INT REFERENCES brokers(id),
  seller INT REFERENCES brokers(id),
  quantity LONG,
  rate DOUBLE,
  amount DOUBLE AS (quantity * rate)
) TIMESERIES(date) PARTITION BY DAY SORT BY (symbol, date) DEDUP KEY (date, transaction_id)"
```

<a id="show-partitions"></a>

## SHOW PARTITIONS FROM

Syntax:

```sql
SHOW PARTITIONS FROM table
SELECT * FROM table_partitions('table')
```

Lists the partitions of one table, oldest first, with QuestDB's columns. Both forms give the same rows.

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `index` | `INT` | 0 for the first partition, then 1, 2, ... |
| `partitionBy` | `STRING` | `DAY`, `MONTH`, `YEAR` or `NONE` |
| `name` | `STRING` | `2026-09-24`, `2026-09`, `2026`; `default` for a table without time partitions |
| `minTimestamp`, `maxTimestamp` | `TIMESTAMP` | the first and last time in it; `NULL` for a table without a time column |
| `numRows` | `LONG` | rows now |
| `diskSize` | `LONG` | bytes: its file, plus its new rows still in the log |
| `diskSizeHuman` | `STRING` | the same, like `12.4 KiB` |
| `readOnly`, `active`, `attached`, `detached`, `attachable` | `BOOL` | `active` is `true` for the newest partition; KarelaDB has no read-only or detached partitions |

- **Notes:** it needs the right to read the table (the row counts and times tell about the rows).

**Example: Trades split by day**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE trades (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, price DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY;
INSERT INTO trades VALUES ('2026-09-24T05:00:00Z', 'CITY', 10), ('2026-09-24T05:03:00Z', 'CITY', 11), ('2026-09-25T05:00:00Z', 'VOLT', 50);
```

```sql
SHOW PARTITIONS FROM trades;
```

Result:

| index (INT) | partitionBy (STRING) | name (STRING) | minTimestamp (TIMESTAMP) | maxTimestamp (TIMESTAMP) | numRows (LONG) | diskSize (LONG) | diskSizeHuman (STRING) | readOnly (BOOL) | active (BOOL) | attached (BOOL) | detached (BOOL) | attachable (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | DAY | 2026-09-24 | 2026-09-24T05:00:00.000Z | 2026-09-24T05:03:00.000Z | 2 | 548 | 548 B | false | false | true | false | false |
| 1 | DAY | 2026-09-25 | 2026-09-25T05:00:00.000Z | 2026-09-25T05:00:00.000Z | 1 | 520 | 520 B | false | true | true | false | false |

(2 rows)

<a id="questdb-meta"></a>

## QuestDB's meta functions

Apps written for QuestDB read the schema with functions in `FROM`. KarelaDB has them with QuestDB 9.4.3's column names and types, so that code runs unchanged.

| Function | One row per | Columns |
|---|---|---|
| `tables()` | table | `id`, `table_name`, `designatedTimestamp`, `partitionBy`, `maxUncommittedRows`, `o3MaxLag`, `walEnabled`, `directoryName`, `dedup`, `ttlValue`, `ttlUnit`, `matView` |
| `table_columns('t')` | column of `t` | `column`, `type`, `indexed`, `indexBlockCapacity`, `symbolCached`, `symbolCapacity`, `designated`, `upsertKey` |
| `wal_tables()` | table | `name`, `suspended`, `writerTxn`, `bufferedTxnSize`, `sequencerTxn`, `errorTag`, `errorMessage`, `memoryPressure` |
| `table_partitions('t')` | partition of `t` | as [SHOW PARTITIONS](#show-partitions) |
| `information_schema.tables()` | table or view | the same as `information_schema.tables` |

- `designatedTimestamp` is the time column of a `TIMESERIES` table, `NULL` for other tables. `dedup` is `true` when the table has a `DEDUP KEY`, and `upsertKey` marks its columns.
- `indexed` is `true` for a column with an index of its own (`ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c ADD INDEX`, or `CREATE INDEX` on that one column).
- `ttlValue`/`ttlUnit` show a TTL as QuestDB does: `SET TTL 14 DAYS` shows `2` `WEEK`; no TTL shows `0` `HOUR`.
- `maxUncommittedRows` (500000), `o3MaxLag` (600000000) and the symbol sizes (256) are QuestDB's defaults: KarelaDB has no such setting per table.
- `wal_tables()`: a KarelaDB commit is applied before it returns, so `writerTxn` always equals `sequencerTxn` and `suspended` is `false`. Code that waits for the two to match goes on at once.

**Example: What a rebuild reads first: time column, partitions, dedup keys**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ticks (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, price DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY DEDUP KEY (symbol, time);
```

```sql
SELECT table_name, designatedTimestamp, partitionBy, dedup FROM tables() WHERE table_name = 'ticks';
SELECT "column", type, indexed, designated, upsertKey FROM table_columns('ticks');
SELECT name, suspended, writerTxn = sequencerTxn AS caught_up FROM wal_tables() WHERE name = 'ticks';
```

Result:

`SELECT table_name, designatedTimestamp, partitionBy, dedup FROM tables() WHERE table_name = 'ticks'`

| table_name (STRING) | designatedTimestamp (STRING) | partitionBy (STRING) | dedup (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ticks | time | DAY | true |

(1 row)

`SELECT column, type, indexed, designated, upsertKey FROM table_columns('ticks')`

| column (STRING) | type (STRING) | indexed (BOOL) | designated (BOOL) | upsertKey (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| time | TIMESTAMP | false | true | true |
| symbol | SYMBOL | false | false | true |
| price | DOUBLE | false | false | false |

(3 rows)

`SELECT name, suspended, writerTxn = sequencerTxn AS caught_up FROM wal_tables() WHERE name = 'ticks'`

| name (STRING) | suspended (BOOL) | caught_up (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|
| ticks | false | true |

(1 row)

**Example: A table that does not exist** (shows an error)

```sql
SELECT * FROM table_columns('tickz');
```

Result:

Error: `table 'tickz' does not exist`

<!-- docs/rules.md -->

# Rules

> Name a check, the trading hours or the dedup choice of a table once, and KarelaDB applies it to every row written - saying which rule refused a row and why.

- Category: Tables
- Keywords: rule, rules, CREATE RULE, ALTER RULE, DROP RULE, SHOW RULES, kdb\_rules, price guard, value range, session hours, trading hours, ON FAIL SKIP, ON FAIL REJECT, dedup\_keep, keep first, check rule
- See also: [CREATE TABLE](create-table.md), [Trading calendars](calendars.md), [Partitions, SORT BY and DEDUP KEY](partitions-and-dedup.md), [Time and time zones](time-and-time-zones.md)

A **rule** is a named check or setting of one table. It applies to every row written to the table - `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `COPY`, `/imp`, `/write` and line protocol - and a row it refuses says **which rule and why**. Rules are listed by `SHOW RULES`, switched off and on by `ALTER RULE`, and saved with the table.

| Kind | Example | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| check | `CHECK (close > 0)` | every new or changed row must not make the condition false |
| session | `SESSION '11:00' TO '15:00' TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kathmandu' CALENDAR nepse` | the row's time must be inside the hours, on a trading day of the calendar |
| setting | `SET dedup_keep = 'first'` | which of two rows with the same DEDUP KEY stays |

<a id="create-rule"></a>

## CREATE RULE

Syntax:

```sql
CREATE RULE [IF NOT EXISTS] name ON table
    CHECK (condition)
  | SESSION 'HH:MM' TO 'HH:MM' [TIME ZONE 'zone'] [CALENDAR calendar]
  | SET dedup_keep = 'first' | 'last'
  [ON FAIL REJECT | SKIP] [MESSAGE 'text']
```

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `CHECK (condition)` | a condition on the values of one row, as a `CHECK` constraint. A condition that is `NULL` passes (standard SQL): write `close IS NOT NULL AND close > 0` to refuse a missing price |
| `SESSION ... TO ...` | the row's time, on the clock of `TIME ZONE` (UTC when not given), from the first time to the second (both included). With `CALENDAR`, only on its trading days ([calendars](calendars.md)). The table needs a time column |
| `ON FAIL REJECT` | the default: the statement fails, and nothing of it is written (PostgreSQL code `23514`) |
| `ON FAIL SKIP` | the row is left out and the statement goes on: the answer says `..., 1 left out by rules (ON FAIL SKIP)`. An `UPDATE` that would break the rule is refused instead (a row already there is never left out) |
| `MESSAGE 'text'` | your words in the refusal, before the reason |
| `SET dedup_keep = 'first'` | a row whose DEDUP KEY the table holds already is left out, whatever the write asked (also `INSERT OR REPLACE` and `/write`). `'last'` is the default: the new row replaces the old one. The table needs a `DEDUP KEY` |

- **Rows already there:** a new rule checks rows written from then on. Find older rows that break it with `SELECT ... WHERE NOT (condition)`.
- **Names:** a rule name is unique in the database. `DROP TABLE` drops the table's rules with it.
- **Role:** `ddl`, like `CREATE TABLE`.
- **Not yet:** `SET null_compare` (comparisons with `NULL` as QuestDB does them) is refused with that reason; comparisons follow standard SQL.

**Example: A price guard: the refused row names its rule** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ohlc (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, open DOUBLE, close DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY;
CREATE RULE price_guard ON ohlc CHECK (open > 0 AND close > 0) MESSAGE 'prices must be above 0';
```

```sql
INSERT INTO ohlc VALUES ('2026-10-01T05:30:00Z', 'NABIL', 500, 0);
```

Result:

Error: `rule 'price_guard' of table 'ohlc' refused the row: prices must be above 0 (open > 0 AND close > 0 is false for the row open='500', close='0')`

**Example: ON FAIL SKIP leaves the bad row out and keeps the others**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ticks (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, price DOUBLE, qty DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY;
CREATE RULE no_negative_qty ON ticks CHECK (qty >= 0) ON FAIL SKIP;
```

```sql
INSERT INTO ticks VALUES ('2026-10-01T05:30:00Z', 'NABIL', 500, 10), ('2026-10-01T05:31:00Z', 'NABIL', 501, -3),
  ('2026-10-01T05:32:00Z', 'NABIL', 502, 7);
```

Result:

```text
2 row(s) inserted, 1 left out by rules (ON FAIL SKIP)
```

**Example: Trading hours of NEPSE: 11:00 to 15:00 in Kathmandu, on its trading days** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE CALENDAR nepse_days (TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kathmandu', ERA FROM '2022-01-01' DAYS sun-thu);
CREATE TABLE trades (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, price DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY;
CREATE RULE nepse_hours ON trades SESSION '11:00' TO '15:00' TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kathmandu' CALENDAR nepse_days;
```

```sql
INSERT INTO trades VALUES ('2026-10-01T10:30:00Z', 'NABIL', 500);
```

Result:

Error: `rule 'nepse_hours' of table 'trades' refused the row: its time 2026-10-01T16:15:00 Asia/Kathmandu is outside the session 11:00 to 15:00`

<a id="alter-rule"></a>

## ALTER RULE

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER RULE [IF EXISTS] name ENABLE | DISABLE | RENAME TO new_name
```

A disabled rule stays, and checks nothing until `ENABLE`.

<a id="drop-rule"></a>

## DROP RULE

Syntax:

```sql
DROP RULE [IF EXISTS] name [, name ...]
```

<a id="show-rules"></a>

## See the rules: SHOW RULES

`SHOW RULES` is `SELECT * FROM kdb_rules`: one row per rule.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `rule`, `table_name` | the rule and its table |
| `kind` | `check`, `session` or `set` |
| `definition` | what follows `ON table` in its `CREATE RULE` |
| `on_fail` | `reject` or `skip` (empty for a setting) |
| `message`, `enabled` | its message, and whether it is on |

**Example: All rules of the database**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE quotes (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, bid DOUBLE, ask DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY;
CREATE RULE spread_ok ON quotes CHECK (ask >= bid) MESSAGE 'ask below bid';
```

```sql
SHOW RULES;
```

Result:

| rule (STRING) | table_name (STRING) | kind (STRING) | definition (STRING) | on_fail (STRING) | message (STRING) | enabled (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| spread_ok | quotes | check | CHECK (ask >= bid) | reject | ask below bid | true |

(1 row)

<!-- docs/trash.md -->

# The trash - UNDROP TABLE

> DROP TABLE keeps the table hidden for some days; UNDROP TABLE brings it back with its rows and indexes.

- Category: Tables
- Keywords: trash, undo drop, undrop, UNDROP, restore table, dropped table, recover table, DROPPED, \_dropped\_, --trash-days, PurgeDroppedTables
- See also: [CREATE TABLE](create-table.md), [ALTER, RENAME and DROP TABLE](alter-table.md), [Protection - timeouts, limits, safe updates, read-only](protection.md), [Backup, check, repair and restore](backup-and-safety.md), [Databases and the data folder](databases.md)

`DROP TABLE` is easy to type by mistake. With the trash, the table is only hidden: its rows stay where they are, and `UNDROP TABLE` brings it back. After the keep time (7 days by default) KarelaDB removes it for good.

`kareladb serve`, `kareladb sql` and `kareladb shell` keep dropped tables for `--trash-days 7`. Programs that use the KarelaDB library set `DatabaseOptions::dropped_table_keep_ms` (0 = off, the default there).

<a id="drop"></a>

## DROP TABLE and the trash

Syntax:

```sql
DROP TABLE [IF EXISTS] <name>                 -- kept in the trash
kareladb serve --trash-days 7                      (0 = DROP TABLE removes at once)
DROP TABLE _dropped_<time>_<name>             -- remove one from the trash for good
```

- **Returns:** `table 't' dropped; UNDROP TABLE t brings it back within 7 days`.
- **Notes:**
  - A new table with the same name, and indexes with the same names, can be made at once.
  - Dropping takes no time and no space: nothing is copied. The rows use disk space until the table is removed for good.
  - When it is removed for good, its files go and so do its entries in the database's list of files; any left by an older build are swept at the next checkpoint or open (`kareladb info` counts them under `manifest keys`).
  - This trash is for tables. [PURGE TRASH](databases.md#purge-trash) empties the database's `_trash` folder of replaced files, and `PURGE TRASH ALL` also the dropped databases; it leaves dropped tables alone.
  - A dropped table is hidden from `SHOW TABLES`, `SHOW INDEXES` and `/api/info`, and nobody can read or change it.
  - A dropped table that REFERENCES another table is removed for good when that other table is dropped.
  - A table with named `UNIQUE` or `PRIMARY KEY` constraints (PostgreSQL style) is dropped for good at once for now.
  - Table grants ([GRANT ... ON TABLE](table-rights.md)) do not come back with `UNDROP TABLE`.

<a id="undrop-table"></a>

## UNDROP TABLE

Syntax:

```sql
UNDROP TABLE <name>
```

Brings back the newest dropped table with this name: its columns, rows and indexes.

- **Returns:** `table 't' is back, with N row(s)`.
- **Notes:** refused while a table or view with that name exists (rename or drop it first), or when an index name is used again meanwhile. Needs role admin on the database.

**Example: Drop by mistake, then bring it back** (sample data: sample)

```sql
DROP TABLE live_data;
SHOW DROPPED TABLES;
UNDROP TABLE live_data;
SELECT count(*) FROM live_data;
```

Result:

`DROP TABLE live_data`

```text
table 'live_data' dropped; UNDROP TABLE live_data brings it back within 7 days
```

`SHOW DROPPED TABLES`

| name (STRING) | dropped (TIMESTAMP) | removed_after (TIMESTAMP) | rows (LONG) | stored_as (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| live_data | 2026-10-24T06:19:39.390Z | 2026-10-31T06:19:39.390Z | 12 | _dropped_1792822779390_live_data |

(1 row)

`UNDROP TABLE live_data`

```text
table 'live_data' is back, with 12 row(s)
```

`SELECT count(*) FROM live_data`

| count(*) (LONG) |
|---|
| 12 |

(1 row)

<a id="show-dropped-tables"></a>

## SHOW DROPPED TABLES

Syntax:

```sql
SHOW DROPPED TABLES
```

The tables in the trash of the current database, newest first.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | the name the table had |
| `dropped` | when it was dropped |
| `removed_after` | when KarelaDB removes it for good |
| `rows` | rows in it |
| `stored_as` | its hidden name, for `DROP TABLE` to remove it at once |

<!-- docs/constraints.md -->

# Constraints

> Rules that keep table data correct: PRIMARY KEY, AUTO, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, DEFAULT, REFERENCES and CHECK.

- Category: Constraints
- Keywords: constraint, rule, column rule, primary key, key, auto increment, autoincrement, serial, identity, sequence, AUTO, not null, required, unique, duplicate, default value, DEFAULT, foreign key, references, REFERENCES, parent row, ON DELETE CASCADE, check, CHECK, CONSTRAINT, validation, data integrity, cannot be NULL, must be unique, has no matching row, still refers to it, CHECK constraint failed, NaN, bad price, price check
- See also: [CREATE TABLE](create-table.md), [ALTER, RENAME and DROP TABLE](alter-table.md), [INSERT](insert.md), [UPDATE and DELETE](update-delete.md), [Indexes](indexes.md), [Transactions](transactions.md)

A **constraint** is a rule for the rows of a table. KarelaDB checks the rules every time a row is written (`INSERT`, `INSERT OR REPLACE`, `UPDATE`, the C++ `InsertRows`, the line protocol). A row that breaks a rule is **not** written, and the whole statement fails. So your app can never store a user without an email, a negative balance, or a trade for a broker that does not exist.

| Rule | Meaning | Error when broken |
|---|---|---|
| [`PRIMARY KEY`](#primary-key) | one row per value; never NULL | `a row with id='1' already exists` |
| [`AUTO`](#auto) | KarelaDB gives the next id | |
| [`NOT NULL`](#not-null) | the column must have a value | `cannot be NULL` |
| [`UNIQUE`](#unique) | no two rows with the same value | `must be unique: ... is already used` |
| [`DEFAULT`](#default) | the value when an INSERT gives none | |
| [`REFERENCES`](#references) | the value must exist in another table | `has no matching row in` / `still refers to it` |
| [`CHECK`](#check) | a condition every row must meet | `CHECK constraint '...' failed` |

A real example: the accounting tables of an app.

**Example: Users, accounts and a ledger with every kind of rule**

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
  id            INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO,
  email         STRING NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  password_hash STRING NOT NULL,
  created       TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id      INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO,
  user_id INT NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  balance DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (balance >= 0)
);
CREATE TABLE ledger (
  id           LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO,
  from_account INT NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),
  to_account   INT NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),
  amount       DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL,
  created      TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now(),
  CONSTRAINT positive_amount CHECK (amount > 0),
  CONSTRAINT two_accounts CHECK (from_account != to_account)
);
SHOW CREATE TABLE ledger;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE users (`

```text
table 'users' created
```

`CREATE TABLE accounts (`

```text
table 'accounts' created
```

`CREATE TABLE ledger (`

```text
table 'ledger' created
```

`SHOW CREATE TABLE ledger`

| create_sql (STRING) |
|---|
| CREATE TABLE ledger (   id LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO,   from_account INT NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),   to_account INT NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),   amount DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL,   created TIM... |

(1 row)

<a id="primary-key"></a>

## PRIMARY KEY

Syntax:

```sql
column TYPE PRIMARY KEY [AUTO]
```

The column that identifies a row. There is **one row per value**. Rows are kept in key order, so finding a row by its key is fast.

- At most one `PRIMARY KEY` per table, on one column. For a key over many columns, use `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` ([indexes](indexes.md)).
- A key can never be `NULL` (you do not need to write `NOT NULL`).
- `UPDATE` may change a key; it is refused when the new value is already used.
- **Returns:** a duplicate key gives `a row with id='...' already exists in 't'`; nothing of that statement is saved. Use `INSERT OR REPLACE` or `INSERT OR IGNORE` to decide what happens ([INSERT](insert.md#duplicates)).
- **Notes:** only for relational tables. A time-series table uses [DEDUP KEY](create-table.md#dedup-key) instead. You cannot add a primary key with `ALTER TABLE` later.

**Example: One row per broker**

```sql
CREATE TABLE brokers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO brokers VALUES (58, 'Northgate Securities'), (1, 'Keystone Securities');
SELECT id, name FROM brokers;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE brokers (`

```text
table 'brokers' created
```

`INSERT INTO brokers VALUES (58, 'Northgate Securities'), (1, 'Keystone Securities')`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT id, name FROM brokers`

| id (INT) | name (STRING) |
|---|---|
| 1 | Keystone Securities |
| 58 | Northgate Securities |

(2 rows)

**Example: The same broker number twice** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE brokers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO brokers VALUES (58, 'Northgate Securities');
```

```sql
INSERT INTO brokers VALUES (58, 'Another Broker');
```

Result:

Error: `a row with id='58' already exists in 'brokers'. Use INSERT OR REPLACE to overwrite it, or INSERT OR IGNORE to skip it`

**Example: A key cannot be NULL** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE securities (symbol SYMBOL PRIMARY KEY, name STRING);
```

```sql
INSERT INTO securities (name) VALUES ('No symbol');
```

Result:

Error: `column 'symbol' (SYMBOL): cannot be NULL`

<a id="auto"></a>

## PRIMARY KEY AUTO

Syntax:

```sql
column BYTE | SHORT | INT | LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO
```

When an `INSERT` gives no value (or `NULL`) for the key, KarelaDB uses the **next number** of the table's counter: 1, 2, 3, ... This is like `SERIAL` or `IDENTITY` in PostgreSQL.

- You may still give an id yourself. A bigger id moves the counter up: after id 10, the next automatic id is 11.
- The counter **only goes up**. The id of a deleted row, of a failed insert, or of a rolled-back transaction is never used again, so there can be gaps (1, 2, 4, ...).
- **Returns:** use `RETURNING id` to get the new id back ([RETURNING](insert.md#returning)).
- **Notes:** only on an integer `PRIMARY KEY`. Do not use AUTO ids to count rows. When the counter passes the type's range (127 for `BYTE`), the insert fails; use `LONG` for big tables.

**Example: New forum posts get ids 1, 2, 3**

```sql
CREATE TABLE posts (id LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO, author STRING NOT NULL, body STRING NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO posts (author, body) VALUES ('ram', 'Is CITY a good buy?'), ('sita', 'I agree, the profit grew 18%.');
INSERT INTO posts (author, body) VALUES ('hari', 'Price is high now.');
SELECT id, author, body FROM posts;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE posts (`

```text
table 'posts' created
```

`INSERT INTO posts (author, body) VALUES ('ram', 'Is CITY a good buy?'), ('sita', 'I agree, the profi`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`INSERT INTO posts (author, body) VALUES ('hari', 'Price is high now.')`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT id, author, body FROM posts`

| id (LONG) | author (STRING) | body (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ram | Is CITY a good buy? |
| 2 | sita | I agree, the profit grew 18%. |
| 3 | hari | Price is high now. |

(3 rows)

**Example: Ids of deleted rows are not used again**

Setup:

```sql

INSERT INTO posts (body) VALUES ('first'), ('second'), ('third');
```

```sql

SELECT id, body FROM posts;
```

Result:

```text

```

```text

```

`INSERT INTO posts (body) VALUES ('new post')`

```text

```

`SELECT id, body FROM posts`

|---|---|
| 1 | first |

(4 rows)

**Example: AUTO needs a whole-number column** (shows an error)

```sql

```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 43: PRIMARY KEY AUTO needs an integer column; expected BYTE, SHORT, INT or LONG but column 'id' is STRING`

<a id="not-null"></a>

## NOT NULL

Syntax:

```sql
column TYPE NOT NULL
```

The column must always have a value. An `INSERT` that gives no value (and there is no `DEFAULT`), or gives `NULL`, fails. An `UPDATE ... SET column = NULL` fails too.

- **Returns:** `column 'name' (STRING): cannot be NULL`.
- **Notes:** a `DEFAULT` fills the column only when the `INSERT` does not name it. An explicit `NULL` is still refused. To add a `NOT NULL` column to a table with rows, give it a `DEFAULT` ([ADD COLUMN](alter-table.md#add-column)). The time column of a time-series table always needs a value: `the time column 'time' needs a value`.

**Example: Every user needs an email**

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (id LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO, email STRING NOT NULL, phone STRING);
INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('ram@example.com');
SELECT id, email, phone FROM users;
```

Result:


| id (LONG) | email (STRING) | phone (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ram@example.com | NULL |

(1 row)

<a id="unique"></a>

## UNIQUE

Syntax:

```sql
column TYPE UNIQUE
```

No two rows may have the same value in this column. `NULL` does not count: many rows may have `NULL`.

- A table may have many `UNIQUE` columns (email, phone, username).
- Checked on `INSERT`, `INSERT OR REPLACE` and `UPDATE`, and also between the rows of one statement.
- **Returns:** `column 'email' must be unique: 'ram@example.com' is already used`.
- **Notes:** `INSERT OR REPLACE` replaces a row with the same **key**, not a row with the same unique value: a clash on a `UNIQUE` column is still an error. For a rule over many columns (one row per symbol, year and quarter), use `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` ([indexes](indexes.md)). Text compares exactly: `'Ram@Example.com'` and `'ram@example.com'` are different; store emails in lower case.

**Example: One account per email; many users without a phone**

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (id LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO, email STRING NOT NULL UNIQUE, phone STRING UNIQUE);
INSERT INTO users (email, phone) VALUES ('ram@example.com', NULL), ('sita@example.com', NULL), ('hari@example.com', '9800000000');
SELECT id, email, phone FROM users;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE users (`

```text
table 'users' created
```

`INSERT INTO users (email, phone) VALUES ('ram@example.com', NULL), ('sita@example.com', NULL), ('har`

```text
3 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT id, email, phone FROM users`

| id (LONG) | email (STRING) | phone (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ram@example.com | NULL |
| 2 | sita@example.com | NULL |
| 3 | hari@example.com | 9800000000 |

(3 rows)

**Example: Register the same email twice** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql

INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('ram@example.com');
```


Error: `column 'email' must be unique: 'ram@example.com' is already used`

**Example: Change an email to one that is taken** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql

INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('ram@example.com'), ('sita@example.com');
```

```sql
UPDATE users SET email = 'ram@example.com' WHERE id = 2;
```

Result:

Error: `column 'email' must be unique: 'ram@example.com' is already used`

<a id="default"></a>

## DEFAULT

Syntax:

```sql
column TYPE DEFAULT expression
```

The value a column gets when an `INSERT` does not name it. Also used by `INSERT OR REPLACE` for columns you do not give, and for old rows by `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN`.

| Default | Example |
|---|---|
| a constant | `DEFAULT 0`, `DEFAULT 'active'`, `DEFAULT FALSE`, `DEFAULT '{}'` for JSON |
| an expression without columns | `DEFAULT -1`, `DEFAULT 60 * 24` |
| a function | `DEFAULT now()`, `DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()`, `DEFAULT random_token()` |

- `now()` and random functions are worked out for **each** inserted row.
- **Notes:** a default cannot use columns (write a computed column `AS (...)` for that) or subqueries. A constant must fit the column type: `INT DEFAULT 'x'` is refused when the table is created. `NOT NULL DEFAULT NULL` is refused. An explicit `NULL` in an `INSERT` does not use the default. There is no `DEFAULT` keyword inside `VALUES (...)`: leave the column out of the column list instead.

**Example: New accounts start active, with 0.00 and a creation time**

```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id      INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO,
  owner   STRING NOT NULL,
  balance DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  status  STRING NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active',
  opened  TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now()
);
INSERT INTO accounts (owner) VALUES ('Ram Sharma');
INSERT INTO accounts (owner, balance, status) VALUES ('Sita Rai', 99.50, 'frozen');
SELECT id, owner, balance, status, opened IS NOT NULL AS has_open_time FROM accounts;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE accounts (`

```text
table 'accounts' created
```

`INSERT INTO accounts (owner) VALUES ('Ram Sharma')`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`INSERT INTO accounts (owner, balance, status) VALUES ('Sita Rai', 99.50, 'frozen')`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT id, owner, balance, status, opened IS NOT NULL AS has_open_time FROM accounts`

| id (INT) | owner (STRING) | balance (DECIMAL(2)) | status (STRING) | has_open_time (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ram Sharma | 0.00 | active | true |
| 2 | Sita Rai | 99.50 | frozen | true |

(2 rows)

**Example: A default of the wrong type** (shows an error)

```sql

```

Result:

Error: `column 'likes' of table 'posts' is INT but its DEFAULT 'none' is text; expected a whole number`

**Example: A default cannot use another column** (shows an error)

```sql

```

Result:

Error: `column 'edited' of table 'posts' has DEFAULT using column 'created'; expected a constant such as 0 or 'n/a', or AS (...) for a computed column`

<a id="references"></a>

## REFERENCES

Syntax:

```sql
column TYPE REFERENCES table(column)
```

The value must exist in the other table (the **parent**). This is a **foreign key**. Use it so a trade cannot point to a broker that does not exist, and a ledger row cannot point to a missing account.

| Argument | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `table` | the parent table; it must exist already (or be the same table) |
| `column` | the parent column; it must be the `PRIMARY KEY` or `UNIQUE`, with the same kind of type (any integer type fits any integer type; a `SYMBOL` may point to a `STRING`) |

What KarelaDB checks:

| Action | Result |
|---|---|
| `INSERT` or `UPDATE` of a child row with a value the parent does not have | error: `column 'buyer' = '99' has no matching row in brokers(id)` |
| `NULL` in the child column | allowed, not checked (add `NOT NULL` to forbid it) |
| `DELETE` of a parent row that children still use, or `UPDATE` of its key | error: `cannot remove brokers(id) = '58': ... still refers to it` |
| `INSERT OR REPLACE` of a parent row with the same key | allowed |
| `DROP TABLE` of the parent | error while a child column references it |

- **Notes:** `ON DELETE` / `ON UPDATE` take `NO ACTION` (the default: refuse while children point to the row), `RESTRICT`, `CASCADE` (delete the children too; ON UPDATE CASCADE follows the new key), `SET NULL` and `SET DEFAULT`. All children are changed in the same statement, or none. Children that `SET NULL`, `SET DEFAULT` or `ON UPDATE CASCADE` change are an update of the child table: its `BEFORE UPDATE` row triggers and `UPDATE` triggers run for them (as in PostgreSQL), and a trigger that refuses stops the whole statement. What such a trigger changes is checked like a plain UPDATE (references, CHECK, the time column); it may not change a UNIQUE or key column there - do that with a separate `UPDATE`. Children `ON DELETE CASCADE` removes fire its `DELETE` triggers. Load the parent table before the child table. A new row cannot point to a row inserted **in the same statement** (a reply and its parent post in one `INSERT`): insert the parent first. REFERENCES checks every new row, so very big imports are faster without it.

**Example: Trades must use real brokers**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE brokers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE trades (id LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO, symbol SYMBOL, buyer INT NOT NULL REFERENCES brokers(id), seller INT REFERENCES brokers(id));
INSERT INTO brokers VALUES (58, 'Northgate Securities'), (45, 'Imperial Securities');
```

```sql
INSERT INTO trades (symbol, buyer, seller) VALUES ('CITY', 58, 45), ('COAST', 45, NULL);
SELECT id, symbol, buyer, seller FROM trades;
```

Result:

`INSERT INTO trades (symbol, buyer, seller) VALUES ('CITY', 58, 45), ('COAST', 45, NULL)`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT id, symbol, buyer, seller FROM trades`

| id (LONG) | symbol (SYMBOL) | buyer (INT) | seller (INT) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | CITY | 58 | 45 |
| 2 | COAST | 45 | NULL |

(2 rows)

**Example: A broker that does not exist** (shows an error)

<a id="check"></a>

## CHECK

Syntax:

```sql
column TYPE [CONSTRAINT name] CHECK (condition)            -- after a column
[CONSTRAINT name] CHECK (condition)                        -- after the columns, for the table
ALTER TABLE table ADD [CONSTRAINT name] CHECK (condition)
ALTER TABLE table DROP CONSTRAINT name
```

A condition that every row must meet. A row where the condition is **false** is not written, and the statement fails. Use it for business rules: a balance is never negative, an amount is positive, a quarter is 1 to 4.

| Part | Rule |
|---|---|
| `condition` | uses the stored columns of the **same row**, operators, `CASE`, `IN`, `BETWEEN`, `LIKE` and built-in functions (`length(email) > 3`) |
| not allowed | other rows, subqueries, aggregates (`sum`), window functions, saved functions, computed columns |
| `CONSTRAINT name` | the name of the rule; without it KarelaDB makes `table_column_check` (after a column) or `table_check` (for the table) |
| `NULL` | a condition that is `NULL` **passes**: add `NOT NULL` when the value must be there |
| NaN | every comparison with a NaN (`=`, `<`, `>=`, `BETWEEN`, `IN`) is **false** here, and `<>` is true: `CHECK (price > 0)` refuses a NaN price, `CHECK (price <> 0)` does not. Write what a good value is, not what a bad one is. (A query compares a NaN as PostgreSQL does, bigger than every number: see [DOUBLE](column-types.md#double).) |

- **Returns:** `CHECK constraint 'name' of table 't' failed: condition is false for the row id='1', balance='-4000.00'`. The message names the rule, the table, the row key and the columns the rule uses.
- **Notes:** table rules come **after** all columns. A column used by a `CHECK` cannot be dropped; `RENAME COLUMN` renames it inside the rule. `SHOW CREATE TABLE` shows every rule with its name. [ADD and DROP CONSTRAINT](alter-table.md#add-check) change the rules later. A rule cannot compare with other rows (like "the sum of all balances is 0"); check that with a query or in a [procedure](procedures.md).

**Example: A withdrawal bigger than the balance is refused** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO, owner STRING NOT NULL, balance DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (balance >= 0));
INSERT INTO accounts (owner, balance) VALUES ('Ram', 1000.00);
```

```sql
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 5000 WHERE id = 1;
```

Result:

Error: `CHECK constraint 'accounts_balance_check' of table 'accounts' failed: balance >= 0 is false for the row id='1', balance='-4000.00'`

**Example: Named rules for a ledger** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ledger (
  id           LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO,
  from_account INT NOT NULL,
  to_account   INT NOT NULL,
  amount       DECIMAL(2) NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT positive_amount CHECK (amount > 0),
  CONSTRAINT two_accounts CHECK (from_account != to_account)
);
```

```sql
INSERT INTO ledger (from_account, to_account, amount) VALUES (1, 2, 250.50);
INSERT INTO ledger (from_account, to_account, amount) VALUES (1, 1, 100.00);
```

Result:

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

Error: `CHECK constraint 'two_accounts' of table 'ledger' failed: from_account != to_account is false for the row id='2', from_account='1', to_account='1'`

**Example: Quarter 1 to 4, and a CHECK lets NULL pass**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE fundamentals (
  symbol STRING NOT NULL,
  quarter INT CHECK (quarter BETWEEN 1 AND 4),
  eps DECIMAL(2)
);
```

```sql

SELECT symbol, quarter, eps FROM fundamentals;
SHOW CREATE TABLE fundamentals;
```

`INSERT INTO fundamentals VALUES ('CITY', 4, 12.10), ('COAST', NULL, 6.35)`

```text

```

|---|---|---|

| COAST | NULL | 6.35 |

(2 rows)

|---|

# INSERT

> Add rows with INSERT, decide what happens with duplicate keys, get new ids back with RETURNING, and write times correctly.

- Category: Writing data
- Keywords: insert, add rows, new row, VALUES, INTO, column list, multi-row insert, upsert, INSERT OR REPLACE, REPLACE, INSERT OR IGNORE, IGNORE, ON CONFLICT, duplicate key, already exists, dedup, RETURNING, returning id, new id, last insert id, time zone, +05:45, Nepal time, UTC, INSERT SELECT, copy rows
- See also: [UPDATE and DELETE](update-delete.md), [Loading many rows](loading-data.md), [Constraints](constraints.md), [Column types](column-types.md), [CREATE TABLE](create-table.md), [Transactions](transactions.md), [Time and time zones](time-and-time-zones.md)

`INSERT` adds rows to a table. One `INSERT` can add many rows, and it is **all or nothing**: when one row is bad, no row of that statement is saved. When KarelaDB says `inserted`, the rows are already on the disk.

| Statement | The key is new | The key is already there |
|---|---|---|
| [`INSERT`](#insert) | row added | **error**, nothing saved |
| [`INSERT OR REPLACE`](#insert-or-replace) | row added | the old row is replaced by the new one |
| [`INSERT OR IGNORE`](#insert-or-ignore) | row added | the new row is skipped |

A real example: today's market candles arrive; one of them was already loaded.

**Example: Load daily candles; a repeated row is replaced, not doubled**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ochl_day (time TIMESTAMP ROUND 1d, symbol SYMBOL, open DOUBLE, high DOUBLE, low DOUBLE, close DOUBLE, volume DOUBLE)
  TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY YEAR DEDUP KEY (symbol, time);
INSERT INTO ochl_day VALUES ('2026-09-13', 'CITY', 505.0, 509.0, 503.1, 508.2, 91000);
```

```sql
INSERT OR REPLACE INTO ochl_day (time, symbol, open, high, low, close, volume) VALUES
  ('2026-09-13', 'CITY', 505.0, 509.0, 503.1, 507.6, 91000),
  ('2026-09-13', 'COAST',  376.0, 379.9, 374.0, 378.5, 120500),
  ('2026-09-13', 'VOLT', 191.0, 194.2, 190.1, 193.7, 64000);
SELECT time, symbol, close FROM ochl_day ORDER BY symbol;
```

Result:

`INSERT OR REPLACE INTO ochl_day (time, symbol, open, high, low, close, volume) VALUES ('2026-09-13',`

```text
2 row(s) inserted, 1 replaced
```

`SELECT time, symbol, close FROM ochl_day ORDER BY symbol`

| time (TIMESTAMP) | symbol (SYMBOL) | close (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-13T00:00:00.000Z | CITY | 507.6 |
| 2026-09-13T00:00:00.000Z | COAST | 378.5 |
| 2026-09-13T00:00:00.000Z | VOLT | 193.7 |

(3 rows)

<a id="insert"></a>

## INSERT INTO ... VALUES

Syntax:

```sql
INSERT INTO table [(column, ...)] VALUES (value, ...) [, (value, ...) ...] [RETURNING ...]
```

Adds one row for each `(...)` after `VALUES`.

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `table` | a table (not a view) |
| `(column, ...)` | optional. The columns the values are for, in any order. Columns you leave out get their `DEFAULT`, or `NULL`, or the next [AUTO](constraints.md#auto) id |
| without a column list | give a value for **every** stored column, in table order; computed columns are skipped |
| `value` | a constant (`'CITY'`, `504.9`, `NULL`, `TRUE`) or an expression without columns (`1 + 1`, `now()`, `CAST('7' AS INT)`) |

- **Returns:** `N row(s) inserted`.
- Each value is converted to the column type; see [column types](column-types.md). Text goes in single quotes; a `'` inside is written `''`.
- **Notes:** many rows in one `INSERT` are **much** faster than one `INSERT` per row. A value cannot be a subquery or use a column. Every row needs the same number of values. The rules of the table ([constraints](constraints.md)) are checked for every row.

**Example: Register two app users; the id and the time come by themselves**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (id LONG PRIMARY KEY AUTO, email STRING NOT NULL UNIQUE, name STRING, created TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now());
```

```sql
INSERT INTO users (email, name) VALUES ('ram@example.com', 'Ram Sharma'), ('sita@example.com', 'Sita Rai');
SELECT id, email, name, created IS NOT NULL AS has_created FROM users;
```

Result:

`INSERT INTO users (email, name) VALUES ('ram@example.com', 'Ram Sharma'), ('sita@example.com', 'Sita`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT id, email, name, created IS NOT NULL AS has_created FROM users`

| id (LONG) | email (STRING) | name (STRING) | has_created (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ram@example.com | Ram Sharma | true |
| 2 | sita@example.com | Sita Rai | true |

(2 rows)

**Example: A forum post with text in another language (Nepali) and a quote inside**


Result:

`INSERT INTO posts (author, body) VALUES ('ram', 'City''s dividend looks good.'), ('sita', 'नमस्ते, य`
