# ORDER BY, LIMIT, OFFSET

> Sort the result, and give back only the first rows or one page of rows.

- Category: Querying
- Keywords: sort, order, sorting, ORDER BY, ASC, DESC, ascending, descending, NULLS FIRST, NULLS LAST, NULLS, FIRST, LAST, LIMIT, OFFSET, top N, first rows, paging, pagination, page, next page, LIMIT a, b, order by, limit, offset, asc, desc, paging
- See also: [SELECT](select.md), [WHERE (row-comparison)](where.md#row-comparison), [GROUP BY and HAVING](group-by.md), [UNION and subqueries (union-all)](union-subqueries.md#union-all), [Window and series functions](functions-window.md), [EXPLAIN](explain.md)

`ORDER BY` sorts the rows of the result. `LIMIT` keeps only the first rows, and `OFFSET` skips rows before them.
They run **last**, after `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and the select list, so they work on the final result.

Without `ORDER BY`, the order of the rows is not promised. Always add `ORDER BY` when the order matters (a "top 10", a page of posts, a report).

**Example: The 3 days with the biggest volume, then the next 3** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT time, symbol, volume FROM ochl_day ORDER BY volume DESC LIMIT 3;
SELECT time, symbol, volume FROM ochl_day ORDER BY volume DESC LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3;
```

Result:

`SELECT time, symbol, volume FROM ochl_day ORDER BY volume DESC LIMIT 3`

| time (TIMESTAMP) | symbol (SYMBOL) | volume (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-09T00:00:00.000Z | COAST | 186330 |
| 2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z | COAST | 186200 |
| 2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z | CITY | 183040 |

(3 rows)

`SELECT time, symbol, volume FROM ochl_day ORDER BY volume DESC LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3`

| time (TIMESTAMP) | symbol (SYMBOL) | volume (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-09T00:00:00.000Z | CITY | 182390 |
| 2026-08-31T00:00:00.000Z | CITY | 159240 |
| 2026-09-03T00:00:00.000Z | VOLT | 145930 |

(3 rows)

<a id="order-by"></a>

## ORDER BY

Syntax:

```sql
ORDER BY sort_key [ASC | DESC] [NULLS FIRST | NULLS LAST], ...
```

A `sort_key` can be:

| Sort key | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| an output column name or alias | `ORDER BY change_pct` | the value of that output column |
| a position | `ORDER BY 2` | the 2nd output column (counts from 1) |
| a table column | `ORDER BY volume` | also when it is not in the select list |
| an expression | `ORDER BY abs(close - open)` | the value of the expression for each row |

With many keys, the second key sorts rows that are equal in the first key, and so on.

- **Returns:** the same rows, sorted.
- **Notes:** text is sorted by its bytes: `'A'` comes before `'B'`, and **every capital letter comes before every small letter** (`'Z'` before `'a'`). This is PostgreSQL's `COLLATE "C"`. For dictionary order write `ORDER BY name COLLATE "en_US"` ([COLLATE](#collate)), or `ORDER BY lower(name)`.
- An alias can be used alone (`ORDER BY move`), but not inside an expression (`ORDER BY abs(move)` is an error in a query without `GROUP BY`): write the expression again.
- After `GROUP BY` or with aggregates, `ORDER BY` can only use the output columns (names, aliases, positions) and expressions of them, like `ORDER BY q / n`.
- After `UNION ALL`, `ORDER BY` can only use output column names or positions (see [UNION ALL](union-subqueries.md#union-all)).
- Rows that are equal in every key keep the order they came in. For stable pages, end with a unique column (like `id`).
- `ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` on a big table only keeps the best `n` rows while it reads, so it is fast. `ORDER BY time DESC LIMIT n` on a time-series table even stops early: it reads the newest rows first (see [LIMIT](performance-tips.md#limit)).

**Example: Top gainers of the day, sorted by an alias** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT symbol, open, close, round((close - open) / open * 100, 2) AS change_pct
FROM ochl_day
WHERE time IN '2026-09-10'
ORDER BY change_pct DESC;
```

Result:

| symbol (SYMBOL) | open (DOUBLE) | close (DOUBLE) | change_pct (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|
| VOLT | 185.6 | 191.2 | 3.02 |
| CITY | 504.6 | 504.9 | 0.06 |
| COAST | 380.1 | 376.1 | -1.05 |

(3 rows)

**Example: Sector first, then symbol inside each sector** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT sector, symbol, name FROM securities ORDER BY sector, symbol;
```

Result:

| sector (STRING) | symbol (SYMBOL) | name (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| Banking | CITY | City Bank Limited |
| Banking | COAST | Coastal Bank Limited |
| Energy | VOLT | Volt River Hydropower Limited |
| Investment | ACME | Acme Investment Company |
| Telecom | TELCO | Northwind Telecom Limited |

(5 rows)

**Example: Sort by a column that is not shown, and by an expression** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT symbol, close FROM ochl_day WHERE time IN '2026-09-10' ORDER BY abs(close - open) DESC;
```

Result:

| symbol (SYMBOL) | close (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|
| VOLT | 191.2 |
| COAST | 376.1 |
| CITY | 504.9 |

(3 rows)

**Example: Newest news first** (sample data: content-news)

```sql
SELECT published_at, symbol, title FROM news ORDER BY published_at DESC LIMIT 3;
```

Result:

| published_at (TIMESTAMP) | symbol (STRING) | title (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-02T03:15:00.000Z | COAST | Coastal Bank merger talks |
| 2026-09-01T02:15:00.000Z | NULL | Market index closes at 2,840 |
| 2026-08-15T04:15:00.000Z | VOLT | Hydropower company plans IPO |

(3 rows)

**Example: Sort by position: the 3rd column (type), then the 2nd (name)** (sample data: query-app)

```sql
SELECT code, name, type FROM accounts WHERE type IN ('income', 'expense') ORDER BY 3, 2;
```

Result:

| code (INT) | name (STRING) | type (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| 5000 | Broker commission | expense |
| 5100 | Office rent | expense |
| 4000 | Dividend income | income |
| 4100 | Gain on sale | income |

(4 rows)

**Example: Capital letters come before small letters; lower() fixes it** (sample data: query-app)

```sql
SELECT email FROM app_users WHERE id IN (2, 4, 6) ORDER BY email;
SELECT email FROM app_users WHERE id IN (2, 4, 6) ORDER BY lower(email);
```

Result:

`SELECT email FROM app_users WHERE id IN (2, 4, 6) ORDER BY email`

| email (STRING) |
|---|
| GITA.RAI@Gmail.com |
| anita_m@hotmail.com |
| sita.k@yahoo.com |

(3 rows)

`SELECT email FROM app_users WHERE id IN (2, 4, 6) ORDER BY lower(email)`

| email (STRING) |
|---|
| anita_m@hotmail.com |
| GITA.RAI@Gmail.com |
| sita.k@yahoo.com |

(3 rows)

**Example: An alias inside an expression is not known** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

```sql
SELECT symbol, close - open AS move FROM ochl_day WHERE time IN '2026-09-10' ORDER BY abs(move);
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 91: unknown column 'move' (table 'ochl_day' has: time symbol open high low close volume)`

**Example: A position must be one of the columns** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

```sql
SELECT id, name FROM brokers ORDER BY 3;
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 39: ORDER BY 3: there are only 2 columns`

<a id="asc-desc"></a>

## ASC, DESC

Syntax:

```sql
ORDER BY sort_key ASC
ORDER BY sort_key DESC
```

`ASC` (ascending) sorts small to big: 1, 2, 3; A, B, C; old times first. It is the default.
`DESC` (descending) sorts big to small: 3, 2, 1; new times first.

- **Notes:** `ASC` or `DESC` belongs to one sort key. `ORDER BY a DESC, b` sorts `a` big first, and `b` small first.
- `DESC` also changes where `NULL` goes by default (see [NULLS FIRST, NULLS LAST](order-by-limit.md#nulls-first-last)).

**Example: Brokers by turnover, biggest first; equal turnover by id, smallest first** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT buyer, sum(amount) AS turnover
FROM trade_log
WHERE date IN '2026-09-10'
GROUP BY buyer
ORDER BY turnover DESC, buyer ASC;
```

Result:

| buyer (INT) | turnover (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|
| 49 | 960370 |
| 45 | 695950 |
| 58 | 260190 |
| 1 | 239420 |
| 34 | 205450 |

(5 rows)

**Example: The last 3 minutes of COAST on 2026-09-10** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT time, close, volume FROM ochl_minutes
WHERE symbol = 'COAST' AND time IN '2026-09-10'
ORDER BY time DESC
LIMIT 3;
```

Result:

| time (TIMESTAMP) | close (DOUBLE) | volume (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-10T09:14:00.000Z | 376.1 | 1060 |
| 2026-09-10T09:13:00.000Z | 376.2 | 1320 |
| 2026-09-10T09:12:00.000Z | 376 | 1150 |

(3 rows)

<a id="collate"></a>

## COLLATE: dictionary order

Syntax:

```sql
sort_key COLLATE "name"
a COLLATE "name" = b      (also <, >, BETWEEN, IN)
```

`COLLATE` picks the order for one `ORDER BY` key or one comparison. Without it, text compares byte by byte.

| Name | Order | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `"C"`, `"POSIX"`, `"default"` | bytes (the same as no `COLLATE`) | `Apple, Zebra, apple` |
| `"en_US"`, `"en_US.utf8"`, `"und-x-icu"`, `"unicode"`, other language names | dictionary: letters first, case and accents only break ties | `apple, Apple, ěa, Zebra` |
| `nocase` | like the dictionary, and `'a' = 'A'` | `'apple' COLLATE nocase = 'APPLE'` is true |
| `natural` | like the dictionary, and digits compare as numbers | `file2, file10` |

- **Returns:** a comparison gives `true` or `false`; `ORDER BY` sorts. `SELECT name COLLATE "en_US"` gives `name` unchanged.
- **Notes:** every language name uses the same dictionary order (a letter with an accent sorts right after the plain letter). An unknown name is an error.
- In `ORDER BY`, write the column or expression with `COLLATE`, not an alias or a position.
- `COLLATE` after a column type in `CREATE TABLE` is still read and ignored: write it in the query.
- Sorting with `COLLATE` works out a sort key for every row, so it is slower than a plain `ORDER BY`.

**Example: Byte order, then dictionary order** (sample data: query-app)

```sql
SELECT email FROM app_users WHERE id IN (2, 4, 6) ORDER BY email;
SELECT email FROM app_users WHERE id IN (2, 4, 6) ORDER BY email COLLATE "en_US";
```

Result:

`SELECT email FROM app_users WHERE id IN (2, 4, 6) ORDER BY email`

| email (STRING) |
|---|
| GITA.RAI@Gmail.com |
| anita_m@hotmail.com |
| sita.k@yahoo.com |

(3 rows)

`SELECT email FROM app_users WHERE id IN (2, 4, 6) ORDER BY email COLLATE en_US`

| email (STRING) |
|---|
| anita_m@hotmail.com |
| GITA.RAI@Gmail.com |
| sita.k@yahoo.com |

(3 rows)

**Example: Case-insensitive match and natural order** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT 'Zebra' < 'apple' AS bytes, 'Zebra' COLLATE "en_US" < 'apple' AS dictionary,
       'apple' COLLATE nocase = 'APPLE' AS same, 'file2' COLLATE natural < 'file10' AS natural;
```

Result:

| bytes (BOOL) | dictionary (BOOL) | same (BOOL) | natural (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|---|
| true | false | true | true |

(1 row)

**Example: An unknown collation** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

```sql
SELECT 'a' COLLATE klingon = 'a';
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 20: collation "klingon" does not exist; KarelaDB knows "C", "en_US" (and other language names), "nocase" and "natural"`

<a id="nulls-first-last"></a>

## NULLS FIRST, NULLS LAST

Syntax:

```sql
ORDER BY sort_key [ASC | DESC] NULLS FIRST
ORDER BY sort_key [ASC | DESC] NULLS LAST
```

Say where rows with a `NULL` sort key go: before all other rows (`NULLS FIRST`) or after them (`NULLS LAST`).

| Written | NULL rows go |
|---|---|
| `ORDER BY x` or `ORDER BY x ASC` | last (like `NULLS LAST`) |
| `ORDER BY x DESC` | first (like `NULLS FIRST`) |
| `ORDER BY x ... NULLS FIRST` | first |
| `ORDER BY x ... NULLS LAST` | last |

- **Notes:** the defaults are the same as in PostgreSQL: `NULL` counts as bigger than every value.
- A common case: "last login, newest first" should show users who never logged in at the end: `ORDER BY last_login DESC NULLS LAST`.

**Example: Recently active users first, never logged in last** (sample data: query-app)

```sql
SELECT username, last_login FROM app_users ORDER BY last_login DESC NULLS LAST;
```

Result:

| username (STRING) | last_login (TIMESTAMP) |
|---|---|
| bikash | 2026-09-11T04:20:00.000Z |
| gita | 2026-09-11T00:45:00.000Z |
| ram | 2026-09-10T14:30:00.000Z |
| suman | 2026-09-10T03:55:00.000Z |
| sita | 2026-09-09T02:15:00.000Z |
| anita | 2026-08-30T06:15:00.000Z |
| hari_99 | NULL |
| test_user | NULL |

(8 rows)

**Example: Without NULLS LAST, DESC puts NULL first** (sample data: query-app)

```sql
SELECT username, last_login FROM app_users ORDER BY last_login DESC LIMIT 3;
```

Result:

| username (STRING) | last_login (TIMESTAMP) |
|---|---|
| hari_99 | NULL |
| test_user | NULL |
| bikash | 2026-09-11T04:20:00.000Z |

(3 rows)

**Example: Securities without a close today at the top** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT s.symbol, d.close
FROM securities s
LEFT JOIN ochl_day d ON d.symbol = s.symbol AND d.time IN '2026-09-10'
ORDER BY d.close NULLS FIRST;
```

Result:

| symbol (SYMBOL) | close (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|
| ACME | NULL |
| TELCO | NULL |
| VOLT | 191.2 |
| COAST | 376.1 |
| CITY | 504.9 |

(5 rows)

**Example: NULLS needs FIRST or LAST** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

```sql
SELECT id FROM brokers ORDER BY id NULLS;
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 41: expected FIRST or LAST after NULLS but found ';'`

<a id="limit"></a>

## LIMIT

Syntax:

```sql
LIMIT n
LIMIT n OFFSET m
LIMIT ALL
LIMIT lo, hi
LIMIT -n
LIMIT -n, -m
FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY
```

Gives back at most `n` rows. With `ORDER BY`, these are the first `n` rows in that order (a "top n").

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `n` | whole number, 0 or more | the most rows to give back; `LIMIT 0` gives no rows (only the columns) |

- **Returns:** the first `n` rows, or fewer when there are fewer.
- **Notes:** `LIMIT` comes after `ORDER BY`, at the very end of the query. With `UNION ALL`, it works on all the rows together.
- `n` must be a plain number: not an expression, not negative.
- `LIMIT ALL` means no limit. The QuestDB form `LIMIT lo, hi` gives rows `lo + 1` to `hi`, so `LIMIT 10, 20` is the same as `LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10`. The standard `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY` works too.
- `LIMIT -n` (QuestDB) gives the **last** `n` rows, still in their own order. On a time-series table these are the newest rows by time, and KarelaDB reads only the newest partitions to find them. `LIMIT -n, -m` gives the last `n` rows without the final `m`: `LIMIT -5, -2` is the 3 rows before the last 2. It cannot be used with `OFFSET` or `FOR UPDATE`.
- Server programs (`kareladb sql`, HTTP `/exec`) also cut very big results; see [limits](limits.md).

**Example: The 5 biggest trades of the trade log** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT transaction_id, symbol, quantity, rate, amount FROM trade_log ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 5;
```

Result:

| transaction_id (LONG) | symbol (SYMBOL) | quantity (LONG) | rate (DOUBLE) | amount (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100001 | TELCO | 1000 | 881 | 881000 |
| 100007 | TELCO | 1000 | 879 | 879000 |
| 100017 | TELCO | 500 | 881 | 440500 |
| 100031 | COAST | 1000 | 402 | 402000 |
| 100015 | COAST | 1000 | 398 | 398000 |

(5 rows)

**Example: Only the column names: LIMIT 0** (sample data: query-app)

```sql
SELECT * FROM app_users LIMIT 0;
```

Result:

| id (INT) | username (STRING) | email (STRING) | full_name (STRING) | city (STRING) | plan (STRING) | created_at (TIMESTAMP) | last_login (TIMESTAMP) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

(0 rows)

**Example: The newest post of the forum** (sample data: content-forum)

```sql
SELECT id, author, body, created_at FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1;
```

Result:

| id (LONG) | author (STRING) | body (STRING) | created_at (TIMESTAMP) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | gita | Which ones? | 2026-09-02T03:25:00.000Z |

(1 row)

**Example: LIMIT -n: the newest 3 daily candles of CITY, oldest first (QuestDB)** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT time, symbol, close FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = 'CITY' LIMIT -3;
```

Result:

| time (TIMESTAMP) | symbol (SYMBOL) | close (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-08T00:00:00.000Z | CITY | 497.5 |
| 2026-09-09T00:00:00.000Z | CITY | 504.6 |
| 2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z | CITY | 504.9 |

(3 rows)

**Example: LIMIT -n, -m: the last 5 rows without the final 2** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT id FROM brokers ORDER BY id LIMIT -5, -2;
```

Result:

| id (INT) |
|---|
| 1 |
| 34 |
| 45 |

(3 rows)

**Example: LIMIT lo, hi gives the rows between them (QuestDB)** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT id FROM brokers ORDER BY id LIMIT 2, 4;
SELECT id FROM brokers ORDER BY id LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2;
SELECT id FROM brokers ORDER BY id FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS ONLY;
```

Result:

`SELECT id FROM brokers ORDER BY id LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2`

| id (INT) |
|---|
| 45 |
| 49 |

(2 rows)

`SELECT id FROM brokers ORDER BY id LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2`

| id (INT) |
|---|
| 45 |
| 49 |

(2 rows)

`SELECT id FROM brokers ORDER BY id LIMIT 2`

| id (INT) |
|---|
| 1 |
| 34 |

(2 rows)

<a id="offset"></a>

## OFFSET

Syntax:

```sql
LIMIT n OFFSET m
```

Skips the first `m` rows, then gives back at most `n` rows.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `m` | whole number, 0 or more | how many rows to skip |

- **Returns:** rows `m + 1` to `m + n`. When `m` is past the end, no rows.
- **Notes:** `OFFSET` may be written after `LIMIT`, or by itself (then there is no limit), or before `LIMIT` as PostgreSQL allows. `OFFSET m ROWS` is accepted too.
- KarelaDB still makes and sorts the skipped rows, so a big `OFFSET` is slow. See [paging](order-by-limit.md#paging).

**Example: Rows 4 to 6 by volume** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT time, symbol, volume FROM ochl_day ORDER BY volume DESC LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3;
```

Result:

| time (TIMESTAMP) | symbol (SYMBOL) | volume (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-09T00:00:00.000Z | CITY | 182390 |
| 2026-08-31T00:00:00.000Z | CITY | 159240 |
| 2026-09-03T00:00:00.000Z | VOLT | 145930 |

(3 rows)

**Example: Past the end: no rows** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT id, name FROM brokers ORDER BY id LIMIT 5 OFFSET 10;
```

Result:

| id (INT) | name (STRING) |
|---|---|

(0 rows)

**Example: OFFSET by itself: skip rows, keep the rest** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT id, name FROM brokers ORDER BY id OFFSET 2;
```

Result:

| id (INT) | name (STRING) |
|---|---|
| 45 | Imperial Securities |
| 49 | Online Securities |
| 58 | Northgate Securities |

(3 rows)

<a id="paging"></a>

## Paging

Syntax:

```sql
-- page p (1, 2, 3, ...) with k rows per page:
ORDER BY key, unique_column LIMIT k OFFSET (p - 1) * k

-- keyset paging: the page after the last row shown
WHERE (key, unique_column) < (last_key, last_unique) ORDER BY key DESC, unique_column DESC LIMIT k
```

An app shows long lists one **page** at a time: 20 forum posts, then the next 20.

There are two ways:

| Way | How | Good | Not good |
|---|---|---|---|
| `LIMIT` + `OFFSET` | page 3 = `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40` | simple; can jump to any page number | slow for deep pages; rows move between pages when new rows arrive |
| keyset paging | "the 20 rows after the last row I showed" with a [row comparison](where.md#row-comparison) | fast on every page; no rows are skipped or shown twice | only "next page" and "previous page" |

- **Notes:** the page order must be **unique**: add a unique column like `id` as the last sort key. Otherwise rows with equal keys can move from one page to another.
- For the offset, KarelaDB needs a whole number: compute `(p - 1) * k` in your program.

**Example: Forum posts, 3 per page: page 1** (sample data: content-forum)

```sql
SELECT id, author, created_at FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 3 OFFSET 0;
```

Result:

| id (LONG) | author (STRING) | created_at (TIMESTAMP) |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | gita | 2026-09-02T03:25:00.000Z |
| 7 | hari | 2026-09-02T03:15:00.000Z |
| 6 | sita | 2026-09-01T06:15:00.000Z |

(3 rows)

**Example: Page 2** (sample data: content-forum)

```sql
SELECT id, author, created_at FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3;
```

Result:

| id (LONG) | author (STRING) | created_at (TIMESTAMP) |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | ram | 2026-09-01T05:45:00.000Z |
| 4 | gita | 2026-09-01T05:15:00.000Z |
| 3 | hari | 2026-09-01T04:35:00.000Z |

(3 rows)

**Example: Page 2 with keyset paging: after post 6, the last row of page 1** (sample data: content-forum)

```sql
SELECT id, author, created_at FROM posts
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-09-01T12:00:00+05:45', 6)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 3;
```

Result:

| id (LONG) | author (STRING) | created_at (TIMESTAMP) |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | ram | 2026-09-01T05:45:00.000Z |
| 4 | gita | 2026-09-01T05:15:00.000Z |
| 3 | hari | 2026-09-01T04:35:00.000Z |

(3 rows)

**Example: A ledger page for the accountant: 5 lines per page, page 2** (sample data: query-app)

```sql
SELECT line_id, entry_date, account, debit, credit, memo
FROM ledger
ORDER BY entry_date, line_id
LIMIT 5 OFFSET 5;
```

Result:

| line_id (INT) | entry_date (TIMESTAMP) | account (INT) | debit (DECIMAL(2)) | credit (DECIMAL(2)) | memo (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | 2026-09-03T00:00:00.000Z | 1100 | NULL | 257500.00 | Pay the broker |
| 7 | 2026-09-03T00:00:00.000Z | 5000 | 1030.00 | NULL | Commission on the CITY buy |
| 8 | 2026-09-03T00:00:00.000Z | 1100 | NULL | 1030.00 | Commission on the CITY buy |
| 9 | 2026-09-04T00:00:00.000Z | 1000 | 30000.00 | NULL | Take cash from the bank |
| 10 | 2026-09-04T00:00:00.000Z | 1100 | NULL | 30000.00 | Take cash from the bank |

(5 rows)

# UNION and subqueries

> Put the rows of two queries together, and use one query inside another.

- Category: Querying
- Keywords: UNION, UNION ALL, ALL, subquery, sub-query, nested query, inner query, EXISTS, NOT EXISTS, IN (SELECT), NOT IN (SELECT), scalar subquery, derived table, correlated subquery, INTERSECT, EXCEPT, UNION DISTINCT, combine results
- See also: [SELECT (from)](select.md#from), [WHERE (in-list)](where.md#in-list), [Joins (join)](joins.md#join), [Joins (left-join)](joins.md#left-join), [GROUP BY and HAVING (group-by)](group-by.md#group-by), [ORDER BY, LIMIT, OFFSET (order-by)](order-by-limit.md#order-by), [Views](views.md)

A **subquery** is a `SELECT` inside another statement, always in `( )`. `UNION ALL` puts the rows of two or more `SELECT`s one after the other.

- A subquery that uses no column of the outer query runs **once**, before the outer query. Then KarelaDB uses the result like a fixed value, a fixed list or a small table.
- A subquery **may use columns of the outer query** (a "correlated" subquery): see [Correlated subqueries](union-subqueries.md#correlated).
- Subqueries work in `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` (also inside `CREATE VIEW` and `EXPLAIN`).
- Subqueries and views can be nested at most 16 levels deep.

**Example: Brokers who bought or sold TELCO: a subquery with UNION ALL inside** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT id, name
FROM brokers
WHERE id IN (SELECT buyer FROM trade_log WHERE symbol = 'TELCO'
             UNION ALL
             SELECT seller FROM trade_log WHERE symbol = 'TELCO')
ORDER BY name;
```

Result:

| id (INT) | name (STRING) |
|---|---|
| 45 | Imperial Securities |
| 1 | Keystone Securities |
| 58 | Northgate Securities |
| 49 | Online Securities |
| 34 | Vision Securities |

(5 rows)

<a id="union-all"></a>

## UNION ALL

Syntax:

```sql
SELECT ... [FROM ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ...]
UNION ALL
SELECT ... [FROM ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ...]
[UNION ALL SELECT ...] ...
[ORDER BY result_column | position [ASC | DESC], ...]
[LIMIT n [OFFSET m]]
```

Runs each `SELECT` and puts all their rows into one result. Rows that are the same are **kept** (that is the meaning of `ALL`).

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| each `SELECT` | a normal query: it can have `FROM`, joins, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `SAMPLE BY`, `HAVING` |
| `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT` at the end | work on **all** rows together |

- **Returns:** the rows of the first part, then the rows of the second part, and so on. The column **names** come from the first part.
- **NULL:** NULL values are kept like any other value.
- **Notes:**
  - Every part must have the same number of columns.
  - KarelaDB does not check that the column types match. Put the same kind of value in the same position, or the column mixes numbers and text.
  - `ORDER BY` after `UNION ALL` can only use a result column name, an alias of the first part, or a position (`ORDER BY 2`). An expression like `ORDER BY amount * 2` is an error.
  - One part cannot have its own `ORDER BY` or `LIMIT`. Wrap that part in `FROM (SELECT ... LIMIT n) t` (example below).
  - `UNION` (without ALL) removes rows that are the same. `INTERSECT` keeps rows found in both parts, `EXCEPT` rows of the first part that are not in the second. With `ALL` they count copies. `INTERSECT` goes before `UNION` and `EXCEPT`.
  - A `UNION` whose parts are plain `SELECT`s of one table (columns with names, no `GROUP BY` or `LIMIT` inside) runs as a `GROUP BY` of every column over the `UNION ALL` of the parts: each part groups its own table in the column engine first. A `UNION` of two tables of 2 and 1 million rows: 539 -> 8 ms. `EXPLAIN` starts with `union: run as a GROUP BY of every column`. A `UNION ALL` after the last `UNION`, or an `INTERSECT` / `EXCEPT`, runs as written.

**Example: Broker 58: what it bought and sold, per symbol** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT symbol, 'buy' AS side, sum(quantity) AS shares FROM trade_log WHERE buyer = 58 GROUP BY symbol
UNION ALL
SELECT symbol, 'sell' AS side, sum(quantity) AS shares FROM trade_log WHERE seller = 58 GROUP BY symbol
ORDER BY symbol, side;
```

Result:

| symbol (SYMBOL) | side (STRING) | shares (LONG) |
|---|---|---|
| CITY | sell | 20 |
| COAST | buy | 760 |
| COAST | sell | 1200 |
| TELCO | buy | 1000 |
| VOLT | buy | 200 |
| VOLT | sell | 50 |

(6 rows)

**Example: Turnover of each broker on one day (bought + sold)** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT broker, sum(amount) AS turnover, count(*) AS trades
FROM (
  SELECT buyer AS broker, amount FROM trade_log WHERE date IN '2026-09-10'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT seller AS broker, amount FROM trade_log WHERE date IN '2026-09-10'
) t
GROUP BY broker
ORDER BY turnover DESC;
```

Result:

| broker (INT) | turnover (DOUBLE) | trades (LONG) |
|---|---|---|
| 45 | 1288160 | 11 |
| 49 | 1173580 | 9 |
| 34 | 773260 | 9 |
| 58 | 761690 | 8 |
| 1 | 726070 | 11 |

(5 rows)

A `GROUP BY` over a `UNION ALL` like the one above is grouped part by part: each part sums its own rows in the column engine and the outer query adds up one row per broker and part, so it costs about as much as the two parts on their own. `EXPLAIN` shows it as `aggregates pushed into the 2 UNION ALL parts`. A view made of such a `UNION ALL` (`CREATE VIEW trades AS SELECT * FROM buys UNION ALL SELECT * FROM sells`) is grouped the same way, `SELECT *` parts too (see [views](views.md#where-pushdown)). See [GROUP BY with many groups](performance-tips.md#many-groups) for what it covers.

Only `sum`, `count`, `min` and `max` can be added up part by part. With `avg`, `first`, `last` or `count(DISTINCT ...)` the parts are not grouped first, but their rows still go straight into the groups without being kept: `EXPLAIN` says `read part by part into the grouping (not kept)`.

**Example: EXPLAIN: grouped part by part, and read part by part** (sample data: sample)

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT broker, sum(amount) AS turnover, count(*) AS trades
FROM (SELECT buyer AS broker, amount FROM trade_log WHERE date IN '2026-09-10'
      UNION ALL
      SELECT seller AS broker, amount FROM trade_log WHERE date IN '2026-09-10') t
GROUP BY broker;
EXPLAIN SELECT broker, avg(amount) AS avg_amount
FROM (SELECT buyer AS broker, amount FROM trade_log WHERE date IN '2026-09-10'
      UNION ALL
      SELECT seller AS broker, amount FROM trade_log WHERE date IN '2026-09-10') t
GROUP BY broker;
```

Result:

`EXPLAIN SELECT broker, sum(amount) AS turnover, count(*) AS trades FROM (SELECT buyer AS broker, amo`

| plan (STRING) |
|---|
| aggregates pushed into the 2 UNION ALL parts: each part groups its own table first |
| scan result of t (0 rows) |
| group by 1 key(s), 2 aggregate(s) |
| engine: row (reads a subquery or view result) |

(4 rows)

`EXPLAIN SELECT broker, avg(amount) AS avg_amount FROM (SELECT buyer AS broker, amount FROM trade_log`

| plan (STRING) |
|---|
| scan rows of t read part by part into the grouping (not kept) |
| group by 1 key(s), 1 aggregate(s) |
| engine: row (reads a subquery or view result) |

(3 rows)

**Example: One activity list from news and forum posts, newest first**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE news (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, title STRING, published_at TIMESTAMP);
CREATE TABLE forum_posts (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, title STRING, created_at TIMESTAMP);
INSERT INTO news VALUES
  (1, 'Market index gains 12 points', '2026-09-10T15:10:00+05:45'),
  (2, 'CITY announces bonus shares', '2026-09-09T16:00:00+05:45');
INSERT INTO forum_posts VALUES
  (10, 'Is VOLT a good buy now?', '2026-09-10T13:20:00+05:45'),
  (11, 'Hydro stocks after the monsoon', '2026-09-08T09:00:00+05:45');
```

```sql
SELECT 'news' AS kind, id, title, published_at AS at FROM news
UNION ALL
SELECT 'forum', id, title, created_at FROM forum_posts
ORDER BY at DESC
LIMIT 3;
```

Result:

| kind (STRING) | id (LONG) | title (STRING) | at (TIMESTAMP) |
|---|---|---|---|
| news | 1 | Market index gains 12 points | 2026-09-10T09:25:00.000Z |
| forum | 10 | Is VOLT a good buy now? | 2026-09-10T07:35:00.000Z |
| news | 2 | CITY announces bonus shares | 2026-09-09T10:15:00.000Z |

(3 rows)

**Example: Different values in the same column: KarelaDB does not stop you**

```sql
SELECT 1 AS n, 'a' AS t
UNION ALL
SELECT 'x', 2;
```

Result:

| n (LONG) | t (STRING) |
|---|---|
| 1 | a |
| x | 2 |

(2 rows)

**Example: LIMIT for one part: wrap it in FROM ( )** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT * FROM (SELECT transaction_id, symbol, amount FROM trade_log WHERE date IN '2026-09-09' ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 1) a
UNION ALL
SELECT * FROM (SELECT transaction_id, symbol, amount FROM trade_log WHERE date IN '2026-09-10' ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 1) b;
```

Result:

| transaction_id (LONG) | symbol (SYMBOL) | amount (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 100001 | TELCO | 881000 |
| 100017 | TELCO | 440500 |

(2 rows)

**Example: Symbols that traded and also have a daily candle (no copies)** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT symbol FROM trade_log
INTERSECT
SELECT symbol FROM ochl_day
ORDER BY 1;
```

Result:

| symbol (SYMBOL) |
|---|
| CITY |
| COAST |
| VOLT |

(3 rows)

**Example: Every part needs the same number of columns** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

```sql
SELECT symbol FROM trade_log
UNION ALL
SELECT symbol, close FROM ochl_day;
```

Result:

Error: `UNION ALL part 2 has 2 columns, the first part has 1`

**Example: ORDER BY after UNION ALL needs a result column** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

```sql
SELECT symbol, quantity FROM trade_log
UNION ALL
SELECT symbol, volume FROM ochl_day
ORDER BY quantity * 2;
```

Result:

Error: `line 4, column 19: ORDER BY after UNION ALL must name a result column or position`

**Example: A part cannot have its own LIMIT** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

```sql
SELECT symbol FROM securities LIMIT 1
UNION ALL
SELECT 'X';
```

Result:

Error: `line 2, column 1: expected OFFSET, ';' or the end of the input but found 'UNION'`

<a id="scalar-subquery"></a>

## (SELECT ...) as a value

Syntax:

```sql
(SELECT expression FROM ... [WHERE ...] [LIMIT 1])
```

A subquery in `( )` where a value is expected: in the `SELECT` list, in `WHERE`, in `HAVING` or in a join's `ON`. It must return **0 or 1 row**.

- **Returns:** the value of the first column of that row.
- **NULL:** when the subquery returns no row, the value is `NULL`.
- **Notes:**
  - More than one row is an error: `subquery returned 3 rows; a value needs exactly one (add LIMIT 1?)`.
  - With more than one column, KarelaDB uses the **first** column and does not complain. Select only one column.
  - The subquery runs once, so every row of the outer query gets the same value.

**Example: Each close next to the best close of the day** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT symbol, close,
       (SELECT max(close) FROM ochl_day WHERE time IN '2026-09-10') AS best_close,
       round(close / (SELECT max(close) FROM ochl_day WHERE time IN '2026-09-10') * 100, 1) AS pct_of_best
FROM ochl_day
WHERE time IN '2026-09-10';
```

Result:

| symbol (SYMBOL) | close (DOUBLE) | best_close (DOUBLE) | pct_of_best (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|
| CITY | 504.9 | 504.9 | 100 |
| COAST | 376.1 | 504.9 | 74.5 |
| VOLT | 191.2 | 504.9 | 37.9 |

(3 rows)

**Example: The trade at the highest CITY rate** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT date, transaction_id, buyer, seller, quantity, rate
FROM trade_log
WHERE symbol = 'CITY'
  AND rate = (SELECT max(rate) FROM trade_log WHERE symbol = 'CITY');
```

Result:

| date (TIMESTAMP) | transaction_id (LONG) | buyer (INT) | seller (INT) | quantity (LONG) | rate (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z | 100029 | 49 | 45 | 200 | 518 |

(1 row)

**Example: The last trading day in the table, without typing the date** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT time, symbol, close
FROM ochl_day
WHERE time = (SELECT max(time) FROM ochl_day)
ORDER BY close DESC;
```

Result:

| time (TIMESTAMP) | symbol (SYMBOL) | close (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z | CITY | 504.9 |
| 2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z | COAST | 376.1 |
| 2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z | VOLT | 191.2 |

(3 rows)

**Example: Symbols with more trades than the average symbol** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT symbol, count(*) AS trades
FROM trade_log
GROUP BY symbol
HAVING count(*) > (SELECT avg(n) FROM (SELECT symbol, count(*) AS n FROM trade_log GROUP BY symbol) t);
```

Result:

| symbol (SYMBOL) | trades (LONG) |
|---|---|
| CITY | 11 |
| COAST | 11 |

(2 rows)

**Example: No row gives NULL** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT (SELECT max(close) FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = 'TELCO') AS telco_best_close;
```

Result:

| telco_best_close (STRING) |
|---|
| NULL |

(1 row)

**Example: More than one row is an error** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

```sql
SELECT symbol, (SELECT close FROM ochl_day WHERE time IN '2026-09-10') AS close
FROM securities;
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 16: subquery returned 3 rows; a value needs exactly one (add LIMIT 1?)`

<a id="in-subquery"></a>

## IN (SELECT ...), NOT IN (SELECT ...)

Syntax:

```sql
expression IN (SELECT column FROM ... [WHERE ...])
expression NOT IN (SELECT column FROM ... [WHERE ...])
```

True when the value is (or is not) one of the values the subquery returns. It works like `IN ('a', 'b', ...)` with the list made by the subquery (see [IN](where.md#in-list)).

- **Returns:** `TRUE` or `FALSE` (or `NULL`, see below).
- **NULL:** a `NULL` on the left gives `NULL`. When the value is not found and the list has a `NULL`, the result is `NULL` too, so `NOT IN` keeps **no** rows. Add `WHERE column IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery.
- **Notes:**
  - An empty subquery gives an empty list: `IN` is false for every row, `NOT IN` is true.
  - With more than one column, KarelaDB uses the **first** column. To match two columns at once, write `(a, b) IN (SELECT x, y FROM ...)` (see [row IN](where.md#row-in)).
  - The subquery can use `UNION ALL`, `GROUP BY`, `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT`.
  - For a symbol column, `IN (SELECT ...)` still lets KarelaDB read only the rows of those symbols (see [EXPLAIN](explain.md#explain)).
  - In `UPDATE` and `DELETE` too: in `SET` and in the `WHERE`.

**Example: Securities with a trade of 1000 shares or more** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT symbol, name
FROM securities
WHERE symbol IN (SELECT symbol FROM trade_log WHERE quantity >= 1000);
```

Result:

| symbol (SYMBOL) | name (STRING) |
|---|---|
| COAST | Coastal Bank Limited |
| TELCO | Northwind Telecom Limited |

(2 rows)

**Example: Securities with no daily candles yet** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT symbol, name, sector
FROM securities
WHERE symbol NOT IN (SELECT symbol FROM ochl_day);
```

Result:

| symbol (SYMBOL) | name (STRING) | sector (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| ACME | Acme Investment Company | Investment |
| TELCO | Northwind Telecom Limited | Telecom |

(2 rows)

**Example: Candles of the 3 symbols with the biggest turnover (TELCO has no candles)** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT time, symbol, close, volume
FROM ochl_day
WHERE time IN '2026-09-10'
  AND symbol IN (SELECT symbol
                 FROM (SELECT symbol, sum(amount) AS turnover FROM trade_log
                       WHERE date IN '2026-09-10' GROUP BY symbol
                       ORDER BY turnover DESC LIMIT 3) top3);
```

Result:

| time (TIMESTAMP) | symbol (SYMBOL) | close (DOUBLE) | volume (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z | CITY | 504.9 | 183040 |
| 2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z | COAST | 376.1 | 186200 |

(2 rows)

**Example: Users who wrote a post, for an app**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE app_users (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, name STRING, banned BOOL);
CREATE TABLE posts (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, user_id LONG, title STRING);
INSERT INTO app_users VALUES (1, 'sita', FALSE), (2, 'ram', FALSE), (3, 'hari', TRUE);
INSERT INTO posts VALUES (100, 1, 'COAST results'), (101, 3, 'Buy now!!!'), (102, 1, 'Hydro outlook');
```

```sql
SELECT id, name FROM app_users WHERE id IN (SELECT user_id FROM posts) ORDER BY id;
SELECT id, name FROM app_users WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM posts);
```

Result:

`SELECT id, name FROM app_users WHERE id IN (SELECT user_id FROM posts) ORDER BY id`

| id (LONG) | name (STRING) |
|---|---|
| 1 | sita |
| 3 | hari |

(2 rows)

`SELECT id, name FROM app_users WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM posts)`

| id (LONG) | name (STRING) |
|---|---|
| 2 | ram |

(1 row)

**Example: A NULL in the list: NOT IN keeps nothing**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE app_users (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, name STRING);
CREATE TABLE posts (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, user_id LONG);
INSERT INTO app_users VALUES (1, 'sita'), (2, 'ram');
INSERT INTO posts VALUES (100, 1), (101, NULL);
```

```sql
SELECT name FROM app_users WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM posts);
SELECT name FROM app_users WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM posts WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL);
```

`SELECT name FROM app_users WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM posts)`

| name (STRING) |
|---|

(0 rows)

`SELECT name FROM app_users WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM posts WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL)`

| name (STRING) |
|---|
| ram |

(1 row)

**Example: Clean up posts of users who are gone**

Setup:


<a id="exists"></a>

## EXISTS, NOT EXISTS

Syntax:

```sql
EXISTS (SELECT ... FROM ... [WHERE ...])
NOT EXISTS (SELECT ... FROM ... [WHERE ...])
```

`EXISTS` is true when the subquery returns at least one row. What the subquery selects does not matter (`SELECT 1` is usual).

- **Returns:** `TRUE` or `FALSE`, never `NULL`.
- **NULL:** a row full of NULL values still counts as a row.
- **Speed:** the subquery stops at its first row, as in PostgreSQL, so you do not need `LIMIT 1`. An `ORDER BY` inside it is skipped when it only names select-list columns and there is no `OFFSET` (any other `ORDER BY` is still checked, then read as a top-1 pass). `GROUP BY` and `HAVING` still run in full before the first group is taken. A `NOT EXISTS` that finds nothing still reads every row it filters.
- **Notes:** the subquery may use the outer row's columns (a correlated `EXISTS`: "securities that have trades"); KarelaDB then runs it as one keyed pass where it can. Without outer columns `EXISTS` is the **same for every row**: all rows are kept or none, an on/off switch ("only if there is any big trade today").

**Example: Show today's candles only if today's trade log is loaded** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT symbol, close
FROM ochl_day
WHERE time IN '2026-09-10'
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM trade_log WHERE date IN '2026-09-10');
```

Result:

| symbol (SYMBOL) | close (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|
| CITY | 504.9 |
| COAST | 376.1 |
| VOLT | 191.2 |

(3 rows)

**Example: As a column: is there any trade of 1000 shares or more?** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM trade_log WHERE quantity >= 1000) AS big_trade,
       NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM trade_log WHERE quantity > 5000) AS no_huge_trade;
```

Result:

| big_trade (BOOL) | no_huge_trade (BOOL) |
|---|---|
| true | true |

(1 row)

**Example: Accounting check: warn when a journal entry does not balance**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE journal (entry_id LONG, line INT, account STRING, debit DECIMAL(2), credit DECIMAL(2));
INSERT INTO journal VALUES
  (1, 1, 'Cash', 5000.00, 0), (1, 2, 'Sales', 0, 5000.00),
  (2, 1, 'Rent', 1200.00, 0), (2, 2, 'Cash', 0, 1000.00);
```

```sql
SELECT EXISTS (SELECT entry_id FROM journal GROUP BY entry_id HAVING sum(debit) != sum(credit)) AS has_unbalanced_entry;
SELECT entry_id, sum(debit) AS debit, sum(credit) AS credit
FROM journal GROUP BY entry_id HAVING sum(debit) != sum(credit);
```

Result:

`SELECT EXISTS (SELECT entry_id FROM journal GROUP BY entry_id HAVING sum(debit) != sum(credit)) AS h`

| has_unbalanced_entry (BOOL) |
|---|
| true |

(1 row)

`SELECT entry_id, sum(debit) AS debit, sum(credit) AS credit FROM journal GROUP BY entry_id HAVING su`

| entry_id (LONG) | debit (DECIMAL(2)) | credit (DECIMAL(2)) |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 1200.00 | 1000.00 |

(1 row)

<a id="from-subquery"></a>

## FROM (SELECT ...) alias

Syntax:

```sql
SELECT ... FROM (SELECT ...) [AS] alias [JOIN ...] [WHERE ...] ...
SELECT ... FROM table t JOIN (SELECT ...) [AS] alias ON condition
```

Uses the result of a query as a table. This is also called a **derived table**. The subquery **needs a name** (the alias).

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `(SELECT ...)` | any query, also with `GROUP BY`, `SAMPLE BY`, window functions, `UNION ALL`, `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` |
| `alias` | the name of the result; write `alias.column` in the outer query |

- **Returns:** the columns of the subquery, with their names or aliases. Give every computed column an alias, so the outer query can name it.
- **Notes:**
  - Use it to work in steps: make candles inside, compute an indicator outside; group inside, filter or join outside.
  - When the subquery has a `TIMESTAMP` column, the outer query can use `SAMPLE BY` on it.
  - A subquery in `FROM` or `JOIN` keeps all its rows in memory. Filter by time **inside** it for big tables.
  - One exception: when the outer query is a `GROUP BY` and the subquery is its only source, and the subquery (or each `UNION ALL` part of it) is a plain `SELECT` of one table with no `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT`, `ORDER BY` or `LIMIT` of its own, its rows go **straight into the groups**, one after another. Only the groups are kept, so millions of rows fit (and very many groups go to disk, see [big GROUP BY](group-by.md#big-group-by)).

**Example: Group inside, filter outside** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT t.symbol, t.trades, t.shares
FROM (SELECT symbol, count(*) AS trades, sum(quantity) AS shares FROM trade_log GROUP BY symbol) t
WHERE t.trades > 5
ORDER BY t.shares DESC;
```

Result:

| symbol (SYMBOL) | trades (LONG) | shares (LONG) |
|---|---|---|
| COAST | 11 | 3070 |
| TELCO | 6 | 2770 |
| CITY | 11 | 2420 |

(3 rows)

**Example: Weekly candles inside, 2-week moving average outside** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT time, close, sma(close, 2) AS sma2
FROM (
  SELECT time, last(close) AS close
  FROM ochl_day
  WHERE symbol = 'CITY' AND time IN '2026'
  SAMPLE BY 1w WEEK START SUNDAY
) w;
```

Result:

| time (TIMESTAMP) | close (DOUBLE) | sma2 (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-23T00:00:00.000Z | 505.9 | NULL |
| 2026-08-30T00:00:00.000Z | 497.9 | 501.9 |
| 2026-09-06T00:00:00.000Z | 504.9 | 501.4 |

(3 rows)

**Example: Join each trade to the symbol's total for the day** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT f.transaction_id, f.symbol, f.quantity, d.total,
       round(f.quantity * 100.0 / d.total, 1) AS pct_of_day
FROM trade_log f
JOIN (SELECT symbol, sum(quantity) AS total FROM trade_log WHERE date IN '2026-09-10' GROUP BY symbol) AS d
  ON d.symbol = f.symbol
WHERE f.date IN '2026-09-10' AND f.symbol = 'COAST'
ORDER BY pct_of_day DESC
LIMIT 4;
```

Result:

| transaction_id (LONG) | symbol (SYMBOL) | quantity (LONG) | total (LONG) | pct_of_day (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100015 | COAST | 1000 | 2850 | 35.1 |
| 100031 | COAST | 1000 | 2850 | 35.1 |
| 100023 | COAST | 500 | 2850 | 17.5 |
| 100026 | COAST | 200 | 2850 | 7 |

(4 rows)

**Example: A cash book from two tables, with a running balance**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE sales (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, day DATE, amount DECIMAL(2));
CREATE TABLE expenses (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, day DATE, amount DECIMAL(2));
INSERT INTO sales VALUES (1, '2026-09-01', 25000.00), (2, '2026-09-03', 18000.00);
INSERT INTO expenses VALUES (1, '2026-09-02', 12000.00), (2, '2026-09-03', 2500.50);
```

```sql
SELECT day, kind, amount, cumsum(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day, kind) AS balance
FROM (
  SELECT day, 'sale' AS kind, amount FROM sales
  UNION ALL
  SELECT day, 'expense', -amount FROM expenses
) book
ORDER BY day, kind;
```

Result:

| day (DATE) | kind (STRING) | amount (DECIMAL(2)) | balance (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-01 | sale | 25000.00 | 25000 |
| 2026-09-02 | expense | -12000.00 | 13000 |
| 2026-09-03 | expense | -2500.50 | 10499.5 |
| 2026-09-03 | sale | 18000.00 | 28499.5 |

(4 rows)

**Example: The subquery needs no name** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT symbol FROM securities);
```

Result:

| count(*) (LONG) |
|---|
| 5 |

(1 row)

<a id="correlated"></a>

## Correlated subqueries

Syntax:

```sql
SELECT ..., (SELECT ... FROM t2 WHERE t2.col = t1.col) FROM t1
SELECT ... FROM t1 WHERE [NOT] EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM t2 WHERE t2.col = t1.col)
SELECT ... FROM t1 LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT ... WHERE t2.col = t1.col) x ON TRUE
```

A **correlated** subquery uses a column of the outer query (`t1.col` above).

- **Speed:** KarelaDB does not run it again for every outer row. When the subquery joins the outer row with `=` (`t2.col = t1.col`), it runs once per **different** outer value first, with that value as a constant, so an index on `t2.col` answers it. Once the outer query has asked for more values than that pays for (one value per 256 rows of `t2` when `col` has an index or is the primary key, at least 8; 8 without an index), KarelaDB reads `t2` once, builds a hash table by `col` and looks every further outer row up in it. So a page about one user costs a few index lookups (0.4 ms where the old plan took 930 ms on 300,000 logins), and a report over every user costs one pass over `t2`. Other subqueries run once per different outer value.
- **Returns:** a value subquery gives NULL when no row matches (`count(*)` gives 0). It is an error when it finds more than one row; add `LIMIT 1` or an aggregate.
- **Names:** an alias hides the table's own name, as in PostgreSQL. In `FROM ochl_day e`, the name `ochl_day.close` does not mean `e`: it means an **outer** `ochl_day`. So a subquery over the same table as the outer query works when you give the inner one an alias. With no outer `ochl_day`, `ochl_day.close` is an error that names the alias to write (`42P01` on the PostgreSQL port).
- **Notes:** a join with `GROUP BY` or a window function (`lag(x) OVER (PARTITION BY ...)`) gives the same answers and is often easier to read.

**Example: The same table inside and outside: how many days closed higher than this one** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT symbol, close,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM ochl_day e
        WHERE e.symbol = ochl_day.symbol AND e.close > ochl_day.close) AS higher_days
FROM ochl_day
WHERE time IN '2026-09-10'
ORDER BY symbol;
```

Result:

| symbol (SYMBOL) | close (DOUBLE) | higher_days (LONG) |
|---|---|---|
| CITY | 504.9 | 10 |
| COAST | 376.1 | 10 |
| VOLT | 191.2 | 4 |

(3 rows)

**Example: The best close of each symbol, as a subquery per row** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT s.symbol,
       (SELECT max(close) FROM ochl_day d WHERE d.symbol = s.symbol) AS best_close
FROM securities s
ORDER BY s.symbol;
```

(5 rows)

**Example: Latest close per symbol compared with the day before: a window function instead** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT symbol, prev_close, close, round((close - prev_close) / prev_close * 100, 2) AS change_pct
FROM (
  SELECT time, symbol, close, lag(close) OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY time) AS prev_close
  FROM ochl_day
) t
WHERE time IN '2026-09-10'
ORDER BY change_pct DESC;
```

Result:

| symbol (SYMBOL) | prev_close (DOUBLE) | close (DOUBLE) | change_pct (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|
| VOLT | 187.3 | 191.2 | 2.08 |
| CITY | 504.6 | 504.9 | 0.06 |
| COAST | 380.1 | 376.1 | -1.05 |

(3 rows)

# EXPLAIN

> See how KarelaDB will read the tables for a query, without running it; with ANALYZE, run it and see what really happened.

- Category: Querying
- Keywords: EXPLAIN, plan, query plan, EXPLAIN ANALYZE, ANALYZE, actual rows, Execution Time, Planning Time, EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON), FORMAT JSON, BUFFERS, VERBOSE, EXPLAIN WITH, EXPLAIN DELETE, EXPLAIN UPDATE, EXPLAIN INSERT, EXPLAIN CALL, depends on runtime value, explain plan, slow query, partitions skipped, key range, full scan, hash join, nested loop, filter while scanning, filter after joins, read only key range(s), use index, no index, a scan is cheaper, skipped by column stats, zone maps, KARELADB\_NO\_ZONE\_MAPS, answer from saved stats, answer from the partition list, KARELADB\_NO\_PARTITION\_ANSWERS, stored column(s) per row, KARELADB\_NO\_COLUMN\_MASK, engine: column, engine: row, column engine, row engine, speed
- See also: [SELECT (from)](select.md#from), [Joins (join)](joins.md#join), [SAMPLE BY (sample-by)](sample-by.md#sample-by), [LATEST ON (latest-on)](latest-on.md#latest-on), [Partitions, SORT BY and DEDUP KEY (partition-by)](partitions-and-dedup.md#partition-by), [Indexes](indexes.md), [UNION and subqueries (from-subquery)](union-subqueries.md#from-subquery), [Transactions](transactions.md), [pg_stat_activity and pg_stat_statements (pg-stat-statements)](server-activity.md#pg-stat-statements)

`EXPLAIN` shows the **plan** of a query: which tables KarelaDB reads, how many partitions it skips, how it joins, groups and sorts. It does not run the query and does not show rows. [`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`](explain.md#explain-analyze) runs it and adds the real rows and times.

Use it when a query is slow. The most important lines are:

- `scan table ... (1 of 2 partitions ...)`: the time filter lets KarelaDB skip whole partition files. "2 of 2" on a big table means **every** file is read. The `about N rows` in that line is an estimate of the whole table's size, not what the query reads.
- `..., 3 skipped by column stats)` inside that bracket: a condition like `rate > 900` ruled those partitions out from the smallest and biggest value each one holds (see [zone maps](explain.md#zone-maps)).
- `read only N key range(s) of each partition`: KarelaDB jumps straight to the rows of the symbols you asked for.
- `answer from saved stats ...` or `answer from the partition list ...`: KarelaDB answers without reading the rows at all (see [answers without reading rows](explain.md#saved-stats)).

**Example: One symbol, one month: KarelaDB reads 1 of 2 partitions, and only CITY's rows** (sample data: sample)

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT time, close FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = 'CITY' AND time IN '2026-09';
```

Result:

| plan (STRING) |
|---|
| scan table ochl_day (1 of 2 partitions, about 57 rows) |
| read only 1 key range(s) of each partition |
| build 3 of 7 stored column(s) per row: time, symbol, close |
| filter while scanning: 2 condition(s) |
| engine: column |

(5 rows)

<a id="explain"></a>

## EXPLAIN

Syntax:

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT ...
EXPLAIN WITH name AS (SELECT ...) SELECT ...
```

Shows the plan of a `SELECT`, one line per step, in a result with one column called `plan`.

- **Returns:** rows of text, one step per row (see [the plan lines](explain.md#plan-lines)).
- **Notes:**
  - The main query does **not** run. But KarelaDB checks it first: an unknown table or column gives the same error as the query itself.
  - A subquery in `FROM`, a view, and `IN (SELECT ...)` / `(SELECT ...)` values **are** run, because the plan needs their results. EXPLAIN of a query on a slow view is slow too.
  - `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and `CALL` can be explained too: see [EXPLAIN INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE](explain.md#explain-change) and [EXPLAIN CALL](explain.md#explain-call). `EXPLAIN SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` is an error.
  - `EXPLAIN SELECT` without `FROM` gives an empty plan.
  - With `UNION ALL`, only the first part is described, plus a line `union all with N more part(s)`.
  - In the command line table format long lines are cut. Use `kareladb sql ... --format csv` to see the whole plan.
  - A user with the `read` role can run EXPLAIN.

**Example: Candles: filter, sample, group, sort and limit** (sample data: sample)

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT time, symbol, first(open) AS open, max(high) AS high, min(low) AS low, last(close) AS close
FROM ochl_minutes
WHERE time IN '2026-09-10'
SAMPLE BY 15m
ORDER BY symbol, time
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 5;
```

Result:

| plan (STRING) |
|---|
| scan table ochl_minutes (1 of 1 partitions, about 956 rows) |
| build 6 of 7 stored column(s) per row: time, symbol, open, high, low, close |
| filter while scanning: 1 condition(s) |
| sample by SAMPLE BY 15m |
| group by 1 key(s), 4 aggregate(s) |
| sort by 2 key(s) |
| limit 10 offset 5 |
| engine: column |

(8 rows)

**Example: Trade log with the buyer and seller names** (sample data: sample)

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT f.transaction_id, b.name AS buyer, s.name AS seller, f.amount
FROM trade_log f
JOIN brokers b ON f.buyer = b.id
LEFT JOIN brokers s ON f.seller = s.id
WHERE f.date IN '2026-09-10' AND b.name LIKE 'N%'
ORDER BY f.amount DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

Result:

| plan (STRING) |
|---|
| scan table trade_log (1 of 2 partitions, about 32 rows) |
| join (key lookup on id) table brokers (1 of 1 partitions, about 5 rows) |
| left join (key lookup on id) table brokers (1 of 1 partitions, about 5 rows) |
| build 6 of 7 stored column(s) per row: date, transaction_id, buyer, seller, quantity, rate |
| filter while scanning: 1 condition(s) |
| sort by 1 key(s) |
| limit 5 |
| engine: row (a join) |

(8 rows)

**Example: Latest live price of each symbol** (sample data: sample)

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT symbol, ltp, pct_change FROM live_data LATEST ON timestamp PARTITION BY symbol;
```

Result:

| plan (STRING) |
|---|
| scan table live_data (1 of 1 partitions, about 12 rows) |
| build 4 of 12 stored column(s) per row: timestamp, symbol, ltp, pct_change |
| latest row per partition on timestamp |
| engine: column |

(4 rows)

**Example: A subquery in FROM is run first: the plan shows its row count** (sample data: sample)

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT t.symbol, t.trades
FROM (SELECT symbol, count(*) AS trades FROM trade_log GROUP BY symbol) t
WHERE t.trades > 5;
```

Result:

| plan (STRING) |
|---|
| scan result of t (3 rows) |
| push 1 condition(s) into subquery t as HAVING |
| filter while scanning: 1 condition(s) |
| engine: row (reads a subquery or view result) |

(4 rows)

**Example: The query is checked: unknown columns are errors** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT time, clsoe FROM ochl_day;
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 22: unknown column 'clsoe' (table 'ochl_day' has: time symbol open high low close volume)`

**Example: Schema statements have no plan** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

```sql
EXPLAIN DROP TABLE trade_log;
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 9: expected SELECT, WITH, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or CALL after EXPLAIN but found 'DROP'`

<a id="explain-analyze"></a>

## EXPLAIN ANALYZE

Syntax:

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE [VERBOSE] SELECT ...        (ANALYSE works too, as in PostgreSQL)
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE [true | false] [, FORMAT TEXT | JSON] [, VERBOSE] [, BUFFERS] [, COSTS] [, TIMING] [, SUMMARY] [, SETTINGS] [, WAL]) SELECT ...
```

Runs the query, then shows its plan and what really happened: the rows and the time of every part of the query, which engine read each table, the partitions read and skipped, and the memory it held.

- **Returns:** the plan lines of [EXPLAIN](explain.md#explain), then:

| Line | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `actual: N row(s) in T ms` | the rows the query gave, and the time it took to run |
| `-> table: N row(s) in T ms, engine: ..., partitions: k of n read (s skipped)` | one line per part of the query that ran: the query itself, then each subquery, view, `WITH` query and `UNION ALL` part, moved in by two spaces per level. `engine:` is `column` or `row (why)`, as in [the plan lines](explain.md#plan-lines). `(no FROM)` for a part without a table |
| `steps: prepare ..., scan and aggregate ..., sort ..., limit and result ...` | where that part's time went. `prepare` binds the query and runs the subqueries it reads; the main step is `scan and filter`, `scan and aggregate`, `scan and sample by`, `scan and window functions`, `scan, join and filter` or `answer from the partition list` |
| `partitions read: N` | partition files read in all, subqueries included |
| `memory: M held at most` | the most the query held at one time, by its own count of kept rows, groups and join tables (the same count the [memory limit](cli-serve.md#memory-limit) uses) |
| `Planning Time: T ms`, `Execution Time: T ms` | as in PostgreSQL: making the plan (with the subqueries it runs), and running the query |

- **Notes:**
  - The query really runs, with its [time limit](protection.md#statement-timeout) and memory limits, and can be cancelled. Its rows are not sent.
  - Only a `SELECT` that changes nothing is run. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` of `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or `CALL`, of `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, and of `WITH x AS (DELETE ...) SELECT ...` is refused, and nothing is changed: use `EXPLAIN` without `ANALYZE` for their plan. (PostgreSQL would run them and change the data.)
  - `VERBOSE`, `BUFFERS`, `COSTS`, `SUMMARY` and `SETTINGS` are accepted; KarelaDB has no costs or buffer counts to add. `TIMING` and `WAL` need `ANALYZE`, as in PostgreSQL. `FORMAT XML` and `YAML` are not supported.
  - Times are wall-clock milliseconds of this run; run it twice to see the effect of files already in memory.

**Example: Where the time of a candle report goes: the column engine, 1 of 2 partitions** (sample data: sample)

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT symbol, max(high) AS high, min(low) AS low FROM ochl_day WHERE time IN '2026-09' GROUP BY symbol ORDER BY symbol;
```

Result:

| plan (STRING) |
|---|
| scan table ochl_day (1 of 2 partitions, about 57 rows) |
| build 4 of 7 stored column(s) per row: time, symbol, high, low |
| filter while scanning: 1 condition(s) |
| group by 1 key(s), 2 aggregate(s) |
| sort by 1 key(s) |
| engine: column |
| actual: 3 row(s) in 0.213 ms |
|   -> ochl_day: 3 row(s) in 0.200 ms, engine: column, partitions: 1 of 2 read (1 skipped) |
|      steps: prepare 0.010 ms, scan and aggregate 0.189 ms |
| partitions read: 1 |
| memory: 2016 bytes held at most (the statement's own count of the rows, groups and joins it keeps) |
| Planning Time: 0.128 ms |
| Execution Time: 0.213 ms |

(13 rows)

**Example: A join runs on the row engine; its subquery is a part of its own** (sample data: sample)

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT b.name, t.trades
FROM (SELECT buyer, count(*) AS trades FROM trade_log GROUP BY buyer) t
JOIN brokers b ON t.buyer = b.id
ORDER BY t.trades DESC LIMIT 3;
```

Result:

| plan (STRING) |
|---|
| scan result of t (5 rows) |
| join (hash on 1 key(s)) table brokers (1 of 1 partitions, about 5 rows) |
| sort by 1 key(s) |
| limit 3 |
| engine: row (a join) |
| actual: 3 row(s) in 0.102 ms |
|   -> t, brokers: 3 row(s) in 0.097 ms, engine: row (a join) |
|      steps: prepare 0.041 ms, scan, join and filter 0.051 ms, sort 0.004 ms, limit and result 0.001 ms |
|     -> trade_log: 5 row(s) in 0.029 ms, engine: row (a condition, group key or aggregate the column engine does not do), partitions: 2 of 2 read |
|        steps: prepare 0.012 ms, scan and aggregate 0.016 ms, result 0.001 ms |
| partitions read: 3 |
| memory: 1059 bytes held at most (the statement's own count of the rows, groups and joins it keeps) |
| Planning Time: 0.321 ms |
| Execution Time: 0.102 ms |

(14 rows)

**Example: A change is not run** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM trade_log;
```

Result:

Error: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the statement to measure it, and KarelaDB does that for SELECT only: an INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or CALL would really change data. Use EXPLAIN without ANALYZE for its plan`

## EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON)

Syntax:

```sql
EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON) SELECT | INSERT | UPDATE | DELETE | CALL ...
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, FORMAT JSON) SELECT ...
```

The plan as one JSON value, for tools: one row in the column `plan`.

- **Returns:** `[{"Plan": {"Node Type": "Query", "Plan Lines": [...]}}]`. With `ANALYZE` the plan also has `"Actual Rows"`, `"Actual Total Time"` and `"Plans"`: one object per part of the query that ran, with `"Relation Name"`, `"Depth"`, `"Engine"`, `"Actual Rows"`, `"Actual Total Time"`, `"Steps"` (`[{"Step": ..., "Time": ...}]`) and, for a table, `"Partitions Total"`, `"Partitions Read"`, `"Partitions Skipped"`, `"Partitions Skipped By Column Stats"`. Next to `"Plan"` come `"Partitions Read"`, `"Peak Memory Bytes"`, `"Planning Time"` and `"Execution Time"`.
- **Notes:** the shape is PostgreSQL's (an array with one object holding `"Plan"`), but KarelaDB's plan is a list of steps, not a tree of costed nodes: its lines are in `"Plan Lines"`. Times are milliseconds.

```sql
EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON) SELECT symbol, last(close) AS close FROM ochl_day GROUP BY symbol;
```

Result:

| plan (STRING) |
|---|
| [{"Plan": {"Node Type": "Query", "Plan Lines": ["scan table ochl_day (2 of 2 partitions, about 57 rows)", "build 3 of 7 stored column(s) per row: time, symbol, close", "group by 1 key(s), 1 aggrega... |

(1 row)

**Example: What really happened, as JSON** (sample data: sample)

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, FORMAT JSON) SELECT count(*) AS trades FROM trade_log WHERE date IN '2026-09-10';
```

Result:

| plan (STRING) |
|---|
| [{"Plan": {"Node Type": "Query", "Plan Lines": ["scan table trade_log (1 of 2 partitions, about 32 rows)", "build 1 of 7 stored column(s) per row: date", "filter while scanning: 1 condition(s)", "g... |

(1 row)

<a id="explain-change"></a>

## EXPLAIN INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE

Syntax:

```sql
EXPLAIN DELETE FROM table [WHERE ...]
EXPLAIN UPDATE table SET ... [WHERE ...]
EXPLAIN INSERT INTO table [(columns)] SELECT ...
EXPLAIN INSERT INTO table [(columns)] VALUES (...), ...
```

Shows how the statement finds its rows: partitions, key ranges, index. **No row is changed.**

- **Returns:** rows of text in the column `plan`.
- **Notes:**
  - `DELETE` and `UPDATE` start with `delete from table t (k of n partitions, about r rows)` or `update table t (...)`. Then come the same lines as for a `SELECT` scan: `use index ...` or `read only k key range(s) ...`, and `filter while scanning: k condition(s)`. `UPDATE` ends with `set k column(s)`.
  - `INSERT ... SELECT` shows `insert into table t the rows of this query:` and the plan of the `SELECT` under it, moved in by two spaces.
  - `INSERT ... VALUES` shows only how many rows it has.
  - Other lines: `run the WITH queries first`, `find the rows with the column engine and take them from its scan` (a big keyed table, a condition without an index that the column engine checks; `KARELADB_NO_VECTOR_MATCHES=1` gives the older `find the rows with the column engine, then read only them by their keys`), `look up the key of every row for a clash` (`ON CONFLICT`, `INSERT OR REPLACE`), `find the target rows by t.id IN (1, 2), then match them with the rows of USING` (or `FROM`; `match every row with the rows of USING` when no part of the WHERE finds them first), `return k item(s) per row` (`RETURNING`).
  - An `UPDATE` or `DELETE` uses an index whenever one fits: it has no `no index: ...` choice. Partitions ruled out by column stats are left out of `k of n`, but the plan does not say how many.
  - The same rights are needed as for the statement itself: `EXPLAIN DELETE` needs `DELETE` on the table.
  - With `UPDATE ... FROM` or `DELETE ... USING`, conditions that use the other table are counted as `filter after matching`.

**Example: Delete one day of one symbol: 1 partition, 1 key range** (sample data: sample)

```sql
EXPLAIN DELETE FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = 'CITY' AND time IN '2026-09-10';
SELECT count(*) AS rows_still_there FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = 'CITY' AND time IN '2026-09-10';
```

Result:

`EXPLAIN DELETE FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = 'CITY' AND time IN '2026-09-10'`

| plan (STRING) |
|---|
| delete from table ochl_day (1 of 2 partitions, about 57 rows) |
| read only 1 key range(s) of each partition |
| filter while scanning: 2 condition(s) |

(3 rows)

`SELECT count(*) AS rows_still_there FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = 'CITY' AND time IN '2026-09-10'`

| rows_still_there (LONG) |
|---|
| 1 |

(1 row)

**Example: An update of the trades of one day** (sample data: sample)

```sql
EXPLAIN UPDATE trade_log SET rate = rate * 1.01 WHERE date IN '2026-09-10' AND symbol = 'CITY';
```

Result:

| plan (STRING) |
|---|
| update table trade_log (1 of 2 partitions, about 32 rows) |
| read only 1 key range(s) of each partition |
| filter while scanning: 2 condition(s) |
| set 1 column(s) |

(4 rows)

**Example: Copy CITY's closes of September into another table** (sample data: sample)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE city_closes (time TIMESTAMP, close DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY MONTH;
```

```sql
EXPLAIN INSERT INTO city_closes SELECT time, close FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = 'CITY' AND time IN '2026-09';
```

Result:

| plan (STRING) |
|---|
| insert into table city_closes the rows of this query: |
|   scan table ochl_day (1 of 2 partitions, about 57 rows) |
|   read only 1 key range(s) of each partition |
|   build 3 of 7 stored column(s) per row: time, symbol, close |
|   filter while scanning: 2 condition(s) |
|   engine: column |

(6 rows)

<a id="explain-call"></a>

## EXPLAIN CALL

Syntax:

```sql
EXPLAIN CALL procedure(argument, ...)
```

Shows the plan of every statement in the [procedure](procedures.md), with the arguments you give. **Nothing runs** and nothing is changed.

- **Returns:** rows of text in the column `plan`: first `procedure name(param = value, ...)`, then `step N: <statement>` for each statement, with its plan moved in under it.
- **Notes:**
  - A variable whose value needs no table (`DECLARE k LONG DEFAULT 5`, `SET d2 = dateadd('d', -1, d)`) is worked out, and its value is shown (`k = 5`).
  - A variable that needs a query (`DEFAULT (SELECT ...)`), a `FETCH` or a loop gets `depends on runtime value`. So does every statement that uses it.
  - An `IF` whose condition is known shows `true` or `false`, and only the branch that would run. Otherwise it shows `depends on runtime value` and every branch.
  - `WHILE` and `FOR` bodies are shown once, as `every pass` or `every row`.
  - A `CALL` of another procedure is not opened: explain that one on its own.
  - `WITH DEBUG` cannot be added: use [CALL ... WITH DEBUG](procedures.md#with-debug) to run the procedure and see what each step did.

**Example: The plan of a procedure that clears one day of one symbol** (sample data: sample)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE PROCEDURE clear_day(d TIMESTAMP, sym SYMBOL) AS BEGIN
  DECLARE left_rows LONG DEFAULT (SELECT count(*) FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = sym);
  DECLARE d_end TIMESTAMP DEFAULT dateadd('d', 1, d);
  DELETE FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = sym AND time >= d AND time < d_end;
  IF left_rows > 100 THEN
    PRINT 'many rows';
  END IF;
END;
```

```sql
EXPLAIN CALL clear_day('2026-09-10T00:00:00Z', 'CITY');
```

Result:

| plan (STRING) |
|---|
| procedure clear_day(d = 2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z, sym = 'CITY') |
| step 1: DECLARE left_rows LONG DEFAULT (SELECT count(*) FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = sym) |
|   left_rows: depends on runtime value |
| step 2: DECLARE d_end TIMESTAMP DEFAULT dateadd('d', 1, d) |
|   d_end = 2026-09-11T00:00:00.000Z |
| step 3: DELETE FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = sym AND time >= d AND time < d_end |
|   delete from table ochl_day (1 of 2 partitions, about 57 rows) |
|   read only 1 key range(s) of each partition |
|   filter while scanning: 3 condition(s) |
| step 4: IF left_rows > 100 THEN: depends on runtime value |
|   step 5: PRINT 'many rows' |

(11 rows)

**Example: EXPLAIN CALL does not take WITH DEBUG** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE PROCEDURE clear_day(d TIMESTAMP, sym SYMBOL) AS BEGIN
  DELETE FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = sym AND time >= d;
END;
```

```sql
EXPLAIN CALL clear_day('2026-09-10T00:00:00Z', 'CITY') WITH DEBUG;
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 9: EXPLAIN CALL does not run the procedure, so WITH DEBUG has nothing to show; use CALL ... WITH DEBUG`

<a id="plan-lines"></a>

## The plan lines

Syntax:

```sql
aggregates pushed into the k UNION ALL parts: each part groups its own table first
window functions over grouped rows: the grouping runs first as a subquery
answer from the partition list of table name (k of n partitions; no other rows read)
scan table name (k of n partitions, about r rows[, s skipped by column stats])
scan result of name (r rows)
push k condition(s) into view | subquery name [after its windows]
push k rank limit(s) into subquery name
time range from the calendar condition(s): col >= 'start' AND < 'end'
use index name (...)
no index: name would read r row(s), a scan is cheaper[; it reads only the storage keys those rows lie between]
no index: the column stats rule out every partition
answer from saved stats of table name: ...
join | left join | asof join | cross join (hash on k key(s) | key lookup on columns | index lookup on column | nested loop) table name (...)
read only k key range(s) of each partition
build k of n stored column(s) per row: columns
filter while scanning: k condition(s)
filter after joins: k condition(s)
latest row per partition on column
sample by SAMPLE BY ...
group by k key(s), m aggregate(s)
k window/series function(s)
distinct
sort by k key(s)
limit n [offset m]
union all with k more part(s)
delete from | update table name (k of n partitions, about r rows)
set k column(s)
insert into table name the rows of this query:
```

The lines come in this order. A line is missing when the query does not have that step.

| Line | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `aggregates pushed into the k UNION ALL parts ...` | A `GROUP BY` over a `UNION ALL` in `FROM`: each part groups its own table first (see [UNION ALL](union-subqueries.md)). |
| `window functions over grouped rows ...` | A window function over a `GROUP BY` result: the grouping runs first. |
| `answer from the partition list ...` | See [answers without reading rows](explain.md#saved-stats). It is then the whole plan, with `sort by` and `limit` after it. |
| `scan table t (k of n partitions, about r rows)` | The first table of `FROM`. KarelaDB reads `k` of its `n` partition files; the others are skipped because of the time filter, the symbols, or [column stats](explain.md#zone-maps). `about r rows` is only an **estimate** of the size of the **whole** table. It is not the number of rows this query reads or matches: for that, run `SELECT count(*)` with the same `WHERE`. |
| `scan result of name (r rows)` | The first source is a subquery or a view. It has already run and gave `r` rows. A subquery without a name (`FROM (SELECT ...)` with no alias) shows as `a subquery`; in part n of a `UNION ALL` it shows as `subquery n`, so the parts can be told apart (also in `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`). |
| `push k condition(s) into ...` | Conditions of your `WHERE` also run inside the view or subquery, so it makes fewer rows (see [views](views.md)). With `after its windows`: they run inside a window query right after its window values are worked out, so it makes only the rows you keep (see [views](views.md#where-pushdown)). |
| `push k rank limit(s) into ...` | `rn <= N` on a `row_number`, `rank` or `dense_rank` column of a window query: the rows above N are dropped inside it, and `row_number()` orders only the first N rows of each partition (see [views](views.md#where-pushdown)). |
| `time range from the calendar condition(s): ...` | `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM ts) = 2026 AND EXTRACT(MONTH FROM ts) = 8`, `year(ts) = 2026`, `date_trunc('month', ts) = '2026-08-01'` and the like on a `TIMESTAMP` column: KarelaDB puts the time range they mean (in UTC) in their place: it keeps exactly the same rows, and partitions, indexes, key ranges and the column engine can use it. |
| `use index name (...)` | A secondary index finds the rows (see [indexes](indexes.md)). |
| `count from the index (no rows read)` | `SELECT count(*)` whose whole `WHERE` the index answers exactly (a [full-text](full-text-search.md) `MATCH`, or the `WHERE` of a partial index): the answer is the index's own count, and no row is read. |
| `index gives the first n row(s) in order` | A `LIMIT` (plus `OFFSET`) the index answers alone, with no `ORDER BY` or one by the table's key: only the first `n` rows the index finds are read. |
| `no index: the column stats rule out every partition` | The [column stats](explain.md#zone-maps) show that no partition can hold a match, so the answer is empty and no index is read. |
| `no index: name would read r row(s), a scan is cheaper` | An index fits, but it finds so many rows that reading the partitions is faster (see [when an index is used](indexes.md#when-used)). |
| `...; it reads only the storage keys those rows lie between` | A relational table with an index on a time column: rows written together have nearby times, so the rows the index finds lie in one stretch of the table. The scan reads only that stretch (the `read only 1 key range(s)` line), on all threads. When the index finds more than a quarter of the table, KarelaDB scans the whole table instead: that is faster than walking the index. |
| `answer from saved stats of table t: ...` | `count`, `sum`, `min`, `max` of whole partitions come from numbers the files keep (see [answers without reading rows](explain.md#saved-stats)). |
| `join (hash on k key(s)) table t` | An inner join. KarelaDB builds a lookup on the `a = b` conditions of `ON`: fast. |
| `join (key lookup on columns) table t` | The `ON` conditions give the first columns of `t`'s key (its `PRIMARY KEY`, or `SORT BY` / `DEDUP KEY` with the time column): each left row reads only its own rows of `t`, and nothing is built first. Chosen when the left side is small next to `t` (see [joins](joins.md#join-speed)). |
| `join (index lookup on column) table t` | The same through an index on that column of `t`. |
| `left join ...`, `asof join ...`, `cross join ...` | The other kinds of [joins](joins.md#join). |
| `(nested loop)` | The join has no `a = b` condition, so every left row is checked with every right row: slow for big tables. |
| `read only k key range(s) of each partition` | Rows are stored sorted (by symbol, then time). `symbol = '...'` or `symbol IN (...)` lets KarelaDB read only those parts of each file. It also follows a `...reads only the storage keys ...` line. |
| `build k of n stored column(s) per row: ...` | The columns KarelaDB takes out of each stored row: only the ones the query uses. A `SELECT *` reads them all and has no such line. |
| `filter while scanning: k condition(s)` | Parts of `WHERE` (joined by `AND`) that use only the first table. They are checked while the rows are read. |
| `filter after joins: k condition(s)` | Parts of `WHERE` that use a joined table. They are checked after the join. |
| `latest row per partition on col` | [LATEST ON](latest-on.md#latest-on). |
| `sample by ...` | [SAMPLE BY](sample-by.md#sample-by) with its options. |
| `group by k key(s), m aggregate(s)` | Grouping. Aggregates in `HAVING` are counted too. |
| `k window/series function(s)` | `sma`, `lag`, `row_number`, ... |
| `distinct`, `sort by k key(s)`, `limit n offset m` | `SELECT DISTINCT`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT` / `OFFSET`. |
| `newest first: reads time >= '...' first, then older time windows only while fewer than n rows are found` | `ORDER BY time DESC LIMIT n` (also the newest `n` buckets of a `SAMPLE BY`) reads the newest rows first and stops once it has `n` (see [LIMIT](performance-tips.md#limit)). The time is where the first stretch starts; when the table has few rows, the line is left out and the query reads them all. After a view or subquery that only filters one table it says `(the view v read as a filter on its table)`. |
| `oldest first: reads time < '...' first, then newer time windows only while fewer than n rows are found` | The same for `ORDER BY time LIMIT n`: the oldest rows or buckets. |
| `union all with k more part(s)` | The other parts of a `UNION ALL`. |
| `engine: column` | The last line. The **column engine** reads the table: whole columns at a time, on all threads. This is the fast way. With window functions it says `engine: column (finds the rows; ...)`: the rows are found that way, then the window functions go row by row. A `GROUP BY` over two joined tables says `engine: column (hash join)` (see [GROUP BY over a join](joins.md#join-column-engine)). |
| `engine: row (why)` | The **row engine** reads the table one row at a time: slower on big tables. The brackets say why, for example `a join`, `an expression in the SELECT list`, `SAMPLE BY months or years`, or `a condition the column engine does not do` (see [WHERE: fast conditions](where.md#fast-conditions)). |

- **Notes:**
  - Only the **first** table in `FROM` skips partitions. A time filter on a joined table does not make it read less: its line always shows all partitions. Put the big time-series table first.
  - A function around the column (`upper(symbol) = 'CITY'`) stops the key ranges: the `read only ...` line disappears.
  - For a `DATE` time column, KarelaDB also reads the partition of the next day, to be safe.
  - The `engine:` line uses the same tests the query uses when it runs. Only the data can still change it: a partition whose `min` / `max` column holds a NaN is read by the row engine. Which conditions keep a query in the fast column engine: see [WHERE: fast conditions](where.md#fast-conditions).

**Example: Good: the symbol is written plainly, so KarelaDB reads 2 key ranges** (sample data: sample)

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT time, symbol, close FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol IN ('CITY', 'COAST') AND time >= '2026-09-01';
```

Result:

| plan (STRING) |
|---|
| scan table ochl_day (1 of 2 partitions, about 57 rows) |
| read only 2 key range(s) of each partition |
| build 3 of 7 stored column(s) per row: time, symbol, close |
| filter while scanning: 2 condition(s) |
| engine: column |

(5 rows)
