# Security functions

> Hash and check passwords, make SHA-256 hashes, random tokens and random ids (UUIDs), and encrypt data with PostgreSQL's pgcrypto functions.

- Category: Functions — security
- Keywords: security, password, hash, salt, pbkdf2, login, register, sign up, session, session token, api key, reset link, uuid, random, crypto, pgcrypto, SHA2, HMAC, webhook signature, digest, sha224, sha384, sha512, sha256 bytea, encode sha256 hex, encrypt, decrypt, encryption, pgp, openpgp, gpg, pgp\_sym\_encrypt, pgp\_sym\_decrypt, crypt, gen\_salt, bcrypt, gen\_random\_bytes, armor, dearmor, aes, base64
- See also: [Users and roles](users-and-roles.md), [Keeping kareladb serve safe](server-security.md), [Bytes, hex and base64](functions-bytes.md), [Constraints](constraints.md), [UPDATE and DELETE](update-delete.md)

These functions help your **app** keep its users safe: people who register and log in to your web site or mobile app.

- A **hash** is a short code made from a text. You can not get the text back from the hash.
- `password_hash` and `password_verify` are for passwords. They are **slow on purpose** (about 0.05 to 0.4 seconds), so a thief who steals the hashes can only try a few guesses per second.
- `sha256` and `hmac_sha256` are **fast**. Use them for tokens and signatures, never for passwords.
- `random_bytes`, `random_token` and `gen_random_uuid` take random bytes from the operating system. They give a new value on every call and for every row.
- A `NULL` argument gives `NULL`.

Database users (who may connect to the KarelaDB server itself) are a different thing: see [Users and roles](users-and-roles.md).

**Example: Register a user, then check the password at login**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE app_users (id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO, email STRING NOT NULL UNIQUE, password_hash STRING NOT NULL);
```

```sql
INSERT INTO app_users (email, password_hash) VALUES ('sita@example.com', password_hash('correct horse battery'));
SELECT id, email, password_hash FROM app_users;
SELECT id FROM app_users
WHERE email = 'sita@example.com' AND password_verify('correct horse battery', password_hash);
```

Result:

`INSERT INTO app_users (email, password_hash) VALUES ('sita@example.com', '$pbkdf2-sha256$i=600000$c6`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT id, email, password_hash FROM app_users`

| id (INT) | email (STRING) | password_hash (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | sita@example.com | $pbkdf2-sha256$i=600000$c6msOKWcpFAoabkNsefsBQ$hDBxFLbDymJf+RuwvjN8/GeCfLjl/l/5hHsvLxAUAr0 |

(1 row)

`SELECT id FROM app_users WHERE email = 'sita@example.com' AND password_verify('correct horse battery`

| id (INT) |
|---|

## password_hash

Syntax:

```sql
password_hash(password)
password_hash(password, iterations)
```

Makes a hash of a password, to store in your users table. Each call uses a new random **salt** (random bytes mixed into the hash), so the same password gives a different hash every time.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `password` | text | the password the user typed. A number is turned into text first. |
| `iterations` | whole number | how many rounds of work: 1000 to 10000000. Default `600000`. More is slower and safer. |

- **Returns:** `STRING` like `$pbkdf2-sha256$i=600000$<salt>$<hash>`. It says how it was made (PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA-256), so `password_verify` can check it later, even after the default changes.
- **NULL:** `NULL` in, `NULL` out.
- **Notes:**
  - With 600000 rounds one call takes about 0.05 to 0.1 seconds on a PC with SHA instructions in the CPU, about 0.4 seconds without them.
  - In `INSERT ... VALUES` and `UPDATE ... SET`, a `password_hash('...')` with plain text is made **before** the statement takes the database lock, so other statements do not wait. The statement KarelaDB shows back has the finished hash, not the password.
  - Because of that, `UPDATE app_users SET password_hash = password_hash('x')` gives **every** changed row the same hash (one salt). Change passwords one row at a time (`WHERE id = ...`).
  - An empty password `''` is accepted. Check the length in your app.
  - Do not compare two hashes with `=`: each hash has its own salt, so they never match. Use `password_verify`.
  - PostgreSQL's pgcrypto way, `crypt(pw, gen_salt('bf'))`, works in KarelaDB too: see [crypt](#crypt). Use it when the hashes must also work in PostgreSQL. MySQL has no safe built-in password hash. KarelaDB's text follows the common `$name$settings$salt$hash` style, but other tools may write the salt and hash a little differently.

**Example: The same password twice gives two different hashes**

```sql
SELECT password_hash('correct horse battery') AS first, password_hash('correct horse battery') AS second;
```

Result:

| first (STRING) | second (STRING) |
|---|---|
| $pbkdf2-sha256$i=600000$hgbdiGcjZ+AI/zkRFOq9fg$KwNhtZo9JkG6lRdyN24P4iG0I3kcaYpgwF8IB1MSi3E | $pbkdf2-sha256$i=600000$J+NW1B6ld7cSs7w1qWFaUg$jVc7enmBehBCAvtmnfD0MtXyGqjKTIcpkRMgrM63FN0 |

(1 row)

**Example: Register: store the hash, never the password**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE app_users (id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO, email STRING NOT NULL UNIQUE, password_hash STRING NOT NULL, created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now());
```

```sql
INSERT INTO app_users (email, password_hash) VALUES ('sita@example.com', password_hash('correct horse battery'));
SELECT id, email, password_hash FROM app_users;
```

Result:

`INSERT INTO app_users (email, password_hash) VALUES ('sita@example.com', '$pbkdf2-sha256$i=600000$sY`

```text

```

`SELECT id, email, password_hash FROM app_users`

|---|---|---|
| 1 | sita@example.com | $pbkdf2-sha256$i=600000$sYMHY1qmILsIUfvV7Wtk+g$fz3X5SckBpn43NcRzF/Ce1JI5r9Nzwj1Fwh8s222Qgw |

## password_verify

Syntax:

```sql
password_verify(password, hash)
```

Checks if a typed password matches a hash made by `password_hash`.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `password` | text | the password the user typed at login |
| `hash` | text | the stored hash, `$pbkdf2-sha256$i=...$...$...` |

- **Returns:** `BOOL`: `true` when the password is right, `false` when it is wrong **or** when the hash is damaged or not a KarelaDB hash. It never gives an error.
- **NULL:** `NULL` when an argument is `NULL`.
- **Notes:**
  - It is as slow as `password_hash`. Call it **once** per login.
  - In `WHERE`, put the email test **first**: `WHERE email = ... AND password_verify(...)`. Then only the one matching row is checked. The other order checks the password of every user.
  - Show the same message for "no such email" and "wrong password" (for example "wrong email or password"), so nobody can find out which emails are registered.
  - It reads the rounds from the hash, so old hashes with other rounds still work.

**Example: Log in: right password gives the id, wrong password gives no row**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE app_users (id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO, email STRING NOT NULL UNIQUE, password_hash STRING NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO app_users (email, password_hash) VALUES ('sita@example.com', password_hash('correct horse battery'));
```

```sql
SELECT id FROM app_users WHERE email = 'sita@example.com' AND password_verify('correct horse battery', password_hash);
SELECT id FROM app_users WHERE email = 'sita@example.com' AND password_verify('wrong guess', password_hash);
```

Result:

`SELECT id FROM app_users WHERE email = 'sita@example.com' AND password_verify('correct horse battery`

| id (INT) |
|---|
| 1 |

(1 row)

`SELECT id FROM app_users WHERE email = 'sita@example.com' AND password_verify('wrong guess', passwor`

| id (INT) |
|---|

(0 rows)

**Example: Wrong, damaged and NULL hashes**

```sql
SELECT password_verify('secret-123', password_hash('secret-123', 1000)) AS right_password,
       password_verify('Secret-123', password_hash('secret-123', 1000)) AS capital_s,
       password_verify('secret-123', 'not a hash') AS damaged,
       password_verify('secret-123', NULL) AS no_hash;
```

Result:

| right_password (BOOL) | capital_s (BOOL) | damaged (BOOL) | no_hash (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|
| true | false | false | NULL |

(1 row)

**Example: Change a password: check the old one, then store a new hash**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE app_users (id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO, email STRING NOT NULL UNIQUE, password_hash STRING NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO app_users (email, password_hash) VALUES ('sita@example.com', password_hash('old password 1'));
```

```sql
SELECT password_verify('old password 1', password_hash) AS old_is_right FROM app_users WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE app_users SET password_hash = password_hash('new password 2') WHERE id = 1;
SELECT password_verify('old password 1', password_hash) AS old_works, password_verify('new password 2', password_hash) AS new_works
FROM app_users WHERE id = 1;
```

Result:

`SELECT password_verify('old password 1', password_hash) AS old_is_right FROM app_users WHERE id = 1`

| old_is_right (BOOL) |
|---|
| true |

(1 row)

```text

```

|---|---|

## sha256

Syntax:

```sql
sha256(text)
sha256(bytes)
sha224(...), sha384(...), sha512(...)
```

The SHA-256 hash of a value. The same value always gives the same hash. It is fast. `sha224`, `sha384` and `sha512` are the other SHA-2 sizes and work the same way.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `text` | text | the value to hash. Numbers, dates and other values are turned into text first. |
| `bytes` | `BYTES` | raw bytes to hash |

- **Returns:**
  - text in: `STRING` of lower-case hex characters (64 for `sha256`), KarelaDB's own handy form.
  - `BYTES` in: `BYTES`, the raw hash (32 bytes for `sha256`), as PostgreSQL's `sha256(bytea)` gives.
- **NULL:** `NULL` in, `NULL` out.
- **Notes:**
  - The text is hashed as UTF-8 bytes, so text in any language (Nepali, Chinese, emoji) works.
  - Never use it for passwords: it is far too fast to guess. Use `password_hash`.
  - Good uses: store the hash of a session token or reset token (a stolen copy of the table can not be used to log in), find the same news article loaded twice, make a short key from a long text.
  - PostgreSQL code works as it is: `encode(sha256(convert_to(token, 'UTF8')), 'hex')` and `encode(sha256('abc'), 'hex')` give the 64 hex characters of the hash (KarelaDB encodes the hash's own bytes, not its hex text again).
  - For other hash kinds by name, use [digest](#digest). MySQL's `SHA2(text, 256)` returns hex like KarelaDB's text form.

**Example**

```sql
SELECT sha256('abc') AS abc, sha256('') AS empty, sha256(NULL) AS null_value;
```

Result:

| abc (STRING) | empty (STRING) | null_value (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad | e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855 | NULL |

(1 row)

**Example: Bytes in, bytes out; the PostgreSQL way to get hex**

```sql
SELECT sha256('abc'::bytea) AS raw_hash,
       encode(sha256(convert_to('abc', 'UTF8')), 'hex') AS pg_style_hex,
       encode(sha256('abc'), 'hex') = sha256('abc') AS same_hex,
       sha512('abc') AS sha512_hex;
```

Result:

| raw_hash (BYTES) | pg_style_hex (STRING) | same_hex (BOOL) | sha512_hex (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|
| \\xba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad | ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad | true | ddaf35a193617abacc417349ae20413112e6fa4e89a97ea20a9eeee64b55d39a2192992a274fc1a836ba3c23a3feebbd454d4423643ce80e2a9ac94fa54ca49f |

(1 row)

**Example: Nepali text, and a number is hashed as its text**

```sql
SELECT sha256('नेपाल') AS nepal, sha256(123) = sha256('123') AS number_as_text, length(sha256('any text at all')) AS hex_chars;
```

Result:

| nepal (STRING) | number_as_text (BOOL) | hex_chars (LONG) |
|---|---|---|
| b57bd645ef34d014bb596b4c4ed6342637d1e2af00e86132ca34fb1673e6135b | true | 64 |

(1 row)

**Example: Find news articles that were loaded twice**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE news (id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO, title STRING, body STRING);
INSERT INTO news (title, body) VALUES
  ('Index up 20 points', 'The index closed higher today.'),
  ('Index gains', 'The index closed higher today.'),
  ('Bank results', 'CITY reported its quarterly profit.');
```

```sql
SELECT sha256(body) AS body_hash, count(*) AS copies
FROM news
GROUP BY sha256(body)
HAVING count(*) > 1;
```

Result:

| body_hash (STRING) | copies (LONG) |
|---|---|
| 4c81bafab2be552b171006f4e3cd1eaf6b94743d2e1ac597e7366a95c394844c | 2 |

(1 row)

## digest

Syntax:

```sql
digest(value, type)
```

The hash of `value` as **bytes**, with the kind named by `type` (PostgreSQL's pgcrypto).

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `value` | text or `BYTES` | what to hash (text as its UTF-8 bytes) |
| `type` | `STRING` | `'md5'`, `'sha1'`, `'sha224'`, `'sha256'`, `'sha384'` or `'sha512'` (big or small letters) |

- **Returns:** `BYTES`. Use `encode(..., 'hex')` for hex text.
- **NULL:** `NULL` in, `NULL` out.
- **Notes:** another `type` is an error. `md5` and `sha1` are broken for security; use them only to match what another system gives.

**Example: The same text, three hash kinds**

```sql
SELECT encode(digest('abc', 'sha1'), 'hex') AS sha1,
       encode(digest('abc', 'md5'), 'hex') AS md5,
       encode(digest('abc', 'sha256'), 'hex') = sha256('abc') AS same_as_sha256;
```

Result:

| sha1 (STRING) | md5 (STRING) | same_as_sha256 (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|
| a9993e364706816aba3e25717850c26c9cd0d89d | 900150983cd24fb0d6963f7d28e17f72 | true |

(1 row)

## hmac_sha256

Syntax:

```sql
hmac_sha256(key, message)
```

A **signature** of a message made with a secret key (HMAC with SHA-256). Only someone who knows the key can make the same signature. Payment gateways and webhooks (a web site that calls your app) use it to prove that a message is real and was not changed.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `key` | text | the secret key |
| `message` | text | the message to sign, for example the body of a request |

- **Returns:** `STRING` of 64 lower-case hex characters.
- **NULL:** `NULL` when an argument is `NULL`.
- **Notes:** the order is **key first**, then the message. PostgreSQL's pgcrypto writes `hmac(message, key, 'sha256')` (message first, returns `BYTEA`); MySQL has no HMAC function.

**Example**

```sql
SELECT hmac_sha256('key', 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog') AS signature;
```

Result:

| signature (STRING) |
|---|
| f7bc83f430538424b13298e6aa6fb143ef4d59a14946175997479dbc2d1a3cd8 |

(1 row)

**Example: Check a webhook: is the signature in the request real?**

```sql
SELECT hmac_sha256('whsec_shop_secret_42', '{"order":1001,"amount":1500}')
         = 'f30505d17def40c02ad9b90fdaef65762d0c6b69cc93843c3228b506340bcfc1' AS real_message,
       hmac_sha256('whsec_shop_secret_42', '{"order":1001,"amount":15}')
         = 'f30505d17def40c02ad9b90fdaef65762d0c6b69cc93843c3228b506340bcfc1' AS amount_changed;
```

Result:

| real_message (BOOL) | amount_changed (BOOL) |
|---|---|
| true | false |

(1 row)

The signature `f30505d1...` came with the request. Only the real message with the right key gives the same signature. Compare signatures in your app with a constant-time compare when you can.

## random_bytes

Syntax:

```sql
random_bytes(n)
```

`n` random bytes from the operating system, written as hex (2 characters per byte).

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `n` | whole number | how many bytes: 1 to 1024. There is no default. |

- **Returns:** `STRING` of `2 * n` hex characters.
- **NULL:** `random_bytes(NULL)` is `NULL`.
- **Notes:** a new value for every call and every row. For tokens in links and cookies, `random_token` is shorter (URL-safe text). For raw `BYTES`, as PostgreSQL gives them, use [gen_random_bytes](#gen-random-bytes).

**Example**

```sql
SELECT random_bytes(4) AS four_bytes, random_bytes(16) AS api_secret, length(random_bytes(16)) AS hex_chars;
```

Result:

| four_bytes (STRING) | api_secret (STRING) | hex_chars (LONG) |
|---|---|---|
| 14c12d79 | 1ea927ae34ba9ef3041ee6710bc821d8 | 32 |

(1 row)

**Example: The number must be from 1 to 1024** (shows an error)

```sql
SELECT random_bytes(0);
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 8: random_bytes: the number of bytes must be a whole number from 1 to 1024`

**Example: The number is required** (shows an error)

```sql
SELECT random_bytes();
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 8: function 'random_bytes' takes 1 argument(s), got 0`

## random_token

Syntax:

```sql
random_token()
random_token(n)
```

`n` random bytes (default 32) as **URL-safe base64** text: letters, digits, `-` and `_`. It can go into a link or a cookie as it is. 32 bytes give 43 characters.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `n` | whole number | how many random bytes: 1 to 1024. Default `32` (256 bits, strong enough for any token). |

- **Returns:** `STRING`.
- **NULL:** `random_token(NULL)` is `NULL`.
- **Notes:**
  - Use it for session tokens, "forgot password" links, email confirm links and API keys.
  - Send the token to the user, but store only `sha256(token)`. Then a stolen copy of the table can not be used.
  - A new value for every call and every row.

**Example**

```sql
SELECT random_token() AS session_token, random_token(16) AS shorter, length(random_token()) AS chars;
```

Result:

| session_token (STRING) | shorter (STRING) | chars (LONG) |
|---|---|---|
| bDvl0YoImFK8pXT_muA8W6Dt1qK4qA7ccfhE2eyAwqo | FiuNkj5OaWCkLFuVbTiI9Q | 43 |

(1 row)

**Example: Forgot password: store the hash of a reset token for 30 minutes**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE password_resets (token_hash STRING PRIMARY KEY, user_id INT NOT NULL, expires_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL);
```

```sql
SELECT random_token() AS token_for_the_email_link;
INSERT INTO password_resets VALUES (sha256('Qm9vSw1mY3Jk0x7Lr2nT5uV8wZ1aB4cD6eF9gH2jK3m'), 1, dateadd('m', 30, now()));
SELECT user_id FROM password_resets
WHERE token_hash = sha256('Qm9vSw1mY3Jk0x7Lr2nT5uV8wZ1aB4cD6eF9gH2jK3m') AND expires_at > now();
```

Result:

`SELECT random_token() AS token_for_the_email_link`

|---|
| ct0BlYus1uOlBh7hm7I2bi3FOJPVzeYKw9X6MZlmsyo |

(1 row)

## gen_random_uuid

Syntax:

```sql
gen_random_uuid()
```

A random id in the standard UUID form (version 4), like `0465d47f-8194-4c94-a372-eda3b70504a0`. Two calls practically never give the same id.

- **Returns:** `STRING` of 36 characters. KarelaDB has no separate UUID column type: use a `STRING` column.
- **NULL:** takes no arguments.
- **Notes:**
  - Good as a public id of a forum post or an order, when you do not want people to guess the next id (`/post/7`, `/post/8`, ...).
  - `DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()` gives each new row its own id.
  - `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN id STRING DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()` gives all **old** rows one and the same value; only new rows get their own.
  - The same name and form as PostgreSQL 13 and newer. MySQL's `UUID()` makes version 1 ids (based on time, not random).

**Example**

```sql
SELECT gen_random_uuid() AS id, length(gen_random_uuid()) AS chars;
```

Result:

| id (STRING) | chars (LONG) |
|---|---|
| 8f5bd1d1-82d8-4369-bd11-b07c46a7a811 | 36 |

(1 row)

**Example: Forum posts with a random public id**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE forum_posts (public_id STRING PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(), author STRING, title STRING);
```

```sql
INSERT INTO forum_posts (author, title) VALUES ('sita', 'CITY dividend news'), ('ram', 'बजार आज कस्तो होला?');
SELECT public_id, author, title FROM forum_posts;
```

Result:

`INSERT INTO forum_posts (author, title) VALUES ('sita', 'CITY dividend news'), ('ram', 'बजार आज कस्त`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT public_id, author, title FROM forum_posts`

| public_id (STRING) | author (STRING) | title (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| 6798f92a-1ec9-484b-903b-bbc986610f62 | sita | CITY dividend news |
| daa5d424-3aec-41a9-8917-9e657563d689 | ram | बजार आज कस्तो होला? |

(2 rows)

**Example: No arguments** (shows an error)

```sql
SELECT gen_random_uuid(4);
```

<a id="pgcrypto"></a>

## PostgreSQL pgcrypto functions

KarelaDB has the functions of PostgreSQL's **pgcrypto** extension, and they give the **same bytes**. Data encrypted in PostgreSQL opens in KarelaDB, and data encrypted in KarelaDB opens in PostgreSQL (and in GnuPG). There is no `CREATE EXTENSION` to run: they are always there.

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| [pgp_sym_encrypt](#pgp-sym-encrypt) / [pgp_sym_decrypt](#pgp-sym-decrypt) | encrypt with a password (OpenPGP). The best choice for secrets you must read back. |
| [encrypt / decrypt](#encrypt) | raw AES, Blowfish or DES with a key you manage yourself |
| [crypt / gen_salt](#crypt) | password hashes: bcrypt `$2a$`, MD5 `$1$`, DES |
| [gen_random_bytes](#gen-random-bytes) | random `BYTES` from the operating system |
| [armor / dearmor](#armor) | encrypted bytes as `-----BEGIN PGP MESSAGE-----` text, and back |
| [base64](#base64) | QuestDB's `base64(data, maxLength)` |

Errors use PostgreSQL's words and codes. Most are SQLSTATE `39000`, for example `Wrong key or corrupt data`.

## pgp_sym_encrypt

Syntax:

```sql
pgp_sym_encrypt(text, password)
pgp_sym_encrypt(text, password, options)
pgp_sym_encrypt_bytea(bytes, password [, options])
```

Encrypts with a password. The result is an **OpenPGP** message (RFC 4880), the format of GnuPG: a key made from the password with a random salt (65536 to 253952 bytes of SHA-1 hashing), AES-128, and a SHA-1 check that finds any change to the message.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `text` / `bytes` | text or `BYTES` | what to encrypt |
| `password` | text | the password |
| `options` | text | optional, like `'cipher-algo=aes256, s2k-count=65536'` (see the table below) |

| Option | Values | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `cipher-algo` | `aes128` (`aes`), `aes192`, `aes256`, `bf`, `3des` | `aes128` |
| `s2k-mode` | `0` plain, `1` salted, `3` salted and repeated | `3` |
| `s2k-count` | 1024 to 65011712 bytes of hashing (with `s2k-mode=3`) | random, 65536 to 253952 |
| `s2k-digest-algo` | `sha1`, `md5`, `sha256`, `sha384`, `sha512` | `sha1` |
| `sess-key` | `1`: a random session key, encrypted with the password key | `0` |
| `s2k-cipher-algo` | cipher for the session key (with `sess-key=1`) | as `cipher-algo` |
| `disable-mdc` | `1`: no integrity check (old format; do not use) | `0` |
| `convert-crlf` | `1`: line ends become `\r\n` | `0` |
| `unicode-mode` | `1`: mark the text as UTF-8 | `0` |
| `compress-algo` | `0` only (KarelaDB does not compress) | `0` |

- **Returns:** `BYTES`. The same text gives different bytes every time (a new salt and a random start).
- **NULL:** `NULL` in, `NULL` out.
- **Notes:**
  - Keep the result in a `BYTES` column. `armor()` turns it into text that GnuPG reads: `gpg --decrypt`.
  - Each call hashes the password again (on purpose, it makes guessing slow): about 0.05 ms per row on a CPU with SHA instructions. For millions of rows, `s2k-count=1024` is about 10 times faster but easier to guess.
  - `cast5`, `twofish` and `compress-algo` 1 or 2 are refused (SQLSTATE `0A000`); PostgreSQL has them. `pgp_pub_encrypt` (public keys) is refused too.

**Example: Encrypt a secret, read it back**

```sql
SELECT pgp_sym_decrypt(pgp_sym_encrypt('secret', 'pw'), 'pw') AS back,
       length(pgp_sym_encrypt('secret', 'pw')) AS bytes;
```

Result:

| back (STRING) | bytes (LONG) |
|---|---|
| secret | 72 |

(1 row)

**Example: Store encrypted phone numbers**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE customers (id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO, name STRING, phone BYTES);
```

```sql
INSERT INTO customers (name, phone) VALUES ('Sita', pgp_sym_encrypt('9841000001', 'shop-key-2026', 'cipher-algo=aes256'));
SELECT name, pgp_sym_decrypt(phone, 'shop-key-2026') AS phone FROM customers;
```

Result:

`INSERT INTO customers (name, phone) VALUES ('Sita', pgp_sym_encrypt('9841000001', 'shop-key-2026', '`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT name, pgp_sym_decrypt(phone, 'shop-key-2026') AS phone FROM customers`

| name (STRING) | phone (STRING) |
|---|---|
| Sita | 9841000001 |

(1 row)

**Example: As text GnuPG reads**

```sql
SELECT armor(pgp_sym_encrypt('hello gpg', 'pw')) AS message;
```

Result:

| message (STRING) |
|---|
| -----BEGIN PGP MESSAGE-----  ww0EBwMC9HknQfda5GZ80joBjNpaOmXyxxtpmk+J5udBOzH4AeGRfx8nK6j6cIvNAmbFxCXxOlxd 9dHMAUKK6P+ZOjrAjyCLkxg3 =c123 -----END PGP MESSAGE-----  |

(1 row)

## pgp_sym_decrypt

Syntax:

```sql
pgp_sym_decrypt(message, password [, options])
pgp_sym_decrypt_bytea(message, password [, options])
```

Opens a message made by `pgp_sym_encrypt`, by PostgreSQL's pgcrypto or by `gpg --symmetric`.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `message` | `BYTES` | the encrypted message (`dearmor()` it first if it is text) |
| `password` | text | the password |
| `options` | text | only `convert-crlf=1` matters here: `\r\n` becomes `\n` |

- **Returns:** `pgp_sym_decrypt` gives `STRING`, `pgp_sym_decrypt_bytea` gives `BYTES`.
- **NULL:** `NULL` in, `NULL` out.
- **Notes:**
  - A wrong password, a changed byte or a cut message all give one error: `Wrong key or corrupt data` (SQLSTATE `39000`). It never gives wrong text.
  - It reads AES-128/192/256, Blowfish and 3DES, all key kinds, and ZIP and ZLIB compression (what GnuPG writes by default).
  - Data encrypted as bytes gives `Not text data` in `pgp_sym_decrypt`: use `pgp_sym_decrypt_bytea`. Text that is not valid UTF-8 gives SQLSTATE `22021`.

**Example: The wrong password is an error, never wrong text** (shows an error)

```sql
SELECT pgp_sym_decrypt(pgp_sym_encrypt('secret', 'pw'), 'pw') AS right_password;
SELECT pgp_sym_decrypt(pgp_sym_encrypt('secret', 'pw'), 'guess') AS wrong_password;
```

Result:

| right_password (STRING) |
|---|
| secret |

(1 row)

Error: `line 2, column 8: Wrong key or corrupt data`

**Example: A message PostgreSQL's pgcrypto made (password foobar)**

```sql
SELECT pgp_sym_decrypt(dearmor('-----BEGIN PGP MESSAGE-----

jA0EBwMCci97v0Q6Z0Zg0kQBsVf5Oe3iC+FBzUmuMV9KxmAyOMyjCc/5i8f1Eest
UTAsG35A1vYs02VARKzGz6xI2UHwFUirP+brPBg3Ee7muOx8pA==
=XtrP
-----END PGP MESSAGE-----'), 'foobar') AS from_postgres;
```

Result:

| from_postgres (STRING) |
|---|
| Secret message. |

(1 row)

## encrypt

Syntax:

```sql
encrypt(data, key, type)
decrypt(data, key, type)
encrypt_iv(data, key, iv, type)
decrypt_iv(data, key, iv, type)
```

Raw encryption with a key you keep yourself. `type` is the cipher, then optionally `-mode` and `/pad:`:

| Part | Values | Default |
|---|---|---|
| cipher | `aes` (key up to 32 bytes: AES-128, 192 or 256 by length), `bf` (Blowfish), `des`, `3des` | - |
| mode | `-cbc`, `-ecb` (`bf-cfb` too) | `-cbc` |
| padding | `/pad:pkcs`, `/pad:none` | `/pad:pkcs` |

- **Returns:** `BYTES`. Use `convert_from(decrypt(...), 'UTF8')` for text.
- **NULL:** `NULL` in, `NULL` out.
- **Notes:**
  - A short key is filled with zero bytes, as pgcrypto does: `'k'` is the AES-128 key `6b000000...`.
  - The same data and key always give the same bytes (the IV is zero). `encrypt_iv` takes your own IV.
  - `decrypt` can **not** tell a wrong key: it gives wrong bytes, as in PostgreSQL. Prefer `pgp_sym_encrypt`, which checks.
  - A wrong `type` gives `Cannot use "...": No such cipher algorithm` (SQLSTATE `22023`).
  - A statement that uses one key for many rows prepares the key once.

**Example: Encrypt and decrypt with AES**

```sql
SELECT encrypt('x', 'k', 'aes') AS encrypted,
       convert_from(decrypt(encrypt('x', 'k', 'aes'), 'k', 'aes'), 'UTF8') AS back;
```

Result:

| encrypted (BYTES) | back (STRING) |
|---|---|
| \\xc7c594ca6690a3fd6861111945a9c1f5 | x |

(1 row)

**Example: The FIPS 197 test: one AES block, no padding**

```sql
SELECT encode(encrypt('\x00112233445566778899aabbccddeeff'::bytea, '\x000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f'::bytea, 'aes-ecb/pad:none'), 'hex') AS block;
```

Result:

| block (STRING) |
|---|
| 69c4e0d86a7b0430d8cdb78070b4c55a |

(1 row)

**Example: Not a cipher** (shows an error)

```sql
SELECT encrypt('x', 'k', 'rot13');
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 8: Cannot use "rot13": No such cipher algorithm`

## crypt

Syntax:

```sql
crypt(password, salt)
gen_salt(type)
gen_salt(type, rounds)
```

pgcrypto's password hashes. `gen_salt` makes a new random salt; `crypt` makes the hash. To check a password later, give `crypt` the stored hash as the salt: the right password gives the same hash back.

| `type` | Hash | `rounds` |
|---|---|---|
| `'bf'` | bcrypt, `$2a$` + 60 characters. The one to use. | 4 to 31, default 6. Each step up doubles the time. |
| `'md5'` | MD5-crypt, `$1$` | fixed |
| `'xdes'` | extended DES, `_` | odd, 1 to 16777215, default 725 |
| `'des'` | old DES: only 8 characters of the password count | fixed |

- **Returns:** `STRING`.
- **NULL:** `NULL` in, `NULL` out.
- **Notes:**
  - The hashes are the same as PostgreSQL's (and Linux's `crypt()`), so users can move between the two.
  - bcrypt uses only the first 72 bytes of a password.
  - A salt it can not use gives `crypt(3) returned NULL` (SQLSTATE `39000`). An unknown type in `gen_salt` gives SQLSTATE `22023`.
  - A high `rounds` can take very long (31 is hours); the statement timeout stops it.
  - KarelaDB's own [password_hash](#password-hash) is the simpler choice when PostgreSQL does not need the hashes.

**Example: Register and log in with bcrypt**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE app_users (email STRING PRIMARY KEY, pw_hash STRING NOT NULL);
```

```sql
INSERT INTO app_users VALUES ('sita@example.com', crypt('correct horse', gen_salt('bf', 8)));
SELECT left(pw_hash, 7) AS kind,
       crypt('correct horse', pw_hash) = pw_hash AS right_password,
       crypt('wrong guess', pw_hash) = pw_hash AS wrong_password
FROM app_users;
```

Result:

`INSERT INTO app_users VALUES ('sita@example.com', crypt('correct horse', gen_salt('bf', 8)))`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT left(pw_hash, 7) AS kind, crypt('correct horse', pw_hash) = pw_hash AS right_password, crypt(`

| kind (STRING) | right_password (BOOL) | wrong_password (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|
| $2a$08$ | true | false |

(1 row)

**Example: The same hash as PostgreSQL and Linux**

```sql
SELECT crypt('pw', '$1$saltsalt') AS md5_crypt, crypt('pw', 'ab') AS old_des;
```

Result:

| md5_crypt (STRING) | old_des (STRING) |
|---|---|
| $1$saltsalt$6SNdNaZLKst2LlSm7oPPL1 | abzlUXK5ed5rs |

(1 row)

**Example: Too few rounds** (shows an error)

```sql
SELECT gen_salt('bf', 3);
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 8: gen_salt: Incorrect number of rounds`

## gen_random_bytes

Syntax:

```sql
gen_random_bytes(n)
```

`n` random bytes from the operating system's secure random generator, as `BYTES` (pgcrypto's form; [random_bytes](#random-bytes) gives hex text).

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `n` | whole number | 1 to 1024 |

- **Returns:** `BYTES`.
- **NULL:** `NULL` in, `NULL` out.
- **Notes:** a new value for every call and every row. Another `n` gives `Length not in range` (SQLSTATE `39000`).

**Example**

```sql
SELECT length(gen_random_bytes(16)) AS bytes, encode(gen_random_bytes(8), 'hex') AS hex;
```

Result:

| bytes (LONG) | hex (STRING) |
|---|---|
| 16 | 631052502e12ab66 |

(1 row)

## armor

Syntax:

```sql
armor(data)
armor(data, keys, values)
dearmor(text)
```

`armor` writes bytes as OpenPGP text: `-----BEGIN PGP MESSAGE-----`, base64 lines of 76 characters and a CRC-24 check line. `dearmor` reads such text back into bytes. `keys` and `values` are two arrays of header lines (`Comment: ...`).

- **Returns:** `armor` gives `STRING`, `dearmor` gives `BYTES`.
- **NULL:** `NULL` in, `NULL` out.
- **Notes:** text with a wrong check line or a character that is not base64 gives `Corrupt ascii-armor` (SQLSTATE `39000`). Text before and after the block is skipped.

**Example: Bytes to text and back**

```sql
SELECT armor('\x01'::bytea) AS text, dearmor(armor('\x01'::bytea)) AS back;
```

Result:

| text (STRING) | back (BYTES) |
|---|---|
| -----BEGIN PGP MESSAGE-----  AQ== =5yUo -----END PGP MESSAGE-----  | \\x01 |

(1 row)

**Example: With a header line**

```sql
SELECT armor('\x01'::bytea, ARRAY['Comment'], ARRAY['made by KarelaDB']) AS text;
```

Result:

| text (STRING) |
|---|
| -----BEGIN PGP MESSAGE----- Comment: made by KarelaDB  AQ== =5yUo -----END PGP MESSAGE-----  |

(1 row)

## base64

Syntax:

```sql
base64(data, maxLength)
```

QuestDB's function: the standard base64 text of the first `maxLength` bytes of `data`.

- **Returns:** `STRING`.
- **NULL:** `NULL` in, `NULL` out.
- **Notes:** `maxLength` must be more than 0. For whole values, `encode(data, 'base64')` and `to_base64(data)` work too.

**Example**

```sql
SELECT base64('ab', 10) AS whole, base64('abcdef', 3) AS first_three;
```

Result:

| whole (STRING) | first_three (STRING) |
|---|---|
| YWI= | YWJj |

(1 row)

<a id="app-login"></a>

## App register, login and sessions

Syntax:

```sql
register:  INSERT ... password_hash('password')
login:     SELECT ... WHERE email = ... AND password_verify('password', password_hash)
session:   random_token()  ->  store sha256(token) with an expiry time
request:   SELECT ... WHERE token_hash = sha256('token') AND expires_at > now()
log out:   DELETE ... WHERE token_hash = sha256('token')
```

The whole way an app lets people register, log in and stay logged in. Your backend (the server program of your app) runs these statements. The browser only ever gets the token.

| Step | What your backend does |
|---|---|
| Register | stores `password_hash(password)`; `UNIQUE` on the email stops a second account |
| Log in | finds the user with `password_verify`; on "no row" says "wrong email or password" |
| Session | makes `random_token()`, sends it as a cookie (`HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`), stores `sha256(token)` with an expiry |
| Every request | finds the user by `sha256(token)` and `expires_at > now()`: fast, no slow hash |
| Log out | deletes the session row |

- **Returns:** see each function above.
- **NULL:** a `NULL` token or password finds no row.
- **Notes:**
  - Always send user text as **parameters** of your driver (`$1`, `$2`), never glued into the SQL text (that allows SQL injection).
  - Count failed logins per email and per IP address in your app and wait longer after each failure. KarelaDB does this for its own logins, not for your tables.
  - Delete old sessions now and then: `DELETE FROM app_sessions WHERE expires_at < now();`
  - After a password change, delete the user's other sessions.

**Example: The complete flow: register, log in, session, request, log out**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE app_users (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO,
  email STRING NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  password_hash STRING NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE TABLE app_sessions (
  token_hash STRING PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INT NOT NULL REFERENCES app_users(id),
  expires_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);
```

```sql
-- 1. register
INSERT INTO app_users (email, password_hash) VALUES ('sita@example.com', password_hash('correct horse battery'));
-- 2. log in: one row means the password is right
SELECT id FROM app_users WHERE email = 'sita@example.com' AND password_verify('correct horse battery', password_hash);
-- 3. make a token for the cookie; below, one fixed token stands for it, so the steps fit together
SELECT random_token() AS token;
INSERT INTO app_sessions VALUES (sha256('mR3v7yJ2nqKx0Qe8i4uX1t9LZbF5cH6aWgD2sP0oVkE'), 1, dateadd('d', 7, now()));
-- 4. every request: who is this?
SELECT u.id, u.email
FROM app_sessions s JOIN app_users u ON u.id = s.user_id
WHERE s.token_hash = sha256('mR3v7yJ2nqKx0Qe8i4uX1t9LZbF5cH6aWgD2sP0oVkE') AND s.expires_at > now();
-- 5. log out
DELETE FROM app_sessions WHERE token_hash = sha256('mR3v7yJ2nqKx0Qe8i4uX1t9LZbF5cH6aWgD2sP0oVkE');
SELECT count(*) AS sessions_left FROM app_sessions;
```

Result:

`INSERT INTO app_users (email, password_hash) VALUES ('sita@example.com', '$pbkdf2-sha256$i=600000$sD`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT id FROM app_users WHERE email = 'sita@example.com' AND password_verify('correct horse battery`

| id (INT) |
|---|
| 1 |

(1 row)

`SELECT random_token() AS token`

| token (STRING) |
|---|
| 0vq7amoP4e_mqykYCt3WXsOYRy6SP_TVc1wX-kqe6UQ |

(1 row)

`INSERT INTO app_sessions VALUES (sha256('mR3v7yJ2nqKx0Qe8i4uX1t9LZbF5cH6aWgD2sP0oVkE'), 1, dateadd('`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT u.id, u.email FROM app_sessions AS s JOIN app_users AS u ON u.id = s.user_id WHERE s.token_ha`

| id (INT) | email (STRING) |
|---|---|
| 1 | sita@example.com |

(1 row)

`DELETE FROM app_sessions WHERE token_hash = sha256('mR3v7yJ2nqKx0Qe8i4uX1t9LZbF5cH6aWgD2sP0oVkE')`

```text
1 row(s) deleted
```

`SELECT count(*) AS sessions_left FROM app_sessions`

| sessions_left (LONG) |
|---|
| 0 |

> Save a query with a name, and select from it like a table.

- Keywords: VIEW, VIEWS, CREATE VIEW, CACHED, CACHED VIEW, CREATE CACHED VIEW, REFRESH, REFRESH ON COMMIT, REFRESH VIEW, REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW, CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW, DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW, REFRESH ON INSERT, SAMPLE BY view, REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY, materialized\_views(), views(), candles from ticks, REFRESH IMMEDIATE, WITH BASE, continuous aggregate, incremental refresh, summary table, DROP VIEW, SHOW VIEWS, IF NOT EXISTS, IF EXISTS, saved query, virtual table, materialized view, CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW, OR REPLACE, ALTER VIEW, change a view, kept the old definition
- See also: [SELECT (from)](select.md#from), [UNION and subqueries (from-subquery)](union-subqueries.md#from-subquery), [SAMPLE BY (sample-by)](sample-by.md#sample-by), [EXPLAIN (explain)](explain.md#explain), [Users and roles](users-and-roles.md)

A **view** is a saved `SELECT` with a name. You use the name in `FROM` like a table. Every time you select from the view, KarelaDB runs its query again, so the view always shows the newest rows.

- Use views for queries you type often: weekly candles, a broker report, the list of active app users.
- A view does not store rows (a [cached view](#cached-view) keeps its result). You cannot `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE` through a view.
- A view and a table cannot have the same name.
- `CREATE VIEW`, `ALTER VIEW` and `DROP VIEW` need the `admin` role, and they cannot be used inside `BEGIN` ... `COMMIT`.

**Example: Weekly candles of a Sunday-to-Thursday trading week, as a view** (sample data: sample)

```sql
CREATE VIEW candles_1w AS
SELECT time, symbol,
       first(open) AS open, max(high) AS high, min(low) AS low, last(close) AS close,
       sum(volume) AS volume
FROM ochl_day
SAMPLE BY 1w WEEK START SUNDAY;

SELECT * FROM candles_1w WHERE symbol = 'VOLT' AND time >= '2026-08-30';
```

Result:

`CREATE VIEW candles_1w AS SELECT time, symbol, first(open) AS open, max(high) AS high, min(low) AS l`

```text
view 'candles_1w' created
```

`SELECT * FROM candles_1w WHERE symbol = 'VOLT' AND time >= '2026-08-30'`

| time (TIMESTAMP) | symbol (SYMBOL) | open (DOUBLE) | high (DOUBLE) | low (DOUBLE) | close (DOUBLE) | volume (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-30T00:00:00.000Z | VOLT | 172.5 | 177.3 | 167.3 | 176 | 368150 |
| 2026-09-06T00:00:00.000Z | VOLT | 174.2 | 192.1 | 172.4 | 191.2 | 486760 |

(2 rows)

<a id="create-view"></a>

## CREATE VIEW

Syntax:

```sql
CREATE [OR REPLACE] VIEW name AS SELECT ...
CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS name AS SELECT ...
CREATE [OR REPLACE] VIEW name AS (SELECT ...)
```

Saves the query under `name`. The query can be any `SELECT`: joins, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `SAMPLE BY`, `LATEST ON`, window functions, subqueries, `UNION ALL`, `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT`.

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `OR REPLACE` | when a view with this name is already there, it gets the **new** query. Otherwise the view is created. |
| `IF NOT EXISTS` | when a view with this name is already there, **nothing changes**: the old query stays, even if you sent a different one. No error. |
| `name` | the view name; like table names it does not care about upper or lower case |
| `AS SELECT ...` | the query. The QuestDB form with brackets, `AS (SELECT ...)`, also works |

- **Returns:** the message `view 'name' created`, `view 'name' replaced` (with `OR REPLACE`), or `view 'name' already exists; kept the old definition` (with `IF NOT EXISTS`). Over the PostgreSQL port the last one also comes as a NOTICE.
- **Notes:**
  - **To change a view, use `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` or [ALTER VIEW](#alter-view), not `IF NOT EXISTS`.** An app that runs `CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS` at startup keeps the first query forever.
  - `OR REPLACE` and `IF NOT EXISTS` cannot be used together.
  - KarelaDB checks the query when you create the view. A query with an error is refused: `the view's query does not work: ...`. A new query may not read the view it replaces.
  - The check reads **no rows**: every table is read as if it were empty, so a view over a table of any size is created at once and never stops at a memory limit. Unknown tables, columns and functions are found by the check. A problem that only the data shows (too many groups, too many rows to keep) comes when the view is read.
  - Give every computed column a name with `AS`. Otherwise the column is called by its expression, like `count(*)`.
  - A name used by a table is refused: `a table named '...' already exists`. `CREATE TABLE` with the name of a view is refused too.
  - Without `OR REPLACE` or `IF NOT EXISTS`, a name that is already a view is refused.
  - A view can use other views (at most 16 levels deep).
  - The query is saved as KarelaDB wrote it back (see [SHOW VIEWS](views.md#show-views)), not with your spaces and line breaks.

**Example: A broker report: buy and sell amount per broker per day** (sample data: sample)

```sql
CREATE VIEW broker_daily AS
SELECT date, broker, round(sum(bought), 2) AS bought, round(sum(sold), 2) AS sold
FROM (
  SELECT date, buyer AS broker, amount AS bought, 0 AS sold FROM trade_log
  UNION ALL
  SELECT date, seller AS broker, 0 AS bought, amount AS sold FROM trade_log
) t
GROUP BY date, broker;

SELECT d.date, b.name, d.bought, d.sold
FROM broker_daily d JOIN brokers b ON b.id = d.broker
WHERE d.date IN '2026-09-10'
ORDER BY d.bought DESC;
```

Result:

`CREATE VIEW broker_daily AS SELECT date, broker, round(sum(bought), 2) AS bought, round(sum(sold), 2`

```text
view 'broker_daily' created
```

`SELECT d.date, b.name, d.bought, d.sold FROM broker_daily AS d JOIN brokers AS b ON b.id = d.broker `

|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z | Online Securities | 960370 | 213210 |
| 2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z | Imperial Securities | 695950 | 592210 |
| 2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z | Northgate Securities | 260190 | 501500 |
| 2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z | Keystone Securities | 239420 | 486650 |
| 2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z | Vision Securities | 205450 | 567810 |

(5 rows)

<a id="alter-view"></a>

## ALTER VIEW

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER VIEW name AS SELECT ...
ALTER VIEW name AS (SELECT ...)
```

Gives a view that is already there a new query. It is the same as `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW`, except that the view **must** exist, and a [cached view](#cached-view) stays cached (with its `REFRESH ON COMMIT`).

- **Returns:** `view 'name' altered` (a cached view adds `(N row(s) cached)`).
- **Notes:**
  - No such view: `view 'name' does not exist; ALTER VIEW changes a view that is there (use CREATE VIEW)`.
  - Only the `AS` form is supported: there is no `ALTER VIEW ... RENAME TO` or `OWNER TO`.

**Example: Add a column to a view** (sample data: sample)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE VIEW banks AS SELECT symbol FROM securities WHERE sector = 'Banking';
```

```sql
ALTER VIEW banks AS SELECT symbol, name FROM securities WHERE sector = 'Banking';
SELECT * FROM banks;
```

Result:

`ALTER VIEW banks AS SELECT symbol, name FROM securities WHERE sector = 'Banking'`

```text
view 'banks' altered
```

`SELECT * FROM banks`

| symbol (SYMBOL) | name (STRING) |
|---|---|
| CITY | City Bank Limited |
| COAST | Coastal Bank Limited |

(2 rows)

**Example: ALTER VIEW needs a view that exists** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

```sql
ALTER VIEW banks AS SELECT symbol FROM securities;
```

Result:

Error: `view 'banks' does not exist; ALTER VIEW changes a view that is there (use CREATE VIEW)`

<a id="select-from-view"></a>

## Selecting from a view

Syntax:

```sql
SELECT ... FROM view_name [alias] [JOIN ...] [WHERE ...] [SAMPLE BY ...] [GROUP BY ...] ...
```

A view name works in `FROM` and in joins, like a table. Its columns are the columns of the view's query.

- **Returns:** the rows of the view's query, then filtered, grouped and sorted by your query.
- **Notes:**
  - The view's query runs every time. Parts of your `WHERE` that are safe to move go **into** the view's query, so it reads fewer rows and partitions (see [WHERE on a view](#where-pushdown)). The rest is applied after the view's query.
  - When the view has a `TIMESTAMP` column, you can use `SAMPLE BY` and `LATEST ON` on the view.
  - When a table, column or other view that the view uses is dropped, the view stays, but selecting from it fails: `view 'name': ... does not exist`.
  - `SHOW COLUMNS FROM view` does not work (it is for tables). Use `SELECT * FROM view LIMIT 1`.
  - `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` on a view fail with `table '...' does not exist`.

**Example: New rows show up at once: the query runs every time** (sample data: sample)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE VIEW city_trades AS SELECT date, transaction_id, quantity, rate FROM trade_log WHERE symbol = 'CITY';
```

```sql
SELECT count(*) AS trades FROM city_trades;
INSERT INTO trade_log (date, transaction_id, symbol, buyer, seller, quantity, rate) VALUES ('2026-09-10', 100033, 'CITY', 58, 1, 30, 519.0);
SELECT count(*) AS trades FROM city_trades;
```

Result:

`SELECT count(*) AS trades FROM city_trades`

| trades (LONG) |
|---|
| 11 |

(1 row)

`INSERT INTO trade_log (date, transaction_id, symbol, buyer, seller, quantity, rate) VALUES ('2026-09`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT count(*) AS trades FROM city_trades`

| trades (LONG) |
|---|
| 12 |

(1 row)

<a id="where-pushdown"></a>

### WHERE on a view

A condition of your `WHERE` also runs **inside** the view (or a `FROM (SELECT ...)` subquery) when that cannot change the result. Then the view builds only the rows you asked for: a weekly candle view filtered to one symbol builds that symbol's weeks, not every symbol's. `EXPLAIN` shows it as `push N condition(s) into view name`.

| A condition on a view column is moved in when the column is | Example |
|---|---|
| a plain column of the view | `SELECT time, symbol, close FROM ochl_day` |
| a `GROUP BY` or `SAMPLE BY` key (not the time column) | `symbol` in `SELECT time, symbol, sum(volume) ... SAMPLE BY 1w` |
| in `PARTITION BY` of every window function | `symbol` in `lag(close) OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY time)` |
| a `LATEST ON ... PARTITION BY` column | `symbol` in `LATEST ON time PARTITION BY symbol` |

It stays outside (the view runs in full first) when:

- the condition uses an aggregate result (`volume > 1000` on `sum(volume) AS volume`), a function, a subquery or the `SAMPLE BY` time column;
- the view has `LIMIT`, `FILL`, `ALIGN TO FIRST OBSERVATION`, `DISTINCT ON`, `UNION` or `WITH`, or a window function without that column in `PARTITION BY`.

**Joins.** A view whose query joins views or subqueries takes a condition on one of its plain columns too (`d.time AS time`), and passes it on to the views it joins. In a query with a join, each view or subquery takes the conditions on its own columns (`WHERE d.time = '2026-10-15'` goes into `d`), and an `ON d.time = t.time` carries a condition on `d.time` over to `t`, as `t.time = '2026-10-15'`. So a join of two daily views read for one day builds one day of each, not every day. This is done for `JOIN`, `LEFT JOIN` and `CROSS JOIN` without `USING`. The right side of a `LEFT JOIN` takes only the carried conditions: a test like `b.n IS NULL` is true on the rows the join fills with NULL, so it stays outside.

A condition on a plain column of a **window** query that cannot move in front of the windows (`time = ...` when the windows are `PARTITION BY symbol`) still runs inside it, right **after** the window values are worked out: `lag()` still sees the rows before, but only the rows you keep are made. `EXPLAIN` shows it as `push N condition(s) into subquery name after its windows`. This happens when every column of the window query is a plain column, or a `row_number`, `rank`, `dense_rank`, `lag`, `lead`, `first_value` or `last_value` of a column (`lag` without a default value).

**lag() and a time range.** When every window function of the view is `lag(x)` or `lag(x, 1)`, all over the same `PARTITION BY` and `ORDER BY time`, and your `WHERE` gives the time a lower end (`time = '2026-10-15'`, `time >= ...`, `time > ...`, `BETWEEN`), the window gets only the rows of that range and, for each partition, its last row before the range. Those rows are read first: the range's rows, then for each of their partitions its last time before the range (`max(time)`, over the 8 days before it, the 16 before those, and so on, the last few partitions looked for by their key values alone), then the rows at those times, a few days per read, each read narrowed to the keys that end there (since 2026-10-17). The day's `lag()` values are the same as over all rows, and what the window holds does not grow with the table: on 2 years of trades a day of a broker-by-symbol view took 0.4 s instead of 2.2 s and about 1 GB. `EXPLAIN` says `the rows of view v's windows read first: the time range and each partition's last row before it, for lag (N rows)`. `KARELADB_NO_LAG_ROWS=1` reads every row of those days instead.

A condition like `rn <= 5` (also `rn < 6`, `rn = 1`, `5 >= rn`) on a `row_number`, `rank` or `dense_rank` column is a **rank limit**: the window query drops every row above the limit as soon as the ranks are known. With `row_number()` it also orders only the first 5 rows of each partition instead of all of them. The usual top-N-per-group query gets fast this way: `SELECT symbol, sum(qty) FROM (SELECT symbol, qty, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY qty DESC) AS rn FROM t WHERE ...) WHERE rn <= 5 GROUP BY symbol`. `EXPLAIN` shows it as `push 1 rank limit(s) into subquery`.

**A view joined to a table, then grouped** (since 2026-10-17). A `GROUP BY` over a view (or subquery) joined to a table, such as the turnover per broker and sector of a daily view joined to a sector map, groups the view first by the columns the rest of the query reads of it (its `GROUP BY`, `ON` and `WHERE` columns), and joins those groups: `SELECT d.broker, s.sector, sum(d.amt) FROM daily d JOIN sector s ON d.symbol = s.symbol GROUP BY d.broker, s.sector` adds up the view per broker and symbol, which a grouped view folds into its own grouping, so a year of the daily view is never built. Only `sum`, `min` and `max` of the view's own columns, every column written with its source's name (`d.amt`), an `INNER` or `LEFT JOIN` of two sources. A year of 006's broker-sector read: 9.3 s and 2.6 GB -> 0.37 s. `EXPLAIN` says `aggregates over a joined view: the view grouped first`. `KARELADB_NO_GROUP_BELOW_JOIN=1` turns it off.

**Only the sums you read.** When a view or `FROM (SELECT ...)` subquery has `GROUP BY`, a `sum`, `count` or `avg` column of it that your query never names is not worked out at all. A daily view with six sums, read for two of them, adds up two: less time, and less memory for the groups.

**A UNION ALL view** (since 2026-10-24). A view whose query is a `UNION ALL` is read the same way as that query written in `FROM (...)`:

- A `GROUP BY` (or a `sum`, `count`, `min`, `max`) over it is grouped **part by part**: each part groups its own table, and your `WHERE` goes into every part (see [UNION ALL](union-subqueries.md#union-all)). `EXPLAIN` says `aggregates pushed into the N UNION ALL parts`.
- A part written `SELECT * FROM t` is read as the columns `t` has **now** (a column added to the tables later shows up through the view), so a `WHERE` goes into it like into a part with a column list.

A one-day sum over a view of two 2-million-row tables took 660 ms and now 3 ms; `SELECT * FROM v WHERE ...` over two `SELECT *` parts 1,130 ms and now 4.5 ms. A cached view keeps handing out its kept rows, and a materialized view is a table, as before.

**Example: A GROUP BY over a UNION ALL view of SELECT * parts: each part groups its own table** (sample data: sample)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE VIEW two_symbols AS SELECT * FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = 'CITY' UNION ALL SELECT * FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = 'VOLT';
```

```sql
SELECT symbol, count(*) AS days, max(close) AS high FROM two_symbols GROUP BY symbol ORDER BY symbol;
EXPLAIN SELECT symbol, count(*) AS days, max(close) AS high FROM two_symbols GROUP BY symbol;
```

Result:

`SELECT symbol, count(*) AS days, max(close) AS high FROM two_symbols GROUP BY symbol ORDER BY symbol`

| symbol (SYMBOL) | days (LONG) | high (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| CITY | 19 | 542.4 |
| VOLT | 19 | 196.4 |

(2 rows)

`EXPLAIN SELECT symbol, count(*) AS days, max(close) AS high FROM two_symbols GROUP BY symbol`

| plan (STRING) |
|---|
| aggregates pushed into the 2 UNION ALL parts: each part groups its own table first |
| scan result of two_symbols (0 rows) |
| group by 1 key(s), 2 aggregate(s) |
| engine: column (the UNION ALL parts grouped as one) |

(4 rows)

The result is always the same as without moving; only the time changes.

**A long time range in parts** (since 2026-10-16). A `GROUP BY` over a view (or a `FROM (SELECT ...)` subquery) for many days, such as a year of a window view summed per symbol, runs the view **a few days at a time** when the time column passes through every step of the view: it is a key of every `GROUP BY`, in the `PARTITION BY` of every window, and comes from the time column of a time-series table partitioned by time. Each part is the view with `time >= a AND time < b` moved inside as above, and its rows go straight into your `GROUP BY`; no window partition and no group can reach across two parts, so the answer is the same. A part holds whole partitions, as many as keep it well under `--max-result-memory` (about 8 KB of memory per row for a view with windows or joins, 512 bytes without); a partition bigger than that (a month of a materialized view) is cut into parts of whole days. A view that joins (since 2026-10-17) is split too when the time is a column of one of its sources (`d.time AS time`) and reaches each other source through an `ON d.time = t.time`, or that source is a small table without a time column (a sector map); after its first part such a view's parts are sized by what that part held. So a range far bigger than the memory limit is answered: 006's pump-and-dump filter over 5 months of 10M trades took 18 s where it stopped at `max_result_memory` before, and its OTM filter (the daily filter joined with a sum of itself) over a year 4.4 s where it ran out of memory. With 2 or more CPUs, two parts run at the same time (since 2026-10-17): the next part is worked out while this one runs or hands its rows on, and the rows still go on in time order, so the answer is the same to the last digit. At 2 CPUs a year of 006's OTM filter over materialized views took 2.0 s instead of 4.3 s, and two years of its Mkt hit view 32 s instead of 63 s. `KARELADB_NO_SPLIT_LANES=1` runs one part at a time. A range that fits in one part runs as before. `KARELADB_NO_TIME_SPLIT=1` turns it off.

| engine: row (reads a subquery or view result) |

(3 rows)

**Example: A table a view reads cannot be dropped** (shows an error)

<a id="cached-view"></a>

## CREATE CACHED VIEW

Syntax:

```sql
CREATE [OR REPLACE] CACHED VIEW name AS SELECT ... [REFRESH ON COMMIT]
CREATE CACHED VIEW IF NOT EXISTS name AS SELECT ... [REFRESH ON COMMIT]
CREATE [OR REPLACE] CACHED VIEW name AS (SELECT ...) [REFRESH ON COMMIT]
```

`OR REPLACE` and `IF NOT EXISTS` work as for [CREATE VIEW](#create-view). A replaced cached view computes its rows again at once.

A cached (materialized) view runs its query once and **keeps the rows**. Selecting from it reads the kept rows, so a slow `GROUP BY` over a big table is paid once, not on every read.

| Form | When the rows are made new |
|---|---|
| `CREATE CACHED VIEW ...` | at `CREATE`, and when you run [REFRESH VIEW](#refresh-view) |
| `CREATE CACHED VIEW ... REFRESH ON COMMIT` | at the first read after a commit changed a table the view reads: `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `POST /write`, `POST /imp`, and rows written by triggers |

- **Returns:** `view 'name' created (N row(s) cached)`.
- **Notes:**
  - The kept rows live in memory. After a restart they are made again at the first read.
  - A `WHERE` on the view filters the kept rows; it does not run the view's query again.
  - `REFRESH ON COMMIT` is only allowed with `CACHED`. On a normal view it is an error.
  - `SHOW VIEWS` lists a cached view with kind `materialized`, and `ON COMMIT` in `refresh` when it has `REFRESH ON COMMIT`.
  - A view whose query fails (a table was dropped) gives the same error as a normal view.

**Example: Trades per symbol as a cached view** (sample data: sample)

```sql
CREATE CACHED VIEW trades_per_symbol AS
SELECT symbol, count(*) AS trades, sum(quantity) AS shares FROM trade_log GROUP BY symbol
REFRESH ON COMMIT;

SELECT * FROM trades_per_symbol ORDER BY trades DESC, symbol;
```

Result:

`CREATE CACHED VIEW trades_per_symbol AS SELECT symbol, count(*) AS trades, sum(quantity) AS shares F`

```text
view 'trades_per_symbol' created (4 row(s) cached)
```

`SELECT * FROM trades_per_symbol ORDER BY trades DESC, symbol`

| symbol (SYMBOL) | trades (LONG) | shares (LONG) |
|---|---|---|
| CITY | 11 | 2420 |
| COAST | 11 | 3070 |
| TELCO | 6 | 2770 |
| VOLT | 4 | 400 |

(4 rows)

<a id="materialized-view"></a>

## CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW

Syntax:

```sql
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW [IF NOT EXISTS] name
    [PARTITION BY DAY | MONTH | YEAR] [TTL n DAYS | ...] [REFRESH ON INSERT | REFRESH IMMEDIATE] [WITH BASE table]
    [INCREMENTAL] [KEY (column)] [LOOKBACK 'time span']
    AS SELECT time_bucket, ..., aggregates [, window calls] FROM table [WHERE ...] GROUP BY time_bucket, ... [HAVING ...]
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW name [KEY (column)] [LOOKBACK 'time span']
    AS SELECT time, ..., window calls FROM table [WHERE ...]
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW [IF NOT EXISTS] name [options]
    AS ( SELECT time, ..., aggregates FROM table [WHERE ...] SAMPLE BY interval [ALIGN TO CALENDAR ...] )
    [TIMESTAMP(time)] [PARTITION BY DAY | MONTH | YEAR] [TTL n DAYS | ...]
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW [CONCURRENTLY] name [WITH DATA]
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW name FULL | INCREMENTAL | RANGE FROM 'time' TO 'time' | FOR 'time' [TO 'time']
DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW [IF EXISTS] name
```

A materialized view is a **real table** that holds the result of a `GROUP BY` or `SAMPLE BY` query. Reading it is a plain table read: fast, and a `WHERE` on its time column skips partitions. The second form is QuestDB's: candles from ticks.

It stays up to date by itself. After each commit that changes rows of its table, a background thread computes again **only the time buckets those rows fall in** and writes only the view rows that changed. A tick at 10:04:31 makes a `SAMPLE BY 1m` view compute the 10:04 minute again, not the day. The commit does not wait for it, and readers and writers of other tables go on while it runs. Writers of the view's own table wait only while the new rows are computed, not while they are written into the view. Changes are applied in commit order. A **read of the view waits** until the view holds every commit made before the read (at most 2 seconds, usually a few milliseconds), so a candle read right after a tick includes that tick. Inside an open transaction the read takes the rows the view has.

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `PARTITION BY` | the view's own partitions. Default: the table's partitioning, or coarser when the time bucket needs it. With `SAMPLE BY`, QuestDB's rule: under an hour `DAY`, under a day `MONTH`, else `YEAR`. `HOUR` and `WEEK` are not supported |
| `TTL` | drop old partitions of the view (see [SET TTL](alter-table.md#set-ttl)) |
| `REFRESH ON INSERT`, `REFRESH IMMEDIATE` | optional; every materialized view is refreshed after inserts, updates and deletes. `REFRESH MANUAL`, `EVERY` and `PERIOD` are not supported |
| `WITH BASE table` | QuestDB: the table the view is refreshed from. It must be the table the query reads |
| `TIMESTAMP(time)` | QuestDB: the view's time column. It must be the time bucket |
| time bucket | with `GROUP BY`: the table's time column, `to_date(time)`, or `date_trunc('year' \| 'quarter' \| 'month' \| 'day' \| 'hour' \| 'minute' \| 'second', time)`. With `SAMPLE BY`: the table's time column in `SELECT`, which holds the start of each bucket |

| Refresh | What it does |
|---|---|
| `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW v`, `... FULL` | drops every row of the view and writes them all again (a view too big for that: part by part, see the notes) |
| `... CONCURRENTLY v` | computes every row, compares, and writes only the rows that differ. Readers keep reading the old rows until it commits (a view too big for that: part by part) |
| `... INCREMENTAL` | now, what the background thread would do next: the buckets that changes of the table made stale |
| `... RANGE FROM 'a' TO 'b'` | the buckets that hold the times `a` to `b`, by difference |
| `... FOR 'a' [TO 'b']` | the view partitions that hold `a` to `b`, by difference |

- **Returns:** `materialized view 'name' created with N row(s), PARTITION BY DAY`.
- **Notes:**
  - The query must read **one** time-series table and `GROUP BY` a time bucket (or, with window calls, show the table's rows with their time column). The bucket must also be a column of the view.
  - **The key.** A view that groups by a `SYMBOL` column of its table (and shows it) has a key: a change marks its time bucket for that symbol only, and the refresh computes only those symbols there. `KEY (column)` names the key yourself (one of the columns the view groups by). `INCREMENTAL` may be written; every materialized view is incremental.
  - **Moving windows.** A view may use window calls that look back a fixed distance: `lag(x, n)`, `sma(x, n)`, `pct_change(x, n)`, or an aggregate over `ROWS BETWEEN n PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` or `RANGE '5 days' PRECEDING`. Every window must `PARTITION BY` the same column (the key) or none, and `ORDER BY` the view's time. A change at time t then computes its key again **from t to the end**, reading first the rows the windows look back over (the n earlier rows of that key, wherever they are, so weekends and holidays never cut a window short). `LOOKBACK '120 days'` makes it read at least that much more history. Refused, saying why: `ema`, `rsi`, `atr`, `cumsum` and ranks (they depend on every earlier row), `lead` and `FOLLOWING` (later rows), and a window without a frame (it reads every earlier row).
  - Refused, with a message that says why: joins, subqueries, `WITH`, `UNION`, `LATEST ON`, `DISTINCT`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`, window calls other than those above, `now()` and `random()`, `date_trunc('week', ...)` (a week can cross a month end), and `SAMPLE BY` with `FILL` or `ALIGN TO FIRST OBSERVATION` (a bucket would depend on the buckets around it).
  - The time bucket is always on the **UTC** clock: a `'day'` bucket is a UTC day, even after `SET TIME ZONE` or with `kareladb serve --timezone`. The view is rebuilt one UTC partition at a time, and a Nepal day (18:15 UTC to 18:15 UTC) would span two.
  - `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and `TRUNCATE` on the view are refused. Change the table instead.
  - `DROP PARTITION` and `TTL` on the **table** do not remove rows from the view. A daily summary can outlive the raw trades. `TRUNCATE` of the table empties the view.
  - The table cannot be dropped or renamed while a view reads it.
  - How far behind a view is shows in `GET /api/stats` under `materialized_views` (`lag_ms`, `pending_ranges`, `pending_partitions`, `last_error`), and in `SELECT * FROM materialized_views()`: `refresh_base_table_txn = base_table_txn` once the view holds every commit of its table.
  - An insert, an `UPDATE` and a `DELETE` mark only the buckets of the rows they change (an `UPDATE` that changes a row's time marks its old and its new bucket). A delete that comes from a foreign key action marks the whole partition it touches; the refresh then compares that partition and still writes only what differs.
  - A refresh locks the view and its table like an `INSERT`. With `kareladb serve --snapshot-reads on`, readers of the view read its rows before the refresh and do not wait.
  - **A bulk load is refreshed once it pauses.** While a table takes a stream of big writes (100,000 rows or more within a second, as `POST /write` with 100k-row bodies from several senders), its views are not refreshed between the requests: each refresh would hold the table for its query, which the loaders then wait for, and compute days the next requests change again. The views catch up in one refresh once no write request is running and none came for 0.3 s, at once when a query reads the view (it waits for that refresh as always), and at the latest 2 minutes after the oldest change. Single rows and small batches are refreshed right away, as before.
  - `SHOW CREATE TABLE name` gives the `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` statement. `SHOW VIEWS` lists it with kind `materialized` and refresh `ON INSERT`.
  - A restart or a power cut never loses a refresh: what was waiting is refreshed after the database opens.
  - `materialized_views()` lists the materialized views with QuestDB's columns (`view_name`, `refresh_type`, `base_table_name`, `view_status`, ...) and KarelaDB's own after them: `rows`, `disk_bytes`, `last_refresh_took_ms`, `refreshes` (since the database opened), `pending_ranges`, `pending_partitions`, `full_refresh_pending` and `lag_ms`. `views()` lists the plain views. To build a view again from nothing: `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW name FULL`.
  - **A view too big to rebuild in one piece** (`FULL`, `CONCURRENTLY`, or the full rebuild after a restart) is rebuilt **part by part**: a few partitions of the table at a time, each part by difference and committed on its own, so the rebuild holds one part in memory, whatever the size of the table. That happens when the view has more rows than one query may make groups (`max_groups`) or keep (`max_result_memory`), or when the one-piece rebuild is stopped by the memory limit. Then the message ends in `, N written`, and while it runs a reader may see some parts rebuilt and others not yet (each part whole). A view that fits is rebuilt in one piece, as before: a reader sees all the old rows or all the new ones.
  - **A `REFRESH` that fails leaves the view as it was**: its rows stay, `view_status` stays `valid`, and only the statement gets the error. `invalid` (with `invalidation_reason`) means the background refresh that keeps the view up to date failed; it is tried again.

**Example: Daily turnover per symbol, kept up to date** (sample data: sample)

**Example: A view needs a time bucket in GROUP BY** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

**Example: Rows of a view come only from its query** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

```sql

```

```sql
DELETE FROM daily_count;
```

Result:

Error: `'daily_count' is a materialized view: its rows come from its query. Change the rows of its table instead, or run REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_count`

<a id="refresh-view"></a>

## REFRESH VIEW

Syntax:

```sql
REFRESH VIEW name
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW name
```

Runs the query of a [cached view](#cached-view) again and keeps the new rows.

- **Returns:** `view 'name' refreshed: N row(s)`.
- **Notes:**
  - It needs the `admin` role, and it cannot be used inside `BEGIN` ... `COMMIT`.
  - `MATERIALIZED` is optional; PostgreSQL writes it.
  - A view made with `REFRESH ON COMMIT` does not need it, but it does no harm.
  - For a [materialized view](#materialized-view) it rebuilds the view from its table; see there for `CONCURRENTLY`, `FULL`, `INCREMENTAL` and `RANGE`.

**Example: Make a cached view new after loading trades** (sample data: sample)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE CACHED VIEW shares_per_symbol AS SELECT symbol, sum(quantity) AS shares FROM trade_log GROUP BY symbol;
```

```sql
REFRESH VIEW shares_per_symbol;
SELECT * FROM shares_per_symbol ORDER BY shares DESC LIMIT 3;
```

Result:

`REFRESH VIEW shares_per_symbol`

```text
view 'shares_per_symbol' refreshed: 4 row(s)
```

`SELECT * FROM shares_per_symbol ORDER BY shares DESC LIMIT 3`

| symbol (SYMBOL) | shares (LONG) |
|---|---|
| COAST | 3070 |
| TELCO | 2770 |
| CITY | 2420 |

(3 rows)

**Example: A normal view has nothing to refresh** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE VIEW banks AS SELECT symbol FROM securities WHERE sector = 'Banking';
```

```sql
REFRESH VIEW banks;
```

Result:

Error: `view 'banks' is not a cached view: it runs its query on every read, so there is nothing to refresh`

<a id="drop-view"></a>

## DROP VIEW

Syntax:

```sql
DROP VIEW [IF EXISTS] name
```

Removes the view. The tables and rows it reads are not touched.

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `IF EXISTS` | no error when there is no such view |

- **Returns:** `view 'name' dropped`, or `view 'name' does not exist` with `IF EXISTS`.
- **Notes:**
  - `DROP VIEW` does not check whether another view uses this view. That other view fails the next time it is used.
  - `DROP VIEW` only drops views. For a table, use `DROP TABLE` (see [create-table](create-table.md)).

**Example: Drop a view, then drop it again safely** (sample data: sample)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE VIEW banks AS SELECT symbol FROM securities WHERE sector = 'Banking';
```

```sql
DROP VIEW banks;
DROP VIEW IF EXISTS banks;
SHOW VIEWS;
```

Result:

`DROP VIEW banks`

```text
view 'banks' dropped
```

`DROP VIEW IF EXISTS banks`

```text
view 'banks' does not exist
```

`SHOW VIEWS`

| name (STRING) | query (STRING) | kind (STRING) | refresh (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|

(0 rows)

**Example: No such view** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

```sql
DROP VIEW banks;
```

Result:

Error: `view 'banks' does not exist`

**Example: Dropping a view that another view uses** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE VIEW broker_names AS SELECT id, name FROM brokers;
CREATE VIEW big_brokers AS SELECT name FROM broker_names WHERE id > 40;
```

```sql
DROP VIEW broker_names;
SELECT * FROM big_brokers;
```

Result:

```text
view 'broker_names' dropped
```

Error: `view 'big_brokers': line 1, column 18: table or view 'broker_names' does not exist`

<a id="show-views"></a>

## SHOW VIEWS

Syntax:

```sql
SHOW VIEWS
```

Lists the views of the current database.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | the view name, as it was written in `CREATE VIEW` |
| `query` | the saved `SELECT`, as KarelaDB writes it back |
| `kind` | `simple`, `complex` or `materialized` (see [kinds of views](#view-kinds)) |
| `refresh` | `ON COMMIT` for a cached view made with `REFRESH ON COMMIT`, `ON INSERT` for a [materialized view](#materialized-view), else NULL |

- **Returns:** one row per view, sorted by name; no rows when there are no views.
- **Notes:** views are not listed by `SHOW TABLES`. The web console shows the same list, split by kind, under **Views** on the left.

**Example: The views of the database, their queries and kinds** (sample data: sample)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE VIEW banks AS SELECT symbol, name FROM securities WHERE sector = 'Banking';
CREATE CACHED VIEW trades_per_symbol AS (SELECT symbol, count(*) AS trades FROM trade_log GROUP BY symbol) REFRESH ON COMMIT;
```

```sql
SHOW VIEWS;
```

Result:

| name (STRING) | query (STRING) | kind (STRING) | refresh (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|
| banks | SELECT symbol, name FROM securities WHERE sector = 'Banking' | simple | NULL |
| trades_per_symbol | SELECT symbol, count(*) AS trades FROM trade_log GROUP BY symbol | materialized | ON COMMIT |

(2 rows)

<a id="view-kinds"></a>

## Simple, complex and materialized views

`SHOW VIEWS` puts every view into one of three kinds. The kind is worked out from the view's query; you do not write it.

| Kind | What the query does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `simple` | reads **one** table (or view) and works one row at a time: picks columns, computes values from one row, filters with `WHERE`, sorts | `SELECT symbol, name FROM securities WHERE sector = 'Energy'` |
| `complex` | anything more: `JOIN`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, `SAMPLE BY`, `LATEST ON`, `DISTINCT`, `UNION`, `WITH`, an aggregate such as `count(*)`, a window function (`OVER`), or a subquery | `SELECT symbol, count(*) FROM trade_log GROUP BY symbol` |
| `materialized` | made with `CREATE CACHED VIEW`, whatever its query is | `CREATE CACHED VIEW ... REFRESH ON COMMIT` |

- In a **simple** view each row is one row of the table, so it is quick and easy to follow.
- A **complex** view makes new rows (one per group, per candle, per joined pair). Put a `WHERE` on the columns it groups by, or on its time column, to keep it fast.
- A **materialized** view keeps its result, so reading it is quick however slow its query is. Its rows are made new by [REFRESH VIEW](#refresh-view), or after each commit with `REFRESH ON COMMIT` (see [CREATE CACHED VIEW](#cached-view)).

**Example: One view of each kind** (sample data: sample)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE VIEW hydro AS SELECT symbol, name FROM securities WHERE sector = 'Energy';
CREATE VIEW trades_with_names AS
SELECT f.symbol, s.name, f.quantity FROM trade_log f JOIN securities s ON s.symbol = f.symbol;
CREATE CACHED VIEW shares_per_symbol AS
SELECT symbol, sum(quantity) AS shares FROM trade_log GROUP BY symbol
REFRESH ON COMMIT;
```

```sql
SHOW VIEWS;
```

Result:

| name (STRING) | query (STRING) | kind (STRING) | refresh (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|
| hydro | SELECT symbol, name FROM securities WHERE sector = 'Energy' | simple | NULL |
| shares_per_symbol | SELECT symbol, sum(quantity) AS shares FROM trade_log GROUP BY symbol | materialized | ON COMMIT |
| trades_with_names | SELECT f.symbol, s.name, f.quantity FROM trade_log AS f JOIN securities AS s ON s.symbol = f.symbol | complex | NULL |

(3 rows)
