# Users and roles

> Database users with passwords, and the roles read, write, ddl and admin for every database or for one.

- Category: Users & security
- Keywords: ALTER USER SET timezone, user time zone, user, users, database user, role, roles, rights, permissions, privileges, GRANT, REVOKE, PASSWORD, ROLE, USER, USERS, IF NOT EXISTS, IF EXISTS, WITH, ALL, admin, ddl, write, read, none, DDL right, schema changes, migrations, \_system, last admin, REVOKE ALL ON DATABASE, 403, permission denied, SET ROLE, RESET ROLE, SET ROLE NONE, current\_user, session\_user
- See also: [Keeping kareladb serve safe](server-security.md), [Security functions](functions-security.md), [kareladb user](cli-users.md), [Logins, tokens and roles over HTTP](http-login.md), [Databases and the data folder](databases.md), [PostgreSQL protocol (port 8832)](postgres-protocol.md)

**Database users** are the people and programs that connect to a running `kareladb serve`: you in the web console, your app's backend, a report script. Each user has a password and a **role** (what it may do).

- As soon as the first user exists, `kareladb serve` asks for a login on every request (see [Keeping kareladb serve safe](server-security.md)).
- The users of **your app** (customers who register on your web site) are something else. Keep them in your own table with [password_hash](functions-security.md#password-hash).
- `kareladb sql` and `kareladb shell` open the files directly. They never ask for a login and can run every statement here. Protect the data folder with the file rights of the operating system.

A small shop with three users: you (admin), the shop's backend (write on one database) and a report script (read everywhere).

**Example: Three users for a small shop**

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER shop_app WITH PASSWORD 'Another-long-secret-42';
GRANT write ON DATABASE demo TO shop_app;
CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD 'Reports-only-secret-7' ROLE read;
SHOW USERS;
```

Result:

`CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD '***' ROLE admin`

```text
user 'admin' created with role admin
```

`CREATE USER shop_app WITH PASSWORD '***'`

```text
user 'shop_app' created with role none
```

`GRANT write ON DATABASE demo TO shop_app`

```text
user 'shop_app' has role write on database 'demo'
```

`CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD '***' ROLE read`

```text
user 'report' created with role read
```

`SHOW USERS`

| name (STRING) | role (STRING) | grants (STRING) | created (TIMESTAMP) | changed (TIMESTAMP) | table_grants (STRING) | two_factor (BOOL) | statement_timeout (STRING) | priority (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| admin | admin | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:44.996Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:44.996Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |
| report | read | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:45.113Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:45.113Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |
| shop_app | none | demo=write | 2026-10-24T06:19:45.052Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:45.054Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |

(3 rows)

`SHOW USERS` lists every user to an admin (anyone else sees only their own row). `SHOW USER name` (QuestDB's form) gives that one user's row, and `SHOW USER` alone the logged-in user's.

**Example: One user's row**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD 'Reports-only-secret-7' ROLE read;
```

```sql
SHOW USER report;
```

Result:

| name (STRING) | role (STRING) | grants (STRING) | created (TIMESTAMP) | changed (TIMESTAMP) | table_grants (STRING) | two_factor (BOOL) | statement_timeout (STRING) | priority (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| report | read | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:45.137Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:45.137Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |

(1 row)

## CREATE USER

Syntax:

```sql
CREATE USER [IF NOT EXISTS] name [WITH] PASSWORD 'secret' [ROLE admin | ddl | write | read | none]
```

Adds a database user with a password. `PASSWORD` and `ROLE` may come in any order.

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `IF NOT EXISTS` | no error when the user is already there (nothing is changed then) |
| `name` | letters, digits, `_` and `-`, 1 to 63 characters. `Bob` and `bob` are the same user. |
| `PASSWORD 'secret'` | at least 12 characters, not the user name, at most 1024 bytes. Write `''` for a `'` inside. Required. |
| `ROLE` | the role on **every** database. Default `none` (nothing until a `GRANT`). |

- **Returns:** a message like `user 'report' created with role read`.
- **Notes:**
  - The **first** user must have `ROLE admin`. Once a user exists, the server asks for a login, and only an admin can manage users.
  - Only a user whose own `ROLE` is `admin` may run it (on a server with users).
  - KarelaDB keeps a PBKDF2 hash of the password (600,000 rounds) and a SCRAM-SHA-256 secret for the PostgreSQL port. The password itself is never stored. The statement KarelaDB shows back reads `PASSWORD '***'`.
  - Hashing takes about 0.1 second, so creating many users is not instant.
  - A name with other characters (a dot, a space, Nepali letters) is refused, also inside double quotes. The name is kept as you wrote it (`Sita-K`), but compared without case.
  - Different from PostgreSQL: there is no `CREATE ROLE`, no `LOGIN`/`NOLOGIN` and no `VALID UNTIL`. MySQL writes `'name'@'host' IDENTIFIED BY '...'`; KarelaDB has no host part.

**Example**

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER IF NOT EXISTS admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER report ROLE read PASSWORD 'Reports-only-secret-7';
```

Result:

`CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD '***' ROLE admin`

```text
user 'admin' created with role admin
```

`CREATE USER IF NOT EXISTS admin WITH PASSWORD '***' ROLE admin`

```text
user 'admin' already exists
```

`CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD '***' ROLE read`

```text
user 'report' created with role read
```

**Example: The first user must be an admin** (shows an error)

```sql
CREATE USER shop_app WITH PASSWORD 'Another-long-secret-42';
```

Result:

Error: `the first user must have ROLE admin (CREATE USER name WITH PASSWORD '...' ROLE admin): once a user exists the server asks for a login, and only an admin can manage users`

**Example: Too short a password** (shows an error)

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'nepal' ROLE admin;
```

Result:

Error: `the password is too short: use at least 12 characters (a password manager can make a long random one)`

**Example: The same name in other letters is the same user** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
```

```sql
CREATE USER Admin WITH PASSWORD 'Another-long-secret-42' ROLE read;
```

Result:

Error: `user 'admin' already exists`

**Example: A password is required** (shows an error)

```sql
CREATE USER report ROLE read;
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 29: CREATE USER needs a password, like CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD '...' ROLE read`

## ALTER USER

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER USER name [WITH] PASSWORD 'new secret'
ALTER USER name ROLE admin | ddl | write | read | none
ALTER USER name [WITH] PASSWORD 'new secret' ROLE read
```

Changes the password, the role, or both.

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | an existing user |
| `PASSWORD 'new secret'` | the new password (at least 12 characters, at most 1024 bytes) |
| `ROLE` | the new role on every database. Grants on single databases stay. |

- **Returns:** a message like `user 'report' changed: new password, role read`.
- **Notes:**
  - **Every user may change their own password.** Changing a role, or another user's password, needs `ROLE admin`.
  - A new password ends every login (session) of that user at once: the web console and `POST /api/login` tokens must log in again.
  - The last user with `ROLE admin` can not lose that role while other users exist. Make another user admin first.

**Example: A new password and a new role**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD 'Reports-only-secret-7' ROLE read;
```

```sql
ALTER USER report WITH PASSWORD 'New-report-secret-8';
ALTER USER report ROLE write;
SHOW USERS;
```

Result:

`ALTER USER report WITH PASSWORD '***'`

```text
user 'report' changed: new password
```

`ALTER USER report ROLE write`

```text
user 'report' changed: role write
```

`SHOW USERS`

| name (STRING) | role (STRING) | grants (STRING) | created (TIMESTAMP) | changed (TIMESTAMP) | table_grants (STRING) | two_factor (BOOL) | statement_timeout (STRING) | priority (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| admin | admin | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:45.535Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:45.535Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |
| report | write | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:45.595Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:45.780Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |

(2 rows)

**Example: The last admin must stay an admin** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD 'Reports-only-secret-7' ROLE read;
```

```sql
ALTER USER admin ROLE read;
```

Result:

Error: `'admin' is the last user with ROLE admin; make another user admin first (ALTER USER <name> ROLE admin), or nobody could manage users any more`

**Example: Nothing to change** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
```

```sql
ALTER USER admin;
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 17: ALTER USER needs PASSWORD '...' or ROLE read|write|ddl|admin`

<a id="statement-timeout"></a>

## ALTER USER ... SET statement_timeout

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER USER name SET statement_timeout = '5s' | 5000 | 0 | DEFAULT
ALTER USER name RESET statement_timeout
```

Gives one user their own time limit for a statement. It takes the place of the server's `--statement-timeout` (60 s unless set) for that user only.

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `'2s'`, `'500ms'`, `'10min'`, `5000` | the time; a plain number is milliseconds |
| `0` | no limit for this user |
| `DEFAULT`, or `RESET` | the server's limit again |

- **Returns:** a message like `statement_timeout of user 'charts' is 2 s (from their next statement)`. `SHOW USERS` shows it in the column `statement_timeout`.
- **Notes:**
  - Needs `ROLE admin`. A user can not change their own limit.
  - It may be longer than the server's limit: a report user may get 10 minutes while every other user keeps 60 s.
  - In a session, the user may still make it **shorter** with `SET statement_timeout`, never longer (an admin user may do both). A longer value or `0` keeps the user's limit; the reply and `SHOW statement_timeout` then show the limit that stays.
  - It counts on the HTTP API and on the PostgreSQL port, from the user's next statement. It is kept in the data folder, so it survives a restart.
  - A per-role limit (all `read` users at once) does not exist; set it on each user.

**Example: Short queries for the chart app, long ones for reports**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER charts WITH PASSWORD 'Chart-app-secret-11' ROLE read;
CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD 'Reports-only-secret-7' ROLE read;
```

```sql
ALTER USER charts SET statement_timeout = '2s';
ALTER USER report SET statement_timeout = '10min';
SHOW USERS;
```

Result:

`ALTER USER charts SET statement_timeout = '2000ms'`

```text
statement_timeout of user 'charts' is 2 s (from their next statement)
```

`ALTER USER report SET statement_timeout = '600000ms'`

```text
statement_timeout of user 'report' is 10 min (from their next statement)
```

`SHOW USERS`

| name (STRING) | role (STRING) | grants (STRING) | created (TIMESTAMP) | changed (TIMESTAMP) | table_grants (STRING) | two_factor (BOOL) | statement_timeout (STRING) | priority (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| admin | admin | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:45.759Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:45.759Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |
| charts | read | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:45.815Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:45.996Z | NULL | false | 2 s | NULL |
| report | read | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:45.871Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:46.001Z | NULL | false | 10 min | NULL |

(3 rows)

**Example: Back to the server's limit**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD 'Reports-only-secret-7' ROLE read;
ALTER USER report SET statement_timeout = '10min';
```

```sql
ALTER USER report RESET statement_timeout;
```

Result:

```text
user 'report' has the server's statement_timeout again
```

**Example: Only a time is accepted** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
```

```sql
ALTER USER admin SET statement_timeout = 'soon';
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 42: statement_timeout needs a time like '30s', '500ms', '2min', 0 (no limit) or DEFAULT, not 'soon'`

<a id="user-timezone"></a>

## ALTER USER ... SET timezone

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER USER name SET timezone = 'Asia/Kathmandu' | 'America/New_York' | '+05:45' | DEFAULT
ALTER USER name SET TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kathmandu'
ALTER USER name RESET timezone
```

The clock one user's sessions start on: `CURRENT_DATE`, `::date`, `date_trunc`, `EXTRACT`, `to_char` and a `DATE` met by a `TIMESTAMP` use it ([time zones](time-and-time-zones.md#session-time-zone)). The user's own `SET TIME ZONE` still changes it for a session. Users without one have the server's zone, which is the computer's own unless `kareladb serve --timezone` names another.

- **Role:** an admin sets it, for any user.
- **Kept:** with the user, across restarts and backups.

**Example: Asha sees days on the Nepal clock, the others on the server's**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER asha WITH PASSWORD 'Asha-Long-Passw0rd' ROLE read;
```

```sql
ALTER USER asha SET timezone = 'Asia/Kathmandu';
```

Result:

```text
time zone of user 'asha' is Asia/Kathmandu (from their next session)
```

## DROP USER

Syntax:

```sql
DROP USER [IF EXISTS] name
```

Removes a user and its grants. Its logins stop working at once.

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `IF EXISTS` | no error when there is no such user |
| `name` | the user to remove |

- **Returns:** `user 'name' dropped`, or `user 'name' does not exist` with `IF EXISTS`.
- **Notes:**
  - Needs `ROLE admin`.
  - The last user with `ROLE admin` can not be dropped while other users exist.
  - When the **last** user is dropped, the server has no users again and stops asking for a login (on `127.0.0.1`).
  - Tables and data are never touched: KarelaDB has no "owner" of a table.

**Example**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD 'Reports-only-secret-7' ROLE read;
```

```sql
DROP USER report;
DROP USER IF EXISTS report;
SHOW USERS;
```

Result:

`DROP USER report`

```text
user 'report' dropped
```

`DROP USER IF EXISTS report`

```text
user 'report' does not exist
```

`SHOW USERS`

| name (STRING) | role (STRING) | grants (STRING) | created (TIMESTAMP) | changed (TIMESTAMP) | table_grants (STRING) | two_factor (BOOL) | statement_timeout (STRING) | priority (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| admin | admin | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:46.267Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:46.267Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |

(1 row)

**Example: The last admin can not be dropped while others exist** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD 'Reports-only-secret-7' ROLE read;
```

```sql
DROP USER admin;
```

Result:

Error: `'admin' is the last user with ROLE admin; make another user admin first (ALTER USER <name> ROLE admin), or nobody could manage users any more`

## SHOW USERS

Syntax:

```sql
SHOW USERS
```

Lists the users with their roles and grants. It never shows passwords or hashes.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | the user name as it was created |
| `role` | the role on every database |
| `grants` | the roles on single databases, like `shop=write, demo=read`; `NULL` when there are none |
| `created` | when the user was made (UTC) |
| `changed` | the last change of password, role or grants (UTC) |
| `table_grants` | [table rights](table-rights.md), like `shop.ledger: -DELETE`; `NULL` when there are none |
| `two_factor` | `true` when the user logs in with a [two-factor code](two-factor-login.md) |
| `statement_timeout` | the user's own [time limit](#statement-timeout), like `2 s` or `off`; `NULL` = the server's |

- **Returns:** one row per user, sorted by name (small and capital letters count the same).
- **Notes:**
  - Every user may run it. A user who is not an admin sees **only their own row**.
  - With no users yet it gives 0 rows.
  - A server or command that opened one database folder by its path (not a data folder) gives an error: users need a data folder.

**Example**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER shop_app WITH PASSWORD 'Another-long-secret-42' ROLE none;
CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD 'Reports-only-secret-7' ROLE read;
CREATE DATABASE shop;
GRANT write ON DATABASE shop TO shop_app;
GRANT read ON DATABASE demo TO shop_app;
```

```sql
SHOW USERS;
```

Result:

| name (STRING) | role (STRING) | grants (STRING) | created (TIMESTAMP) | changed (TIMESTAMP) | table_grants (STRING) | two_factor (BOOL) | statement_timeout (STRING) | priority (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| admin | admin | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:46.417Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:46.417Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |
| report | read | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:46.537Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:46.537Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |
| shop_app | none | demo=read, shop=write | 2026-10-24T06:19:46.478Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:46.560Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |

(3 rows)

## GRANT

Syntax:

```sql
GRANT read | write | ddl | admin | ALL ON DATABASE db TO name
```

Gives a user a role on **one** database. `ALL` is the same as `admin`.

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| role | `read`, `write`, `ddl`, `admin` or `ALL` |
| `db` | an existing database |
| `name` | an existing user |

- **Returns:** a message like `user 'shop_app' has role write on database 'shop'`.
- **Notes:**
  - A user has **one** grant per database. A new `GRANT` on the same database replaces the old one (also a weaker one: `GRANT read` after `GRANT admin` leaves `read`).
  - The user may use the **stronger** of its own `ROLE` and the grant. A grant can never take away what `ROLE` gives.
  - `GRANT admin ON DATABASE shop` gives all rights **inside** `shop`, but not creating or dropping databases, and not managing users. Those need `ROLE admin`.
  - Needs `ROLE admin`.
  - `DROP DATABASE` also removes every grant on that database.
  - A `GRANT` of a role is per database. For single tables use [table rights](table-rights.md): `GRANT SELECT ON TABLE prices TO u`, `REVOKE DELETE ON TABLE ledger FROM app`. There are no column or row rights.

**Example: The app may write in its own database only**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER shop_app WITH PASSWORD 'Another-long-secret-42';
CREATE DATABASE shop;
```

```sql
GRANT write ON DATABASE shop TO shop_app;
GRANT ALL ON DATABASE demo TO shop_app;
SHOW USERS;
```

Result:

`GRANT write ON DATABASE shop TO shop_app`

```text
user 'shop_app' has role write on database 'shop'
```

`GRANT admin ON DATABASE demo TO shop_app`

```text
user 'shop_app' has role admin on database 'demo'
```

`SHOW USERS`

| name (STRING) | role (STRING) | grants (STRING) | created (TIMESTAMP) | changed (TIMESTAMP) | table_grants (STRING) | two_factor (BOOL) | statement_timeout (STRING) | priority (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| admin | admin | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:46.484Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:46.484Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |
| shop_app | none | demo=admin, shop=write | 2026-10-24T06:19:46.543Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:46.705Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |

(2 rows)

**Example: DROP DATABASE removes the grants on it**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER shop_app WITH PASSWORD 'Another-long-secret-42';
CREATE DATABASE shop;
GRANT write ON DATABASE shop TO shop_app;
```

```sql
DROP DATABASE shop;
SHOW USERS;
```

Result:

`DROP DATABASE shop`

```text
database 'shop' dropped; its folder was moved to kdb-data/_trash/1792822786932-shop
```

`SHOW USERS`

| name (STRING) | role (STRING) | grants (STRING) | created (TIMESTAMP) | changed (TIMESTAMP) | table_grants (STRING) | two_factor (BOOL) | statement_timeout (STRING) | priority (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| admin | admin | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:46.728Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:46.728Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |
| shop_app | none | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:46.784Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:46.936Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |

(2 rows)

**Example: The database must exist** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER shop_app WITH PASSWORD 'Another-long-secret-42';
```

```sql
GRANT write ON DATABASE accounts TO shop_app;
```

Result:

Error: `database 'accounts' does not exist`

**Example: none is not a role to grant: use REVOKE** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
```

```sql
GRANT none ON DATABASE demo TO admin;
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 7: expected a role (read, write, ddl or admin, or ALL) in GRANT, found 'none'`

## REVOKE

Syntax:

```sql
REVOKE [read | write | ddl | admin | ALL] ON DATABASE db FROM name
```

Removes the user's grant on one database.

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| role | optional, and only for reading comfort: the whole grant on `db` goes, whatever role you write |
| `db` | the database. It may already be gone. |
| `name` | an existing user |

- **Returns:** `user 'name' has no grant on database 'db' now` (also when there was no grant).
- **Notes:**
  - It does **not** change the user's own `ROLE`. A user with `ROLE read` can still read `db` after `REVOKE`. Use `ALTER USER name ROLE none` for that.
  - `REVOKE read ...` on a user with a `write` grant removes the `write` grant too; there is no "step down". To give less, `GRANT` the smaller role instead.
  - KarelaDB also accepts `TO name` instead of `FROM name`.
  - Needs `ROLE admin`.

**Example**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER shop_app WITH PASSWORD 'Another-long-secret-42';
GRANT write ON DATABASE demo TO shop_app;
```

```sql
REVOKE ALL ON DATABASE demo FROM shop_app;
SHOW USERS;
```

Result:

`REVOKE ALL ON DATABASE demo FROM shop_app`

```text
user 'shop_app' has no grant on database 'demo' now
```

`SHOW USERS`

| name (STRING) | role (STRING) | grants (STRING) | created (TIMESTAMP) | changed (TIMESTAMP) | table_grants (STRING) | two_factor (BOOL) | statement_timeout (STRING) | priority (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| admin | admin | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:46.965Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:46.965Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |
| shop_app | none | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:47.021Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:47.145Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |

(2 rows)

**Example: REVOKE does not touch the user's own ROLE**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD 'Reports-only-secret-7' ROLE read;
GRANT write ON DATABASE demo TO report;
```

```sql
REVOKE read ON DATABASE demo FROM report;
SHOW USERS;
```

Result:

`REVOKE read ON DATABASE demo FROM report`

```text
user 'report' keeps role write on database 'demo': REVOKE read takes away only a read grant; use REVOKE write or REVOKE ALL. Nothing was revoked
```

`SHOW USERS`

| name (STRING) | role (STRING) | grants (STRING) | created (TIMESTAMP) | changed (TIMESTAMP) | table_grants (STRING) | two_factor (BOOL) | statement_timeout (STRING) | priority (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| admin | admin | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:47.208Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:47.208Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |
| report | read | demo=write | 2026-10-24T06:19:47.268Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:47.270Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |

(2 rows)

<a id="set-role"></a>

## SET ROLE

Syntax:

```sql
SET ROLE name          -- from now on, statements use the rights of user `name`
SET ROLE NONE          -- back to the login user's rights
RESET ROLE             -- the same
```

An app that logs in as an admin (for its start-up migrations) can drop to the rights of its own user for everything else. The session keeps the role until `RESET ROLE`, as in PostgreSQL.

| Who logged in | May take |
|---|---|
| the token, or a server without users | any user |
| a user whose own `ROLE` is `admin` | any user |
| any other user | only itself |

- **Returns:** `statements now use the rights of user 'name' (RESET ROLE goes back)`.
- **Errors:** a name that is no user: `role "name" does not exist` (`22023`). Someone else, without `ROLE admin`: `permission denied to set role "name"` (`42501`).
- **Notes:**
  - Every statement is checked against the rights of the role: its `ROLE`, its database `GRANT`s and its [table rights](table-rights.md).
  - Over the PostgreSQL protocol `current_user` gives the role and `session_user` the login user. The audit log names both (`admin (as report)`).
  - It changes the rights of SQL. HTTP routes that are not SQL (`/api/...`) still use the login.
  - It lasts for the HTTP session or the PostgreSQL connection. Without a session it lasts for the one request.

**Example: An admin session takes the rights of a report user** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD 'Reports-only-secret-7' ROLE read;
```

```sql
SET ROLE report;
SELECT 1 AS reading_is_fine;
CREATE TABLE made_by_report (id INT);
```

Result:

```text
statements now use the rights of user 'report' (RESET ROLE goes back)
```

Error: `CREATE TABLE needs role ddl on database 'demo'; user 'report' has read`

**Example: RESET ROLE goes back to the login user's rights**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD 'Reports-only-secret-7' ROLE read;
```

```sql
SET ROLE report;
RESET ROLE;
CREATE TABLE made_after_reset (id INT);
```

Result:

`SET role = 'report'`

```text
statements now use the rights of user 'report' (RESET ROLE goes back)
```

`SET role = ''`

```text
back to the rights of the login user
```

`CREATE TABLE made_after_reset (`

```text
table 'made_after_reset' created
```

<a id="roles"></a>

## Roles: what each one may do

Syntax:

```sql
none  <  read  <  write  <  ddl  <  admin
```

Each role may do everything of the roles before it.

| Role | May do |
|---|---|
| `none` | nothing (until a `GRANT`). It may still log in, change its own password and see its own row in `SHOW USERS`. |
| `read` | `SELECT`, `SHOW ...`, `EXPLAIN`, `USE`, CSV export, cursors (`DECLARE`, `FETCH`, `CLOSE`), `BEGIN` / `COMMIT` / `ROLLBACK` / `SAVEPOINT`, `/api/info`, list backups |
| `write` | also `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` (with `RETURNING`), `TRUNCATE`, `CALL` of procedures, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, line protocol (`POST /write`) |
| `ddl` | also the schema: `CREATE` / `ALTER` / `DROP` / `RENAME` of tables, views, indexes, sequences, functions, procedures and triggers, `REFRESH VIEW`, a new table with `POST /imp`. No users, no server settings, no backups, no audit log. |
| `admin` | also `BACKUP`, `CHECK TABLE`, `SHOW AUDIT`, `ALTER TABLE ... SET AUDIT`, `ALTER DATABASE`, `TRUNCATE ALL TABLES`, the trigger queue (`RETRY` / `SKIP`) |

The HTTP routes that are not SQL need these roles:

| Needs | Routes |
|---|---|
| a login only | `GET /api/me`, `POST /api/feedback` (send a comment) |
| `read` on the database | `GET /api/info`, `GET /api/disk`, `GET /api/backups`, `GET /api/stats`, `GET /api/trigger-queue`, `GET /api/timers`, `GET /api/pins`, cursors |
| `write` on the database | `POST /write`, `POST /api/v2/write`, `POST /imp` (`ddl` when it creates the table) |
| `admin` on the database | `POST /api/check`, `POST /api/backup`, save, run, turn off or delete a [timer](timers.md), pin or unpin a [statement](pinned-queries.md) |
| the user's own `ROLE admin` | `GET` and `POST /api/settings`, `POST /api/restart`, `POST` and `DELETE /api/databases`, `GET /api/feedback`, `POST /api/feedback/<id>`, `GET /api/audit` (with `kind=data`: `admin` on that database is enough) |

Two places give a role:

| Where | For | Written |
|---|---|---|
| the user's own `ROLE` | **every** database | `CREATE USER ... ROLE read`, `ALTER USER ... ROLE read` |
| a grant | **one** database | `GRANT write ON DATABASE shop TO shop_app` |

- **Returns:** a statement without the needed role is refused before any of it runs, with HTTP status 403 and a message like `INSERT needs role write on database 'shop'; user 'report' has read`.
- **Notes:**
  - Only a user whose own `ROLE` is `admin` may create and drop databases and manage users (`CREATE USER`, `ALTER USER ... ROLE`, `DROP USER`, `GRANT`, `REVOKE`). The message then says `needs role admin as its own ROLE (it acts on the whole server)`.
  - `SHOW DATABASES` lists only the databases the user may read.
  - A `--token` of the server works like a full admin.
  - Give each program only what it needs: your app's backend `write` on its own database, a report script `read`, a migration tool `ddl`. Keep `admin` for yourself.
  - `ddl` is for a developer or a migration tool (Flyway, Alembic, Prisma) that changes tables but must not manage users or settings. It is kept by its name, like the other roles. An older KarelaDB reads a `ddl` user as `none`: that user loses rights there, it never gains them.
  - `CALL` needs `write`: a procedure can only change rows (it can not hold `CREATE` or `DROP`).
  - A view, procedure or trigger saved by a `ddl` user may only read and change what that user may. `CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT * FROM _audit_log` needs `admin`, like reading `_audit_log` itself. See [table rights](table-rights.md#revoke-on-table).
  - Only `kareladb serve` (HTTP, web console and PostgreSQL port) checks roles. `kareladb sql` and `kareladb shell` do not.

**Example: A report user that may read every database, and an app that may write one**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
```

```sql
CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD 'Reports-only-secret-7' ROLE read;
CREATE USER shop_app WITH PASSWORD 'Another-long-secret-42' ROLE none;
GRANT write ON DATABASE demo TO shop_app;
SHOW USERS;
```

Result:

`CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD '***' ROLE read`

```text
user 'report' created with role read
```

`CREATE USER shop_app WITH PASSWORD '***' ROLE none`

```text
user 'shop_app' created with role none
```

`GRANT write ON DATABASE demo TO shop_app`

```text
user 'shop_app' has role write on database 'demo'
```

`SHOW USERS`

| name (STRING) | role (STRING) | grants (STRING) | created (TIMESTAMP) | changed (TIMESTAMP) | table_grants (STRING) | two_factor (BOOL) | statement_timeout (STRING) | priority (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| admin | admin | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:47.396Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:47.396Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |
| report | read | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:47.579Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:47.579Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |
| shop_app | none | demo=write | 2026-10-24T06:19:47.659Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:47.662Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |

(3 rows)

**Example: A migration user may change tables, not users** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER migrate WITH PASSWORD 'Migrations-only-secret-9' ROLE ddl;
```

```sql
SET ROLE migrate;
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, total DOUBLE);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN placed TIMESTAMP;
CREATE INDEX orders_placed ON orders (placed);
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 12.5, '2026-09-25T10:00:00Z');
CREATE USER intern WITH PASSWORD 'Intern-long-secret-3';
```

Result:

`SET role = 'migrate'`

```text
statements now use the rights of user 'migrate' (RESET ROLE goes back)
```

`CREATE TABLE orders (`

```text
table 'orders' created
```

`ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN placed TIMESTAMP`

```text
table 'orders' altered
```

`CREATE INDEX orders_placed ON orders (placed)`

```text

```

`INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 12.5, '2026-09-25T10:00:00Z')`

```text

```

Error: `CREATE USER needs role admin as its own ROLE (it acts on the whole server); user 'migrate' has ddl`

**Example: A writer may change rows but not the schema** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER shop_app WITH PASSWORD 'Another-long-secret-42' ROLE write;
```

```sql
SET ROLE shop_app;
CREATE TABLE app_made (id INT);
```

Result:

```text

```

Error: `CREATE TABLE needs role ddl on database 'demo'; user 'shop_app' has write`

<a id="system-database"></a>

## Where users are kept

Syntax:

```sql
<data folder>/_system/        the hidden database with the table users
```

Users belong to the **data folder**, not to one database. KarelaDB keeps them in a hidden database named `_system` inside the data folder. All databases of that folder share the users.

| Column of `users` | Holds |
|---|---|
| `name`, `role`, `grants` | what `SHOW USERS` shows |
| `password_hash` | `$pbkdf2-sha256$i=600000$...` (the same form as `password_hash()`) |
| `scram` | `SCRAM-SHA-256$4096:...` for PostgreSQL clients |
| `created_at`, `changed_at` | times |

- **Returns:** not a statement: `USE _system` and `CREATE DATABASE _system` are refused.
- **Notes:**
  - A server that opened **one database folder by its path** (`kareladb serve D:\kdb\market`) has no users. Use `--data-dir <folder>`.
  - Anyone who can read the data folder or a backup can read the password hashes. Keep the folder and backups private (`chmod 700` on Linux).
  - `kareladb user add | passwd | role | list | remove` work on the same users while the server is stopped (see [kareladb user](cli-users.md)). While `kareladb serve` runs, use SQL in its console.
  - Logins (sessions) and [API tokens](api-tokens.md) are kept here too, as hashes only, so a restart logs nobody out.
  - An old `kareladb` program made before users existed does not know `_system` and would serve the data **without** a login. Update every `kareladb` program first.

**Example: _system is not a normal database** (shows an error)

```sql
USE _system;
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 5: bad database name '_system': '_system' is where KarelaDB keeps its users`

**Command line: kareladb user and SQL see the same users**

```bash
kareladb user add admin --role admin
> Long-Admin-Passw0rd
> Long-Admin-Passw0rd
kareladb user list
kareladb sql kdb-data/shop "CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY)"
kareladb sql shop "CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD 'Reports-only-secret-7' ROLE read; SHOW USERS"
```

Output:

`> kareladb user add admin --role admin`

```text
user 'admin' added with role admin in ./kdb-data
```

`> kareladb user list`

```text
USER                     ROLE   GRANTS                         CHANGED
admin                    admin  -                              2026-10-24 12:04:47
1 user in ./kdb-data
```

`> kareladb sql kdb-data/shop "CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY)"`

```text
table 'orders' created
```

`> kareladb sql shop "CREATE USER report WITH PASSWORD 'Reports-only-secret-7' ROLE read; SHOW USERS"`

```text
user 'report' created with role read

name   | role  | grants | created                  | changed                  | table_grants | two_factor | statement_timeout | priority
-------+-------+--------+--------------------------+--------------------------+--------------+------------+-------------------+---------
admin  | admin | NULL   | 2026-10-24T06:19:47.866Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:47.866Z | NULL         | false      | NULL              | NULL    
report | read  | NULL   | 2026-10-24T06:19:48.261Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:48.261Z | NULL         | false      | NULL              | NULL    
(2 rows, 0.0 ms)
```

Here the data folder is `kdb-data`. The first `kareladb sql` makes the database `shop` in it by its path. After that, the plain name `shop` means the database in the data folder, so the user statements work. A plain name that is **not** in the data folder is taken as a new folder in the current folder, and then user statements say `users need a data folder`.

<!-- docs/table-rights.md -->

# Table rights - GRANT ON TABLE

> Give a user rights on one table (GRANT SELECT ON TABLE prices), on some of its columns (GRANT SELECT (id, name) ON staff) or on some of its rows (CREATE POLICY), or take some rights of the role away (REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE ON TABLE ledger).

- Category: Users & security
- Keywords: table rights, table privileges, per-table grant, column rights, column privileges, GRANT SELECT (, column\_privileges, has\_column\_privilege, hide a column, permissions, GRANT SELECT, GRANT INSERT, REVOKE DELETE, REVOKE UPDATE, PRIVILEGES, DEFAULT, append-only table, ledger rights, read one table, row rights, row-level security, RLS, CREATE POLICY, DROP POLICY, ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, pg\_policies, row\_security, multi-tenant, own rows only
- See also: [Users and roles](users-and-roles.md), [Audit log](audit-log.md), [Protection - timeouts, limits, safe updates, read-only](protection.md), [Keeping kareladb serve safe](server-security.md)

A user's [role](users-and-roles.md#roles) gives rights on a whole database. Table rights change that for one table of the current database:

```text
allowed = (the role allows it AND it was not revoked on the table) OR it was granted on the table
```

| Right | Needed for |
|---|---|
| `SELECT` | reading the table in `SELECT`, subqueries, `JOIN`, `EXPLAIN`, cursors, and `RETURNING` |
| `INSERT` | `INSERT`, and the line protocol (`POST /write`) |
| `UPDATE` | `UPDATE` |
| `DELETE` | `DELETE` |

They are checked once per statement, before it runs (and before the result cache), never per row.

<a id="grant-on-table"></a>

## GRANT ... ON TABLE

Syntax:

```sql
GRANT SELECT | INSERT | UPDATE | DELETE | ALL [PRIVILEGES] [, ...] ON TABLE <table> TO <user>
GRANT DEFAULT ON TABLE <table> TO <user>
```

Adds rights on one table of the current database (`USE`). `DEFAULT` removes every table right of the user on that table: the role decides again.

- **Returns:** `granted SELECT on table 'prices' of database 'shop' to user 'viewer'`.
- **Notes:** needs a server admin. Works for views too (a view gives what it shows).

**Example: A user who may only read one table** (sample data: sample)

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER viewer WITH PASSWORD 'Viewer-password-42';
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE securities TO viewer;
SHOW USERS;
```

Result:

`CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD '***' ROLE admin`

```text
user 'admin' created with role admin
```

`CREATE USER viewer WITH PASSWORD '***'`

```text
user 'viewer' created with role none
```

`GRANT SELECT ON TABLE securities TO viewer`

```text
granted SELECT on table 'securities' of database 'demo' to user 'viewer'
```

`SHOW USERS`

| name (STRING) | role (STRING) | grants (STRING) | created (TIMESTAMP) | changed (TIMESTAMP) | table_grants (STRING) | two_factor (BOOL) | statement_timeout (STRING) | priority (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| admin | admin | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:36.328Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:36.328Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |
| viewer | none | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:36.383Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:36.416Z | demo.securities: +SELECT | false | NULL | NULL |

(2 rows)

<a id="revoke-on-table"></a>

## REVOKE ... ON TABLE

Syntax:

```sql
REVOKE SELECT | INSERT | UPDATE | DELETE | ALL [, ...] ON TABLE <table> FROM <user>
```

Takes rights away on one table, even when the role allows them. For an accounting ledger that must only grow: the app's user has role `write`, and `REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE ON TABLE ledger FROM app`.

- **Returns:** `revoked UPDATE, DELETE on table 'ledger' of database 'shop' from user 'app'`. A refused statement gets `DELETE on table 'ledger' was revoked for user 'app'` (HTTP 403, SQLSTATE `42501`).
- **Notes:**
  - `DROP TABLE` removes the table rights of that table; `RENAME TABLE` keeps them under the new name. A new table with an old name does not get old rights.
  - Views, procedures (`CALL`) and triggers run without the rights of whoever uses them, like PostgreSQL's `SECURITY DEFINER`. So when a `ddl` user saves one, KarelaDB checks what it reads and changes against that user's rights: a view of a revoked table, or a procedure that deletes from it, is refused. The same holds for `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT`.
  - A statement that reads a second table needs `SELECT` on it too: `INSERT ... SELECT`, `UPDATE ... FROM`, `DELETE ... USING` and `WITH`.
  - Older KarelaDB programs refuse a data folder with table rights (they would ignore them).

**Example: The ledger only grows** (sample data: query-app)

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER app WITH PASSWORD 'App-password-12345';
GRANT write ON DATABASE demo TO app;
REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE ON TABLE ledger FROM app;
SHOW USERS;
```

Result:

`CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD '***' ROLE admin`

```text
user 'admin' created with role admin
```

`CREATE USER app WITH PASSWORD '***'`

```text
user 'app' created with role none
```

`GRANT write ON DATABASE demo TO app`

```text
user 'app' has role write on database 'demo'
```

`REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE ON TABLE ledger FROM app`

```text
revoked UPDATE, DELETE on table 'ledger' of database 'demo' from user 'app'
```

`SHOW USERS`

| name (STRING) | role (STRING) | grants (STRING) | created (TIMESTAMP) | changed (TIMESTAMP) | table_grants (STRING) | two_factor (BOOL) | statement_timeout (STRING) | priority (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| admin | admin | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:36.346Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:36.346Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |
| app | none | demo=write | 2026-10-24T06:19:36.402Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:36.455Z | demo.ledger: -UPDATE -DELETE | false | NULL | NULL |

(2 rows)

**Example: A revoked table can not be wrapped in a view** (sample data: query-app; shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER migrate WITH PASSWORD 'Migrations-only-secret-9' ROLE ddl;
REVOKE SELECT ON TABLE ledger FROM migrate;
```

```sql
SET ROLE migrate;
CREATE VIEW all_ledger AS SELECT * FROM ledger;
```

Result:

```text
statements now use the rights of user 'migrate' (RESET ROLE goes back)
```

Error: `SELECT on table 'ledger' was revoked for user 'migrate' (REVOKE SELECT ON TABLE ledger)`

<a id="column-rights"></a>

## Column rights

Syntax:

```sql
GRANT SELECT | INSERT | UPDATE | ALL (<column> [, ...]) [, ...] ON [TABLE] <table> TO <user>
REVOKE SELECT | INSERT | UPDATE | ALL (<column> [, ...]) [, ...] ON [TABLE] <table> FROM <user>
```

A right can name columns. Then it is about those columns only. Each right has its own list: `GRANT SELECT (id, name), UPDATE (name) ON staff TO clerk`.

```text
column allowed = not revoked on the column AND (the table allows it OR it was granted on the column)
```

| You want | Write |
|---|---|
| A user who reads only some columns | `GRANT SELECT (id, name) ON staff TO temp` (no role on the database) |
| Hide one column from a role | `REVOKE SELECT (salary) ON staff FROM clerk` |
| Let a user change only one column | `REVOKE UPDATE ON staff FROM clerk; GRANT UPDATE (name) ON staff TO clerk` |
| Back to the role | `GRANT DEFAULT ON TABLE staff TO clerk` (removes the table's column rights too) |

Every column a statement names is checked: the `SELECT` list, `WHERE`, `JOIN ... ON`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, `ORDER BY`, subqueries, `WITH`, `RETURNING`, the columns an `INSERT` fills and the columns an `UPDATE` sets. A refused statement gets `permission denied for column "salary" of table "staff"` (HTTP 403, SQLSTATE `42501`).

- **Returns:** `revoked SELECT on column 'salary' of table 'staff' of database 'hr' from user 'clerk'`.
- **Notes:**
  - `SELECT *` (and `RETURNING *`) reads every column, so it is refused when one of them is not allowed, as in PostgreSQL. Name the columns instead. `count(*)` reads no column and is fine.
  - An `INSERT` without a column list fills every column: it needs `INSERT` on all of them.
  - `DELETE` takes whole rows, so it cannot name columns.
  - A user whose role on the database is `admin` is never held back by column rights.
  - The rights are checked each time a statement runs, also for a prepared statement or a plan kept in the cache.
  - `RENAME COLUMN` keeps the rights under the new name; `DROP COLUMN` removes them.
  - A table of another database (`otherdb.t`) with a column you may not read is refused as a whole; `USE` that database to read the other columns.
  - `has_column_privilege()` and `information_schema.column_privileges` show the same rights.
  - The rights are kept in `_system`. Older KarelaDB programs refuse a data folder once a column right was granted there (they would ignore it).

**Example: An auditor who reads some columns of the ledger** (sample data: query-app)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER auditor WITH PASSWORD 'Auditor-password-77';
GRANT SELECT (line_id, entry_date, account) ON ledger TO auditor;
```

```sql
SET ROLE auditor;
SELECT line_id, account FROM ledger ORDER BY line_id LIMIT 3;
```

Result:

`SET role = 'auditor'`

```text
statements now use the rights of user 'auditor' (RESET ROLE goes back)
```

`SELECT line_id, account FROM ledger ORDER BY line_id LIMIT 3`

| line_id (INT) | account (INT) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 1100 |
| 2 | 3000 |
| 3 | 1200 |

(3 rows)

**Example: SELECT * needs every column** (sample data: query-app; shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER auditor WITH PASSWORD 'Auditor-password-77';
GRANT SELECT (line_id, entry_date, account) ON ledger TO auditor;
```

```sql
SET ROLE auditor;
SELECT * FROM ledger;
```

Result:

```text
statements now use the rights of user 'auditor' (RESET ROLE goes back)
```

Error: `permission denied for column "entry_id" of table "ledger": SELECT * (or RETURNING *) reads every column, and user 'auditor' may not SELECT this one; name the columns instead`

**Example: What the current user may do with each column** (sample data: query-app)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER app WITH PASSWORD 'App-password-12345';
GRANT write ON DATABASE demo TO app;
REVOKE SELECT (credit) ON ledger FROM app;
```

```sql
SET ROLE app;
SELECT column_name, privilege_type FROM information_schema.column_privileges
WHERE table_name = 'ledger' AND column_name IN ('debit', 'credit') ORDER BY 1, 2;
```

Result:

`SET role = 'app'`

```text
statements now use the rights of user 'app' (RESET ROLE goes back)
```

`SELECT column_name, privilege_type FROM "information_schema.column_privileges" WHERE table_name = 'l`

| column_name (STRING) | privilege_type (STRING) |
|---|---|
| credit | INSERT |
| credit | UPDATE |
| debit | INSERT |
| debit | SELECT |
| debit | UPDATE |

(5 rows)

<a id="row-rights"></a>

## Row rights (row-level security)

Syntax:

```sql
CREATE POLICY <name> ON <table> [AS PERMISSIVE] [FOR ALL | SELECT | INSERT | UPDATE | DELETE]
    [TO <user> | PUBLIC [, ...]] [USING (<condition>)] [WITH CHECK (<condition>)]
DROP POLICY [IF EXISTS] <name> ON <table>
ALTER TABLE <table> ENABLE | DISABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY
```

A policy decides which rows of a table a user sees and may change. It acts once the table's row-level security is on (`ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`). Then, for every user who is not an admin of the database:

| Statement | What the policies do |
|---|---|
| `SELECT` (also joins, subqueries, `WITH`, views, `EXPLAIN`, `CREATE TABLE ... AS`) | only rows where a `USING` condition is true are read |
| `UPDATE`, `DELETE` | only those rows are changed; others are left alone, without an error |
| `INSERT`, and the new version of an updated row | must pass a `WITH CHECK` condition (or the `USING` of a policy without one), else `new row violates row-level security policy for table "t"` (HTTP 403, SQLSTATE `42501`) |

The policies of a table are joined with `OR`: one that lets a row in is enough. A table with row-level security on and no policy for the user shows them no rows at all.

- **Returns:** `policy 'own' created on table 'orders'`; `row-level security of table 'orders' is on`.
- **Notes:**
  - Needs role `admin` on the database. An admin is never held back by the policies (`FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` is accepted and changes nothing).
  - `current_user` in a condition is the user running the statement, so one policy serves every user.
  - A view shows each reader the rows their own policies allow (like PostgreSQL's `security_invoker` views).
  - `SET row_security = off`: a statement a policy would change fails instead (`query would be affected by row-level security policy`), as in PostgreSQL. Use it to be sure a dump gets every row.
  - Bulk paths that do not run SQL refuse such a table for these users: `/cursor`, `POST /write`, `/imp` and `COPY FROM`. A `DO` block is refused too. Use `SELECT` and `INSERT`.
  - A `WITH CHECK` condition looks at the one row only (no subqueries).
  - Results of these users never come from the result cache, so a cached answer is never shared between users.
  - `RENAME TABLE` keeps the policies; `DROP TABLE` removes them. `pg_policies`, `pg_policy` and `pg_tables.rowsecurity` show them.
  - Only `PERMISSIVE` policies (`AS RESTRICTIVE` is refused). Statements inside procedures and triggers are not filtered; their `WITH CHECK` still applies.
  - The policies are kept in `_system`. Older KarelaDB programs refuse a data folder once a policy was made there (they would ignore it).

**Example: Each user sees only their own rows** (sample data: query-app)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER ann WITH PASSWORD 'Ann-password-12345';
GRANT write ON DATABASE demo TO ann;
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, owner STRING, amount DOUBLE);
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'ann', 10), (2, 'bo', 20), (3, 'ann', 30);
CREATE POLICY own ON orders TO ann USING (owner = current_user);
ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
```

```sql
SET ROLE ann;
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY id;
```

Result:

`SET role = 'ann'`

```text
statements now use the rights of user 'ann' (RESET ROLE goes back)
```

`SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE owner = current_user) AS orders ORDER BY id`

| id (INT) | owner (STRING) | amount (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ann | 10 |
| 3 | ann | 30 |

(2 rows)

**Example: A row for someone else is refused** (sample data: query-app; shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER ann WITH PASSWORD 'Ann-password-12345';
GRANT write ON DATABASE demo TO ann;
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, owner STRING, amount DOUBLE);
CREATE POLICY own ON orders TO ann USING (owner = current_user);
ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
```

```sql
SET ROLE ann;
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (4, 'bo', 5);
```

Result:

```text
statements now use the rights of user 'ann' (RESET ROLE goes back)
```

Error: `new row violates row-level security policy for table "orders"`

**Example: The policies of a database** (sample data: query-app)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER ann WITH PASSWORD 'Ann-password-12345';
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, owner STRING, amount DOUBLE);
CREATE POLICY own ON orders TO ann USING (owner = current_user);
CREATE POLICY big ON orders FOR SELECT TO PUBLIC USING (amount > 100);
```

```sql
SELECT policyname, cmd, roles, qual FROM pg_policies ORDER BY policyname;
```

Result:

| policyname (STRING) | cmd (STRING) | roles (STRING) | qual (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|
| big | SELECT | {public} | amount > 100 |
| own | ALL | {ann} | owner = current_user |

(2 rows)

<a id="revoke-role"></a>

## REVOKE role ON DATABASE

Syntax:

```sql
REVOKE read | write | admin ON DATABASE <db> FROM <user>
REVOKE ALL ON DATABASE <db> FROM <user>
```

`REVOKE <role>` takes away exactly a grant of that role. A stronger grant stays: `REVOKE read` does not remove a `write` grant (the message says so). `REVOKE ALL` removes any grant on the database.

- **Returns:** `user 'u' has no grant on database 'shop' now`, or `user 'u' keeps role write on database 'shop': REVOKE read takes away only a read grant; use REVOKE write or REVOKE ALL. Nothing was revoked`.

<!-- docs/api-tokens.md -->

# API tokens

> Named, revocable secrets for apps - each acts as one user, and DROP TOKEN stops it at once.

- Category: Users & security
- Keywords: API token, api tokens, token, tokens, CREATE TOKEN, DROP TOKEN, SHOW TOKENS, revoke, revoke token, kdbt\_, Bearer, Authorization, EXPIRES, personal access token, service token, app token, 401
- See also: [Users and roles](users-and-roles.md), [Logins, tokens and roles over HTTP](http-login.md), [Keeping kareladb serve safe](server-security.md), [Protection - timeouts, limits, safe updates, read-only](protection.md)

An **API token** is a long secret an app sends with every request, like the server's `--token`. The difference: you can have **many**, each has a **name**, each acts as **one user** (with that user's rights), and you can **remove one** without touching the others.

| | `--token` of `kareladb serve` | API token |
|---|---|---|
| How many | one | as many as you like |
| Rights | everything | the rights of its user |
| Change or revoke | restart the server with another one | `DROP TOKEN name`, at once |
| Kept | on the command line | in the data folder (only its hash) |

Give each app its own token. When one app is retired or its secret leaks, drop that token; the other apps go on.

**Example: A token for the chart app, a read-only user**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER charts WITH PASSWORD 'Chart-app-secret-11' ROLE read;
```

```sql
CREATE TOKEN chart_app FOR USER charts EXPIRES IN 90 DAYS;
SHOW TOKENS;
```

Result:

`CREATE TOKEN chart_app FOR USER charts EXPIRES IN 90 DAYS`

| name (STRING) | user (STRING) | token (STRING) | expires (TIMESTAMP) |
|---|---|---|---|
| chart_app | charts | kdbt_ldRrx-53itbKjFzTlM6dgh3aJ_ypgE0El9E_LnN8pNM | 2027-01-22T06:18:44.626Z |

(1 row)

```text
token 'chart_app' for user 'charts' created: copy it now, it is shown only this once. Send it as Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

`SHOW TOKENS`

| name (STRING) | user (STRING) | prefix (STRING) | created (TIMESTAMP) | expires (TIMESTAMP) | expired (BOOL) | created_by (STRING) | last_used (TIMESTAMP) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| chart_app | charts | kdbt_ldRr... | 2026-10-24T06:18:44.630Z | 2027-01-22T06:18:44.626Z | false | NULL | NULL |

(1 row)

## CREATE TOKEN

Syntax:

```sql
CREATE TOKEN name [FOR USER user] [EXPIRES IN n DAYS]
```

Makes a new token and shows its secret **once**.

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | letters, digits, `_` and `-`, 1 to 63 characters; unique (case does not matter). Say which app uses it. |
| `FOR USER user` | the user it acts as. Without it: the user who runs the statement. |
| `EXPIRES IN n DAYS` | it stops working after that many days (1 to 99999). Without it: never. |

- **Returns:** one row `name`, `user`, `token`, `expires`. The `token` looks like `kdbt_` and 43 more letters. Copy it now: KarelaDB keeps only its SHA-256, so nobody can show it again.
- **Notes:**
  - Any user may make a token for **themselves**. A token for another user needs `ROLE admin`.
  - The app sends it as `Authorization: Bearer kdbt_...` on the HTTP API (`/exec`, `/write`, `/imp`, `/api/...`). It is not a password for the PostgreSQL port; use the user's password there.
  - It can do exactly what its user can do, including [table rights](table-rights.md), the user's [time limit](users-and-roles.md#statement-timeout) and [rate limit](protection.md#rate-limits). For a read-only app, make a user with `ROLE read` and a token for it.
  - A new password for the user does **not** end the user's tokens (apps keep working). `DROP USER` removes the user's tokens.
  - The session that runs it needs a user: with the server's `--token` or in `kareladb sql`, write `FOR USER`.

**Example: Two apps, two tokens for one user**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER loader WITH PASSWORD 'Loader-secret-long-5' ROLE write;
```

```sql
CREATE TOKEN price_feed FOR USER loader;
CREATE TOKEN backfill FOR USER loader EXPIRES IN 7 DAYS;
```

Result:

`CREATE TOKEN price_feed FOR USER loader`

| name (STRING) | user (STRING) | token (STRING) | expires (TIMESTAMP) |
|---|---|---|---|
| price_feed | loader | kdbt_PZF-2vtd9GEZZ2lsSFMgqYWFOhHX_wc8qCQAoauhLww | NULL |

(1 row)

```text
token 'price_feed' for user 'loader' created: copy it now, it is shown only this once. Send it as Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

`CREATE TOKEN backfill FOR USER loader EXPIRES IN 7 DAYS`

| name (STRING) | user (STRING) | token (STRING) | expires (TIMESTAMP) |
|---|---|---|---|
| backfill | loader | kdbt_t8yav6WSkclo9teXXdQkqF9Q-xxYDctXFGUsQu-87es | 2026-10-31T06:18:44.715Z |

(1 row)

```text
token 'backfill' for user 'loader' created: copy it now, it is shown only this once. Send it as Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

**Example: The name is taken** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE TOKEN price_feed FOR USER admin;
```

```sql
CREATE TOKEN price_feed FOR USER admin;
```

Result:

Error: `token 'price_feed' already exists`

**Example: A token acts as a user** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
```

```sql
CREATE TOKEN price_feed;
```

Result:

Error: `CREATE TOKEN needs FOR USER <name> here: this session has no user (the server's --token, or a local tool), and a token always acts as one user`

## DROP TOKEN

Syntax:

```sql
DROP TOKEN [IF EXISTS] name
```

Revokes a token. Every request with it gets `401` from then on: `the API token is wrong, has expired or was dropped (SHOW TOKENS)`.

- **Returns:** `token 'name' dropped: it stops working at once`.
- **Notes:** a user may drop their own tokens; other users' tokens need `ROLE admin`.

**Example**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE TOKEN price_feed FOR USER admin;
```

```sql
DROP TOKEN price_feed;
DROP TOKEN IF EXISTS price_feed;
```

Result:

`DROP TOKEN price_feed`

```text
token 'price_feed' dropped: it stops working at once
```

`DROP TOKEN IF EXISTS price_feed`

```text
token 'price_feed' does not exist
```

## SHOW TOKENS

Syntax:

```sql
SHOW TOKENS
```

Lists the tokens. Never the secrets: only the first letters, so you can tell which one an app has.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name`, `user` | the token and the user it acts as |
| `prefix` | its first letters, like `kdbt_Ab3x...` |
| `created`, `expires` | when it was made; when it stops (`NULL` = never) |
| `expired` | `true` once `expires` has passed |
| `created_by` | who made it (`NULL`: the `--token` or a local tool) |
| `last_used` | its last request since the server started (`NULL`: none yet) |

- **Notes:** an admin sees every token; other users see their own. The web console lists them on the **Settings** page, where you can make and remove them too.

**Example**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE TOKEN price_feed FOR USER admin EXPIRES IN 30 DAYS;
```

```sql
SHOW TOKENS;
```

Result:

| name (STRING) | user (STRING) | prefix (STRING) | created (TIMESTAMP) | expires (TIMESTAMP) | expired (BOOL) | created_by (STRING) | last_used (TIMESTAMP) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| price_feed | admin | kdbt_JI05... | 2026-10-24T06:18:44.862Z | 2026-11-23T06:18:44.857Z | false | NULL | NULL |

(1 row)

<a id="kept"></a>

## Where tokens and logins are kept

Both live in the hidden `_system` database of the data folder, as **hashes only**:

| Table | Holds |
|---|---|
| `api_tokens` | name, user, the SHA-256 of the secret, its first letters, times |
| `login_sessions` | the SHA-256 of each login token of `POST /api/login` and the console, its user and when it ends |

So a server restart logs nobody out, and apps with a token go on. A login still ends after 12 hours, at logout, or when the user gets a new password or is dropped. An older KarelaDB program does not know these tables: there, tokens do not work and everyone logs in again.


---

<!-- docs/two-factor-login.md -->

# Two-factor login (TOTP)

> A database user can log in to the console and POST /api/login with a password and a 6-digit code from an authenticator app.

- Category: Users & security
- Keywords: two-factor, 2FA, TOTP, step-up, step\_up\_actions, step\_up\_minutes, X-KDB-TOTP, /api/step-up, step\_up\_required, one-time code, authenticator app, Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, otpauth, ENABLE TOTP, DISABLE TOTP, code, lost phone, reset-2fa, password policy, password rules, 12 characters
- See also: [Users and roles](users-and-roles.md), [Logins, tokens and roles over HTTP](http-login.md), [Keeping kareladb serve safe](server-security.md), [kareladb user](cli-users.md), [Audit log](audit-log.md)

With two-factor login, a stolen password is not enough: the login also needs the 6-digit code that an authenticator app on the phone shows (it changes every 30 seconds, RFC 6238).

Use it for **people** (admins in the web console). Programs keep a user without two-factor login: HTTP Basic and the PostgreSQL port cannot ask for a code, so they refuse a two-factor user.

<a id="enable-totp"></a>

## ALTER USER ... ENABLE TOTP

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER USER <name> ENABLE TOTP
ALTER USER <name> DISABLE TOTP
```

Makes a new secret for the user and turns two-factor login on. The answer has an `otpauth://` URI and the secret: put one of them into the authenticator app **now**. It is shown only this once.

- **Returns:** one row `user`, `otpauth_uri`, `secret`, and the message `two-factor login is on for user 'boss': ...`.
- **Notes:**
  - Users may do it for themselves; admins for everyone. `DISABLE TOTP` turns it off.
  - The console and `POST /api/login` then ask for the code after a right password: `{"error":"enter the 6-digit code from your authenticator app","totp":true}`. Send it as `"code"` with the password.
  - A code works once, 30 seconds before or after its time too. Wrong codes count as failed logins (after 5 the address must wait) and are in the [audit log](audit-log.md).
  - Older KarelaDB programs refuse a data folder with two-factor users.

**Example: Turn two-factor login on for an admin**

```sql
CREATE USER boss WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
ALTER USER boss ENABLE TOTP;
```

Result:

`CREATE USER boss WITH PASSWORD '***' ROLE admin`

```text
user 'boss' created with role admin
```

`ALTER USER boss ENABLE TOTP`

| user (STRING) | otpauth_uri (STRING) | secret (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| boss | otpauth://totp/KarelaDB:boss?secret=VXT5WJTFQSUXCJDJFURU5NFQ3DJDGCK6&issuer=KarelaDB&algorithm=SHA1&digits=6&period=30 | VXT5WJTFQSUXCJDJFURU5NFQ3DJDGCK6 |

(1 row)

```text
two-factor login is on for user 'boss': add the otpauth URI (or the secret) to an authenticator app now; it is shown only once
```

<a id="kareladb-user-reset-2fa"></a>

## kareladb user reset-2fa

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb user reset-2fa <name> [--data-dir <folder>]
```

Turns two-factor login off for a user who lost the phone, while `kareladb serve` is stopped. The user logs in with the password only until `ALTER USER <name> ENABLE TOTP` is run again.

- **Returns:** `two-factor login is off for user 'boss'; ...`, or `user 'boss' has no two-factor login; nothing to do`.
- **Notes:** the change is written to the audit log of the data folder.

**Command line: A user without two-factor login: nothing to do**

```bash
kareladb user add admin --role admin
> Long-Admin-Passw0rd
> Long-Admin-Passw0rd
kareladb user reset-2fa admin
```

Output:

`> kareladb user add admin --role admin`

```text
user 'admin' added with role admin in ./kdb-data
```

`> kareladb user reset-2fa admin`

```text
user 'admin' has no two-factor login; nothing to do
```

<a id="password-policy"></a>

## Password policy

Syntax:

```sql
at least 12 characters, at most 1024 bytes, not the user name
```

KarelaDB refuses a new password of a database user that is too short or is the user name. Characters are counted, not bytes (12 letters of any language, such as Nepali, are fine). Passwords set before this rule keep working.

**Example: A too short password is refused** (shows an error)

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'ktm-2026' ROLE admin;
```

Result:

Error: `the password is too short: use at least 12 characters (a password manager can make a long random one)`

<a id="token-rotation"></a>

## Session tokens

Every login gets a new random token. When the login request still carries an old login (the `kdb_login` cookie or a Bearer token), that old login ends: a token somebody planted before the login is worth nothing afterwards.

<a id="step-up"></a>

## Step-up codes for dangerous actions

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb.conf:    "step_up_actions": "on", "step_up_minutes": 5
environment: KARELADB_STEP_UP_ACTIONS=on  KARELADB_STEP_UP_MINUTES=5
```

A console left open is a risk: anyone at that desk could drop a table. With `step_up_actions` on, a few dangerous actions also need a two-factor code typed in the last `step_up_minutes` (5 by default). It is off by default.

| Needs a fresh code | |
|---|---|
| SQL | `DROP TABLE`, `DROP DATABASE`, `CREATE USER`, `ALTER USER`, `DROP USER`, `GRANT`, `REVOKE`, `ALTER SYSTEM` |
| HTTP | `POST /api/settings`, `DELETE /api/databases/<name>` |

- **How to give the code:** the console shows a code box by itself and then runs the action again. Programs send the header `X-KDB-TOTP: 123456` with the request, or call `POST /api/step-up` with `{"code": "123456"}` once; the code then counts for that login for `step_up_minutes`.
- **Without a code:** the answer is 403 with `"code": "step_up_required"`, the action, and `"totp": true`.
- **A login with a code counts too:** right after logging in, the first dangerous action needs no second code.
- **Users without two-factor login** are refused with `"totp": false` and a message to enrol: `ALTER USER <name> ENABLE TOTP`. Enrolling yourself never needs a code.
- **Not asked:** the server's access token (`--token`) and a local server without logins have no user to ask.
- **Changing it:** `POST /api/settings` with `{"step_up_actions": "on"}` or `{"step_up_minutes": 10}` saves to kareladb.conf and works at once. `step_up_minutes` also takes a time like `"30s"`.
- **Not covered yet:** the PostgreSQL port. A user with two-factor login cannot log in there at all; keep other users off it, or give them no admin role, while step-up matters.

```text
POST /exec   DROP TABLE trades
-> 403 {"error":"DROP TABLE needs a fresh two-factor code: send it as the header X-KDB-TOTP, or once with
        POST /api/step-up {\"code\": \"123456\"} (good for 5 minutes)","code":"step_up_required",
        "action":"DROP TABLE","totp":true,"step_up_minutes":5}
```
