<!-- docs/server-security.md -->

# Keeping kareladb serve safe

> Keep the server on 127.0.0.1, use users or a token, put HTTPS in front, and pick strong passwords.

- Category: Users & security
- Keywords: security, safe, secure, KARELADB\_TOKEN, Docker, internet, vps, firewall, --bind, --token, bind address, 0.0.0.0, 127.0.0.1, localhost, access token, login, log in, logout, HTTP Basic, Bearer, cookie, kdb\_login, kdb\_auth, X-KDB-CSRF, HTTPS, TLS, SSL, certificate, reverse proxy, Caddy, nginx, SSH tunnel, X-Forwarded-Proto, failed logins, too many failed logins, 429, 401, 403, cross-site, CSRF, DNS rebinding, password rules, SCRAM, checklist
- See also: [Users and roles](users-and-roles.md), [Security functions](functions-security.md), [kareladb serve](cli-serve.md), [kareladb user](cli-users.md), [Logins, tokens and roles over HTTP](http-login.md), [PostgreSQL protocol (port 8832)](postgres-protocol.md), [Backup, check, repair and restore](backup-and-safety.md)

`kareladb serve` gives full access to your data over the network: the HTTP API, the web console and the PostgreSQL port. This page says how to keep strangers out.

The short rules:

1. Keep the default `--bind 127.0.0.1`. Then only programs on the same computer can connect.
2. Create **users** with long passwords (see [Users and roles](users-and-roles.md)). Then every request needs a login.
3. For access from other computers, turn on [TLS](tls.md) (`--tls-cert`: https and `sslmode=require`), or put a web server with HTTPS in front, or use an SSH tunnel.
4. Keep the data folder and the backups private: whoever can read them can read everything, without a login.

| Server | Login needed? |
|---|---|
| `--bind 127.0.0.1` (default), no `--token`, no users | **No.** Only programs on this computer can connect. |
| the data folder has users | **Yes**, for every request except `/health`, `POST /api/login` and the console page itself |
| started with `--token <secret>` | **Yes.** The token works like an admin. With users too, both work. |
| `--bind 0.0.0.0` (or any address that is not `127.x`) with no token and no users | **Refused:** `kareladb serve` does not start |

**HTTP: Is a login needed on this server?**

```http
GET /health
```

Response:

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{
  "status": "ok",
  "version": "0.2.0-dev",
  "product": "KarelaDB",
  "server_time_ms": 1792822761317,
  "auth_required": false,
  "login": false,
  "tls": false,
  "ready": true,
  "standby": false,
  "role": "leader"
}
```

<a id="bind"></a>

## --bind

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb serve [--bind 127.0.0.1 | --bind <address>] ...
```

The network address the server listens on. It is used for the HTTP port and the PostgreSQL port.

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `127.0.0.1` | the default. Only programs on the same computer can connect. |
| `0.0.0.0` | every network card: other computers can connect too |
| one address, like `192.168.1.20` | only that network card |

- **Returns:** nothing; the start-up lines show the console address.
- **Notes:**
  - Any address that does not start with `127.` needs users or `--token`, or `kareladb serve` refuses to start. (`localhost` counts as local.)
  - Your app's backend on the same VPS reaches KarelaDB on `127.0.0.1`. You almost never need `0.0.0.0`.
  - The [Docker image](install-packages.md#docker) must listen on `0.0.0.0`, because a published port cannot reach the container's own `127.0.0.1`. So it refuses to start without `KARELADB_TOKEN` (`-e KARELADB_TOKEN=<token>`). Publish the port only to where it is needed, for example `-p 127.0.0.1:9900:9900`.
  - Also close ports 9900 (HTTP) and 8832 (PostgreSQL) in the firewall. Open only SSH, 80 and 443.
  - Without a login, KarelaDB still refuses requests that a browser marks as coming from another web site, and requests whose `Host` is not `localhost` or `127.x` (a trick called DNS rebinding). So a bad web page open in your browser can not reach your local server.

**Command line: 0.0.0.0 without users and without a token is refused** (shows an error)

```bash
kareladb serve --bind 0.0.0.0
```

Output:

```text
cold store 'archive': folder ./cold-archive
error: --bind 0.0.0.0 without --token and without users would let anyone who can reach this computer
read, change and delete every database. Do one of these first:
  1. create an admin user:   kareladb user add <name> --role admin
  2. or start with a secret:  --token <long random text>
  3. or keep --bind 127.0.0.1 and put a web server with HTTPS in front of KarelaDB
See docs/tutorial/16-users-passwords-security.md
```

exit code 1

**HTTP: A request from another web site is refused**

```http
GET /exec?query=SELECT%201
Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site
```

Response:

HTTP 403 (application/json)

```text
{"error": "cross-site requests are not allowed"}
```

**HTTP: A request sent by a page of another web site is refused**

```http
GET /exec?query=SELECT%201
Origin: http://evil.example.com
```

Response:

HTTP 403 (application/json)

```text
{"error": "cross-origin requests are not allowed"}
```

<a id="token"></a>

## --token

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb serve --token <long random text>
```

A secret that every request must send, as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. It gives **full** rights (like an admin on every database).

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `<token>` | text | the secret. Use 32 or more random characters, for example from `SELECT random_token()`. |

- **Returns:** nothing; the start-up line `access` says `token required`.
- **Notes:**
  - The token is **one** secret for everybody. Users are better: each program gets its own password and only the role it needs, and you can remove one user without changing the others.
  - With users **and** a token, both work. PostgreSQL clients can use the token as the password.
  - Other people on the same computer can see command lines (`ps`, Task Manager). Start the server from a file only you can read (for example a systemd unit), or use users.
  - The web console asks for the token and the server keeps it in an `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict` cookie (`kdb_auth`), so page scripts cannot read it. Changes sent with that cookie also need the `X-KDB-CSRF` header ([CSRF](http-login.md#csrf)); the console sends it by itself.

**Example: Make a strong token or password**

```sql
SELECT random_token() AS token_for_kdb_serve, random_token(24) AS password_for_a_program;
```

Result:

| token_for_kdb_serve (STRING) | password_for_a_program (STRING) |
|---|---|
| deuwByspuEItGPl1w7cq3RdfI30aIoN7CAykocwafVw | L2HuHi1_9T2RCbI6ySbVaBpgR0839UFB |

(1 row)

**Command line: A server with a token**

```bash
kareladb serve --token 3kD9vQx7LmN2pR8sT4wY6zA1bC5eF0gH
```

Output:

```text
cold store 'archive': folder ./cold-archive
KarelaDB 0.2.0-dev
  console   http://127.0.0.1:9900
  data      ./kdb-data (from KDB_DATA_DIR; one folder per database)
  default   default (used when a request names no database)
  backups   ./kdb-data/_backups/<database name> (from default)
  access    token required
  capacity  32 HTTP threads (default), 500 PostgreSQL connections (default), lock wait 5 s (default)
  lanes     reads using 100 ms of CPU (three times in a row) wait for one of 16 heavy slots, at most 16 HTTP in line (--lanes on)
  reads     32 reads run at once (the CPUs, at least 2; follows the CPU limit), the rest wait in line (--read-slots)
  commits   synced to disk before they are confirmed (--sync-commits always)
  time zone Asia/Katmandu (the computer's); also timers and backup schedules
  readers   read while a long trigger or CALL writes (--reader-yield on); idle open transaction rolled back after 30 s (default)
  memory    26.95 GB for the whole process (85% of the machine's memory); table data 512.0 MB of it (--memory)
  cpu       32 CPUs (the machine's); 16 query threads (half of the CPUs, follows the limit), limits checked every 10 s
  limits    statement timeout 1 min, result memory 1.00 GB, 5000000 groups, 32 statements per user
  safety    writes allowed; DROP TABLE kept 7 days (UNDROP TABLE); audit log on (SHOW AUDIT)
  logs      slow queries >= 1000 ms to ./kdb-data/_logs/slow_queries.jsonl; pg_stat_statements on; metrics at /metrics
  recovery  the default database is created when it is first used

Press Ctrl+C to stop.
```

<a id="logins"></a>

## Users and logins

Syntax:

```sql
HTTP Basic:   Authorization: Basic base64(user:password)
Log in once:  POST /api/login  {"user": "...", "password": "..."}   ->  token
Then:         Authorization: Bearer <token>     (or the kdb_login cookie in a browser)
Log out:      POST /api/logout
```

When the data folder has users, every request needs a login. Create users with [CREATE USER](users-and-roles.md#create-user) or [kareladb user add](cli-users.md). The details of each route are in [HTTP login](http-login.md).

| Way | Used by | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **HTTP Basic** (user and password on each request) | scripts, `curl -u` | KarelaDB remembers a good password for 10 minutes, so it is not slow |
| **`POST /api/login`**, then `Authorization: Bearer <token>` | apps | the token is random (256 bits); KarelaDB keeps only its SHA-256, in memory |
| **Cookie** `kdb_login` | the web console | `HttpOnly` (page scripts can not read it) and `SameSite=Strict` (other sites can not use it). A change also needs the `X-KDB-CSRF` header ([CSRF](http-login.md#csrf)). |
| **SCRAM-SHA-256** | PostgreSQL drivers on port 8832 | the password never crosses the network |

- **Returns:** a wrong login gets HTTP 401 `{"error":"wrong user name or password","login":true}`. A statement the user may not run gets HTTP 403 (see [roles](users-and-roles.md#roles)).
- **Notes:**
  - A login ends after **12 hours**, at log out, when the server restarts, and when the user's password changes or the user is dropped.
  - **Failed logins:** after 5 failures for one user from one address (or 20 from one address for any users), that address must wait: 1 second, then 2, 4, 8, ... up to 15 minutes. Meanwhile the answer is HTTP 429 `too many failed logins; try again in 1 s`. A good login ends the wait for that user.
  - Every failed login is written to the server's output with the user name and the address, never the password: `login failed: user 'admin' from 127.0.0.1 (wrong password; 5 failures in a row); next try allowed in 1 s`.
  - The answer for an unknown user takes as long as for a wrong password, so nobody can find out which names exist.
  - Behind a reverse proxy every request comes from `127.0.0.1`, so the waiting is shared by everyone who tries the same user name.
  - `kareladb sql` and `kareladb shell` never ask for a login. They open the files directly.
  - Users belong to a data folder. A server started with one database folder by its path (`kareladb serve D:\kdb\market`) has no users; use `--data-dir`.

**Command line: With a user, the server asks for a login**

```bash
kareladb user add admin --role admin
> Long-Admin-Passw0rd
> Long-Admin-Passw0rd
kareladb serve
```

Output:

`> kareladb user add admin --role admin`

```text
user 'admin' added with role admin in ./kdb-data
```

`> kareladb serve`

```text
cold store 'archive': folder ./cold-archive
KarelaDB 0.2.0-dev
  console   http://127.0.0.1:9900
  data      ./kdb-data (from KDB_DATA_DIR; one folder per database)
  default   default (used when a request names no database)
  backups   ./kdb-data/_backups/<database name> (from default)
  access    login required (1 user)
  capacity  32 HTTP threads (default), 500 PostgreSQL connections (default), lock wait 5 s (default)
  lanes     reads using 100 ms of CPU (three times in a row) wait for one of 16 heavy slots, at most 16 HTTP in line (--lanes on)
  reads     32 reads run at once (the CPUs, at least 2; follows the CPU limit), the rest wait in line (--read-slots)
  commits   synced to disk before they are confirmed (--sync-commits always)
  time zone Asia/Katmandu (the computer's); also timers and backup schedules
  readers   read while a long trigger or CALL writes (--reader-yield on); idle open transaction rolled back after 30 s (default)
  memory    26.95 GB for the whole process (85% of the machine's memory); table data 512.0 MB of it (--memory)
  cpu       32 CPUs (the machine's); 16 query threads (half of the CPUs, follows the limit), limits checked every 10 s
  limits    statement timeout 1 min, result memory 1.00 GB, 5000000 groups, 32 statements per user
  safety    writes allowed; DROP TABLE kept 7 days (UNDROP TABLE); audit log on (SHOW AUDIT)
  logs      slow queries >= 1000 ms to ./kdb-data/_logs/slow_queries.jsonl; pg_stat_statements on; metrics at /metrics
  recovery  the default database is created when it is first used

Press Ctrl+C to stop.
```

**HTTP: A server without users has nothing to log in to**

```http
POST /api/login
Content-Type: application/json

{"user": "admin", "password": "Long-Admin-Passw0rd"}
```

Response:

HTTP 400 (application/json)

```text
{
  "error": "this server has no users yet; create one with CREATE USER <name> WITH PASSWORD '...' ROLE admin"
}
```

<a id="https"></a>

## HTTPS in front

Syntax:

```sql
browser  --HTTPS-->  Caddy or nginx (port 443)  --HTTP-->  kareladb serve on 127.0.0.1:9900
```

Over plain HTTP, anyone on the network path can read passwords and tokens. When people or programs on **other** computers must reach KarelaDB, either turn on KarelaDB's own [TLS](tls.md), or put a web server with HTTPS (a **reverse proxy**) in front and keep KarelaDB on `127.0.0.1`. A proxy also gets free certificates by itself and renews them.

- **Returns:** not a KarelaDB setting.
- **Notes:**
  - Caddy gets a free certificate by itself (see the first block below). With nginx, also send `X-Forwarded-Proto` (second block).
  - When the proxy sends `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`, KarelaDB marks its login cookie `Secure` (only sent over HTTPS).
  - KarelaDB still asks for the login behind the proxy. Create users first.
  - Even simpler for yourself: do not open the console to the internet at all. Use an **SSH tunnel** from your PC: `ssh -L 9900:127.0.0.1:9900 you@your-vps`, then open `http://127.0.0.1:9900` on your PC.
  - A proxy does not cover the PostgreSQL port. Turn on KarelaDB's [TLS](tls.md) for it (`sslmode=require`), or reach it through an SSH tunnel.

Caddy, file `/etc/caddy/Caddyfile`:

```text
kdb.example.com {
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:9900
}
```

nginx, inside the `server { listen 443 ssl; ... }` block:

```text
location / {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:9900;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
}
```

<a id="password-rules"></a>

## Password rules

Syntax:

```sql
at least 12 characters, not the user name, at most 1024 bytes;  long and random is best
```

What KarelaDB needs from the password of a database user, and what is wise.

| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| KarelaDB refuses | fewer than 12 characters, the user name itself, or more than 1024 bytes |
| Wise for people | 16 or more characters; a few random words are easy to remember. Admins: also [two-factor login](two-factor-login.md) |
| Wise for programs | 20 or more random characters from a password manager or `random_token(24)`; programs keep them in their settings |
| Never | the same password as your email or bank; a password on the command line; a password in a web page's JavaScript |

- **Returns:** a too short password gets `the password is too short: use at least 12 characters (a password manager can make a long random one)`. Passwords set before this rule keep working.
- **Notes:**
  - KarelaDB keeps two things per user: a PBKDF2-SHA-256 hash with 600,000 rounds (slow to guess), and a SCRAM-SHA-256 secret with only 4,096 rounds (the PostgreSQL default, faster to guess). This is why database users should have **long random** passwords.
  - `kareladb user add` reads the password from a prompt or a pipe (`echo "the password" | kareladb user add report --role read`), never from the command line.
  - SQL text with `PASSWORD '...'` may end up in your own scripts and logs. The web console's history and KarelaDB's statement echo show `PASSWORD '***'`.
  - The passwords of **your app's** users are a different matter: store them with [password_hash](functions-security.md#password-hash).

**Example: A too short password is refused** (shows an error)

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'ktm2026' ROLE admin;
```

Result:

Error: `the password is too short: use at least 12 characters (a password manager can make a long random one)`

<a id="checklist"></a>

## Checklist

Syntax:

```sql
bind 127.0.0.1  +  users  +  HTTPS or SSH tunnel  +  firewall  +  private data and backups
```

A small Linux VPS with your app and KarelaDB on the same machine. [Chapter 16](../tutorial/16-users-passwords-security.md) shows each step with commands.

| Check | Why |
|---|---|
| KarelaDB runs as its own system user; data and backups are `chmod 700` (on Linux and macOS KarelaDB makes new files `0600` and new folders `0700` itself; folders made by an older version keep their rights, so `chmod -R go-rwx` them once) | a file copy needs no login |
| `--bind 127.0.0.1` (the default); ports 9900 and 8832 closed in the firewall | strangers can not even connect |
| an `admin` user with a long random password; each app has its own user with the smallest role | one leaked password does not open everything |
| [TLS](tls.md), HTTPS (Caddy or nginx) or an SSH tunnel for the console and the PostgreSQL port | passwords are not sent in plain text |
| every `kareladb` program updated before the first user was created | old versions do not know users and would serve without a login |
| app passwords stored with `password_hash`; session tokens random and stored as `sha256` | a stolen table does not give the passwords |
| nightly backup copied to another place, restore tested | backups hold the password hashes: keep them private too |
| server output checked for `login failed` now and then | see who tries to guess |

- **Returns:** not a statement.
- **Notes:** rights are per database; [table rights](table-rights.md) change them for single tables (no column or row rights). Logins are kept in the data folder (hashes only), so a restart logs nobody out. Give each app its own [API token](api-tokens.md). More protection (timeouts, audit log, scheduled backups): [protection](protection.md).

<!-- docs/tls.md -->

# TLS (https and sslmode=require)

> Encrypt both ports with one certificate - https:// for the HTTP API and the console, sslmode=require for PostgreSQL clients.

- Category: Users & security
- Keywords: TLS, SSL, https, certificate, cert, key, PEM, self-signed, --tls-cert, --tls-key, --tls-required, KARELADB\_TLS\_CERT, KARELADB\_TLS\_KEY, KARELADB\_TLS\_REQUIRED, tls\_cert, tls\_key, sslmode, require, verify-full, sslrootcert, sslnegotiation, direct, encryption, 28000, Secure cookie, curl -k, Lets Encrypt, openssl
- See also: [Keeping kareladb serve safe](server-security.md), [PostgreSQL protocol (port 8832)](postgres-protocol.md), [kareladb serve](cli-serve.md), [Logins, tokens and roles over HTTP](http-login.md), [API tokens](api-tokens.md)

With TLS on, everything between a client and KarelaDB is encrypted: passwords, tokens and data. One certificate serves **both** ports.

| Port | Clients connect with |
|---|---|
| HTTP (9900) | `https://host:9900` (browsers, `curl`, HTTP libraries) |
| PostgreSQL (8832) | `sslmode=require` (or `verify-full`), also `sslnegotiation=direct` of PostgreSQL 17 |

- TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only. It needs a `kareladb` built with OpenSSL: `kareladb --version` shows `tls: OpenSSL ...` (the Docker image and the packages have it).
- Without TLS, keep KarelaDB on `127.0.0.1` and put a web server with HTTPS in front, or use an SSH tunnel ([server security](server-security.md#https)).

<a id="turn-on"></a>

## Turn it on

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb serve --tls-cert cert.pem --tls-key key.pem [--tls-required on|off]
kareladb serve --tls-cert auto
kareladb.conf:  "tls_cert": "/data/cert.pem", "tls_key": "/data/key.pem"
env:       KARELADB_TLS_CERT=/data/cert.pem  KARELADB_TLS_KEY=/data/key.pem  KARELADB_TLS_REQUIRED=on
```

| Setting | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `--tls-cert FILE` | the certificate in PEM: the server's first, then the chain | off |
| `--tls-key FILE` | its private key in PEM (without a passphrase) | - |
| `--tls-cert auto` | KarelaDB makes a **self-signed** certificate once, in `<data folder>/_tls/`, and keeps using it | - |
| `--tls-required on\|off` | `on`: plain connections are refused, except from this computer (`127.x`) | `on` |

- A flag wins, then `kareladb.conf`, then the environment. They are read when the server starts; after renewing a certificate, restart the server.
- The start-up lines say what is used: `console https://...`, `postgres ... (TLS: sslmode=require ...)` and a `tls` line with the file.
- A wrong file stops the server with the reason, for example `a certificate needs its key too` or `the TLS key does not belong to the certificate`.
- Plain connections from `127.x` still work with `--tls-required on`, so a health check or a tool on the same computer needs no certificate.

```bash
kareladb serve --data-dir kdb-data --bind 0.0.0.0 --token "long-random-secret-1" --tls-cert auto
```

<a id="auto"></a>

## A self-signed certificate (auto)

`--tls-cert auto` makes `kdb-cert.pem` and `kdb-key.pem` in `<data folder>/_tls/` the first time (EC P-256, valid 10 years, for `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and the `--bind` address), and uses the same pair after every restart.

- The data is encrypted, but a client can not tell by itself that it talks to **your** server. Tell it which certificate to trust:
  - `curl --cacert kdb-data/_tls/kdb-cert.pem https://localhost:9900/health`
  - `psql "host=localhost port=8832 sslmode=verify-full sslrootcert=kdb-data/_tls/kdb-cert.pem ..."`
- `sslmode=require` and `curl -k` encrypt without checking the certificate.
- A browser warns once for a self-signed certificate. For people on the internet, use a real certificate (Let's Encrypt, or your company's) with `--tls-cert` and `--tls-key`.
- In Docker: `-e KARELADB_TLS_CERT=auto`. The pair is kept in the `/data` volume, so it survives a rebuild.

<a id="clients"></a>

## What changes for clients

| Client | Before | With TLS |
|---|---|---|
| browser, console | `http://host:9900` | `https://host:9900` |
| `curl` | `curl http://...` | `curl https://...` (`-k` or `--cacert` for self-signed) |
| psql, DBeaver, drivers | `sslmode=disable` | `sslmode=require`, or `verify-full` with the certificate |
| plain `http://` from another computer | answered | `400`: `This KarelaDB server speaks HTTPS only: use https:// ...` |
| plain PostgreSQL from another computer | answered | SQLSTATE `28000`: `this server requires TLS: connect with sslmode=require` |

- Over https the login cookie is marked `Secure` (the browser sends it only over https). `GET /health` says `"tls": true` for a request that came over TLS.
- With `--tls-required off`, one port takes both: a client that starts with TLS gets TLS, a plain one gets plain.
- A PostgreSQL client that sends more bytes right after its SSL request, before the handshake, is disconnected (that is how a man in the middle could slip commands in; CVE-2021-23214 in PostgreSQL).

<a id="docker"></a>

## Docker

Inside a container KarelaDB must listen on all addresses (`--bind 0.0.0.0`), so the published ports decide who can reach it:

| `docker run` | Reachable from |
|---|---|
| `-p 9900:9900 -p 8832:8832` | every computer that can reach this one |
| `-p 127.0.0.1:9900:9900 -p 127.0.0.1:8832:8832` | this computer only |

Through Docker's port mapping, clients reach KarelaDB from Docker's own address, not from `127.x`: with TLS on, they must use TLS. The image's health check runs inside the container on `127.0.0.1`, so it keeps working.

<!-- docs/encryption.md -->

# Encryption at rest

> CREATE DATABASE x WITH (encryption = on) - every file, log record and backup of it is encrypted; without the master key a copied disk shows nothing.

- Category: Users & security
- Keywords: encryption, encrypted, encryption at rest, at rest, encrypt, AES, AES-256, AES-256-GCM, GCM, ChaCha20, ChaCha20-Poly1305, master key, data key, key file, KARELADB\_MASTER\_KEY, KARELADB\_MASTER\_KEY\_FILE, KARELADB\_MASTER\_KEY\_PREVIOUS, KARELADB\_MASTER\_KEY\_PREVIOUS\_FILE, \_encryption.key, kareladb key, key rotation, rotate key, WITH (encryption , TDE, stolen disk, snapshot
- See also: [Databases and the data folder](databases.md), [TLS (https and sslmode=require)](tls.md), [Keeping kareladb serve safe](server-security.md), [Backup, check, repair and restore](backup-and-safety.md), [kareladb info, check, repair, dump-file](cli-maintenance.md)

An **encrypted database** keeps every file on disk encrypted: the tables, the log, the manifests and its backups. Someone who copies the disk, a VPS snapshot or a backup sees only random bytes. Only a KarelaDB server that has the **master key** can read it.

It is **off by default**. You choose it for each database when you create it.

| | Plain database | Encrypted database |
|---|---|---|
| Files on disk | readable with a hex editor | random bytes |
| Backups | readable | encrypted too, and useless without the master key |
| Needs | nothing | the master key when the server starts |
| Queries | - | the same SQL, the same results |
| Speed | - | see [speed](#speed) |

Not covered: someone logged in to the running server as the `kareladb` system user or as root can read the key and the memory. [Users and roles](users-and-roles.md) and [TLS](tls.md) protect the running server; encryption at rest protects the disk.

<a id="turn-on"></a>

## Turn it on

1. Make a master key once, and keep it **outside** the data folder:

```bash
kareladb key new > /etc/kareladb/master.key        # 64 hex characters
chmod 600 /etc/kareladb/master.key
```

2. Give it to the server, in one of these ways:

Syntax:

```sql
KARELADB_MASTER_KEY=<64 hex characters, or base64 of 32 bytes>
KARELADB_MASTER_KEY_FILE=<a file holding the key as text, or 32 raw bytes>
```

3. Create the database encrypted:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE payroll WITH (encryption = on);
USE payroll;
CREATE TABLE salaries (name STRING, amount DECIMAL(2));
```

- **Returns:** `database 'payroll' created encrypted`.
- `WITH (encryption = on, pg_compat = on)` gives both options together ([CREATE DATABASE](databases.md#create-database)).
- Without a master key, `CREATE DATABASE ... WITH (encryption = on)` fails with `encryption = on needs a master key` and makes nothing.
- A database is encrypted or plain for its whole life. `ALTER DATABASE` cannot switch it, and `CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS ... WITH (encryption = on)` leaves a plain database that exists plain. To encrypt data you have, create an encrypted database and copy the tables into it (`INSERT INTO new_db.t SELECT * FROM old_db.t`).
- `GET /api/databases` shows `"encrypted": true` for each encrypted database.

In Docker, pass the key file as a secret and point `KARELADB_MASTER_KEY_FILE` at it, for example `-v /etc/kareladb/master.key:/run/secrets/kdb_master_key:ro -e KARELADB_MASTER_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/kdb_master_key`. Never put it in the data volume.

<a id="keys"></a>

## Keys

There are two keys, so that changing the master key never rewrites your data:

| Key | What it is | Where it is |
|---|---|---|
| master key | 256 bits you give the server | `KARELADB_MASTER_KEY` or `KARELADB_MASTER_KEY_FILE`, never in the data folder |
| data key | 256 random bits, one per database | `<database>/_encryption.key`, **wrapped** (encrypted) by the master key |

- The server refuses to start when `KARELADB_MASTER_KEY_FILE` is inside the data folder: a copy of the folder would hold the key too.
- An encrypted database opened without the master key, or with another one, is refused with a clear message (`... is encrypted: give the server its master key ...`). It is never reported as damage, and nothing is changed.
- **Keep the master key safe and keep a copy.** Without it the data cannot be read by anyone, KarelaDB included.

<a id="rotate"></a>

## Change the master key

Do this when a key may have leaked, or someone who knew it left:

1. `kareladb key new` for the new key.
2. Start the server with the **new** key in `KARELADB_MASTER_KEY` and the **old** one in `KARELADB_MASTER_KEY_PREVIOUS` (or the `..._FILE` forms).
3. Each encrypted database re-wraps its data key with the new master key when it opens. It takes milliseconds, and no data file is rewritten. The server log says `the data key is now wrapped by the new master key`.
4. Re-wrap the backups too: `kareladb key rotate <backups folder>` (same variables).
5. Remove `KARELADB_MASTER_KEY_PREVIOUS`.

```bash
KARELADB_MASTER_KEY_FILE=/etc/kareladb/new.key KARELADB_MASTER_KEY_PREVIOUS_FILE=/etc/kareladb/old.key \
  kareladb key rotate /data/_backups/payroll
```

Backups you do not re-wrap still need the old key. Keep old keys as long as backups that need them exist.

<a id="backups"></a>

## Backups and restore

- A backup of an encrypted database is encrypted too. Its files are copied as the encrypted bytes they are, and it takes the wrapped data key along (`_encryption.key`).
- `kareladb verify-backup`, `kareladb restore` and `POST /api/restore` need the master key. The restored database is encrypted with the same data key.
- A copy made off the machine (`--backup-copy`) is encrypted too.

<a id="what"></a>

## What is encrypted

| Part | How |
|---|---|
| table files, catalog, manifests, backup manifests, temporary GROUP BY files | the whole file, in 64 KB pieces, each with AES-256-GCM and its own check |
| the log (`wal/`, `wal_archive/`) | every record body on its own. Record headers (length, number, checksum) and commit times stay plain, so recovery after a crash works exactly as before |
| `kdb.lock`, `_encryption.key` | not encrypted (the key file holds only the wrapped key) |
| memory | not encrypted (see above) |

- Every file gets a key of its own, made from the data key and a random value in the file's header. Every piece has a fresh random nonce.
- Any changed byte, a piece moved inside a file, or a piece taken from another file fails its check and is reported as damage. A plain file put into an encrypted database is refused, never read as data.
- The cipher is **AES-256-GCM** where the CPU has AES instructions (every x86-64 CPU since about 2010). Without them, new files use **ChaCha20-Poly1305**, which is fast in plain code. Each file says which one it uses, so a database moved between computers still opens.

<a id="speed"></a>

## Speed

Measured on the development PC (Windows, x86-64 with AES instructions), a table of 1 million rows in 12 day partitions, a GROUP BY over all of it:

| Work | Plain | Encrypted |
|---|---|---|
| AES-256-GCM on one core | - | about 3-3.9 GB/s |
| scan of loaded data (in memory) | 292 ms | 302 ms (about +3%, within noise) |
| first scan after opening (reads and decrypts the files) | 749 ms | 883 ms (about +18%) |
| size of the data files | 60.2 MB | 61.6 MB (+2.3%) |

- **The first read after opening misses the goal.** The goal was at most 10% slower than a plain database; the first scan after opening was about 18% slower in this measurement. Work to close that gap is still open.
- Queries on data already in memory do not decrypt anything: they cost the same.
- Reading files, writing files (checkpoints, loads) and the log cost a little more CPU. A disk is slower than the cipher.
- Without AES instructions (old or small CPUs) ChaCha20-Poly1305 runs at about 550 MB/s on one core.

<!-- docs/protection.md -->

# Protection - timeouts, limits, safe updates, read-only

> Stop slow statements (timeout and cancel), limit the memory of one query and the statements of one user, refuse UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE, and make a database read-only.

- Category: Users & security
- Keywords: protection, statement timeout, statement\_timeout, timeout, cancel, cancel query, stop query, kill query, CancelRequest, 57014, query\_canceled, X-KDB-Request-Id, X-KDB-Statement-Timeout, X-KDB-Safe-Updates, memory limit, too many rows, too many groups, 54000, max\_result\_memory, max\_groups, safe updates, safe\_updates, read-only, READ, ONLY, WRITE, --statement-timeout, --max-result-memory, --max-groups, --max-queries-per-user, --rate-limit-ip, --rate-limit-user, rate limit, 53400, --safe-updates, --read-only, 408, 413, 429, 503, Retry-After, drain, --drain-timeout, graceful shutdown
- See also: [Keeping kareladb serve safe](server-security.md), [Audit log](audit-log.md), [The trash - UNDROP TABLE](trash.md), [Table rights - GRANT ON TABLE](table-rights.md), [Two-factor login (TOTP)](two-factor-login.md), [Backups on a schedule](backup-schedule.md), [kareladb serve](cli-serve.md), [PostgreSQL protocol (port 8832)](postgres-protocol.md), [Run SQL over HTTP (/exec, /exp)](http-exec.md)

These settings keep one bad query, one busy user or one typing mistake from hurting the server. They cost almost nothing: a running query looks at one flag every 16,384 rows, never at every row.

| Protection | Turn it on | Default of `kareladb serve` |
|---|---|---|
| statement timeout | `--statement-timeout 30s`, `SET statement_timeout = '5s'`, `ALTER USER u SET statement_timeout = '2s'` | 60 s |
| cancel a running statement | Postgres cancel (pgx context, psql Ctrl+C), `DELETE /exec/<id>`, closing the HTTP connection | on |
| memory of one query | `--max-result-memory 1GB`, `--max-groups 5000000` | 1 GB, 5,000,000 groups |
| memory of the whole server | `--memory-limit 3GB` ([memory limit](cli-serve.md#memory-limit)) | 85% of a container's limit, else of the machine's memory |
| statements per user | `--max-queries-per-user 32` | 32 |
| requests per second | `--rate-limit-ip 50`, `--rate-limit-user 20` ([rate limits](#rate-limits)) | no limit |
| safe updates | `--safe-updates`, `SET safe_updates = on` | off |
| read-only | `--read-only`, `ALTER DATABASE x SET READ ONLY` | off |

`kareladb sql`, `kareladb shell` and programs that use the KarelaDB library have no limits unless they set `DatabaseOptions`.

<a id="statement-timeout"></a>

## SET statement_timeout

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb serve --statement-timeout 60s          (0 = no limit)
SET statement_timeout = '5s' | 5000 | 0 | DEFAULT
HTTP header:  X-KDB-Statement-Timeout: 5s
```

A statement (one request, or one Postgres query message) that runs longer is stopped. Nothing of a stopped change is written: an `UPDATE` stopped halfway changes no row.

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `'5s'`, `'500ms'`, `'2min'`, `5000` | the time; a plain number is milliseconds (like PostgreSQL) |
| `0` | no limit (only admins; others keep the server's limit) |
| `DEFAULT` | the server's `--statement-timeout` again |

- **Returns:** the error `canceling statement due to statement timeout (5 s); ...`. HTTP 408, PostgreSQL SQLSTATE `57014`.
- **Notes:**
  - A user who is not an admin can only make the limit shorter.
  - An admin can give one user their own limit, shorter or longer than the server's: `ALTER USER charts SET statement_timeout = '2s'` (see [Users and roles](users-and-roles.md#statement-timeout)). That limit then stands in for `--statement-timeout` for that user.
  - Over HTTP, `SET statement_timeout` lasts for the rest of the request (a shorter time counts at once, a longer one from the next request), or for the whole [HTTP session](http-sessions-and-cursors.md) when one is used. The header works for one request.
  - Waiting for another session's transaction (at most 5 s) counts too. A statement that waits for another writer (a long `CALL`, a trigger job, a load) stops at its time limit or when cancelled, within a few milliseconds, not when that writer is done.
  - The limit is checked inside every long loop: table scans, rows made by `generate_series`, joins, `GROUP BY`, window functions, `WHILE` loops and each statement of a `CALL`. A statement stops within a fraction of a second after its time is up. Sorting millions of rows, or freeing the memory they took, can add a little.
  - A `CALL` stopped inside its body says where first (`procedure 'p', line 4: canceling statement due to statement timeout ...`). It is still HTTP 408 and SQLSTATE `57014`.
  - [Triggers](triggers.md#time-limit) count toward the timeout of the statement that fired them. This is also true for `POST /write` and `POST /imp`: the header `X-KDB-Statement-Timeout` works there too, with the same rules. A trigger that runs too long gives `trigger <name>: statement timeout (<N> s)` (HTTP 408), and nothing of the request is written.

**Example: A time for the rest of this session** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SET statement_timeout = '5s';
SELECT count(*) FROM ochl_day;
```

Result:

`SET statement_timeout = '5s'`

```text
statement_timeout is 5 s for this session
```

`SELECT count(*) FROM ochl_day`

| count(*) (LONG) |
|---|
| 57 |

(1 row)

<a id="cancel"></a>

## Cancel a running statement

Syntax:

```sql
PostgreSQL:  CancelRequest (pgx: cancel the context; psql: Ctrl+C)
HTTP:        POST /exec with X-KDB-Request-Id: <id>, then DELETE /exec/<id>
HTTP:        close the connection (the browser or program gave up)
SQL:         SELECT pg_cancel_backend(pid)   (pid from pg_stat_activity; pg_terminate_backend also closes it)
```

Stops a statement that is running now.

- **Returns:** the stopped statement gets `canceling statement due to user request` (HTTP 408, SQLSTATE `57014`).
- **Notes:**
  - The Postgres port answers the CancelRequest of the connection's key only, like PostgreSQL.
  - When an HTTP client closes the connection, KarelaDB notices it within a fifth of a second and stops the statement.
  - From SQL, over either port: find the statement in [pg_stat_activity](server-activity.md#pg-stat-activity) and stop it with [pg_cancel_backend](server-activity.md#pg-cancel-backend). Users may stop only their own; admins every one.

<a id="delete-exec"></a>

## DELETE /exec/<id>

Syntax:

```sql
DELETE /exec/<id>
```

Stops the `/exec` request that was sent with the header `X-KDB-Request-Id: <id>`. The id is chosen by the program (for example a random text).

- **Returns:** `{"request_id":"<id>","cancelled":true}`, or HTTP 404 when no request with that id is running (it finished).
- **Notes:** users may stop only their own requests; admins may stop every request. A second request with the same id while the first runs gets HTTP 409.

**HTTP: Nothing with this id is running**

```http
DELETE /exec/report-17
```

Response:

HTTP 404 (application/json)

```text
{"error": "no running request has the id 'report-17' (it may have finished)"}
```

<a id="memory-limits"></a>

## Memory limits

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb serve --max-result-memory 1GB --max-groups 5000000        (0 = no limit)
```

Stops a query that would keep too much in memory: the rows of the result, rows waiting for `ORDER BY`, `DISTINCT` or window functions, and the groups of `GROUP BY`, `SAMPLE BY` and `LATEST ON`.

- **Returns:** `the query keeps too many rows in memory (about N MB; the limit is M MB, max_result_memory)` or `the query makes more than N groups (max_groups)`. HTTP 413, SQLSTATE `54000`.
- **Notes:** add a `WHERE` or a `LIMIT`, group by fewer columns, or read a big result in parts with a [cursor](cursors.md).
- **Big answers over the Postgres port** stream: a plain read (no `ORDER BY`, `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT` or `OFFSET`) sends its rows while it reads them, so this limit does not stop it ([big answers stream](postgres-protocol.md#streaming)).
- **INSERT ... SELECT:** a plain copy (no `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT`, window, `ORDER BY` or `LIMIT`) writes the rows while it reads them, so this limit does not stop it ([INSERT ... SELECT](insert.md#insert-select)).
- **GROUP BY and SAMPLE BY bigger than memory:** when the groups of a query need more than half of `--max-result-memory`, the rows of the groups that are not in memory yet go to sorted temporary files in the database folder (`_tmp/`) and are added up after the scan, one group at a time. The result is exactly the same, only slower. The files are removed when the query ends, fails or is cancelled, and when the database opens after a crash. One query may write at most 16 GB of them (`DatabaseOptions::max_spill_bytes`); past that it stops with `the GROUP BY needs more than N MB of temporary files (max_spill_bytes)`. A read-only database never writes them.

<a id="max-queries-per-user"></a>

## --max-queries-per-user

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb serve --max-queries-per-user 32        (0 = no limit)
```

How many statements one user may run at the same time, over HTTP and the Postgres port together.

- **Returns:** HTTP 429 `user 'x' already runs 32 statements at the same time`; on the Postgres port SQLSTATE `55P03`.
- **Notes:** the `--token` and a server without users are not counted. A connection pool of your app normally stays below the limit.

<a id="rate-limits"></a>

## --rate-limit-ip and --rate-limit-user

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb serve --rate-limit-ip 50 --rate-limit-user 20       (requests per second, 0 = no limit)
kareladb.conf:  "rate_limit_ip": 50, "rate_limit_user": 20
env:       KARELADB_RATE_LIMIT_IP=50  KARELADB_RATE_LIMIT_USER=20
```

How many requests one client address, and one user, may send per second. Both are off unless set.

| Counts as one request | Where |
|---|---|
| one HTTP request to `/exec`, `/exp`, `/write`, `/imp`, `/cursor`, `/api/...` and `POST /api/login` | HTTP port |
| one Query message, or one Execute of a prepared statement | PostgreSQL port |

- **Returns:** HTTP `429` with a `Retry-After` header (whole seconds) and `rate limit: user 'charts' sends more than 20 requests per second (--rate-limit-user); try again in 1 s`. On the PostgreSQL port SQLSTATE `53400`. Nothing of the request runs. Inside `BEGIN ... COMMIT` on the PostgreSQL port the refusal is an error like any other: the transaction is aborted, and `COMMIT` rolls it back.
- **Notes:**
  - Each address and each user has a "bucket" of N requests that refills at N per second. A client may send N at once, then N per second on average.
  - The address limit is checked **before** the login, so a flood of wrong passwords is slowed too. The user limit is checked after it.
  - Requests from this computer (`127.x`) are never limited by address, so the console and health checks always get through. The `--token` (no user) is limited only by address.
  - The web console's files, `/health` and `/help` are not counted.
  - **Behind Docker's port mapping or a proxy**, every client may reach KarelaDB from the same address. Then use `--rate-limit-user`, or set `--rate-limit-ip` high.
  - Read when the server starts. The Settings page shows the values in use.

<a id="safe-updates"></a>

## SET safe_updates

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb serve --safe-updates
SET safe_updates = on | off
HTTP header:  X-KDB-Safe-Updates: on | off
```

Refuses `UPDATE` and `DELETE` without `WHERE`, the classic mistake that changes every row.

- **Returns:** `safe updates are on: an UPDATE without WHERE would change every row of 't'. Add a WHERE ...`
- **Notes:** `WHERE true` changes every row on purpose. `--safe-updates` makes it the start value of every session; a session can turn it off.

**Example: UPDATE without WHERE is refused** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

```sql
SET safe_updates = on;
UPDATE securities SET name = 'oops';
```

Result:

```text
safe updates are on for this session
```

Error: `safe updates are on: an UPDATE without WHERE would change every row of 'securities'. Add a WHERE (WHERE true changes every row on purpose), or turn safe updates off for this session: SET safe_updates = off`

<a id="read-only"></a>

## ALTER DATABASE ... SET READ ONLY

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER DATABASE <name> SET READ ONLY
ALTER DATABASE <name> SET READ WRITE
kareladb serve --read-only
```

A read-only database takes no changes: `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, DDL, `CALL`, the line protocol, a CSV import (`/imp`). `SELECT`, backups and checks work.

- **Returns:** `database 'x' is read-only now: only reads are allowed`. A refused change gets `the database is read-only (...)`, HTTP 403, SQLSTATE `25006`.
- **Notes:**
  - Needs a server admin. The setting is kept in the data folder (`_system`) and holds after a restart. A read-only database cannot be dropped.
  - `kareladb serve --read-only` makes **every** database read-only, and refuses new databases and user changes. Good for a report server on a copy of the data.

**Example: Read-only, then writable again** (shows an error)

```sql
ALTER DATABASE demo SET READ ONLY;
SELECT count(*) FROM securities;
INSERT INTO brokers VALUES (99, 'New broker');
```

Result:

```text
database 'demo' is read-only now: only reads are allowed
```

Error: `the database is read-only (ALTER DATABASE demo SET READ ONLY; undo with SET READ WRITE): only reads are allowed`

<a id="drain"></a>

## Stopping the server without cutting requests off

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb serve --drain-timeout 30s          (0 = do not wait; env KARELADB_DRAIN_TIMEOUT; 5s in the Docker image)
```

When the server is asked to stop (Ctrl+C, SIGTERM, `docker stop`), it does not drop what is running:

| Request | What happens |
|---|---|
| already running | finishes and gets its real answer, for up to `--drain-timeout`; then its connection closes |
| arrives during the stop | HTTP **503** with `Retry-After: 2`; nothing of it is run |
| still running after `--drain-timeout` | cancelled like a [statement timeout](#statement-timeout); nothing half-done is written |

- `GET /health` also answers 503 while the server stops, so a load balancer or Docker's health check stops sending traffic.
- The 503 body is `{"error": "the server is shutting down; send the request again in a moment"}`, and the server log shows the request with `503 0 ms (stopping)`.
- There is no drain when the server restarts itself ([POST /api/restart](http-server-info.md#api-restart)) or when its Windows console window is closed (Windows gives it only about 4 seconds). Running statements are cancelled at once then.
- The log says `stopping: running requests finished in N ms`, or `stopping: requests still running after 30s (--drain-timeout); they are cancelled`.
- Clients should send a request again after a 503, a refused connection or a connection closed before the reply. A cut-off `/write` or `/exec` is rolled back as a whole, so repeating it is safe.
- Keep the drain time below how long your service manager waits before it kills the process. See [Docker](install-packages.md#docker-stop).

<!-- docs/audit-log.md -->

# Audit log

> KarelaDB writes security events (logins, users, DDL, backups, refused rights) and, for chosen tables, every changed row with who, when, old and new values.

- Category: Users & security
- Keywords: audit, audit log, audit trail, hash chain, tamper, tamper-evident, SHOW AUDIT VERIFY, verify, user agent, User-Agent, application\_name, agent, --token-name, KARELADB\_TOKEN\_NAME, who changed, history of changes, login history, failed logins, lockout, \_audit\_log, AUDIT, SET AUDIT ON, SET AUDIT OFF, old values, new values, accounting, compliance, --audit, --audit-keep-days, retention, erase user, delete user data, right to be forgotten, GDPR, privacy, personal data, erasure
- See also: [Protection - timeouts, limits, safe updates, read-only](protection.md), [Users and roles](users-and-roles.md), [Keeping kareladb serve safe](server-security.md), [Table rights - GRANT ON TABLE](table-rights.md), [Two-factor login (TOTP)](two-factor-login.md), [Logins, tokens and roles over HTTP](http-login.md)

The audit log is a table named `_audit_log`. KarelaDB writes it; nobody can change, delete or drop its rows (it is **append-only**). It goes through the log like any change, so it survives crashes, and backups hold it.

| What | Where | Turn it on |
|---|---|---|
| logins (good, failed, lockouts), user and grant changes, `CREATE`/`DROP`/`ALTER` of tables, indexes, views, functions, procedures, triggers and databases, backups, timers, pinned statements, partitions a TTL dropped, refused rights | `_audit_log` of the hidden `_system` database | `kareladb serve --data-dir ...` (default `--audit on`) |
| every row a statement adds, changes or deletes in one table | `_audit_log` of that database | `ALTER TABLE t SET AUDIT ON` |

Columns of `_audit_log`: `time`, `event`, `user`, `client`, `db`, `object`, `detail`, `row_key`, `old_values` (JSON), `new_values` (JSON), `session`, `ok`, `seq`, `hash`, `agent`.

`client` is the address and protocol (`10.0.0.5 (http)`). `agent` is the program that sent the request: the HTTP `User-Agent` header (`curl/8.4.0`, the browser of the web console), or the PostgreSQL `application_name` (`psql`, `DBeaver`). It is at most 200 characters, and `NULL` when the client sent none. A client can write anything there, so it helps to tell programs apart but proves nothing.

An action done with the server's `--token` is written with `user` = `token`, or the name given with `--token-name` (or `KARELADB_TOKEN_NAME`), never with an empty user.

| event | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `login`, `login_failed`, `lockout` | a login, a wrong password or code, an address that must wait |
| `user`, `ddl`, `protection`, `backup`, `server` | user statements, schema changes, protection settings, backups, server start, stop and restart |
| `timer` | a [timer](timers.md) saved, run now, turned on or off, or deleted |
| `pin` | a [pinned statement](pinned-queries.md) pinned or unpinned |
| `ttl_drop` | partitions a table's [TTL](alter-table.md#set-ttl) dropped by itself |
| `denied` | a statement the user's rights did not allow |
| `insert`, `update`, `delete` | a row of a table with `SET AUDIT ON` |

<a id="show-audit"></a>

## SHOW AUDIT

Syntax:

```sql
SHOW AUDIT [LIMIT n] [WHERE <condition>] [LIMIT n]
```

The newest security events first (100 when there is no `LIMIT`). The condition uses the columns above.

- **Returns:** rows of `_audit_log` of `_system` (on a server that opened one folder by its path: of that database).
- **Notes:** needs a server admin. The condition may only use the audit rows: no subqueries of other tables.

**Example: Failed logins of the last day**

```sql
SHOW AUDIT WHERE event = 'login_failed' AND time > dateadd('d', -1, now()) LIMIT 20;
```

Result:

| time (TIMESTAMP) | event (STRING) | user (STRING) | client (STRING) | db (STRING) | object (STRING) | detail (STRING) | row_key (STRING) | old_values (JSON) | new_values (JSON) | session (LONG) | ok (BOOL) | seq (LONG) | hash (STRING) | agent (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

(0 rows)

```text
no audit events yet
```

<a id="set-audit"></a>

## ALTER TABLE ... SET AUDIT ON

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER TABLE <name> SET AUDIT ON
ALTER TABLE <name> SET AUDIT OFF
```

From now on, every row a statement adds, changes or deletes in the table is also written to `_audit_log` of the database, **in the same transaction** as the change: there is never a change without its audit row, or an audit row without its change.

| Column | Holds |
|---|---|
| `event` | `insert`, `update` or `delete` |
| `user`, `client`, `agent`, `session` | who: the logged-in user, the address and protocol, the client program, the session |
| `detail` | the statement (a big INSERT is shortened) |
| `row_key` | the key of the row: `id='5'`, or `rowid=7` for a table without a key |
| `old_values`, `new_values` | the row before and after, as JSON. Columns whose name holds `password`, `secret`, `token`, `scram` or `totp` show `"***"`. |

- **Returns:** `audit is on for table 'accounts': every changed row is written to _audit_log`.
- **Notes:**
  - Tables without `SET AUDIT ON` cost nothing extra. An audited table's writes cost one row lookup and one audit row per changed row.
  - An `UPDATE` that changes nothing in a row writes no audit row. Rolled back transactions write none.
  - Read the rows with `SELECT ... FROM _audit_log` (needs role admin on the database).
  - Older KarelaDB programs refuse a database with an audited table (the setting would be lost).

**Example: Audit an accounts table**

```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (id INT PRIMARY KEY, owner STRING, balance DECIMAL(2));
ALTER TABLE accounts SET AUDIT ON;
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (1, 'Sita', 100.00);
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 25 WHERE id = 1;
SELECT event, row_key, old_values, new_values FROM _audit_log ORDER BY time;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE accounts (`

```text
table 'accounts' created
```

`ALTER TABLE accounts SET AUDIT ON`

```text
audit is on for table 'accounts': every changed row is written to _audit_log
```

`INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (1, 'Sita', 100.00)`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 25 WHERE id = 1`

```text
1 row(s) updated
```

`SELECT event, row_key, old_values, new_values FROM _audit_log ORDER BY time`

| event (STRING) | row_key (STRING) | old_values (JSON) | new_values (JSON) |
|---|---|---|---|
| insert | id='1' | NULL | {"id":1,"owner":"Sita","balance":100.00} |
| update | id='1' | {"id":1,"owner":"Sita","balance":100.00} | {"id":1,"owner":"Sita","balance":75.00} |

(2 rows)

**Example: Nobody can change the audit rows** (shows an error)

```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (id INT PRIMARY KEY, balance DECIMAL(2));
ALTER TABLE accounts SET AUDIT ON;
DELETE FROM _audit_log;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE accounts (`

```text
table 'accounts' created
```

`ALTER TABLE accounts SET AUDIT ON`

```text
audit is on for table 'accounts': every changed row is written to _audit_log
```

Error: `the audit table _audit_log is append-only: KarelaDB writes it, nobody can change or drop it (old rows are removed by the audit retention setting)`

<a id="hash-chain"></a>

## The hash chain

Every row gets a number and a hash, so a row changed or removed outside KarelaDB (by editing the files) is found.

| Column | Holds |
|---|---|
| `seq` | 1, 2, 3 ... in the order the rows were written |
| `hash` | SHA-256 (hex) of the previous row's hash and this row's values |

A changed row no longer matches its hash. A removed row leaves a gap in `seq`. `SHOW AUDIT VERIFY`, `kareladb check <database>` and `POST /api/check` check the whole chain and name the rows that do not fit.

- **Returns:** `kareladb check` prints `audit chain: N row(s) checked, seq 1 to N, newest hash ...`, or a `TAMPERED:` line per problem (exit code 2).
- **Notes:**
  - Note the newest hash somewhere else now and then (a ticket, an email). Then even the newest rows cannot be cut off unseen.
  - Rows written before KarelaDB had the chain keep `seq` and `hash` empty; the check counts them apart.
  - When `--audit-keep-days` removes old months, the check starts at the oldest row left.
  - The `agent` column came after the chain. It is in the hashed values only when it has a value: older rows (no agent) keep the hash they were written with, and a row's agent can not be changed or cleared unseen.

**Example: The chain of an audited table**

```sql
CREATE TABLE ledger (id INT PRIMARY KEY, amount DECIMAL(2));
ALTER TABLE ledger SET AUDIT ON;
INSERT INTO ledger VALUES (1, 10.00), (2, 20.00);
SELECT seq, event, row_key, length(hash) AS hash_length FROM _audit_log ORDER BY seq;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE ledger (`

```text
table 'ledger' created
```

`ALTER TABLE ledger SET AUDIT ON`

```text
audit is on for table 'ledger': every changed row is written to _audit_log
```

`INSERT INTO ledger VALUES (1, 10.00), (2, 20.00)`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT seq, event, row_key, length(hash) AS hash_length FROM _audit_log ORDER BY seq`

| seq (LONG) | event (STRING) | row_key (STRING) | hash_length (LONG) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | insert | id='1' | 64 |
| 2 | insert | id='2' | 64 |

(2 rows)

<a id="show-audit-verify"></a>

## SHOW AUDIT VERIFY

Syntax:

```sql
SHOW AUDIT VERIFY
```

Checks the hash chain from SQL, the same check as `kareladb check`, without stopping the server.

| Column | Holds |
|---|---|
| `log` | which `_audit_log`: `_system` (the security events), or the database of the session (its `SET AUDIT ON` rows) |
| `ok` | `true` when every row matches its hash and no `seq` is missing |
| `rows_checked` | the rows with a `seq` |
| `unchained` | older rows written before the chain existed |
| `first_seq`, `last_seq` | the range of `seq` checked |
| `first_broken` | the `seq` of the first row that does not fit; `NULL` when all fit |
| `problems` | what is wrong, row by row |
| `last_hash` | the newest hash: note it somewhere else to also catch a cut at the end |

- **Returns:** one row per audit log, and the message `the audit hash chain is intact (N rows checked)` or `the audit hash chain is broken: ...`.
- **Notes:**
  - Needs a server admin, like `SHOW AUDIT`.
  - It reads the whole chain: on a log of millions of rows it takes a few seconds.

**Example: Check the chain of an audited table**

```sql
CREATE TABLE ledger (id INT PRIMARY KEY, amount DECIMAL(2));
ALTER TABLE ledger SET AUDIT ON;
INSERT INTO ledger VALUES (1, 10.00), (2, 20.00);
UPDATE ledger SET amount = 15.00 WHERE id = 1;
SHOW AUDIT VERIFY;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE ledger (`

```text
table 'ledger' created
```

`ALTER TABLE ledger SET AUDIT ON`

```text
audit is on for table 'ledger': every changed row is written to _audit_log
```

`INSERT INTO ledger VALUES (1, 10.00), (2, 20.00)`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`UPDATE ledger SET amount = 15.00 WHERE id = 1`

```text
1 row(s) updated
```

`SHOW AUDIT VERIFY`

| log (STRING) | ok (BOOL) | rows_checked (LONG) | unchained (LONG) | first_seq (LONG) | last_seq (LONG) | first_broken (LONG) | problems (STRING) | last_hash (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| demo | true | 3 | 0 | 1 | 3 | NULL | NULL | e9c0d4c5a945caae22fa31b4a97371e9421cd054b1631fef3444e6ec24cfb94c |

(1 row)

```text
the audit hash chain is intact (3 rows checked)
```

<a id="audit-keep-days"></a>

## --audit-keep-days

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb serve [--audit on|off] [--audit-keep-days N]
```

`--audit off` writes no security events. `--audit-keep-days N` removes security events older than N days, a whole month at a time, once a day (0 = keep forever, the default).

- **Notes:**
  - Security events (`login_failed`, `lockout`, `denied`, `user`, `protection`) are written to disk before the request that caused them gets its answer. A successful `login` and the other events (`ddl`, `timer`, `backup` ...) are written in groups every 200 ms, so a crash can lose the events of that moment. A new connection does not wait for a disk write.
  - Keep the audit log of accounting for as long as the law asks (often several years).
  - `--audit-keep-days` only removes **security events** (the `_audit_log` of `_system`). The data-change rows of `SET AUDIT ON` tables, in each database's own `_audit_log`, are kept as long as the database lives (see [erase one user's data](#erase-user)).

<a id="erase-user"></a>

## Erase one user's data

A person asks you to delete everything you hold about them. Three steps: find the tables, delete the rows, and know what the audit log keeps.

**1. Find every table with a user column.** `information_schema.columns` lists the columns of every table.

**Example: Which tables hold a user id or an email?**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE app_users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, email STRING NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, user_id INT REFERENCES app_users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, amount DECIMAL(2));
CREATE TABLE page_views (time TIMESTAMP, user_id INT, page STRING) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY;
```

```sql
SELECT table_name, column_name FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE column_name IN ('user_id', 'email') ORDER BY table_name;
```

Result:

| table_name (STRING) | column_name (STRING) |
|---|---|
| app_users | email |
| orders | user_id |
| page_views | user_id |

(3 rows)

**2. Delete the rows in one transaction.** Tables that point to the user with `REFERENCES ... ON DELETE CASCADE` lose their rows together with the user's row ([REFERENCES](constraints.md#references)). Tables without such a key (a time-series table of page views, for example) need their own `DELETE`. One `BEGIN ... COMMIT` makes it all or nothing.

**Example: Delete user 1 everywhere, then check**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE app_users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, email STRING NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, user_id INT REFERENCES app_users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, amount DECIMAL(2));
CREATE TABLE page_views (time TIMESTAMP, user_id INT, page STRING) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY;
INSERT INTO app_users VALUES (1, 'ram@example.com'), (2, 'sita@example.com');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10, 1, 250.00), (11, 2, 99.50), (12, 1, 10.00);
INSERT INTO page_views VALUES ('2026-09-24T10:00:00Z', 1, '/home'), ('2026-09-24T10:01:00Z', 2, '/home');
```

```sql
BEGIN;
DELETE FROM page_views WHERE user_id = 1;
DELETE FROM app_users WHERE id = 1;
COMMIT;
SELECT 'orders' AS table_name, count(*) AS rows_left FROM orders WHERE user_id = 1
UNION ALL SELECT 'page_views', count(*) FROM page_views WHERE user_id = 1
UNION ALL SELECT 'app_users', count(*) FROM app_users WHERE id = 1;
```

Result:

`BEGIN`

```text
transaction started
```

`DELETE FROM page_views WHERE user_id = 1`

```text
1 row(s) deleted
```

`DELETE FROM app_users WHERE id = 1`

```text
1 row(s) deleted
```

`COMMIT`

```text
transaction committed: 4 change(s) saved
```

`SELECT 'orders' AS table_name, count(*) AS rows_left FROM orders WHERE user_id = 1 UNION ALL SELECT `

| table_name (STRING) | rows_left (LONG) |
|---|---|
| orders | 0 |
| page_views | 0 |
| app_users | 0 |

(3 rows)

**3. What the audit log keeps.** If a table has `SET AUDIT ON`, its `_audit_log` row for the `DELETE` holds the deleted row in `old_values`, and the older `insert` and `update` rows hold it too. **These rows cannot be erased with SQL.** The log is append-only on purpose: `DELETE`, `UPDATE`, `TRUNCATE` and `DROP` of `_audit_log` are refused, and every row is linked to the one before by the [hash chain](#hash-chain), so a row removed by editing the files is reported by `kareladb check`. `--audit-keep-days` does not reach these rows either: it only removes security events.

**Example: The deleted row is still in old_values**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE app_users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, email STRING NOT NULL);
ALTER TABLE app_users SET AUDIT ON;
INSERT INTO app_users VALUES (1, 'ram@example.com');
```

```sql
DELETE FROM app_users WHERE id = 1;
SELECT event, row_key, old_values FROM _audit_log WHERE event = 'delete';
```

Result:

`DELETE FROM app_users WHERE id = 1`

```text
1 row(s) deleted
```

`SELECT event, row_key, old_values FROM _audit_log WHERE event = 'delete'`

| event (STRING) | row_key (STRING) | old_values (JSON) |
|---|---|---|
| delete | id='1' | {"id":1,"email":"ram@example.com"} |

(1 row)

| What you can do | How |
|---|---|
| Keep personal data out of audited tables | Put names, emails and phone numbers in a table **without** `SET AUDIT ON`, and audit the table of money or orders that holds only the user's id. The audit rows then hold an id that means nothing once the user row is gone. |
| Hide secrets | Columns whose name holds `password`, `secret`, `token`, `scram` or `totp` are always written as `"***"`. |
| Stop recording | `ALTER TABLE t SET AUDIT OFF` writes no new rows. The rows already there stay. |
| Remove everything | `DROP DATABASE`, then `PURGE TRASH ALL`, removes the database and its `_audit_log`. There is no way to remove only some rows. |

- **Notes:** backups hold the deleted rows too, until the [backup schedule](backup-schedule.md) removes the old backups (`backup_keep_daily`, `backup_keep_weekly`).
- **Notes:** in many places the law lets you keep records you must keep for accounting or security, even after an erasure request. Say in your privacy policy that the audit log keeps the changes of audited tables, and for how long.

# Troubleshooting a running server

> What to look at, and what to change, when the server is slow, readers wait, memory or disk grows, the start is slow, a timer or a backup does not run, or data must come back.

- Category: Backup, check, repair, restore
- Keywords: troubleshooting, runbook, production problem, incident, server slow, slow server, slow queries, readers wait, reads wait, busy, table is busy, 55P03, 40001, lock timeout, memory high, out of memory, memory full, disk full, disk growing, disk space, trash, keep\_versions, last shutdown: not clean, slow start, start-up slow, log replay, timer not running, timer did not run, backup failed, restore, what to do, symptom
- See also: [Monitor panel (memory, processor, caches)](console-monitor.md), [Health, info, check and backup over HTTP (metrics)](http-server-info.md#metrics), [Health, info, check and backup over HTTP (slow-queries)](http-server-info.md#slow-queries), [Transactions (lock-timeout)](transactions.md#lock-timeout), [kareladb serve (memory-limit)](cli-serve.md#memory-limit), [Databases and the data folder (purge-trash)](databases.md#purge-trash), [Timers](timers.md), [Backups on a schedule](backup-schedule.md), [Backup, check, repair and restore (after-damage)](backup-and-safety.md#after-damage)

Each part below is one **symptom**: what you see, where to **check**, and the **fix**. Start with the console's [Monitor](console-monitor.md): it shows memory, the statements running now and the slow statements on one page.

The checks use three routes. Send the token as for any route: `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

| Route | Shows |
|---|---|
| [`GET /api/stats`](http-server-info.md#api-stats) | memory, running statements, waits, snapshot reads, databases that are still opening |
| [`GET /metrics`](http-server-info.md#metrics) | the same counters for Prometheus or Grafana |
| [`GET /api/slow-queries`](http-server-info.md#slow-queries) | the statements that took longer than `--slow-query-ms` (1 second unless set) |

<a id="slow"></a>

## The server is slow

| Check | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| Monitor, **Statements running now** | one long statement that holds everything up. **Cancel** stops it. |
| `GET /api/slow-queries?limit=20` | which statements are slow, who sent them, how many rows they gave |
| `kdb_slow_statements_total` in `/metrics` | whether slow statements are new or have always been there |
| `kdb_gate_waits_total{mode}`, `kdb_gate_wait_seconds_total{mode}` | time spent **waiting for a lock**, not working: see [readers wait](#readers-wait) |
| `kdb_partition_loads_total` rising fast | data is read from disk again and again: `--memory` is too small for what is queried |
| `EXPLAIN <the slow query>` | whether the query reads every partition (`scan table t (120 of 120 partitions ...)`) |

- **Fix:** give a time range to queries of big time-series tables, add an [index](indexes.md) for lookups by one column, and see [performance tips](performance-tips.md). Stop a runaway statement with **Cancel**, and limit them with `--statement-timeout` ([protection](protection.md)).

**HTTP: The newest slow statements**

```http
GET /api/slow-queries?limit=5
```

Response:

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{
  "threshold_ms": 1000,
  "recorded": 0,
  "queries": []
}
```

**Example: How much of the table a query reads**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ticks (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, price DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY;
INSERT INTO ticks VALUES ('2026-09-23T10:00:00Z', 'CITY', 510), ('2026-09-24T10:00:00Z', 'CITY', 512);
```

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT max(price) FROM ticks WHERE time IN '2026-09-24';
```

Result:

| plan (STRING) |
|---|
| scan table ticks (1 of 2 partitions, about 2 rows) |
| answer from saved stats of table ticks: 1 of 1 partitions from the partition list and their files' stats (0 in memory, 0 partitions loaded, 1 file headers read); 0 partitions scanned |
| build 2 of 3 stored column(s) per row: time, price |
| filter while scanning: 1 condition(s) |
| group by 0 key(s), 1 aggregate(s) |
| engine: column |

(6 rows)

<a id="readers-wait"></a>

## Readers wait for a writer

A `SELECT` that is quick at night takes seconds by day, while a load, a trigger or a long `CALL` writes the same table.

| Check | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| The start-up lines, `readers ...` | whether [reader yield](transactions.md#reader-yield) is on |
| `kdb_gate_wait_seconds_total{mode="read"}` | how long readers waited in total |
| `snapshot_reads` in `/api/stats` | whether [snapshot reads](transactions.md#snapshot-reads) are on and used |

- **Fix:**
  - Keep reader yield on (`--reader-yield on`, `KARELADB_READER_YIELD=on`; on unless set). Readers then get in between the writer's statements.
  - Turn on snapshot reads (`--snapshot-reads on`, `KARELADB_SNAPSHOT_READS=on`) so readers do not wait even for one long statement, also on tables with an index of up to 1,000,000 rows (`--snapshot-index-rows`).
  - Split one huge statement (`INSERT ... SELECT` of millions of rows) into smaller ones: readers can only get in between statements.

<a id="busy"></a>

## Errors 55P03 and 40001: the table is busy

`table 'x' is busy: another transaction has held it for N ms` means a writer waited the [lock timeout](transactions.md#lock-timeout) (5 seconds unless set) for another writer of the same table. Nothing of the statement was done.

| Code | When | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `55P03` (HTTP 503) | a statement outside `BEGIN ... COMMIT` | send it again |
| `40001` (HTTP 503) | inside `BEGIN ... COMMIT` | `ROLLBACK` and run the whole transaction again; drivers retry this code by themselves |
| `40P01` | two transactions that would wait for each other | run it again |

| Check | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| Monitor, **Statements running now** | the transaction that holds the table, and for how long |
| `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` | a client that sent `BEGIN` and then nothing keeps the table until it is rolled back (30 s unless set, see [idle transactions](transactions.md#idle-timeout)) |

- **Fix:** keep transactions short. For many small writers of one table that should queue instead of failing, raise the wait for them: `SET lock_timeout = '20s'` in the session, `X-KDB-Lock-Timeout: 20s` on one request, or `--lock-timeout` for the server.

**Example: Let this session wait longer for a busy table, then go back to the server's wait**

```sql
SET lock_timeout = '20s';
SET lock_timeout = DEFAULT;
```

Result:

`SET lock_timeout = '20s'`

```text
lock_timeout is 20 s for this session
```

`SET lock_timeout = 'DEFAULT'`

```text
lock_timeout is the server's default again
```

<a id="memory"></a>

## Memory is high

| Check | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| Monitor, **Memory in RAM** and **Most it ever held** | what the process holds now, and at its peak |
| `kdb_memory_bytes{kind}` in `/metrics` | which part is big: `table_data`, `key_maps`, `indexes`, `pending`, `result_cache`, `allocator` ... |
| `kdb_memory_level` | 0 green, 1 yellow, 2 red: near the [memory limit](cli-serve.md#memory-limit) |
| errors `memory full: ...` (HTTP 503) | the limit stopped new work instead of the process being killed |

| Setting | What it limits |
|---|---|
| `--memory <MB>` (`KARELADB_MEMORY`) | table data kept loaded. Data over it is read from disk again. |
| `--memory-limit <size>` (`KARELADB_MEMORY_LIMIT`) | everything together. Keep `--memory` at about half of it. |
| `--max-result-memory` | one query's result ([protection](protection.md#memory-limits)) |
| `GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.arena_max=8:glibc.malloc.trim_threshold=67108864` | Linux and Docker: how much freed memory the C library keeps; without it the process can hold far more than it uses |

- **Fix:** `allocator` big: set `GLIBC_TUNABLES` as above (see [Docker](install-packages.md#docker)). `table_data` big: lower `--memory`. A query that needs much memory: add a time range or a `LIMIT`. A transaction that fails with `transaction too big for memory`: split it.

<a id="disk"></a>

## The disk keeps growing

| Check | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| [`GET /api/disk`](http-server-info.md#api-disk), or the console's [Keep data](console-keep-data.md) page | the size of the data, of older file versions, of the trash, and of the log |
| `kdb_database_disk_bytes{database,kind}` in `/metrics` | the same, over time |

| Big part | Why | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `previous_bytes` | every checkpoint keeps older versions of each file for repairs (`keep_versions`, 2 unless set) | `PURGE VERSIONS KEEP 1`, or a lower `keep_versions` in `kareladb.conf` ([versions](databases.md#purge-versions)) |
| `trash_bytes` | replaced files wait `trash_keep_hours` (1 hour), dropped databases wait for ever | `PURGE TRASH`, or `PURGE TRASH ALL` for dropped databases ([trash](databases.md#purge-trash)) |
| dropped tables | `DROP TABLE` keeps a table for `--trash-days` (7) so `UNDROP TABLE` works | `SHOW DROPPED TABLES`, then `DROP TABLE _dropped_...` ([the trash](trash.md)) |
| `wal_archive_bytes` | the old log is kept for point-in-time restores | a shorter `WAL_ARCHIVE` ([databases](databases.md#wal-archive)) |
| `data_bytes` | the rows themselves | a [TTL](alter-table.md#set-ttl) or `DROP PARTITION` for old days |

**HTTP: What a database takes on disk**

Setup:

```text
CREATE TABLE ticks (time TIMESTAMP, price DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY;
INSERT INTO ticks VALUES ('2026-09-24T10:00:00Z', 1.5);
```

```http
GET /api/disk
```

Response:

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{
  "database": "demo",
  "data_files": 1,
  "data_bytes": 236,
  "tail_files": 0,
  "tail_bytes": 0,
  "delta_files": 0,
  "delta_bytes": 0,
  "previous_files": 0,
  "previous_bytes": 0,
  "trash_folders": 0,
  "trash_bytes": 0,
  "wal_bytes": 1048640,
  "wal_archive_bytes": 0,
  "total_bytes": 1048876,
  "trash_purged_bytes": 0
}
```

**Example: Free older file versions and the trash**

Setup:

```sql

INSERT INTO ticks VALUES ('2026-09-24T10:00:00Z', 1.5);
```

```sql

PURGE TRASH;
```

Result:

`PURGE VERSIONS KEEP 1`

```text

```

`PURGE TRASH`

```text

```

<a id="slow-start"></a>

## The start is slow, or says "last shutdown: not clean"

`last shutdown: not clean (crash or kill)` in the start-up lines means the server was killed, not stopped. That is not damage: KarelaDB replays the log, and every confirmed change comes back. Replaying a long log takes time.

| Check | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| the `recovery` start-up line | clean or not, and how many log records were replayed |
| `opening_databases` in `/api/stats` | databases still opening, and for how long |

- **Fix:** stop the server so it can finish: Ctrl+C, `docker stop`, or a service stop. A Docker container needs `--stop-timeout 60` when it is **created**; without it, Docker Desktop kills it about 1 second after asking it to stop, and every start replays the log ([Docker](install-packages.md#docker), [stopping](cli-serve.md#stop)). Do not use `docker rm -f` or `docker kill` on a running server.

<a id="timer"></a>

## A timer does not run

| Check | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| [`GET /api/timers`](timers.md#get-api-timers) | `enabled`, `next_run_ms` (0 = off), `last_run_ms`, `last_ok`, `last_error` |
| `kdb_timer_failures_total`, `kdb_timer_late_seconds_max` | failed runs, and how late runs started |

| Cause | Fix |
|---|---|
| the timer is off | turn it on (**Timers** page, or `POST /api/timers/<name>/enable`) |
| it runs at the wrong hour | times are the server's clock; a container runs on UTC. Set `--timezone Asia/Kathmandu` |
| `last_error` says why | fix the SQL, or the rights of the user who saved it last (it runs with them) |
| the run before is still going | a run is skipped when the one before has not finished. Make the SQL faster; a run stops after 10 minutes |
| its database was dropped | delete the timer |

**HTTP: Every timer, with its last run and error**

```http
GET /api/timers
```

Response:

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{
  "now_ms": 1792822781578,
  "timers": []
}
```

<a id="backup"></a>

## A backup failed

| Check | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| `backup_schedule` in [`GET /api/info`](backup-schedule.md#backup-status) | `last_run_ok`, `warning` (`the last good backup of 'x' is N hours old`), and per database `error` |
| `backup_command` in `/api/info` | the copy command's exit code and the end of what it printed |
| `kareladb backups <dir>` | the backups there, and whether each is whole |

| Cause | Fix |
|---|---|
| disk full | free space, or keep fewer backups (`backup_keep_daily`, `backup_keep_weekly`) ([when the disk is full](backup-and-safety.md#disk-full)) |
| the folder is not there, or not writable | inside Docker it must be under a mounted volume |
| the copy command failed | run the command by hand with the same folder |

Then run one backup now to see that it works: `POST /api/backup`, or **Back up now** in the console.

<a id="restore"></a>

## Getting data back

| What happened | Steps |
|---|---|
| a table was dropped | `UNDROP TABLE t` within `--trash-days` ([the trash](trash.md)) |
| a bad `UPDATE` or `DELETE` | [restore while the server runs](backup-and-safety.md#restore-online): `POST /api/restore` with `"until"` one second before the mistake into a new name, check it, then `POST /api/databases/swap` |
| damaged files (`failed its checksum`, `DAMAGED`) | stop, copy the folder, `kareladb check`, `kareladb repair --backups <dir>` ([after damage](backup-and-safety.md#after-damage)) |
| the whole folder is lost | `kareladb restore <newest backup> <new folder>`, `kareladb check <new folder>`, then start the server on it ([kareladb restore](backup-and-safety.md#kareladb-restore)) |

**Command line: Check a database, then repair it from the backups** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb check market
kareladb repair market --backups backups
```

Output:

`> kareladb check market`

```text
checked 14 files (76.1 KB) and 1 log segments
OK: no damage found
```

`> kareladb repair market --backups backups`

```text
manifest copy: a, last shutdown: clean
replayed 0 transactions after LSN 30, last LSN 30

Nothing to repair.
```
