<!-- docs/backup-and-safety.md -->

# Backup, check, repair and restore

> How KarelaDB keeps your data safe, how to make and test backups, and how to get the data back after damage or a mistake.

- Category: Backup, check, repair, restore
- Keywords: backup, backups, CHECKPOINT, checkpoint now, settle after a load, restore, point-in-time restore, PITR, point-in-time window, restore drill, monthly restore, test restore, restore while running, online restore, /api/restore, swap database, /api/databases/swap, wal\_archive\_mb, undo, bad import, UPDATE without WHERE, verify, verified backup, hard links, retention, keep daily, keep weekly, prune, daily backup, Task Scheduler, cron, damage, disk failure, safety, --hard-links, --keep-daily, --keep-weekly, --logs-from, --until, backup.kdb, /api/backup, /api/check, Backup now, Check now, disk full, 507, 53100, no space, out of memory, ENOMEM, Cannot allocate memory, 53200, try again, compressed log, compressed\_log, log compression, WAL compression, KARELADB\_WAL\_COMPRESS, packed log records, kdb\_wal\_packed\_input\_bytes\_total
- See also: [kareladb info, check, repair, dump-file](cli-maintenance.md), [How KarelaDB stores data](data-formats.md), [kareladb serve](cli-serve.md), [Transactions](transactions.md), [Health, info, check and backup over HTTP](http-server-info.md)

KarelaDB is built so that a crash, a power cut or a bad disk block never gives you wrong data without telling you.
But only **backups on another disk** protect you from a dead disk or a big mistake (a wrong `UPDATE`, a bad import).
This page shows how to make backups, check them, and restore from them.

Most commands here need the database **closed** (no `kareladb serve`, no `kareladb shell` on it). With a running server, use `BACKUP DATABASE`, the console's **Backup now**, `POST /api/backup` and `POST /api/check`, and [restore while the server runs](#restore-online).

<a id="protection"></a>

## How KarelaDB protects your data

| Danger | What KarelaDB does |
|---|---|
| Power cut or crash while writing | Every change goes into the **log** (WAL, write-ahead log) first. The log is on the disk before KarelaDB says "done". At the next start KarelaDB replays the log. |
| A file only half written | Data files are **never changed**. KarelaDB writes a new version, checks it, and then switches to it. |
| A bad bit on the disk | Every block of every file has a **checksum** (CRC32C, a short number made from the bytes). KarelaDB notices one wrong bit and names the file and block. |
| A damaged data file | The **repair ladder**: the previous version of the file plus the log, then a copy from a backup plus the log. See [kareladb repair](cli-maintenance.md#kareladb-repair). |
| A damaged list of files | The list (the **manifest**) is saved **twice**. One good copy is always left. |
| A mistake (wrong UPDATE, bad import) | **Point-in-time restore**: a backup plus the log, up to the second before the mistake. See [restore while running](#restore-online) and [kareladb restore](#kareladb-restore). |
| The whole disk dies | Only backups on another disk help. |
| The disk is full | KarelaDB stops accepting writes when less than 64 MB is free, so nothing is left half written. See [when the disk is full](#disk-full). |

More details: [data formats](data-formats.md) and [chapter 9](../tutorial/09-backup-and-safety.md).

<a id="compressed-log"></a>

## The log is compressed

A commit has to wait until its log records are on the disk. For a big commit (a whole-history rewrite of one symbol: `DELETE` 240,000 rows and `INSERT ... SELECT` them again) that is tens of MB, and the wait for the disk was most of the commit's time. Since 2026-10-02 KarelaDB packs such records before it writes them.

| What | How |
|---|---|
| which commits | those whose log records hold **64 KB or more**; smaller commits are written exactly as before, so they cost nothing extra |
| how much smaller | about **a third** of the bytes for candle rows and deletes (measured: 44 MB of log became 14 MB) |
| how fast | packing runs on up to 8 threads (at most half the CPUs); measured on that rewrite, its `COMMIT` took 41 ms instead of 89 ms |
| never bigger | a group of records that does not get smaller (random bytes) is written as before |
| safe | every record inside is checked again (its checksum) when it is read; a torn end after a power cut is found as before |
| encrypted databases | the records are packed first, then [encrypted](encryption.md) |
| everything that reads the log | recovery, `kareladb check`, backups and restore, [standby copies](standby.md), [change streams](change-stream.md) and `AS OF` read packed records like any others |
| watch it | `/metrics`: `kdb_wal_packed_input_bytes_total` (what the records would have taken) and `kdb_wal_packed_output_bytes_total` (what was written) |
| turn it off | `KARELADB_WAL_COMPRESS=off` in the environment of `kareladb serve` (or any `kareladb` command) |

Packed records are a stored-format feature (`compressed_log`, see [versions](versions.md)): a build from before 2026-10-02 refuses them as "needs a newer KDB" (its name then), never as damage. [kareladb downgrade](versions.md#downgrade) to such a KarelaDB turns packing off by itself while it works, so it leaves no packed record that the older KarelaDB would have to read.

<a id="disk-full"></a>

## When the disk is full

Syntax:

```sql
HTTP:        507 Insufficient Storage   (/exec: {"error": ...}; POST /write: {"code": "disk full", "message": ..., ...})
PostgreSQL:  SQLSTATE 53100 (disk_full)
```

KarelaDB looks at the free space of the data disk before it writes, at most once a second. Below **64 MB** free it refuses the write with `only N MB free on disk; KarelaDB pauses writes below 64 MB so nothing is half-written`. A write the disk itself refuses (it filled up in between) gets the same HTTP code and SQLSTATE, with the system's message.

| What | What happens |
|---|---|
| the refused write | nothing of it is saved; the whole request or transaction is rolled back |
| reads | go on as usual |
| the database | is not damaged and needs no repair |
| later writes | work again as soon as there is room; no restart is needed |

- Free room: delete old backups on that disk, empty the [trash](trash.md), drop old partitions, or move the data folder to a bigger disk (the [Settings page](console-settings.md)).
- A loader should treat 507 like 503: wait, then send the same request again. It was not applied.
- One exception: when the disk fills while the log is being flushed, the 507 message says `The rows of this write are applied in memory and reach the log once disk space is freed`. Those rows are already there (reads show them) and are saved once space is back. For a table with a key, sending them again is harmless; for a table without one, do not send them again.

<a id="out-of-memory"></a>

## When the system is short of memory

Syntax:

```sql
HTTP:        503 Service Unavailable, Retry-After: 1   (not applied: send it again)
HTTP:        500, no Retry-After   ("... The rows of this write are applied in memory ...": do not send it again)
PostgreSQL:  SQLSTATE 53200 (out_of_memory)
```

Sometimes the operating system refuses a write to a file for a moment: `Cannot allocate memory` (ENOMEM). A Docker VM whose memory is full of file cache does this. It is not a broken disk, and since 2026-10-02 KarelaDB treats it so:

| What | What happens |
|---|---|
| a read, write or truncate of a file | tried again after a short pause, for about 2 s, before it counts as failed |
| a write to the log | undone and tried again, for about 3 s more |
| a write that still fails | gets 503 with `Retry-After` (it was not applied: send it again in a moment); the database does **not** stop and needs no reopen |
| reads, `/health` | go on as usual |
| later writes | work again by themselves when memory is back |

- One exception, as with a full disk: when the shortage hits the shared flush of the log, the rows are already in the table. That answer is **500 without `Retry-After`**, and its message says `The rows of this write are applied in memory`. Reads show those rows, and KarelaDB writes them to the log as soon as it can. Do not send them again to a table without a key: it would hold them twice.
- `kdb_io_retries_total` in [/metrics](http-server-info.md#metrics) counts the calls that were tried again.

## BACKUP DATABASE

Syntax:

```sql
BACKUP DATABASE
```

Makes a backup of the current database **while it stays open**, then reads the whole backup again to check it.
It works in `kareladb serve` (console, `POST /exec`), in `kareladb shell` and in `kareladb sql`, when there is a backup folder. `kareladb serve` always has one unless it is started with `--backups off` (`_backups` in the data folder, `_backups/<folder name>` next to a folder served by its path, or `--backups <dir>`; see [where the settings come from](backup-schedule.md#backup-settings)). `kareladb shell` and `kareladb sql` need `--backups <dir>`.

| Result column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `backup` | The new backup folder. Its name is the **UTC** time: `20260911-081906-660`. |
| `files` | Data files in the backup |
| `bytes` | Size of the backup |
| `log_lsn` | The backup holds every change up to this log position |

- **Deletes old backups:** after a good backup it keeps the newest backup of each of the last 7 days and of the last 4 weeks, and deletes the rest of that folder.
- In a server with a data folder, a database backs up into `<dir>/<database name>`.
- Needs the `admin` role when the server has users.
- Without a backup folder (`kareladb sql` without `--backups`, or a server started with `--backups off`): `no backup folder is set`.
- A server with a [copy command](backup-schedule.md#backup-command) copies each new backup off the server.

**Command line: In kareladb shell, started with a backup folder** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb shell market --backups backups
> BACKUP DATABASE;
```

Output:

```text
KarelaDB 0.2.0-dev shell on market
End statements with ';'. Type .help for commands, .exit to quit.
kareladb> backup                      | files | bytes  | log_lsn
----------------------------+-------+--------+--------
backups/20261024-061845-094 |     9 | 194519 |      30
(1 row, 17.6 ms)
backup created and verified
kareladb>
```

**Example: No backup folder was given** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

```sql
BACKUP DATABASE;
```

Result:

Error: `no backup folder is set; start KarelaDB with a backup folder (for example --backups D:/kdb_backups)`

## CHECK TABLE

Syntax:

```sql
CHECK TABLE <table>
```

Reads every block of every data file and every log record, and checks the checksums. It changes nothing.

- **Result:** a column `problem` with one row per problem (no rows when all is well), and the message `OK: no damage found in N files` or `N problem(s) found`.
- **It always checks the whole database**, whatever table you name. The name is not even checked.
- The same as `.check` in `kareladb shell`, **Check now** in the console, `POST /api/check`, and [kareladb check](cli-maintenance.md#kareladb-check) for a closed database.
- Needs the `admin` role when the server has users.

**Example: Check the database** (sample data: sample)

```sql
CHECK TABLE ochl_day;
```

Result:

| problem (STRING) |
|---|

(0 rows)

```text
OK: no damage found in 14 files
```

<a id="checkpoint"></a>

## CHECKPOINT

Syntax:

```sql
CHECKPOINT
```

Writes every change of the current database that waits in memory (and in the log) to its data files, and answers only when that is done. It is PostgreSQL's `CHECKPOINT`. A benchmark or a loader sends it after a bulk load, so that what comes next does not run beside the background writing of that load.

| What | How |
|---|---|
| a checkpoint already running | it waits for that one to end first, then writes what is still waiting |
| nothing waiting | answers at once: `nothing to write: every change is in the files already` (no file is written) |
| readers | go on while the files are written; writers wait until it is done |
| the answer | no rows; the message `checkpoint done: every change is in the files`. Over the PostgreSQL port the command tag is `CHECKPOINT` |
| where | HTTP `POST /exec`, the PostgreSQL port, the console, `kareladb shell` |
| rights | the `ddl` role (or `admin`) when the server has users, as for `COMPRESS TABLE` |

- Send it **alone**: `CHECKPOINT; SELECT 1` is refused with `CHECKPOINT runs alone`.
- Not inside a transaction block: after `BEGIN` it is refused (SQLSTATE `25001`); `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK` first.
- Your changes are safe without it: every commit is in the log on the disk before KarelaDB answers. `CHECKPOINT` only moves the work of writing the data files to a moment you choose. See [data formats](data-formats.md) for when KarelaDB checkpoints by itself.
- On a read-only database there is nothing to write, and it answers at once.

**Example: Write out what a load left waiting** (sample data: sample)

```sql
CHECKPOINT;
```

Result:

```text
checkpoint done: every change is in the files
```

## kareladb backup

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb backup <db> <backups-dir> [--hard-links] [--keep-daily N] [--keep-weekly N] [--data-dir <folder>]
```

Makes a backup of a **closed** database into a new folder inside `<backups-dir>`, then reads the whole backup again. Only then it prints `backup created and verified`.

| Option | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `<db>` | A database name in the data folder, or a folder path | required |
| `<backups-dir>` | The folder for backups. It is created when missing. For a database **name**, the backup goes to `<backups-dir>/<name>`. | required |
| `--hard-links` | Hard links instead of copies for the data files: very fast, no extra space, but **no protection** from disk damage (see below). The log files are always copied. | copies |
| `--keep-daily N` | After the backup, keep the newest backup of each of the last `N` days | 7 (when only `--keep-weekly` is given) |
| `--keep-weekly N` | After the backup, keep the newest backup of each of the last `N` weeks (weeks start on Sunday, UTC) | 4 (when only `--keep-daily` is given) |

- **Exit code:** `0` = the backup is made and verified. `1` = error (for example `the database is open in another program`). `2` = damage (the backup failed its check).
- **Without `--keep-daily` and `--keep-weekly` nothing is deleted.** With one of them, backups that no rule keeps are deleted, and each one prints `removed old backup ...`. The newest backup is always kept. Days count only days that have a backup.
- **Backup folder names are UTC time**: `20260911-081906-660` = 2026-09-11 08:19:06.660 UTC = 14:04 in Nepal (+05:45).
- Inside: `backup.kdb` (the list, written last), `files/` (the data files) and `wal/` (the log needed). A folder whose name ends in `.partial` is an unfinished backup; it is never used.
- **Put the backups on another disk** (`E:\kdb_backups`). One broken disk must not destroy both.
- **Hard links** share the same disk sectors as the database. If the disk goes bad, both are lost. Use them only as an extra undo point before a big import, never as the only backup.
- A running server has the database open, so `kareladb backup` fails with `the database is open in another program. Stop it first, or run BACKUP DATABASE in that server's console or API.`
- **Watch the path:** `kareladb backup` on a folder that does not exist makes a new empty database there and backs it up (`0 files`) with exit code `0`. Check the output of a scheduled backup.

**Command line: A daily backup that keeps 7 daily and 4 weekly backups** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb backup market backups --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 4
kareladb backups backups
```

Output:

`> kareladb backup market backups --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 4`

```text

  9 files, 190.0 KB, log up to 30
```

`> kareladb backups backups`

```text

20261024-061845-161    2026-10-24 12:03:45       9   190.0 KB           30
1 backups
```

kareladb backup market backups
kareladb backup market backups --keep-daily 1 --keep-weekly 1

## kareladb backups

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb backups <backups-dir>
```

Lists the finished backups in a folder, **newest first**.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `BACKUP` | Folder name (UTC time) |
| `CREATED` | When it was made, in the **local time** of this computer |
| `FILES`, `SIZE` | Data files and total size (data and log) |
| `LOG LSN` | The backup holds every change up to this log position |

- **Exit code:** `0`; `1` when the folder does not exist.
- Unfinished (`.partial`) and unreadable folders are not listed. It does **not** check the backups: use [kareladb verify-backup](#kareladb-verify-backup).
- For a database name in the data folder, list `<backups-dir>/<name>`.

**Command line** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb backup market backups
kareladb backups backups
```

Output:

`> kareladb backup market backups`

```text
backup created and verified: backups/20261024-061845-233
  9 files, 190.0 KB, log up to 30
```

`> kareladb backups backups`

```text
BACKUP                 CREATED               FILES       SIZE      LOG LSN
20261024-061845-233    2026-10-24 12:03:45       9   190.0 KB           30
1 backups
```

**Command line: A folder that does not exist** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb backups no-such-folder
```

Output:

```text
error: Not found: list 'no-such-folder': Windows error 3
```

exit code 1

## kareladb verify-backup

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb verify-backup <backup-dir>
```

Reads **one** whole backup again: every data file and block against its checksum, every log file, and that the log reaches the end the backup promises.

- **Exit code:** `0` = `OK: backup is intact`. `2` = problems, one `PROBLEM:` line each. A folder that is not a backup also gives `2`.
- `<backup-dir>` is one backup folder, like `E:\kdb_backups\20260911-081906-660`, not the folder of all backups.
- A backup you never tested is not a backup. Verify old backups now and then, and do a test restore once a month.

The help build cannot know the name of a new backup folder, so this is real output from [chapter 9](../tutorial/09-backup-and-safety.md):

```powershell
$newest = Get-ChildItem backups -Directory | Sort-Object Name | Select-Object -Last 1
kareladb verify-backup "backups\$($newest.Name)"
"exit code: $LASTEXITCODE"
```

```text
OK: backup is intact
exit code: 0
```

**Command line: The folder of all backups is not one backup** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb backup market backups
kareladb verify-backup backups
```

Output:

`> kareladb backup market backups`

```text
backup created and verified: backups/20261024-061845-303
  9 files, 190.0 KB, log up to 30
```

`> kareladb verify-backup backups`

```text
PROBLEM: backup.kdb: open 'backups/backup.kdb': Windows error 2
error: Corruption: backup.kdb: open 'backups/backup.kdb': Windows error 2
```

exit code 2

## kareladb restore

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb restore <backup-dir> <new-folder> [--logs-from <old-db-folder>] [--until "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM[:SS]"]
```

Makes a **new** database folder from a backup. The old database is not touched.

| Option | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `<backup-dir>` | One backup folder (`backups\20260911-081906-660`) | required |
| `<new-folder>` | The new database folder. It must not exist, or be empty. | required |
| `--logs-from <old-db-folder>` | Also take the **newer log** from the old database, so changes made **after** the backup come back too | only the backup |
| `--until "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM[:SS]"` | Replay the log only up to this time, in the **local time** of this computer. Changes made in that second are included. | the end of the log |

- **Exit code:** `0` = restored. `1` = error (the target is not empty, a wrong `--until`). `2` = the backup is damaged (`pick another one`). A wrong backup path gives the same message and `2`.
- **First it verifies the backup.** Every copied file is checked again.
- `--until` earlier than the backup itself is refused: `this backup already contains changes made after the requested time; pick an older backup`.
- `--logs-from` only uses a log of the **same** database and history; another database's log is ignored with a note.
- The log is replayed the first time the new database is opened. Run `kareladb check <new-folder>` before you use it.
- A restored database has no older file versions yet; they appear again as data changes.
- `<new-folder>` is a folder path. To use it as a database in the data folder, restore into `<data folder>\<name>`.

**A story: an UPDATE without WHERE.** At about 14:05 someone ran `UPDATE ochl_day SET close = 0`. The newest backup was from 14:04. Restore the backup, add the newer log from the old database, and stop one second before the mistake. Real commands and output from [chapter 9](../tutorial/09-backup-and-safety.md) (the help build cannot run this, because it cannot know the backup's folder name):

```powershell
$backup = Get-ChildItem backups -Directory | Sort-Object Name | Select-Object -Last 1
kareladb restore "backups\$($backup.Name)" market-restored --logs-from market --until "2026-09-11 14:05:10"
kareladb sql market-restored "SELECT time, symbol, close FROM ochl_day WHERE time >= '2026-09-10' ORDER BY symbol, time"
```

```text
stopped at the requested time: changes after LSN 36 are not restored
restored 9 data files from backups\20260911-142715-556 plus 1 newer log segments; the log (up to LSN 36) is replayed on first open
restored into market-restored
time                     | symbol | close
-------------------------+--------+------
2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z | CITY  | 504.9
2026-09-13T00:00:00.000Z | CITY  | 508.2
2026-09-14T00:00:00.000Z | CITY  |   511
2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z | COAST   | 376.1
2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z | VOLT  | 191.2
(5 rows, 0.2 ms)
```

The prices are back. The row of 2026-09-14 was added **after** the backup but **before** the mistake, and it is there too.

Then switch over: stop the server, rename `market` to `market-broken` and `market-restored` to `market`, start the server. Keep `market-broken` until you are sure. With a running server, [restore while running](#restore-online) does all of this without a stop.

A target folder that is not empty (real output from chapter 9):

```text
error: Already exists: restore target is not empty: market-restored
```

**Command line: --until must be a local time like 2026-09-11 14:30** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb restore backups/20260911-081906-660 market-restored --until "11.09.2026 14:30"
```

Output:

```text
error: --until must look like "2026-09-11 14:30" or "2026-09-11 14:30:15"
```

exit code 1

**Command line: Not a backup folder** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb restore no-such-backup market-restored
```

Output:

```text
error: Corruption: the backup is damaged; pick another one
  backup.kdb: open 'no-such-backup/backup.kdb': Windows error 3
```

exit code 2

<a id="restore-online"></a>

## Restore while the server runs

Syntax:

```sql
POST /api/restore            {"database": "market", "as": "market_check", "until": "2026-09-24 14:05:09"}
POST /api/databases/swap     {"database": "market", "with": "market_check"}
```

The same as `kareladb restore`, without stopping anything:

1. **Restore** a backup of `market` into a **new** database `market_check`. `market` keeps running and is not touched.
2. **Check** `market_check`: run a few queries, `CHECK TABLE`.
3. **Swap**: `market` gets the restored data, `market_check` the data `market` had. Users, rights and settings (read-only, dialect, old log, timers, pins) stay with the name `market`.
4. Drop `market_check` when you are sure.

| `until` | What comes back |
|---|---|
| not given | the backup as it was |
| a time (`2026-09-24 14:05:09`, UTC unless it ends in `Z` or `+05:45`), or `until_ms` | the backup, then `market`'s own log up to that time: **point in time** |
| `latest` | the backup, then all of `market`'s log: a copy as of now |

- The newest backup made before `until` is used, or name one with `"backup": "20260924-120000-000"`.
- In the console: **Health** > **Restore a backup**, then **Swap in**.
- The swap needs both databases unused: an open PostgreSQL connection or session on either gives `in use`; close it and try again.
- Details: [POST /api/restore](http-server-info.md#api-restore) and [POST /api/databases/swap](http-server-info.md#api-swap).

<a id="pitr-window"></a>

### How far back a point in time can go

A restore to a time starts from a backup made **before** it and replays the database's log from there. The log older than the data files is kept in `wal_archive`, up to its size limit (`wal_archive_mb`, 1 GB per database by default; [Settings](console-settings.md#wal-archive)). When the oldest kept log starts after a backup ended, that backup can only be restored as it was.

`GET /api/backups` says how far back you can go now:

Syntax:

```sql
"point_in_time": {"possible": true, "from": "2026-09-23T10:00:00.000Z", "from_backup": "20260923-100000-000", ...}
```

- `from` is the earliest time you can restore to; anything from there to now works.
- `possible: false` with `why`: the kept log does not reach the newest backup. Make a backup now, and raise `wal_archive_mb` or back up more often.
- Rule of thumb: `wal_archive_mb` must hold the log written between **two** backups. A database that writes 300 MB of log a day and backs up daily needs at least 300 MB; 100 MB gives a point in time only for the last few hours.

<a id="restore-drill"></a>

## A monthly restore drill

A backup you never restored is a hope, not a backup. Once a month, with the server running:

| Step | How | Pass when |
|---|---|---|
| 1. restore the newest backup into a new name | `POST /api/restore {"database":"market","as":"drill_2026_09"}` (or **Health** > **Restore a backup**) | `"opened": true` |
| 2. check it | `POST /api/check?db=drill_2026_09` | `"ok": true` |
| 3. compare | `SELECT count(*)` of the main tables in both, and the newest row time | the counts match the backup's time |
| 4. a point in time | the same with `"until"` an hour ago | it opens, rows up to that hour |
| 5. the copy off the server | copy one backup back from the remote (rclone, S3) into the backup folder and restore it | it restores |
| 6. clean up | `DROP DATABASE drill_2026_09` | |
| 7. write it down | date, backup used, time taken | |

Time step 1: that is how long a real restore takes. If `point_in_time` says `possible: false`, raise `wal_archive_mb`.

**HTTP: Step 1 and 6 of a drill: restore the newest backup, then drop the copy** (sample data: sample)

```http
POST /api/backup
###
POST /api/restore
Content-Type: application/json

{"as": "drill_check"}
###
POST /exec?db=drill_check
Content-Type: text/plain

SELECT count(*) FROM ochl_day
###
DELETE /api/databases/drill_check
```

<a id="daily-plan"></a>

## A daily backup plan

Syntax:

```sql
after the market closes:  kareladb backup <db> <other disk> --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 4
right after:               kareladb check <db>
once a week:               copy the newest backup to a third place
once a month:              a restore drill (below), then a few queries
```

The plan below is for market data that stops arriving at 15:00 local time (the examples use Nepal time and a Sunday-to-Thursday trading week, as on some exchanges). For logs, sensor readings or an app, pick the quietest hour of your own day. Do this every working day:

| When (local time) | What | How |
|---|---|---|
| after 15:00, when imports are done | Backup to **another disk** | `kareladb backup` (server stopped) or `POST /api/backup` (server running). Keep 7 daily + 4 weekly. |
| right after the backup | Check the database | `kareladb check` or `POST /api/check`. Exit code `2` or `"ok":false`: act now. |
| every day | Read the log of the backup script | |
| after each backup | Copy it to a third place (another PC, NAS, cloud) | [--backup-command](backup-schedule.md#backup-command), or `robocopy`, `rsync` or your backup tool |
| once a month | **Test restore** and run a few queries | the [restore drill](#restore-drill), or `kareladb restore <backup> D:\restore-test`, then `kareladb sql D:\restore-test "SELECT count(*) FROM ochl_day"` |
| before a big import or a schema change | An extra backup | `kareladb backup ... --hard-links` is fine here |

**The script** (Windows PowerShell; save as `D:\kdb-work\daily-backup.ps1`; not run here):

```powershell
# daily-backup.ps1 - backup and check after the market closes. Use full paths in a scheduled task.
$Kdb     = "D:\KarelaDB\build\bin\kareladb.exe"
$Data    = "D:\kdb\market"
$Backups = "E:\kdb_backups"
$Log     = "D:\kdb-work\backup-log.txt"

Add-Content $Log "---- $(Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss')"

$out = & $Kdb backup $Data $Backups --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 4 2>&1 | ForEach-Object { "$_" }
$code = $LASTEXITCODE
Add-Content $Log $out
if ($code -ne 0) { Add-Content $Log "BACKUP FAILED (exit code $code)"; exit $code }

$out = & $Kdb check $Data 2>&1 | ForEach-Object { "$_" }
$code = $LASTEXITCODE
Add-Content $Log $out
if ($code -ne 0) { Add-Content $Log "CHECK FOUND A PROBLEM (exit code $code)"; exit $code }
```

**Windows Task Scheduler**, Sunday to Thursday at 15:30 (run PowerShell as Administrator; not run here):

```powershell
$action  = New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute "powershell.exe" `
             -Argument "-NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File D:\kdb-work\daily-backup.ps1" `
             -WorkingDirectory "D:\kdb-work"
$trigger = New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Weekly -DaysOfWeek Sunday,Monday,Tuesday,Wednesday,Thursday -At 15:30
Register-ScheduledTask -TaskName "KarelaDB daily backup" -Action $action -Trigger $trigger
Start-ScheduledTask -TaskName "KarelaDB daily backup"     # test it once, then read the log
```

**Linux cron** (`crontab -e`; Sunday=0 to Thursday=4, computer time; not run here):

```bash
30 15 * * 0-4  /usr/local/bin/kareladb backup /srv/kareladb/data/market /mnt/backup/kdb --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 4 >> /var/log/kdb-backup.log 2>&1 && /usr/local/bin/kareladb check /srv/kareladb/data/market >> /var/log/kdb-backup.log 2>&1
```

**If `kareladb serve` runs all day**, let the server do it: `--backups E:\kdb_backups --backup-schedule "daily 15:30" --backup-copy F:\kdb_copy` makes, checks and copies a backup of every database each day, with no script (see [backups on a schedule](backup-schedule.md)). To do it from a script instead, ask the server. It keeps 7 daily and 4 weekly backups by itself (not run here):

```powershell
$r = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri "http://127.0.0.1:9900/api/backup?db=market"
$c = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri "http://127.0.0.1:9900/api/check?db=market"
if (-not $c.ok) { "CHECK FOUND A PROBLEM: $($c.problems -join '; ')"; exit 2 }
```

With `--token` or users, add `-Headers @{ Authorization = "Bearer <token>" }` (see [HTTP login](http-login.md)).

<a id="after-damage"></a>

## After damage: what to do

Syntax:

```sql
1. stop       2. copy the folder       3. kareladb check <db>
4. kareladb repair <db> --backups <dir>     5. kareladb check <db>
6. if still damaged: kareladb restore <newest backup> <new folder> --logs-from <db>
```

Messages like `failed its checksum`, `DAMAGED`, `the end of the log is damaged`, or exit code `2`:

1. **Stop** the server and every program that uses the database.
2. **Copy** the whole database folder to a safe place (`Copy-Item D:\kdb\market E:\damaged-copy -Recurse`). Then nothing you try can make it worse.
3. `kareladb check <db>` to see what is damaged.
4. `kareladb repair <db> --backups <backups-dir>`. It uses the previous file version, then the backups, and replays the log. See [kareladb repair](cli-maintenance.md#kareladb-repair).
5. `kareladb check <db>` again. When it says `OK: no damage found`, start the server again.
6. If the repair says `Some damage could not be repaired`: `kareladb restore <newest backup> <new folder> --logs-from <db>`, check the new folder, and switch folders.
7. If needed log records are damaged and no backup has them: `kareladb restore ... --logs-from` keeps everything up to the damage. `kareladb repair <db> --accept-log-loss` is the **last** choice: it opens the database and the changes in the damaged part are lost.
8. Find out **why**: disk errors in the Windows Event Viewer, a failing SSD (`smartctl`). Replace bad hardware.

- After a crash or a killed server, `last shutdown: not clean` is normal: KarelaDB replays the log, and confirmed changes are not lost. That is not damage.
- A write that the crash cut in half at the very end of the log is dropped by itself, as if the power had gone a moment earlier.

**Command line: Steps 3 to 5 on a healthy database** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb check market
kareladb repair market --backups backups
kareladb check market
```

Output:

`> kareladb check market`

```text
checked 14 files (76.1 KB) and 1 log segments
OK: no damage found
```

`> kareladb repair market --backups backups`

```text
manifest copy: a, last shutdown: clean
replayed 0 transactions after LSN 30, last LSN 30

Nothing to repair.
```

`> kareladb check market`

```text
checked 14 files (76.1 KB) and 1 log segments
OK: no damage found
```

<!-- docs/backup-schedule.md -->

# Backups on a schedule

> kareladb serve makes a verified backup of every database at set times, checks a second copy on another disk, runs your command to copy each backup off the server, and warns when the last good backup is old.

- Category: Backup, check, repair, restore
- Keywords: backup schedule, scheduled backup, nightly backup, daily backup, automatic backup, second copy, copy to another disk, offsite, off-site, S3, rclone, scp, remote storage, backup command, backup status, backup warning, default backup folder, \_backups, KARELADB\_BACKUP\_DIR, KARELADB\_BACKUP\_SCHEDULE, KARELADB\_BACKUP\_COMMAND, KARELADB\_BACKUP\_KEEP\_DAILY, KARELADB\_BACKUP\_KEEP\_WEEKLY, backup\_dir, backup\_schedule, backup\_command, --backups, --backup-schedule, --backup-copy, --backup-command, --backup-warn-hours, --keep-daily, --keep-weekly, daily, hourly, every
- See also: [Backup, check, repair and restore](backup-and-safety.md), [kareladb serve](cli-serve.md), [kareladb info, check, repair, dump-file](cli-maintenance.md), [Health, info, check and backup over HTTP](http-server-info.md), [Protection - timeouts, limits, safe updates, read-only](protection.md), [Audit log](audit-log.md)

You do not need a scheduled task outside KarelaDB: `kareladb serve` makes the backups itself.

A backup does not stop the database. KarelaDB waits for an open transaction to end, writes a checkpoint, and then copies the files while reads and writes go on.

<a id="backup-settings"></a>

## Where the settings come from

Each backup setting is read when the server starts. The first of these wins: a flag, `kareladb.conf` (the [Settings page](console-settings.md#backups) saves it there), the environment, the default.

| Setting | Flag | `kareladb.conf` | Environment | Default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| backup folder | `--backups <dir>` | `backup_dir` | `KARELADB_BACKUP_DIR` | `_backups` in the data folder (one folder served by its path: `_backups/<folder name>` next to it) |
| schedule | `--backup-schedule` | `backup_schedule` | `KARELADB_BACKUP_SCHEDULE` | `off` |
| daily backups kept | `--keep-daily` | `backup_keep_daily` | `KARELADB_BACKUP_KEEP_DAILY` | 7 |
| weekly backups kept | `--keep-weekly` | `backup_keep_weekly` | `KARELADB_BACKUP_KEEP_WEEKLY` | 4 |
| copy command | `--backup-command` | `backup_command` | `KARELADB_BACKUP_COMMAND` | none |

- A server with a data folder always has a backup folder: `<data folder>/_backups`, one sub-folder per database. In Docker that is `/data/_backups`, inside the volume, so a rebuild keeps it. `BACKUP DATABASE` and **Backup now** work without any setting.
- `off` as the folder turns backups off. `_backups` cannot be a database name.
- The default folder is on the **same disk** as the data. Copy the backups off the server too: [--backup-command](#backup-command) or [--backup-copy](#backup-copy).
- A folder served by its path (`kareladb serve D:\kdb\market`) backs up into `D:\kdb\_backups\market`: the folder a data-folder server in `D:\kdb` would use for the database `market`, so both keep one set of backups. It is next to the database folder, never inside it.
- The Settings page can save the schedule and what is kept, not the copy command: a command runs programs on the server, so only whoever can edit `kareladb.conf` (or the server's start command) sets it.

**Command line: The default backup folder in the start-up lines**

```bash
kareladb serve
```

Output:

```text
cold store 'archive': folder ./cold-archive
KarelaDB 0.2.0-dev
  console   http://127.0.0.1:9900
  data      ./kdb-data (from KDB_DATA_DIR; one folder per database)
  default   default (used when a request names no database)
  backups   ./kdb-data/_backups/<database name> (from default)
  access    no token
  capacity  32 HTTP threads (default), 500 PostgreSQL connections (default), lock wait 5 s (default)
  lanes     reads using 100 ms of CPU (three times in a row) wait for one of 16 heavy slots, at most 16 HTTP in line (--lanes on)
  reads     32 reads run at once (the CPUs, at least 2; follows the CPU limit), the rest wait in line (--read-slots)
  commits   synced to disk before they are confirmed (--sync-commits always)
  time zone Asia/Katmandu (the computer's); also timers and backup schedules
  readers   read while a long trigger or CALL writes (--reader-yield on); idle open transaction rolled back after 30 s (default)
  memory    26.95 GB for the whole process (85% of the machine's memory); table data 512.0 MB of it (--memory)
  cpu       32 CPUs (the machine's); 16 query threads (half of the CPUs, follows the limit), limits checked every 10 s
  limits    statement timeout 1 min, result memory 1.00 GB, 5000000 groups, 32 statements per user
  safety    writes allowed; DROP TABLE kept 7 days (UNDROP TABLE); audit log on (SHOW AUDIT)
  logs      slow queries >= 1000 ms to ./kdb-data/_logs/slow_queries.jsonl; pg_stat_statements on; metrics at /metrics
  recovery  the default database is created when it is first used

Press Ctrl+C to stop.
```

<a id="daily-recipe"></a>

## Set a daily backup

Backups are on by default, but nothing makes one by itself until there is a schedule. Three steps:

1. Open **Settings > Backups** in the console, type `daily 16:30` as the schedule and press **Save**. Or send it with the token:

Syntax:

```sql
POST /api/settings   {"backup_schedule": "daily 16:30"}   ->  {"saved": true, "restart_required": true, ...}
```

2. The schedule is saved in `kareladb.conf` and used **from the next start**. Restart the server (the **Restart** button on the Settings page, or restart the service or container).
3. Check it: `GET /api/info` shows `"backup_schedule": {"schedule": "daily 16:30", "next_run_ms": ...}`, and the Settings page shows the schedule from `kareladb.conf`.

- In a container the time is UTC unless `kareladb serve --timezone` is set: `daily 16:30` is 22:15 in Nepal.
- Pick a time after the day's data is in. A backup does not stop reads or writes.
- Then set a [copy command](#backup-command), so a lost disk does not take the backups with it.

<a id="backup-schedule"></a>

## --backup-schedule

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb serve [--backups <dir>] --backup-schedule "daily 16:00" [--keep-daily 7] [--keep-weekly 4]
```

| Schedule | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `daily 16:00` | every day at 16:00 |
| `daily 02:00,14:00` | several times a day |
| `hourly`, `hourly :30` | every hour, at minute 0 (or 30) |
| `every 6h`, `every 30m` | counted from midnight, 5 minutes to 24 hours |
| `off` | no scheduled backups (the default) |

Times are the **local time of the computer**, or the zone of `kareladb serve --timezone` when it is set (in a zone without daylight saving, such as Nepal `+05:45`, `daily 16:00` is always the same hour; pick a time after your data for the day is in).

- **Returns:** the start-up lines show `schedule  backups daily 16:00, next 2026-09-12 16:00:00`. Each backup writes a line: `backup of 'market' OK: 12 files, 3.4 MB, 850 ms, ...` or `backup of 'market' FAILED: ...`.
- **Notes:**
  - Every database of the data folder and `_system` (users, audit log) are backed up into `<dir>/<name>`. Each backup is read back and checked before it counts.
  - Old backups are removed by `--keep-daily` and `--keep-weekly` (7 and 4).
  - Each backup is in the [audit log](audit-log.md) (`event = 'backup'`).

| Start error | Why |
|---|---|
| `a backup schedule needs a backup folder: add --backups <dir> (or KARELADB_BACKUP_DIR)` | a schedule with the folder `off` |
| `--backup-copy needs a backup schedule (the copy is made after each scheduled backup)` | a copy without a schedule |
| `the backup schedule (--backup-schedule): the backup interval must be from 5 minutes to 24 hours` | `every 1m` and the like |

These stop the start only when the flags themselves clash. When the folder
`off` comes from `kareladb.conf` or `KARELADB_BACKUP_DIR`, the server starts anyway with
`warning: backups are off ... starting without scheduled backups`, so the
console stays reachable to fix it. The Settings page refuses to save such a
clash: send `{"backup_dir": "off", "backup_schedule": "off"}` to turn both off.

**Command line: Backups every day at 16:00 local time**

```bash
kareladb serve --backups backups --backup-schedule "daily 16:00"
```

Output:

```text
cold store 'archive': folder ./cold-archive
KarelaDB 0.2.0-dev
  console   http://127.0.0.1:9900
  data      ./kdb-data (from KDB_DATA_DIR; one folder per database)
  default   default (used when a request names no database)
  backups   backups/<database name> (from --backups)
  access    no token
  capacity  32 HTTP threads (default), 500 PostgreSQL connections (default), lock wait 5 s (default)
  lanes     reads using 100 ms of CPU (three times in a row) wait for one of 16 heavy slots, at most 16 HTTP in line (--lanes on)
  reads     32 reads run at once (the CPUs, at least 2; follows the CPU limit), the rest wait in line (--read-slots)
  commits   synced to disk before they are confirmed (--sync-commits always)
  time zone Asia/Katmandu (the computer's); also timers and backup schedules
  readers   read while a long trigger or CALL writes (--reader-yield on); idle open transaction rolled back after 30 s (default)
  memory    26.95 GB for the whole process (85% of the machine's memory); table data 512.0 MB of it (--memory)
  cpu       32 CPUs (the machine's); 16 query threads (half of the CPUs, follows the limit), limits checked every 10 s
  limits    statement timeout 1 min, result memory 1.00 GB, 5000000 groups, 32 statements per user
  safety    writes allowed; DROP TABLE kept 7 days (UNDROP TABLE); audit log on (SHOW AUDIT)
  logs      slow queries >= 1000 ms to ./kdb-data/_logs/slow_queries.jsonl; pg_stat_statements on; metrics at /metrics
  schedule  backups daily 16:00, next 2026-10-24 16:00:00

Press Ctrl+C to stop.
```

**Command line: A schedule with backups turned off is refused**

```bash
kareladb serve --backups off --backup-schedule "daily 16:00"
```

Output:

```text
cold store 'archive': folder ./cold-archive
error: a backup schedule needs a backup folder: add --backups <dir> (or KARELADB_BACKUP_DIR)
```

exit code 1

<a id="backup-copy"></a>

## --backup-copy

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb serve --backups <dir> --backup-schedule "..." --backup-copy <dir on another disk>
```

After each scheduled backup, KarelaDB copies it to a second folder (another disk, a USB disk, a mounted network drive) and checks the copy there: every block checksum and every log checksum is read back from the copy. A backup on the same disk is lost with the disk.

- **Returns:** the log line says `copy checked: E:/kdb_copy/market/...` or `COPY FAILED: ...`.
- **Notes:** the copy keeps old backups by the same `--keep-daily` / `--keep-weekly`. For a cloud or another computer, use [--backup-command](#backup-command).

<a id="backup-command"></a>

## --backup-command

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb serve --backup-command "<command with {dir}, {database}, {name}>"
```

After **every** backup the server makes (the schedule, `BACKUP DATABASE`, **Backup now**, `POST /api/backup`), it runs this command to copy the backup off the server. KarelaDB has no cloud code of its own: the command is any tool you have installed and logged in (rclone, the AWS CLI, scp, robocopy).

| In the command | Becomes |
|---|---|
| `{dir}` | the new backup folder, full path |
| `{database}` | the database's name |
| `{name}` | the backup folder's own name, like `20260924-160000-123` |

- Each value is put in quotes for the shell. Without any placeholder the folder is added at the end.
- The command runs through `/bin/sh` (Linux, Docker) or `cmd.exe` (Windows). Exit code `0` is success.
- It never holds up the database: the backup is finished when the command starts. Commands run one at a time, in order; at most 100 wait.
- **Returns:** a line in the server log (`backup copy command for 'market' OK in 5200 ms: ...` or `FAILED (exit code 1) ... - <its last line>`), an event in the activity log, and `backup_command` in `/api/info` (below). The console shows `(copy failed)` next to **Last backup**.
- The tool must be inside the Docker image or on the host's `PATH`. Test the command by hand once.

Syntax:

```sql
rclone:   --backup-command "rclone copy {dir} remote:kdb/{database}/{name}"
AWS S3:   --backup-command "aws s3 cp --recursive {dir} s3://my-bucket/kdb/{database}/{name}"
scp:      --backup-command "scp -r {dir} backup@10.0.0.9:/srv/kareladb/{database}/"
Windows:  --backup-command "robocopy {dir} \\nas\kdb\{name} /E"
```

A copy made with `--backup-command` is a plain folder: to use it, copy it back and restore it ([kareladb restore](backup-and-safety.md#kareladb-restore), or put it in the backup folder and use [POST /api/restore](http-server-info.md#api-restore)).

**Command line: A command after each backup: here it only prints the folder**

```bash
kareladb serve --backup-command "echo copy {database} {name}"
```

Output:

```text
cold store 'archive': folder ./cold-archive
KarelaDB 0.2.0-dev
  console   http://127.0.0.1:9900
  data      ./kdb-data (from KDB_DATA_DIR; one folder per database)
  default   default (used when a request names no database)
  backups   ./kdb-data/_backups/<database name> (from default)
  copy      after each backup: echo copy {database} {name} (from --backup-command)
  access    no token
  capacity  32 HTTP threads (default), 500 PostgreSQL connections (default), lock wait 5 s (default)
  lanes     reads using 100 ms of CPU (three times in a row) wait for one of 16 heavy slots, at most 16 HTTP in line (--lanes on)
  reads     32 reads run at once (the CPUs, at least 2; follows the CPU limit), the rest wait in line (--read-slots)
  commits   synced to disk before they are confirmed (--sync-commits always)
  time zone Asia/Katmandu (the computer's); also timers and backup schedules
  readers   read while a long trigger or CALL writes (--reader-yield on); idle open transaction rolled back after 30 s (default)
  memory    26.95 GB for the whole process (85% of the machine's memory); table data 512.0 MB of it (--memory)
  cpu       32 CPUs (the machine's); 16 query threads (half of the CPUs, follows the limit), limits checked every 10 s
  limits    statement timeout 1 min, result memory 1.00 GB, 5000000 groups, 32 statements per user
  safety    writes allowed; DROP TABLE kept 7 days (UNDROP TABLE); audit log on (SHOW AUDIT)
  logs      slow queries >= 1000 ms to ./kdb-data/_logs/slow_queries.jsonl; pg_stat_statements on; metrics at /metrics
  recovery  the default database is created when it is first used

Press Ctrl+C to stop.
```

<a id="backup-warn-hours"></a>

## --backup-warn-hours

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb serve ... --backup-schedule "..." --backup-warn-hours 26        (0 = no warning)
```

Each database is checked on its own. When a database's newest good backup is older than this, the log says so once an hour, naming the database: `WARNING: the last good backup of 'sales' is 30 hours old ...`. `/api/info` and the console show the same warning.

- A database with no backup at all counts from when the server first saw it: `WARNING: database 'test_01' has no good backup yet (known for 27 hours) ...`. A database made after today's round is backed up by the next one, so it is not overdue before that.
- When several databases are overdue, the one waiting longest is named and the rest are counted: `... (and 12 more databases)`.
- The server reads the backup folders at start and every hour after, so a backup made by hand (`BACKUP DATABASE`) counts too. It never opens a database to do so.

<a id="backup-status"></a>

## Backup status in /api/info

Syntax:

```sql
GET /api/info  ->  "backup_schedule": {"schedule", "copy_to", "next_run_ms", "last_run_ms", "last_run_ok",
                                       "last_ok_ms", "running", "warning", "databases": [...]}
```

- **Returns:** `null` when there is no schedule. `databases` lists the last round: `database`, `ok`, `error`, `dir`, `files`, `bytes`, `started_ms`, `took_ms`, `copy_dir`, `copy_ok`, `copy_error`.
- `warning` is `""`, `the last good backup of 'x' is N hours old` or `database 'x' has no good backup yet (known for N hours)`, with `(and N more databases)` when several are overdue. `databases_overdue` is how many are.
- `last_ok_ms` is the newest good backup of the database whose newest backup is oldest (0 when a database has none).

Syntax:

```sql
GET /api/info  ->  "backup_command": {"set", "runs", "failed", "dropped", "queued", "running",
                                      "last": {"database", "dir", "ok", "exit_code", "output", "started_ms", "took_ms"}}
```

- `null` without a copy command. `output` is the end of what the command printed, shown to admins only (`""` for other users).

# Versions and upgrades

> A new KarelaDB opens the data of an older KarelaDB. An older KarelaDB refuses the data of a newer KarelaDB with "needs a newer KarelaDB" and changes nothing.

- Category: Backup, check, repair, restore
- Keywords: version, versions, upgrade, kareladb upgrade, kareladb version, SHOW VERSION, VERSION, feature list, stored-format feature, needs a newer KarelaDB, needs a newer KDB, newer KarelaDB, older KarelaDB, old data, compatibility, exit code 3, Newer format, 0A000, KDB\_TEST\_HIDE\_FEATURES, partition\_format\_2, block\_stats, auto\_meta, table\_grants, pg\_catalog\_parts, batched\_log\_sync, database\_settings, dedup\_change, plpgsql\_triggers, symbol\_partitions, round\_time\_zone, no feature name, catalog part, downgrade, kareladb downgrade, kareladb features, going back, older version, go back to an older KarelaDB, rollback
- See also: [Backup, check, repair and restore](backup-and-safety.md), [kareladb info, check, repair, dump-file](cli-maintenance.md), [The kareladb program (exit-codes)](cli-overview.md#exit-codes), [How KarelaDB stores data](data-formats.md), [Versions and upgrades (downgrade)](versions.md#downgrade)

The rule:

- A **newer** KarelaDB opens the data of an **older** KarelaDB, as it is. Nothing to convert.
- An **older** KarelaDB refuses the data of a **newer** KarelaDB with the message `this database needs a newer KarelaDB: it uses <feature>` (a build from before the KarelaDB name, 2026-10-22, says `needs a newer KDB`). It does not call the data damaged, it repairs nothing and it changes nothing.

How it works: every database keeps a **feature list** in its manifest. A feature is one change to what KarelaDB writes on disk, for example `json` (a JSON column) or `sequences` (`CREATE SEQUENCE`). KarelaDB adds a feature to the list **before** it writes the first data that needs it. When a database opens, KarelaDB reads the list first. A name it does not know means: a newer KarelaDB wrote this. Only schema statements (`CREATE`, `ALTER`, ...), first uses and checkpoints look at the list, so rows cost nothing extra.

A database made by a KarelaDB **before** feature lists (before 2026-09-12) has no list. It opens as always. KarelaDB works out its list from the tables, files and log, and saves it at the next checkpoint (or now, with [kareladb upgrade](#kareladb-upgrade)).

<a id="kareladb-version"></a>

## kareladb version <db>

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb version
kareladb version <db> [--data-dir <folder>]
```

Without `<db>`: this KarelaDB and every feature it can read. With `<db>`: the feature list of that database (read from its manifest, so it also works while a server has the database open).

- **Exit code:** `0`. `3` when the database uses a feature this KarelaDB does not know. `1` when the folder is not a database.
- A database without a list yet says `feature list: not saved yet`.

**Command line: This KarelaDB and the features it reads**

```bash
kareladb version
```

Output:

```text

  block_stats          0.2.0-dev (2026-09-11)   column stats section in partition files (count, min, max, sum per column)
  runs                 0.2.0-dev (2026-09-11)   log record 'C': rows of a bulk upsert kept as columns

  database_settings    0.2.0-dev (2026-09-12)   ALTER DATABASE ... SET READ ONLY (_system.database_settings)
  dialects             0.2.0-dev (2026-09-12)   ALTER DATABASE ... SET dialect (_system.database_dialects)
  pg_catalog_parts     0.2.0-dev (2026-09-12)   PostgreSQL column types, multi-column keys, foreign keys, expression and partial indexes (catalog parts 'T', 'K', 'F', 'X')
  sequences            0.2.0-dev (2026-09-12)   CREATE SEQUENCE: the "sequences" file and its log records
  batched_log_sync     0.2.0-dev (2026-09-11)   log segments in the batched format (header flag 1, 16-byte commit records): group commit and --sync-commits batch
  dedup_change         0.2.0-dev (2026-09-12)   ALTER TABLE ... DEDUP ENABLE / DISABLE: the DEDUP KEY of a table that already holds rows
  plpgsql_triggers     0.2.0-dev (2026-09-12)   PostgreSQL plpgsql trigger functions and FOR EACH ROW triggers in the "routines" file
  cached_views         0.2.0-dev (2026-09-13)   CREATE CACHED VIEW: which views are cached, and REFRESH ON COMMIT, in the "views" file

A database that uses a feature not in this list needs a newer KarelaDB (kareladb check exits with 3).
```

## SHOW VERSION

Syntax:

```sql
SHOW VERSION
```

This KarelaDB's version, and for the current database: the features it uses now and the list saved in its manifest. Every user may run it (it shows no data).

| item | value |
|---|---|
| `kareladb version` | the version of this KarelaDB |
| `database` | the current database |
| `features used` | what the database uses now |
| `feature list` | `saved: ...`, or `not saved yet (written by an older KarelaDB)` |
| `features this KarelaDB reads` | how many, and their names |

**Example: SHOW VERSION** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SHOW VERSION;
```

Result:

| item (STRING) | value (STRING) |
|---|---|
| kdb version | 0.2.0-dev |
| database | demo |
| features used | batched_log_sync, block_stats, compressed_log, partition_format_2 |
| feature list | saved: batched_log_sync, block_stats, compressed_log, partition_format_2 |
| features this KDB reads | 52: views, partition_format_2, block_stats, runs, auto_meta, json, bytes, check, indexes, routines, users, audit, table_grants, totp, trash, database_settings, dialects, pg_catalog_parts, sequences... |

(5 rows)

## kareladb upgrade

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb upgrade <db> [--backups <dir>] [--data-dir <folder>]
```

Makes a database ready for this KarelaDB, in three steps:

1. A **verified backup** into `--backups <dir>` (default: a folder `<db folder>-backups` next to the database; for a name in the data folder `<data folder>-backups/<name>`). Older backups there are kept.
2. Saves the database's **feature list** (and writes anything a newer format needs; this version needs nothing more).
3. Runs [kareladb check](cli-maintenance.md#kareladb-check).

- **Exit code:** `0` = done. `3` = the database needs a newer KarelaDB (nothing was done, no backup). `2` = the check found damage (the backup from step 1 is named). `1` = it could not run (for example the database is open in a server: stop it first).
- You do not have to run it: KarelaDB saves the list by itself at the next checkpoint. Run it when you want the backup, or before you give the folder to another KarelaDB.
- After an upgrade, an older KarelaDB that does not know one of the listed features refuses the database. Keep the backup if you may need to go back to that older KarelaDB.

**Command line: Upgrade a database** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb upgrade market --backups backups
```

Output:

```text
KarelaDB 0.2.0-dev, database market
saved feature list: batched_log_sync, block_stats, compressed_log, partition_format_2
1/3 verified backup into backups ...
    backups/20261024-061947-810 (9 files, 190.0 KB)
2/3 saving the feature list ...
    features used: batched_log_sync, block_stats, compressed_log, partition_format_2
    (no files need to be written again for this KarelaDB version)
3/3 check ...
checked 14 files (76.1 KB) and 1 log segments
OK: no damage found

Upgrade done. An older KarelaDB build that does not know one of these features now refuses this database with "needs a newer KarelaDB".
```

<a id="downgrade"></a>

## Going back to an older version

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb features <db> | --data-dir <folder>
kareladb downgrade <db> | --data-dir <folder> --to <version> [--backups <dir>] [--no-backup]
kareladb downgrade <db> | --data-dir <folder> --known <feature,feature,...>
```

An older KarelaDB opens a database again when the data uses nothing newer than that KarelaDB reads. The feature list only grows, so it may still name a feature you stopped using: a dropped column, a dropped procedure. `kareladb downgrade` takes those names off.

`kareladb features` shows what each database uses **now**, and what uses it. It changes nothing.

`kareladb downgrade` works in three steps:

1. A **verified backup** (as [kareladb upgrade](#kareladb-upgrade) makes it). `--no-backup` skips it.
2. A checkpoint, so nothing waits in the log. Then the feature list becomes exactly what the data uses.
3. [kareladb check](cli-maintenance.md#kareladb-check).

| Option | What it means |
|---|---|
| `--to 2026-09-24` | a KarelaDB built on that day: it reads every feature written since that day or before |
| `--to 0.2.0-dev` | the last KarelaDB of that version |
| `--known views,indexes,...` | exactly these features: the names `kareladb version` of the older KarelaDB prints |
| `--data-dir <folder>` without `<db>` | every database of the data folder, `_system` too. All are checked before any is changed. |

- **Refused** when the data uses a feature the older KarelaDB does not read. It names the table, column, index, view or routine that uses it, and how to remove it. Nothing is changed, and no backup is made.
- A dropped table stays in the [trash](trash.md) and still counts. Remove it for good with `DROP TABLE _dropped_<time>_<name>`.
- It never rewrites data into an older form. To go back, first stop using the newer feature, for example `ALTER TABLE prices DROP COLUMN amount` for a `NUMERIC(30, 4)` column.
- A dropped column stays in the table's files written before the drop, and an older KarelaDB refuses such a file. `kareladb features` names these files ("a dropped or changed ... column still in N partition file(s)"). You do nothing: in step 2, `kareladb downgrade` writes those partitions again without the column, and says how many.
- Stop the server first. Then start the older KarelaDB on the data.
- **Exit code:** `0` = done. `1` = refused, or it could not run. `2` = the check found damage (the backup is named).

**Command line: What a database uses now** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb features market
```

Output:

```text
database market
in use now (4):
  partition_format_2     0.2.0-dev (2026-09-11)
      used by: the table files
  block_stats            0.2.0-dev (2026-09-11)
      used by: the table files
  batched_log_sync       0.2.0-dev (2026-09-11)
      used by: the log (group commit writes every log segment this way)
  compressed_log         0.2.0-dev (2026-10-02)
      used by: the log (big commits are written as packed records)
```

**Command line: Let a KarelaDB of 24 Sep 2026 open the data** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb downgrade market --to 2026-09-24 --backups backups
```

Output:

```text
KarelaDB 0.2.0-dev: downgrade to 2026-09-24

database market
1/3 verified backup into backups ...
    backups/20261024-061947-962 (9 files, 190.0 KB)
2/3 checkpoint, then the feature list ...
    list before: batched_log_sync, block_stats, compressed_log, partition_format_2
    list now:    batched_log_sync, block_stats, partition_format_2
    taken off (no longer used): compressed_log
3/3 check ...
checked 14 files (76.1 KB) and 1 log segments
OK: no damage found

Downgrade done. Stop this KarelaDB and start the older one on the data. Opening the data with this KarelaDB again is fine: it adds features to the list as they are used.
```

**Command line: Refused: a 128-bit NUMERIC column is in use**

Setup:

```text
CREATE TABLE prices (id LONG, amount NUMERIC(30, 4));
```

```bash
kareladb downgrade market --to 2026-09-24 --no-backup
```

Output:

```text
KarelaDB 0.2.0-dev: downgrade to 2026-09-24

database market uses features the older KarelaDB does not read:
  decimal128             0.2.0-dev (2026-09-25)
      used by: column 'amount' of table 'prices' (NUMERIC with more than 18 digits)
      to remove: ALTER TABLE prices DROP COLUMN amount

Nothing was changed. Remove what is listed (a dropped table stays in the trash until DROP TABLE _dropped_<time>_<name>), or keep this KarelaDB. The command only goes back when the data uses nothing newer.
```

exit code 1

<a id="needs-newer"></a>

## "needs a newer KarelaDB"

Syntax:

```sql
error: this database needs a newer KarelaDB: it uses <feature> (a stored-format feature this KarelaDB build does not know). Nothing was changed
```

The database was written by a newer KarelaDB. **It is not damaged.**

A build from before the KarelaDB name (2026-10-22) says the same with the old name: `this database needs a newer KDB: it uses <feature> (a stored-format feature this KDB build does not know)`.

- Open it with that KarelaDB or a newer one. `kareladb version` on both programs shows what each can read.
- Do **not** run `kareladb repair` or `kareladb restore`: they would refuse too (exit code `3`).
- The same message comes for other things only a newer KarelaDB writes: a newer manifest or file format version, a log record type or a catalog part this KarelaDB does not know, a file name it does not know, or a backup of such a database.
- `kareladb check`, `kareladb repair`, `kareladb sql`, `kareladb version <db>` and `kareladb upgrade` end with **exit code 3**. Over HTTP it is status 500; on the PostgreSQL port SQLSTATE `0A000`.

<a id="features"></a>

## The features

| Feature | What a database with it has | Written since |
|---|---|---|
| `views` | `CREATE VIEW` (the "views" file) | 0.2.0-dev (2026-09-10) |
| `partition_format_2` | table partition files in format 2 | 2026-09-11 |
| `block_stats` | count, min, max and sum per column in partition files | 2026-09-11 |
| `runs` | log records of bulk upserts kept as columns (line protocol) | 2026-09-11 |
| `auto_meta` | AUTO id counters in the manifest | 2026-09-11 |
| `json`, `bytes` | `JSON` and `BYTES` columns | 2026-09-11 |
| `check` | `CHECK` constraints | 2026-09-11 |
| `indexes` | `CREATE INDEX`, `UNIQUE`, `FULLTEXT` | 2026-09-11 |
| `routines` | saved functions, procedures, triggers | 2026-09-11 |
| `users` | server users (in `_system`) | 2026-09-11 |
| `batched_log_sync` | log files in the batched form: group commit (the default) and `--sync-commits batch` write them, so every database has it | 2026-09-11 |
| `audit` | `ALTER TABLE ... SET AUDIT ON`, `_audit_log` | 2026-09-12 |
| `table_grants`, `totp` | `GRANT ... ON TABLE`, two-factor logins (in `_system`) | 2026-09-12 |
| `trash` | dropped tables kept for `UNDROP TABLE` | 2026-09-12 |
| `database_settings`, `dialects` | `ALTER DATABASE ... SET READ ONLY` / `SET dialect` (in `_system`) | 2026-09-12 |
| `pg_catalog_parts` | PostgreSQL types, multi-column keys, foreign keys, expression and partial indexes | 2026-09-12 |
| `sequences` | `CREATE SEQUENCE` | 2026-09-12 |
| `dedup_change` | `ALTER TABLE ... DEDUP ENABLE` / `DISABLE` on a table that already holds rows | 2026-09-12 |
| `plpgsql_triggers` | PostgreSQL `plpgsql` trigger functions and `FOR EACH ROW` triggers | 2026-09-12 |
| `cached_views` | `CREATE CACHED VIEW`: which views are cached and `REFRESH ON COMMIT`, kept in the "views" file | 2026-09-13 |
| `deferred_triggers` | `CREATE TRIGGER ... DEFERRED`: job records in the log, and the "trigger_queue" and "q/..." files of waiting jobs | 2026-09-13 |
| `materialized_views` | `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW`: the view's query in the catalog, refresh records in the log, waiting partitions in the manifest | 2026-09-13 |
| `table_ttl` | `TTL n DAYS` on a table, kept in the catalog | 2026-09-13 |
| `read_only_procedures` | `CREATE PROCEDURE ... READ ONLY`, kept with the procedure | 2026-09-24 |
| `dedup_insert` | `WITH (dedup_insert = 'upsert')` on a table, kept in the catalog | 2026-09-24 |
| `decimal128` | `NUMERIC(p, s)` columns with more than 18 digits (128 bits each) | 2026-09-25 |
| `uuid` | `UUID` columns, 16 bytes per value ([UUID](column-types.md#uuid)) | 2026-10-02 |
| `column_grants` | `GRANT SELECT (a, b) ON TABLE t` ([column rights](table-rights.md#column-rights); in `_system`, only once one is granted) | 2026-10-02 |
| `row_policies` | `CREATE POLICY`, `ALTER TABLE t ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` ([row rights](table-rights.md#row-rights); in `_system`, only once one is made) | 2026-10-02 |
| `dedup_generated_key` | a stored generated column in a `DEDUP KEY`, like [the minute of the time](partitions-and-dedup.md#minute-key) | 2026-09-25 |
| `symbol_partitions` | `PARTITION BY ..., SYMBOL(col)` ([split by symbol](partitions-and-dedup.md#partition-by-symbol)) | 2026-09-25 |
| `round_time_zone` | a column `TIMESTAMP ROUND 1d TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kathmandu'` ([TIME ZONE](sample-by.md#time-zone)) | 2026-09-25 |
| `enum_types` | `CREATE TYPE ... AS ENUM`: the types and their labels, kept in the catalog | 2026-09-25 |
| `row_ttl` | `WITH (ttl_column = c)`: [rows that expire](create-table.md#row-ttl), kept in the catalog | 2026-09-25 |
| `column_compression` | `SET (compression = on)` on a table and its packed partition files ([compression](partitions-and-dedup.md#compression)); `kareladb downgrade` writes the files plain again once the table is set to `off` | 2026-09-25 |
| `calendars` | `CREATE CALENDAR`: [trading calendars](calendars.md) (eras, holidays, extra trading days), kept in the catalog | 2026-09-25 |
| `materialized_view_sample_by` | a [materialized view](views.md#materialized-view) over a `SAMPLE BY` query (QuestDB's form) | 2026-09-26 |
| `comments` | `COMMENT ON TABLE / COLUMN`: [the comments](functions-postgres.md#comments) of tables and columns, kept in the catalog; `COMMENT ON ... IS NULL` removes one | 2026-09-26 |
| `partition_tails` | [tail files](partitions-and-dedup.md#tail-files) (`kareladb serve --tail-files on`): rows appended to a partition saved in extra files next to it; `kareladb downgrade` writes those partitions whole again | 2026-10-02 |
| `partition_deltas` | [delta files](partitions-and-dedup.md#delta-files) (on unless `KARELADB_NO_PARTITION_DELTA=1`): a few rows of a partition replaced, updated or deleted, saved in one extra file next to it; `kareladb downgrade` writes those partitions whole again | 2026-10-02 |
| `compressed_log` | [compressed log](backup-and-safety.md#compressed-log): a big commit's log records written packed (on unless `KARELADB_WAL_COMPRESS=off`), so every database this KarelaDB opens has it; `kareladb downgrade` to an older KarelaDB turns packing off by itself while it works | 2026-10-02 |
| `search_analyzer` | `CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX ... WITH (language = 'english')`: the [word analyzer](full-text-search.md#language) of a full-text index, kept in the catalog | 2026-10-02 |
| `fulltext_segments` | the words of full-text and JSON indexes saved in the folder `fts/` ([segments on disk](full-text-search.md#segments)). **Never put in a database's list:** an older KarelaDB ignores the folder, so it still opens the database; `kareladb downgrade` to a KarelaDB without it moves the folder's files to `_trash` | 2026-10-02 |
| `endpoints` | `CREATE ENDPOINT`: [saved queries served at GET /v/name](http-endpoints.md), kept with the functions and procedures | 2026-10-03 |
| `cold_storage` | `SET (cold_storage = ...)` on a table and its partitions moved to an object store ([cold storage](cold-storage.md)), kept as small stub files; an older build would take a stub for a damaged partition. The way back: `RESET (cold_storage)`, then `ALTER TABLE ... MOVE PARTITION ... FROM COLD` | 2026-10-22 |

- A feature stays in the list once it is there, even when you drop the table that used it. [kareladb downgrade](#downgrade) takes such names off.
- Programs made **before** feature lists do not read the list. They still refuse most new data (catalog parts, file formats) but not all of it: do not open new data with them.
- For tests only: the environment variable `KDB_TEST_HIDE_FEATURES=name,name` makes kareladb act like an older build that does not know those features.

<a id="no-feature-name"></a>

## Two options named late

Two table options were saved for a while as a new **part** of a table in the catalog, without a feature name. Since 2026-09-25 they have one: `symbol_partitions` and `round_time_zone`. KarelaDB adds the name to the list at the next checkpoint.

| Table option | Saved as | Written since | Named since |
|---|---|---|---|
| a column `TIMESTAMP ROUND 1d TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kathmandu'` | catalog part `R` | 2026-09-13 | 2026-09-25 (`round_time_zone`) |
| `PARTITION BY ..., SYMBOL(col)` | catalog part `P` | 2026-09-18 | 2026-09-25 (`symbol_partitions`) |

- Only a database with such a table gets the name. Every other database opens in an older KarelaDB as before.
- A build from before the feature name still refuses such a database safely: it finds a catalog part it does not know and stops with `needs a newer KDB` (its name then).

<a id="no-format-change"></a>

## Changes that need no format change

These newer changes write nothing an older KarelaDB cannot read. An older KarelaDB that knows the features in the database's list still opens it.

| Change | Since | Why the files stay the same |
|---|---|---|
| tables without a `DEDUP KEY` loaded as sorted runs | 2026-09-23 | the same run log record (`runs`) as tables with a key |
| skipping partitions and blocks by column stats, `count`/`min`/`max`/`sum` from saved stats | 2026-09-23 | partition files already had the stats (`block_stats`) |
| table write locks, group commit, reader yield | 2026-09-23 | only how writers take turns in memory |
| keys of dropped tables removed from the manifest | 2026-09-23 | fewer keys of a kind the manifest already had. See [manifest keys](data-formats.md#manifest-keys). |
| indexes built at open | 2026-09-23 | indexes are never stored |
| [pinned queries](pinned-queries.md) | 2026-09-23 | kept as rows of an ordinary table, `_pinned_queries` (in `_system`, or in the database of a server without a data folder) |
