<!-- docs/standby.md -->

# Standby server: a live read-only copy (--standby-of, kareladb promote)

> A second KarelaDB server that copies every database of a primary from its log, a moment behind, and serves reads.

- Category: Backup, check, repair, restore
- Keywords: standby, hot standby, replica, read replica, replication, failover, streaming, long poll, KARELADB\_STANDBY\_WAIT\_MS, --standby-of, --standby-token, KARELADB\_STANDBY\_OF, KARELADB\_STANDBY\_TOKEN, GET /api/wal, api/wal, GET /api/standby, api/standby, in\_hot\_standby, wal, log shipping, lsn, kareladb promote, POST /api/promote, api/promote, promote, failover, lag, replication lag, kdb\_standby\_lag\_seconds, 25006, read\_only\_sql\_transaction
- See also: [Cluster: automatic failover (--cluster-peers, kareladb witness)](cluster.md), [Backup, check, repair and restore](backup-and-safety.md), [Change stream and live subscriptions: changes('t'), GET /api/changes, GET /api/subscribe](change-stream.md), [kareladb serve](cli-serve.md), [Databases and the data folder](databases.md)

A **standby** is a second `kareladb serve` that keeps a copy of every database of another server, the **primary**. It reads the primary's log (the WAL) over HTTP and applies each transaction in order. The primary sends each commit as soon as it is on its disk, so the copy is usually a few milliseconds behind. Users of the standby can read; every change is made on the primary.

Use it to keep reports and dashboards off the primary, and to have a second copy on another computer.

A standby does not take over by itself when the primary dies: a person runs `kareladb promote`. For automatic failover, run a [cluster](cluster.md) instead: two data nodes and a small witness, where the leader is elected and a new one takes writes within about 6 seconds (3.6 to 6 s measured) ([what was tested](cluster.md#failures)).

<a id="start"></a>

## Start a standby

```bash
# the primary: any kareladb serve with a token
kareladb serve --data-dir D:/kdb-data --token <secret>

# the standby: another folder (another computer), pointing at the primary
kareladb serve --data-dir E:/kdb-copy --standby-of http://primary:9900 --standby-token <secret>
```

| Setting | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--standby-of URL` (`KARELADB_STANDBY_OF`) | the primary's address, `http://host:port` or `https://host:port` |
| `--standby-token T` (`KARELADB_STANDBY_TOKEN`) | what the standby sends to the primary: the primary's `--token`, or an API token of an admin |
| `KARELADB_STANDBY_WAIT_MS` | how long one request waits at the primary for the next commit (default 25000 ms, at least 1000, at most 55000). `0` turns streaming off: the standby then asks every `KARELADB_STANDBY_POLL_MS` |
| `KARELADB_STANDBY_POLL_MS` | how often an up-to-date standby asks again when it cannot wait at the primary (default 100 ms) |

<a id="streaming"></a>

## Streaming: how fast the copy follows

Each database is copied by a thread of its own. The thread asks the primary for the log after its last LSN and says it will wait (`wait=`). When nothing is new, the request waits on the primary. The primary's commit wakes it the moment the commit is on disk, and the answer goes out at once.

| | Before 2026-10-22 | Now |
|---|---|---|
| how the standby asks | every 100 ms, database after database | one waiting request per database |
| a big load in one database | the others waited for it | the others go on |
| requests while nothing changes | 10 a second per database | one every 25 s per database |

Measured on one PC (primary and standby on 2 CPUs each, in WSL), from the moment the primary confirmed a one-row commit until the standby showed the row:

| Load on the primary | Before (median / p99) | Now (median / p99) |
|---|---|---|
| none | 69 / 110 ms | 3.2 / 5.0 ms |
| a bulk load (500-row inserts) in another database | 1,435 / 1,945 ms | 1.1 / 7.6 ms |
| a bulk load in the same database | 855 / 1,405 ms | 150 / 278 ms |

With a bulk load in the same database, the standby has to apply all of that load first, one transaction after another, so the lag is the time to apply it. The primary's write speed was the same with and without the change.

A waiting request costs the primary a sleeping thread, not a worker: while it waits, another HTTP thread serves in its place (one kept from an earlier wait, so a commit does not start and end a thread), so `/exec` has all its `--http-threads` workers however many databases the standbys copy. At most 64 requests wait at once. A request that finds all 64 places taken is answered at once (`X-KDB-Waited: 0`), and that thread asks again after `KARELADB_STANDBY_POLL_MS`, as before.

A waiting request does not keep its database open: `DROP DATABASE` on the primary works while a standby waits on it.

The standby only asks the primary to wait when the primary's list of databases says it can (the header `X-KDB-Wal-Wait: 1`). A primary on a version before 2026-10-22 does not say so: the standby then asks it every `KARELADB_STANDBY_POLL_MS`, as before, and its waiting places stay free for `GET /api/changes`. Upgrade the primary too to get streaming.

The standby copies:

| What | How |
|---|---|
| rows: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, loads | as logged, in commit order, one whole transaction at a time |
| schema changes: CREATE, ALTER, DROP TABLE, indexes, views | as logged |
| partitions dropped by a TTL or `DROP PARTITION` | as logged by the primary |
| new and dropped databases | a new one is copied; a dropped one goes to `_trash` |
| users, rights and API tokens (`_system`) | as logged; logins on the standby use them |

<a id="read-only"></a>

## Read-only

On a standby every change is refused with `this server is a standby of http://...: it only reads; make changes on the primary`. That covers INSERT, DDL, `CREATE DATABASE` and user statements.

| Where | Answer |
|---|---|
| `POST /exec` | HTTP 403, `"sqlstate": "25006"` |
| `POST /write`, `POST /imp` | HTTP 403, `"sqlstate": "25006"` (before the body is read) |
| PostgreSQL port | error `25006` (read_only_sql_transaction), as on a PostgreSQL hot standby |

Timers, TTL checks, trigger jobs, materialized view refreshes and the audit log do not run there: the primary runs them, and their results come in its log.

PostgreSQL drivers see `in_hot_standby = on` and `default_transaction_read_only = on`, so `target_session_attrs=read-only` picks the standby.

<a id="status"></a>

## How far is it?

The lag, over every database:

| Where | Fields |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/stats` (any login) | `standby.lag_lsn`, `standby.lag_bytes`, `standby.lag_seconds`, `standby.connected` |
| `GET /metrics` | `kdb_standby`, `kdb_standby_connected`, `kdb_standby_lag_lsn`, `kdb_standby_lag_bytes`, `kdb_standby_lag_seconds`, `kdb_standby_applied_transactions_total` |
| the console | the status bar: `Standby (read-only) - lag 0.1 s` |

`lag_lsn` counts the log entries the primary has and the copy has not applied. `lag_bytes` is those entries in bytes, estimated from the bytes per entry copied so far. `lag_seconds` is how long the oldest of them has waited; when the primary cannot be reached, at least the time since it last answered. All three are 0 when the copy is up to date.

`GET /api/standby` (server admins) on the standby gives the detail:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `lag_lsn`, `lag_bytes`, `lag_seconds` | as above |
| `promoted` | `kareladb promote` ran: this server is a primary now |
| `connected`, `error` | the last request to the primary worked, or why not |
| `fetch_threads` | the threads copying a database each (streaming) |
| `databases[].applied_lsn` | the last LSN of the primary this copy holds |
| `databases[].primary_lsn`, `behind_lsn` | the end of the primary's log when last asked, and the difference |
| `databases[].last_commit_ms` | when the last applied transaction committed on the primary |
| `databases[].received_bytes` | log bytes copied since the standby started |
| `databases[].error` | why this database stopped copying |

<a id="promote"></a>

## Promote: the standby becomes the primary

When the primary is lost, make the standby the primary:

```bash
kareladb promote --url http://standby:9900 --token <secret>
```

That sends `POST /api/promote` (server admins). The standby stops copying (a transaction being applied ends first), and from that moment:

| What | After the promote |
|---|---|
| writes (HTTP, `/write`, `/imp`, PostgreSQL) | taken; the log goes on from the last LSN copied |
| PostgreSQL | new connections see `in_hot_standby = off` |
| TTL checks, sweeps, refreshes, trigger jobs, timers | run here (the Timers page shows up after the next restart) |
| `CREATE DATABASE`, users | allowed |
| `GET /api/standby` | `"promoted": true` |

A second promote answers 409. A server that is no standby answers 409 too.

To have this done by itself, with no person at 3 a.m., run a [cluster](cluster.md): two data nodes and a witness elect a new leader when the old one dies, and fence it so the two never both write.

Before you promote:

- Make sure the old primary is really gone, or stop it. Two primaries take different writes, and the copies cannot be joined again.
- Look at `lag_lsn`: what the primary committed and the standby had not copied is lost.

After the promote, start the server again **without** `--standby-of` (and drop `KARELADB_STANDBY_OF`); with it, it would be a standby again. To get a new standby, start one against the new primary. The old primary's folder cannot follow the new one: copy it again from a backup of the new primary.

<a id="seed"></a>

## Starting from a backup

From an empty data folder the standby copies each database from the start of its log. That works only while the primary still keeps its whole log (`ALTER DATABASE ... SET WAL_ARCHIVE`). Otherwise start the standby on a copy of the primary's data: a restored backup, or the data folder copied while the primary was stopped. The standby asks for the log from where that copy ends.

When the primary no longer keeps the log a database needs, or the two no longer fit (the primary's database was dropped and made again, or restored), that database stops copying and `databases[].error` says so: copy it again from a backup of the primary. The other databases go on. Equal LSNs are not trusted alone: with each request the standby sends the commit time of the last transaction it holds, and the primary checks that its own log has that same transaction there. A database the primary cannot open for a moment is left as it is on the standby, never dropped.

<a id="api-wal"></a>

## GET /api/wal

What the standby reads. Server admins only: it holds every row, and the users' password hashes.

| Request | Answer |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/wal` | the databases and where each one's log ends (`format=tsv`: one line each; `-` or `null` when the primary cannot open it right now) |
| `GET /api/wal?db=x&from=<lsn>[&max_bytes=n][&wait=ms][&prev_ms=t]` | the committed transactions of `x` from LSN `from` on, binary; `410` when that part of the log is gone; `409` when the transaction at LSN `from - 1` did not commit at `prev_ms` (another log) |

With `wait=ms` and nothing new yet, the answer waits up to that long and goes out as soon as the next commit is on disk. These headers come with each answer:

| Header | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `X-KDB-Durable-Lsn` | where the primary's log on disk ended when it was read |
| `X-KDB-More` | `1`: there is more right now, ask again at once |
| `X-KDB-Waited` | with `wait=`: `1` it waited, `0` every waiting place was taken and it answered at once |

The list (`GET /api/wal`) carries `X-KDB-Wal-Wait: 1`: this primary honours `wait=`.

Use HTTPS (`--tls-cert`) between computers: the log is sent as it is.

<!-- docs/cluster.md -->

# Cluster: automatic failover (--cluster-peers, kareladb witness)

> Two or three KarelaDB servers and a witness elect a leader; when the leader's computer dies, another takes over by itself in about 5 to 10 seconds.

- Category: Backup, check, repair, restore
- Keywords: cluster, failover, automatic failover, high availability, ha, leader, follower, election, raft, term, witness, kareladb witness, quorum, majority, lease, fencing, split brain, --cluster-peers, --node-id, --cluster-token, KARELADB\_CLUSTER\_PEERS, KARELADB\_NODE\_ID, KARELADB\_CLUSTER\_TOKEN, KARELADB\_ELECTION\_TIMEOUT\_MS, KARELADB\_LEASE\_MS, KARELADB\_CLUSTER\_HEARTBEAT\_MS, GET /api/cluster, api/cluster, 421, 25006, 08007, \_diverged, kareladb cluster diverged, DELETE /api/cluster/diverged, copy id
- See also: [Standby server: a live read-only copy (--standby-of, kareladb promote)](standby.md), [Backup, check, repair and restore](backup-and-safety.md), [kareladb serve](cli-serve.md)

A **cluster** is three voters that choose one **leader** among them. The leader is a primary: it takes every change. The other data nodes are its [standbys](standby.md): they copy its log and serve reads. When the leader's computer dies, the others notice within about 5 seconds and elect a new leader, which takes changes from then on. Nobody has to run `kareladb promote`.

Two leaders never both write: a leader that loses touch with the others stops taking changes **before** anyone else can be elected (see [Fencing](#fencing)).

<a id="shape"></a>

## The shape

| Layout | Computers | Good | Not so good |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 data nodes + 1 witness | 2 big, 1 tiny | cheap: the witness holds no data, only votes (a few MB of memory) | after one data node dies there is one copy until it is back |
| 3 data nodes | 3 big | still two copies after one dies | 3 times the disk and memory |

Two voters alone are not safe: when they lose contact, neither can tell "the other is dead" from "the cable is cut". A third voter breaks the tie, so `--cluster-peers` needs at least 3.

<a id="start"></a>

## Start a cluster

Every node gets the same list of voters, each as `id=http://host:port`, and its own `--node-id`:

```bash
PEERS=a=http://10.0.0.1:9900,b=http://10.0.0.2:9900,w=http://10.0.0.3:9900

# data node a
kareladb serve --data-dir /data --bind 0.0.0.0 --token <secret> --node-id a --cluster-peers $PEERS
# data node b
kareladb serve --data-dir /data --bind 0.0.0.0 --token <secret> --node-id b --cluster-peers $PEERS
# the witness (no data)
kareladb witness --data-dir /witness --bind 0.0.0.0 --port 9900 --token <secret> --node-id w --cluster-peers $PEERS
```

| Setting | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--cluster-peers LIST` (`KARELADB_CLUSTER_PEERS`) | every voter, this one too: `id=http://host:port`, comma-separated. An entry without `id=` uses `host:port` as its id |
| `--node-id ID` (`KARELADB_NODE_ID`) | this node's id in the list |
| `--cluster-token T` (`KARELADB_CLUSTER_TOKEN`) | what the nodes send each other. Default: `--token`. Every node must accept it as an admin's token, because followers read the leader's log with it |
| `KARELADB_ELECTION_TIMEOUT_MS` | how long a node waits without hearing the leader before it asks to be elected (default 5000, random +-20%) |
| `KARELADB_LEASE_MS` | how long a leader may write after a majority last answered it (default 3000) |
| `KARELADB_CLUSTER_HEARTBEAT_MS` | how often the leader says "I am here" (default 500) |
| `KARELADB_SYNC_STANDBYS` | `1` or `prefer` (default): a commit is confirmed once a standby holds it too, or by the leader alone while no standby copies; `required`: never by the leader alone; `0`: the leader alone ([sync commit](#sync)) |
| `KARELADB_SYNC_WAIT_MS` | with `required`: how long a written commit waits for a standby before it fails (default 10000) |
| `KARELADB_ON_LEADER`, `KARELADB_ON_FOLLOWER` | a command run on each role change ([clients](#clients)) |
| `KARELADB_ROLE_SCRIPT_TIMEOUT_MS` | `30000` (default): a role script that runs longer is killed and logged |

The lease plus one heartbeat must end before the shortest election timeout (3000 + 500 < 4000 with the defaults). A node refuses to start otherwise, because then two leaders could write at once. Give every node the same three settings: each message carries the sender's lease and shortest timeout, and a node refuses votes and heartbeats from a node whose settings do not fit beside its own (its log says why).

A node starts as a follower that copies nothing. Within the election timeout one data node is elected; it says so in its log (`cluster: this node is the leader in term 1`), and the others start copying it.

A list of two voters is refused, because two nodes alone cannot fail over safely:

**Command line: Two voters are not enough**

```bash
kareladb serve --data-dir data --token T --node-id a --cluster-peers a=http://10.0.0.1:9900,b=http://10.0.0.2:9900
```

Output:

```text
error: --cluster-peers needs at least 3 voters (two data nodes and a witness, or three data nodes): two alone cannot tell a dead node from a cut cable
```

exit code 1

A witness needs the same list of voters as the data nodes:

**Command line: A witness without --cluster-peers**

```bash
kareladb witness --data-dir witness --node-id w --token T
```

Output:

```text
error: kareladb witness needs --cluster-peers (every voter, this one too; env KARELADB_CLUSTER_PEERS)
```

exit code 1

<a id="connect"></a>

## Connection strings

Give clients **both data nodes** (not the witness: it holds no data). The driver tries them in order and keeps the one that takes writes.

| Client | Connection string |
|---|---|
| psql, libpq, Python psycopg | `postgresql://user:pass@10.0.0.1:8832,10.0.0.2:8832/default?target_session_attrs=read-write` |
| Go pgx | `postgres://user:pass@10.0.0.1:8832,10.0.0.2:8832/default?target_session_attrs=read-write` |
| Java JDBC | `jdbc:postgresql://10.0.0.1:8832,10.0.0.2:8832/default?targetServerType=primary` |
| Node `pg` | one host per pool; on error `25006` or a closed connection, connect to the other node |
| HTTP (`/exec`, `/write`) | send to either node; a follower answers `421` with `X-KarelaDB-Leader: <url>`: send it again there |
| A load balancer | health check `GET /health?role=leader` (writes) or `?role=follower` (reads) |
| Reads only | `target_session_attrs=any` (or `prefer-standby`): any node answers reads. A follower says true to `pg_is_in_recovery()` and on to `in_hot_standby` and `transaction_read_only`, as a PostgreSQL standby does, so every driver tells it from the leader |

After a failover the driver's open connections to the old leader break. A
connection pool opens new ones and finds the new leader by itself; a client
that keeps one connection should connect again on error and send the write
again only if it was not confirmed (see [what a commit does](#sync)).

Any server answers `/health` without a token. A plain server (no cluster) says it leads:

**HTTP: The role check a load balancer uses**

```http
GET /health?role=leader
```

Response:

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{
  "status": "ok",
  "version": "0.2.0-dev",
  "product": "KarelaDB",
  "server_time_ms": 1792822728141,
  "auth_required": false,
  "login": false,
  "tls": false,
  "ready": true,
  "standby": false,
  "role": "leader"
}
```

**HTTP: Asked for a follower, the leader answers 503**

```http
GET /health?role=follower
```

Response:

HTTP 503 (application/json)

```text
{
  "status": "ok",
  "version": "0.2.0-dev",
  "product": "KarelaDB",
  "server_time_ms": 1792822728177,
  "auth_required": false,
  "login": false,
  "tls": false,
  "ready": true,
  "standby": false,
  "role": "leader"
}
```

<a id="election"></a>

## How the leader is chosen

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| 1 | The leader sends a heartbeat to every other voter every 500 ms (`POST /api/cluster/heartbeat`, on the same port). |
| 2 | A node that hears nothing for its election timeout first asks the others whether they **would** vote for it. A voter that heard a leader, or gave a vote, less than 4 s ago says no, to this question and to a real vote. So a node that was only cut off cannot disturb a working cluster when it comes back, and no second leader is elected while the first may still write. |
| 3 | If a majority would, it adds 1 to the **term** (an election counter), votes for itself and asks for real votes (`POST /api/cluster/vote`). |
| 4 | A voter gives one vote per term, and only to a candidate whose log is at least as far as its own **for every database**, and as far as what the leader last said a majority holds. The witness keeps that list. A log's end is the term of the leader that wrote its last entry, then its LSN: a newer term wins over a longer log from an older term. So the most up-to-date node wins. Before both comes the database's **copy id**, which making of the database the log belongs to: a database dropped and made again (even within one term) starts its LSNs again from 1, and a node that only holds the dropped one never wins over a node holding the new one, however long its old log is. |
| 5 | With a majority (2 of 3) the candidate is the leader. Every database becomes a primary's, in place, and its log goes on in a new history named by the term. Timers start. |
| 6 | The other data node becomes its follower and copies its log. |

The term, the vote and the last leader are in `<data>/_cluster/state`. A node writes and syncs this file **before** it answers a vote, so it never votes twice in one term, even across a crash. If the file is damaged, the node refuses to start rather than guess.

A node that replays a long log after a crash still votes: nothing is applied to a database while it opens, so the end its open's log check read (before the replay starts) is its log end, and the node answers votes with it. Only until that check has read the log does it say `this voter's own log ends are still being read`.

<a id="fencing"></a>

## Fencing: two leaders never write

| Layer | How |
|---|---|
| Lease | The leader may write only while a majority answered a heartbeat it sent in the last 3 s (a steady clock, not the time of day). When the lease runs out, every database refuses commits at once, with SQLSTATE `25006`, and the node steps down. Others can be elected only after 4 s without a heartbeat, which is after the lease ended. |
| Term on every log request | A follower sends its term with each request for the log (`GET /api/wal?term=`). A leader that sees a higher term steps down at once and answers `421`. A follower never applies a log from an older term. |

A follower that was the leader before (it lost its lease, or the cluster moved on while it was away) becomes a follower in place: its databases turn into copies again and it copies from the new leader. Nothing has to be copied by hand, even when its log no longer fits the new leader's (next section).

<a id="rejoin"></a>

## When the old leader comes back

A leader that was cut off, or whose computer stopped, may have logged commits the new leader never got. In async mode some of them may have been confirmed to a client. When it comes back, it takes the new leader's history by itself, database by database:

| Its copy | What it does |
|---|---|
| Fits the new leader's log | copies on from where it is. |
| Has commits after the point where the two logs part (the fork) | cuts its log back to the fork and copies on from there. Its data files are linked, not copied, so this takes a moment even for a big database. |
| Its files no longer hold the data as it was at the fork (a checkpoint ran after it), or the new leader no longer keeps the log it needs | copies the database again: `GET /api/snapshot?db=` on the leader sends a consistent copy while writes go on there; the node checks every file, restores it and follows from its end. |

The fork is found from the log terms of both nodes (which leader wrote which part of the log) and checked with the commit at the fork and the database's copy id, so a database made again under the same name is never taken for the same one: it is copied again, and the old copy is kept whole in `_diverged`.

Nothing is deleted. When the old copy held commits the leader never got, its whole folder (its log too) moves to `<data>/_diverged/<database>-<time>`, with:

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `diverged.txt` | the database, the fork LSN, how many commits only this node had, and when it moved |
| `diverged.kdbwal` | those commits, in the form `GET /api/wal` sends |
| the rest | the database as this node held it: open it with `kareladb sql --data-dir` to look at the rows |

Look at them, and delete one when you no longer need it, with the node running or stopped:

```bash
kareladb cluster diverged list --data-dir /data
# folder                                   database                 fork_lsn      end_lsn     txns  how          moved
# default-20261023-021530                  default                     98012        98140      128  cut back     2026-10-23 02:15:30
kareladb cluster diverged drop default-20261023-021530 --data-dir /data
# deleted /data/_diverged/default-20261023-021530
```

On a running node the same is `DELETE /api/cluster/diverged?folder=<folder>` with the cluster token (`404` when `_diverged` holds no such folder; a path is refused). KarelaDB never deletes a `_diverged` folder by itself.

A copy that only fell behind (nothing of its own, and the leader confirmed the last transaction they share) goes to `<data>/_trash` instead, as a dropped database does. When the leader cannot confirm it (it no longer keeps that part of its log), the whole old copy is kept in `_diverged`. A rejoin that fails (no disk space for the leader's snapshot, the leader busy sending one) is tried again after 5 seconds, then twice as long each time, up to 10 minutes. `GET /api/cluster` lists every `_diverged` folder under `diverged`.

A power cut at any step leaves a usable node: the old folder stays in place until the new copy is complete, and a swap that was under way is finished at the next start. The users database (`_system`) is not copied again while the server runs: if it went apart, `GET /api/standby` says so; stop the node, move `<data>/_system` away and start it again.

<a id="status"></a>

## Watch it

`GET /api/cluster` (with the cluster token) on any node:

```json
{"node":"a","witness":false,"role":"leader","term":3,"leader":"a","leader_url":"http://10.0.0.1:9900",
 "voted_for":"a","lease_left_ms":2950,
 "peers":[{"id":"b","url":"http://10.0.0.2:9900","reachable":true,"last_answer_ms_ago":40,"error":null},
          {"id":"w","url":"http://10.0.0.3:9900","reachable":true,"last_answer_ms_ago":41,"error":null}],
 "log_ends":{"_system":{"term":3,"lsn":120},"default":{"term":2,"lsn":7},"trades":{"term":3,"lsn":98012}},
 "majority_holds":{"_system":{"term":3,"lsn":120},"default":{"term":2,"lsn":7},"trades":{"term":3,"lsn":98012}},
 "lag":{"_system":0,"default":0,"trades":0},
 "sync_commit":{"wanted":true,"on":true,"waits":51200,"wait_us":40960000,"acks":9800,"fallbacks":0}}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `role` | `leader`, `follower`, `pre-candidate` (asking whether it could win) or `candidate` |
| `term` | the election counter; it goes up by one for each election |
| `lease_left_ms` | the leader: how much longer it may write without another answer from a majority |
| `log_ends` | where each database's log ends on this node: its last LSN and the term of the leader that wrote it (0: before the cluster) |
| `majority_holds` | per database, the log a majority of the voters holds (the leader works it out; others show what it last said) |
| `lag` | per database, log entries not yet on the standby (on the leader) or not yet on this node (on a follower) |
| `sync_commit` | `wanted`: `KARELADB_SYNC_STANDBYS` is not `0`; `on`: commits wait for a standby now (this node leads); `mode`: `off`, `prefer` or `required`; how many waited, for how long in all, the standby acks, the `fallbacks` (commits confirmed without a standby) and the `refused` (commits refused or failed with `required`) |
| `diverged` | a data node: the copies kept in `<data>/_diverged` because they held commits the leader never got ([rejoin](#rejoin)); `folder` is the name `DELETE /api/cluster/diverged?folder=` takes, `path` where it is |
| `unopenable` | a data node: databases that could not be opened (a damaged manifest, a missing key), with the error. They are left out of this node's log ends, so they never keep it out of an election; the open is tried again now and then |
| `followers` | the followers that do not vote, from `KARELADB_CLUSTER_FOLLOWERS` ([reading from followers](#reads)) |

Without a token:

| Request | Answer |
|---|---|
| `GET /health` | adds `"role":"leader"` or `"follower"` and `"cluster":{"node","term","leader"}`; the console's status bar shows it (`Leader - term 3`, `Follower - term 3 - leader a`) |
| `GET /health?role=leader` | `200` only on the leader, else `503`: point a load balancer's health check at it to send writes to the leader alone. `?role=follower` is the opposite. |

`/metrics` adds `kdb_cluster_leader` (1 on the leader), `kdb_cluster_term`, `kdb_cluster_lag_lsn{db="..."}`, `kdb_cluster_sync_on`, `kdb_cluster_sync_acks_total`, `kdb_cluster_sync_waits_total`, `kdb_cluster_sync_wait_seconds_total`, `kdb_cluster_sync_fallback_total`, `kdb_cluster_sync_required` (1 with `required`) and `kdb_cluster_sync_refused_total`.

A follower's copy and its lag show in `GET /api/standby`, `/api/stats` and `/metrics`, as on any [standby](standby.md#status).

<a id="sync"></a>

## Sync commit: a confirmed commit is on two disks

| `KARELADB_SYNC_STANDBYS` | A commit is confirmed once | Lost when the leader's computer dies |
|---|---|---|
| `required` | it is on the leader's disk **and** on a standby's disk. Never by the leader alone: with no standby copying, writes are refused | nothing that was confirmed |
| `1` or `prefer` (the default in a cluster) | it is on the leader's disk **and** on a standby's disk, while a standby copies. While none copies, by the leader alone (below) | nothing confirmed while a standby copies. Commits confirmed while none copied: lost if the leader's disk dies before a standby copies them |
| `0` | it is on the leader's disk | when its computer dies: what the standby had not copied yet, usually the last few ms. When it is only cut off from the network: everything it confirmed until its lease ran out, up to 3 s of commits |

A session can still say `SET synchronous_commit = off`: its commits are then confirmed at once, without waiting for any disk, as in PostgreSQL.

How it works: a standby syncs its log before it asks the leader for more, so its next request says "I hold everything before this". A commit waits for that. Writers that commit at the same time share one wait, so many writers pay it once together. Measured on one computer (2 data nodes and a witness, one INSERT per commit over the PostgreSQL port):

| | `KARELADB_SYNC_STANDBYS=0` | `1` |
|---|---|---|
| 1 client, time per commit (median) | 0.67 ms | 1.47 ms |
| 32 clients, commits per second | 15,700 | 9,300 |

When no standby copies - only the witness is reachable, or the standby is down - waiting would stop every write. With `1` (`prefer`) the leader then confirms commits without a standby (async), writes `WARNING: sync commit: no standby is copying ...` in its log (at most every 10 s) and counts each in `kdb_cluster_sync_fallback_total`. The first commit after a standby dies waits up to the lease (3 s) before that, and so does the first commit of each database after a node becomes leader, after `CREATE DATABASE` and after a database is opened again: the standby gets that long to find it. Sync commit comes back by itself as soon as a standby copies again. With `required` it refuses them instead ([below](#sync-required)).

<a id="sync-required"></a>

### `required`: never confirmed alone

Use `KARELADB_SYNC_STANDBYS=required` for data where a refused write is better than a confirmed write that may vanish (orders, payments).

| Case | What the commit does |
|---|---|
| A standby copies | the same as `1`: confirmed once the standby holds it |
| No standby copies (for longer than the lease) | refused **before it is written**: SQLSTATE `25006`, HTTP `500`, `no standby holds this database's log now ... nothing of it was written`. Send it again once a standby copies (`GET /api/cluster`) |
| The standby goes away while the commit waits | the commit waits up to `KARELADB_SYNC_WAIT_MS` (10 s) or its `statement_timeout`, then fails: `25006`, `no standby holds this commit ... it is on the leader's disk ... not confirmed`. It stays on the leader and the standby copies it when it comes back. Check whether it is there before you send it again |
| `SET synchronous_commit = off` | not refused and not waited for, as with `1`: the session asked for no wait |

Each refused or failed commit counts in `kdb_cluster_sync_refused_total`, and the log says `WARNING: sync commit: ... required: commits are refused` at most every 10 s. Reads always go on. PostgreSQL's synchronous standby makes a commit wait forever (or, cancelled, keeps it with a warning); MySQL's semi-sync falls back to async after a timeout. `required` instead refuses up front once it knows no standby copies, so a client never hangs and never hears "done" for a commit only one disk holds.

Only a voting standby confirms a commit. A follower that does not vote (`KARELADB_CLUSTER_FOLLOWERS`) copies the same log, but an election never looks at it, so its copy does not count.

| Case | What the commit does |
|---|---|
| The standby is up but its copy makes no progress (its disk is full, every apply fails) | counts as "no standby copies": async after the lease, with the warning |
| The leader still reaches the witness | async: the commits are confirmed by the leader alone. No second leader can write meanwhile (the witness still backs this one), but if the leader's computer is lost before a standby copies them, they are lost - the same as `KARELADB_SYNC_STANDBYS=0` for that time. The warning in the log says so |
| The leader reaches no one | waits; when the lease ends the node steps down and the commit fails |
| The leader steps down while a commit waits | the commit fails with `committed on this node's disk but not confirmed by a standby ... may be lost` (HTTP `500`, SQLSTATE `08007`, "transaction resolution unknown"). It is on the old leader's disk only: check on the new leader whether it is there before you send it again. The old leader itself goes on: it becomes a follower, and if the new leader never got that commit, the old leader's copy goes to [`_diverged`](#rejoin) and it takes the new leader's history. |

Reads never wait for a standby. A node that stepped down with a commit no standby confirmed refuses reads of that database (`503`, try again) until it follows the new leader again (a few seconds): its rows are not shown to other clients while the cluster may still drop them. A node that restarts in between does not know this any more.

`CREATE DATABASE` and `DROP DATABASE` are not covered by sync commit: the leader confirms them alone, and a standby makes or drops its copy on its next look at the leader's list (within a second). If the leader's computer dies in that second, the new leader may still have a dropped database (with its rows) or lack a new one. Check after a failover, or wait a second after either before you count on it.

<a id="clients"></a>

## Clients

| Client | How it finds the leader |
|---|---|
| PostgreSQL drivers | list every data node: `host=10.0.0.1,10.0.0.2 target_session_attrs=read-write` (libpq, pgx, JDBC). A follower says `in_hot_standby = on` and `transaction_read_only = on`, so the driver skips it. |
| HTTP | a write sent to a follower is answered `421 Misdirected Request` with the leader's address in the header `X-KarelaDB-Leader`; the body is the same `25006` error as before. Send the request again there. |
| The console | on a `421` it offers once to open the leader's console |
| `kareladb exec` | `kareladb exec --url http://10.0.0.2:9900 --token T "INSERT ..."` follows a `421` once to the leader |
| A virtual address | `KARELADB_ON_LEADER` and `KARELADB_ON_FOLLOWER` name a command the node runs on each role change, with the role, the term and the leader's id: `move-ip.sh leader 3 a`. Use it to move a keepalived or cloud floating IP address to the leader. The scripts run one at a time, in order, and never hold up the election. Only the newest role's script runs when several changes come at once; one that runs longer than `KARELADB_ROLE_SCRIPT_TIMEOUT_MS` (30 s) is killed with everything it started. |

<a id="reads"></a>

## Reading from followers

Every follower answers reads, so reads can be spread over the nodes. Add as
many more read copies as you like: a **learner** copies the leader like any
follower but never votes, so the election stays the same with or without it.

```bash
# a learner: its --node-id is not in --cluster-peers
kareladb serve --data-dir /data/f1 --token T --node-id f1 \
  --cluster-peers a=http://10.0.0.1:9900,b=http://10.0.0.2:9900,w=http://10.0.0.3:9900 --cluster-learner
```

Or list the learners on every node with `KARELADB_CLUSTER_FOLLOWERS=f1=http://10.0.0.4:9900,f2=http://10.0.0.5:9900`:
a node whose id is there is a learner, and `GET /api/cluster` on a voter lists them.
A learner asks the voters who leads every heartbeat and follows the newest
leader; `GET /api/cluster` on it says `"role":"learner"`, the leader and `lag_ms`.

**Read your own write.** A copy is a few ms behind the leader, so a read sent
there right after a write may not see it yet. The cluster leader answers every
write that changed something (`POST /exec`, `/write`, `/imp`, `/api/v2/write`)
with `X-KarelaDB-Lsn`: where that database's log ends with the write in it.
Send it back as `X-KarelaDB-Min-Lsn` with the read (same database), and the
follower waits until it has applied that far. Only a cluster leader sends it:
a plain primary with [standbys](standby.md) does not.

The key-value store (`/kv`, `kv_get()` and the other `kv_*` functions) answers
on the leader only. It keeps its keys in memory, and a follower copies the
leader's `_kv` rows into the table, not into that memory, so a follower
refuses every key command, reads too: `/kv` answers `421` with the leader's
address in `X-KarelaDB-Leader`, as a write does. When a follower becomes the
leader it reads its keys again from `_kv` before it takes a command, so it
goes on from the keys the old leader had, not from the ones it held when it
started.

```bash
curl -si -X POST http://leader:9900/exec -H "Authorization: Bearer T" -d "INSERT INTO trades VALUES (...)" | grep -i x-kareladb-lsn
# X-KarelaDB-Lsn: 98012
curl -s "http://follower:9900/exec?query=SELECT%20count(*)%20FROM%20trades" -H "Authorization: Bearer T" -H "X-KarelaDB-Min-Lsn: 98012"
```

| Setting | Default | What it does on a follower or standby |
|---|---|---|
| `KARELADB_READ_WAIT_MS` | 2000 (10000 at most) | the longest a read with `X-KarelaDB-Min-Lsn` waits; after that it answers `503` (with `Retry-After`) so the client reads from the leader. At most 64 reads wait at once on a node; the next is told `503` at once |
| `KARELADB_MAX_READ_LAG_MS` | 0 (no limit) | a node further behind than this answers HTTP reads with `503`, so clients and load balancers go to another node. A node copying from nobody (during an election, or before it has reached a leader) counts as too far behind |

Both apply to HTTP reads only (`/exec`, `/v/...`, `/exp` and `POST /cursor`),
after the token check; the leader ignores them. The PostgreSQL port does not
read them: a lagging follower still answers there. The lag is the one
`GET /api/standby` shows.

A follower applies the leader's log a run of transactions at a time, with one
disk sync per run. Measured on one machine (two writers committing small
transactions as fast as they could): the copy stayed a median of 96 log
entries behind and caught up 15 ms after the load stopped (one sync per
transaction: 5,700 entries behind, 2.5 s to catch up). A read on the follower
waits only while a run is applied: p99 20 us during that load (1.1-1.7 ms
before).

<a id="failures"></a>

## What happens when something breaks

Each row was tested on one computer with two data nodes and a witness, with
four clients writing all the time (`tools/cluster_check` in the source; it cuts
links with its own proxies). With sync commit (the default) not one confirmed
row was lost in any of them, both data nodes always ended with the same rows,
and no term ever had two leaders.

| What broke | What the cluster did |
|---|---|
| The leader's computer died (`kill -9`) | the other data node led and took writes again 3.6 to 6 s later (90 failovers in a 22-minute run) |
| The leader died in the middle of a big transaction (200,000 rows), a `CHECKPOINT` or an `ALTER TABLE` | the same; the transaction or the new column is there whole or not at all |
| The leader died while the `COMMIT` of a spilled transaction (past `--txn-spill-mb`) wrote it into the log | the same: the transaction is there whole or not at all |
| The leader was cut off from both others | it stopped confirming writes at once (they waited, then failed); the other data node led 3.9 s later. When the cable came back, the old leader followed the new one |
| The witness was cut off | nothing changed: same leader, same term, writes went on |
| A link that went down and up every 0.2 to 1.5 s, for 40 s | no election at all (the term stayed the same) |
| A slow link to the follower (20 ms more per packet) | sync commits got slower (1,600 to 225 rows a second for four clients), none failed |
| All three stopped (power cut or clean stop), then started in any order | the same history; writes were taken again 1 to 4.4 s after the last node started |

With `KARELADB_SYNC_STANDBYS=0` (async) the same tests lose confirmed rows, as expected:

| What broke | Lost with async (four clients) |
|---|---|
| The leader's computer died | 100 rows: what the follower had not copied yet |
| The leader was cut off from both others | 29,635 and 74,704 rows in two runs: everything it confirmed in the 3 s until its lease ran out. They are in its `_diverged` folder |

Use sync commit (the default) when a confirmed row must never be lost.

<a id="limits"></a>

## What it does not do yet

| | |
|---|---|
| `KARELADB_SYNC_STANDBYS=0`, or `1` with only the witness reachable (`required` refuses instead) | a commit the follower had not copied when the leader's computer died is lost from the cluster (usually the last few ms). A leader that is only cut off goes on confirming until its lease ends: those commits (up to 3 s of them) are kept in its `_diverged` folder when it comes back, not in the cluster. |
| An old leader's users database (`_system`) with commits the new one never got | it stops copying `_system` and says so; move `<data>/_system` away while the node is stopped. Every other database takes the leader's history by itself ([rejoin](#rejoin)). |
| `kareladb promote` | refused on a cluster node: the leader is elected. |
| Reads during an apply | a read on a follower waits while a run of the leader's transactions is applied (usually microseconds, at most a few ms): it does not read a snapshot there, which could show half a transaction. |

## See also

# The kareladb program

> What the kareladb program is, how it finds your databases, and what its exit codes mean.

- Category: Command line
- Keywords: command line, CLI, kareladb.exe, usage, exit code, $LASTEXITCODE, data folder, KARELADB\_DATA\_DIR, --data-dir, --config, kareladb.conf, database name, folder path, --help, -h, --version, kareladb help, kareladb help tutorial
- See also: [kareladb sql and kareladb shell](cli-sql-and-shell.md), [kareladb serve](cli-serve.md), [kareladb info, check, repair, dump-file](cli-maintenance.md), [kareladb user](cli-users.md), [Backup, check, repair and restore](backup-and-safety.md), [Databases and the data folder](databases.md)

`kareladb` is the one program you need. It runs SQL, the interactive shell, the server, backups and repairs.
It works in PowerShell, CMD, bash and zsh, on Windows, Linux and macOS.

A **database** is a folder on the disk. Many databases can live in one **data folder** (one sub-folder per database).
Most commands take a `<db>` argument: the **name** of a database in the data folder, or the **path** of a database folder.

| Command | What it does | Help |
|---|---|---|
| `kareladb sql` | Runs SQL once and prints the result | [kareladb sql](cli-sql-and-shell.md#kareladb-sql) |
| `kareladb shell` | A prompt where you type SQL | [kareladb shell](cli-sql-and-shell.md#kareladb-shell) |
| `kareladb serve` | The server: web console, HTTP API, PostgreSQL port | [kareladb serve](cli-serve.md#kareladb-serve) |
| `kareladb info`, `kareladb check`, `kareladb repair`, `kareladb dump-file` | Look at a database, find and fix damage | [maintenance](cli-maintenance.md) |
| `kareladb backup`, `kareladb backups`, `kareladb verify-backup`, `kareladb restore` | Backups | [backup and safety](backup-and-safety.md) |
| `kareladb user ...` | Users of the server | [kareladb user](cli-users.md) |
| `kareladb version`, `kareladb help [<topic>]` | Version; the list of commands and of every help topic, one topic, or a tutorial chapter, in the terminal | below |
| `kareladb upgrade` | Make an older database ready for this KarelaDB (backup, feature list, check) | [versions and upgrades](versions.md) |
| `kareladb features` | The stored-format features a database uses now, and what uses them | [going back](versions.md#downgrade) |
| `kareladb downgrade` | Let an older KarelaDB open the data again, when it uses nothing newer (backup, feature list, check) | [going back](versions.md#downgrade) |
| `kareladb skill`, `kareladb skill install` | Print, or install for Claude Code, the file that teaches an AI assistant how to use KarelaDB | [the Claude skill](install-packages.md#skill) |

<a id="help"></a>

## kareladb help

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb
kareladb help
kareladb --help
kareladb -h
kareladb help <topic>
kareladb help tutorial [<chapter>]
```

Prints the version and a short list of every command and option, then the list of help topics - the same pages a running server shows at `/help` - with their titles. `kareladb help <topic>` prints one topic in the terminal (the Markdown source in a source checkout, the built page as text in a package); a word that is not a topic lists the topics whose name contains it. `kareladb help tutorial` lists the tutorial chapters and `kareladb help tutorial 17` prints one (the tutorial is part of the source checkout only).

- **Exit code:** `0` for `kareladb help`, `--help` and `-h`. `1` for `kareladb` with no command, for an unknown command, and for a topic that does not exist.
- **Notes:** an unknown command (for example a typing mistake like `kareladb bakup`) also prints this list, with exit code `1`. The topics come from the help folder the program finds (`help_dir` in kareladb.conf, `KARELADB_HELP_DIR`, next to the program, or the checkout's `docs/help/site`); without one, only the command list is printed.

**Command line: The list of commands**

```bash
kareladb help
```

Output:

```text
KarelaDB 0.2.0-dev (KARELA DataBase)

Usage:
  kareladb info    <db>                          show files, versions and log position
  kareladb check   <db> [--no-audit-chain]       read every block and log record, report damage;
                                                 then check the hash chain of _audit_log

              [--pg-port 8832] [--pg-timestamptz] PostgreSQL protocol for Postgres drivers and tools (0 = off)
                                                 (Ctrl+C stops). Without <db>: every database in the data folder
  kareladb exec [--url http://localhost:9900] [--token <t>] [--db <name>] "SQL"
              run SQL on a running server and print its JSON answer; a cluster follower's 421 is followed
              once to the leader it names
  kareladb promote [--url http://localhost:9900] [--token <t>]  make the standby at --url a primary: it stops
                                                 copying and takes changes (when the primary is lost)

              the copies a cluster node kept in _diverged when it took the leader's history; drop deletes one
  kareladb shell   [<db>] [--backups <dir>] [--memory <MB>]  interactive SQL prompt (end statements with ;)
  kareladb sql     <db> "SQL" [--format table|csv|json] [--max-rows N]
                                                 run SQL and print results (use - to read SQL from stdin)
  kareladb user add <name> [--role admin|ddl|write|read]  add a server user; the password is asked for (or read
                                                 from a pipe), never given on the command line
  kareladb user passwd <name>                    set a new password
  kareladb user role <name> admin|ddl|write|read|none change the role
  kareladb user list                             users and roles (never passwords)
  kareladb user remove <name>
  kareladb user reset-2fa <name>                 turn two-factor login off (a lost phone)
                                                 (kareladb user works on the data folder while kareladb serve is stopped;
                                                 while it runs, use CREATE USER ... in its console)
  kareladb version [<db>]                        this build and the stored-format features it reads;
                                                 with <db>: the features that database uses
  kareladb upgrade <db> [--backups <dir>]        verified backup, then save the database's feature list, then check
  kareladb features <db> | --data-dir <folder>   the stored-format features each database uses now, and what uses them
  kareladb downgrade <db> | --data-dir <folder> --to <version> [--backups <dir>] [--no-backup]
                                                 let an older KarelaDB open the data (--to 2026-09-13, or --known
                                                 <names> from the older kareladb version); refused, naming what uses
                                                 each newer feature, when the data needs one
  kareladb key new                               print a new random master key (64 hex characters) for
                                                 encrypted databases: keep it in KARELADB_MASTER_KEY or a key file
                                                 (KARELADB_MASTER_KEY_FILE) outside the data folder
  kareladb key rotate <folder>                   re-wrap the data key of an encrypted database folder, or of
                                                 every backup in a folder of backups, with KARELADB_MASTER_KEY
                                                 (the old key in KARELADB_MASTER_KEY_PREVIOUS); no data file changes
  kareladb help [<topic> | tutorial [<chapter>]]     the help topics (and, in a source checkout, the tutorial)
                                                 in the terminal; without a topic: the list of topics
  kareladb skill [install] [--dir <d>] [--url <u>] [--token <t>] [--home <checkout>]
                                                 print, or install into ~/.claude/skills/kareladb, the file that
                                                 teaches an AI assistant in another project how to use KarelaDB

<db>: a database name in the data folder (market), or the path of a database folder (D:\kdb\market, ./market).
Data folder: --data-dir <folder>, else kareladb.conf, else the KARELADB_DATA_DIR environment variable,
  else "data" next to kareladb.
--config <file>: kareladb.conf, the JSON file the console's Settings page and ALTER SYSTEM write
  (default: kareladb.conf next to kareladb). A flag on the command line always wins over it, and it wins over
  the environment. It may hold: data_dir, wal_dir, wal_archive_mb, cache_mb, keep_versions, trash_keep_hours,
  trash_max_mb, slow_query_ms, http_threads, max_connections, lock_timeout_ms,
  idle_in_transaction_timeout_ms, rate_limit_ip, rate_limit_user, timer_workers, timezone,
  http_functions, http_timeout_ms, ilp_auto_create, step_up_actions, step_up_minutes, alert_webhook,
  tls_cert, tls_key, the backup_*
  settings, and "system" (what ALTER SYSTEM SET saved; SELECT pg_reload_conf() puts it in use).
  A database folder served by its path (kareladb serve D:\kdb\market) reads only the three folders below.
  web_dir, help_dir and skill_dir name the folders of the console, the help and the Claude skill
  (else KARELADB_WEB_DIR, KARELADB_HELP_DIR, KARELADB_SKILL_DIR, else web/, help/ and skill/ next to kareladb).
--memory <MB>: memory for table data kept loaded (default 512). More is faster on big tables.
--memory-limit <size>: one limit for everything the server holds (table data, unsaved changes,
  indexes, results, caches, what the allocator keeps), like 3GB or 3072 (MB). Near it, memory is
  given back (the result cache too); at it, quick statements still run in a small reserve and
  others get 'memory full' (HTTP 503, PostgreSQL 53200); over it, the running statement that
  holds the most is stopped with 'memory full'. Default: 85% of a container's
  memory limit, else of the machine's memory (env KARELADB_MEMORY_LIMIT; 0 or off = no limit).
--threads <N>: threads for big queries and writes (default and most: half of the CPU threads).
--cache-mb <MB>: memory for results of repeated queries, all databases together (default 256,
  0 = off; else kareladb.conf cache_mb, else env KARELADB_CACHE_MB). A result is used again only while no
  table it read has changed; a quick one (under 1 ms) is kept when asked twice. Queries with
  random() are never kept; with now() only for a caller that takes an older answer
  (/exec?cache_now_ms=500, SET result_cache_now_ms = 500). One result may use a quarter of it,
  a pinned one three quarters. ALTER DATABASE db SET RESULT_CACHE = '256MB' gives a database
  a space of its own.
--pg-compat on|off: PostgreSQL 14's answers for every database without its own ALTER DATABASE ...
  SET pg_compat (default off; env KARELADB_PG_COMPAT): 7 / 2 = 3, 1.005 is an exact NUMERIC, a window
  with ORDER BY counts ties together, text sorts like en_US. A session can choose with
  SET kdb.pg_compat = on | off.
--pg-int-division on|off: on the Postgres port, whole number / whole number gives a whole
  number (7 / 2 = 3) as in PostgreSQL (default off; env KARELADB_PG_INT_DIVISION). A session can
  still choose with SET int_division = integer | float.
--reader-yield on|off: readers do not wait for a long trigger or CALL; they read the last
  committed rows (default on; env KARELADB_READER_YIELD). Off: readers wait for the writer's statement.
--per-table-reads on|off: a reader waits only for writers of the tables it reads, and not while
  a checkpoint writes its files (default on; env KARELADB_PER_TABLE_READS). Off: it waits for every writer.
--pin-threads auto|on|off: auto (default): on Linux, inside a CPU quota (docker --cpus, cgroup cpu.max)
  smaller than the CPUs the process may run on, every thread is pinned to the quota's worth of CPUs,
  one per core, and moved back when the quota goes (docker update --cpus); 32 connections on a 2-CPU
  quota of a 32-CPU host no longer run on all 32 and stall when the time is spent. on: each HTTP
  worker, PostgreSQL connection and query thread runs on one CPU of its own, taken in turn from as
  many CPUs as KarelaDB may use, out of the cpuset; background threads stay on those CPUs. off: nothing is
  pinned (env KARELADB_PIN_THREADS). Ignored on Windows.
--read-only-calls on|off: a CALL of a procedure that changes nothing runs like a SELECT: no table
  locks, no transaction (default on; env KARELADB_READ_ONLY_CALLS).
--scoped-ddl on|off: CREATE/ALTER/DROP TABLE, INDEX and TRIGGER, TRUNCATE, CREATE TABLE AS and
  materialized views lock only the tables they touch; views, procedures and functions lock none
  (default on; env KARELADB_SCOPED_DDL). Off: every schema change locks every table.
--ddl-beside-writers on|off: with --scoped-ddl, CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, RENAME TABLE and CREATE/DROP
  INDEX run beside a writer of other tables that is inside one long statement (default on; env
  KARELADB_DDL_BESIDE_WRITERS). Off: they wait until that writer pauses between two statements.
--log-lock-waits on|off: a statement that waits for a table lock longer than --deadlock-timeout
  writes one line to the log naming itself, the lock and who holds it (default off; env
  KARELADB_LOG_LOCK_WAITS; a session: SET log_lock_waits = on).
--deadlock-timeout 1s: when --log-lock-waits writes its line (default 1s; env KARELADB_DEADLOCK_TIMEOUT;
  a session: SET deadlock_timeout). Deadlocks are found at once whatever it is.
--skip-locked-beside on|off: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED inside BEGIN reads beside other open
  transactions that hold the table and returns the rows they did not touch (default off; env
  KARELADB_SKIP_LOCKED_BESIDE). Its UPDATE of such a row waits for their COMMIT. Off: no rows there.
--table-writers one|many: many: several users change one table at the same time when each of their
  statements on it touches single rows by the primary key (one-row INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE ... WHERE
  id = x, a CALL or trigger of such statements); the same row is waited for, as in PostgreSQL. Anything
  else on the table waits for the whole table, as before (default one; env KARELADB_TABLE_WRITERS).
--snapshot-reads on|off: a reader of a table that a long CALL, trigger job or bulk write is changing
  does not wait: it reads a snapshot of the committed rows (default off; env KARELADB_SNAPSHOT_READS).
  Tables with an index too, while a writer is busy on them, at any size: the read uses the index
  on the snapshot (an idle BEGIN is taken out and the index used, as before).
--tail-files on|off: a checkpoint saves rows appended after the end of a partition in a small tail file
  instead of writing the whole partition again (default off; env KARELADB_TAIL_FILES). A database with tail
  files needs a KarelaDB from 2026-10-02 or later (kareladb downgrade merges them back).
--snapshot-index-rows 1000000: a table with a full-text/JSON index, or an index not built yet, is
  scanned on a snapshot: only up to this many rows, a bigger one waits for its writer as before
  (default 1000000; 0 = indexed tables never get snapshots; env KARELADB_SNAPSHOT_INDEX_ROWS).
--txn-spill-mb 64: a transaction's log records past this many MB (or 1/16 of --memory-limit) go to a
  temporary file in the database's _tmp folder until COMMIT (default 64; 0 = never; env KARELADB_TXN_SPILL_MB).
--lanes on|off: priority lanes (default on; env KARELADB_LANES). A read whose shape used --heavy-ms of
  CPU or more the last three times it ran is heavy: only --heavy-slots of those run at once, at a
  lower CPU priority, and the rest wait in line. Charts and other short statements never wait. SET kdb.priority = high|normal|low, the X-KDB-Priority header
  and ALTER USER ... SET kdb.priority choose a lane by hand. Off: every statement runs at once.
--heavy-ms 100: the CPU time a read shape must use to count as heavy (env KARELADB_HEAVY_MS).
--heavy-slots N: heavy statements that run at once (default half the CPUs, at least 1; env
  KARELADB_HEAVY_SLOTS).
--heavy-queue N: heavy HTTP requests that may wait at once (default half the HTTP threads, at
  least 4; env KARELADB_HEAVY_QUEUE). Past it a request sent with priority low gets 503; a read heavy by
  its history runs at once. PostgreSQL statements are not counted: they wait up to their timeout.
--read-slots auto|off|N: reads (outside BEGIN) that run at once; the rest wait in line. A read holds
  its slot for at most 10 ms, so a long one never holds the line up (default auto = the CPUs the
  process may use, at least 2, following docker update --cpus; env KARELADB_READ_SLOTS). Off: every read
  starts at once, as before.
--timezone Asia/Kathmandu: the clock of CURRENT_DATE, ::date, date_trunc, EXTRACT and to_char, and of
  timer and backup schedules (default: the computer's own zone; env
  KARELADB_TIMEZONE; kareladb.conf "timezone"). Times are still stored as UTC. A session: SET TIME ZONE.
  Default: the computer's own zone. Zones with summer time (America/New_York) need the system's
  zone files (tzdata); per user: ALTER USER name SET timezone = 'zone'.
--warm-indexes on|off: build every index right after a database opens, on a background thread,
  so the first query finds them ready (default on; env KARELADB_WARM_INDEXES). Off: on first use.
--sync-commits always: every write is on disk before it is confirmed (default).
--sync-commits batch: writes are confirmed at once and put on disk every 10 ms. Much faster for
  many small writes; a power cut can lose the last confirmed writes, but never damages the data.
Protection of kareladb serve (docs/tutorial/21-protection.md):
  --statement-timeout 60s      stop statements that run longer (default 60s, 0 = no limit)
  --max-result-memory 1GB      rows one query may keep in memory (default 1GB, 0 = no limit)
  --max-groups N               GROUP BY groups of one query (default 5000000, 0 = no limit)
  --max-queries-per-user N     statements one user runs at the same time (default 32, 0 = no limit)
  --safe-updates               refuse UPDATE and DELETE without WHERE (SET safe_updates = off per session)
  --read-only                  the whole server only reads
  --standby-of URL             this server is a standby: it copies every database of the primary at URL
                               (http://host:9900) from its log, and only reads (env KARELADB_STANDBY_OF)
  --standby-token T            the token the standby sends to the primary: its --token or an admin's API
                               token (env KARELADB_STANDBY_TOKEN)
  --cluster-peers LIST         this server is a cluster node: id=http://host:port of every voter, this one too
                               (a=http://a:9900,b=http://b:9900,w=http://w:9900); the leader is elected and
                               takes over by itself when it dies (env KARELADB_CLUSTER_PEERS)
  --node-id ID                 this node's id in --cluster-peers (env KARELADB_NODE_ID)
  --cluster-token T            the token the nodes send each other (default --token; every node must accept
                               it as an admin's) (env KARELADB_CLUSTER_TOKEN)
                               a cluster node also reads KARELADB_SYNC_STANDBYS=0|1|required (1: a commit is
                               confirmed once a standby holds it, or alone when none copies; default 1;
                               required: never alone, refused when no standby copies, failed after
                               KARELADB_SYNC_WAIT_MS, 10000) and KARELADB_ON_LEADER / KARELADB_ON_FOLLOWER
                               (a command run on each role change: <cmd> leader|follower <term> <leader-id>)
  --cluster-learner            a cluster follower that does not vote: one more copy to read from; its
                               --node-id is not in --cluster-peers (env KARELADB_CLUSTER_LEARNER=on, or list
                               it in KARELADB_CLUSTER_FOLLOWERS=f1=http://h4:9900,...). Reads on any follower:
                               KARELADB_MAX_READ_LAG_MS (answer 503 when further behind), KARELADB_READ_WAIT_MS
                               (how long X-KarelaDB-Min-Lsn waits; default 2000)
  --trash-days N               DROP TABLE keeps the table N days for UNDROP TABLE (default 7; also sql, shell)
  --audit on|off               audit log of logins, users, DDL, backups in _system (default on)
  --audit-keep-days N          remove audit rows older than N days (default 0 = keep forever)
  --activity-log-size N        recent events for the console's activity panel, in memory (default 5000, 0 = off)
  --slow-query-ms N            statements taking N ms or more go to <data>/_logs/slow_queries.jsonl
                               (GET /api/slow-queries; default 1000, 0 = off; env KARELADB_SLOW_QUERY_MS)
  --stat-statements on|off     pg_stat_statements: totals per statement shape, in memory
                               (default on; env KARELADB_STAT_STATEMENTS)
  --token-name NAME            what the audit log calls whoever uses the --token (default token; env KARELADB_TOKEN_NAME)
  --trash-max-mb N             a database's _trash may hold N MB; beyond it the oldest go at once
                               (default: a quarter of the data, at least 256 MB; 0 = no limit;
                               env KARELADB_TRASH_MAX_MB, kareladb.conf trash_max_mb)
  --drain-timeout 30s          on stop, running requests may finish this long; new ones get 503 (default 30s)
  --tls-cert FILE --tls-key FILE  TLS on both ports: https:// and PostgreSQL sslmode=require (PEM files;
                               --tls-cert auto: a self-signed pair made in <data>/_tls; env KARELADB_TLS_CERT,
                               KARELADB_TLS_KEY; kareladb.conf tls_cert, tls_key)
  --tls-required on|off        with TLS, refuse plain connections except from 127.x (default on;
                               env KARELADB_TLS_REQUIRED)
  --rate-limit-ip N            requests per second one client address may send, HTTP and PostgreSQL
                               (default 0 = no limit; 127.x is never limited; env KARELADB_RATE_LIMIT_IP)
  --rate-limit-user N          requests per second one user may send (default 0 = no limit;
                               env KARELADB_RATE_LIMIT_USER). Over a limit: HTTP 429 with Retry-After
  --http-threads N             HTTP requests handled at once (default: the CPU threads, at least 8; env KARELADB_HTTP_THREADS)
  --http-gzip remote|on|off    gzip answers of 2 KB or more for clients that send Accept-Encoding: gzip:
                               clients on other computers (remote, the default), all, or none (env KARELADB_HTTP_GZIP)
  --timer-workers N            timers that may run at the same time (1 to 64, default 3; env KARELADB_TIMER_WORKERS)
  --tcp-keepalives-idle S      TCP keepalive of every connection: seconds idle before the first probe,
  --tcp-keepalives-interval S  seconds between probes, and probes before a vanished client is dropped
  --tcp-keepalives-count N     (0 = the system's, the default; env KARELADB_TCP_KEEPALIVES_IDLE, ...)
  --ilp-auto-create on|off     POST /write creates a table it does not find, as QuestDB does (default on;
                               kareladb.conf "ilp_auto_create"; env KARELADB_ILP_AUTO_CREATE)
  --max-connections N          PostgreSQL logins at once, all databases (default 100, 0 = no limit; env KARELADB_MAX_CONNECTIONS)
  --lock-timeout 5s            a writer waits this long for a busy table (default 5s, 0 = no limit; env KARELADB_LOCK_TIMEOUT;
                               a session: SET lock_timeout = '20s')
  --idle-in-transaction-timeout 30s  an open BEGIN ... COMMIT that sends nothing this long is rolled
                               back (default 30s, 0 = never; env KARELADB_IDLE_IN_TRANSACTION_TIMEOUT;
                               a session: SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '5min')
  --trigger-retries N          a failed deferred trigger job runs again N times (1 s, 2 s, 4 s ... apart) before
                               its queue stops (default 3, 0 = never; env KARELADB_TRIGGER_RETRIES)
  --max-trigger-jobs N         deferred trigger jobs waiting per database; a write past it is refused with the
                               reason (default 10000, 0 = no limit; env KARELADB_MAX_TRIGGER_JOBS)
  --alert-webhook URL          POST failed trigger jobs as JSON to http://<IPv4>:<port>/<path>
                               (env KARELADB_ALERT_WEBHOOK, kareladb.conf alert_webhook)
  --backups <dir>              backup folder (default <data folder>/_backups; "off" = none; or KARELADB_BACKUP_DIR)
  --backup-schedule "daily 16:00"  verified backups of every database (local time; or KARELADB_BACKUP_SCHEDULE)
  --backup-command "<cmd>"     run after each backup to copy it off the server: {dir} {database} {name}
                               (or KARELADB_BACKUP_COMMAND), e.g. "rclone copy {dir} remote:kdb/{database}/{name}"
  --backup-copy <dir>          a second, checked copy of each scheduled backup (another disk)
  --backup-warn-hours N        warn in the log when the last good backup is older (default 26)
  --keep-daily N --keep-weekly N   backups kept (default 7 and 4; or KARELADB_BACKUP_KEEP_DAILY / _WEEKLY)
Exit codes: 0 OK, 1 error, 2 damage found, 3 the database needs a newer KarelaDB (nothing was changed).

Help topics (0), from ./help-placeholder. "kareladb help <topic>" prints one; a running server has them at /help:
```
## kareladb version

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb version
kareladb --version
kareladb version <db>
```

Prints the version of KarelaDB and the stored-format features it can read. `crc32c hardware: yes` means the CPU computes checksums (CRC32C) with special fast instructions. `no` also works, only slower.
With `<db>` it shows the features that database uses ([versions and upgrades](versions.md)).

- **Exit code:** `0`. With `<db>`: `3` when the database needs a newer KarelaDB.

**Command line**

```bash
kareladb version
```

Output:


<a id="db-argument"></a>

## <db>: a name or a folder path

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb sql market "..."          -- a name: the database 'market' in the data folder
kareladb sql ./market "..."        -- a path: the folder 'market' in the current folder
kareladb sql D:\kdb\market "..."   -- a path: always that folder
```

The commands `sql`, `shell`, `serve`, `info`, `check`, `repair` and `backup` take `<db>`. KarelaDB decides like this:

| You write | KarelaDB uses |
|---|---|
| A name (only letters, digits, `_` and `-`), and the data folder has a database with that name | That database in the data folder. Upper or lower case does not matter. |
| A name, and the data folder has **no** database with that name | The folder with that name in the **current** folder. It is created when it does not exist. |
| A path (it has `\`, `/`, `:` or `.`) | Always that folder. It is created when it does not exist (not by `kareladb info` and `kareladb check`). |
| Nothing (only `kareladb shell` and `kareladb serve`) | The data folder: `kareladb shell` opens the database `default`; `kareladb serve` serves all databases. |

- **Notes:** a wrong name does **not** give an error. `kareladb sql markett "..."` makes a new, empty database `markett`, and then says `table ... does not exist`. Write `./market` when you want to be sure you mean a folder.
- With a **name**, `kareladb backup` and `kareladb repair --backups` use the sub-folder `<backups-dir>/<name>`, the same place `kareladb serve` uses.
- Database names are 1 to 64 characters. `Market` and `market` are the same database.

**Command line: A name in the data folder, and a path in the current folder**

```bash
kareladb shell
> CREATE DATABASE reports;
kareladb sql reports "CREATE TABLE daily (day DATE PRIMARY KEY, trades LONG); INSERT INTO daily VALUES ('2026-09-10', 32)"
kareladb info reports
kareladb sql ./reports "SHOW TABLES"
```

Output:

`> kareladb shell`

```text
KarelaDB 0.2.0-dev shell on default (data folder ./kdb-data)
End statements with ';'. Type .help for commands, .exit to quit.
kareladb> database 'reports' created
kareladb>
```

`> kareladb sql reports "CREATE TABLE daily (day DATE PRIMARY KEY, trades LONG); INSERT INTO daily VALUES ('2026-09-10', 32)"`

```text
table 'daily' created

1 row(s) inserted
```

`> kareladb info reports`
