(1 row)

<a id="kv-collections"></a>

## Hashes, sets, sorted sets and lists

A key can hold more than one text. The commands and answers are Redis 7's; `COMMAND DOCS HSET` shows the syntax of each one.

| Type | Commands | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| hash | `HSET`, `HGET`, `HMGET`, `HGETALL`, `HDEL`, `HEXISTS`, `HLEN`, `HKEYS`, `HVALS`, `HINCRBY`, `HINCRBYFLOAT`, `HSETNX`, `HSTRLEN`, `HRANDFIELD`, `HSCAN` | a record: a user, a cart, the fields of one session |
| set | `SADD`, `SREM`, `SMEMBERS`, `SISMEMBER`, `SMISMEMBER`, `SCARD`, `SINTER`, `SUNION`, `SDIFF` (and `...STORE`), `SINTERCARD`, `SMOVE`, `SPOP`, `SRANDMEMBER`, `SSCAN` | tags, who is online, unique visitors |
| sorted set | `ZADD`, `ZINCRBY`, `ZREM`, `ZSCORE`, `ZMSCORE`, `ZCARD`, `ZCOUNT`, `ZRANK`, `ZREVRANK`, `ZRANGE` (`BYSCORE`, `BYLEX`, `REV`, `LIMIT`, `WITHSCORES`), `ZRANGEBYSCORE`, `ZPOPMIN`, `ZPOPMAX`, `ZUNION`, `ZINTER`, `ZDIFF` (and `...STORE`), `ZREMRANGEBY...`, `ZRANDMEMBER`, `ZSCAN` | leaderboards, things due at a time (score = Unix time) |
| list | `LPUSH`, `RPUSH`, `LPOP`, `RPOP`, `LLEN`, `LRANGE`, `LINDEX`, `LSET`, `LINSERT`, `LREM`, `LPOS`, `LTRIM`, `LMOVE`, `LMPOP`, `RPOPLPUSH` | queues, the last n events |
| any of them | `SORT key [BY pattern] [LIMIT o n] [GET pattern ...] [ASC \| DESC] [ALPHA] [STORE dst]`, `SORT_RO` | the values sorted, or values of other keys they point to |

```js
await fetch('/kv', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify([
  ['HSET', 'user:1', 'name', 'a', 'age', '3'],
  ['HINCRBY', 'user:1', 'age', '2'],
  ['HGETALL', 'user:1'],
  ['ZADD', 'board', 10, 'a', 20, 'b'],
  ['ZRANGE', 'board', 0, -1, 'WITHSCORES'],
]) });                                   // -> [2, 5, {"name":"a","age":"5"}, 2, ["a","10","b","20"]]
```

**Example: A hash and a leaderboard from SQL**

```sql
SELECT kv('HSET', 'user:1', 'name', 'Sita', 'age', '30'), kv('HINCRBY', 'user:1', 'age', '1'), kv('HGETALL', 'user:1');
SELECT kv('ZADD', 'board', '10', 'ram', '25', 'sita'), kv('ZRANGE', 'board', '0', '-1', 'REV', 'WITHSCORES');
```

Result:

`SELECT kv('HSET', 'user:1', 'name', 'Sita', 'age', '30'), kv('HINCRBY', 'user:1', 'age', '1'), kv('H`

| kv('HSET', 'user:1', 'name', 'Sita', 'age', '30') (LONG) | kv('HINCRBY', 'user:1', 'age', '1') (LONG) | kv('HGETALL', 'user:1') (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 31 | {"name":"Sita","age":"31"} |

(1 row)

`SELECT kv('ZADD', 'board', '10', 'ram', '25', 'sita'), kv('ZRANGE', 'board', '0', '-1', 'REV', 'WITH`

| kv('ZADD', 'board', '10', 'ram', '25', 'sita') (LONG) | kv('ZRANGE', 'board', '0', '-1', 'REV', 'WITHSCORES') (STRING) |
|---|---|
| 2 | ["sita","25","ram","10"] |

(1 row)

- `HGETALL` answers a JSON **object**; scores are texts (`"10"`, `"1.5"`), and `WITHSCORES` lists are flat: `[member, score, ...]`.
- `SMEMBERS`, `SINTER`, `SUNION` and `SDIFF` answer the members **sorted**, so the answer is the same every time (Redis's order changes).
- A command on a key of another type answers `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value`; so does `GET` of a hash.
- A hash, set or list that becomes empty is deleted, as in Redis. `EXPIRE`, `TTL`, `DEL`, `RENAME`, `COPY` and `TYPE` work on every type.
- They count toward the [memory cap](#kv-memory) like strings, and eviction may take a whole hash, set or list.

<a id="kv-blocking"></a>

### Waiting for a value: BLPOP

`BLPOP key [key ...] timeout` takes the first value of the first list that has one. When all are empty it **waits** until another client pushes, up to `timeout` seconds (`0.5` works; `0` = no limit), then answers `null`. `BRPOP`, `BLMOVE`, `BRPOPLPUSH`, `BLMPOP`, `BZPOPMIN`, `BZPOPMAX` and `BZMPOP` wait the same way.

```js
// a worker: waits up to 5 s for a job
const [job] = await (await fetch('/kv', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify(['BLPOP', 'jobs', 5]) })).json();
// -> ["jobs", "job-17"] as soon as someone runs ['RPUSH', 'jobs', 'job-17'], or null after 5 s
```

- The wait holds one HTTP thread: many waiting workers need more threads (`kareladb serve --http-threads`).
- From SQL (`kv('BLPOP', ...)`) a blocking pop never waits: it answers at once, so a statement cannot hang.

<a id="kv-watch"></a>

### WATCH, MULTI and EXEC

`MULTI` queues the commands after it and `EXEC` runs them together: no other client's command comes in between. `WATCH key ...` before `MULTI` makes `EXEC` answer `null` (and run nothing) when another client changed one of those keys meanwhile, so you read again and retry: an **optimistic lock**.

A Redis connection keeps its `WATCH` from one command to the next. Over HTTP, give your requests a **session** name: `POST /kv?session=name`. Requests with the same name (from the same user) share their `WATCH` and `MULTI`; a session ends 10 minutes after its last request. Without `session`, they last for that one request.

```js
// request 1: read the stock and watch it
POST /kv?session=order-7   [["WATCH","stock"],["GET","stock"]]            // -> ["OK","5"]
// request 2: write it only if nobody changed it since
POST /kv?session=order-7   [["MULTI"],["SET","stock","4"],["EXEC"]]       // -> ["OK","QUEUED",["OK"]], or [..., null] to retry
```

- A command refused while queued (unknown, wrong number of words, no right to write) makes `EXEC` answer `EXECABORT` and run nothing, as in Redis.
- `UNWATCH` forgets the watched keys; `DISCARD` drops the queue.

<a id="kv-sql"></a>

## From SQL: kv_get, kv_set, kv_incr

Syntax:

```sql
kv_get(key)                     -- GET
kv_set(key, value [, seconds])  -- SET key value [EX seconds]
kv_incr(key [, n])              -- INCRBY key n (1 when left out)
kv_del(key)                     -- DEL
kv_expire(key, seconds)         -- EXPIRE
kv_ttl(key)                     -- TTL
kv(command, word, ...)          -- any command: kv('MGET', 'a', 'b')
```

The same store, from any SQL client and the PostgreSQL port. A list answer (`MGET`, `KEYS`, `LRANGE`) comes as JSON text, and `HGETALL` as a JSON object. A NULL word gives NULL and changes nothing.

**Example: A counter and a code that expires**

```sql
SELECT kv_incr('page:home');
SELECT kv_incr('page:home', 10);
SELECT kv_set('otp:42', '815204', 120), kv_get('otp:42'), kv_ttl('otp:42');
SELECT kv('MGET', 'page:home', 'otp:42', 'nothing');
```

Result:

`SELECT kv_incr('page:home')`

| kv_incr('page:home') (LONG) |
|---|
| 1 |

(1 row)

`SELECT kv_incr('page:home', 10)`

| kv_incr('page:home', 10) (LONG) |
|---|
| 11 |

(1 row)

`SELECT kv_set('otp:42', '815204', 120), kv_get('otp:42'), kv_ttl('otp:42')`

| kv_set('otp:42', '815204', 120) (STRING) | kv_get('otp:42') (STRING) | kv_ttl('otp:42') (LONG) |
|---|---|---|
| OK | 815204 | 120 |

(1 row)

`SELECT kv('MGET', 'page:home', 'otp:42', 'nothing')`

| kv('MGET', 'page:home', 'otp:42', 'nothing') (STRING) |
|---|
| ["11","815204",null] |

(1 row)

**Example: A counter needs a number** (shows an error)

```sql
SELECT kv_set('name', 'sita'), kv_incr('name');
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 32: kv_incr: ERR value is not an integer or out of range`

- **Rights:** `kv_get`, `kv_ttl` and reading commands need role `read`; the others need role `write`, and so does `kv()` when its command is not written out as text (as in `kv(col, 'k')`). A read-only transaction (`BEGIN READ ONLY`) refuses them.
- **On disk:** the client's statement returns once its changes are on disk. Inside an open `BEGIN ... COMMIT` (and with `SET synchronous_commit = off`) it does not wait; the change is written within milliseconds. A key change is **not** part of the transaction: a `ROLLBACK` does not take it back.

<a id="kv-table"></a>

## The table _kv

The keys live in the table `_kv` of the database, made at the first change:

| Column | Type | |
|---|---|---|
| `k` | `STRING PRIMARY KEY` | the key |
| `v` | `STRING` | the value |
| `expires_at` | `TIMESTAMP` | when it expires; `NULL` = never ([row TTL](create-table.md#row-ttl)) |

- `SELECT` reads it like any table: `SELECT k, v FROM _kv WHERE k LIKE 'session:%'`. Expired keys are not in it.
- Only the store changes it: `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `TRUNCATE`, `DROP` and `ALTER` of `_kv` are refused (`42501`). Empty it with `FLUSHDB`. [TRUNCATE ALL TABLES](databases.md#truncate-all-tables) empties the store too.
- It is in the log and in backups like any table, and the keys are back after a restart: the store reads `_kv` into memory when the database opens.
- **Memory:** every key and value is held in memory while the database is open, as in Redis. Keep big documents in tables, or set a [cap](#kv-memory).

Hashes, sets, sorted sets and lists are in a second table, `_kv_items`, made when the first one is: one row with the key's type (`t`) and expiry, and **one row per field, member or list item** (`f`, `v`). So `HSET` of one field writes one row, however big the hash is.

```sql
SELECT k, t, f, v FROM _kv_items WHERE k = 'user:1';
-- user:1 | hash | NULL | NULL
-- user:1 | NULL | age  | 31
-- user:1 | NULL | name | Sita
```

Only the store changes `_kv_items` too.

<!-- docs/http-sessions-and-cursors.md -->

# Sessions and cursors over HTTP

> Keep a transaction open over several HTTP requests with a session, and read a big result a part at a time with a cursor.

- Category: HTTP API
- Keywords: session, /session, X-KDB-Session, transaction over HTTP, BEGIN COMMIT over HTTP, idle\_timeout\_ms, cursor, /cursor, fetch, done, big result, paging, read in parts, snapshot, database is busy, 503
- See also: [Transactions](transactions.md), [Cursors](cursors.md), [Run SQL over HTTP (/exec, /exp)](http-exec.md), [HTTP API overview](http-overview.md)

Normally every HTTP request stands alone: a `BEGIN` in one `/exec` request cannot be finished by a `COMMIT` in the next one. Two tools help:

- A **session** keeps a transaction (`BEGIN` ... `COMMIT`: several changes that are saved all together or not at all) open between requests. Open one with `POST /session`, then send its id in the header `X-KDB-Session` with each `/exec`.
- A **cursor** runs one `SELECT` once, keeps its rows on the server, and gives them to you a few at a time. Use it for results too big for one answer.

More about transactions: [Transactions](transactions.md). SQL cursors inside procedures (`DECLARE ... CURSOR`): [Cursors](cursors.md).

## POST /session

Syntax:

```sql
POST /session
```

Opens a session and gives back its id. Send the id with every request that belongs to it:

Syntax:

```sql
X-KDB-Session: <id>        (a header on /exec)
/exec?session=<id>         (or a URL parameter or form field)
```

| Parameter | Where | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| (none) | - | The request has no body | - |

| Answer field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `session` | The session id: 32 random hex characters. Keep it secret: it is like a key to the open transaction. |
| `idle_timeout_ms` | A session unused this long is closed, and its open transaction is rolled back (undone). 600,000 ms = 10 minutes. |

- **Status codes:** 200; 401 without a needed login; 503 too many open sessions (at most 1,000): close unused ones.
- **Notes:**
  - A session belongs to the user who opened it. Another user's session id answers 404, as if it did not exist.
  - A session may run SQL on several databases (`db=` on each request); `DELETE /session/<id>` ends it on all of them.
  - **One writer per table:** while a session has an open `BEGIN`, other changes to the tables it used (other requests, the line protocol) **wait** up to the lock timeout (5 seconds unless set: `SET lock_timeout = '20s'` in the session, or the header `X-KDB-Lock-Timeout: 20s` on one request; see [lock timeout](transactions.md#lock-timeout)), then fail with HTTP 503 `table 'x' is busy: ...`. Changes to other tables go on. Reads do not wait: they see the rows as they were before the open transaction. Keep transactions short.
  - An open transaction with no statement for **30 seconds** is rolled back by the database. The session then gets an error until it sends `ROLLBACK`.
  - Without a session, a transaction cannot stay open after its request: a `BEGIN` without `COMMIT` is rolled back at the end of the request, and the answer is an error (see the example below). Send `BEGIN; ...; COMMIT` in one `POST /exec`, or use a session.

**HTTP: Without a session: BEGIN without COMMIT is rolled back** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

```http
POST /exec?compat=0

INSERT INTO brokers VALUES (72, 'Never Saved Securities')
```

A transfer between two accounts in Python, with the `requests` library:

```python
import requests

KarelaDB = "http://127.0.0.1:9900"

def run(sql, session=None):
    headers = {"Content-Type": "text/plain; charset=utf-8"}
    if session:
        headers["X-KDB-Session"] = session
    r = requests.post(f"{KarelaDB}/exec", params={"compat": 0, "db": "shop"}, data=sql.encode("utf-8"), headers=headers)
    body = r.json()
    if r.status_code != 200:
        raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {r.status_code}: {body['error']}")
    return body["results"]

session = requests.post(f"{KarelaDB}/session").json()["session"]
try:
    run("BEGIN", session)
    run("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1", session)
    balance = run("SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1", session)[0]["dataset"][0][0]
    if float(balance) < 0:
        run("ROLLBACK", session)          # not enough money: undo
    else:
        run("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 2", session)
        run("COMMIT", session)
finally:
    requests.delete(f"{KarelaDB}/session/{session}")   # rolls back anything still open
```

```js
// Node 18+
const KarelaDB = "http://127.0.0.1:9900";
const { session } = await (await fetch(`${KarelaDB}/session`, { method: "POST" })).json();
const run = async (sql) => {
  const res = await fetch(`${KarelaDB}/exec?compat=0`, { method: "POST", headers: { "X-KDB-Session": session }, body: sql });
  const body = await res.json();
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(body.error);
  return body.results;
};
try {
  await run("BEGIN");
  await run("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'CITY', 10)");
  await run("COMMIT");
} finally {
  await fetch(`${KarelaDB}/session/${session}`, { method: "DELETE" });
}
```

```powershell
$kdb = "http://127.0.0.1:9900"
$s = (Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post "$kdb/session").session
$h = @{ "X-KDB-Session" = $s }
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post "$kdb/exec?compat=0" -Headers $h -ContentType "text/plain" -Body "BEGIN; INSERT INTO brokers VALUES (71, 'Test')" | Out-Null
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post "$kdb/exec?compat=0" -Headers $h -ContentType "text/plain" -Body "COMMIT" | Out-Null
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Delete "$kdb/session/$s" | Out-Null
```

<a id="delete-session"></a>

## DELETE /session/<id>

Syntax:

```sql
DELETE /session/<id>
```

Closes a session. Its open transaction is **rolled back** (nothing of it is saved) and its SQL cursors are closed.

| Parameter | Where | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `<id>` | path | The id from `POST /session` | required |

| Answer field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `session` | The id |
| `closed` | `true` |

- **Status codes:** 200; 401 without a needed login; 404 no such session (already closed, closed after 10 minutes unused, or opened by another user).
- **Notes:** always close sessions you opened (in a `finally` block), even after an error. A request with a closed session id answers 404 `session '...' does not exist: it was closed, or unused for more than 600 s (its open transaction was rolled back). Open a new one with POST /session`. A server restart closes every session.

**HTTP: Closing the session undoes the open transaction** (sample data: sample)

```http

BEGIN;
DELETE FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = 'CITY'
###
DELETE /session/{{session}}
###
GET /exec?compat=0&query=SELECT count(*) AS city_days_still_there FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = 'CITY'
```

## POST /cursor

Syntax:

```sql
POST /cursor[?db=<name>]
body: one SELECT
```

Runs one `SELECT`, keeps all its rows on the server, and answers with the cursor's id. Read the rows with [GET /cursor/&lt;id&gt;](http-sessions-and-cursors.md#get-cursor).

| Parameter | Where | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| body | body | Exactly one `SELECT` (or a form field `query=`) | required |
| `db` | URL | The database (or the header `X-KDB-Database`). Use the same database for all requests of this cursor. | the default database |

| Answer field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `cursor` | The cursor id (16 hex characters, hard to guess) |
| `columns[]` | `name` and `type` of each column |
| `rows` | How many rows the cursor holds |

- **Status codes:** 200; 400 not exactly one SELECT, bad SQL, more than 10,000,000 rows, or too many open cursors; 401/403 login or role (needs `read`); 404 unknown database.
- **Notes:**
  - The rows are a **snapshot**: changes after `POST /cursor` do not change them. A cursor never sees a transaction that is still open.
  - The rows stay in the server's memory until the cursor is closed or done, so close it when you are finished.
  - At most 16 cursors per database are open at the same time (SQL cursors of procedures count too). An unused cursor closes after 10 minutes.
  - At most 10,000,000 rows per cursor: narrow the SELECT with `WHERE`.

**HTTP: Open a cursor, read 3 rows twice, close it** (sample data: sample)

```http
POST /cursor

SELECT time, symbol, close FROM ochl_minutes WHERE time IN '2026-09-10' ORDER BY time, symbol
###
GET /cursor/{{cursor}}?fetch=3
###
GET /cursor/{{cursor}}?fetch=3
###
DELETE /cursor/{{cursor}}
```

Response:

`POST /cursor`

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
  "columns": [
```

<a id="get-cursor"></a>

## GET /cursor/<id>

Syntax:

```sql
GET /cursor/<id>[?fetch=N]
```

Gives the next `N` rows of the cursor. It only reads rows that are already kept, so GET is right here.

| Parameter | Where | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `<id>` | path | The id from `POST /cursor` | required |
| `fetch` | URL | How many rows: 1 or more, at most 1,000,000 | 1,000 |
| `db` | URL | The same database as `POST /cursor` (or the header `X-KDB-Database`) | the default database |

| Answer field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `cursor` | The id |
| `columns[]` | `name` and `type` of each column |
| `dataset` | The rows, in the same form as [/exec](http-exec.md#get-exec) |
| `count` | Number of rows in this answer |
| `done` | `true` when no rows are left after these |

- **Status codes:** 200; 400 `fetch must be a number of rows, 1 or more`; 401/403 login or role; 404 no such cursor (closed, unused for 10 minutes, or another database).
- **Notes:** after `done` is `true`, the kept rows are freed, but the id stays until you close it (further GETs give 0 rows). Read in a loop until `done`.

**HTTP: Read until done** (sample data: sample)


Reading a big result in Python, 5,000 rows at a time:

```python
import requests

KarelaDB = "http://127.0.0.1:9900"
params = {"db": "market"}
c = requests.post(f"{KarelaDB}/cursor", params=params,
                  data="SELECT time, symbol, close FROM ochl_minutes ORDER BY time".encode("utf-8")).json()
if "error" in c:
    raise RuntimeError(c["error"])
print("rows:", c["rows"])
try:
    while True:
        page = requests.get(f"{KarelaDB}/cursor/{c['cursor']}", params={**params, "fetch": 5000}).json()
        for time, symbol, close in page["dataset"]:
            pass  # use the row
        if page["done"]:
            break
finally:
    requests.delete(f"{KarelaDB}/cursor/{c['cursor']}", params=params)
```

```csharp
using var http = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri("http://127.0.0.1:9900") };
var open = await http.PostAsync("/cursor?db=market", new StringContent("SELECT time, close FROM ochl_minutes ORDER BY time", Encoding.UTF8, "text/plain"));
var cursor = JsonDocument.Parse(await open.Content.ReadAsStringAsync()).RootElement.GetProperty("cursor").GetString();
try
{
    while (true)
    {
        var page = JsonDocument.Parse(await http.GetStringAsync($"/cursor/{cursor}?db=market&fetch=5000")).RootElement;
        foreach (var row in page.GetProperty("dataset").EnumerateArray()) { /* use row[0], row[1] */ }
        if (page.GetProperty("done").GetBoolean()) break;
    }
}
finally
{
    await http.DeleteAsync($"/cursor/{cursor}?db=market");
}
```

<!-- docs/http-import.md -->

# CSV import over HTTP (POST /imp)

> Send a CSV file to kareladb serve and it loads the rows, making the table from the file when it is new - QuestDB's /imp.

- Category: HTTP API
- Keywords: /imp, imp, CSV import, timings, Server-Timing, parse\_ms, lock\_wait\_ms, wal\_ms, apply\_ms, durable\_ms, durable, queued, gzip upload, import CSV, upload CSV, load a file, QuestDB import, multipart, form-data, overwrite, atomicity, skipCol, skipRow, abort, forceHeader, partitionBy, delimiter, fmt, rowsImported, rowsRejected, schema
- See also: [Line protocol (POST /write)](line-protocol.md), [Loading many rows](loading-data.md), [Run SQL over HTTP (/exec, /exp)](http-exec.md), [HTTP API overview](http-overview.md), [CREATE TABLE](create-table.md), [Partitions, SORT BY and DEDUP KEY](partitions-and-dedup.md)

`POST /imp` loads a **CSV file** into a table. It is QuestDB's import route, so a QuestDB script or the QuestDB web console can send here without changes.

- A table that is **not there yet** is made from the file: the column names come from the first line, the types from the values.
- A table that **is** there gets the rows added (upserted, like the [line protocol](line-protocol.md#post-write)).
- Everything is written in **one transaction**: after a good answer all rows are in, after an error nothing changed.

For SQL, use [POST /exec](http-exec.md#post-exec). For a fast live feed, use the [line protocol](line-protocol.md). More ways to load data: [loading data](loading-data.md).

## POST /imp

Syntax:

```sql
POST /imp?name=<table>[&db=<name>]
         [&overwrite=true][&atomicity=skipCol|skipRow|abort]
         [&timestamp=<column>&partitionBy=DAY|MONTH|YEAR|NONE]
         [&delimiter=,][&forceHeader=true][&fmt=json]
body: the CSV itself, or multipart/form-data with a file part named "data"
```

Reads the CSV, makes the table when it is new, and writes the rows.

| Parameter | Where | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | URL | The table to load into. Without it, the file name of the upload (without `.csv`) is used. | required |
| `db` | URL | The database (or the header `X-KDB-Database`). Without it: the one database that already has the table ([which database](#which-database)). | see the left |
| `overwrite` | URL | `true`: drop the table first and make it again from the file. | `false` |
| `atomicity` | URL | What a value that does not fit its column does: `skipCol` the value becomes `NULL`, `skipRow` the whole row is left out, `abort` nothing at all is written. | `skipCol` |
| `dedup` | URL | `skip`: no duplicate lookups in days that already hold rows. **A key already stored may then be there twice**; the answer has `dedupSkipped` ([dedup=skip](partitions-and-dedup.md#dedup-skip)). | `on` |
| `timestamp` | URL | Which column is the time column of a **new** table (`TIMESERIES(...)`). | none |
| `partitionBy` | URL | `NONE`, `DAY`, `MONTH` or `YEAR` for a **new** table. Anything but `NONE` needs `timestamp=`. | `NONE` |
| `delimiter` | URL | The character between the values; `\t` or `tab` for a tab. Without it KarelaDB guesses from the first lines. | guessed |
| `forceHeader` | URL | `true`: the first line is column names. Without it KarelaDB decides: names that match the table, or a first line with nothing that looks like data. | guessed |
| `fmt` | URL | `json`: answer as JSON. Anything else: a short text answer. | text |
| `schema` | form part | JSON that sets column types: `[{"name": "close", "type": "DOUBLE"}]`. | types guessed |

| Answer (with `fmt=json`) | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `status` | `"OK"`, or the error message |
| `database` | the database the rows went into |
| `location` | the table the rows went into |
| `rowsImported` | how many rows were written |
| `rowsRejected` | how many rows were left out (`atomicity=skipRow`) |
| `header` | whether the first line was read as column names |
| `partitionBy`, `timestamp` | the table's partitioning and time column |
| `columns` | one entry per column: `name`, `type`, `size` in bytes, `errors` (values that did not fit) |
| `timings` | where the time of the request went, in milliseconds ([timings](#timings)) |

- **Status codes:** 200 loaded (read `rowsRejected`: a 200 can still have left rows out); 400 a bad CSV, a bad parameter, an unknown column, `atomicity=abort` with a bad value, or no `db` when the database cannot be worked out; 401/403 login or role (403 also when a [table right](table-rights.md) does not allow inserts into this table); 404 unknown database; 405 for a `GET`; 408 a trigger ran past the statement timeout; 413 body over 64 MB (counted after unpacking); 500 server trouble (nothing written); 503 while the server is stopping; 507 the disk is full: free space, then send the same file again, unless the message says `do not send it again` (the disk filled while the log was flushed: the rows are already in the table and are saved once space is back, see [backup and safety](backup-and-safety.md)).
- **Roles:** loading into a table that is there needs the **write** role. Making a table (a new name, or `overwrite=true`) needs **admin**.
- **Types of a new table:** `BOOLEAN`, `LONG`, `DOUBLE`, `DATE`, `TIMESTAMP`, else `STRING`. Send `schema` (or make the table yourself with [CREATE TABLE](create-table.md)) when you want `SYMBOL`, `DECIMAL(2)` or a `PRIMARY KEY`.
- **Notes:**
  - Rows are **upserted**: a row with the same `PRIMARY KEY` or `DEDUP KEY` replaces the old one, so sending the same file twice makes no duplicates.
  - The first 5000 lines are read first, to find the header and the types. A column whose later values do not fit follows `atomicity`.
  - The body may be compressed with `Content-Encoding: gzip` or `deflate`. The 64 MB limit counts the unpacked CSV. A damaged body gives 400 and imports nothing. With curl: `gzip -c prices.csv | curl --data-binary @- -H "Content-Encoding: gzip" "http://127.0.0.1:9900/imp?name=prices"`.
  - [Triggers](triggers.md) run once for the whole request, like the line protocol. Their time counts toward the [statement timeout](protection.md#statement-timeout); send `X-KDB-Statement-Timeout` for a longer one (admins only). A trigger that runs too long gives status 408 and `trigger <name>: statement timeout (<N> s) (nothing was imported)`.

<a id="timings"></a>

### When the OK comes, and where the time went

An OK from `/imp` (200) or [`/write`](line-protocol.md#post-write) (204) means the rows are **written and safe on disk**. Nothing is queued for later: the answer waits for the log's disk sync. A server crash right after the OK loses none of these rows.

Each answer says where its time went. `/imp` with `fmt=json` has a `timings` object; `/write` answers 204 with no body, so it sends the same numbers in the standard `Server-Timing` header (browser developer tools show it). All are milliseconds with 3 decimals.

| Field | `Server-Timing` | What the time was spent on |
|---|---|---|
| `parse_ms` | `parse` | reading the body (after unpacking gzip) and building the rows, before any lock |
| `lock_wait_ms` | `lock` | waiting behind other writes of the same tables, or for a transaction that holds one |
| `wal_ms` | `wal` | writing the log and waiting for its disk sync. Writers that arrive together share one sync |
| `apply_ms` | `apply` | checking the rows (keys, rules) and putting them in the table |
| `trigger_ms` | `trigger` | [triggers](triggers.md) the rows fired inside the request |
| `durable_ms` | | from the start until the rows were on disk: the moment the OK can go out |
| `total_ms` | `total` | the whole request |

The five steps add up to `total_ms`. A slow load then shows at a glance what to fix:

- a large `lock_wait_ms`: other writers or a long transaction hold the table. Send fewer, bigger requests, or write to separate tables.
- a large `wal_ms`: the disk is slow to sync. Bigger requests share one sync between more rows.
- a large `parse_ms`: the body is big. Several senders at once parse in parallel.

The activity log (`GET /api/activity`) keeps the same numbers for each write event, and `GET /api/stats` adds them up since the start under `writes` (`line_protocol` and `csv_import`: `requests`, `rows` and the sum of each step; a step's average is its sum divided by `requests`). `bench/parallel-write.mjs` sends from 1, 2, 4 and 8 senders at once and prints rows per second with the average of each step.

<a id="which-database"></a>

### Which database, without db=

A QuestDB client has no `db=` to send, so `/imp` works out the database from the table name:

| The server has | Without `db=` the rows go to |
|---|---|
| one database | that database |
| several, and one of them has the table | that database (the default one wins when it is among several that have it) |
| several, and more than one has the table (not the default) | nothing: 400, add `db=` |
| several, and none has the table | nothing: 400, add `db=` or create the table first |

KarelaDB refuses rather than guessing, so a load meant for another database never makes a new table with guessed types in the default one. The answer's `database` says where the rows went.

**HTTP: A new table straight from a CSV of daily closes**

```http
POST /imp?name=day_closes&timestamp=time&partitionBy=YEAR&fmt=json
Content-Type: text/csv

time,symbol,close
2026-09-09T00:00:00Z,CITY,502.10
2026-09-09T00:00:00Z,COAST,374.80
2026-09-10T00:00:00Z,CITY,504.90
2026-09-10T00:00:00Z,COAST,376.10
###
GET /exec?compat=0&query=SELECT * FROM day_closes ORDER BY time, symbol
```

```python
    raise RuntimeError(answer["status"])
print(answer["rowsImported"], "rows in", answer["location"])
```

<!-- docs/pinned-queries.md -->

# Pinned queries

> Pin a SELECT so its result is always ready in the result cache - computed when the database opens, never pushed out, computed again after a write.

- Category: HTTP API
- Keywords: pin, pinned query, pinned statement, pins, keep a result ready, warm cache, preload, dashboard slow query, GET /api/pins, POST /api/pins, DELETE /api/pins, \_pinned\_queries, cache\_pinned
- See also: [Performance tips (result-cache)](performance-tips.md#result-cache), [Run SQL over HTTP (/exec, /exp)](http-exec.md), [Timers](timers.md), [Indexes (warm)](indexes.md#warm), [Monitor panel (memory, processor, caches)](console-monitor.md)

A **pinned query** is a `SELECT` the server keeps ready. Pin the slow question a dashboard asks on every load, and from then on every request for it is answered from the [result cache](performance-tips.md#result-cache):

- It is computed **when the database opens**, right after the indexes are [built at open](indexes.md#warm), before anyone asks.
- It is **never pushed out** of the result cache by other results, and it may take up to **three quarters** of the cache (an ordinary result is kept only up to a quarter).
- After a **write** to a table it reads, the server computes it again by itself once the database has been quiet for half a second, so the next request finds it fresh. On a database that is written all the time and is never quiet, it does so at the latest two seconds after the first write that made the result old. A request that comes before that computes it, as any query would.
- Pins are saved in the table `_pinned_queries` of the hidden `_system` database (like [timers](timers.md)), or of the served database when `kareladb serve` runs on one folder, so they survive restarts and are part of every backup.

The rules of the cache still apply: the statement must be one cacheable `SELECT` of this database (no `now()`, no random functions, no other database), and the **row limit is part of the key**: pin it with the `max_rows` the requests use (`/exec` sends 10,000 unless `limit=` says otherwise; the console sends 10,000).

A pin is saved code that later runs by itself, without a rights check: only a server **admin** can pin or unpin, and every change is written to the [audit log](audit-log.md) (event `pin`).

Pins are a feature of `kareladb serve`. A server started without them answers `/api/pins` with 404.

<a id="get-api-pins"></a>

## GET /api/pins

Syntax:

```sql
GET /api/pins[?db=<name>]
```

The pins of one database (the default database without `db=`). Needs read rights on the database.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `database`, `sql`, `max_rows`, `enabled` | the pin as saved |
| `created_ms`, `created_by` | when it was saved and by whom; empty = the token |
| `open` | the database is open now; the fields below are live only then |
| `cached`, `cached_bytes` | its result is in the cache right now, and its size |
| `last_run_ms`, `last_ok`, `last_error` | the last time the server computed it by itself (at open, or after a write); `last_ok` is `null` before the first |
| `error` | why the database refused the pin when it was applied (a column that no longer exists, for example); empty when it took it |

`now_ms` at the top is the server's clock. `GET /api/stats` shows `cache_pinned` per database: how many pinned results are in the cache now.

<a id="post-api-pins"></a>

## POST /api/pins

Syntax:

```sql
POST /api/pins[?db=<name>]
Content-Type: application/json

{"sql": "SELECT ...", "max_rows": 10000, "enabled": true}
```

Pins a statement, or replaces the pin with the same SQL. Returns the pin.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `sql` | one `SELECT`, at most 64 KB |
| `max_rows` | optional, 1 to 1,000,000 (default 10,000): the row limit the requests use |
| `enabled` | optional (default `true`); `false` keeps the pin saved without applying it |

A statement that is not one `SELECT`, does not parse, or reads another database is a 400 that says so. So is a `max_rows` out of range.

**HTTP: Pin the totals a dashboard shows on every load**

Setup:

```text
CREATE TABLE trades (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, symbol SYMBOL, qty LONG, price DOUBLE);
INSERT INTO trades VALUES (1, 'CITY', 100, 510.5), (2, 'CITY', 50, 512), (3, 'VOLT', 200, 301);
```

```http
POST /api/pins
Content-Type: application/json

{"sql": "SELECT symbol, sum(qty) AS qty, sum(qty * price) AS amount FROM trades GROUP BY symbol ORDER BY symbol"}
###
GET /api/pins
```

Response:

`POST /api/pins`

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{
  "database": "demo",
  "sql": "SELECT symbol, sum(qty) AS qty, sum(qty * price) AS amount FROM trades GROUP BY symbol ORDER BY symbol",
  "max_rows": 10000,
  "enabled": true,
  "created_ms": 1792822768156,
  "created_by": "",
  "open": true,
  "cached": false,
  "cached_bytes": 0,
  "last_run_ms": 1792822768157,
  "last_ok": true,
  "last_error": "",
  "error": ""
}
```

`GET /api/pins`

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{
  "now_ms": 1792822768208,
  "pins": [
    {
      "database": "demo",
      "sql": "SELECT symbol, sum(qty) AS qty, sum(qty * price) AS amount FROM trades GROUP BY symbol ORDER BY symbol",
      "max_rows": 10000,
      "enabled": true,
      "created_ms": 1792822768156,
      "created_by": "",
      "open": true,
      "cached": false,
      "cached_bytes": 0,
      "last_run_ms": 1792822768157,
      "last_ok": true,

      "error": ""
    }
  ]
```

<!-- docs/revisions.md -->

# Change revisions: GET /api/rev and kdb_rev()

> A cheap number per table and per symbol that changes when committed rows change, so a chart polls it and reads its candles again only when they changed.

- Category: HTTP API
- Keywords: revision, revisions, rev, GET /api/rev, api/rev, kdb\_rev, candle rev, candle-rev, change signal, did it change, poll, polling, chart refresh, table\_rev, boot, rev column, per-symbol revision
- See also: [Performance tips (result-cache)](performance-tips.md#result-cache), [Pinned queries](pinned-queries.md), [Run SQL over HTTP (/exec, /exp)](http-exec.md), [CREATE TABLE](create-table.md)

A chart that shows NABIL's candles does not need to read them every few seconds. It can ask for NABIL's **revision** instead, and read the candles again only when the revision changed.

- A revision is a short text such as `a67f6ff8e720.1532`. Compare it for **equality** only; the number is not a count and not a time.
- It changes after every **committed** change of rows holding that value: `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `POST /write`, `POST /imp`, a trigger, a `CALL`.
- A change **inside an open transaction** does not move it. It moves at `COMMIT`. A rollback may move it too; the rows are then the same as before, and a read again simply gives them.
- Another value's writes never move it: a new NEPSE candle leaves NABIL's revision alone.
- A **restart** changes every revision (the part before the dot is new).
- It never waits for the database lock: it answers in well under a millisecond, even while a long `CALL` or bulk load writes.

<a id="rev-column"></a>

## Which column has revisions

Each table keeps revisions for the values of **one** column, when it has one of these:

| Table | Column with revisions |
|---|---|
| `PARTITION BY ..., SYMBOL(symbol)` | `symbol` (the column named in `SYMBOL(...)`) |
| `SORT BY (symbol, time)`, `DEDUP KEY (symbol, time)`, or a `PRIMARY KEY` whose first column is a `SYMBOL` | that first column |
| anything else (`SORT BY (time, symbol)`, no SYMBOL key) | none: every value gets the table's revision |

A table without a rev column still works: its values then change together, whenever any row of the table changes.

Revisions per value are for columns with **up to 10,000 values**, such as the symbols of a market. They live in memory, outside `--memory`. When a table's rev column gets more values than that (a `SYMBOL` primary key of customer ids, say), the table drops its list and goes on as if it had no rev column: every write then moves every value's revision. `rev_values` in `GET /api/stats` counts the values kept.

The same values decide what the [result cache](performance-tips.md#result-cache) keeps: a cached `WHERE symbol = 'NABIL'` result stays valid while only other symbols are written.

<a id="api-rev"></a>

## GET /api/rev

Syntax:

```sql
GET /api/rev?table=<name>&symbol=<value>[&symbol=<value> ...][&column=<name>][&db=<name>]
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `table` | the table (required) |
| `symbol` | a value of the rev column; repeat it for more (up to 1000). `value=` is the same |
| `column` | optional: the rev column's name. A different name is a 400 that names the right one |
| `db` | the database; the default database without it |

The answer:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `table`, `column` | the table and its rev column (`null` when it has none) |
| `boot` | changes when the database opens again |
| `table_rev` | changes after every committed change of the table |
| `revs` | one revision per value asked for |

It needs read rights on the table: role `read` on the database, or `GRANT SELECT` on the table. An unknown table is a 404.

**HTTP: The revisions of two symbols**

Setup:

```text
CREATE TABLE candles (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, close DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time)
  PARTITION BY YEAR, SYMBOL(symbol) SORT BY (symbol, time) DEDUP KEY (symbol, time);
INSERT INTO candles VALUES ('2026-09-24T10:00:00Z', 'NABIL', 1510), ('2026-09-24T10:00:00Z', 'NEPSE', 2750);
```

```http
GET /api/rev?table=candles&symbol=NABIL&symbol=NEPSE
```

Response:

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{
  "database": "demo",
  "table": "candles",
  "column": "symbol",
  "boot": "f13844fa1885",
  "table_rev": "f13844fa1885.0",
  "revs": {"NABIL": "f13844fa1885.0", "NEPSE": "f13844fa1885.0"}
}
```

**HTTP: Asking by the wrong column says which one has revisions**

Setup:

```text
CREATE TABLE candles (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, close DOUBLE) TIMESERIES(time)
  PARTITION BY YEAR, SYMBOL(symbol) SORT BY (symbol, time) DEDUP KEY (symbol, time);
```

```http
GET /api/rev?table=candles&column=close&symbol=NABIL
```

Response:

HTTP 400 (application/json)

```text
{"error": "table 'candles' keeps revisions per value of column 'symbol', not 'close'"}
```

A page that polls:

```js
let seen = null;
setInterval(async () => {
  const r = await (await fetch('/api/rev?table=candles&symbol=NABIL')).json();
  if (r.revs.NABIL !== seen) {
    seen = r.revs.NABIL;
    drawChart(await readCandles('NABIL'));  // only when NABIL changed
  }
}, 2000);
```

<a id="kdb_rev"></a>

## kdb_rev

Syntax:

```sql
kdb_rev('<table>')
kdb_rev('<table>', '<value>')
```

The same revisions in SQL, for clients that only speak the [PostgreSQL protocol](postgres-protocol.md). With one argument: the table's revision (`table_rev`). With two: the revision of that value of the rev column. It gives the same text as `GET /api/rev`, and needs the same right: reading the table (a user whose `SELECT` on it was revoked gets an error). Unlike the route it runs as a statement, so it waits for the database lock like any `SELECT`. A NULL argument gives NULL; an unknown table is an error.

**Example: A symbol's revision and the table's** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT length(kdb_rev('ochl_minutes', 'CITY')) > 0 AS has_rev,
       kdb_rev('ochl_minutes', 'CITY') = kdb_rev('ochl_minutes', 'CITY') AS stable;
```

Result:

| has_rev (BOOL) | stable (BOOL) |
|---|---|
| true | true |

(1 row)

<!-- docs/change-stream.md -->

# Change stream and live subscriptions: changes('t'), GET /api/changes, GET /api/subscribe

> Every committed INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE of a table as an ordered stream you can resume from its LSN, in SQL or over HTTP, and queries that push their changed rows.

- Category: HTTP API
- Keywords: change stream, changes, cdc, change data capture, GET /api/changes, api/changes, GET /api/subscribe, api/subscribe, subscribe, SUBSCRIBE, live query, push, server-sent events, sse, EventSource, Last-Event-ID, lsn, resume, exactly once, wal\_archive
- See also: [Change revisions: GET /api/rev and kdb_rev()](revisions.md), [Backup, check, repair and restore](backup-and-safety.md), [Run SQL over HTTP (/exec, /exp)](http-exec.md), [Databases and the data folder](databases.md)

Every committed change of a table is already in KarelaDB's log, in commit order, numbered by a **log sequence number** (LSN). The change stream reads it back:

- in SQL: `SELECT * FROM changes('t')`
- over HTTP: `GET /api/changes?table=t&from=<lsn>`, as server-sent events or JSON

A reader keeps the LSN it read last and asks for what came after it. It gets **every change exactly once, in commit order**, also after a restart or a crash of the server, because the stream only shows commits that are safe on disk and the log is what the server itself replays.

Nothing extra is written for this: a commit costs what it cost before.

<a id="changes"></a>

## changes('t')

Syntax:

```sql
SELECT * FROM changes('<table>' [, after_lsn [, max_rows]])
```

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `lsn` | the transaction's commit LSN. All rows of one transaction share it |
| `seq` | the row's place inside its transaction (0, 1, 2, ...) |
| `committed_at` | when the transaction committed |
| `op` | `upsert`, `delete` or `ddl` |
| `key` | `delete`: the row's partition and key (hex); `ddl`: the statement; otherwise NULL |
| the table's columns | `upsert`: the row as it is after the change; NULL for `delete` and `ddl` |

A table column named like one of the first five (a column `lsn`) is shown as `row_lsn`.

| op | Made by |
|---|---|
| `upsert` | `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `POST /write`, `POST /imp`, `COPY`, a trigger. The log keeps the row after the change, so an INSERT and an UPDATE look the same |
| `delete` | `DELETE`, and the old row of an UPDATE that moved it to another key. The log keeps the key, not the old row |
| `ddl` | a schema change that names the table: `TRUNCATE`, `ALTER TABLE`, `DROP PARTITION`, `CREATE TABLE`; also a `DELETE` that removed whole partitions ([DELETE](update-delete.md#delete)), as `ALTER TABLE ... DROP PARTITION` |

Arguments:

| Argument | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `after_lsn` | only changes committed after this LSN. `0` or none: from the oldest change the kept log still holds |
| `max_rows` | stop after about this many rows. It stops **between transactions**, never inside one, so reading on from the last `lsn` never skips a row. A transaction bigger than `max_rows` comes whole on its own |

Without `max_rows`, a read of more than 100,000 rows is an error: read in parts. `WHERE lsn > x` and a plain `LIMIT n` are passed down, so they read only what they need:

**Example: Every change of a table, in order**

```sql
CREATE TABLE acct (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING, bal DOUBLE);
INSERT INTO acct VALUES (1, 'Asha', 10), (2, 'Bikash', 20);
UPDATE acct SET bal = 15 WHERE id = 1;
DELETE FROM acct WHERE id = 2;
SELECT seq, op, id, name, bal FROM changes('acct') WHERE op <> 'ddl';
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE acct (`

```text
table 'acct' created
```

`INSERT INTO acct VALUES (1, 'Asha', 10), (2, 'Bikash', 20)`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`UPDATE acct SET bal = 15 WHERE id = 1`

```text
1 row(s) updated
```

`DELETE FROM acct WHERE id = 2`

```text
1 row(s) deleted
```

`SELECT seq, op, id, name, bal FROM changes('acct') WHERE op != 'ddl'`

| seq (INT) | op (STRING) | id (INT) | name (STRING) | bal (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | upsert | 1 | Asha | 10 |
| 1 | upsert | 2 | Bikash | 20 |
| 0 | upsert | 1 | Asha | 15 |
| 0 | delete | NULL | NULL | NULL |

(4 rows)

To read on, remember the largest `lsn` you have **fully** read and ask for `changes('acct', that_lsn)` or `WHERE lsn > that_lsn`. Be careful with a SQL `LIMIT`: it cuts exactly, maybe inside a transaction. The `max_rows` argument and `GET /api/changes` never do.

<a id="api-changes"></a>

## GET /api/changes

Syntax:

```sql
GET /api/changes?table=<name>[&from=<lsn>][&limit=<n>][&wait=<ms>][&format=sse|json][&db=<name>]
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `table` | the table (required) |
| `from` | read after this LSN (`0` or none: from the oldest kept). Without it the `Last-Event-ID` header is used, which a browser's `EventSource` sends when it asks again |
| `limit` | about this many rows at most (default 1000); whole transactions only |
| `wait` | with nothing new, wait up to this many ms for a commit (default 25000 for events, 0 for JSON; at most 55000) |
| `format` | `sse` (default): server-sent events. `json`: one JSON object |

As **server-sent events**, each change is an event `change` whose data is `{"lsn", "seq", "committed_at", "op", "key", "row"}`. The last change of each transaction carries `id: <lsn>`. The answer ends with an event `position` whose id is where to read on. A browser needs nothing more than:

```js
const es = new EventSource('/api/changes?table=trades');
es.addEventListener('change', (e) => apply(JSON.parse(e.data)));
// EventSource asks again by itself, sending the last id it saw:
// nothing is missed and nothing comes twice.
```

Each request waits for a commit, answers, and ends; the client then asks again (`retry: 1000`). A change arrives within milliseconds of its commit. At most a quarter of the server's HTTP threads (`--threads`) wait at once; the others answer at once with what there is, so waiting readers never take the threads `/exec` needs.

As **JSON** (`format=json`): `{"table", "changes": [...], "next", "more", "durable_lsn", "oldest_lsn"}`. Read on with `from=<next>`; `more: true` means more is ready now.

**HTTP: The changes of a table as JSON**

Setup:

```text
CREATE TABLE acct (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING, bal DOUBLE);
INSERT INTO acct VALUES (1, 'Asha', 10);
```

```http
GET /api/changes?table=acct&format=json
```

Response:

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{
  "table": "acct",
  "changes": [
    {
      "lsn": 2,
      "seq": 0,
      "committed_at": "2026-10-24T06:18:46.271Z",
      "op": "ddl",
      "key": "CREATE TABLE acct (\n  id INT PRIMARY KEY,\n  name STRING,\n  bal DOUBLE\n)",
      "row": null
    },
    {
      "lsn": 4,
      "seq": 0,
      "committed_at": "2026-10-24T06:18:46.275Z",
      "op": "upsert",
      "key": null,
      "row": {"id": 1, "name": "Asha", "bal": 10}
    }
  ],
  "next": 4,
  "more": false,
  "durable_lsn": 4,
  "oldest_lsn": 1
}
```

It needs read rights on the table: role `read` on the database, or `GRANT SELECT` on the table. An unknown table is a 404.

<a id="retention"></a>

## How long changes are kept

The stream reads the log, and the log is kept as long as the database's `wal_archive` setting allows: `ALTER DATABASE ... SET WAL_ARCHIVE = '2GB'`, the server default `KARELADB_WAL_ARCHIVE_MB` / `wal_archive_mb` in `kareladb.conf` (1 GB unless set). A reader that falls further behind than that is **never** given a stream with a hole: `changes()` fails and `GET /api/changes` answers **410 Gone**, with `gone_before`, the first LSN still kept. Such a reader starts again from a fresh copy of the table (`SELECT *`) and then reads on from `oldest_lsn`.

A slow or lost reader cannot fill the disk: it keeps no log for itself. While one read runs (milliseconds), only the log after its position stays where it is; older log and replaced data files are cleaned up as usual. Readers never slow down writers: a poll does not list the log folders.

<a id="api-subscribe"></a>

## GET /api/subscribe

A **live query**: the answer of one `SELECT`, and afterwards only the rows a commit changed.

Syntax:

```sql
GET /api/subscribe?query=SUBSCRIBE SELECT ...[&wait=<ms>][&db=<name>]
```

1. The first request answers at once with an event `snapshot`: `{"table", "symbol", "columns", "rows"}` and an id: `<subscription>.<version>`, naming the subscription and the answer the client has.
2. Asked again with that id (`Last-Event-ID`, or `&id=`), the request waits until a commit changes the table, runs the query again, and sends an event `rows`: `{"columns", "rows", "removed"}` with the rows that are **new or changed**, and how many rows left the answer. A candle query over `date_trunc` buckets gets the one bucket a trade changed, as its new version.
3. With nothing changed before `wait` ends, the answer has no `rows` event, only the id to ask again with.

An answer lost on the way (a dropped connection, a proxy timeout) is not lost for the client: it asks again with the id it really has, and gets the same change again. An id with a version the server no longer keeps gets a fresh `snapshot`, which replaces everything the client has. A client that reconnects while its old request still waits takes over: the old request ends and the new one answers, so an `EventSource` never gets an error and stops.

When the `WHERE` picks one value of the table's [revision column](revisions.md#rev-column) (`WHERE symbol = 'NABIL'`), only a commit of that symbol wakes the subscriber: a NEPSE trade does not. Otherwise any commit of the table does.

```js
const q = encodeURIComponent(`SUBSCRIBE SELECT date_trunc('minute', time) AS m, first(price) AS open,
  max(price) AS high, min(price) AS low, last(price) AS close
  FROM trades WHERE symbol = 'NABIL' GROUP BY m ORDER BY m`);
const es = new EventSource('/api/subscribe?query=' + q);
es.addEventListener('snapshot', (e) => drawAll(JSON.parse(e.data).rows));
es.addEventListener('rows', (e) => JSON.parse(e.data).rows.forEach(upsertCandle));
```

Limits: one table (no joins, subqueries in `FROM`, `UNION` or `WITH`); at most 10,000 rows in the answer; 10,000 subscriptions per server (when that is reached, the one asked for longest ago makes room, and its client gets a fresh `snapshot` when it asks again); a subscription nobody asked for in 2 minutes is dropped, and asking with an unknown id gives a fresh `snapshot`. The query runs with the caller's rights, like `/exec`.

`SUBSCRIBE` sent to `/exec` or the PostgreSQL port is an error that points here: those answer once and cannot push.

<!-- docs/http-login.md -->

# Logins, tokens and roles over HTTP

> How a program or the console proves who it is - the access token, HTTP Basic, POST /api/login - and the 401, 403 and 429 answers.

- Category: HTTP API
- Keywords: login, logout, api/login, api/logout, api/me, api/session, whoami, token, --token, Bearer, Authorization, HTTP Basic, curl -u, cookie, kdb\_login, kdb\_auth, kdb\_token, CSRF, X-KDB-CSRF, remember me, HttpOnly, SameSite, 401, 403, 429, Retry-After, WWW-Authenticate, roles, read, write, admin, password, session token, failed logins
- See also: [Users and roles](users-and-roles.md), [Keeping kareladb serve safe](server-security.md), [HTTP API overview (auth)](http-overview.md#auth), [kareladb user](cli-users.md), [PostgreSQL protocol (port 8832) (passwords)](postgres-protocol.md#passwords)

A server can be open, need a **token**, or need a **user login**. This page shows how to send each one over HTTP.

| Server | Login needed? |
|---|---|
| `kareladb serve` on `127.0.0.1` (the default), no `--token`, no users | **No.** Only programs on the same computer can connect. |
| started with `--token <secret>` | **Yes**: the token. It may do everything. |
| the data folder has **users** (`CREATE USER`, `kareladb user add`) | **Yes**: a user name and password, or a login token. Each user may do only what their role allows. With `--token` too, the token also works. |
| `--bind 0.0.0.0` (not 127.x) without `--token` and without users | the server does not start |

- `GET /health`, `POST /api/login`, `POST /api/session`, `POST /api/logout` and the console page need no login. `/health` says `auth_required` and `login` (users exist).
- Making users and roles: [users and roles](users-and-roles.md). Keeping a server on the internet safe: [server security](server-security.md).
- Tutorial: [chapter 16, users, passwords and security](../tutorial/16-users-passwords-security.md).

The examples below that need users or a token run on their own new `kareladb serve` (a fresh data folder), so you see the real answers. On a new server without users, the first `CREATE USER ... ROLE admin` can be sent without a login; from then on every request needs one.

<a id="ways"></a>

## Ways to send a login

| How | Send | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| The access token | header `Authorization: Bearer <token>` | a server started with `--token` |
| HTTP Basic | header `Authorization: Basic <base64 of user:password>` (`curl -u user:password`) | scripts. A good password is remembered for 10 minutes, so it is not slow. |
| A login token | `POST /api/login` once, then `Authorization: Bearer <token>` | apps that make many requests |
| An API token | `CREATE TOKEN app FOR USER u` once, then `Authorization: Bearer kdbt_...` ([API tokens](api-tokens.md)) | apps and services: many named tokens, each revoked on its own |
| The login cookie | `POST /api/login` sets the cookie `kdb_login` | browsers: the web console |
| The token cookie | `POST /api/session` turns a token into the cookie `kdb_auth` | browsers: the web console, when you paste a token |

- **Base64** is a way to write any bytes as plain letters; `curl -u` and every HTTP library do it for you.
- A **cookie** is a small value the browser keeps and sends back by itself. KarelaDB's cookies are `HttpOnly` (JavaScript in the page cannot read them) and `SameSite=Strict` (other web sites cannot make the browser send them).
- A change sent with a cookie (not a `GET`) also needs the header `X-KDB-CSRF`. See [CSRF](http-login.md#csrf). A header login needs nothing extra.
- On a server that needs no login, the `Authorization` header is not checked at all.

## POST /api/login

Syntax:

```sql
POST /api/login
body: {"user": "<name>", "password": "<password>"[, "code": "<6 digits>"]}
   or user=<name>&password=<password>[&code=<6 digits>]  (Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded)
```

Checks a user name and password. On success it starts a **login session** (12 hours), sets the cookie `kdb_login`, and gives back a token for `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

| Parameter | Where | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `user` | JSON body or form field | The user name (case is ignored) | required |
| `password` | JSON body or form field | The password | required |
| `code` | JSON body or form field | The code of the authenticator app, for a user with [two-factor login](two-factor-login.md) | - |
| `X-KDB-Console` | header | Sent by the web console: then the answer has no `token` (the console uses only the cookie) | not sent |

| Answer field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `user` | The user name as it is stored |
| `role` | The user's own ROLE: `admin`, `write`, `read` or `none` (for every database) |
| `grants` | Roles on single databases, like `{"shop": "write"}` |
| `expires_ms` | When the login ends (ms since 1970, UTC) |
| `token` | The login token (43 characters). Send it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. |
| `csrf` | The `X-KDB-CSRF` value for changes sent with the cookie ([CSRF](http-login.md#csrf)) |
| header `Set-Cookie` | `kdb_login=<token>; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Max-Age=43200` (and `Secure` over [TLS](tls.md), or when a proxy sends `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`) |

- **Status codes:** 200 logged in; 400 no user name, or the server has no users; 401 `{"error": "wrong user name or password", "login": true}` (the same text for an unknown user, so nobody can find out which names exist); 403 the request comes from another web site; 429 too many failed logins, with a `Retry-After` header (seconds to wait).
- **Notes:**
  - A login ends after 12 hours, at `POST /api/logout`, or when the user gets a new password or is dropped. A server restart does not end it: logins are kept in the data folder, as hashes only ([where](api-tokens.md#kept)).
  - KarelaDB keeps only the SHA-256 of the token, never the token itself.
  - After 5 failed logins for one user from one address, that user must wait before the next try from that address: 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, ... up to 15 minutes. A good login ends the waiting for that user.
  - After 20 failed logins for one user from all addresses together, that user waits everywhere (someone is guessing from many machines).
  - Only the user who failed waits. Other users, and the right `--token` (with any name, on the [PostgreSQL port](postgres-protocol.md#passwords) too), still work from the same address. This matters behind Docker or a NAT, where every client has the same address.
  - Every failed login is printed in the server's output with the user name and address (never the password).
  - The same users log in on the [PostgreSQL port](postgres-protocol.md#passwords).

**HTTP: The first user, a login, the token, and logout**

```http
POST /exec?compat=0

CREATE USER boss WITH PASSWORD 'boss-secret-1' ROLE admin
###
GET /exec?compat=0&query=SELECT 1 AS one
###
POST /api/login
Content-Type: application/json

{"user": "boss", "password": "boss-secret-1"}
###
GET /exec?compat=0&query=SELECT 1 AS one
Authorization: Bearer {{token}}
###
POST /api/logout
Authorization: Bearer {{token}}
###
GET /exec?compat=0&query=SELECT 1 AS one
Authorization: Bearer {{token}}
```

Log in once, then use the token (Python, `requests`):

```python
import requests

KarelaDB = "http://127.0.0.1:9900"
r = requests.post(f"{KarelaDB}/api/login", json={"user": "shop_app", "password": "Another-long-secret-42"})
if r.status_code == 429:
    raise RuntimeError(f"too many failed logins: wait {r.headers['Retry-After']} s")
if r.status_code != 200:
    raise RuntimeError(r.json()["error"])
auth = {"Authorization": "Bearer " + r.json()["token"]}

rows = requests.post(f"{KarelaDB}/exec", params={"db": "shop", "compat": 0},
                     data="SELECT count(*) FROM orders", headers=auth).json()
print(rows["results"][0]["dataset"])

requests.post(f"{KarelaDB}/api/logout", headers=auth)
```

```js
// Node 18+
const KarelaDB = "http://127.0.0.1:9900";
const login = await fetch(`${KarelaDB}/api/login`, {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ user: "shop_app", password: process.env.KARELADB_PASSWORD }),
});
const me = await login.json();
if (!login.ok) throw new Error(me.error);
const auth = { Authorization: `Bearer ${me.token}` };
const res = await fetch(`${KarelaDB}/exec?db=shop&compat=0`, { method: "POST", headers: auth, body: "SELECT 1" });
console.log(res.status, (await res.json()).results);
```

```powershell
$login = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post "http://127.0.0.1:9900/api/login" -ContentType "application/json" `
  -Body (@{ user = "shop_app"; password = $env:KARELADB_PASSWORD } | ConvertTo-Json)
$auth = @{ Authorization = "Bearer $($login.token)" }
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post "http://127.0.0.1:9900/exec?db=shop&compat=0" -Headers $auth -ContentType "text/plain" -Body "SELECT 1"
```

```csharp
using var http = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri("http://127.0.0.1:9900") };
var login = await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/api/login", new { user = "shop_app", password = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("KARELADB_PASSWORD") });
var body = await login.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<JsonElement>();
if (!login.IsSuccessStatusCode) throw new Exception(body.GetProperty("error").GetString());
http.DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization = new AuthenticationHeaderValue("Bearer", body.GetProperty("token").GetString());
```

<a id="logout"></a>

## POST /api/logout

Syntax:

```sql
POST /api/logout
```

Ends a login session: the one of the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header, and the one of the `kdb_login` cookie. It also ends the console session of the `kdb_auth` cookie on the server, and tells the browser to forget the cookies `kdb_login` and `kdb_auth`.

| Parameter | Where | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Authorization: Bearer <token>` | header | The login token to end | - |
| `kdb_login` | cookie | The login cookie to end | - |

| Answer field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `logged_out` | always `true` |
| header `Set-Cookie` | `kdb_login=; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Max-Age=0` and the same for `kdb_auth` (removes the cookies) |

- **Status codes:** always 200, also when there was no login.
- **Notes:** after logout the token answers 401 `the login token is wrong or has expired; log in again (POST /api/login)`. HTTP Basic has nothing to log out: just stop sending the password. The `--token` cannot be logged out.

**HTTP: Log out (here without a login: still 200)**

```http
POST /api/logout
```

Response:

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{"logged_out": true}
```

## GET /api/me

Syntax:

```sql
GET /api/me
```

Who am I? The user of this request's login, and the role. The web console shows it at the top ("boss (admin)").

| Parameter | Where | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a login) | header or cookie | Any of the [ways to send a login](http-login.md#ways) | - |

| Answer field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `user` | The user name, or `null` (the token, or a server without login) |
| `role` | The user's own ROLE; `admin` for full access |
| `grants` | Roles on single databases: `{"shop": "write"}` |
| `full_access` | `true` for the `--token`, and on a server without login |
| `two_factor` | `true` when this user has [two-factor login](two-factor-login.md) on |
| `login_required` | `true` when requests need a login or token |
| `users` | `true` when the data folder has users |
| `cookie` | `true` when this request logged in with a cookie |
| `csrf` | Only with a cookie login: the `X-KDB-CSRF` value for changes ([CSRF](http-login.md#csrf)) |

- **Status codes:** 200; 401 without a needed login (the answer then has `"login": true` when users exist).
- **Notes:** a program can call it after start to check that its password or token works.

**HTTP: On a server without token and users: full access**

```http
GET /api/me
```

Response:

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text

  "user": null,
  "role": "admin",
  "grants": {},
  "full_access": true,
  "two_factor": false,

  "users": false,
  "cookie": false,
  "step_up_actions": false,
  "step_up_minutes": 5,
  "step_up_until_ms": 0
}
```

<a id="token"></a>

## The access token (--token)

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb serve --token <long random secret>
Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

The simplest protection: one secret for everything. Whoever sends it may do **everything**, like an admin.

| Situation | Answer |
|---|---|
| no token sent | 401 `{"error": "access token required"}` |
| a wrong token | 401 `{"error": "wrong access token"}` |
| the right token | the normal answer |

- The 401 answer has the header `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="kdb"`.
- The web console asks for the token once and hands it to [`POST /api/session`](http-login.md#session). The server keeps the token and gives the browser an `HttpOnly` cookie with a random session id, so no script in the page can read the token, and the cookie never holds it. CSV downloads work with that cookie too.
- Older consoles kept the token in the browser's storage and in a cookie `kdb_token`. The new console moves it into the `HttpOnly` cookie once and deletes both. The server still reads `kdb_token` for one more release.
- The token is compared in constant time, so it cannot be guessed by measuring answer times.
- It is also the password of the [PostgreSQL port](postgres-protocol.md#passwords) when there are no users.
- Pick a long random token (20 or more characters). For programs that should only read, or only use one database, use **users** instead.

**HTTP: A server started with --token change-me-please** (shows an error)

```http
GET /health
###
GET /exec?compat=0&query=SELECT 1 AS one
###
GET /exec?compat=0&query=SELECT 1 AS one
Authorization: Bearer wrong
###
GET /exec?compat=0&query=SELECT 1 AS one
Authorization: Bearer change-me-please
```

Response:

`GET /health`

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{
  "status": "ok",
  "version": "0.2.0-dev",
  "product": "KarelaDB",
  "server_time_ms": 1792822760568,
  "auth_required": true,
  "login": false,
  "tls": false,
  "ready": true,
  "standby": false,
  "role": "leader"
}
```

`GET /exec?compat=0&query=SELECT 1 AS one`

HTTP 401 (application/json)

```text
{"error": "access token required"}
```

`GET /exec?compat=0&query=SELECT 1 AS one`

HTTP 401 (application/json)

```text
{"error": "wrong access token"}
```

`GET /exec?compat=0&query=SELECT 1 AS one`

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{
  "query": "SELECT 1 AS one",
  "results": [
    {
      "statement": "SELECT 1 AS one",
      "columns": [
        {"name": "one", "type": "LONG"}
      ],
      "dataset": [
        [1]
      ],
      "count": 1,
      "truncated": false,
      "rows_affected": 0,
      "message": "",
      "timings": {"parse_us": 19, "execute_us": 62}
    }
  ],
  "timings": {"parse_us": 19, "execute_us": 62}
}
```

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer change-me-please" "http://127.0.0.1:9900/exec?compat=0&query=SELECT%201"
```

```powershell
$h = @{ Authorization = "Bearer $env:KARELADB_TOKEN" }
Invoke-RestMethod "http://127.0.0.1:9900/api/info" -Headers $h
```

<a id="session"></a>

## POST /api/session

Syntax:

```sql
POST /api/session[?remember=1]
Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

Starts a console session for a token and gives the browser the cookie `kdb_auth`. The web console calls it when you paste a token. The server keeps the token in its memory; the cookie holds only a random session id. The cookie is `HttpOnly`, so no script in the page can read it.

| Parameter | Where | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Authorization: Bearer <token>` | header | The `--token`, an [API token](api-tokens.md) or a login token | required |
| `remember` | query | `1`: the session lasts 30 days. Without it the session lasts 12 hours, and the browser forgets the cookie when it closes. | not sent |

A console session ends when:

| What happens | Why |
|---|---|
| its time is up (12 hours, or 30 days with `remember`) | a forgotten browser does not stay logged in |
| [`POST /api/logout`](http-login.md#logout) with the cookie | the server forgets the id: a copied cookie stops working too |
| the pasted token stops working (`DROP TOKEN`, an ended login) | the session has the token's rights, checked on every request |
| the server restarts | sessions live in memory only: paste the token again |

- A cookie from an older KarelaDB held the token itself. The server no longer takes it: the console asks for the token once more.

| Answer field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `user` | The token's user, or `null` for the `--token` |
| `role` | The role; `admin` for the `--token` |
| `full_access` | `true` for the `--token` |
| `remember` | `true` when the cookie is kept 30 days |
| `csrf` | The `X-KDB-CSRF` value for changes sent with the cookie ([CSRF](http-login.md#csrf)) |
| header `Set-Cookie` | `kdb_auth=<session id>; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` (with `Max-Age=2592000` for `remember`, and `Secure` over [TLS](tls.md)) |

- **Status codes:** 200; 400 no `Authorization: Bearer` header; 401 a wrong token; 403 the request comes from another web site.
- **Notes:** programs do not need it. They send `Authorization: Bearer <token>` with every request. [`POST /api/logout`](http-login.md#logout) makes the browser forget the cookie.

**HTTP: The console hands over a token and gets a session cookie**

```http
POST /api/session
Authorization: Bearer change-me-please
```

Response:

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{
  "user": null,
  "role": "admin",
  "full_access": true,
  "remember": false,
  "csrf": "81b743e1ada9d4737dbcca49af366fdb"
}
```

<a id="csrf"></a>

## CSRF: the X-KDB-CSRF header

A browser sends cookies by itself, even when another web site makes it send a request. That is called **CSRF** (cross-site request forgery). So a request that logged in with a **cookie** and changes something must also send the header `X-KDB-CSRF`.

| Request | Needs `X-KDB-CSRF`? |
|---|---|
| `GET` or `HEAD` (only reads) | no |
| `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE` with the cookie `kdb_login` or `kdb_auth` | **yes** |
| any request with `Authorization: Bearer` or `Basic` | no: another web site cannot set that header |
| the old cookie `kdb_token` | no, but the request must come from the console (`X-KDB-Console`) |

- The value comes in the `csrf` field of [`POST /api/login`](http-login.md#post-api-login), [`POST /api/session`](http-login.md#session) and [`GET /api/me`](http-login.md#get-api-me). Another web site cannot read it.
- The value belongs to the cookie. A new login gives a new value.
- The web console sends it by itself (`window.KdbConsole.api`).
- Without it the answer is 403 with `"csrf": true`.

**HTTP: A change with the cookie: refused without the header, done with it** (shows an error)

```http
POST /api/session
Authorization: Bearer change-me-please
###
POST /exec?compat=0
Cookie: kdb_auth=change-me-please

CREATE TABLE notes (id INT, text STRING)
###
POST /exec?compat=0
Cookie: kdb_auth=change-me-please
X-KDB-CSRF: {{csrf}}

CREATE TABLE notes (id INT, text STRING)
```

Response:

`POST /api/session`

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{
  "user": null,
  "role": "admin",
  "full_access": true,
  "remember": false,
  "csrf": "d3c9e83750a0e697791d5de24878f1b0"
}
```

`POST /exec?compat=0`

HTTP 401 (application/json)

```text
{"error": "the saved access token is no longer accepted; enter it again"}
```

`POST /exec?compat=0`

HTTP 401 (application/json)

```text
{"error": "the saved access token is no longer accepted; enter it again"}
```

<a id="basic"></a>

## HTTP Basic

Syntax:

```sql
Authorization: Basic <base64 of name:password>
curl -u <name>:<password> ...
```

Sends the user name and password with **every** request. KarelaDB checks the password once and then remembers it for 10 minutes, so it stays fast.

- Good for scripts and tools that cannot keep a token.
- A wrong password: 401 `wrong user name or password`. Many wrong passwords: 429 with `Retry-After`.
- On a server with users, a request with no login gets `WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="kdb"`, so a browser shows its own password box. The console sends `X-KDB-Console: 1` and gets `Bearer` instead (no browser box).
- On a server without users, Basic is refused: 401 `this server has no users yet`.

The header below is the base64 of `reader:reader-secret-1`, what `curl -u reader:reader-secret-1` sends. The user `reader` has role `read`, so reading works and writing is refused:

**HTTP: HTTP Basic with a read-only user** (sample data: sample)

```http
POST /exec?compat=0

CREATE USER boss WITH PASSWORD 'boss-secret-1' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER reader WITH PASSWORD 'reader-secret-1' ROLE read
###
GET /exec?compat=0&query=SELECT symbol, name FROM securities ORDER BY symbol LIMIT 2
Authorization: Basic cmVhZGVyOnJlYWRlci1zZWNyZXQtMQ==
###
POST /exec?compat=0
Authorization: Basic cmVhZGVyOnJlYWRlci1zZWNyZXQtMQ==

INSERT INTO brokers VALUES (99, 'Not Allowed Securities')
```

Response:

`POST /exec?compat=0`

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{
  "query": "CREATE USER boss WITH PASSWORD 'boss-secret-1' ROLE admin;\nCREATE USER reader WITH PASSWORD 'reader-secret-1' ROLE read",
  "results": [
    {
      "statement": "CREATE USER boss WITH PASSWORD '***' ROLE admin",
      "columns": [],
      "dataset": [],
      "count": 0,
      "truncated": false,
      "rows_affected": 0,
      "message": "user 'boss' created with role admin",
      "timings": {"parse_us": 0, "execute_us": 114321}
    },
    {
      "statement": "CREATE USER reader WITH PASSWORD '***' ROLE read",
      "columns": [],
      "dataset": [],
      "count": 0,
      "truncated": false,
      "rows_affected": 0,
      "message": "user 'reader' created with role read",
      "timings": {"parse_us": 0, "execute_us": 57251}
    }
  ],
  "timings": {"parse_us": 0, "execute_us": 171572}
}
```

<a id="roles"></a>

## Roles: what each route needs

Each user has a **role**: `none`, `read`, `write` or `admin`. The user's own ROLE counts for every database; a `GRANT ... ON DATABASE` gives a role on one database. KarelaDB uses the stronger of the two.

| Route | Needs |
|---|---|
| `GET /health`, `POST /api/login`, `POST /api/logout`, the console files | nothing |
| `GET /api/me`, `POST /session`, `DELETE /session/<id>`, `POST /api/feedback` | any login |
| `/exec` and `/exp` with SQL that reads, `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`/`ROLLBACK` | `read` on the database |
| `GET /api/info`, `GET /api/disk`, `GET /api/backups`, `GET /api/trigger-queue`, `GET /api/stats`, `GET /api/timers`, `GET /api/pins`, `/cursor` | `read` |
| `/exec` with `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `CALL`; `POST /write`, `POST /imp` into a table that is there | `write` |
| `/exec` with `CREATE`/`ALTER`/`DROP` of tables, views, functions, procedures, triggers, indexes; `BACKUP DATABASE`, `CHECK TABLE`; `POST /api/check`, `POST /api/backup`; a new table with `POST /imp`; saving, running and removing [timers](timers.md); pinning and unpinning [statements](pinned-queries.md) | `admin` on the database |
| `POST /api/databases`, `DELETE /api/databases/<name>`, `GET /api/settings`, `POST /api/settings`, `POST /api/restart`, `GET /api/audit`, `GET /api/feedback`, `POST /api/feedback/<id>`, `CREATE USER`, `GRANT`, ... | the user's own ROLE `admin` |
| `GET /api/databases` | any login; lists only the databases the user may read |

- A session (`POST /session`) can only be used by the user who opened it.
- Rights are per database, and per table with [table rights](table-rights.md); not per column or row.
- Users with [two-factor login](two-factor-login.md) send `"code"` with `POST /api/login`; without it the answer is 401 with `"totp": true`.

<a id="errors"></a>

## 401, 403 and 429 answers

| Answer | Means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| 401 `{"error": "login required: log in (POST /api/login), or send a user name and password (HTTP Basic)", "login": true}` | no login on a server with users | log in |
| 401 `{"error": "wrong user name or password", "login": true}` | a wrong name or password | check them |
| 401 `{"error": "the login token is wrong or has expired; log in again (POST /api/login)"}` | an old or wrong login token | log in again |
| 401 `{"error": "your login has expired; log in again"}` | an old login cookie | log in again |
| 401 `{"error": "access token required"}` / `{"error": "wrong access token"}` | a server with `--token` | send the right token |
| 403 `{"error": "INSERT needs role write on database 'shop'; user 'report' has read"}` | logged in, but the role is too weak | use another user, or `GRANT` |
| 403 `{"error": "cross-site requests are not allowed"}` | a browser request from another site | call KarelaDB from your backend |
| 403 `{"error": "this change came with a login cookie but without the right X-KDB-CSRF header; ...", "csrf": true}` | a change sent with a cookie but no `X-KDB-CSRF` | send the `csrf` value, see [CSRF](http-login.md#csrf) |
| 429 `{"error": "too many failed logins; try again in 4 s", "login": true}` and `Retry-After: 4` | too many failed logins | wait that many seconds |

The 403 role message is shown for real in [HTTP Basic](http-login.md#basic). In a 401 answer, `"login": true` tells a program that the server has users (so it should log in, not ask for a token).

**HTTP: A request from another web site is refused before any login check**

```http
POST /api/login
Content-Type: application/json
Origin: http://evil.example

{"user": "boss", "password": "boss-secret-1"}
```

Response:

HTTP 403 (application/json)

```text
{"error": "cross-origin requests are not allowed"}
```
