<!-- docs/functions-postgres.md -->

# PostgreSQL-compatible functions

> Functions a PostgreSQL app expects: arrays, sequence numbers (nextval), who you are and what you may do (current_user, has_table_privilege), comments (COMMENT ON), advisory locks and session settings, so app code runs on KarelaDB without changes.

- Category: Postgres protocol
- Keywords: PostgreSQL functions, to\_regclass, pg\_relation\_size, pg\_total\_relation\_size, pg\_table\_size, pg\_indexes\_size, pg\_database\_size, pg\_size\_pretty, table size, database size, current\_database, postgres compatibility, array, ARRAY\[\], arrays, list of values, watchlist, tags, sequence, auto number, order number, invoice number, advisory lock, named lock, job lock, one worker at a time, pg\_advisory, nextval, currval, lastval, setval, unnest, cardinality, current\_setting, set\_config, SET LOCAL, session setting, custom setting, current\_user, session\_user, current\_role, current\_schema, current\_schemas, current\_catalog, version, has\_table\_privilege, has\_column\_privilege, has\_database\_privilege, has\_schema\_privilege, pg\_has\_role, privileges, rights, COMMENT ON, comment, description, obj\_description, col\_description, pg\_get\_indexdef, pg\_get\_constraintdef, pg\_get\_viewdef, pg\_get\_expr, format\_type, pg\_table\_is\_visible
- See also: [PostgreSQL protocol (port 8832)](postgres-protocol.md), [JSON functions](functions-json.md), [Text functions](functions-text.md), [Date and time functions](functions-date-time.md), [Constraints](constraints.md), [Transactions](transactions.md)

A PostgreSQL app sends more than plain SQL. It also calls **arrays**, **sequences** and **advisory locks**.
KarelaDB answers all three with the PostgreSQL names, so the same app code runs here.

- An **array** is a list of values in one value: `ARRAY['CITY', 'COAST']`. KarelaDB keeps an array as a [JSON](functions-json.md) list, so a `JSON` column can hold one and every JSON function still works on it.
- A **sequence** is a counter the database keeps for you: order numbers, invoice numbers. `nextval` gives the next one. See `CREATE SEQUENCE` in [constraints](constraints.md#auto) for how to make one.
- An **advisory lock** is a name (a number) your app takes so two copies of it do not do the same job twice.

The other PostgreSQL function names live with their own kind: the JSON ones in [JSON functions](functions-json.md), the time ones in [date and time](functions-date-time.md), `initcap`, `md5`, `to_str` and `string_to_array` in [text functions](functions-text.md).

**Example: A watchlist as one array value** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT ARRAY['CITY', 'COAST', 'VOLT'] AS watchlist,
       cardinality(ARRAY['CITY', 'COAST', 'VOLT']) AS how_many,
       array_to_string(ARRAY['CITY', 'COAST', 'VOLT'], ', ') AS shown;
```

Result:

| watchlist (TEXT[]) | how_many (LONG) | shown (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| ["CITY","COAST","VOLT"] | 3 | CITY, COAST, VOLT |

(1 row)

<a id="arrays"></a>

## Arrays in KarelaDB

Syntax:

```sql
ARRAY[value, value, ...]        an array value
'["CITY","COAST"]'              JSON text an array function reads as an array
'{CITY,COAST}'                  PostgreSQL array text an array function reads too
```

An array is a list of values kept as one value. KarelaDB stores it as a JSON list, so `ARRAY['CITY','COAST']` shows as `["CITY","COAST"]` and fits in a `JSON` column.

- **Counting starts at 1**, as in PostgreSQL: the first element is number 1.
- An array may hold text, numbers, `TRUE`/`FALSE` and `NULL` mixed together. KarelaDB does not check that all elements are of one type.
- The functions on this page also read **text**: text that starts with `[` as JSON, text that starts with `{` as PostgreSQL array text (`'{CITY,COAST}'`). So a value a PostgreSQL driver sends still works.
- A `JSON` **column** keeps JSON only. To save a PostgreSQL array text in one, read it first: `string_to_array(t, ',')`, or `array_cat(t, ARRAY[])`.
- There are no arrays of arrays with their own functions. `array_length(a, 2)` (a second dimension) always gives `NULL`.
- To store a list, use a `JSON` column. To take a list apart into rows, use [unnest](functions-postgres.md#unnest).

**Example: A watchlist column an app reads and writes** (sample data: sample)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE watchlists (user_id INT PRIMARY KEY, symbols JSON);
INSERT INTO watchlists VALUES (1, '["CITY","COAST"]'), (2, array_cat('{VOLT,ACME}', ARRAY[]));
```

```sql
SELECT user_id, symbols, cardinality(symbols) AS how_many,
       symbols ->> 0 AS first_symbol
FROM watchlists ORDER BY user_id;
```

Result:

| user_id (INT) | symbols (JSON) | how_many (LONG) | first_symbol (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ["CITY","COAST"] | 2 | CITY |
| 2 | ["VOLT","ACME"] | 2 | VOLT |

(2 rows)

## array_append

Syntax:

```sql
array_append(array, value)
```

The array with one more value at the **end**.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `array` | array (`JSON` list, or array text) | the list to add to |
| `value` | any | the value to put at the end |

- **Returns:** the new array (`JSON`). The old one is not changed.
- **NULL:** `array_append(NULL, 'CITY')` is `["CITY"]` (a NULL array counts as empty). A `NULL` value is added as JSON `null`.
- **Notes:** PostgreSQL writes this as `array || value`. In KarelaDB `||` joins text, so use the function name.

**Example: Add a company to a user's watchlist** (sample data: sample)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE watchlists (user_id INT PRIMARY KEY, symbols JSON);
INSERT INTO watchlists VALUES (1, '["CITY","COAST"]');
```

```sql
UPDATE watchlists SET symbols = array_append(symbols, 'VOLT') WHERE user_id = 1;
SELECT user_id, symbols FROM watchlists;
```

Result:

`UPDATE watchlists SET symbols = array_append(symbols, 'VOLT') WHERE user_id = 1`

```text
1 row(s) updated
```

`SELECT user_id, symbols FROM watchlists`

| user_id (INT) | symbols (JSON) |
|---|---|
| 1 | ["CITY","COAST","VOLT"] |

(1 row)

## array_prepend

Syntax:

```sql
array_prepend(value, array)
```

The array with one more value at the **front**. The value comes first, the array second (as in PostgreSQL).

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `value` | any | the value to put in front |
| `array` | array | the list to add to |

- **Returns:** the new array (`JSON`).
- **NULL:** a `NULL` array counts as empty. A `NULL` value is put in front as JSON `null`.

**Example** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT array_prepend('ACME', ARRAY['CITY', 'COAST']) AS watchlist;
```

Result:

| watchlist (JSON) |
|---|
| ["ACME","CITY","COAST"] |

(1 row)

## array_cat

Syntax:

```sql
array_cat(array1, array2)
```

The two arrays joined into one, in order.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `array1` | array | the first list |
| `array2` | array | the list added after it |

- **Returns:** the joined array (`JSON`).
- **NULL:** only when **both** are `NULL`. One `NULL` counts as an empty list.

**Example: One watchlist for two users** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT array_cat(ARRAY['CITY', 'COAST'], ARRAY['VOLT']) AS together,
       array_cat(NULL, ARRAY['TELCO']) AS one_side_null,
       array_cat(NULL, NULL) AS both_null;
```

Result:

| together (TEXT[]) | one_side_null (TEXT[]) | both_null (TEXT[]) |
|---|---|---|
| ["CITY","COAST","VOLT"] | ["TELCO"] | NULL |

(1 row)

## array_remove

Syntax:

```sql
array_remove(array, value)
```

The array without **every** element equal to `value`.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `array` | array | the list |
| `value` | any | the value to take out (all of them) |

- **Returns:** the shorter array (`JSON`). Nothing equal: the same array.
- **NULL:** `array_remove(NULL, x)` is `NULL`. `array_remove(a, NULL)` takes the `null` elements out.

**Example: A user removes a company from the watchlist** (sample data: sample)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE watchlists (user_id INT PRIMARY KEY, symbols JSON);
INSERT INTO watchlists VALUES (1, '["CITY","COAST","CITY"]');
```

```sql
UPDATE watchlists SET symbols = array_remove(symbols, 'CITY') WHERE user_id = 1;
SELECT user_id, symbols FROM watchlists;
```

Result:

`UPDATE watchlists SET symbols = array_remove(symbols, 'CITY') WHERE user_id = 1`

```text
1 row(s) updated
```

`SELECT user_id, symbols FROM watchlists`

| user_id (INT) | symbols (JSON) |
|---|---|
| 1 | ["COAST"] |

(1 row)

## array_position

Syntax:

```sql
array_position(array, value [, start])
```

Which place `value` has in the array. The first place is `1`.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `array` | array | the list to look in |
| `value` | any | the value to find |
| `start` | `INT` | look from this place on (default `1`) |

- **Returns:** `LONG`, the place of the **first** match, or `NULL` when the value is not there.
- **NULL:** a `NULL` array gives `NULL`. `array_position(a, NULL)` finds a `null` element.

**Example: Where is VOLT in the watchlist?** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT array_position(ARRAY['CITY', 'COAST', 'VOLT'], 'VOLT') AS at_place,
       array_position(ARRAY['CITY', 'COAST', 'VOLT'], 'TELCO') AS not_there,
       array_position(ARRAY['CITY', 'COAST', 'CITY'], 'CITY', 2) AS from_place_2;
```

Result:

| at_place (LONG) | not_there (STRING) | from_place_2 (LONG) |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | NULL | 3 |

(1 row)

<a id="array_length"></a>

## array_length, array_upper

Syntax:

```sql
array_length(array, dimension)
array_upper(array, dimension)
```

How many elements the array has. `dimension` must be `1`; KarelaDB has one dimension only. `array_upper` gives the number of the last place, which is the same number.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `array` | array | the list |
| `dimension` | `INT` | always `1` |

- **Returns:** `LONG`.
- **NULL:** an **empty** array gives `NULL` (that is what PostgreSQL does; use `cardinality` for `0`). A `NULL` array, or a dimension that is not `1`, also gives `NULL`.

**Example** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT array_length(ARRAY['CITY', 'COAST'], 1) AS how_many,
       array_upper(ARRAY['CITY', 'COAST'], 1) AS last_place,
       array_length(ARRAY[], 1) AS empty_list,
       array_length(ARRAY['CITY'], 2) AS no_second_dimension;
```

Result:

| how_many (LONG) | last_place (LONG) | empty_list (STRING) | no_second_dimension (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 2 | NULL | NULL |

(1 row)

## cardinality

Syntax:

```sql
cardinality(array)
```

How many elements the array has, counting an empty array as `0`.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `array` | array | the list |

- **Returns:** `LONG`.
- **NULL:** `cardinality(NULL)` is `NULL`. An empty array gives `0`, not `NULL`.
- **Notes:** this is the safe one to use in `WHERE`: `cardinality(symbols) > 0`.

**Example: How many companies each user follows** (sample data: sample)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE watchlists (user_id INT PRIMARY KEY, symbols JSON);
INSERT INTO watchlists VALUES (1, '["CITY","COAST"]'), (2, '[]'), (3, NULL);
```

```sql
SELECT user_id, cardinality(symbols) AS follows, array_length(symbols, 1) AS same_but_null_when_empty
FROM watchlists ORDER BY user_id;
```

Result:

| user_id (INT) | follows (LONG) | same_but_null_when_empty (LONG) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2 | 2 |
| 2 | 0 | NULL |
| 3 | NULL | NULL |

(3 rows)

## array_to_string

Syntax:

```sql
array_to_string(array, separator [, null_text])
```

The elements written one after the other with `separator` between them.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `array` | array | the list |
| `separator` | `STRING` | text put between two elements |
| `null_text` | `STRING` | what a `NULL` element is written as; without it `NULL` elements are left out |

- **Returns:** `STRING`.
- **NULL:** a `NULL` array or a `NULL` separator gives `NULL`.

**Example: A watchlist in one line for an email** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT array_to_string(ARRAY['CITY', 'COAST', 'VOLT'], ', ') AS watchlist,
       array_to_string(ARRAY['CITY', NULL, 'VOLT'], ', ') AS nulls_left_out,
       array_to_string(ARRAY['CITY', NULL, 'VOLT'], ', ', '?') AS nulls_shown;
```

Result:

| watchlist (STRING) | nulls_left_out (STRING) | nulls_shown (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| CITY, COAST, VOLT | CITY, VOLT | CITY, ?, VOLT |

(1 row)

## unnest

Syntax:

```sql
unnest(array)
```

Turns one array into **many rows**, one row per element, in order.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `array` | array | the list to take apart |

- **Returns:** one row per element.
- **NULL:** a `NULL` array gives **no rows**.
- **Notes:** this is how a PostgreSQL app sends a list of symbols in one parameter: `WHERE symbol IN (SELECT unnest($1))`.

**Example: One row per company in the list** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT unnest(ARRAY['CITY', 'COAST', 'VOLT']) AS symbol;
```

Result:

| symbol (STRING) |
|---|
| CITY |
| COAST |
| VOLT |

(3 rows)

**Example: An app sends a watchlist and asks for those companies** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT symbol, name, sector
FROM securities
WHERE symbol IN (SELECT unnest(ARRAY['CITY', 'VOLT']))
ORDER BY symbol;
```

Result:

| symbol (SYMBOL) | name (STRING) | sector (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| CITY | City Bank Limited | Banking |
| VOLT | Volt River Hydropower Limited | Energy |

(2 rows)

## nextval

Syntax:

```sql
nextval('sequence_name')
```

The next number of a sequence. Each call gives a number that was never given before, even when many connections ask at the same time.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `sequence_name` | `STRING` | the sequence name in **single quotes**; `'public.orders_id_seq'` and `'"Name"'` are accepted too |

- **Returns:** `LONG`.
- **NULL:** a `NULL` name gives `NULL`.
- **Notes:** make the sequence first with `CREATE SEQUENCE order_no_seq START WITH 1001`. A number that was given is never given again, also when the transaction is rolled back - so there can be gaps. A sequence that does not exist is an error. For a simple id column, `PRIMARY KEY AUTO` is easier (see [constraints](constraints.md#auto)).

**Example: Order numbers from a sequence**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE SEQUENCE order_no_seq START WITH 1001;
CREATE TABLE orders (order_no LONG PRIMARY KEY, symbol SYMBOL, quantity LONG);
```

```sql
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (nextval('order_no_seq'), 'CITY', 100),
                          (nextval('order_no_seq'), 'COAST', 50);
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY order_no;
```

Result:

`INSERT INTO orders VALUES (nextval('order_no_seq'), 'CITY', 100), (nextval('order_no_seq'), 'COAST',`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY order_no`

| order_no (LONG) | symbol (SYMBOL) | quantity (LONG) |
|---|---|---|
| 1001 | CITY | 100 |
| 1002 | COAST | 50 |

(2 rows)

## currval

Syntax:

```sql
currval('sequence_name')
```

The number this connection got **last** from that sequence. It does not move the sequence on.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `sequence_name` | `STRING` | the sequence name in single quotes |

- **Returns:** `LONG`.
- **NULL:** a `NULL` name gives `NULL`.
- **Notes:** it is an error before this connection has called `nextval` on that sequence. Another connection's numbers are never shown, so `currval` is safe to read after an insert.

**Example: The order number just given**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE SEQUENCE order_no_seq START WITH 1001;
CREATE TABLE orders (order_no LONG PRIMARY KEY, symbol SYMBOL);
```

```sql
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (nextval('order_no_seq'), 'CITY');
SELECT currval('order_no_seq') AS my_order_no;
```

Result:

`INSERT INTO orders VALUES (nextval('order_no_seq'), 'CITY')`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT currval('order_no_seq') AS my_order_no`

| my_order_no (LONG) |
|---|
| 1001 |

(1 row)

**Example: currval before nextval is an error** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE SEQUENCE order_no_seq;
```

```sql
SELECT currval('order_no_seq');
```

Result:

Error: `currval of sequence 'order_no_seq' is not yet defined in this session (call nextval first)`

## lastval

Syntax:

```sql
lastval()
```

The number this connection got last from **any** sequence.

- **Returns:** `LONG`.
- **NULL:** never `NULL`.
- **Notes:** it is an error before this connection has called `nextval` at all. With more than one sequence, `currval('name')` says clearly which one you mean.

**Example: The last number of any sequence**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE SEQUENCE order_no_seq START WITH 1001;
CREATE SEQUENCE invoice_no_seq START WITH 500;
```

```sql
SELECT nextval('order_no_seq') AS order_no, nextval('invoice_no_seq') AS invoice_no;
SELECT lastval() AS last_of_any, currval('order_no_seq') AS last_order_no;
```

Result:

`SELECT nextval('order_no_seq') AS order_no, nextval('invoice_no_seq') AS invoice_no`

| order_no (LONG) | invoice_no (LONG) |
|---|---|
| 1001 | 500 |

(1 row)

`SELECT lastval() AS last_of_any, currval('order_no_seq') AS last_order_no`

| last_of_any (LONG) | last_order_no (LONG) |
|---|---|
| 500 | 1001 |

(1 row)

## setval

Syntax:

```sql
setval('sequence_name', value)
setval('sequence_name', value, is_called)
```

Sets the sequence to `value`. Use it after loading old rows, so new numbers start above them.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `sequence_name` | `STRING` | the sequence name in single quotes |
| `value` | `LONG` | the number to set |
| `is_called` | `BOOL` | `TRUE` (default): `value` counts as already given, so the next `nextval` is `value + 1`. `FALSE`: the next `nextval` gives `value` itself. |

- **Returns:** `LONG`, the `value` you gave.
- **NULL:** a `NULL` name or a `NULL` value gives `NULL` and changes nothing.
- **Notes:** a value outside the sequence's `MINVALUE`/`MAXVALUE` is an error. `setval` is written to disk at once; a `ROLLBACK` does not take it back.

**Example: Move the counter above the order numbers already loaded**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE SEQUENCE order_no_seq START WITH 1;
CREATE TABLE orders (order_no LONG PRIMARY KEY, symbol SYMBOL);
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (5000, 'CITY'), (5001, 'COAST');
```

```sql
SELECT setval('order_no_seq', (SELECT max(order_no) FROM orders)) AS set_to;
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (nextval('order_no_seq'), 'VOLT');
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY order_no;
```

Result:

`SELECT setval('order_no_seq', (SELECT max(order_no) FROM orders)) AS set_to`

| set_to (LONG) |
|---|
| 5001 |

(1 row)

`INSERT INTO orders VALUES (nextval('order_no_seq'), 'VOLT')`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY order_no`

| order_no (LONG) | symbol (SYMBOL) |
|---|---|
| 5000 | CITY |
| 5001 | COAST |
| 5002 | VOLT |

(3 rows)

**Example: is_called = FALSE: the next number is the one you gave**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE SEQUENCE order_no_seq;
```

```sql
SELECT setval('order_no_seq', 7000, FALSE) AS set_to;
SELECT nextval('order_no_seq') AS next_number;
```

Result:

`SELECT setval('order_no_seq', 7000, FALSE) AS set_to`

| set_to (LONG) |
|---|
| 7000 |

(1 row)

`SELECT nextval('order_no_seq') AS next_number`

| next_number (LONG) |
|---|
| 7000 |

(1 row)

<a id="sizes"></a>

## Names and sizes: to_regclass, pg_relation_size, ...

Syntax:

```sql
to_regclass('name')
pg_relation_size(relation [, 'main'])
pg_table_size(relation)
pg_indexes_size(relation)
pg_total_relation_size(relation)
pg_database_size(name_or_oid)
pg_size_pretty(bytes)
current_database()
```

| Function | Returns |
|---|---|
| `to_regclass('name')` | the name of the table, index, view or sequence, or `NULL` when there is none |
| `pg_relation_size`, `pg_table_size`, `pg_total_relation_size` | `LONG` bytes of the table on disk |
| `pg_indexes_size` | `LONG`, always `0` |
| `pg_database_size` | `LONG` bytes of every file of the database: tables, the log, kept versions |
| `pg_size_pretty(bytes)` | text like `8192 bytes`, `24 kB`, `1536 MB`, exactly as PostgreSQL writes it |
| `current_database()` | the database's name |

- **Arguments:** a relation is a name in single quotes (`'public.orders'` and `'"Orders"'` work) or an oid from `pg_class`.
- **Returns:** a table's size is its partition files plus its new rows that are still in the log (they move into the files at the next checkpoint), so a table that was just filled is never `0`.
- **NULL:** a `NULL` argument, or an oid nothing has, gives `NULL`. A name that does not exist is an error (`42P01`), as in PostgreSQL.
- **Notes:** KarelaDB keeps indexes in memory only (built from the rows when the database opens), so they take `0` bytes on disk. `pg_database_size` measures only the database the statement runs in.
- **Waits:** a size reads the table the way a query of it does. `pg_total_relation_size('t')` waits for a statement that is writing `t` (never for writers of other tables), even with snapshot reads on. With an oid or a column instead of a name in quotes - `pg_total_relation_size(c.oid)` over `pg_class` - the size waits for every writer, as `SHOW TABLES` does.

**Example: How big are the tables?**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, symbol SYMBOL, quantity LONG);
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'CITY', 100), (2, 'VOLT', 50);
```

```sql
SELECT to_regclass('orders') AS found, to_regclass('orderz') AS missing,
       pg_total_relation_size('orders') > 0 AS has_bytes,
       pg_size_pretty(10240) AS ten_kb, pg_size_pretty(1610612736) AS big;
```

Result:

| found (STRING) | missing (STRING) | has_bytes (BOOL) | ten_kb (STRING) | big (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| orders | NULL | true | 10 kB | 1536 MB |

(1 row)

<a id="session-info"></a>

## Who and where: current_user, version()

Syntax:

```sql
current_user   current_role   user   session_user
current_schema   current_schemas(include_implicit)   current_catalog
version()
```

| Function | Returns |
|---|---|
| `current_user`, `current_role`, `user` | the user whose rights your statements use: after `SET ROLE` that user, else who logged in |
| `session_user` | who logged in, whatever `SET ROLE` did |
| `current_schema`, `current_schema()` | `public`: every table is in it |
| `current_schemas(false)` | `{public}`; with `true` also `pg_catalog`, which is searched first |
| `current_catalog` | the database's name, like `current_database()` |
| `version()` | `PostgreSQL 14.0 (KDB ...), compatible server` - drivers read the `14` |

- The same answers over HTTP [`/exec`](http-exec.md) and the [Postgres port](postgres-protocol.md). With an [API token](api-tokens.md) you are its user.
- **No user:** with the server's `--token` or a local tool (`kareladb sql`) there is no user; the name is `kareladb`. On the Postgres port of a server without users it is the name the client connected as.
- Write the first four without brackets, as SQL does. A column of that name wins: `SELECT user FROM _audit_log` reads the column.

**Example: Who am I, and on what?**

```sql
SELECT current_user, session_user, current_schema, current_catalog,
       version() LIKE 'PostgreSQL 14%' AS pg14;
```

Result:

| current_user (STRING) | session_user (STRING) | current_schema (STRING) | current_catalog (STRING) | pg14 (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| kdb | kdb | public | demo | true |

(1 row)

<a id="pg_typeof"></a>

## pg_typeof

Syntax:

```sql
pg_typeof(value)
```

The PostgreSQL name of a value's type, as text: `integer`, `bigint`, `numeric`, `double precision`, `text`, `character varying`, `timestamp with time zone`, `jsonb`, `text[]` ...

- **Returns:** text.
- **Notes:**
  - The name comes from what the value is: a column gives its declared type (`VARCHAR(10)` is `character varying`), a cast its target, `now()` is `timestamp with time zone`. Arithmetic widens as in PostgreSQL: `integer * integer` is `integer`, `integer + 1.5` is `numeric`.
  - A whole number that fits 32 bits is `integer`, as in PostgreSQL, although KarelaDB keeps every whole number in 64 bits. A text constant alone is `unknown`, as in PostgreSQL.
  - Anything else is named from its value (`text`, `bigint`, `double precision`, ...).

**Example: What PostgreSQL type does each value have?**

```sql
SELECT pg_typeof(1) AS one, pg_typeof(3000000000) AS big, pg_typeof(1.5) AS decimal_literal,
       pg_typeof(1 + 1) AS sum, pg_typeof(now()) AS now, pg_typeof(CAST(1 AS DOUBLE)) AS float8;
```

Result:

| one (STRING) | big (STRING) | decimal_literal (STRING) | sum (STRING) | now (STRING) | float8 (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| integer | bigint | numeric | integer | timestamp with time zone | double precision |

(1 row)

<a id="privileges"></a>

## Rights: has_table_privilege and friends

Syntax:

```sql
has_table_privilege([user,] table, privilege)
has_column_privilege([user,] table, column, privilege)
has_database_privilege([user,] database, privilege)
has_schema_privilege([user,] schema, privilege)
pg_has_role([user,] role, privilege)
```

`TRUE` when the user may do it now: the same rules the statements are checked with - the user's [role](users-and-roles.md), changed by [GRANT / REVOKE ... ON TABLE](table-rights.md).

| Function | Privileges | `TRUE` when |
|---|---|---|
| `has_table_privilege` | `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `TRUNCATE`, `REFERENCES`, `TRIGGER` | `SELECT` needs role `read`, the changes `write` (`TRUNCATE` counts as `DELETE`), each changed by the table's grants; `REFERENCES` and `TRIGGER` need `ddl` |
| `has_column_privilege` | `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `REFERENCES` | as for the table: KarelaDB has no rights per column |
| `has_database_privilege` | `CONNECT`, `TEMPORARY` (`TEMP`), `CREATE` | any role on that database; `CREATE` needs `ddl` |
| `has_schema_privilege` | `USAGE`, `CREATE` | `USAGE` of `public` needs a role; `pg_catalog` and `information_schema` are open to all. `CREATE` in `public` needs `ddl` |
| `pg_has_role` | `MEMBER`, `USAGE` | the role is the user, or one of `read`, `write`, `ddl`, `admin` the user has here |

- **user:** a user name; without it, the current user. `public` is PostgreSQL's everyone and has no rights. A user whose own `ROLE` is `admin` has every right, as a PostgreSQL superuser.
- **privilege:** one word or a list, `'SELECT, INSERT'`: `TRUE` when any of them is allowed. `... WITH GRANT OPTION` is `TRUE` only for an admin: KarelaDB has no grant options.
- **Objects:** a name (`'orders'`, `'public.orders'`) or an oid from `pg_class` or `pg_database`. An oid nothing has gives `NULL`; a name that does not exist is an error.
- **Errors**, as PostgreSQL: `22023` unrecognized privilege type, `42704` a user that does not exist, `42P01` a table, `42703` a column, `3D000` a database, `3F000` a schema.

**Example: What a read-only user may do**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER charts WITH PASSWORD 'Chart-app-secret-11' ROLE read;
CREATE TABLE orders (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, quantity LONG);
```

```sql
SELECT has_table_privilege('charts', 'orders', 'SELECT') AS reads,
       has_table_privilege('charts', 'orders', 'INSERT') AS writes,
       has_schema_privilege('charts', 'public', 'CREATE') AS creates,
       pg_has_role('charts', 'read', 'MEMBER') AS is_reader;
```

Result:

| reads (BOOL) | writes (BOOL) | creates (BOOL) | is_reader (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|---|
| true | false | false | true |

(1 row)

**Example: A privilege PostgreSQL does not have** (shows an error)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders (id LONG PRIMARY KEY);
```

```sql
SELECT has_table_privilege('orders', 'DROP');
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 8: has_table_privilege: unrecognized privilege type: "DROP"`

<a id="comments"></a>

## Comments and definitions: COMMENT ON, obj_description, pg_get_indexdef

Syntax:

```sql
COMMENT ON TABLE table IS 'text' | NULL
COMMENT ON COLUMN table.column IS 'text' | NULL
obj_description(table [, 'pg_class'])       col_description(table, column_number)
pg_get_indexdef(index [, column, pretty])   pg_get_constraintdef(constraint_oid [, pretty])
pg_get_viewdef(view [, pretty])             format_type(type_oid, typmod)
pg_table_is_visible(relation)               pg_get_expr(text, relation)
```

`COMMENT ON` keeps a description with a table or a column. It stays after a restart, and `\d+` in psql shows it. `IS NULL` (or `IS ''`) removes it. It needs role `ddl`, like `ALTER TABLE`.

| Function | Returns |
|---|---|
| `obj_description(t, 'pg_class')` | the table's comment, `NULL` when none |
| `col_description(t, n)` | the comment of column `n` (1 = the first), `NULL` when none |
| `pg_get_indexdef(i)` | the `CREATE INDEX` line of an index (also of `t_pkey`); with a column number, that key only |
| `pg_get_constraintdef(oid)` | `PRIMARY KEY (id)`, `CHECK (...)`, `FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES ...`, by the oid in `pg_constraint` |
| `pg_get_viewdef(v)` | the view's `SELECT`; `NULL` for a table |
| `format_type(oid, typmod)` | the type as PostgreSQL writes it: `integer`, `character varying(45)`, `numeric(10,2)` |
| `pg_table_is_visible(oid)` | `TRUE`: everything is in `public` |

- `COMMENT ON` other objects (an index, a function, a schema) is accepted and says it is not kept. A view is not a table: `COMMENT ON TABLE v` is error `42809`.
- `pg_get_partkeydef` and `pg_get_functiondef` give `NULL`: KarelaDB tables are not PostgreSQL partitioned tables and `pg_proc` lists no functions. `pg_get_serial_sequence('t', 'id')` gives `public.t_id_seq` for a `SERIAL` column: that is the name of the column's counter, which `nextval`, `currval`, `setval`, `lastval` and `ALTER SEQUENCE ... RESTART WITH n` take, so a `pg_dump` restore that ends with `SELECT setval('t_id_seq', max)` works as it is. The counter only goes up: a `setval` below the ids already in the table means their largest + 1.
- Over HTTP, `'orders'::regclass` stays the name `'orders'`; these functions take the name as well as an oid.

**Example: Describe a table and a column**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, quantity LONG);
```

```sql
COMMENT ON TABLE orders IS 'one row per order';
COMMENT ON COLUMN orders.quantity IS 'shares, never negative';
SELECT obj_description('orders'::regclass, 'pg_class') AS about_table,
       col_description('orders'::regclass, 2) AS about_quantity;
```

Result:

`COMMENT ON TABLE orders IS 'one row per order'`

```text
COMMENT
```

`COMMENT ON COLUMN orders.quantity IS 'shares, never negative'`

```text
COMMENT
```

`SELECT obj_description(CAST('orders' AS STRING), 'pg_class') AS about_table, col_description(CAST('o`

| about_table (STRING) | about_quantity (STRING) |
|---|---|
| one row per order | shares, never negative |

(1 row)

**Example: The SQL behind an index, a key and a type**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, symbol VARCHAR(12));
CREATE INDEX orders_symbol ON orders (symbol);
```

```sql
SELECT pg_get_indexdef('orders_symbol'::regclass) AS index_sql,
       pg_get_indexdef('orders_pkey'::regclass) AS key_sql,
       format_type(1043, 16) AS symbol_type;
```

Result:

| index_sql (STRING) | key_sql (STRING) | symbol_type (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| CREATE INDEX orders_symbol ON public.orders USING btree (symbol) | CREATE UNIQUE INDEX orders_pkey ON public.orders USING btree (id) | character varying(12) |

(1 row)

<a id="advisory-locks"></a>

## Advisory locks

Syntax:

```sql
pg_advisory_lock(key)            take a lock, wait if someone else has it
pg_try_advisory_lock(key)        take it only if it is free (TRUE / FALSE)
pg_advisory_unlock(key)          give it back
```

An **advisory lock** is a name your app agrees on. It locks **no table and no row** - it only stops two copies of your program from doing the same job at the same time.

Say your app closes the trading day at 15:05: it reads the trade log and writes the daily candles. If two copies of the app run, the job must run once. Each copy asks for the lock `918273`; the one that gets it does the job, the other one skips it.

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `key` | the lock name as a whole number (`BIGINT`), for example `918273` |
| `key1, key2` | two `INT` numbers instead of one; they are a **different** set of names (so `(1, 2)` and the single number 1 never meet) |
| `_shared` | many holders at the same time (readers); a lock without `_shared` waits until no one holds the key |
| `_xact` | the lock ends by itself with the transaction |
| `pg_try_*` | never waits: `TRUE` when the lock was taken, `FALSE` when someone else has it |

- Locks of **different databases** never meet, even with the same number.
- A session lock is held until it is given back **as many times as it was taken**, or until the connection closes. Over HTTP, a statement without a [session](http-sessions-and-cursors.md#post-session) is its own session, so its locks end with the statement.
- Waiting has a limit of **30 seconds** (PostgreSQL waits forever). After that the statement fails with a "locked" error; try again later.
- A `SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(...)` sent on its own waits **without holding up the database**, also inside `BEGIN ... COMMIT`: other readers and writers go on, and the waiter gets the lock as soon as the holder commits. A lock call inside a procedure or a longer statement list waits in place.
- On the Postgres port, `pg_try_*` and `pg_advisory_unlock*` are typed `bool` before they run, so a driver can read them into a boolean (Go: `bool`).
- `SET statement_timeout` also ends the wait (see [protection](protection.md#statement-timeout)).

**Example: Only one copy of the app closes the day** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(918273) AS i_do_the_job;
SELECT count(*) AS trades_to_sum FROM trade_log;
SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(918273) AS given_back;
```

Result:

`SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(918273) AS i_do_the_job`

| i_do_the_job (BOOL) |
|---|
| true |

(1 row)

`SELECT count(*) AS trades_to_sum FROM trade_log`

| trades_to_sum (LONG) |
|---|
| 32 |

(1 row)

`SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(918273) AS given_back`

| given_back (BOOL) |
|---|
| true |

(1 row)

<a id="pg_advisory_lock"></a>

## pg_advisory_lock, pg_advisory_lock_shared

Syntax:

```sql
pg_advisory_lock(key)
pg_advisory_lock(key1, key2)
pg_advisory_lock_shared(key)
pg_advisory_lock_shared(key1, key2)
```

Takes a **session** lock and waits until it is free. The lock is held until `pg_advisory_unlock` gives it back, or the connection closes.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `key` | `LONG` | the lock name as one whole number |
| `key1`, `key2` | `INT` | the lock name as two numbers (a different set of names) |

- **Returns:** nothing (PostgreSQL calls this `void`; KarelaDB shows an empty value).
- **NULL:** a `NULL` key gives `NULL` and takes no lock.
- **Notes:** `_shared` lets several connections hold the same key at once; a lock without `_shared` waits for all of them. Taking the same key twice in one connection works and needs two unlocks. Waiting stops after 30 seconds with an error.

**Example: Take the day-close lock, do the work, give it back** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT pg_advisory_lock(918273) AS taken;
SELECT symbol, sum(quantity) AS shares FROM trade_log GROUP BY symbol ORDER BY symbol;
SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(918273) AS given_back;
```

Result:

`SELECT pg_advisory_lock(918273) AS taken`

| taken (STRING) |
|---|
|  |

(1 row)

`SELECT symbol, sum(quantity) AS shares FROM trade_log GROUP BY symbol ORDER BY symbol`

| symbol (SYMBOL) | shares (LONG) |
|---|---|
| CITY | 2420 |
| COAST | 3070 |
| TELCO | 2770 |
| VOLT | 400 |

(4 rows)

`SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(918273) AS given_back`

| given_back (BOOL) |
|---|
| true |

(1 row)

<a id="pg_advisory_xact_lock"></a>

## pg_advisory_xact_lock, pg_advisory_xact_lock_shared

Syntax:

```sql
pg_advisory_xact_lock(key)
pg_advisory_xact_lock(key1, key2)
pg_advisory_xact_lock_shared(key)
pg_advisory_xact_lock_shared(key1, key2)
```

The same, but the lock ends **with the transaction**. There is no unlock function for it.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `key` | `LONG` | the lock name as one whole number |
| `key1`, `key2` | `INT` | the lock name as two numbers |

- **Returns:** nothing (`void`).
- **NULL:** a `NULL` key gives `NULL` and takes no lock.
- **Notes:** `COMMIT` and `ROLLBACK` free it. A statement outside `BEGIN ... COMMIT` is its own transaction, so the lock ends with that statement. This is the safest kind: a crash in the middle cannot leave the lock behind.

**Example: The lock is gone after COMMIT** (sample data: sample)

Setup:

```sql
BEGIN;
SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(918273) AS taken_for_this_transaction;
COMMIT;
```

```sql
SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(918273) AS free_again;
```

Result:

| free_again (BOOL) |
|---|
| true |

(1 row)

<a id="pg_try_advisory_lock"></a>

## pg_try_advisory_lock, pg_try_advisory_lock_shared

Syntax:

```sql
pg_try_advisory_lock(key)
pg_try_advisory_lock(key1, key2)
pg_try_advisory_lock_shared(key)
pg_try_advisory_lock_shared(key1, key2)
```

Takes a **session** lock only if it is free right now. It never waits.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `key` | `LONG` | the lock name as one whole number |
| `key1`, `key2` | `INT` | the lock name as two numbers |

- **Returns:** `BOOL`. `TRUE` the lock is yours, `FALSE` someone else holds it.
- **NULL:** a `NULL` key gives `NULL`.
- **Notes:** this is the one to use for "do this job only if nobody else is doing it". Remember to call `pg_advisory_unlock` with the same key when the job is done.

**Example: Skip the job when another copy already has the lock** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(918273) AS first_call,
       pg_try_advisory_lock(918273) AS same_connection_again;
SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(918273) AS unlock_1, pg_advisory_unlock(918273) AS unlock_2;
```

Result:

`SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(918273) AS first_call, pg_try_advisory_lock(918273) AS same_connection_a`

| first_call (BOOL) | same_connection_again (BOOL) |
|---|---|
| true | true |

(1 row)

`SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(918273) AS unlock_1, pg_advisory_unlock(918273) AS unlock_2`

| unlock_1 (BOOL) | unlock_2 (BOOL) |
|---|---|
| true | true |

(1 row)

<a id="pg_try_advisory_xact_lock"></a>

## pg_try_advisory_xact_lock, pg_try_advisory_xact_lock_shared

Syntax:

```sql
pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(key)
pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(key1, key2)
pg_try_advisory_xact_lock_shared(key)
pg_try_advisory_xact_lock_shared(key1, key2)
```

Takes a **transaction** lock only if it is free right now. It never waits, and it ends with the transaction.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `key` | `LONG` | the lock name as one whole number |
| `key1`, `key2` | `INT` | the lock name as two numbers |

- **Returns:** `BOOL`. `TRUE` the lock is yours until the transaction ends, `FALSE` someone else holds it.
- **NULL:** a `NULL` key gives `NULL`.
- **Notes:** nothing to unlock: `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK` frees it.

**Example: Take it only if free, inside a transaction** (sample data: sample)

```sql
BEGIN;
SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(918273) AS got_it;
COMMIT;
```

Result:

`BEGIN`

```text
transaction started
```

`SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(918273) AS got_it`

| got_it (BOOL) |
|---|
| true |

(1 row)

`COMMIT`

```text
transaction committed: 0 change(s) saved
```

<a id="pg_advisory_unlock"></a>

## pg_advisory_unlock, pg_advisory_unlock_shared

Syntax:

```sql
pg_advisory_unlock(key)
pg_advisory_unlock(key1, key2)
pg_advisory_unlock_shared(key)
pg_advisory_unlock_shared(key1, key2)
```

Gives back one **session** lock this connection holds.

| Argument | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `key` | `LONG` | the lock name as one whole number |
| `key1`, `key2` | `INT` | the lock name as two numbers |

- **Returns:** `BOOL`. `TRUE` a lock was given back, `FALSE` this connection did not hold that key.
- **NULL:** a `NULL` key gives `NULL`.
- **Notes:** use `_shared` for a lock taken with `pg_advisory_lock_shared`. A key taken twice needs two unlocks. Transaction locks (`_xact`) cannot be unlocked this way; they end with the transaction.

**Example: Unlocking a key you do not hold gives FALSE** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(918273) AS taken;
SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(918273) AS given_back,
       pg_advisory_unlock(918273) AS again,
       pg_advisory_unlock(55) AS never_held;
```

Result:

`SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(918273) AS taken`

| taken (BOOL) |
|---|
| true |

(1 row)

`SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(918273) AS given_back, pg_advisory_unlock(918273) AS again, pg_advisory_un`

| given_back (BOOL) | again (BOOL) | never_held (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|
| true | false | false |

(1 row)

## pg_advisory_unlock_all

Syntax:

```sql
pg_advisory_unlock_all()
```

Gives back **every** session lock this connection holds.

- **Returns:** nothing (`void`).
- **NULL:** never `NULL`.
- **Notes:** transaction locks are not touched; they end with the transaction. A closing connection does this by itself, so you rarely need to call it.

**Example: Clean up after a job** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT pg_advisory_lock(918273) AS lock_1;
SELECT pg_advisory_lock(918274) AS lock_2;
SELECT pg_advisory_unlock_all() AS all_given_back;
SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(918273) AS free_again;
```

Result:

| lock_1 (STRING) |
|---|
|  |

|  |

(1 row)

| all_given_back (STRING) |

|  |

<a id="settings"></a>

## Session settings: current_setting, set_config

Syntax:

```sql
current_setting(name)               the value, an error when it was never set
current_setting(name, missing_ok)   the value, or NULL when missing_ok is TRUE
set_config(name, value, is_local)   sets it and returns the value
SET name = 'value'                  the same as set_config(name, value, FALSE) (Postgres port)
SET LOCAL name = 'value'            the same as set_config(name, value, TRUE) (Postgres port)
```

A **setting** is a named text value your connection keeps. Apps use names of their own with a dot in them, like `app.allow_edit`, to tell a [trigger](triggers.md) what the next statement may do.

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | the setting's name, any case; your own names have a dot: `nchartpro.allow_identity_update` |
| `value` | text |
| `is_local` | `TRUE`: only until the transaction ends (`COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`); `FALSE`: until the connection closes |
| `missing_ok` | `TRUE`: a name never set gives `NULL` instead of an error |

- A value belongs to **one connection** (over HTTP, one [session](http-sessions-and-cursors.md#post-session)). Another connection never sees it.
- Triggers and procedures that your statement sets off see your values. Triggers made `DEFERRED` run later, outside your connection, so they do not.
- A `LOCAL` value outside `BEGIN ... COMMIT` lasts for the call only, as each call is its own transaction. On the Postgres port, `SET LOCAL` outside a transaction does nothing and sends warning `25P01`, as PostgreSQL does.
- After a `LOCAL` value ends, the name reads `''` (empty text), as in PostgreSQL.
- Built-in names answer too: `current_setting('TimeZone')` is the session's zone (`UTC` unless `SET TIME ZONE` or `kareladb serve --timezone` names one).

**Example: Set a value, read it back, and ask for one never set** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT set_config('app.allow_edit', 'on', TRUE) AS set_to,
       current_setting('app.allow_edit') AS read_back,
       current_setting('app.never_set', TRUE) AS missing,
       current_setting('TimeZone') AS time_zone;
```

Result:

| set_to (STRING) | read_back (STRING) | missing (STRING) | time_zone (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|
| on | on | NULL | UTC |

(1 row)

A trigger that lets a DBA through only when the statement asked for it:

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION guard_email() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  IF current_setting('app.allow_edit', true) = 'on' THEN
    RETURN NEW;
  END IF;
  IF NEW.email IS DISTINCT FROM OLD.email THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'email is write-once';
  END IF;
  RETURN NEW;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

-- the DBA, on the Postgres port:
BEGIN;
SET LOCAL app.allow_edit = 'on';
UPDATE users SET email = 'new@x.com' WHERE id = 7;
COMMIT;   -- the setting ends here
```

<!-- docs/server-activity.md -->

# pg_stat_activity and pg_stat_statements

> See who is connected and what runs now (pg_stat_activity, query_activity(), GET /api/sessions), stop a statement or close a connection (pg_cancel_backend, pg_terminate_backend, CANCEL QUERY, DELETE /api/sessions/<pid>), close idle and vanished clients (idle_session_timeout, tcp_keepalives_*), and see the totals of every statement shape (pg_stat_statements).

- Category: Postgres protocol
- Keywords: query\_activity, CANCEL QUERY, cancel\_query, pg\_sleep, idle\_session\_timeout, client\_connection\_check\_interval, tcp\_keepalives\_idle, tcp\_keepalives\_interval, tcp\_keepalives\_count, keepalive, 57P01, 57P05, 57014, /api/sessions, CLIENT LIST, CLIENT KILL, kill session, pg\_stat\_activity, pg\_stat\_statements, pg\_stat\_statements\_reset, pg\_cancel\_backend, pg\_terminate\_backend, pg\_backend\_pid, running queries, running statements, idle in transaction, wait\_event, wait\_event\_type, kill query, kill connection, terminate connection, statement statistics, query statistics, slow statements, query totals, --stat-statements, KARELADB\_STAT\_STATEMENTS, queryid, mean\_exec\_time, total\_exec\_time, 42501
- See also: [Protection - timeouts, limits, safe updates, read-only (cancel)](protection.md#cancel), [EXPLAIN (explain-analyze)](explain.md#explain-analyze), [Health, info, check and backup over HTTP (slow-queries)](http-server-info.md#slow-queries), [Monitor panel (memory, processor, caches)](console-monitor.md), [PostgreSQL protocol (port 8832)](postgres-protocol.md), [Sessions and cursors over HTTP](http-sessions-and-cursors.md)

These are the views and functions PostgreSQL tools use to watch a server. They work the same over the [Postgres port](postgres-protocol.md) and over HTTP (`POST /exec`), and they show both kinds of client.

| View or function | What it gives |
|---|---|
| `pg_stat_activity` | one row per connection and HTTP session, and per HTTP request while it runs |
| `pg_cancel_backend(pid)` | stops the statement that backend runs |
| `pg_terminate_backend(pid)` | also closes its connection or HTTP session |
| `pg_backend_pid()` | the pid of your own connection (or HTTP request) |
| `query_activity()`, `CANCEL QUERY id`, `cancel_query(id)` | QuestDB's names: the running statements, and stopping one of them |
| `pg_sleep(seconds)` | waits; a cancel or a timeout stops it at once |
| `GET /api/sessions`, `DELETE /api/sessions/<pid>` | the same list as JSON, and closing one (Redis' `CLIENT LIST` and `CLIENT KILL`) |
| `pg_stat_statements` | calls, times and rows of every statement shape since the server started |
| `pg_stat_statements_reset()` | starts the totals again |
| `pg_locks`, `pg_blocking_pids(pid)` | the table locks held and waited for, with the same pids; who a waiting pid waits for ([LOCK TABLE and pg_locks](transactions.md#lock-table)) |

`kareladb sql` and `kareladb shell` have no server around them: there the views are empty and the functions answer `false`.

<a id="pg-stat-activity"></a>

## pg_stat_activity

Syntax:

```sql
SELECT pid, usename, application_name, client_addr, state, wait_event_type, wait_event, query_start, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
[WHERE pid <> pg_backend_pid()]
```

The columns are PostgreSQL 14's, in its order.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `pid` | the backend's number. A Postgres connection's is its `pg_backend_pid()` (the key of its cancel requests). An HTTP request without a session gets one of its own, from 1073741824 up |
| `datname`, `usename` | the database and the user (for a login without KarelaDB users: the login name) |
| `application_name` | the Postgres `application_name`, or the HTTP `User-Agent` |
| `client_addr` | the client's address (`client_port` and `client_hostname` are NULL) |
| `backend_start`, `xact_start`, `query_start`, `state_change` | when the connection opened, its transaction began, its statement began, its state last changed |
| `state` | `active` (a statement runs), `idle`, `idle in transaction`, `idle in transaction (aborted)` |
| `wait_event_type`, `wait_event` | what an active statement waits for: `Lock` / `relation` (another statement's tables), `Lock` / `tuple` (a row another transaction locked), `Lock` / `advisory`; an idle Postgres connection shows `Client` / `ClientRead`. NULL when not waiting |
| `query` | the running statement, or the last one when idle (up to 1024 characters) |
| `backend_type` | `client backend` |

- **Rights:** an admin (and the `--token`) sees every row in full. Other users see every row, but only their own rows' details: for another user's backend `query` is `<insufficient privilege>` and the times, state, address and wait columns are NULL, as in PostgreSQL.
- **Notes:**
  - An HTTP session ([POST /session](http-sessions-and-cursors.md)) is one backend from its start to its close. An HTTP request without a session is listed only while it runs.
  - `datid` and `usesysid` are the oids `pg_database` and `pg_roles` show; use `datname` and `usename`.
  - The same list, as JSON, is in [`GET /api/stats`](http-server-info.md) (`running`), which the console's Monitor panel shows.

**Example: Without a server (kareladb sql) nobody else is connected**

```sql
SELECT count(*) AS others FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE pid <> pg_backend_pid();
```

Result:

| others (LONG) |
|---|
| 0 |

(1 row)

<a id="pg-cancel-backend"></a>

## pg_cancel_backend and pg_terminate_backend

Syntax:

```sql
pg_cancel_backend(pid)
pg_terminate_backend(pid [, timeout])
```

`pg_cancel_backend` stops the statement the backend runs now; the connection stays. `pg_terminate_backend` also closes it: a Postgres connection gets `FATAL: terminating connection due to administrator command` (SQLSTATE `57P01`) and is closed at once (an open transaction is rolled back), an HTTP session is closed as [DELETE /session](http-sessions-and-cursors.md) closes it.

- **Returns:** `true` when a backend has that pid (also when it is idle and there was nothing to stop), `false` when none has, NULL for a NULL pid.
- **Rights:** an admin may stop every backend; other users only their own. Otherwise: `must be a member of the role whose query is being canceled or member of pg_signal_backend` (SQLSTATE `42501`, HTTP 403).
- **Notes:**
  - The stopped statement gets `canceling statement due to user request` (SQLSTATE `57014`, HTTP 408), as with a [cancel request](protection.md#cancel). It stops within milliseconds: the scans look at the stop flag once per batch of rows.
  - `timeout` is accepted and not waited for.
  - Over TLS a terminated idle connection is closed without the `57P01` message (two threads must not write one TLS session).

**Example: No backend has this pid**

```sql
SELECT pg_cancel_backend(12345) AS cancelled, pg_terminate_backend(12345) AS terminated;
```

Result:

| cancelled (BOOL) | terminated (BOOL) |
|---|---|
| false | false |

(1 row)

Syntax:

```sql
-- Stop everything user etl has run for more than 5 minutes
SELECT pid, pg_cancel_backend(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE usename = 'etl' AND state = 'active' AND query_start < now() - INTERVAL '5 minutes';

-- Close the connections left idle in a transaction
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'idle in transaction';
```

<a id="query-activity"></a>

## query_activity, CANCEL QUERY and cancel_query

Syntax:

```sql
SELECT query_id, worker_id, worker_pool, username, query_start, state_change, state, is_wal, query
FROM query_activity()
CANCEL QUERY query_id
cancel_query(query_id)
```

QuestDB's way to see and stop running statements. `query_activity()` has one row per statement running now, over HTTP and the Postgres port, itself included.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `query_id` | the statement's number: new for every statement, never used twice while the server runs |
| `worker_id` | the `pid` of its connection or request, as `pg_stat_activity` shows it |
| `worker_pool` | `pgwire` (the Postgres port) or `http` |
| `username`, `query` | who runs it, and its text (up to 1024 characters) |
| `query_start`, `state_change` | when it started |
| `state` | `active`, or `cancelled` while a stopped statement winds down |
| `is_wal` | always `false`: KarelaDB applies a commit before it returns, so it has no WAL apply jobs |

- **Returns:** `CANCEL QUERY` answers `true` or fails with `query to cancel not found in registry [id=...]` (SQLSTATE `42704`) when no statement runs with that id. `cancel_query(id)` answers `true` when it stopped one, `false` when none runs with that id, NULL for NULL.
- **Rights:** an admin sees and stops every statement; other users see only their own and may stop only their own (otherwise SQLSTATE `42501`, HTTP 403).
- **Notes:** the stopped statement ends with `canceling statement due to user request` (`57014`); its connection stays. `pg_stat_activity`'s own `query_id` column is PostgreSQL's (a number for the statement's shape) and stays NULL.

**Example: Without a server (kareladb sql) nothing else runs**

```sql
SELECT count(*) AS running FROM query_activity();
```

Result:

| running (LONG) |
|---|
| 0 |

(1 row)

**Example: No statement runs with this id**

```sql
SELECT cancel_query(123456) AS cancelled;
```

Result:

| cancelled (BOOL) |
|---|
| false |

(1 row)

Syntax:

```sql
-- Stop every statement that has run for more than a minute
SELECT query_id, cancel_query(query_id) FROM query_activity()
WHERE query_start < now() - INTERVAL '1 minute' AND query NOT LIKE '%query_activity%';
```

<a id="pg-sleep"></a>

## pg_sleep

Syntax:

```sql
pg_sleep(seconds)
```

Waits that many seconds (a fraction is fine), then returns an empty value, as PostgreSQL's `void`. A cancel, `pg_terminate_backend`, `CANCEL QUERY` or the [statement timeout](protection.md) stops it within about 10 ms. NULL or 0 returns at once.

**Example: A short wait**

```sql
SELECT pg_sleep(0.01) IS NOT NULL AS waited;
```

Result:

| waited (BOOL) |
|---|
| true |

(1 row)

<a id="idle-clients"></a>

## Idle and vanished clients

Syntax:

```sql
SET idle_session_timeout = '10min'             -- 0 = off (the default)
SET client_connection_check_interval = '5s'    -- 0 = off (the default)
SET tcp_keepalives_idle = 60                   -- seconds; 0 = the server's
SET tcp_keepalives_interval = 10
SET tcp_keepalives_count = 5
kareladb serve --tcp-keepalives-idle 60 --tcp-keepalives-interval 10 --tcp-keepalives-count 5
```

PostgreSQL 14's settings, for one Postgres connection.

| Setting | What it does |
|---|---|
| `idle_session_timeout` | A connection that waits longer than this for its next query, **outside** a transaction, is closed with `FATAL: terminating connection due to idle-session timeout` (SQLSTATE `57P05`). An open `BEGIN` counts under `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` instead ([idle transactions](transactions.md#idle-timeout)). Milliseconds as a number, or `'2s'`, `'5min'`. |
| `client_connection_check_interval` | While a statement runs, the server looks this often whether the client is still there, and stops the statement when it went away, so a long query does not run on for nobody. At most about 5 times a second. |
| `tcp_keepalives_idle`, `_interval`, `_count` | TCP keepalive of this connection: seconds without traffic before the first probe, seconds between probes, probes before the connection is given up. `SHOW` reads the value back from the socket. `0` = the server's (the `--tcp-keepalives-*` flags, `KARELADB_TCP_KEEPALIVES_*`, `tcp_keepalives_*` in `kareladb.conf`), else the system's. |

- **Notes:**
  - Keepalive is on for every HTTP and Postgres connection, as in PostgreSQL, so a client that vanished without closing (a laptop shut, a NAT that forgot it) is noticed and its locks are given back. The server flags set the timings for both ports.
  - A wrong value is refused with SQLSTATE `22023` and changes nothing. Idle and interval go up to 32767 s, the count up to 127.
  - The connections the server closed are in the [activity log](http-server-info.md) (`GET /api/activity`, kind `session`).
  - These are settings of the Postgres port. `SHOW idle_session_timeout` there answers `0` until it is set, then as PostgreSQL writes it (`2s`, `1min`).

<a id="api-sessions"></a>

## GET /api/sessions and DELETE /api/sessions/<pid>

Syntax:

```sql
GET /api/sessions
GET /api/activity?sessions=1
DELETE /api/sessions/<pid>
```

`GET /api/sessions` is `pg_stat_activity` as JSON: every Postgres connection, HTTP session and running HTTP request, with `pid`, `protocol` (`pg` or `http`), `user`, `database`, `application_name`, `client_addr`, `state`, `wait_event_type`, `wait_event`, `query`, the times in Unix milliseconds (`backend_start_ms`, `xact_start_ms`, `query_start_ms`, `state_change_ms`) and `query_id` (the running statement's, for `CANCEL QUERY`; null when idle). `GET /api/activity?sessions=1` adds the same list to the activity log's answer, so one poll shows what happened and what runs now.

`DELETE /api/sessions/<pid>` is `pg_terminate_backend(<pid>)`: the statement stops, an open transaction rolls back, a Postgres client gets `57P01`. It answers `{"pid":..,"terminated":true}`, `404` when no session has that pid, `403` when it is another user's and you are not an admin, `400` for a pid that is not a number.

Syntax:

```sql
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KARELADB_TOKEN" http://localhost:9900/api/sessions
curl -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer $KARELADB_TOKEN" http://localhost:9900/api/sessions/42
```

<a id="pg-stat-statements"></a>

## pg_stat_statements

Syntax:

```sql
SELECT query, calls, total_exec_time, mean_exec_time, max_exec_time, rows
FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10
pg_stat_statements_reset([userid, dbid, queryid])
kareladb serve --stat-statements on|off          (env KARELADB_STAT_STATEMENTS; default on)
```

The totals of every statement **shape** the server ran: the statement with each literal replaced by `$1`, `$2`, ..., so `WHERE id = 5` and `WHERE id = 7` count together. Spacing, comments and the case of words do not make a new shape. No extension needs to be created.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `queryid` | the shape's number: the same for every user |
| `query` | the shape, as its user first sent it (up to 1024 characters) |
| `calls`, `rows` | how often it ran, and the rows it returned or changed in all |
| `total_exec_time`, `min_exec_time`, `max_exec_time`, `mean_exec_time`, `stddev_exec_time` | milliseconds |
| `usename`, `datname` | KarelaDB's own columns: the user and the database (`userid` and `dbid` are the same oid for everyone) |
| `plans`, `*_plan_time`, `shared_blks_*`, `local_blks_*`, `temp_blks_*`, `blk_*_time`, `wal_*` | PostgreSQL's columns KarelaDB does not count: 0 |

- **Returns:** one row per user, database and shape.
- **Notes:**
  - Only statements that ended without an error count, as in PostgreSQL. The console's own polling does not count.
  - One HTTP request is one statement, even when it holds several.
  - At most 5000 shapes are kept (PostgreSQL's `pg_stat_statements.max`). When a new one comes, the 5% least-called make room. The totals are kept in memory: a restart starts them again. Statements a procedure or trigger runs count in the `CALL` or write that ran them (`pg_stat_statements.track` is `top`).
  - It costs a few hundred nanoseconds per statement: the first 16 KB of the text are read once for the shape. `--stat-statements off` switches it off; the view is then empty.
  - Other users' shapes show `<insufficient privilege>` instead of the text to a user who is not an admin.
  - `pg_stat_statements_reset()` needs an admin. With a `queryid` (the third argument, `0` = all) only that shape starts again.

**Example: Without a server (kareladb sql) nothing is counted**

```sql
SELECT count(*) AS shapes FROM pg_stat_statements;
```

Result:

| shapes (LONG) |
|---|
| 0 |

(1 row)

<!-- docs/listen-notify.md -->

# LISTEN and NOTIFY

> Send a message to every client that listens on a channel when a transaction commits - over the PostgreSQL port (LISTEN) or HTTP (GET /listen, server-sent events).

- Category: Postgres protocol
- Keywords: LISTEN, NOTIFY, UNLISTEN, UNLISTEN \*, pg\_notify, notification, notifications, pub/sub, pubsub, publish, subscribe, PUBLISH, SUBSCRIBE, PSUBSCRIBE, pattern, pmessage, redis, push, event, events, channel, payload, NotificationResponse, GET /listen, /listen, server-sent events, SSE, EventSource, text/event-stream, payload string too long, channel name cannot be empty, 54000, trigger notify, LISTEN needs a connection that stays open
- See also: [PostgreSQL protocol (port 8832)](postgres-protocol.md), [Triggers](triggers.md), [Transactions](transactions.md), [Run SQL over HTTP (/exec, /exp)](http-exec.md), [CREATE TABLE (row-ttl)](create-table.md#row-ttl), [Key-value store (Redis-like) (kv-pubsub)](kv.md#kv-pubsub)

`NOTIFY` sends a short message on a **channel**. Every client that listens on that channel gets it, the moment the sending transaction commits. It works as in PostgreSQL 14, and web pages can listen over HTTP too.

| | How |
|---|---|
| Send | `NOTIFY orders, 'order 42 paid'` or `SELECT pg_notify('orders', 'order 42 paid')`, from any client, a [trigger](triggers.md) or a procedure |
| Listen (PostgreSQL port) | `LISTEN orders` on a connection that stays open ([below](#listen-pg)) |
| Listen (HTTP, web pages) | `GET /listen?channel=orders`: server-sent events ([below](#listen-http)); `?pattern=price.*` for every channel a pattern matches |
| Redis-style | `PUBLISH`, `PUBSUB` and keyspace events through `POST /kv` ([key-value store](kv.md#kv-pubsub)): the same channels, sent at once |

The rules, the same as PostgreSQL's:

- A message is delivered when its transaction **commits**, never after a `ROLLBACK`. `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT` drops the ones sent after the savepoint.
- The same channel and payload sent twice in one transaction arrive **once**. Otherwise the order is kept.
- Channels belong to one database: a `NOTIFY` in `market` never reaches a listener of `app`.
- A message is a signal for clients connected **now**: nothing is stored, and nothing is sent again after a restart. Read the table after a message to get the data.

<a id="notify"></a>

## NOTIFY and pg_notify()

Syntax:

```sql
NOTIFY channel [, 'payload']
pg_notify(channel_text, payload_text)
```

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `channel` | a name. Without quotes it is lower case (`NOTIFY Orders` goes to `orders`); `"Orders"` keeps its case |
| `payload` | text of at most 7999 bytes; none = empty |
| `pg_notify(...)` | the same as a function, for a value made in the query. It takes the channel as written (no lower case) |

- **Returns:** `NOTIFY`; `pg_notify()` gives `NULL`.
- **Errors:** `payload string too long`, `channel name cannot be empty`, `channel name too long` (more than 63 bytes).
- Anyone who may read the database may send and listen, as in PostgreSQL.

**Example: Send inside a transaction: it goes out at COMMIT**

```sql
BEGIN;
NOTIFY orders, 'order 42 paid';
SELECT pg_notify('orders', 'order ' || 43 || ' paid');
COMMIT;
```

Result:

`BEGIN`

```text
transaction started
```

`NOTIFY orders, 'order 42 paid'`

```text
notification on channel 'orders': sent to its listeners when the transaction commits
```

`SELECT pg_notify('orders', 'order ' || 43 || ' paid')`

| pg_notify('orders', 'order ' \|\| 43 \|\| ' paid') (STRING) |
|---|
| NULL |

(1 row)

`COMMIT`

```text
transaction committed: 0 change(s) saved
```

**Example: A payload that is too long** (shows an error)

```sql
SELECT pg_notify('orders', repeat('x', 8000));
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 8: pg_notify: payload string too long`

<a id="notify-trigger"></a>

### From a trigger

A [trigger](triggers.md) can send a message for each new row. It is part of the statement's transaction: a failed insert sends nothing.

**Example: Tell the listeners about every paid order**

```sql
CREATE TABLE payments (id LONG PRIMARY KEY, amount DOUBLE);
CREATE TRIGGER tell_paid AFTER INSERT ON payments EXECUTE BEGIN
  SELECT pg_notify('payments', 'paid ' || id) FROM NEW;
END;
INSERT INTO payments VALUES (1, 250.0), (2, 99.5);
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE payments (`

```text
table 'payments' created
```

`CREATE TRIGGER tell_paid AFTER INSERT ON payments EXECUTE BEGIN`

```text
trigger 'tell_paid' created on table 'payments'
```

`INSERT INTO payments VALUES (1, 250.0), (2, 99.5)`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT pg_notify('payments', 'paid ' || id) FROM NEW`

| pg_notify('payments', 'paid ' \|\| id) (STRING) |
|---|
| NULL |
| NULL |

(2 rows)

<a id="listen-pg"></a>

## LISTEN on the PostgreSQL port

Syntax:

```sql
LISTEN channel
UNLISTEN channel | *
```

- The connection gets a `NotificationResponse` (channel, payload, the sender's process id) for each message. Drivers show them their own way: psql prints `Asynchronous notification "orders" with payload "..." received from server process with PID 17.`, pgx has `WaitForNotification`, psycopg `conn.notifies()`, node-pg the `notification` event.
- An idle connection gets it at once. A connection inside `BEGIN ... COMMIT` gets it when that transaction ends, as in PostgreSQL. Its own messages come right after its `COMMIT`.
- `LISTEN` inside `BEGIN ... COMMIT` starts at `COMMIT`, and not at all after `ROLLBACK`. `DISCARD ALL` stops every listen.

<a id="listen-http"></a>

## GET /listen: server-sent events

Syntax:

```sql
GET /listen?channel=orders[&channel=payments][&pattern=price.*][&db=name]
```

The reply is `text/event-stream` and stays open. A browser reads it with `EventSource`:

```js
const es = new EventSource('/listen?channel=orders');
es.onmessage = (e) => {
  const n = JSON.parse(e.data);  // {"channel":"orders","payload":"order 42 paid","pid":0}
  refreshOrders();
};
```

| Event | When |
|---|---|
| `listen` | once, when listening started: `{"channels":[...],"patterns":[...],"database":"..."}` |
| (message) | one per notification: `{"channel","payload","pid"}`; `pid` is 0 for a sender that is not a PostgreSQL connection; `"pattern"` too when it came through a pattern |
| `: ping` (a comment) | every 15 s, so a proxy keeps the stream open |
| `error` | the stream ends after it (see [limits](#limits)) |

- It needs a login, like [/exec](http-exec.md) (`Authorization: Bearer ...`, or the console's cookie). Up to 64 channels and patterns in one stream; the names are taken as written.
- `channel=` is Redis's `SUBSCRIBE`, `pattern=` its `PSUBSCRIBE`: a glob as `KEYS` takes it (`*` any text, `?` one character, `[abc]`, `\` before a special character). `/listen?pattern=price.*` gets `price.NABIL`, `price.HDL`, ... A message that matches a channel and a pattern of the same stream comes once for each.
- Over HTTP a channel may be up to 4096 bytes long (a [keyspace event](kv.md#kv-events) holds the whole key); `NOTIFY` keeps PostgreSQL's 63.
- `LISTEN` sent through `/exec` is refused with the way to do it: a request has no connection that stays open to be told.

<a id="limits"></a>

## Limits

- A listener that does not read keeps up to 32 MB of messages. Past that, it is **cut off**: the PostgreSQL connection ends with SQLSTATE `54000`, the HTTP stream with an `error` event. Nothing is lost quietly: connect again, `LISTEN` again, and read the table.
- At most 256 HTTP streams at once (`503` beyond).
- Messages of one sending connection arrive in commit order. Messages of two connections that commit at the same moment may arrive in either order.

# Settings - SET, SHOW ALL, ALTER SYSTEM

> One list of the server's settings behind pg_settings, SHOW ALL, SHOW PARAMETERS and GET /api/settings; SET for a session, ALTER SYSTEM and pg_reload_conf() for the server.

- Category: Postgres protocol
- Keywords: settings, pg\_settings, SHOW ALL, SHOW PARAMETERS, SET, RESET, ALTER SYSTEM, pg\_reload\_conf, current\_setting, work\_mem, max\_parallel\_workers\_per\_gather, enable\_hashjoin, enable\_nestloop, enable\_indexscan, log\_statement, plan\_cache\_mode, plan cache, kareladb.conf, kdb\_settings, QuestDB, parameters, txn\_spill\_mb, memory\_limit
- See also: [PostgreSQL protocol (port 8832)](postgres-protocol.md), [PostgreSQL-compatible functions](functions-postgres.md), [kareladb serve](cli-serve.md), [Settings page (data folder, old log, capacity, program files and users)](console-settings.md), [Limits](limits.md), [Joins](joins.md), [Indexes](indexes.md)

KarelaDB keeps **one list** of its settings. The same list is behind:

| Where | Shows |
|---|---|
| `SELECT * FROM pg_settings` | PostgreSQL's view: name, setting, unit, context, source, ... |
| `SHOW ALL` | name, value (as `SHOW` writes it: `4MB`, `5s`) and description |
| `SHOW PARAMETERS` | QuestDB's view: property path, environment variable, value, where it came from |
| `SELECT * FROM kdb_settings` | all of the above in one table, to filter with `WHERE` |
| `GET /api/settings` | the list under `"parameters"`, with the server's values |
| `SHOW work_mem`, `current_setting('work_mem')` | one setting, for this session |

Each setting says what KarelaDB does with it (the `use` column of `kdb_settings`):

| use | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `applied` | KarelaDB acts on it (`statement_timeout`, `work_mem`, `enable_hashjoin`, ...) |
| `shown` | kept and shown for clients, but KarelaDB works the same either way (`DateStyle`, `search_path`) |
| `ignored` | accepted so PostgreSQL scripts run, with a NOTICE (`shared_buffers` in a session, `enable_seqscan`, `jit`, ...) |

<a id="set"></a>

## Change a setting for this session

Syntax:

```sql
SET name = value          SET name TO value
SET LOCAL name = value    until COMMIT or ROLLBACK
RESET name                RESET ALL
SHOW name                 SHOW ALL
```

A value can have a unit, as in PostgreSQL: `SET work_mem = '64MB'`, `SET statement_timeout = '5s'`. `SHOW` gives it back the same way. A bad value gives `22023`, an unknown name on `SHOW` gives `42704`.

The `context` column says when a setting may change:

| context | Changes with |
|---|---|
| `user` | `SET` in any session |
| `superuser` | `SET` by an admin (`log_statement`) |
| `sighup` | `ALTER SYSTEM` and `SELECT pg_reload_conf()` |
| `postmaster` | a restart: a `kareladb serve` flag, `kareladb.conf` or an environment variable (`55P02` on `SET`) |
| `internal` | never (`server_version`, `block_size`) |

Over HTTP, a `SET` lasts for the rest of the same request (and for the whole session when you use one: [sessions](http-sessions-and-cursors.md)).

**Example: Set and read a setting**

```sql
SET work_mem = '64MB';
SHOW work_mem;
SELECT name, setting, unit, source FROM pg_settings WHERE name IN ('work_mem', 'enable_hashjoin');
```

Result:

`SET work_mem = '64MB'`

```text
work_mem is 64MB for this session
```

`SHOW work_mem`

| work_mem (STRING) |
|---|
| 64MB |

(1 row)

`SELECT name, setting, unit, source FROM pg_settings WHERE name IN ('work_mem', 'enable_hashjoin')`

| name (STRING) | setting (STRING) | unit (STRING) | source (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|
| enable_hashjoin | on | NULL | default |
| work_mem | 65536 | kB | session |

(2 rows)

<a id="planner"></a>

## The planner settings KarelaDB applies

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `work_mem` | `0` | how much a `GROUP BY` keeps in memory before its groups go to temporary files. `0` = half of the statement's working memory. Never more than three quarters of it |
| `max_parallel_workers_per_gather` | the server's threads | threads one statement's scans and aggregates may use, its own included. `0` or `1` = one thread |
| `enable_hashjoin` | `on` | `off`: equality joins compare every pair of rows (a nested loop) instead of building a hash |
| `enable_nestloop` | `on` | `off`: a join does not look each row's match up by key or index; it builds a hash |
| `enable_indexscan` | `on` | `off`: no secondary index finds rows; the table is scanned. A full-text search keeps its index |
| `log_statement` | `none` | `ddl`, `mod` or `all`: statements go to the server's log as `LOG:  statement: ...` (admins only) |
| `plan_cache_mode` | `auto` | `force_custom_plan`: this session's statements are parsed every time; they neither use nor fill the [plan cache](#plan-cache). `auto` and `force_generic_plan` use it |

The switches are there to compare answers and times, as in PostgreSQL. They are read once per statement, never per row.

<a id="memory"></a>

## Memory settings set at start

These change only with a restart (`postmaster`): a `kareladb serve` flag or an environment variable.

| Setting | Default | Flag / variable | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `memory_limit` | none | `--memory-limit`, `KARELADB_MEMORY_LIMIT` | one limit for everything the server holds |
| `shared_buffers` | 512 MB | `--memory`, `KARELADB_MEMORY` | table data kept loaded |
| `txn_spill_mb` | `64` | `--txn-spill-mb`, `KARELADB_TXN_SPILL_MB` | a transaction's log records past this many MB (or 1/16 of `memory_limit`) go to a temporary file until `COMMIT`. `0` = never. See [big transactions](transactions.md#txn-spill) |

**Example: Read the memory settings**

```sql
SELECT name, setting, unit, context FROM pg_settings WHERE name IN ('memory_limit', 'txn_spill_mb') ORDER BY name;
```

Result:

| name (STRING) | setting (STRING) | unit (STRING) | context (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|
| memory_limit | 0 | kB | postmaster |
| txn_spill_mb | 64 | MB | postmaster |

(2 rows)

<a id="plan-cache"></a>

## The plan cache

An app sends the same small statement again and again: a key lookup, a price, a session check. Parsing it can take as long as running it. So the server keeps the parse of a statement it has seen, by its exact text, and the next run of the same text skips the parse.

| What | How |
|---|---|
| Who uses it | every client: `POST /exec`, `GET /exec` and the PostgreSQL port's simple query (prepared statements keep their own parse per connection) |
| What is kept | one `SELECT` the first time; one `INSERT ... VALUES`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE` when the same text comes a second time. Not `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, a `WITH` that changes rows, or a statement that names another database |
| Same statement, other values | an `INSERT ... VALUES`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or `CALL` is also kept by its *shape* - the text with its numbers and `'strings'` left out - the first time, per connection (or HTTP worker). The next text of that shape, `INSERT INTO t VALUES (1018, 'open')` after `(1017, 'paid')`, runs the kept parse with its own values put in: the same tree a parse would make, without the parse. Only when every value is a plain value; a `LIMIT`, a cast's precision, a `SIMILAR TO` pattern or a `GROUP BY` keeps the text parsed every time |
| Per database | each database has its own entries, even for the same text |
| After a schema change | `CREATE`, `ALTER` or `DROP` of a table: the next run parses the text again |
| Size | up to 2,048 texts of at most 2 KB each; when full, one not used lately goes |
| Planned on each run | which index, which engine and which partitions are worked out again every time, with the values of that run |

The answers never change: only the time to parse is saved. `GET /api/stats` shows it under `"plan_cache"`:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `hits` | runs that skipped the parse |
| `misses` | statements it could keep that had to be parsed: the first time, or after a schema change |
| `entries` | parses kept now |
| `capacity` | texts it keeps at most |

To leave it out for one session, as PostgreSQL does for its own plan cache:

**Example: Parse every statement of this session**

```sql
SET plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan;
SHOW plan_cache_mode;
```

Result:

`SET plan_cache_mode = 'force_custom_plan'`

```text
plan_cache_mode is force_custom_plan for this session
```

`SHOW plan_cache_mode`

| plan_cache_mode (STRING) |
|---|
| force_custom_plan |

(1 row)

<a id="alter-system"></a>

## Change a setting for the server

Syntax:

```sql
ALTER SYSTEM SET name = value
ALTER SYSTEM RESET name
ALTER SYSTEM RESET ALL
SELECT pg_reload_conf();
```

`ALTER SYSTEM` saves the value in `kareladb.conf`, under `"system"`. It is in use after `SELECT pg_reload_conf()` (or the next start) for every new statement of every session that did not `SET` it itself. Only a server admin may run either. `ALTER SYSTEM` cannot run inside `BEGIN ... COMMIT`.

```text
ALTER SYSTEM SET work_mem = '256MB';
ALTER SYSTEM SET log_statement = 'ddl';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();       -- true
```

`kareladb.conf` then holds:

```text
{
  "data_dir": "/data",
  "system": {"log_statement": "ddl", "work_mem": "262144"}
}
```

- Settings that only change with a restart (`port`, `shared_buffers`, `max_connections`, ...) give `55P02` and name the flag or `kareladb.conf` key to use.
- A database folder served by its path (`kareladb serve D:\kdb\market`) has no `kareladb.conf` of its own: `ALTER SYSTEM` says so.
- A value in `kareladb.conf` that is no longer valid is skipped with a warning in the server's log; the default is used.

<a id="fixes"></a>

## Also fixed on 2026-09-26

- `KARELADB_NO_ZONE_MAPS=0` (and every other `KARELADB_NO_*` switch set to `0`, `off`, `no` or `false`) now means **off**: the speed-up stays on. Some switches used to turn off for any value.
- An on/off variable set but empty (`KARELADB_SCOPED_DDL=` in a compose file) no longer stops the server: it counts as not set. `true`/`false`, `yes`/`no` and `1`/`0` work too.
- `kareladb serve <folder>` (a database folder by its path) no longer takes `alert_webhook` from the default `kareladb.conf`, like every other `kareladb.conf` setting.
- `KARELADB_INDEX_MAX_VISITS` must be a whole number of 1 or more; any other value is ignored with a warning, instead of making ordered index reads give up at once.
- `kareladb help` lists what `kareladb.conf` may hold.
