# Grafana and Prometheus

> Draw KarelaDB data in Grafana through the PostgreSQL port, watch the server with Prometheus, and use the two ready dashboards.

- Category: Postgres protocol
- Keywords: Grafana, grafana-oss, dashboard, dashboards, panel, panels, Prometheus, scrape, /metrics, Telegraf, PostgreSQL data source, grafana-postgresql-datasource, data source, datasource, provisioning, $\_\_timeFilter, $\_\_timeGroup, $\_\_timeGroupAlias, $\_\_timeFrom, $\_\_timeTo, $\_\_unixEpochFilter, $\_\_unixEpochGroup, $\_\_interval, $\_\_rate\_interval, template variable, \_\_text, \_\_value, multi-value, candlestick, candles, OHLC, TimescaleDB, time\_bucket, array\_lower, function in FROM, kdb\_snapshot\_reads\_total, integrations/grafana, docker compose, outputs.http, chunked
- See also: [PostgreSQL protocol (port 8832)](postgres-protocol.md), [Health, info, check and backup over HTTP (metrics)](http-server-info.md#metrics), [Line protocol (POST /write)](line-protocol.md), [SAMPLE BY](sample-by.md), [LATEST ON](latest-on.md), [Performance tips](performance-tips.md), [API tokens](api-tokens.md), [Users and roles](users-and-roles.md)

Grafana draws charts from databases. KarelaDB works with it in two ways:

| What | How | Grafana data source |
|---|---|---|
| Your data: prices, trades, sensor readings | SQL over the [PostgreSQL port](postgres-protocol.md) (8832) | the built-in **PostgreSQL** data source |
| The server's health: requests, latency, memory | Prometheus reads [GET /metrics](http-server-info.md#metrics) | **Prometheus** |

Two ready dashboards, the data source files and a `docker-compose.yml` are in the folder `integrations/grafana` of the KarelaDB source. Everything on this page was run with Grafana 11.6.0 and Prometheus 3.1.0 on 2026-10-22: every panel of both dashboards came back with rows through Grafana's own `/api/ds/query`.

<a id="data-source"></a>

## Connect the PostgreSQL data source

In Grafana: **Connections**, **Data sources**, **Add data source**, **PostgreSQL**.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Host URL | `127.0.0.1:8832`; Grafana in Docker and KarelaDB on the same computer: `host.docker.internal:8832`; in `docker-compose.yml`: `kareladb:8832` |
| Database name | a KarelaDB database, like `market` |
| Username | a KarelaDB user with `ROLE read` (below); without KarelaDB users, any name |
| Password | that user's password (the server's token also works, but it gives Grafana full rights: below) |
| TLS/SSL Mode | `disable` without TLS; `require` when `kareladb serve` runs with [TLS](tls.md) |
| Version | `14` (KarelaDB says it is PostgreSQL 14) |
| TimescaleDB | **off** (KarelaDB has no `time_bucket`; [macros](#macros)) |

**Save & test** answers `Database Connection OK`.

- Grafana only reads. Give it a user that may only read, so a panel can never change data. Anyone who may edit a panel can send any SQL through the data source, so with the server's token (`KARELADB_TOKEN`, `--token`, full rights) as the password they could `DROP` or `DELETE` anything: use the token only for a quick try on your own computer.

**Example: A read-only user for Grafana** (sample data: sample)

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER grafana WITH PASSWORD 'Grafana-reads-only-7' ROLE read;
SHOW USERS;
```

Result:

`CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD '***' ROLE admin`

```text
user 'admin' created with role admin
```

`CREATE USER grafana WITH PASSWORD '***' ROLE read`

```text
user 'grafana' created with role read
```

`SHOW USERS`

| name (STRING) | role (STRING) | grants (STRING) | created (TIMESTAMP) | changed (TIMESTAMP) | table_grants (STRING) | two_factor (BOOL) | statement_timeout (STRING) | priority (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| admin | admin | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:19.006Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:19.006Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |
| grafana | read | NULL | 2026-10-24T06:19:19.085Z | 2026-10-24T06:19:19.085Z | NULL | false | NULL | NULL |

(2 rows)

- An API token is not a password for the PostgreSQL port ([API tokens](api-tokens.md)): Grafana logs in with the user's password.
- The query editor lists tables and columns for the **Builder** mode. KarelaDB answers the exact catalog SQL Grafana 11 sends (it reads the `search_path` with `array_lower` and with `string_to_array(...)` used as a table).

Instead of clicking, Grafana can read the data source from a file at start (`integrations/grafana/provisioning/datasources/kareladb.yaml`). Grafana fills `${...}` from its own environment, so the password is not in the file. Never put the server's token in Grafana's environment:

```yaml
apiVersion: 1
datasources:
  - name: KarelaDB
    type: grafana-postgresql-datasource
    uid: kareladb-pg
    url: ${KARELADB_PG_HOST}          # 127.0.0.1:8832
    user: grafana
    jsonData:
      database: ${KARELADB_DATABASE}  # market
      sslmode: disable
      postgresVersion: 1400
      timescaledb: false
    secureJsonData:
      password: ${KARELADB_GRAFANA_PASSWORD}   # the grafana user's (ROLE read)
```

<a id="macros"></a>

## The macros

Grafana changes its macros into plain SQL before it sends the query. The table shows what KarelaDB receives for a dashboard showing 2026-09-09 to 2026-09-11.

| Macro | KarelaDB receives | Works |
|---|---|---|
| `$__timeFilter(time)` | `time BETWEEN '2026-09-09T00:00:00Z' AND '2026-09-11T00:00:00Z'` | yes |
| `$__timeFrom()`, `$__timeTo()` | `'2026-09-09T00:00:00Z'`, `'2026-09-11T00:00:00Z'` | yes |
| `$__time(time)` | `time AS "time"` | yes |
| `$__timeEpoch(time)` | `extract(epoch from time) as "time"` | yes |
| `$__timeGroup(time, 1h)` | `floor(extract(epoch from time)/3600)*3600` | yes, on the column engine |
| `$__timeGroupAlias(time, 1h)` | the same with `AS "time"` | yes, on the column engine |
| `$__timeGroup(time, 1h, 0)`, `NULL`, `previous` | the same; Grafana fills the missing buckets itself | yes |
| `$__unixEpochFilter(col)`, `$__unixEpochFrom()`, `$__unixEpochTo()` | `col >= 1788912000 AND col <= 1789084800` | yes, for a column of whole seconds |
| `$__unixEpochGroup(col, 1h)`, `$__unixEpochGroupAlias` | `floor((col)/3600)*3600` | yes |
| `$__interval`, `$__interval_ms` | `2m`, `120000`: the width of one point on the panel | yes |
| TimescaleDB on: `$__timeGroup` as `time_bucket(...)` | `time_bucket('3600.000s',time)` | **no**: keep TimescaleDB off |

- `$__unixEpochFilter(extract(epoch from time))` does not work: Grafana's macro reader stops at the first `)`. Use `$__timeFilter(time)` on a time column.
- `$__timeGroup` is the same SQL for every database, so it comes from Grafana's own code. KarelaDB sees the shape `floor(extract(epoch from col)/N)*N` and groups it in the column engine like `date_trunc`, with exactly the rows the row-by-row engine gives (4 million rows into 3,169 five-minute buckets: 34 ms instead of 6.2 s). That is for buckets of whole seconds and of 1/2, 1/4 or 1/8 second. A bucket like `0.1` (Grafana's `100ms`, `50ms`, `1ms` intervals) is not exact in a computer's floating point, so `floor(.../0.1)` must be worked out row by row to give the same edges as PostgreSQL; such a query runs on the row engine. A panel **Min interval** of `1s` keeps every panel on the fast path.

The panel query and what reaches KarelaDB, run on the sample data:

```text
SELECT $__timeGroupAlias(time, 1h), symbol AS metric, last(close) AS close
FROM ochl_minutes
WHERE $__timeFilter(time)
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1
```

**Example: $__timeGroupAlias(time, 1h) as KarelaDB receives it** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT floor(extract(epoch from time)/3600)*3600 AS "time", symbol AS metric, last(close) AS close
FROM ochl_minutes
WHERE time BETWEEN '2026-09-09T00:00:00Z' AND '2026-09-11T00:00:00Z'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1
LIMIT 6;
```

Result:

| time (DOUBLE) | metric (SYMBOL) | close (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 1788930000 | CITY | 507.8 |
| 1788930000 | COAST | 392.9 |
| 1788933600 | CITY | 506 |
| 1788933600 | COAST | 387.7 |
| 1788937200 | CITY | 509.4 |
| 1788937200 | COAST | 382.3 |

(6 rows)

(The `LIMIT 6` only keeps this page short.) `time` comes back as seconds since 1970, which Grafana reads as a time.

<a id="formats"></a>

## Time series and table panels

| Format (under the query) | What the query must give |
|---|---|
| **Time series** | a column named `time` (a `TIMESTAMP`, or seconds since 1970), then number columns. A text column named `metric` makes one line per value (`symbol AS metric`). Rows sorted by `time`. |
| **Table** | any columns; Grafana shows them as they come |

- Several numbers per row without a `metric` column make one line per number column.
- A `TIMESTAMP` column is sent as PostgreSQL `timestamp` (UTC). Set the dashboard's time zone, not the query's.

<a id="variables"></a>

## Template variables

A variable is a list the dashboard user picks from. Its query runs over the same data source.

| Variable query | Gives |
|---|---|
| `SELECT DISTINCT symbol FROM ochl_minutes ORDER BY 1` | one value per row |
| `SELECT name AS __text, symbol AS __value FROM securities ORDER BY symbol` | `__text` is shown, `__value` goes into the SQL |

**Example: A variable with names shown and symbols used** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT name AS __text, symbol AS __value FROM securities ORDER BY symbol;
```

Result:

| __text (STRING) | __value (SYMBOL) |
|---|---|
| Acme Investment Company | ACME |
| City Bank Limited | CITY |
| Coastal Bank Limited | COAST |
| Northwind Telecom Limited | TELCO |
| Volt River Hydropower Limited | VOLT |

(5 rows)

How Grafana puts a variable into the SQL:

| Variable | Write | KarelaDB receives |
|---|---|---|
| one value | `symbol = '$symbol'` | `symbol = 'CITY'` |
| multi-value or **All** | `symbol IN ($symbols)` | `symbol IN ('CITY','COAST')` (Grafana adds the quotes) |

**Example: A multi-value variable as KarelaDB receives it** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT symbol, sum(quantity) AS volume, sum(amount) AS amount
FROM trade_log
WHERE date BETWEEN '2026-09-09T00:00:00Z' AND '2026-09-11T00:00:00Z' AND symbol IN ('CITY','COAST')
GROUP BY symbol
ORDER BY symbol;
```

Result:

| symbol (SYMBOL) | volume (LONG) | amount (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| CITY | 2420 | 1247230 |
| COAST | 3070 | 1227510 |

(2 rows)

<a id="candles"></a>

## Candles with SAMPLE BY

[SAMPLE BY](sample-by.md) cuts the time into equal buckets and is the fastest way to draw candles: one bucket per point of the panel with `SAMPLE BY $__interval`. Give the panel a **Min interval** of the data's own step (`1m` for one-minute candles), so a narrow time range does not ask for buckets smaller than the data. Use Grafana's **Candlestick** panel: it finds the columns `open`, `high`, `low`, `close` and `volume` by name.

```text
SELECT time, first(open) AS open, max(high) AS high, min(low) AS low, last(close) AS close, sum(volume) AS volume
FROM ochl_minutes
WHERE $__timeFilter(time) AND symbol = '$symbol'
SAMPLE BY $__interval
```

**Example: Thirty-minute candles of CITY, as KarelaDB receives them** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT time, first(open) AS open, max(high) AS high, min(low) AS low, last(close) AS close, sum(volume) AS volume
FROM ochl_minutes
WHERE time BETWEEN '2026-09-09T00:00:00Z' AND '2026-09-11T00:00:00Z' AND symbol = 'CITY'
SAMPLE BY 30m
LIMIT 5;
```

Result:

| time (TIMESTAMP) | open (DOUBLE) | high (DOUBLE) | low (DOUBLE) | close (DOUBLE) | volume (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-09T05:00:00.000Z | 512 | 512.4 | 509.8 | 510.7 | 13730 |
| 2026-09-09T05:30:00.000Z | 510.7 | 511.5 | 507 | 507.8 | 22270 |
| 2026-09-09T06:00:00.000Z | 507.8 | 507.8 | 504.2 | 504.8 | 24120 |
| 2026-09-09T06:30:00.000Z | 504.8 | 506.3 | 504 | 506 | 20990 |
| 2026-09-09T07:00:00.000Z | 506 | 508.9 | 505.8 | 507.6 | 25210 |

(5 rows)

<a id="fast-panels"></a>

## Fast panels

A dashboard runs every panel's query on each refresh, for every person looking at it. These keep each query short:

| Do | Why |
|---|---|
| `WHERE $__timeFilter(time)` on the table's [designated time column](partitions-and-dedup.md) | only the partitions in the time range are read ([EXPLAIN](explain.md) says "1 of 2 partitions") |
| `SAMPLE BY $__interval` or `$__timeGroupAlias(time, $__interval)` | one row per point of the panel, worked out in the column engine; never thousands of raw rows for Grafana to thin out |
| `symbol = '$symbol'` or `symbol IN ($symbols)` on a `SYMBOL` column | a SYMBOL compare is a number compare ([SYMBOL columns](performance-tips.md#symbol)) |
| [LATEST ON](latest-on.md) for "last price" tables and stat panels | reads the newest rows of each symbol, not the whole range |
| A **Min interval** on the panel, and `LIMIT` on table panels | a narrow range or a big table cannot ask for a million rows |
| TimescaleDB off, no `time_bucket` | `$__timeGroup` is grouped by the column engine; `time_bucket` does not exist |

**Example: Only the day in the time range is read, in the column engine** (sample data: sample)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ticks (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, price DOUBLE, qty LONG) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY DAY;
INSERT INTO ticks SELECT CAST(1788912000000 + (x - 1) * 60000 AS TIMESTAMP), CASE WHEN x % 2 = 0 THEN 'CITY' ELSE 'COAST' END, 100 + x % 7, x % 50
FROM long_sequence(2880);
```

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT floor(extract(epoch from time)/300)*300 AS "time", symbol AS metric, sum(qty) AS volume
FROM ticks
WHERE time BETWEEN '2026-09-10T00:00:00Z' AND '2026-09-10T23:59:59Z'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1;
```

Result:

| plan (STRING) |
|---|
| scan table ticks (1 of 2 partitions, about 2880 rows) |
| build 3 of 4 stored column(s) per row: time, symbol, qty |
| filter while scanning: 1 condition(s) |
| group by 2 key(s), 1 aggregate(s) |
| sort by 1 key(s) |
| engine: column |

(6 rows)

(Two days of one-minute ticks, so the table has two day partitions.)

- A table with a computed column (`amount DOUBLE AS (quantity * rate)`, like the sample's `trade_log`) is still grouped row by row, even when the query does not read that column; `EXPLAIN` says `engine: row`.
- Grafana's relative ranges (`now-6h`) give new times on every refresh, so the [result cache](performance-tips.md#result-cache) seldom answers them. A fixed range (a past day) is answered from the cache after the first look.
- The PostgreSQL port has its own line in the server dashboard (statement latency, `pg`). A slow panel shows up in `GET /api/slow-queries` with its full SQL, macros already replaced.

<a id="prometheus"></a>

## Prometheus: the server's health

[GET /metrics](http-server-info.md#metrics) gives the server's counters in Prometheus's text format: requests, statement latency (HTTP and PostgreSQL), memory, result cache, WAL and checkpoint writes, lock waits, snapshot reads per database (`kdb_snapshot_reads_total`), slow statements and disk use. A scrape never waits for a database lock. Metric names start with `kdb_` and stay that way, so alerts and dashboards keep working.

`/metrics` needs only the `read` right, so never give Prometheus the server's token. Make a read-only user; Prometheus logs in with its name and password, or with an [API token](api-tokens.md) of it:

**Example: A token for Prometheus** (sample data: sample)

Setup:

```sql
CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD 'Long-Admin-Passw0rd' ROLE admin;
CREATE USER monitor WITH PASSWORD 'Monitor-reads-only-9' ROLE read;
```

```sql
CREATE TOKEN prometheus FOR USER monitor;
```

Result:

| name (STRING) | user (STRING) | token (STRING) | expires (TIMESTAMP) |
|---|---|---|---|
| prometheus | monitor | kdbt_Bc0KKJR2cVv-t6I-MoYT37corGH_z7ydKOZkkF87rjQ | NULL |

(1 row)

```text
token 'prometheus' for user 'monitor' created: copy it now, it is shown only this once. Send it as Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

Put the user's password in a file next to `prometheus.yml`, one line, and point the scrape job at the HTTP port:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: kareladb
    metrics_path: /metrics
    basic_auth:
      username: monitor
      password_file: /etc/prometheus/kareladb_password
    # or the token: authorization: { type: Bearer, credentials_file: /etc/prometheus/kareladb_token }
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["127.0.0.1:9900"]
```

- In Prometheus, **Status**, **Targets** shows the job `up`. A `401` there is a wrong or missing token.
- Add Prometheus to Grafana as a **Prometheus** data source (`http://127.0.0.1:9090`).
- Only open databases have per-database lines (`database="market"`); counters start at 0 when the server starts, which `rate()` handles.

<a id="dashboards"></a>

## The ready dashboards

| File in `integrations/grafana/dashboards` | Data source | Panels |
|---|---|---|
| `kareladb-server.json` (KarelaDB server) | Prometheus | version, uptime, requests per second and by status, HTTP latency p50 / p95 / p99, statement latency by protocol, statements and errors, slow statements, lock waits, memory by kind, resident memory and limit, processor, WAL and checkpoint writes, snapshot reads, result cache and partition loads, disk use |
| `kareladb-market.json` (KarelaDB market example) | PostgreSQL | candles of a symbol (SAMPLE BY), last daily close (LATEST ON), volume per day, close by symbol (`$__timeGroupAlias` with fill), traded amount, trades; variables for the symbol and a multi-value symbol list |

The market dashboard reads the help's [sample data](sample-data.md) in a database named `market` ([quick start](quick-start.md#sample-data) loads it); its time range is 2026-09-09 to 2026-09-11, the days the sample holds.

**Import one by hand:** **Dashboards**, **New**, **Import**, upload the JSON file. Each dashboard has a data source picker at the top (`KarelaDB`, `Prometheus`); pick yours there.

**Load them at start (provisioning):** mount the folders into Grafana:

| Folder | Mount at |
|---|---|
| `integrations/grafana/provisioning` | `/etc/grafana/provisioning` |
| `integrations/grafana/dashboards` | `/var/lib/grafana/dashboards/kareladb` |

They appear in a **KarelaDB** folder. Set `KARELADB_PG_HOST`, `KARELADB_DATABASE`, `KARELADB_GRAFANA_PASSWORD` (the read-only user's) and `KARELADB_PROMETHEUS_URL` in Grafana's environment.

**All three together:** `integrations/grafana/docker-compose.yml` builds the `kareladb` image from the source and starts KarelaDB, Prometheus and Grafana. A one-off step makes the users `admin`, `grafana` (`ROLE read`) and `monitor` (`ROLE read`); only KarelaDB and that step see the server's token:

```bash
cd integrations/grafana
export KARELADB_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
export KARELADB_ADMIN_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -hex 16)
export KARELADB_GRAFANA_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -hex 16)
export KARELADB_MONITOR_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -hex 16)
printf %s "$KARELADB_MONITOR_PASSWORD" > prometheus/kareladb_password
docker compose up -d --build
# Grafana: http://127.0.0.1:3000 (admin / admin)
```

Then load the sample data into the database `market` and open **Dashboards**, **KarelaDB**. `node verify.mjs http://admin:<password>@127.0.0.1:3000` runs every panel query and every variable through Grafana and says which ones gave rows.

<a id="telegraf"></a>

## Telegraf

Telegraf collects metrics (processor, memory, disks, many services) and can write them to KarelaDB with the [line protocol](line-protocol.md). Each measurement becomes a table that `POST /write` makes by itself; Grafana then reads it with SQL. Use Telegraf's **http** output:

```toml
[[outputs.http]]
  url = "http://127.0.0.1:9900/write?db=metrics&precision=ns"
  method = "POST"
  data_format = "influx"
  [outputs.http.headers]
    Authorization = "Bearer ${KARELADB_TELEGRAF_TOKEN}"   # an API token of a user with write on metrics
    Content-Type = "text/plain; charset=utf-8"
```

- Make the database first (`CREATE DATABASE metrics`); `/write` makes tables, not databases.
- Telegraf's `influxdb` and `influxdb_v2` outputs send the body in chunks without a length, which KarelaDB answers with `501 chunked request bodies are not supported`; the `http` output sends the length. The `influxdb_v2` output also sends `Authorization: Token ...`, and KarelaDB takes only `Bearer`.
- Tested with Telegraf 1.33.0: `inputs.cpu` and `inputs.mem` made the tables `cpu` and `mem`, with a `timestamp` column for `$__timeFilter(timestamp)`.

<a id="troubleshooting"></a>

## When it does not work

| Grafana says | Why | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `password authentication failed for user "grafana"` | wrong password, or a user that is not a KarelaDB user on a server with users | the user's password, or the token on a server without users |
| `pq: SSL is not enabled on the server` | TLS/SSL Mode `require` on a server without TLS | `disable`, or turn [TLS](tls.md) on |
| `connections from other computers need a password` | no token and no users, and Grafana runs in Docker (another address) | start the server with a token or make a user |
| `database 'x' does not exist` | the Database name field | a database from `SHOW DATABASES` |
| `unknown function 'time_bucket'` | TimescaleDB is on in the data source | turn it off; `$__timeGroup` works without it |
| `db has no time column` | Time series format without a `time` column | `AS "time"`, `$__time(col)` or `$__timeGroupAlias(...)` |
| Prometheus target `down`, `401` | a wrong password in `password_file`, or a wrong token | the password or a token of a user with `read` |

<!-- docs/c-api.md -->

# C API (kdb.h)

> Use KarelaDB inside your own program with no server - open a folder, run SQL, read rows as text or native numbers - through the C header include/kdb.h and the kdb_c library.

- Category: C API
- Keywords: C API, kdb.h, kdb\_c, kdb.dll, libkdb.so, libkdb.dylib, embedded, embed, library, shared library, cgo, Go, golang, go-embedded, MinGW, database/sql, Rust, Python, ctypes, C#, P/Invoke, Swift, kdb\_open, kdb\_close, kdb\_exec, kdb\_exec\_values, kdb\_append, kdb\_result, kdb\_result\_free, kdb\_errmsg, kdb\_sqlstate, kdb\_last\_error, kdb\_session\_open, SQLSTATE, KDB\_BUILD\_C\_API, thread safety
- See also: [SQL basics](sql-basics.md), [Transactions](transactions.md), [INSERT](insert.md), [PostgreSQL protocol (port 8832)](postgres-protocol.md), [Run SQL over HTTP (/exec, /exp)](http-exec.md)

The C API puts the whole KarelaDB engine inside your own program. There is no server, no port and no token: your program opens a database folder and runs SQL on it directly. The same SQL works as over HTTP or the PostgreSQL port.

| Part | Where |
|---|---|
| The header | `include/kdb.h` - plain C, so C, C++, Go (cgo), Rust, Python (ctypes), C# (P/Invoke) and Swift can call it |
| The library | `kdb.dll` (Windows), `libkdb.so` (Linux), `libkdb.dylib` (macOS) - the CMake target `kdb_c` |
| A full example | `tests/test_c_api.c` in the source |

Only the `kdb_` functions of the header leave the library. The ABI is stable: functions are only ever added, never changed or removed. `kdb_abi_version()` says which set a library has (1 today).

<a id="build"></a>

## Build the library

On Windows the library is built with the rest of KarelaDB. On Linux and macOS ask for it, because it needs position-independent code, which costs the server program a little speed:

```text
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DKDB_BUILD_C_API=ON
cmake --build build --target kdb_c
```

The library lands in `build/bin`. On Windows it carries the C++ runtime inside, so `kdb.dll` needs no other DLL beside it.

<a id="exec"></a>

## Open, run SQL, read rows

```c
#include "kdb.h"
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
  kdb_db* db;
  if (kdb_open("D:/data/app", "{\"memory_mb\": 256}", &db) != KDB_OK) {
    printf("open failed: %s\n", kdb_errmsg());
    return 1;
  }
  kdb_exec(db, "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS prices (sym SYMBOL, close DOUBLE, ts TIMESTAMP)", NULL, NULL);
  kdb_exec(db, "INSERT INTO prices VALUES ($1, $2, $3)", "[\"AAPL\", 101.5, \"2026-10-02T09:15:00Z\"]", NULL);

  kdb_result* r;
  if (kdb_exec(db, "SELECT sym, close, ts FROM prices WHERE close > $1", "[100]", &r) == KDB_OK) {
    for (int64_t i = 0; i < kdb_result_rows(r); i++)
      printf("%s %g %s\n", kdb_result_text(r, i, 0, NULL), kdb_result_double(r, i, 1),
             kdb_result_text(r, i, 2, NULL));
    kdb_result_free(r);
  }
  return kdb_close(db);
}
```

- `kdb_open` makes the folder when it is not there. One process at a time may open a folder; do not point it at the folder a running `kareladb serve` uses.
- `kdb_exec` returns every row (there is no row limit). With several statements separated by `;`, the result is the last one's.
- Parameters `$1, $2, ...` come as a JSON array, or typed with `kdb_exec_values` and the helpers `kdb_int`, `kdb_double`, `kdb_text`, `kdb_bool`, `kdb_null`. A value never becomes SQL, so it is safe from SQL injection.
- Pass `NULL` for the result when you do not need it.

<a id="options"></a>

### Options of kdb_open

`options_json` may be `NULL` or an object with any of these. A name it does not know is an error, so a typo is never silently ignored.

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `memory_mb` | 512 | saved partition data kept in memory |
| `read_only` | false | open without writing anything |
| `sync_commits` | true | false: a commit returns before the disk sync (a power cut can lose the last ~10 ms) |
| `background` | true | false: no background threads (idle checkpoints, TTL, index warm-up, view refresh) - for short tools |
| `statement_timeout_ms` | 0 | stop a statement after this long (0 = no limit) |
| `lock_timeout_ms` | the engine's | how long a writer waits for a busy table |
| `min_free_mb` | 64 | refuse writes when the disk has less free |
| `encryption` | false | make a new database encrypted (needs `KARELADB_MASTER_KEY`) |

<a id="result"></a>

## Reading a result

| Function | Gives |
|---|---|
| `kdb_result_columns`, `kdb_result_rows` | the size |
| `kdb_result_column_name`, `kdb_result_column_type` | `"close"`, `"DOUBLE"` (the SQL type) |
| `kdb_result_type` | `KDB_NULL`, `KDB_BOOL`, `KDB_INT`, `KDB_DOUBLE` or `KDB_TEXT` |
| `kdb_result_int64`, `kdb_result_double` | the value as a native number |
| `kdb_result_text` | the value as text; `NULL` for SQL NULL |
| `kdb_result_rows_affected`, `kdb_result_message` | for INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and DDL |

A TIMESTAMP is a `KDB_INT` of Unix milliseconds (UTC), and its text is `2026-10-02T09:15:00.000Z`. A DATE is days since 1970-01-01, text `2026-10-02`. A DECIMAL is exact text (`"512.40"`); `kdb_result_double` reads it as a number. A row or column out of range reads as NULL - never a crash.

Every pointer a result gives stays valid until `kdb_result_free`, even after `kdb_close`.

<a id="errors"></a>

## Errors and SQLSTATE

Every call that can fail returns a `kdb_code`: `KDB_OK` (0), `KDB_NOTFOUND`, `KDB_INVALID`, `KDB_LOCKED`, `KDB_MISUSE` (a NULL handle, bad JSON, an unknown option) and a few more. The message and the PostgreSQL SQLSTATE of the last failure on the calling thread stay until that thread's next call:

```c
if (kdb_exec(db, "INSERT INTO users (id) VALUES (1)", NULL, NULL) != KDB_OK) {
  if (strcmp(kdb_sqlstate(), "23505") == 0) puts("that id is taken");
  else printf("%s: %s\n", kdb_sqlstate(), kdb_errmsg());
}
```

| SQLSTATE | Means |
|---|---|
| `42P01` | no such table |
| `42703` | no such column |
| `42601` | a syntax error |
| `23505` | a duplicate key |
| `23503` | a REFERENCES row is missing |
| `23502` | NULL in a NOT NULL column |
| `55P03` | a lock wait ran out |

These are the same codes the PostgreSQL port sends. A call that works sets `00000`.

<a id="append"></a>

## Bulk rows: kdb_append

`kdb_append` writes many rows in one commit without any SQL text - the fastest way in. Values go row after row:

```c
const char* cols[] = {"sym", "close", "ts"};
kdb_value rows[] = {
  kdb_text("AAPL"), kdb_double(101.5), kdb_text("2026-10-02T09:15:00Z"),
  kdb_text("MSFT"), kdb_double(410.2), kdb_text("2026-10-02T09:15:00Z"),
};
uint64_t written;
kdb_append(db, "prices", cols, 3, rows, 2, KDB_APPEND_ERROR, &written);
```

All rows or none are written. The mode says what a row with a key that is taken does: `KDB_APPEND_ERROR` (fail, like INSERT), `KDB_APPEND_REPLACE`, `KDB_APPEND_IGNORE`, or `KDB_APPEND_UPSERT` (like REPLACE, faster).

<a id="sessions"></a>

## Transactions: sessions

Each `kdb_exec` is its own connection: a `BEGIN` there is rolled back when the call ends. To keep a transaction open across calls, open a session:

```c
uint64_t s;
kdb_session_open(db, &s);
kdb_exec_session(db, s, "BEGIN", NULL, NULL);
kdb_exec_session(db, s, "UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 10 WHERE id = 1", NULL, NULL);
kdb_exec_session(db, s, "UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 10 WHERE id = 2", NULL, NULL);
kdb_exec_session(db, s, "COMMIT", NULL, NULL);
kdb_session_close(db, s);  /* rolls back anything still open */
```

<a id="threads"></a>

## Threads

| Thing | Rule |
|---|---|
| A `kdb_db` | any number of threads at once; reads run side by side, writes one at a time per table, as in the server |
| A `kdb_result` | never changes after it is returned: many threads may read it; free it once |
| A session | one connection: use one per thread |
| Errors | kept per thread, so threads never see each other's message |
| `kdb_close` | the last call on a `kdb_db`: no other thread may still use it |

<a id="go"></a>

## From Go: the cgo package

`examples/go-embedded` in the source is a Go package over `kdb.h`. It gives Go code the shape of `database/sql`, with no server:

```go
db, err := kdb.Open("D:/data/app", &kdb.Options{MemoryMB: 256})
if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
defer db.Close()

db.Exec("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS prices (sym SYMBOL, close DOUBLE, ts TIMESTAMP)")
db.Exec("INSERT INTO prices VALUES ($1, $2, $3)", "AAPL", 101.5, time.Now())

rows, err := db.Query("SELECT sym, close, ts FROM prices WHERE close > $1", 100)
if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
defer rows.Close()
for rows.Next() {
  var sym string
  var close float64
  var ts time.Time
  if err := rows.Scan(&sym, &close, &ts); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
}
```

| Go | Does |
|---|---|
| `kdb.Open(path, opts)`, `db.Close()` | `kdb_open`, `kdb_close`; `opts` may be `nil` |
| `db.Exec(sql, args...)` | runs SQL; returns `RowsAffected` and `Message` |
| `db.Query(sql, args...)` | `Rows` with `Next`, `Scan`, `Columns`, `Value`, `Close` |
| `db.QueryRow(sql, args...).Scan(...)` | the first row; `kdb.ErrNoRows` when there is none |
| `db.Session()` | a session: `BEGIN ... COMMIT` across calls; `Close` rolls back what is still open |
| `db.Append(table, cols, rows, mode)` | `kdb_append`: many rows in one commit, no SQL text |

- Parameters may be `nil`, `bool`, any integer, `float32`/`float64`, `string`, `[]byte` and `time.Time` (sent as UTC text, which a TIMESTAMP or DATE column reads).
- `Scan` takes `*string`, `*[]byte`, `*int64`, `*int`, `*int32`, `*float64`, `*float32`, `*bool`, `*time.Time`, `*any`, and `sql.NullString`, `sql.NullInt64`, `sql.NullTime`, ... (anything with a `Scan` method). A NULL into a plain type is an error, as in `database/sql`.
- A TIMESTAMP or DATE column scans into `time.Time` (UTC).
- An error is a `*kdb.Error` with `Code`, `SQLState` and `Message`; `kdb.IsSQLState(err, "23505")` asks for one code.
- One `*kdb.DB` may be used by many goroutines at once. The package reads the error of a call inside the same C call, so a goroutine that Go moves to another thread never gets another call's SQLSTATE.
- A result holds all its rows, so `Next` never waits on the engine. A `Rows` that is never closed is freed later by the garbage collector; close it to free it at once.

<a id="go-build"></a>

### Building it

cgo needs a C compiler on `PATH` when the package is built, and the library when the program runs.

1. Build the library (see [Build the library](#build)). The package looks for it in `build/bin` (on Windows also the import library in `build/lib`) of the same source tree. For a library somewhere else, set `CGO_CFLAGS=-I<folder of kdb.h>` and `CGO_LDFLAGS=-L<folder of the library>`.
2. Build or test it with cgo on:

```text
cd examples/go-embedded
go test ./...
```

| System | Notes |
|---|---|
| Windows | cgo needs MinGW-w64 gcc on `PATH` (for example MSYS2: `C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin`); MSVC does not work with cgo. `kdb.dll` must be found when the program starts: put it next to your `.exe`, or `build\bin` on `PATH`. It carries its C++ runtime, so it needs no other DLL. |
| Linux | gcc or clang; build the library with `-DKDB_BUILD_C_API=ON`. The package sets an rpath to `build/bin`; a program you ship needs `libkdb.so` beside it or on `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`. |
| macOS | clang (the Xcode command line tools); as Linux, with `libkdb.dylib`. |

cgo is on by default when Go finds a C compiler. A cross build (another `GOOS` or `GOARCH`) turns it off, so build on the kind of system the program runs on.

To use the package from your own module, point at it with two lines in your `go.mod` - `require kdb v0.0.0` and `replace kdb => ../KDB/examples/go-embedded` - and `import "kdb"`.

# Web console

> The browser page of kareladb serve - run SQL, see results as a grid or a chart, switch databases, check health, make backups and open this help.

- Category: Web console
- Keywords: console, web console, browser, pages, tabs, Home menu, SQL page, Dashboards, Data page, View data, Monitor panel, Settings page, right side, flyout, panel, pin, Samples, Databases panel, Tools panel, Purge trash, Delete all data, Terminal, activity log, log, Timers tab, New timer, Run now, Keep data for, object tabs, web folder, web\_dir, KARELADB\_WEB\_DIR, console not installed, editor, Run, Run all, Ctrl+Enter, Ctrl+Shift+Enter, F1, history, grid, result grid, chart, candles, Export CSV, table list, health box, Check now, Backup now, database picker, New database, login form, Log out, token box, theme, dark, light, Help menu, Documentation, Examples, Keyboard shortcuts, About KarelaDB, #sql, link with SQL, Try in console, dashboard
- See also: [Dashboard page (many charts on one page)](console-dashboards.md), [View data page (browse and edit rows)](console-data-page.md), [Keep data page (how long tables keep their rows)](console-keep-data.md), [Monitor panel (memory, processor, caches)](console-monitor.md), [Settings page (data folder, old log, capacity, program files and users)](console-settings.md), [Comments and suggestions](feedback.md), [HTTP API overview (get)](http-overview.md#get), [Run SQL over HTTP (/exec, /exp)](http-exec.md), [Logins, tokens and roles over HTTP](http-login.md), [Databases over HTTP (/api/databases)](http-databases.md), [Health, info, check and backup over HTTP](http-server-info.md), [kareladb serve](cli-serve.md), [Databases and the data folder](databases.md)

The **web console** is a web page inside `kareladb serve`. Open it in a browser to write SQL, run it, and look at the results. It needs no internet and no other software. Its files are plain files in the folder `web/` next to the kareladb program, not inside the program ([where kareladb finds them](install-packages.md#folders)).

Pick a page from the **Home** menu at the top left. The button shows where you are, for example `Home / Dashboard`.

| Menu item | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **Home** | write and run statements, see results as a grid or a chart (this page) |
| **Dashboard** | [many charts on one page](console-dashboards.md), saved in the database |
| **View data** | [browse tables and change rows](console-data-page.md) with forms instead of SQL |
| **Keep data** | [how long each table keeps its rows](console-keep-data.md): keep the last months or years, drop what is older |
| **Settings** | [where the data is kept, how much old log each database keeps, and who may log in](console-settings.md) |

The buttons down the right side open panels over the page: **Monitor**, **Health**, **Samples**, **Databases**, **Tools** and the **Terminal** ([right side](#right-side)).

**Comments and suggestions** in the [Help menu](#help-menu) opens one more page: a form to send a message to whoever runs the server ([feedback](feedback.md)).

The page you were on last opens again when you come back.

- Start the server, then open `http://127.0.0.1:9900` in Chrome, Edge or Firefox.
- Everything the console does goes through the [HTTP API](http-overview.md), so everything it can do, a program can do too.
- Tutorial: [chapter 6, web console](../tutorial/06-web-console.md).

**Command line: Start the server; the console address is on the second line**

```bash
kareladb serve --backups backups
```

Output:

```text
cold store 'archive': folder ./cold-archive
KarelaDB 0.2.0-dev
  console   http://127.0.0.1:9900
  data      ./kdb-data (from KDB_DATA_DIR; one folder per database)
  default   default (used when a request names no database)
  backups   backups/<database name> (from --backups)
  access    no token
  capacity  32 HTTP threads (default), 500 PostgreSQL connections (default), lock wait 5 s (default)
  lanes     reads using 100 ms of CPU (three times in a row) wait for one of 16 heavy slots, at most 16 HTTP in line (--lanes on)
  reads     32 reads run at once (the CPUs, at least 2; follows the CPU limit), the rest wait in line (--read-slots)
  commits   synced to disk before they are confirmed (--sync-commits always)
  time zone Asia/Katmandu (the computer's); also timers and backup schedules
  readers   read while a long trigger or CALL writes (--reader-yield on); idle open transaction rolled back after 30 s (default)
  memory    26.95 GB for the whole process (85% of the machine's memory); table data 512.0 MB of it (--memory)
  cpu       32 CPUs (the machine's); 16 query threads (half of the CPUs, follows the limit), limits checked every 10 s
  limits    statement timeout 1 min, result memory 1.00 GB, 5000000 groups, 32 statements per user
  safety    writes allowed; DROP TABLE kept 7 days (UNDROP TABLE); audit log on (SHOW AUDIT)
  logs      slow queries >= 1000 ms to ./kdb-data/_logs/slow_queries.jsonl; pg_stat_statements on; metrics at /metrics
  recovery  the default database is created when it is first used

Press Ctrl+C to stop.
```

<a id="open"></a>

## Open the console

Syntax:

```sql
kareladb serve [<database folder>] [--data-dir <folder>] [--port 9900] [--bind 127.0.0.1] [--backups <folder>] [--token <secret>]
http://127.0.0.1:9900/
```

| Server started as | What the console shows |
|---|---|
| `kareladb serve` or `kareladb serve --data-dir <folder>` | every database of the data folder; **New database** is there |
| `kareladb serve D:\kdb\market` (one folder) | just that database; no **New database** |
| with a data folder (or `--backups <folder>`) | **Backup now** and **Restore a backup** work |
| with `--token <secret>` | a box that asks for the token once |
| on a data folder with users | a **Log in** form |

- Keep the server window open while you use the console. Stop the server with **Ctrl+C**.
- From another computer, do not open the port to the network: use an SSH tunnel (`ssh -L 9900:127.0.0.1:9900 you@server`) and open `http://127.0.0.1:9900` on your own PC ([server security](server-security.md)).
- The page only loads files from the KarelaDB server itself (its `Content-Security-Policy` says so), and it cannot be put inside another site's page.
- The console files are read from the `web` folder when the browser asks for them. When that folder is missing, the server still runs and the API works; the page at `/` says the console is not installed and lists the folders KarelaDB looked in. The banner of `kareladb serve` says so too.
- Copying a new console into the folder shows at the next page load, with no restart. The browser keeps its copy only until the file changes (the server answers `304 Not Modified` while it is the same).

**HTTP: The console page is there (HEAD: only the headers)**

```http
HEAD /
```

Response:

HTTP 200 (text/html)

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| Top bar | the **Home** menu, the database picker, **New database**, folder and version, the logged-in user and **Log out**, the connection state, **Help**, the theme button |
| Left side | one tab each for [Tables, Views, Triggers, Procedures, Functions and Timers](#tables) |
| Editor | where you write SQL, with the **Run**, **Run all**, **History** buttons and the **Rows** limit |
| Results | one tab per statement; each result as a **Grid** or a **Chart**; **Export CSV** |
| Terminal | a live log of what the server does ([terminal](#terminal)); shown and hidden with the **Terminal** button |
| Right side | buttons that open the [Monitor, Health, Samples, Databases and Tools panels](#right-side) |
| Status bar | rows, times, and the server's clock |

The lines between the editor, the results and the terminal can be dragged; the console remembers the sizes.

<a id="editor"></a>

## Editor

Write SQL here. Keywords, text and numbers get colors, and lines have numbers.

| Button or key | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Run** or `Ctrl+Enter` | Runs the statement under the cursor. When text is selected, runs only the selection. |
| **Run all** or `Ctrl+Shift+Enter` | Runs everything in the editor |
| **Rows** | The most rows each statement gives back: 1,000, 10,000 (default), 100,000 or 1,000,000 |
| `Tab` | Puts in two spaces |

- Statements are split at `;`. "The statement under the cursor" is the text between the `;` before and after the cursor.
- The editor text is kept in your browser, so it is still there next time.
- With many statements, each result gets a **tab** (`1 SELECT ...`, `2 ...`).
- When a statement fails, a red **error bar** shows the message. Its position (`line 2, column 8`) is counted in **your editor**, the line number turns red, and clicking the position moves the cursor there. The statements before the error ran and are kept: the error tab says `Before it: 1 statement(s) ran and are kept`.
- Statements like `INSERT` show their message (`3 row(s) inserted`) and the rows affected.
- After `CREATE`, `DROP`, `ALTER` or `RENAME`, the table list reloads by itself. After `USE name;` the database picker switches to that database.
- Ready statements to start with, with **Insert** and **Run** buttons, are in the **Samples** panel on the right. It opens by itself on your first visit.

The console runs each statement with [POST /exec](http-exec.md#post-exec)`?compat=0&limit=<Rows>`.

<a id="history"></a>

## History

**History** lists the last 50 statements you ran, newest first, with the time. Click one to put it back at the end of the editor.

- The history is kept only in this browser.
- Passwords are never kept: `PASSWORD 'secret'` and the text in `password_hash('...')` and `password_verify('...')` are saved as `'***'`.
- `Escape` closes the list.

<a id="grid"></a>

## Results grid

The grid shows the rows of one result.

| Action | What it does |
|---|---|
| Click a column header | Sort: small to big, then big to small, then back to the first order (sorting uses the rows already loaded) |
| Drag the right edge of a header | Change the column width |
| Click a cell | Select it |
| `Ctrl+C`, or double-click a cell | Copy its value |
| Hover over long text | See all of it |

- The header shows the column's name and type (`DOUBLE`, `TIMESTAMP`, ...). Numbers are right-aligned.
- NULL shows as `null`. Times are UTC, as the API sends them.
- When the result was cut by the **Rows** limit, the bar says `Row limit reached: showing the first N rows.`
- The grid draws only the rows you can see, so it stays fast with a million rows.

<a id="chart"></a>

## Chart

Click **Chart** above a result. The console looks at the columns and picks the chart that fits best: **candles** for `time, open, high, low, close` (with volume bars when there is a `volume` column), a **line** for a time column with numbers, a **bar** chart for a text column with numbers, and so on. The button is off when no chart fits (a chart needs at least one number column).

The bar above the chart:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| Chart type list | Choose another chart. Types that do not fit the columns are greyed out and say what they need. |
| **Columns** | Choose which column is the time or category, the values, the series (one line per value of a text column), and "One chart per" |
| Symbol list | When a text column has several values (many symbols), the chart shows one of them; pick it here |
| **Indicators** | (time charts) Add SMA, EMA, Bollinger bands, RSI, MACD or stochastic, and set their periods |
| **Log** | A logarithmic value scale (values must be above 0) |
| **No gaps** | (time charts) Leave out time without rows (nights, weekends, holidays), so every row has the same width |
| Legend | Click a name to hide or show that series |
| **Reset**, **PNG**, **CSV**, **Full screen** | Reset the zoom; save the chart as a picture; save the chart's rows as a CSV file (from the browser, no new query); fill the whole screen |
| **Add to dashboard** | Put this statement and this chart on a [dashboard](console-dashboards.md) as a new panel |

Chart types:

| Group | Types |
|---|---|
| Price | Candlestick, OHLC bars |
| Time | Line, Step line, Area, Stacked area |
| Compare | Bar (vertical), Bar (horizontal), Grouped bar, Stacked bar |
| Spread | Histogram, Box plot, Scatter, Bubble |
| Share | Pie, Donut, Treemap |
| Heatmap | Calendar heatmap, Matrix heatmap |
| Number | KPI number, Gauge |
| Table | A table with green/red change columns, color scales and a sparkline (a small price line) per row |

| Mouse or key (on the chart) | What it does |
|---|---|
| Mouse wheel, or `+` and `-` | Zoom in and out |
| Drag, or `Shift` + arrow keys | Move |
| Double-click, `Home` or `0` | Reset the zoom |
| Move the mouse, or arrow keys | A crosshair and a tooltip with the values of that row |
| Two fingers (touch screen) | Pinch to zoom |
| `F` | Full screen; `Esc` leaves it |

- Times on the chart are in **your computer's time zone** (for example Nepal time on a PC set to Nepal). The grid shows UTC.
- Big price series (100,000 bars) still zoom and move smoothly.
- The console remembers your chart settings for each statement, and whether you last used Grid or Chart.
- The chart follows the dark or light theme.

**Example: A good query for candles** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT time, open, high, low, close, volume
FROM ochl_day
WHERE symbol = 'CITY'
ORDER BY time;
```

Result:

| time (TIMESTAMP) | open (DOUBLE) | high (DOUBLE) | low (DOUBLE) | close (DOUBLE) | volume (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-12-28T00:00:00.000Z | 540.3 | 542.5 | 539.2 | 542.2 | 85290 |
| 2025-12-29T00:00:00.000Z | 540.6 | 542.1 | 538.8 | 539.7 | 52010 |
| 2025-12-30T00:00:00.000Z | 538.5 | 540.5 | 536.4 | 539.3 | 95460 |
| 2025-12-31T00:00:00.000Z | 540.4 | 546.2 | 538.9 | 542.4 | 22330 |
| 2026-08-23T00:00:00.000Z | 505 | 508.4 | 502 | 507.9 | 125050 |

(first 5 of 19 rows)

<a id="dashboards"></a>

## Charts and dashboards

A chart you like can go on a **dashboard**: a page of several charts, each from its own query, that refresh by themselves. Click **Add to dashboard** on the chart bar, pick a dashboard (or **A new dashboard**) and give the panel a title. The dashboard opens with the new panel; click **Save** there to keep it. The dashboard page is explained in [dashboards](console-dashboards.md).

**Example: Rows for a bar chart: shares traded per symbol** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT symbol, sum(quantity) AS shares
FROM trade_log
GROUP BY symbol
ORDER BY shares DESC;
```

Result:

| symbol (SYMBOL) | shares (LONG) |
|---|---|
| COAST | 3070 |
| TELCO | 2770 |
| CITY | 2420 |
| VOLT | 400 |

(4 rows)

<a id="export-csv"></a>

## Export CSV

**Export CSV** downloads all rows of the shown result as a CSV file.

- It runs the statement **again** on the server with [GET /exp](http-exec.md#get-exp) (up to 1,000,000 rows, not only the rows in the grid). So it is offered only for `SELECT`, `SHOW` and `EXPLAIN`.
- The file name comes from the table after `FROM`, for example `ochl_day.csv` (else `kdb-export.csv`).
- Times are UTC. NULL is an empty field.

<a id="tables"></a>

## Object list

The left side lists the objects of the chosen database, one tab for each kind: **Tables**, **Views**, **Triggers**, **Procedures**, **Functions** and **Timers**. Each tab shows how many there are. The console remembers the tab you picked.

- **Indexes** are in the Tables tab, under the tables. Click **Indexes** to close or open that group.
- Click the small arrow of a view, trigger, procedure or function to see its statement. **Open in editor** puts the statement into the editor.
- A procedure or function also has **Run on a timer...**: it opens the [timer form](#timers) with `CALL name(...)` or `SELECT name(...)` filled in.

**Folders.** A database with many objects can be tidied into folders: **+ Folder** at the top of a tab makes one, and you drag a table, view, trigger, procedure or function onto it. A folder exists in every tab, so `floorsheet` can hold the floor-sheet tables in the Tables tab and the floor-sheet procedures in the Procedures tab. Hover a folder's heading to rename (✎) or remove (×) it; removing a folder only puts its objects back in the plain list. Folders change nothing but this list: no name, statement or query is affected. They are saved in the table `_console_groups` of the database, so every browser sees the same folders; the first folder creates that table, which needs the admin role, and dragging needs the write role.

**Tables**

| Mark | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `TS` badge | a time-series table (with its partition: `DAY`, `MONTH`, `YEAR`) |
| `REL` badge | a relational table |
| `TS` on a column | the table's time column |
| `PK` | primary key |
| `FK` | `REFERENCES` another table (hover to see which) |
| `FX` | a computed column |

| Action | What it does |
|---|---|
| Click the small arrow | Show the columns and their types |
| Click a table or column name | Put the name into the editor at the cursor |
| Double-click a table name | Run `SHOW COLUMNS FROM <table>` |
| **Refresh** | Reload the object lists and the health panel |

The list comes from [GET /api/info](http-server-info.md#get-api-info). It also reloads every 30 seconds while the page is visible.

<a id="timers"></a>

## Timers

A **timer** runs SQL by itself on a schedule, for example `CALL refresh_prices();` every 5 minutes, so a table stays up to date without anybody running anything. The server runs it, so it goes on when no browser is open. Full details: [timers](timers.md).

| In the Timers tab | What it does |
|---|---|
| **New timer** | A form: name, schedule, the SQL, and whether it is turned on. **Run** picks a procedure or function of this database. |
| **Keep data for...** | Pick time-series tables and how long they keep their rows. It sets a TTL, or makes a monthly timer that drops old partitions. The [Keep data page](console-keep-data.md) does the same for one table at a time. |
| **Reload** | Reads the list again (it also refreshes by itself while the tab is open) |
| The dot before a name | green: the last run worked; red: it failed; blue: running now; dashed: turned off |
| Click the arrow | Next run, last run, how long it took, rows, the error, and how many runs |
| **Run now** | Runs it once now, whatever the schedule says |
| **Turn off** / **Turn on** | Stops or starts running it on the schedule |
| **Edit**, **Delete** | Change the schedule or the SQL; delete the timer (the procedure stays) |

Schedules: `every 30s`, `every 5m`, `every 2h`, `hourly`, `hourly :15`, `daily 16:00`, `daily 02:00,13:30`, `weekdays 11:00`, `monthly 1 02:00`. The form offers the common ones as quick picks. Times are the server computer's local time.

- A run that is still going when the next one is due is skipped, never started twice.
- A timer belongs to the database chosen at the top, and runs with the rights of the user who saved it.
- Any user who may read the database sees its timers. Saving, changing, deleting and **Run now** need the `admin` role on that database, and each of them is written to the [audit log](audit-log.md).

<a id="right-side"></a>

## Right side: Monitor, Health, Samples, Databases

The buttons down the right side open a **panel** over the page. The same button closes it again; so do the **x** and `Esc`.

| Button | The panel |
|---|---|
| **Monitor** | memory, processor, caches and the statements running now ([Monitor](console-monitor.md)) |
| **Health** | damaged files, backups, **Check now** and **Backup now** ([health](#health-box)); the button gets a red dot while a file is damaged |
| **Samples** | ready statements with **Insert** and **Run** |
| **Databases** | every database with its tables, size, folder and old log (`wal_archive`: its limit, whether it is its own or the server default, and the size on disk); click one to use it; **New database**; **Old log** sets a database's own limit, **Off**, or the server default again ([SET WAL_ARCHIVE](databases.md#wal-archive)); **Delete** |
| **Tools** | **Purge trash** frees disk space in the whole data folder ([PURGE TRASH ALL](databases.md#purge-trash)); **Delete all data** empties every table of the chosen database after you type its name ([TRUNCATE ALL TABLES](databases.md#truncate-all-tables)) |
| **Terminal** | not a panel: shows or hides the [terminal](#terminal) at the bottom of Home |

- A panel floats over the page and closes when you click somewhere else. The **pin** button keeps it open beside the page instead.
- Drag its left edge to make it wider. Double-click the edge for the normal width.
- The console remembers the open panel, the pin and the widths.

<a id="terminal"></a>

## Terminal

The **terminal** at the bottom of Home is a live log of what the server does: every statement, write, timer run, login and backup, as it happens. It shows where the data comes from, for example a program on the PostgreSQL port or a timer.

```text
14:19:02.114  PG     10.0.0.5 app    market   3 ms       1 row  SELECT price FROM ochl_day WHERE ...
14:19:02.530  HTTP   10.0.0.9        market  12 ms  12,000 rows  12,000 rows into trade_log (line protocol)
14:20:00.004  TIMER  refresh_prices  market  41 ms    350 rows  CALL refresh_prices();
```

| Column or control | What it is |
|---|---|
| Time | when it finished, with milliseconds, in your computer's time zone |
| Source | `HTTP` (statements, `/write` and CSV imports), `PG` (PostgreSQL port), `TIMER`, `BACKUP` (a scheduled backup), `DEFERRED` (a job of a [deferred trigger](triggers.md)), or the kind, such as `LOGIN` |
| From | the address of the program, and the user |
| Database, time, rows | where it ran, how long it took, how many rows |
| **All**, **Queries**, **Writes**, **Timers**, **Errors** | show only that kind of line |
| **This database** | only lines of the database chosen at the top |
| Filter text | only lines with that text |
| **Pause**, **Clear**, **x** | stop adding lines, empty the list, hide the terminal |

- The terminal is hidden when the page opens. It shows up by itself when you **Run** a statement, and the **Terminal** button shows or hides it any time.
- Click a line to see all of its text; double-click a statement to put it into the editor. Failed lines are red.
- While the terminal is hidden, the **Terminal** button counts the new lines.
- The console's own background reads (the lists on the left, the monitor) are not logged, so they do not fill it.
- Users who are not admins see only their own lines.

<a id="health-box"></a>

## Health panel

| Line | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `OK - no damaged files` (green) or `DAMAGED (n)` (red) | files KarelaDB knows are damaged, with their names |
| **Last backup** | how long ago (`just now`, `3 h ago`), `never`, or `no backup folder`; `(copy failed)` when the [copy command](backup-schedule.md#backup-command) failed. Hover it for the folder, the schedule and the last copy. |
| **Data** | size and number of the data files |
| **Log LSN** | the number of the last change in the log; it grows with every change |
| **Opened** | when the server opened the database |
| **Recovery at open** | what KarelaDB did when it opened the database (it opens by itself when something was wrong) |
| **Check now** | reads every block of every file and the log ([POST /api/check](http-server-info.md#post-api-check)). Example message: `OK: 11 files (76.1 KB) and 1 log segments read in 1.50 ms. No damage.` |
| **Backup now** | makes a verified backup ([POST /api/backup](http-server-info.md#post-api-backup)). Example message: `Backup 20260911-083519-806 created and verified: 9 files, 222.3 KB.` The button is off when backups are off (`--backups off`). |
| **Restore a backup** | opens a small form: the backups of this database, how far back a restore **up to** a time can go ([the window](backup-and-safety.md#pitr-window)), a time (empty = the backup as it was) and a **new** name. **Restore** makes the new database while this one keeps running ([POST /api/restore](http-server-info.md#api-restore)). Then **Swap ... in** gives this database the restored data and the new one the old data ([swap](http-server-info.md#api-swap)); it asks first. |

If **Check now** finds damage: stop the server and run `kareladb repair` ([backup and safety](backup-and-safety.md)).

<a id="databases"></a>

## Database picker and New database

- The **Database** list at the top shows the databases of the server. Everything on the page uses the chosen one: the editor, the object lists, the health panel, timers and backups. The console adds `db=<name>` to each request.
- The **Databases** panel on the right shows the same databases with their tables, size and folder. Click one to use it.
- The browser remembers the choice. When that database is gone, the console uses the server's default database.
- **New database** asks for a name (letters, digits, `_` and `-`, at most 64; `_trash` and Windows device names like `con` are not allowed). The new, empty database is chosen right away. It uses [POST /api/databases](http-databases.md#post-api-databases).
- `USE demo;`, `CREATE DATABASE x;` and `DROP DATABASE x;` in the editor also update the list. Dropping the chosen database moves the console back to the default database. A dropped database's folder moves to `_trash`.
- With users, the list shows only the databases you may read, and **New database** only for a user with ROLE `admin`.

<a id="login"></a>

## Login form and token box

**Users.** When the data folder has users, the console shows **Log in**. Type the user name and password.

- After the login, the top bar shows the user and role, for example `boss (admin)`, and a **Log out** button.
- The login is kept in a cookie that scripts cannot read (`HttpOnly`) and that works only on this site (`SameSite=Strict`). It ends after 12 hours, at **Log out**, when the server restarts, or when the password changes.
- A wrong password keeps the form open with `Wrong user name or password.` After 5 wrong tries, wait a moment.
- Each statement runs with your role. A refused one shows the error, for example `INSERT needs role write on database 'shop'; user 'report' has read`.

**Token.** On a server started with `--token`, the console shows **Access token required**. Type the token once.

- The server keeps it in a cookie that scripts cannot read (`HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict`). CSV downloads work with it too.
- **Remember on this computer for 30 days** is on at first. Clear it and the browser forgets the token when it closes.
- **Log out** at the top makes this browser forget the token.
- A token an older console kept in the browser's storage is moved into the cookie once, then deleted there.
- The console sends the `X-KDB-CSRF` header with every change by itself ([CSRF](http-login.md#csrf)).

The connection state at the top says `Connected`, `Offline` (the server does not answer), `Token required` or `Login required`. More: [logins and tokens](http-login.md).

<a id="theme"></a>

## Theme

The button at the top right switches between the **dark** theme (the default) and the **light** theme. The browser remembers the choice. The help panel and charts follow the theme.

<a id="help-menu"></a>

## Help menu

The **Help** button in the top bar opens a menu:

| Item | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Documentation** | Opens this help in a panel on the right side of the console. Drag its left edge to make it wider; **Open in new tab** shows it as a full page; **Close** or `Esc` closes it. |
| **Help for word under cursor** (`F1`) | Opens the help for the keyword or function at the cursor in the editor: on `round(` it opens the function `round`, on `ORDER` in `ORDER BY` it opens `ORDER BY`. Inside a text `'...'` or a `--` comment, it opens the help's start page. |
| **Examples...** | A list of the ready examples of this help, with a search box and a preview. **Insert into editor** puts the chosen example (with the tables it needs) at the end of the editor; then press `Ctrl+Enter`. **Open in help** shows it in the help. |
| **Keyboard shortcuts** | The table below |
| **Comments and suggestions** | A form to send a comment, a problem or an idea to whoever runs this server. An admin also sees the messages sent so far and marks them read or done ([feedback](feedback.md)). |
| **About KarelaDB** | The version, the database and its folder, the data folder, number of tables, the backup folder, how you are logged in, the help's version, and the server address |

- In the help panel, every SQL example has **Insert into editor**, which puts that SQL (with its setup) into the console editor.
- The help comes from [GET /help/](http-overview.md#get-help): a folder of pages next to the kareladb program, not inside it. When no help folder is installed, the panel says so and how to build it.
- The menu works with the keyboard: `Arrow down` opens it, arrows move, `Enter` chooses, `Esc` closes.

<a id="shortcuts"></a>

## Keyboard shortcuts

| Keys | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Ctrl+Enter` | Run the statement under the cursor (or the selected text) |
| `Ctrl+Shift+Enter` | Run every statement in the editor |
| `Tab` | Put two spaces in the editor |
| `F1` | Help for the keyword or function under the cursor |
| `Ctrl+C` (in the grid) | Copy the selected cell |
| Double-click a cell | Copy that cell |
| `Esc` | Close a menu, the History list, a dialog or the help panel |
| `/` (in the help) | Jump to the help's search box |

On a Mac, use `Cmd` instead of `Ctrl`.

<a id="sql-link"></a>

## Open the console with SQL in the editor

Syntax:

```sql
http://127.0.0.1:9900/#sql=<URL-encoded SQL>
```

A link of this form opens the console and puts the SQL at the end of the editor, selected, ready for `Ctrl+Enter`. It does **not** run the SQL by itself.

- **URL-encoded** means special characters are written as `%` codes: a space is `%20`, a `'` is `%27`, a `,` is `%2C`. JavaScript's `encodeURIComponent`, Python's `urllib.parse.quote` and PowerShell's `[uri]::EscapeDataString` do it.
- The `#sql=...` part is removed from the address after it is read, so reloading the page does not add the SQL again.
- The **Try in console** button of examples in this help (when the help is opened as a page, not inside the console) uses such a link.
- The part after `#` never goes to the server, so the SQL does not appear in server logs.

```text
http://127.0.0.1:9900/#sql=SELECT%20symbol%2C%20close%20FROM%20ochl_day%20WHERE%20symbol%20%3D%20%27CITY%27%20LIMIT%205
```

```powershell
$sql = "SELECT symbol, close FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = 'CITY' LIMIT 5"
Start-Process ("http://127.0.0.1:9900/#sql=" + [uri]::EscapeDataString($sql))
```

```python
import urllib.parse, webbrowser
sql = "SELECT symbol, close FROM ochl_day WHERE symbol = 'CITY' LIMIT 5"
webbrowser.open("http://127.0.0.1:9900/#sql=" + urllib.parse.quote(sql, safe=""))
```

# Dashboard page (many charts on one page)

> Put many charts on one page, each from its own query, with pickers such as $symbol at the top and an automatic refresh. Dashboards are saved in the database.

- Category: Web console
- Keywords: dashboard, dashboards, Dashboard page, panel, chart panel, text note, Add panel, Add to dashboard, Edit, Variables, $symbol, $from, variable, picker, Auto refresh, refresh, Save, \_dashboards, Export JSON, Import JSON, Copy JSON, Duplicate, example dashboards, Market overview, Stock view, Portfolio, today-30d
- See also: [Web console](web-console.md), [View data page (browse and edit rows)](console-data-page.md), [Monitor panel (memory, processor, caches)](console-monitor.md), [SELECT](select.md), [Users and roles](users-and-roles.md)

The **Dashboard** page of the [web console](web-console.md) (Home menu) shows many charts on one page. Each chart is a **panel**: one `SELECT` and the chart settings for it. The panels refresh by themselves, and pickers at the top (a symbol, a date range) change every panel at once.

- A dashboard belongs to the database chosen at the top. It is saved in the table `_dashboards` of that database, so backups keep it and roles apply.
- The list always holds three **example** dashboards: **Market overview**, **Stock view** and **Portfolio**. They are made for the [sample data](sample-data.md). **Save** on an example makes your own copy.
- A panel only reads: it runs its SQL with `GET /exec`, which refuses statements that change data. Each panel reads at most 10,000 rows; **Rows** in its editor picks 100, 1,000, 10,000 or 100,000.

<a id="screen"></a>

## The screen

```text
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| [Stock view v] [Stock view        ]          Auto refresh [30 s v] Refresh Edit Add panel Variables Save More |
| Symbol [CITY v]   From [2025-09-23]   To [2026-09-23]                                        |
| +------------------------------------------------------------+                              |
| | Candles, volume, RSI and MACD                          ... |                              |
| |  (chart)                                                   |                              |
| +------------------------------------------------------------+                              |
| +------------------+ +---------------------------------------+                              |
| | Last close   ... | | Daily move % (calendar)           ... |                              |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| Dashboard list | Opens another dashboard: yours, then the examples |
| Title box | The dashboard's name |
| **Auto refresh** | Runs every panel again every 5 s, 10 s, 30 s, 1 min, 5 min or 15 min, or **Off** |
| **Refresh** | Runs every panel again now |
| **Edit** | Turns on moving and resizing panels |
| **Add panel** | Opens the panel editor for a new panel |
| **Variables** | The pickers at the top ([variables](#variables)) |
| **Save** | Writes the dashboard to `_dashboards` |
| **More** | **New dashboard**, **Duplicate**, **Export JSON file**, **Copy JSON**, **Import JSON**, **Delete** |

The panels sit on a grid of 12 columns. In **Edit** mode, drag a panel by its move handle, or drag its bottom right corner to resize it. With the keyboard: arrow keys move it, `Shift` + arrow keys resize it.

<a id="panels"></a>

## Panels

Each panel has a **...** menu:

| Item | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Edit** | Opens the panel editor |
| **Refresh** | Runs this panel again |
| **Open SQL in editor** | Puts the panel's SQL, with the variables filled in, into the SQL editor on Home |
| **Save PNG**, **Save CSV** | The chart as a picture, or its rows as a CSV file |
| **Full screen**, **Reset zoom** | As on the [chart](web-console.md#chart) of the SQL editor |
| **Duplicate** | A copy of the panel |
| **Remove** | Takes the panel off (in **Edit** mode only) |

The panel editor has a title, a kind and, for a chart, the SQL. **Chart from SQL** is one `SELECT` and a chart; **Text note** is a few lines of text, for example how to use the dashboard. **Run preview** (or `Ctrl+Enter`) runs the SQL and shows the chart, with the same chart types and settings as the SQL editor.

The quickest way to make a panel: run a query on Home, pick a chart, and click **Add to dashboard** on the chart bar.

**Example: A good panel query: one symbol, a time range** (sample data: sample)

```sql
SELECT time, open, high, low, close, volume
FROM ochl_day
WHERE symbol = 'CITY'
ORDER BY time;
```

Result:

| time (TIMESTAMP) | open (DOUBLE) | high (DOUBLE) | low (DOUBLE) | close (DOUBLE) | volume (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-12-28T00:00:00.000Z | 540.3 | 542.5 | 539.2 | 542.2 | 85290 |
| 2025-12-29T00:00:00.000Z | 540.6 | 542.1 | 538.8 | 539.7 | 52010 |
| 2025-12-30T00:00:00.000Z | 538.5 | 540.5 | 536.4 | 539.3 | 95460 |
| 2025-12-31T00:00:00.000Z | 540.4 | 546.2 | 538.9 | 542.4 | 22330 |
| 2026-08-23T00:00:00.000Z | 505 | 508.4 | 502 | 507.9 | 125050 |

(first 5 of 19 rows)

<a id="variables"></a>

## Variables

A **variable** is a picker at the top of the dashboard. Write `$name` (or `${name}`) in a panel's SQL and the picker's value goes there. **Variables** opens the list: a name, a label, a type and a default value.

| Type | The picker | Goes into the SQL as |
|---|---|---|
| Text | a text box | a quoted text: `'CITY'` |
| List of values | a list of values you type (`CITY, COAST, VOLT`) | a quoted text |
| Values from SQL | a list filled by a query (`SELECT DISTINCT symbol FROM ochl_day ORDER BY symbol`) | a quoted text |
| Number | a number box | the number |
| Date | a date box; the default may be `today`, `today-30d`, `today-1y` | a quoted date: `'2026-09-11'` |
| Table or column name | a text box | the name as it is (letters, digits and `_` only) |
| Interval | a text box: `1d`, `15m`, `1M` | as it is, for `SAMPLE BY $step` |

- Text is always quoted, and a `'` in it is doubled, so a picker can never change what the statement does.
- A list can allow **several** values; they go in as `'CITY', 'COAST'`, for `WHERE symbol IN ($symbols)`.
- `$name` inside a quoted text or a comment is left alone.
- A value that does not fit its type (a word in a number box) stops the panel with a message; nothing is sent.

**Example: What a panel with $symbol, $from and $to runs** (sample data: sample)

```sql
-- The panel SQL:  ... WHERE symbol = $symbol AND time >= $from AND time < $to
SELECT time, close
FROM ochl_day
WHERE symbol = 'CITY' AND time >= '2025-01-01' AND time < '2026-01-01'
ORDER BY time;
```

Result:

| time (TIMESTAMP) | close (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|
| 2025-12-28T00:00:00.000Z | 542.2 |
| 2025-12-29T00:00:00.000Z | 539.7 |
| 2025-12-30T00:00:00.000Z | 539.3 |
| 2025-12-31T00:00:00.000Z | 542.4 |

(4 rows)

<a id="save"></a>

## Saving, and who may do what

| Role on the database | Can |
|---|---|
| `read` | open and look at dashboards; export them as JSON |
| `write` | also save, change and delete them |
| `admin` | also save the **first** dashboard, which creates the table `_dashboards` |

- The first **Save** in a database runs `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS _dashboards (...)`. That needs the `admin` role. A `write` user who is first is asked to let an admin save one dashboard first, or to use **More > Export JSON file**.
- A changed dashboard says `Changed, not saved` next to its title. Opening another one first asks whether to drop the changes.
- **Export JSON file** and **Import JSON** move a dashboard to another database or another server. An imported dashboard opens at once; **Save** keeps it.

**Example: The table the first Save creates**

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS _dashboards (id STRING PRIMARY KEY, title STRING NOT NULL, body STRING NOT NULL, updated TIMESTAMP, updated_by STRING);
SHOW COLUMNS FROM _dashboards;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS _dashboards (`

```text
table '_dashboards' created
```

`SHOW COLUMNS FROM _dashboards`

| name (STRING) | type (STRING) | primary_key (BOOL) | not_null (BOOL) | computed (BOOL) | references (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| id | STRING | true | false | false | NULL |
| title | STRING | false | true | false | NULL |
| body | STRING | false | true | false | NULL |
| updated | TIMESTAMP | false | false | false | NULL |
| updated_by | STRING | false | false | false | NULL |

(5 rows)

<!-- docs/console-data-page.md -->

# View data page (browse and edit rows)

> Look at the rows of a table in the console and change them with forms - add, edit and delete - without writing SQL.

- Category: Web console
- Keywords: data page, View data, browse, browser, table browser, edit row, change row, add row, insert row, delete row, new table, phpMyAdmin, WHERE filter, paging, per page, sort column, primary key, read-only, time-series, no primary key, Open in SQL
- See also: [Web console](web-console.md), [Settings page (data folder, old log, capacity, program files and users)](console-settings.md), [Monitor panel (memory, processor, caches)](console-monitor.md), [INSERT](insert.md), [UPDATE and DELETE](update-delete.md), [Constraints](constraints.md), [CREATE TABLE](create-table.md), [Table rights - GRANT ON TABLE](table-rights.md)

The **View data** page of the [web console](web-console.md) (Home menu) shows the tables of the chosen database and the rows inside them. You can add, change and delete rows with a form instead of writing [INSERT](insert.md), [UPDATE and DELETE](update-delete.md) by hand.

Everything it does goes through `/exec`, so a user may only do what their [role](users-and-roles.md) allows: a `read` user sees the rows and no buttons, a `write` user may change them, and an `admin` may also make tables.

<a id="screen"></a>

## The screen

```text
+--------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| TABLES             | trades  timeseries - by DAY          [Add row] [Open in SQL] [Refresh]  |
| [Find a table   ]  | WHERE [ qty > 10                          ] [Apply] [Filter columns...] |
|  trades    69.3M   |      | date       | symbol   | broker   | qty  | rate   |               |
|  items         5   |      | [(all)  v] | [CITY v] | [(all) v]| LONG | DOUBLE |               |
|                    |      | 2026-09-11 | CITY     | 58       |  100 | 512.40 |               |
|                    |      | 2026-09-11 | CITY     | 12       |   50 | 512.00 |               |
| [New table]        | Rows 1-50 of 4,112   < 1 2 3 ... 83 > Last     Per page [50 v]         |
+--------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| Left list | every table of the database, with its row count. Type in the box to find one. |
| **New table** | a small form for `CREATE TABLE`; it shows the statement it will run before it runs it (admins only) |
| **WHERE** box | an extra condition, exactly as you would write it in SQL. Press Enter or **Apply**. |
| **Filter columns...** | tick the columns that get a list of their values in the heading (symbol, date, broker ...). Pick a value from a list to see only its rows; several lists combine. The list holds each different value once, newest first for a time column, at most 500. |
| Column heads | click one to sort the **whole table** by it (not only the page); click again for the other direction. A time-series table opens newest first. |
| **Edit** / **Delete** | change or remove that one row |
| **Add row** | a form with one box per column |
| **Open in SQL** | puts the `SELECT` this page is showing into the Home page ([SQL editor](web-console.md#editor)), to change it by hand |
| Pager | page numbers, `<` `>` and **Last**; 25 to 500 rows a page; how many rows the filters found |

The page remembers the table you were looking at, the rows-per-page and each table's filter columns, so coming back opens where you left off. A value list is one `SELECT DISTINCT` per column, read once per table (and again on **Refresh**): on a table of many million rows it takes a moment, and the rows show first.

<a id="editable"></a>

## Which tables can be edited

To change or delete **one** row, KarelaDB has to be able to name that row on its own. That is what a [`PRIMARY KEY`](constraints.md#primary-key) is for.

| Table | Browse | Add a row | Edit or delete one row |
|---|---|---|---|
| relational, with `PRIMARY KEY` | yes | yes | **yes** |
| relational, without a key | yes | yes | no |
| time-series (`TIMESERIES(...)`) | yes | yes | no |

A [time-series table](create-table.md) has a `DEDUP KEY`, not a primary key, and the same key may appear more than once. A form that edited "the row" could quietly change several, so the page does not offer it and says why instead. Use the SQL editor on Home with a `WHERE` you have checked, and run the matching `SELECT` first to see what it will hit.

- The primary key column itself cannot be changed in the edit form: it is the name the row is found by. Delete the row and add a new one to change a key.
- A `PRIMARY KEY AUTO` column is left out of the add form; the server hands the value out.
- Computed columns are left out too: the engine works them out.

<a id="sql"></a>

## What it sends

Nothing is hidden. Each button sends one ordinary statement:

| Button | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Add row** | `INSERT INTO items (name, qty) VALUES ('bolt', 12)` |
| **Save** (edit) | `UPDATE items SET qty = 137 WHERE id = 2` |
| **Delete** | `DELETE FROM items WHERE id = 2` |
| **New table** | the `CREATE TABLE` shown in the form |

- Only the boxes you actually changed go into the `SET` list.
- An empty box means `NULL`.
- Text is quoted and `'` inside it is doubled. A number box that does not hold a number is refused before anything is sent, with a message that says which column.
- Anything the server refuses (a `NOT NULL` column left empty, a `CHECK` that fails, a missing `REFERENCES` row, a role that is too weak) is shown as it came back, so the reason is the server's own.

**Example: A table the View data page can fully edit**

```sql
CREATE TABLE items (
  id     INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO,
  name   STRING NOT NULL,
  qty    INT,
  price  DOUBLE
);
INSERT INTO items (name, qty, price) VALUES ('bolt', 12, 0.45), ('nut', 40, 0.12);
SELECT * FROM items;
```

Result:

`CREATE TABLE items (`

```text
table 'items' created
```

`INSERT INTO items (name, qty, price) VALUES ('bolt', 12, 0.45), ('nut', 40, 0.12)`

```text
2 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT * FROM items`

| id (INT) | name (STRING) | qty (INT) | price (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | bolt | 12 | 0.45 |
| 2 | nut | 40 | 0.12 |

(2 rows)

<a id="notes"></a>

## Notes

- The row count under the pager is a real `SELECT count(*)` with the same filter, so it is the true number, not an estimate.
- Big values are cut off in the grid; the full text is in the cell's tooltip. For the whole value use the SQL editor on Home.
- The page reads at most one page of rows at a time, so opening a table with millions of rows costs the same as opening a small one.
- Rights per table ([table rights](table-rights.md)) apply here as everywhere else: a table you may not read is not listed.
