<!-- docs/console-keep-data.md -->

# Keep data page (how long tables keep their rows)

> See every table of a database with how long it keeps its rows, and set "keep only the last N months or years": the older days, months or years are dropped, the newest stay.

- Category: Web console
- Keywords: keep data, retention, Save disk, /api/disk, disk usage, older copies, trash, keep the last, keep only, old data, drop old data, TTL, months, years, drop partition older than, disk space, save disk, free space, purge
- See also: [Web console](web-console.md), [ALTER, RENAME and DROP TABLE](alter-table.md), [Timers](timers.md), [Partitions, SORT BY and DEDUP KEY](partitions-and-dedup.md), [Databases and the data folder](databases.md), [View data page (browse and edit rows)](console-data-page.md)

The **Keep data** page of the [web console](web-console.md) (Home menu) lists every table of the chosen database and lets you say how long each keeps its rows. Nothing is dropped from the start of the table: it keeps the **newest** data and lets the oldest go.

<a id="screen"></a>

## The screen

```text
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Keep data   database nchart006                                                [Refresh]  |
| [x] all   For the 3 ticked: keep the last [6] [months v]  [Keep] [Keep everything] [Drop older now] |
|                                                                                          |
|   | table         | kind              | rows   | on disk | data from / to           | keeps           |                              |
| [x]| Daily_Filter  | time-series, DAY  | 11.5M  | 890 MB  | 2022-01-25 to 2026-09-11 | the last 6 months | [6][months v] [Keep] [Drop older now] [Everything] |
| [ ]| floorsheet_v1 | time-series, DAY  | 69.3M  | 5.3 GB  | 2022-01-25 to 2026-09-11 | everything        | [6][months v] [Keep] [Drop older now]              |
| [ ]| bg_config     | relational        | 2      | 4 KB    | no partitions            | everything (no partitions to drop)                                    |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| rows, on disk | the table's row count and the bytes its files take |
| data from / to | the oldest and newest time in the table (read from the block statistics, so it costs nothing) |
| keeps | `everything`, or `the last 6 months`: the table's [TTL](alter-table.md#set-ttl) |
| **Keep** | sets the TTL: `ALTER TABLE t SET TTL 6 MONTHS`. From then on KarelaDB drops, every minute and by itself, every partition whose last moment is older than that |
| **Everything** | takes the TTL off: `ALTER TABLE t SET TTL NONE` |
| **Drop older now** | one drop, now: `ALTER TABLE t DROP PARTITION OLDER THAN 6 MONTHS`. It shows the statement and asks first |
| the top bar | the same three for every ticked table at once (**Keep everything** takes the TTL off them) |
| **Refresh** | reads the tables and the disk box again |

The period is a number and a unit: `days`, `weeks`, `months` or `years`.

- Only time-series tables with `PARTITION BY DAY`, `MONTH` or `YEAR` can keep "the last N": everything else has no partitions to drop, is listed greyed, and keeps everything. Use [DELETE](update-delete.md#delete) there.
- A partition goes when its **last** moment is older than the period, so "the last 6 months" always holds at least 6 full months. Months and years follow the calendar.
- Whole partitions go, never single rows, and a dropped partition cannot be brought back. Every drop is written to the audit log.
- A `read` user sees the page; the buttons need `write`.

<a id="disk"></a>

## Disk space

The box at the top says what the database takes on disk, part by part. It reads [GET /api/disk](http-server-info.md#api-disk), which walks the trash folder, so it is asked for on this page only. Hover a part to see how many files it holds.

| Part | What it is | Field of `/api/disk` |
|---|---|---|
| On disk | everything below together | `total_bytes` |
| data | the current version of every data file: the rows. Of those, [tail files](partitions-and-dedup.md#tail-files) are rows appended after a partition's file, folded back into it later, and [delta files](partitions-and-dedup.md#delta-files) the rows of a partition replaced or deleted | `data_bytes`, `data_files`; tails `tail_bytes`, `tail_files`; deltas `delta_bytes`, `delta_files` |
| older copies | older versions of the data files, kept so a damaged file can be repaired from one of them (2 per file unless `keep_versions` says otherwise; a version whose old log is gone can repair nothing and goes by itself) | `previous_bytes`, `previous_files` |
| trash | replaced files nothing needs any more; the server removes them by itself once they are older than `trash_keep_hours` (1 hour unless set), or when the trash is over `trash_max_mb` (a quarter of the data, at least 256 MB, unless set) | `trash_bytes`, `trash_folders` |
| log | the current log, and old log kept for repairs and backups ([wal_archive](console-settings.md#wal-archive)) | `wal_bytes` + `wal_archive_bytes` |

**Save disk** (admin) runs [PURGE VERSIONS KEEP 1](databases.md#purge-versions), which leaves one older copy per file, then [PURGE TRASH](databases.md#purge-trash), and shows the space that came back. Dropping partitions frees their files the same way: they go to the trash first, and the trash goes on its own.

**Example: What the Keep button runs**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE trades (time TIMESTAMP, symbol SYMBOL, qty LONG) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY MONTH;
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE trades SET TTL 6 MONTHS;
SHOW CREATE TABLE trades;
```

Result:

`ALTER TABLE trades SET TTL 6 MONTHS`

```text
table 'trades' drops partitions older than 6 MONTHS
```

`SHOW CREATE TABLE trades`

| create_sql (STRING) |
|---|
| CREATE TABLE trades (   time TIMESTAMP,   symbol SYMBOL,   qty LONG ) TIMESERIES(time) PARTITION BY MONTH SORT BY (symbol, time) TTL 6 MONTHS |

(1 row)

<!-- docs/console-monitor.md -->

# Monitor panel (memory, processor, caches)

> What the server is doing right now - memory it holds, processor it uses, what each database keeps in memory, deferred trigger queues, and the statements running this second.

- Category: Web console
- Keywords: monitor, timers, timer failures, late timer, Monitor panel, monitoring, memory, RAM, resident, working set, processor, CPU, threads, uptime, running statements, cancel statement, kill query, result cache, cache hits, cached results, memory budget, loaded partitions, pending rows, checkpoint, open cursors, log position, LSN, deferred trigger queue, trigger lag, failed job, /api/stats, activity, activity log, server log, terminal, what the server is doing, GET /api/activity, --activity-log-size, X-KDB-Quiet, slow statements, slow queries, --slow-query-ms, disk use, on disk, trash, metrics
- See also: [Web console](web-console.md), [Settings page (data folder, old log, capacity, program files and users)](console-settings.md), [View data page (browse and edit rows)](console-data-page.md), [Health, info, check and backup over HTTP](http-server-info.md), [Performance tips](performance-tips.md), [Protection - timeouts, limits, safe updates, read-only](protection.md), [kareladb serve](cli-serve.md), [Triggers](triggers.md)

The **Monitor** panel of the [web console](web-console.md) shows the inside of a running `kareladb serve`: how much memory the process holds, how busy the processor is, what each open database keeps in memory, and which statements are running right now. Open it with the **Monitor** button on the [right side](web-console.md#right-side) of the console. It is a panel, not a page: pin it to keep it open beside the page you work on.

It reads [`GET /api/stats`](http-server-info.md#api-stats) every couple of seconds. Everything there is a counter already in memory, so asking often costs almost nothing: no file is read and no database is opened to answer it.

- Any login that may **read** can see the panel. A `read` user sees only their own running statements, because statement text can hold values; an `admin` sees everyone's.
- **Refresh** at the top picks 2, 5, 10 or 30 seconds, or **Off**; **Now** reads the numbers at once. The panel stops asking while it is closed or the browser tab is hidden.
- `/api/stats` holds more than the panel shows, for example the zone map counters (`zone_partition_skips`, `zone_block_skips`), `cache_pinned` and the memory of each database by kind. Read it from a script for those ([GET /api/stats](http-server-info.md#api-stats)).

<a id="opening"></a>

## Warnings and databases opening

At the top, in a yellow frame, the server's `warnings`: today, a database far bigger than `--memory` ([why it matters](cli-serve.md#memory-warning)).

Below them, one card per database being opened right now. A big database replays the log written after its last checkpoint, which over a slow disk takes minutes, and its first request waits that long. The card shows what the open does now (`checking log`, `replaying log`, `loading tables`, ...), for how long, how much of the log is replayed, and how many table files it went through. When the numbers move, the open is working; the card goes away when the database is open.

In a database's card, a **Checkpoint** line shows a checkpoint writing changes to partition files: the table, partitions written of how many, and for how long. **Busy** means a write or a checkpoint held the database when the panel asked: the memory numbers are live, the tables and queues are from the reading before. The panel never waits for a busy database.

<a id="process"></a>

## The server process

| Number | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Memory in RAM** | what the operating system says this process holds now (Windows: working set; Linux: `VmRSS`). The bar is its share of the RAM in the computer. |
| **Most it ever held** | the highest that number has been since the server started |
| **Processor** | share of one processor used between the last two readings. 100 % means one processor fully busy; on 8 processors the most is 800 %. It is blank until the panel has asked twice. |
| **Running for** | how long the process has been up |
| **Threads** | threads the process runs now: the query threads (`--threads`), the HTTP server (one thread that accepts connections and a pool of workers that answer requests, `--http-threads`), the PostgreSQL port, and the background threads (checkpoints, timers, the audit log) |
| **Open handles** | open files and sockets |
| **Free RAM on this computer** | what a program could still get. Inside a container this is the container's limit, not the host's RAM. |
| **Processors** | processors the process may use |

Memory in RAM is bigger than the memory budget below it: the budget covers **table data**, while the process also holds indexes, results being built, and the program itself.

<a id="running"></a>

## Statements running now

One line per statement, over HTTP and the [PostgreSQL port](postgres-protocol.md) together:

| Column | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Elapsed** | how long it has been running |
| **Lane** | `fast`, `normal` or `heavy` ([priority lanes](cli-serve.md#lanes)); `heavy (waiting)` while a report waits for a heavy slot |
| **User** | the user who sent it, or `(token)` for the [access token](http-login.md#token) |
| **Database** | which database it runs against |
| **From** | the address it came from, and which port (`http` or `pg`) |
| **Statement** | the first 200 characters |
| **Cancel** | stops it: `DELETE /exec/<id>`. It becomes `stopping` until it winds down. |

**Cancel** needs a name to cancel by, which is the `X-KDB-Request-Id` header the client sent. A client that sent none shows `no id` instead; it still stops on its own [statement timeout](protection.md). The console itself always sends one. There is no **Cancel** at all on a server started without query protection (`can_cancel` is `false` in `/api/stats`).

A statement that is stuck is usually one of the things in [performance tips](performance-tips.md): a `SELECT` with no time range on a big time-series table, a join without a matching key, or a `GROUP BY` over too many groups.

<a id="lanes"></a>

## Lanes

Shown while [priority lanes](cli-serve.md#lanes) are on: the heavy slots in use, how many reports wait for one, how many statement shapes are known to be heavy, and whether heavy statements run at a lower CPU priority here. The table has one line per lane: how many run and wait now, how many started since the server did, how many had to wait and for how long (average and longest), how many were refused because the HTTP line was full (only requests sent with priority `low`), how many ran at once because it was full (heavy only by history), and how many gave up waiting (a timeout or a cancel).

<a id="slow"></a>

## Slow statements

The newest 20 statements that took at least the slow-query threshold (`kareladb serve --slow-query-ms`, 1 second by default), from [`GET /api/slow-queries`](http-server-info.md#slow-queries). They are kept in a file on disk, so last night's slow statement is still here in the morning, after a restart too.

| Column | What it is |
|---|---|
| **When** | when it ended |
| **Took** | how long it ran |
| **User**, **Database** | who sent it (the token's name for the [access token](audit-log.md)), and where |
| **Statement** | the statement; `failed:` in front when it did not succeed. Point at it for the whole text and the error. |

The list is read every 10 seconds at most, and at once with **Now**.

<a id="timers"></a>

## Timers

Every [timer](timers.md) of the databases you may read, also of databases not open yet. Timers in trouble come first: failing now, then failed in the last 24 hours, then the latest to start. The title counts the timers with failures.

| Column | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Timer** | `database.name`; `(off)` when it is turned off. Point at it for the schedule, the next run and the SQL. |
| **Last run** | how long ago it last ran and whether that run was `ok` or `failed` (red); `running now` while it runs |
| **Late** | how many seconds after its due time the last run got its write in; yellow above 5 s. Point at it for the worst since the server started. |
| **Failed 24 h** | runs that failed in about the last 24 hours (red when not 0). Point at it for the count since the server started. |
| **Last error** | the last run's error, or `-` |

The numbers come with the rest of `/api/stats` (`timers`), from memory: nothing is read from disk for them.

<a id="databases"></a>

## Each database

Only databases that are **open** are listed. A database opens the first time it is used, so a server that has just started may show none - that is not a fault.

| Number | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Rows held in memory** | saved partition data kept in memory, against the budget (`--memory`, 512 MB by default). When it is full, the partitions used longest ago are dropped and read again when next needed. |
| **Waiting to be written** | changes that are in the log but not yet in the partition files. A checkpoint writes them; it starts by itself at a quarter of the memory budget. |
| **Result cache** | memory holding results of repeated queries (`--cache-mb` or `cache_mb` in kareladb.conf, 256 MB by default; 0 turns it off) |
| **Cache hits** | share of queries answered from that cache since the database was opened |
| **Cached results** | how many results are in that cache now |
| **Open cursors** | [cursors](cursors.md) a client has open (`POST /cursor`) |
| **Log position** | the last change written to the log (the LSN) |
| **On disk** | what the database takes on disk. The bar is the share that is data; point at it for the parts: data, older versions, trash, log, old log. Measured once a minute. Older versions and trash go by themselves (`keep_versions`, `trash_keep_hours`, `trash_max_mb` in [kareladb.conf](cli-serve.md#kareladb-conf)); the [Keep data page](console-keep-data.md) frees them at once. |
| **Open for** | how long ago the server opened this database |

A database with [deferred triggers](triggers.md#deferred) also shows **Deferred trigger queues**, one line per trigger:

| Column | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Trigger**, **Table** | the trigger and the table it watches |
| **Waiting** | jobs not finished yet |
| **Lag** | how long the oldest waiting job has waited (`-` when none waits) |
| **Running** | the job running now and its rows, or `-` |
| **Failed job** | a job that failed and stopped the queue, with its error. Fix the cause, then run `RETRY TRIGGER QUEUE <trigger>`. |

The same numbers come from [GET /api/trigger-queue](http-server-info.md#api-trigger-queue), which can also wait until the jobs are done.

**Tables** opens a line per table:

| Column | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Rows** | rows saved in partition files |
| **In memory** | how much of that table's data is in memory now |
| **Partitions** / **Loaded** | how many partitions the table has, and how many are in memory |
| **Not yet written** | rows changed since the last checkpoint |

This is the quickest way to see which table is using the memory budget, and whether a big load has been written to disk yet.

<a id="activity"></a>

## Server activity

The [terminal](web-console.md#terminal) at the bottom of the Home page shows what the server has done lately, newest at the bottom: every statement that ended, every bulk load and where it came from, timer runs, deferred trigger jobs, logins and backups. It reads `GET /api/activity`, described here.

| Kind | One event for |
|---|---|
| `query` | a statement over HTTP (`/exec`, `/exp`, `/cursor`) or the [PostgreSQL port](postgres-protocol.md), when it ends |
| `write` | a `POST /write` ([line protocol](line-protocol.md)) or `POST /imp` ([CSV import](http-import.md)) request: its rows and tables |
| `timer` | a run of a [timer](timers.md) |
| `trigger` | a job of a [deferred trigger](triggers.md#deferred) that finished or failed (client `(deferred trigger)`) |
| `login` | a login that worked, a failed login, a lockout |
| `backup` | a backup made from the console or the [backup schedule](backup-schedule.md) |
| `server` | the server started or stops |

- It is kept **in memory only**: the last 5,000 events (`kareladb serve --activity-log-size N`, `0` turns it off). A restart starts it empty. For a record that is kept, use the [audit log](audit-log.md).
- Passwords, secrets and tokens in SQL show as `'***'`, and long statements are cut to 300 characters.
- A bulk load is **one** event per request, never one per row, so logging does not slow loading down.
- Requests with the header `X-KDB-Quiet: 1` are not logged. The console sends it with its own background refreshes.

Syntax:

```sql
GET /api/activity[?after=<seq>][&limit=<n>][&db=<name>]
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `after` | only events with a larger `seq`. Leave it out for the newest events. |
| `limit` | at most this many events (default 500, at most 2000) |
| `db` | only events of this database |

The reply is `{"seq", "dropped", "events"}`. `seq` is the newest event's number: send it back as `after` to get only what is new. `dropped` is `true` when some events after `after` were already pushed out of memory.

| Event field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `seq`, `ms` | its number, and when it happened (Unix milliseconds) |
| `kind`, `level` | see the table above; `level` is `info`, `ok` or `error` |
| `user` | who did it; empty for the access token |
| `client` | where it came from: `10.0.0.5 (pg)`, `127.0.0.1 (http)`, `(timer refresh_prices)` |
| `database`, `text` | the database, and the statement or a message like `12,000 rows into trade_log (line protocol)` |
| `rows`, `took_ms`, `error` | rows changed or returned (`-1` = not known), how long it took, and the error |

An admin (or the token) sees every event; any other user sees only their own.

**HTTP: Run a statement, then read the newest events**

```http
POST /exec?compat=0

SELECT 1 + 1 AS two
###
GET /api/activity?limit=2
```

Response:

`POST /exec?compat=0`

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{
  "query": "SELECT 1 + 1 AS two",
  "results": [
    {
      "statement": "SELECT 1 + 1 AS two",
      "columns": [
        {"name": "two", "type": "LONG"}
      ],
      "dataset": [
        [2]
      ],
      "count": 1,
      "truncated": false,
      "rows_affected": 0,
      "message": "",
      "timings": {"parse_us": 26, "execute_us": 59}
    }
  ],
  "timings": {"parse_us": 26, "execute_us": 59}
}
```

`GET /api/activity?limit=2`

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{
  "seq": 3,
  "dropped": false,
  "events": [
    {
      "seq": 2,
      "ms": 1792822726274,
      "kind": "query",
      "level": "ok",
      "user": "",
      "client": "127.0.0.1 (http)",
      "database": "h119",
      "text": "CREATE TABLE acct (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING, bal DOUBLE); INSERT INTO acct VALUES (1, 'Asha', 10);",
      "rows": 1,
      "took_ms": 3,
      "error": ""
    },
    {
      "seq": 3,
      "ms": 1792822729715,
      "kind": "query",
      "level": "ok",
      "user": "",
      "client": "127.0.0.1 (http)",
      "database": "demo",
      "text": "SELECT 1 + 1 AS two",
      "rows": 1,
      "took_ms": 0,
      "error": ""
    }
  ]
}
```

<a id="not"></a>

## What it does not show

- Numbers of the past: the panel keeps nothing, so a reload starts fresh. For a history, let Prometheus read [`GET /metrics`](http-server-info.md#metrics), or read `/api/stats` from a script every minute and keep the rows in a table.
- Statements that finished long ago. The [activity](#activity) keeps only the recent ones in memory; the [audit log](audit-log.md) (`SHOW AUDIT`) keeps who changed what.
- Damage and backups; those are in the [Health panel](web-console.md#health-box) on the right side of the console and in [`/api/info`](http-server-info.md#get-api-info).

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KARELADB_TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:9900/api/stats
```

<!-- docs/console-settings.md -->

# Settings page (data folder, old log, capacity, program files and users)

> Where the server keeps its data, how to point it at another folder, and who may log in - all from the console.

- Category: Web console
- Keywords: settings, settings page, data folder, move data, change data folder, kareladb.conf, config file, --config, restart, restart server, add user, change password, remove user, grants, roles, free space, disk space, wal\_archive, wal\_archive\_mb, KARELADB\_WAL\_ARCHIVE\_MB, old log, cache\_mb, KARELADB\_CACHE\_MB, result cache size, program files, web\_dir, help\_dir, skill\_dir, KARELADB\_WEB\_DIR, KARELADB\_HELP\_DIR, KARELADB\_SKILL\_DIR, command line, Docker, KARELADB\_DATA\_DIR, capacity, http\_threads, max\_connections, lock\_timeout\_ms, idle\_in\_transaction\_timeout\_ms, rate\_limit\_ip, rate\_limit\_user, timer\_workers, http\_functions, KARELADB\_HTTP\_FUNCTIONS
- See also: [Web console](web-console.md), [Monitor panel (memory, processor, caches)](console-monitor.md), [View data page (browse and edit rows)](console-data-page.md), [Users and roles](users-and-roles.md), [kareladb user](cli-users.md), [kareladb serve](cli-serve.md), [Databases and the data folder](databases.md), [Keeping kareladb serve safe](server-security.md), [Install packages and the Claude skill](install-packages.md), [Health, info, check and backup over HTTP](http-server-info.md)

The **Settings** page of the [web console](web-console.md) has these parts: **Storage** (where the databases live), **Old log kept per database** (the `wal_archive` size), **Result cache** (`cache_mb`), **Backups**, **Calls from SQL** (`http_functions`), **Capacity and waits** (HTTP threads, PostgreSQL connections, the lock timeout, the drain time), **Program files** (the folders of the console, the help and the Claude skill) and **Users** (who may log in). Only a user whose own `ROLE` is `admin` may open it; everybody else sees a line saying so.

<a id="storage"></a>

## Storage

The top of the page shows the **data folder** in use, and a badge saying where that choice came from. Under it: how many databases are in it, how much they use, and how much room is left on that disk.

Where the data folder comes from, strongest first:

| Source | Badge | Set by |
|---|---|---|
| `--data-dir <folder>` | `--data-dir on the command line` | the command that started the server |
| `kareladb.conf` | `this Settings page (kareladb.conf)` | **Save** on this page |
| `KARELADB_DATA_DIR` | `the KARELADB_DATA_DIR environment variable` | the environment |
| the default | `program folder` | `data` next to `kareladb` |

**A flag always wins.** When the server was started with `--data-dir`, the page says so in a yellow banner: a folder saved here will only be used once the server is started without that flag. This is worth reading before pressing anything - it is the difference between a setting that works and one that quietly does nothing.

**How this server was started** folds open to show the settings file (`config_path`) and the whole command line (`command_line`), as [GET /api/settings](http-server-info.md#api-settings) gives them.

**In Docker** the image passes the data folder as the environment variable `KARELADB_DATA_DIR=/data`, not as `--data-dir`, on purpose: a flag would always win, and this page could then never change the folder. The image also keeps `kareladb.conf` in the volume (`--config /data/kareladb.conf`), so a setting saved here survives a new image and a new container. A folder you choose here must be under a mounted volume too; anywhere else is inside the container and is lost with it ([Docker](install-packages.md#docker)).

<a id="change"></a>

### Changing the folder

Type a folder and press **Save**. Before anything is written, the server:

1. makes the folder if it is not there,
2. writes a small file in it and removes it again, to be sure it can write there,
3. refuses a folder that is itself **one database** (it holds a `_manifest.a`) - the data folder is the one **above** those, the one with a folder per database.

Only then is the folder written to `kareladb.conf`. A folder that fails any of those checks is refused with the reason, and the file is not touched.

```json
{"data_dir":"E:/kdb-data"}
```

**Nothing is copied.** The databases in the old folder stay exactly where they are; the server simply looks somewhere else from the next start. To take them along:

1. Save the new folder here.
2. Stop the server.
3. Move the database folders yourself.
4. Start it again.

<a id="restart"></a>

### Restart

**Restart the server** closes every database cleanly and starts again **in the same process**. No service manager, Docker restart policy or supervisor is needed, and the server keeps the same port, so the console reconnects by itself after a few seconds.

- Statements that are running are stopped and open transactions are rolled back, exactly as at a normal shutdown.
- The server prints `restarting...`, then `databases closed cleanly (N ms)`, then its usual banner.
- Restarting is written to the [audit log](audit-log.md).

If the saved folder cannot be used when the server starts again - an unplugged disk, a renamed share - the server does **not** refuse to boot. It prints a warning and starts on the usual folder instead, so there is always a console to fix the setting in:

```text
warning: the data folder saved in 'C:/kdb/kareladb.conf' cannot be used: cannot make the folder 'Z:/gone'
         starting with the usual folder instead. Fix it on the Settings page.
```

<a id="read-only"></a>

### When it cannot be changed here

The page shows the folder without a **Save** button when the settings file cannot be written - a read-only program folder, for instance, as in some container images. It then says why, and the folder is set with `--data-dir` or `KARELADB_DATA_DIR` as before. `--config <file>` puts the settings file somewhere writable:

```bash
kareladb serve --config /var/lib/kdb/kareladb.conf
```

A server started on **one database folder** (`kareladb serve D:\kdb\market`) has no data folder to change, so Storage is read-only there too.

<a id="wal-archive"></a>

## Old log kept per database

Each database keeps old log files in its `wal_archive` folder. They are only used to repair a damaged file and by backups; the data does not need them. This part of the page sets how much each database keeps: a size in MB, or **Off**.

| Where the value comes from, strongest first | Shown as |
|---|---|
| `wal_archive_mb` in `kareladb.conf` (**Save** here) | `this page (kareladb.conf)` |
| the environment variable `KARELADB_WAL_ARCHIVE_MB` | `KARELADB_WAL_ARCHIVE_MB` |
| the default | `the default (1 GB)` |

- **Save** works at once, with no restart. A smaller size removes the oldest files of every open database now.
- **Off** keeps no old log. A damaged file can then only be repaired from a backup.
- A database with its own setting keeps it: [`ALTER DATABASE ... SET WAL_ARCHIVE`](databases.md#wal-archive), or **Old log** in the console's **Databases** panel. There you can also pick **Server default** again.

```json
{"data_dir":"E:/kdb-data","wal_archive_mb":100}
```

<a id="result-cache"></a>

## Result cache

The [result cache](performance-tips.md#result-cache) keeps the results of repeated `SELECT`s in memory. This part of the page sets its size for all databases together, in MB; `0` turns it off.

| Where the value comes from, strongest first | Shown as |
|---|---|
| `--cache-mb` on the command line (the page cannot change it then) | `--cache-mb` |
| `cache_mb` in `kareladb.conf` (**Save** here) | `this page (kareladb.conf)` |
| the environment variable `KARELADB_CACHE_MB` | `KARELADB_CACHE_MB` |
| the default | `the default (256 MB)` |

- **Save** works at once, with no restart. A smaller size drops the oldest results now.
- One result may use a quarter of the space, a [pinned](pinned-queries.md) one three quarters.
- A database with a space of its own keeps it: [`ALTER DATABASE ... SET RESULT_CACHE`](databases.md#result-cache).

<a id="backups"></a>

## Backups

The backup folder, the schedule, how many backups are kept, and the command that copies each backup off the server. Each line says where its value came from: a flag, this page (`kareladb.conf`), the environment or the default ([where the settings come from](backup-schedule.md#backup-settings)).

| Line | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Folder** | where backups go; `_backups` in the data folder by default |
| **Schedule** | when the server makes backups by itself (`daily 02:00`, `every 6h`, `off`) |
| **Kept** | the newest backup of each of the last N days and weeks |
| **Copy off the server** | the [backup command](backup-schedule.md#backup-command), or `none` with a warning: backups on the same disk are lost with it |

- **Save** writes the schedule and the two counts to `kareladb.conf`. They are used from the next start: use **Restart** under Storage.
- The folder and the copy command are shown, not edited. A command runs programs on the server, so it is set in `kareladb.conf` by hand, with `--backup-command` or `KARELADB_BACKUP_COMMAND`.
- Keep enough old log (above) to cover the time between two backups, or a restore to a moment in between is not possible ([the window](backup-and-safety.md#pitr-window)).

```json
{"data_dir":"/data","backup_schedule":"daily 02:00","backup_keep_daily":14,"backup_command":"aws s3 cp --recursive {dir} s3://my-bucket/kdb/{database}/{name}"}
```

<a id="http-functions"></a>

## Calls from SQL

Which hosts [`http_get` and `http_post`](http-functions.md) may call, and how long one call may take.

- Type the hosts separated by commas (`api.example.com, 10.0.0.5:8080`), or `off`.
- **Save** writes `http_functions` and `http_timeout_ms` to `kareladb.conf`. They apply at once, no restart.
- **Set by** says where the list came from: this page (`kareladb.conf`), `KARELADB_HTTP_FUNCTIONS`, or the default (off).

<a id="capacity"></a>

## Capacity and waits

What the server was started with, and where each value came from. It is read-only: the server reads these when it starts, so a change needs a restart.

| Line | Setting | Set with, strongest first |
|---|---|---|
| **HTTP requests at once** | `http_threads` | `--http-threads`, then `kareladb.conf`, then `KARELADB_HTTP_THREADS`, then the CPU threads (at least 8) |
| **PostgreSQL connections** | `max_connections` | `--max-connections`, then `kareladb.conf`, then `KARELADB_MAX_CONNECTIONS`, then 500 |
| **Wait for a busy table** | `lock_timeout_ms` | `--lock-timeout`, then `kareladb.conf`, then `KARELADB_LOCK_TIMEOUT`, then 5 s. A session changes its own with [`SET lock_timeout`](transactions.md#lock-timeout). |
| **Idle open transaction rolled back after** | `idle_in_transaction_timeout_ms` | `--idle-in-transaction-timeout`, then `kareladb.conf`, then `KARELADB_IDLE_IN_TRANSACTION_TIMEOUT`, then 30 s. A session: [`SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`](transactions.md#idle-timeout). |
| **Time to finish on stop** | `--drain-timeout` | `--drain-timeout`, then `KARELADB_DRAIN_TIMEOUT`, then 30 s ([stopping](cli-serve.md#stop)) |
| **Requests per second per address** | `rate_limit_ip` | `--rate-limit-ip`, then `kareladb.conf`, then `KARELADB_RATE_LIMIT_IP`, then no limit ([rate limits](protection.md#rate-limits)) |
| **Requests per second per user** | `rate_limit_user` | `--rate-limit-user`, then `kareladb.conf`, then `KARELADB_RATE_LIMIT_USER`, then no limit |
| **Timers running at once** | `timer_workers` | `--timer-workers`, then `kareladb.conf`, then `KARELADB_TIMER_WORKERS`, then 3 ([timers](timers.md)) |
| **TCP keepalive: idle before the first probe**, **between probes**, **probes before giving up** | `tcp_keepalives_idle`, `tcp_keepalives_interval`, `tcp_keepalives_count` | `--tcp-keepalives-*`, then `kareladb.conf`, then `KARELADB_TCP_KEEPALIVES_*`, then the system's. A Postgres session: [`SET tcp_keepalives_idle`](server-activity.md#idle-clients). |

To change one, write its key into `kareladb.conf` by hand and press **Restart** under Storage; a flag or an environment variable changes only when the server is started again. Every option of the server, with its flag, variable and key, is in [every option](cli-serve.md#all-options).

```json
{"data_dir":"E:/kdb-data","http_threads":32,"max_connections":300,"lock_timeout_ms":20000}
```

<a id="program-files"></a>

## Program files

The web console, the help pages and the Claude skill are folders of plain files next to the kareladb program, not part of it. This part shows which folder the server uses for each, and what chose it. It is read-only.

| Line | Folder | Chosen by, strongest first |
|---|---|---|
| **Web console** | `web_dir` | `kareladb.conf` `"web_dir"`, then `KARELADB_WEB_DIR`, then `web/` next to the program, then `share/kareladb/web` beside the program folder, then a source checkout |
| **Help pages** | `help_dir` | the same, with `"help_dir"`, `KARELADB_HELP_DIR` and `help/` |
| **Claude skill** | `skill_dir` | the same, with `"skill_dir"`, `KARELADB_SKILL_DIR` and `skill/` |

- After each folder the page says where it came from: `from kareladb.conf`, `from KARELADB_WEB_DIR`, `next to the program`, `in share/kareladb beside the program folder` or `from the source checkout`. `not found` means none of the places had the files.
- To use other folders, write them into `kareladb.conf` by hand, or set the environment variables, and restart the server. More: [where kareladb finds the console, the help and the skill](install-packages.md#folders).

```json
{"data_dir":"E:/kdb-data","web_dir":"E:/kdb/web","help_dir":"E:/kdb/help","skill_dir":"E:/kdb/skill"}
```

<a id="users"></a>

## Users

The same users as [`CREATE USER`](users-and-roles.md) and [`kareladb user`](cli-users.md) - this page just sends that SQL for you.

| Button | What it sends |
|---|---|
| **Add a user** | `CREATE USER name WITH PASSWORD '...' ROLE read` |
| **Change** | `ALTER USER name WITH PASSWORD '...' ROLE write` (only the parts you filled in) |
| **Grants** | `GRANT write ON DATABASE shop TO name`, or `REVOKE ALL ON DATABASE shop FROM name` |
| **Remove** | `DROP USER name` |

On a server with no users yet, the page says so and offers **Add the first user**. That first user must have `ROLE admin`, so the role box is fixed. **As soon as that user exists, every request needs a login** - the console notices at once and shows its login form, so have the password ready.

The rules the server enforces, which the page simply reports:

- A password must be at least 12 characters and must not be the user name.
- `Bob` and `bob` are the same user.
- The last user with `ROLE admin` cannot be removed or made weaker while other users exist.
- A new password ends that user's open logins at once.

Roles, and what each one may do, are in [users and roles](users-and-roles.md). Keeping a server reachable from outside safe is in [server security](server-security.md).

<!-- docs/feedback.md -->

# Comments and suggestions

> How people who use a KarelaDB server send comments, suggestions and problem reports, and how its admins read them.

- Category: Web console
- Keywords: feedback, comment, comments, suggestion, suggestions, problem report, bug report, send feedback, contact, POST /api/feedback, GET /api/feedback, POST /api/feedback/\<id\>, \_feedback
- See also: [Web console](web-console.md), [Logins, tokens and roles over HTTP](http-login.md), [Users and roles](users-and-roles.md), [About KarelaDB](about-kareladb.md)

Anyone who may use a KarelaDB server can send its admins a **comment**, a **suggestion** or a **problem** report. The message is saved on that server, in the table `_feedback`, so it survives restarts and is part of every backup.

| Who | What they can do | Where |
|---|---|---|
| anyone who can open the console (logged in, or with the token) | send a message | **Help > Comments and suggestions** |
| a server admin (the user's own `ROLE admin`, or the token) | read every message and mark it read or done | the same page, under **Received** |
| a program | the same, over HTTP | [POST /api/feedback](#post-api-feedback), [GET /api/feedback](#get-api-feedback), [POST /api/feedback/<id>](#mark-feedback) |

- Messages go to the admins of **this** server, not to the makers of KarelaDB.
- A message can be up to 4,000 characters. A name or email for an answer is optional.
- One user can send at most 10 messages in 10 minutes (without a user name: one client address), so a script cannot fill the table.
- Messages are kept in the hidden `_system` database when the server has a data folder, or in the served database when `kareladb serve` runs on one folder.

<a id="page"></a>

## The page in the console

Open **Help > Comments and suggestions**.

1. Pick what it is: **Comment**, **Suggestion** or **Problem**.
2. Write the message. **Ctrl+Enter** sends it too.
3. Optionally add a name or email, if you would like an answer.
4. Press **Send**. The page says which number the message was saved as.

A server admin also sees **Received**: every message, newest first, with its kind, time, sender and state. **New**, **Read**, **Done** and **All** filter the list; **Mark read**, **Mark done** and **Mark new** change a message's state.

<a id="post-api-feedback"></a>

## POST /api/feedback

Syntax:

```sql
POST /api/feedback
Content-Type: application/json

{"kind": "comment | suggestion | problem", "message": "...", "contact": "...", "page": "..."}
```

Saves one message. Needs a login or the token, like every `/api` route; no role is needed.

| Field | Needed | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `kind` | no (default `comment`) | `comment`, `suggestion` or `problem` |
| `message` | yes | 1 to 4,000 characters, no control characters except line breaks and tabs |
| `contact` | no | up to 200 characters |
| `page` | no | where it was sent from, up to 200 characters |

- **Returns:** `{"id": 12, "saved": true}`.
- **Errors:** 400 with a message that says which field is wrong; 401 without a login; 429 after 10 messages in 10 minutes from one user (or one address, for the token).
- The server adds the time, the user name and the client address itself.

```text
curl -s -X POST "$KARELADB_URL/api/feedback" -H "Authorization: Bearer $KARELADB_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-binary '{"kind":"suggestion","message":"Please add a CSV export to dashboards.","contact":"ram@example.com"}'

{"id":1,"saved":true}
```

<a id="get-api-feedback"></a>

## GET /api/feedback

Syntax:

```sql
GET /api/feedback[?status=new|read|done][&limit=N]
```

Reads the messages, newest first, as columns and rows like [/exec](http-exec.md). Needs a **server admin**: the user's own `ROLE admin` or the token, because messages can hold names and email addresses.

| Parameter | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `status` | only messages in this state: `new`, `read` or `done` | all |
| `limit` | at most this many rows; more than 1,000 counts as 1,000 | `100` |

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | `LONG` | the message number |
| `time` | `TIMESTAMP` | when it was sent (UTC) |
| `kind` | `STRING` | `comment`, `suggestion` or `problem` |
| `status` | `STRING` | `new`, `read` or `done` |
| `message` | `STRING` | the text |
| `contact` | `STRING` | the name or email given, or `NULL` |
| `page` | `STRING` | where it was sent from |
| `user` | `STRING` | the logged-in user, or `NULL` for the token |
| `client` | `STRING` | the client address |

- **Returns:** `{"columns": [...], "dataset": [[...], ...], "count": N}`. A server where nobody has sent anything yet answers with no rows.
- **Errors:** 400 for an unknown `status`; 401 without a login; 403 for a user who is not a server admin.

<a id="mark-feedback"></a>

## POST /api/feedback/<id>

Syntax:

```sql
POST /api/feedback/<id>
Content-Type: application/json

{"status": "new | read | done"}
```

Changes the state of one message. `status` can also be a query or form field (`?status=done`). Needs a **server admin**, like reading.

- **Returns:** `{"id": 12, "status": "done"}`.
- **Errors:** 400 when `<id>` is not a whole number above 0, or `status` is not `new`, `read` or `done`; 403 for a user who is not a server admin; 404 `there is no message #<id>`.

**HTTP: Send a suggestion, read the new ones, mark it done**

```http
POST /api/feedback
Content-Type: application/json

{"kind":"suggestion","message":"Please add a CSV export to dashboards.","contact":"ram@example.com","page":"console"}
###
GET /api/feedback?status=new
###
POST /api/feedback/{{id}}
Content-Type: application/json

{"status":"done"}
```

Response:

`POST /api/feedback`

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{"id": 1, "saved": true}
```

`GET /api/feedback?status=new`

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{
  "columns": [
    {"name": "id", "type": "LONG"},
    {"name": "time", "type": "TIMESTAMP"},
    {"name": "kind", "type": "STRING"},
    {"name": "status", "type": "STRING"},
    {"name": "message", "type": "STRING"},
    {"name": "contact", "type": "STRING"},
    {"name": "page", "type": "STRING"},
    {"name": "user", "type": "STRING"},
    {"name": "client", "type": "STRING"}
  ],
  "dataset": [
    [
      1,
      "2026-10-24T06:18:54.065Z",
      "suggestion",
      "new",
      "Please add a CSV export to dashboards.",
      "ram@example.com",
      "console",
      null,
      "127.0.0.1 (http)"
    ]
  ],
  "count": 1
}
```

`POST /api/feedback/{{id}}`

HTTP 200 (application/json)

```text
{"id": 1, "status": "done"}
```

**HTTP: A message number that does not exist**

```http
POST /api/feedback/999
Content-Type: application/json

{"status":"read"}
```

Response:

HTTP 404 (application/json)

```text
{"error": "there is no message #999"}
```

<!-- docs/geometry-and-cad.md -->

# Survey, CAD and 3D data: points, drawings, blocks, meshes

> How to keep survey points, 2D drawings (lines, arcs, polylines, blocks, layers) and 3D meshes in KarelaDB, load only the part a canvas can see, and do distance, area and volume maths in SQL - with the rule that the camera stays in the client.

- Category: Geometry & CAD
- Keywords: survey, land survey, survey data, control point, control line, traverse, total station, northing, easting, elevation, coordinates, coordinate system, projection, datum, CAD, drawing, DXF, DWG, entity, line, arc, circle, polyline, vertex, vertices, bulge, layer, block, block insert, group, 2D, 3D, mesh, triangle, TIN, terrain, point cloud, solid, bounding box, bbox, viewport, partial load, level of detail, LOD, pan, zoom, camera, canvas, WebGL, hit test, selection, area, shoelace, perimeter, bearing, distance, volume, cross section, geometry, spatial, GIS, PostGIS, R-tree
- See also: [Database models: relational, hierarchical, network, NoSQL, object](data-models.md), [Column types](column-types.md), [Constraints](constraints.md), [Triggers](triggers.md), [Views](views.md), [Math functions](functions-math.md), [Window and series functions](functions-window.md), [Time travel and branches: SELECT ... AS OF, CREATE DATABASE ... BRANCH OF](as-of-and-branches.md), [Change stream and live subscriptions: changes('t'), GET /api/changes, GET /api/subscribe](change-stream.md), [JSON functions](functions-json.md), [Indexes](indexes.md)

KarelaDB has no geometry type and no spatial index, but it has what a drawing really is made of: numbers, ordered lists, keys, rules and history. This topic shows one layout that works for survey work, 2D CAD and 3D objects, and what to leave to the program that draws.

| You want to keep | Use | Why |
|---|---|---|
| a coordinate | `DOUBLE` columns `x`, `y`, `z` (or `DECIMAL(12,4)` for legal plans) | fast maths, plain to read, indexable |
| a list of vertices | one row per vertex with a `seq` number, or a `DOUBLE[]` when the list is only ever read whole | rows can be changed one at a time; an array is one value |
| what an entity is | a `kind` column and a few typed columns (`radius`, `start_angle`, ...) | no parsing, every value queryable |
| style, text, anything free-form | a `JSON` column | one place for the long tail, still searchable with `json_value()` |
| the shape's extent | four columns `min_x`, `min_y`, `max_x`, `max_y`, kept by a trigger | the "what is in view" query needs only these |
| a mesh | a vertex table and a face table | partial loads, volumes and sections stay SQL |
| who changed what and when | `AS OF`, the change stream, a branch | history comes with the database |

What is **not** in KarelaDB today: `ST_Intersects`, buffers, projections between datums, and an R-tree. The bounding-box columns and a B-tree index on them do the job up to a few hundred thousand entities per drawing; beyond that a grid index would be new engine work.

Setup used by the examples below:

```sql
CREATE TABLE projects (
  id    INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name  TEXT NOT NULL,
  crs   TEXT NOT NULL,              -- the one coordinate system every number in this project is in
  units TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'm'
);
CREATE TABLE points (
  project   INT NOT NULL REFERENCES projects(id),
  id        INT NOT NULL,
  x         DOUBLE NOT NULL,        -- easting
  y         DOUBLE NOT NULL,        -- northing
  z         DOUBLE,                 -- elevation, NULL when not measured
  code      TEXT NOT NULL,          -- CP control, TP traverse, SP spot shot, ...
  note      TEXT,
  observed  TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (project, id)
);
CREATE TABLE drawings (
  id      INT PRIMARY KEY,
  project INT NOT NULL REFERENCES projects(id),
  name    TEXT NOT NULL,
  props   JSON
);
CREATE TABLE layers (
  drawing INT NOT NULL REFERENCES drawings(id),
  name    TEXT NOT NULL,
  color   TEXT,
  visible BOOL NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,
  locked  BOOL NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE,
  PRIMARY KEY (drawing, name)
);
CREATE TABLE entities (
  id          UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  drawing     INT NOT NULL REFERENCES drawings(id),
  layer       TEXT NOT NULL,
  kind        TEXT NOT NULL,        -- line, polyline, arc, circle, text, insert
  closed      BOOL NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE,
  cx          DOUBLE, cy DOUBLE,    -- circle and arc: centre; text and insert: position
  radius      DOUBLE,
  start_angle DOUBLE, end_angle DOUBLE,   -- degrees, counter-clockwise from +x
  rotation    DOUBLE NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  scale       DOUBLE NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  block       INT,                  -- kind = 'insert': the block placed here
  parent      UUID,                 -- the group this entity belongs to, if any
  props       JSON,                 -- colour, line weight, text value, ...
  min_x       DOUBLE, min_y DOUBLE, max_x DOUBLE, max_y DOUBLE,
  updated     TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX entities_view ON entities (drawing, min_x, min_y);
CREATE TABLE vertices (
  entity UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES entities(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  seq    INT NOT NULL,
  x      DOUBLE NOT NULL,
  y      DOUBLE NOT NULL,
  z      DOUBLE,
  bulge  DOUBLE NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, -- a curved segment to the next vertex, as DXF writes it
  PRIMARY KEY (entity, seq)
);
CREATE TRIGGER vertices_box_i AFTER INSERT ON vertices EXECUTE BEGIN
  UPDATE entities SET min_x = s.x0, min_y = s.y0, max_x = s.x1, max_y = s.y1, updated = now()
  FROM (SELECT entity, min(x) AS x0, min(y) AS y0, max(x) AS x1, max(y) AS y1
        FROM vertices WHERE entity IN (SELECT entity FROM NEW) GROUP BY entity) s
  WHERE entities.id = s.entity;
END;
CREATE TRIGGER vertices_box_u AFTER UPDATE ON vertices EXECUTE BEGIN
  UPDATE entities SET min_x = s.x0, min_y = s.y0, max_x = s.x1, max_y = s.y1, updated = now()
  FROM (SELECT entity, min(x) AS x0, min(y) AS y0, max(x) AS x1, max(y) AS y1
        FROM vertices WHERE entity IN (SELECT entity FROM NEW) GROUP BY entity) s
  WHERE entities.id = s.entity;
END;
INSERT INTO projects VALUES (1, 'Riverside plot 12', 'EPSG:32645', 'm');
INSERT INTO points (project, id, x, y, z, code) VALUES
  (1, 1, 1000.000, 2000.000, 100.50, 'CP'),
  (1, 2, 1100.000, 2000.000, 101.20, 'CP'),
  (1, 3, 1100.000, 2080.000,  99.80, 'CP'),
  (1, 4, 1000.000, 2080.000, 100.10, 'CP'),
  (1, 5, 1052.300, 2041.700, 100.90, 'SP');
INSERT INTO drawings VALUES (1, 1, 'Site plan', '{"scale":"1:500"}');
INSERT INTO layers (drawing, name, color) VALUES (1, 'BOUNDARY', 'red'), (1, 'ROAD', 'grey'), (1, 'TEXT', 'black');
```

<a id="coordinates"></a>

## Coordinates and the one rule

Keep every coordinate of a project in **one** coordinate system, and write its name down in the project row (`crs`). Mixing a local site grid with a national grid in the same table is the most common survey data error, and no query can repair it later. Store x = easting, y = northing, z = elevation, as `DOUBLE`: 15-16 significant digits hold a millimetre at the size of a country.

**Example: The project says which coordinate system its numbers are in**

```sql
SELECT name, crs, units FROM projects;
```

Result:

| name (STRING) | crs (STRING) | units (STRING) |
|---|---|---|
| Riverside plot 12 | EPSG:32645 | m |

(1 row)

- **Notes:**
  - For legal boundary plans, where a value must print back exactly as surveyed, use `DECIMAL(12, 4)` instead ([column-types](column-types.md#decimal)). Maths on `DOUBLE` is faster.
  - A point that must be unique by its number within a project gets the composite key `(project, id)` as above; a point id can then repeat in another project.

<a id="points"></a>

## Survey points and control

One row per shot: number, x, y, z, a code and when it was observed. Control points, traverse stations and spot shots live in the same table and differ by `code`, so one index and one query serve them all. A control **line** is an ordered pair (or list) of control points, kept in its own small table.

**Example: Control points, and the distance and bearing between two of them**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE control_lines (project INT, id INT, from_pt INT, to_pt INT, PRIMARY KEY (project, id));
INSERT INTO control_lines VALUES (1, 1, 1, 2), (1, 2, 2, 3);
```

```sql
SELECT l.id,
       round(sqrt((b.x - a.x) * (b.x - a.x) + (b.y - a.y) * (b.y - a.y)), 3) AS distance,
       round(degrees(atan2(b.x - a.x, b.y - a.y)), 4)                       AS bearing_deg
FROM control_lines l
JOIN points a ON a.project = l.project AND a.id = l.from_pt
JOIN points b ON b.project = l.project AND b.id = l.to_pt
ORDER BY l.id;
```

Result:

| id (INT) | distance (DOUBLE) | bearing_deg (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 100 | 90 |
| 2 | 80 | 0 |

(2 rows)

- **Notes:**
  - Surveyors measure bearing clockwise from north, so it is `atan2(dx, dy)`, not the mathematician's `atan2(dy, dx)`. A negative result is a bearing west of north: add 360.
  - `round(..., 3)` is for the page; keep the full `DOUBLE` in the table.

<a id="observations"></a>

## Raw observations, reduced in SQL

Keep what the instrument gave: station, bearing (or horizontal angle), slope distance, vertical angle, instrument and target heights. Coordinates are **computed** from them. When a setup turns out wrong, change one row and recompute, instead of hunting the points it touched.

**Example: A total-station shot, reduced to a coordinate**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE observations (
  id       INT PRIMARY KEY,
  project  INT, station INT,
  bearing  DOUBLE,     -- degrees from north
  vertical DOUBLE,     -- zenith angle, 90 = level
  slope    DOUBLE,     -- slope distance
  hi       DOUBLE DEFAULT 0,  -- instrument height
  ht       DOUBLE DEFAULT 0   -- target height
);
INSERT INTO observations VALUES (1, 1, 1, 45.0, 88.5, 70.711, 1.5, 1.8);
```

```sql
SELECT o.id,
       round(s.x + o.slope * sin(radians(o.vertical)) * sin(radians(o.bearing)), 3) AS x,
       round(s.y + o.slope * sin(radians(o.vertical)) * cos(radians(o.bearing)), 3) AS y,
       round(s.z + o.hi + o.slope * cos(radians(o.vertical)) - o.ht, 3)             AS z
FROM observations o
JOIN points s ON s.project = o.project AND s.id = o.station;
```

Result:

| id (INT) | x (DOUBLE) | y (DOUBLE) | z (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1049.983 | 2049.983 | 102.051 |

(1 row)

A traverse closure is the same maths summed over the legs: `sum()` of the easting and northing differences, compared with the known end point. `WITH RECURSIVE` ([union-subqueries](union-subqueries.md)) walks a traverse that is stored leg by leg.

<a id="entities"></a>

## Drawings, layers and entities

One `entities` row per thing a CAD program would call an entity. The `kind` column says which of the typed columns are meaningful; the bounding box columns are filled by a trigger from the vertices, or directly for circles and text. Layers are a table too, so visibility and lock state are data, not a convention.

**Example: A polyline from four vertices: the trigger fills its bounding box**

Setup:

```sql
INSERT INTO entities (id, drawing, layer, kind, closed) VALUES ('0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100', 1, 'BOUNDARY', 'polyline', TRUE);
INSERT INTO vertices (entity, seq, x, y) VALUES
  ('0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100', 1, 1000, 2000),
  ('0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100', 2, 1100, 2000),
  ('0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100', 3, 1100, 2080),
  ('0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100', 4, 1000, 2080);
```

```sql
SELECT layer, kind, closed, min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y FROM entities;
```

Result:

| layer (STRING) | kind (STRING) | closed (BOOL) | min_x (DOUBLE) | min_y (DOUBLE) | max_x (DOUBLE) | max_y (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BOUNDARY | polyline | true | 1000 | 2000 | 1100 | 2080 |

(1 row)

**Example: A circle and a text label have no vertices: write their box directly**

Setup:

```sql
INSERT INTO entities (drawing, layer, kind, cx, cy, radius, min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y)
  VALUES (1, 'ROAD', 'circle', 1050, 2040, 6, 1044, 2034, 1056, 2046);
INSERT INTO entities (drawing, layer, kind, cx, cy, rotation, props, min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y)
  VALUES (1, 'TEXT', 'text', 1052.3, 2041.7, 0, '{"text":"MH 5","height":1.5}', 1052.3, 2041.7, 1058.3, 2043.2);
```

```sql
SELECT kind, cx, cy, radius, json_value(props, '$.text') AS text FROM entities WHERE kind IN ('circle', 'text') ORDER BY kind;
```

Result:

| kind (STRING) | cx (DOUBLE) | cy (DOUBLE) | radius (DOUBLE) | text (STRING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| circle | 1050 | 2040 | 6 | NULL |
| text | 1052.3 | 2041.7 | NULL | MH 5 |

(2 rows)

**Example: Moving a vertex moves the box with it**

Setup:

```sql
INSERT INTO entities (id, drawing, layer, kind) VALUES ('0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100', 1, 'ROAD', 'line');
INSERT INTO vertices (entity, seq, x, y) VALUES ('0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100', 1, 0, 0), ('0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100', 2, 10, 0);
```

```sql
UPDATE vertices SET x = 25, y = 12 WHERE entity = '0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100' AND seq = 2;
SELECT kind, min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y FROM entities;
```

Result:

`UPDATE vertices SET x = 25, y = 12 WHERE entity = '0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100' AND seq = 2`

```text
1 row(s) updated
```

`SELECT kind, min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y FROM entities`

| kind (STRING) | min_x (DOUBLE) | min_y (DOUBLE) | max_x (DOUBLE) | max_y (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| line | 0 | 0 | 25 | 12 |

(1 row)

**Example: Deleting an entity deletes its vertices**

Setup:

```sql
INSERT INTO entities (id, drawing, layer, kind) VALUES ('0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100', 1, 'ROAD', 'line');
INSERT INTO vertices (entity, seq, x, y) VALUES ('0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100', 1, 0, 0), ('0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100', 2, 10, 0);
```

```sql
DELETE FROM entities WHERE id = '0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100';
SELECT count(*) AS vertices_left FROM vertices;
```

Result:

`DELETE FROM entities WHERE id = '0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100'`

```text
1 row(s) deleted
```

`SELECT count(*) AS vertices_left FROM vertices`

| vertices_left (LONG) |
|---|
| 0 |

(1 row)

- **Notes:**
  - Arcs: `cx`, `cy`, `radius`, `start_angle`, `end_angle` in degrees, counter-clockwise from +x, the way DXF stores them. The start point is `(cx + radius * cos(radians(start_angle)), cy + radius * sin(radians(start_angle)))`; the arc length is `radius * radians(end_angle - start_angle)`.
  - A curved polyline segment is a `bulge` on the vertex it starts at (tangent of a quarter of the included angle, again DXF's convention). Keeping DXF's conventions makes import and export a straight copy.
  - A box is a cheap over-estimate: a circle's box includes its corners, an arc's box can be computed exactly but the full circle's box is good enough to find it.
  - `props` holds colour, line weight, line type, text value, text height, and anything a plugin adds. `json_value(props, '$.text')` reads one field; an index on it is not possible, so a field you filter on often gets its own column.

<a id="blocks"></a>

## Blocks and groups

A **block** is a drawing that other drawings place. An `insert` entity names the block and where it goes (`cx`, `cy`, `rotation`, `scale`); the block's own entities are rows of the block's drawing. A **group** is an entity whose children carry its id in `parent`. `WITH RECURSIVE` resolves nesting to any depth.

**Example: A block placed twice, and the recursive query that expands both**

Setup:

```sql
INSERT INTO drawings VALUES (2, 1, 'MANHOLE', '{"block":true}');
INSERT INTO layers (drawing, name) VALUES (2, '0');
INSERT INTO entities (drawing, layer, kind, cx, cy, radius, min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y) VALUES (2, '0', 'circle', 0, 0, 0.6, -0.6, -0.6, 0.6, 0.6);
INSERT INTO entities (drawing, layer, kind, block, cx, cy, rotation, scale, min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y) VALUES
  (1, 'ROAD', 'insert', 2, 1020, 2010, 0, 1, 1019.4, 2009.4, 1020.6, 2010.6),
  (1, 'ROAD', 'insert', 2, 1080, 2060, 0, 1, 1079.4, 2059.4, 1080.6, 2060.6);
```

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE placed(drawing, kind, block, cx, cy, depth) AS (
  SELECT drawing, kind, block, cx, cy, 0 FROM entities WHERE drawing = 1 AND kind = 'insert'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.drawing, e.kind, e.block, p.cx + e.cx, p.cy + e.cy, p.depth + 1
  FROM placed p JOIN entities e ON e.drawing = p.block
  WHERE p.depth < 8
)
SELECT kind, cx, cy, depth FROM placed ORDER BY depth, cx;
```

Result:

| kind (STRING) | cx (DOUBLE) | cy (DOUBLE) | depth (LONG) |
|---|---|---|---|
| insert | 1020 | 2010 | 0 |
| insert | 1080 | 2060 | 0 |
| circle | 1020 | 2010 | 1 |
| circle | 1080 | 2060 | 1 |

(4 rows)

- **Notes:**
  - The example adds positions; a real insert also rotates and scales (`cx + scale * (x * cos(r) - y * sin(r))`). Do that in the client when drawing, or in a saved function ([saved-functions](saved-functions.md)) when you need it in SQL.
  - `depth < 8` stops a block that (by mistake) contains itself.
  - Groups are the same query over `parent` instead of `block`.

<a id="viewport"></a>

## Partial load: only what the canvas can see

The canvas never loads a whole drawing. It asks for the entities whose box overlaps the window it shows, plus a margin, and asks again only when the view moves out of that margin. The index on `(drawing, min_x, min_y)` narrows the scan; the other three conditions filter the rest.

**Example: Everything on visible layers that overlaps a 60 x 40 m window**

Setup:

```sql
INSERT INTO entities (drawing, layer, kind, cx, cy, radius, min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y) VALUES
  (1, 'ROAD', 'circle', 1010, 2010, 2, 1008, 2008, 1012, 2012),
  (1, 'ROAD', 'circle', 1090, 2070, 2, 1088, 2068, 1092, 2072),
  (1, 'TEXT', 'text', 1050, 2040, NULL, 1050, 2040, 1056, 2042);
UPDATE layers SET visible = FALSE WHERE drawing = 1 AND name = 'TEXT';
```

```sql
SELECT e.kind, e.layer, e.min_x, e.min_y
FROM entities e JOIN layers l ON l.drawing = e.drawing AND l.name = e.layer
WHERE e.drawing = 1 AND l.visible
  AND e.max_x >= 1000 AND e.min_x <= 1060    -- the window, x
  AND e.max_y >= 2000 AND e.min_y <= 2040    -- the window, y
ORDER BY e.layer, e.min_x;
```

Result:

| kind (STRING) | layer (STRING) | min_x (DOUBLE) | min_y (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|
| circle | ROAD | 1008 | 2008 |

(1 row)

**Example: Far out, skip what would be smaller than a pixel**

Setup:

```sql
INSERT INTO entities (drawing, layer, kind, cx, cy, radius, min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y) VALUES
  (1, 'ROAD', 'circle', 1010, 2010, 0.05, 1009.95, 2009.95, 1010.05, 2010.05),
  (1, 'ROAD', 'circle', 1090, 2070, 4, 1086, 2066, 1094, 2074);
```

```sql
SELECT kind, radius FROM entities
WHERE drawing = 1 AND kind = 'circle'
  AND greatest(max_x - min_x, max_y - min_y) >= 0.5   -- 0.5 m per pixel at this zoom
ORDER BY radius;
```

Result:

| kind (STRING) | radius (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|
| circle | 4 |

(1 row)

- **Notes:**
  - Ask with a margin of about one screen around the window, so small pans need no query at all.
  - For big polylines keep a simplified copy for far zooms (a `vertices_lod` table with every 10th vertex, or a `DOUBLE[]` in `props`); the client picks by zoom.
  - The HTTP API returns JSON the canvas can draw straight away ([http-exec](http-exec.md)); the Postgres port serves desktop CAD and GIS tools ([postgres-protocol](postgres-protocol.md)).

<a id="camera"></a>

## The camera stays in the client

Pan, zoom, the view matrix, hover and window selection change sixty times a second. None of that goes through the database: a commit costs a disk sync and a query a round trip, and the GPU or a loop over an in-memory array does the matrix multiply a thousand times faster than SQL could. The split is:

| In memory (client) | In KarelaDB |
|---|---|
| world-to-screen matrix, camera position | the entities, as the source of truth |
| hit testing under the mouse, window selection | "what exists in this region" |
| the working set of loaded entities | levels of detail, history, who changed what |
| redraw on every frame | one query when the view leaves the loaded region |

Save the camera as a **view**, not as live state: one row per user and drawing, written when the user stops moving or closes the drawing, read when it is opened. Named views and layout viewports are rows of the same table.

**Example: A saved view: where the user left the drawing**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE saved_views (drawing INT, owner TEXT, name TEXT, cx DOUBLE, cy DOUBLE, scale DOUBLE, rotation DOUBLE DEFAULT 0, saved TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now(), PRIMARY KEY (drawing, owner, name));
```

```sql
INSERT INTO saved_views (drawing, owner, name, cx, cy, scale) VALUES (1, 'amrit', 'last', 1050, 2040, 0.25);
SELECT cx, cy, scale FROM saved_views WHERE drawing = 1 AND owner = 'amrit' AND name = 'last';
```

Result:

`INSERT INTO saved_views (drawing, owner, name, cx, cy, scale) VALUES (1, 'amrit', 'last', 1050, 2040`

```text
1 row(s) inserted
```

`SELECT cx, cy, scale FROM saved_views WHERE drawing = 1 AND owner = 'amrit' AND name = 'last'`

| cx (DOUBLE) | cy (DOUBLE) | scale (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|
| 1050 | 2040 | 0.25 |

(1 row)

<a id="history"></a>

## Save, open, undo and history

A save is a transaction: all the rows of the edit, or none ([transactions](transactions.md)). Opening is the viewport query above plus the layers and the saved view. For undo across sessions and "who moved this", KarelaDB's own history does the work: `AS OF` reads a table as it was at a time, the change stream lists every committed change with its LSN, and a branch gives a writable copy of a whole database to try a redesign on.

```sql
-- The client noted the time before the edit (or the commit LSN from changes('entities')).
UPDATE entities SET cx = 1060, min_x = 1054, max_x = 1066 WHERE id = '0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100';
SELECT cx FROM entities AS OF TIMESTAMP '2026-10-15 14:29:58.250' WHERE id = '0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100';  -- 1050
SELECT cx FROM entities                                            WHERE id = '0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100';  -- 1060
-- Undo it for everyone: put the old rows back.
INSERT OR REPLACE INTO entities SELECT * FROM entities AS OF TIMESTAMP '2026-10-15 14:29:58.250' WHERE drawing = 1;
```

- **Notes:**
  - Every committed change of `entities` and `vertices` is in `changes('entities')` ([change-stream](change-stream.md)); a second client subscribed to it redraws what others change without polling.
  - A long design alternative is a branch: `CREATE DATABASE plan_b BRANCH OF site` ([as-of-and-branches](as-of-and-branches.md#branch)).

<a id="three-d"></a>

## 3D: vertices, faces, volumes

A mesh is a vertex table and a face table; a solid is a closed mesh; a terrain (TIN) is a mesh whose faces come from the survey points. Rows, not one big JSON: a 16 MB document cannot be loaded in part or changed one triangle at a time, rows can.

**Example: A pyramid as a mesh, its extent and its volume**

Setup:

```sql
CREATE TABLE mesh_vertices (mesh INT, id INT, x DOUBLE, y DOUBLE, z DOUBLE, PRIMARY KEY (mesh, id));
CREATE TABLE mesh_faces (mesh INT, id INT, a INT, b INT, c INT, PRIMARY KEY (mesh, id));
INSERT INTO mesh_vertices VALUES (1,1, 0,0,0), (1,2, 10,0,0), (1,3, 10,10,0), (1,4, 0,10,0), (1,5, 5,5,9);
INSERT INTO mesh_faces VALUES (1,1, 1,2,5), (1,2, 2,3,5), (1,3, 3,4,5), (1,4, 4,1,5), (1,5, 1,3,2), (1,6, 1,4,3);
```

```sql
SELECT mesh, count(*) AS vertices, min(x) AS min_x, max(x) AS max_x, min(z) AS min_z, max(z) AS max_z
FROM mesh_vertices GROUP BY mesh;
SELECT f.mesh,
       round(abs(sum(va.x * (vb.y * vc.z - vc.y * vb.z)
                   - va.y * (vb.x * vc.z - vc.x * vb.z)
                   + va.z * (vb.x * vc.y - vc.x * vb.y)) / 6), 3) AS volume
FROM mesh_faces f
JOIN mesh_vertices va ON va.mesh = f.mesh AND va.id = f.a
JOIN mesh_vertices vb ON vb.mesh = f.mesh AND vb.id = f.b
JOIN mesh_vertices vc ON vc.mesh = f.mesh AND vc.id = f.c
GROUP BY f.mesh;
```

Result:

`SELECT mesh, count(*) AS vertices, min(x) AS min_x, max(x) AS max_x, min(z) AS min_z, max(z) AS max_`

| mesh (INT) | vertices (LONG) | min_x (DOUBLE) | max_x (DOUBLE) | min_z (DOUBLE) | max_z (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5 | 0 | 10 | 0 | 9 |

(1 row)

`SELECT f.mesh, round(abs(sum(va.x * (vb.y * vc.z - vc.y * vb.z) - va.y * (vb.x * vc.z - vc.x * vb.z)`

| mesh (INT) | volume (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 300 |

(1 row)

- **Notes:**
  - The volume is the signed-tetrahedron sum over a **closed** mesh with faces wound the same way; the pyramid's 10 x 10 base and height 9 give 300.
  - Earthworks: two terrains, the same formula on each, the difference is cut or fill. A cross section is the vertices (or the face edges) within a thin box along the section line.
  - A point cloud is `points` with a `code` of its own, or a time-series table when scans arrive continuously ([create-table](create-table.md)).
  - Keep the 3D bounding box too (`min_z`, `max_z`) when a 3D viewport loads in part.

<a id="measure"></a>

## Measurements in SQL

Length, perimeter and area need only the vertices and two window functions ([functions-window](functions-window.md)): `lag()` for the vertex before, and the first vertex again to close a polygon.

**Example: Length of each polyline, perimeter and area of the closed one**

Setup:

```sql
INSERT INTO entities (id, drawing, layer, kind, closed) VALUES ('0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100', 1, 'BOUNDARY', 'polyline', TRUE);
INSERT INTO vertices (entity, seq, x, y) VALUES
  ('0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100', 1, 1000, 2000), ('0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100', 2, 1100, 2000),
  ('0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100', 3, 1100, 2080), ('0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100', 4, 1000, 2080);
INSERT INTO entities (id, drawing, layer, kind) VALUES ('1f1e1d1c-1b1a-4918-9716-151413121110', 1, 'ROAD', 'polyline');
INSERT INTO vertices (entity, seq, x, y) VALUES
  ('1f1e1d1c-1b1a-4918-9716-151413121110', 1, 1000, 2010), ('1f1e1d1c-1b1a-4918-9716-151413121110', 2, 1030, 2050), ('1f1e1d1c-1b1a-4918-9716-151413121110', 3, 1100, 2050);
```

```sql
WITH walk AS (
  SELECT v.entity, e.closed, v.x, v.y,
         lag(v.x) OVER (PARTITION BY v.entity ORDER BY v.seq) AS px,
         lag(v.y) OVER (PARTITION BY v.entity ORDER BY v.seq) AS py,
         first_value(v.x) OVER (PARTITION BY v.entity ORDER BY v.seq) AS fx,
         first_value(v.y) OVER (PARTITION BY v.entity ORDER BY v.seq) AS fy,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY v.entity ORDER BY v.seq DESC) AS from_end
  FROM vertices v JOIN entities e ON e.id = v.entity
)
SELECT entity, closed,
       round(sum(CASE WHEN px IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE sqrt((x - px) * (x - px) + (y - py) * (y - py)) END)
             + CASE WHEN closed THEN sum(CASE WHEN from_end = 1 THEN sqrt((fx - x) * (fx - x) + (fy - y) * (fy - y)) ELSE 0 END) ELSE 0 END, 3) AS length,
       CASE WHEN closed THEN round(abs(sum(CASE WHEN px IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE px * y - x * py END)
                                   + sum(CASE WHEN from_end = 1 THEN x * fy - fx * y ELSE 0 END)) / 2, 3) END AS area
FROM walk GROUP BY entity, closed ORDER BY closed DESC;
```

Result:

| entity (UUID) | closed (BOOL) | length (DOUBLE) | area (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0f0e0d0c-0b0a-4908-8706-050403020100 | true | 360 | 8000 |
| 1f1e1d1c-1b1a-4918-9716-151413121110 | false | 120 | NULL |

(2 rows)

**Example: The nearest control point to a clicked spot**

```sql
SELECT id, x, y, round(sqrt((x - 1052.3) * (x - 1052.3) + (y - 2041.7) * (y - 2041.7)), 3) AS distance
FROM points WHERE project = 1 AND code = 'CP'
ORDER BY distance LIMIT 1;
```

Result:

| id (INT) | x (DOUBLE) | y (DOUBLE) | distance (DOUBLE) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 1100 | 2080 | 61.173 |

(1 row)

- **Notes:**
  - The area is the shoelace formula; `closed` decides whether the last vertex joins back to the first.
  - A nearest-point search over many points first narrows by box (`x BETWEEN cx - r AND cx + r AND y BETWEEN ...`), then sorts the few that remain.
  - Spot heights, slopes and volumes between terrains are `GROUP BY` queries over the same tables; keep them as views ([views](views.md)) so the canvas and a report read the same numbers.

<a id="limits"></a>

## Limits and what would come next

| Today | Works up to | Beyond that |
|---|---|---|
| box columns + B-tree index | a few hundred thousand entities per drawing | a grid or R-tree index in the engine |
| maths in SQL (`sin`, `cos`, `atan2`, `sqrt`, windows) | distance, bearing, area, volume, closure | intersections, buffers, offsets: client side or a saved function |
| one `crs` per project | one grid per project | datum transformations are not built in |
| `JSON` props | free-form attributes | a field you filter on often becomes a column |

Nothing in this layout would change if a geometry type arrived later: the typed columns and the vertex rows would feed it as they are.
