<a id="http"></a>

## Server and HTTP

Syntax:

```sql
request body     64 MB (also after gzip or deflate is unpacked)
request headers  64 KB
idle connection  closed after 30 seconds
worker threads   one per CPU thread, at least 8 (--http-threads)
pg connections   500 (--max-connections)
```

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| HTTP request body (SQL text, line protocol, CSV) | 64 MB. A body sent with `Content-Encoding: gzip` or `deflate` is unpacked first, and the unpacked body is also at most 64 MB. Send big loads in several requests. |
| HTTP replies | not compressed |
| HTTP request headers | 64 KB |
| Requests handled at the same time | one worker thread per CPU thread, at least 8 and at most 64 by default. Set it with `kareladb serve --http-threads N` (1 to 1024), `KARELADB_HTTP_THREADS` or `http_threads` in `kareladb.conf`. Fast and slow requests share the workers: more slow statements than workers make other requests wait for a free one (in a test with 8 workers, 12 slow scans made a `SELECT 1` wait 18.6 s). |
| PostgreSQL connections | 500 logged-in connections for the whole server, all databases together. Set it with `kareladb serve --max-connections N` (`0` = no limit), `KARELADB_MAX_CONNECTIONS` or `max_connections` in `kareladb.conf`. A closed connection's place is free again at once. One more gets `53300`. |
| A keep-alive connection with no new request | closed after 35 seconds (answers advertise `Keep-Alive: timeout=30`; the 5 extra seconds keep a request sent right at 30 seconds from meeting the close) |
| A started request must arrive within | 30 seconds |
| Failed logins | after 5 failures for one user from one address (or 20 from one address), waits of 1 s, 2 s, 4 s ... up to 15 minutes |
| Web console login | 12 hours |
| HTTPS | `--tls-cert` ([TLS](tls.md)), or a reverse proxy |

See [server security](server-security.md) and [HTTP exec](http-exec.md).

**Command line: The server's defaults are in its banner** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb serve ./market
```

Output:

```text
cold store 'archive': folder ./cold-archive
KarelaDB 0.2.0-dev
  console   http://127.0.0.1:9900
  data      ./market
  backups   ./_backups/market (from default)
  access    no token
  capacity  32 HTTP threads (default), 500 PostgreSQL connections (default), lock wait 5 s (default)
  lanes     reads using 100 ms of CPU (three times in a row) wait for one of 16 heavy slots, at most 16 HTTP in line (--lanes on)
  reads     32 reads run at once (the CPUs, at least 2; follows the CPU limit), the rest wait in line (--read-slots)
  commits   synced to disk before they are confirmed (--sync-commits always)
  time zone Asia/Katmandu (the computer's); also timers and backup schedules
  readers   read while a long trigger or CALL writes (--reader-yield on); idle open transaction rolled back after 30 s (default)
  memory    26.95 GB for the whole process (85% of the machine's memory); table data 512.0 MB of it (--memory)
  cpu       32 CPUs (the machine's); 16 query threads (half of the CPUs, follows the limit), limits checked every 10 s
  limits    statement timeout 1 min, result memory 1.00 GB, 5000000 groups, 32 statements per user
  safety    writes allowed; DROP TABLE kept 7 days (UNDROP TABLE); audit log off
  logs      slow queries >= 1000 ms to ./market/_logs/slow_queries.jsonl; pg_stat_statements on; metrics at /metrics
  recovery  manifest copy: a, last shutdown: clean
  open      opened in 1 ms: manifest 0 ms, 1 files read 0 ms (8 table files left for their first use), log check 1 ms, replay 0 ms (0 transactions), clean-up 0 ms

Press Ctrl+C to stop.
```

<a id="disk-memory"></a>

## Disk and memory

Syntax:

```sql
free disk space     writes stop below 64 MB free
disk full           HTTP 507 {"code":"disk full"}, PostgreSQL SQLSTATE 53100
old file versions   2 per file, then _trash for 1 hour
log archive         1 GB per database by default; SET WAL_ARCHIVE changes it
memory for data     --memory, default 512 MB for all open databases together
```

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Free disk space | writes (and checkpoints) are refused when less than 64 MB is free; they work again when there is space |
| A full disk | the write fails with HTTP 507 `{"code":"disk full", ...}` (PostgreSQL port: SQLSTATE `53100`). Rows already committed stay, and nothing is half written. |
| A full disk with the default log mode | `kareladb serve` commits with a group flush (`--sync-commits always`). If that flush hits a full disk, the writes in it get 507 with `The rows of this write are applied in memory and reach the log once disk space is freed`. Reads go on, later writes get 507 until there is room, and then everything works again with no restart. Those refused rows are lost only if the server stops before space is freed. Rarely (the disk refuses the flush after it took the data), the log stops instead: reads go on, writes say `reopen the database to recover`. |
| A full disk with `--sync-commits batch` | reads go on, and writes work again when there is space. But if the disk fills at the moment the log is flushed, the writes confirmed since the last flush (every 10 ms) are lost, and the database must be reopened. |
| An `INSERT` that got 507 | can still be committed: the checkpoint that runs after a commit can fail on its own and report the full disk. Count the rows before you send them again. |
| Previous versions of each data file | 2 (for the repair ladder; `keep_versions` in `kareladb.conf` or `KARELADB_KEEP_VERSIONS`, 0 to 10); fewer once the old log they need is gone |
| Replaced files in `_trash` | removed after 1 hour (`trash_keep_hours` in `kareladb.conf` or `KARELADB_TRASH_KEEP_HOURS`), or sooner beyond `trash_max_mb` (a quarter of the data, at least 256 MB, unless set) |
| A dropped table | kept 7 days for `UNDROP TABLE` (`--trash-days`) |
| Old log files (`wal_archive`) | 1 GB per database by default; the oldest are deleted. Change it per database with [ALTER DATABASE ... SET WAL_ARCHIVE](databases.md#wal-archive), or for all with `wal_archive_mb` on the [Settings page](console-settings.md#wal-archive). `OFF` keeps none. |
| One log file (`wal/*.log`) | 64 MB, then a new file starts |
| One log record | 256 MB (big changes are split into several records) |
| Memory for loaded table data | `--memory`, default 512 MB for all open databases of `kareladb serve` together |
| Memory for one plain or full-text index | 2 GB (`index_memory_bytes`); a bigger index is not built and queries read the table |
| Memory for repeated query results | `--cache-mb`, default 64 MB for all open databases together. One result may use an eighth of it, a [pinned query](pinned-queries.md) half. |
| Temporary files of one big `GROUP BY` or `SAMPLE BY` | 16 GB (`max_spill_bytes`), in `_tmp/` of the database folder; used when the groups need more than half of `--max-result-memory`, removed when the query ends |
| Temporary files of one `INSERT ... SELECT ... ORDER BY` | the same 16 GB (`max_spill_bytes`), in `_tmp/`; the rows are sorted in batches of up to 64 MB, removed when the statement ends |
| Full-text search: one word | 256 bytes (a longer word is cut) |
| [Zone maps](performance-tips.md#zone-maps) | skip only partitions that are in memory. A partition not loaded since the open is read, unless a whole-table `count`, `sum`, `min` or `max` is answered from [saved stats](performance-tips.md#saved-stats). |

**Command line: Sizes and log positions of the files** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb info market
```

Output:

```text
database        market
manifest        copy a, sequence 9
last shutdown   clean
log position    30 (saved in files up to 30)
newest change   2026-10-24 12:03:43
features        batched_log_sync, block_stats, compressed_log, partition_format_2
manifest keys   26

FILE                                      VERSION       SIZE          LSN  STATUS
catalog                                         6     2.1 KB           30  ok
t/1/all                                         7      777 B           30  ok
t/2/all                                         8      556 B           30  ok
t/3/2025                                        9     1.7 KB           30  ok
t/3/2026                                       10     3.6 KB           30  ok
t/4/2026-09                                    11    57.0 KB           30  ok
t/5/2026-09-09                                 12     1.4 KB           30  ok
t/5/2026-09-10                                 13     2.4 KB           30  ok
t/6/2026-09-10                                 14     2.7 KB           30  ok

9 files, 72.1 KB, 0 marked damaged
(STATUS is what the manifest records. To read every block and find new damage, run: kareladb check)
```

<a id="switches"></a>

## Switches for measuring

These environment variables turn one speed-up off, so you can time a query with and without it. The answers are the same either way. Set them for `kareladb serve` only while you measure.

| Variable | Turns off |
|---|---|
| `KARELADB_NO_ZONE_MAPS=1` | skipping partitions by their min and max, and answers from [saved stats](performance-tips.md#saved-stats) |
| `KARELADB_NO_COLUMN_MASK=1` | building only the columns a query reads ([column mask](performance-tips.md#column-mask)) |
| `KARELADB_NO_UNION_PUSHDOWN=1` | grouping a `GROUP BY` over a `UNION ALL` part by part |

For one query, `/exec?cache=0` skips the result cache (see [performance tips](performance-tips.md#measure)).

<a id="not-supported"></a>

## Not supported yet

Syntax:

```sql
NATURAL JOIN   DDL in a transaction
```

Short list. The details, and the ways around each one, are in [known limitations](../tutorial/known-limitations.md).

| Area | Not there yet |
|---|---|
| Statements | `CREATE`/`DROP`/`ALTER` inside a transaction or procedure; `SELECT ... INTO` |
| Changing a table | `PARTITION BY` and `SORT BY` of an existing table; the type of the time column or of a `SORT BY` / `DEDUP KEY` column; dropping the `PRIMARY KEY` |
| Queries | `NATURAL JOIN` (write `JOIN ... USING (columns)`); `ASOF JOIN ... TOLERANCE`; a series function inside another (`lag(sma(x, 3))`); `GROUPS` frames, named windows, `IGNORE NULLS` |
| Procedures and triggers | exception handlers, `LOOP`, `OUT` parameters, functions that return tables, `INSTEAD OF` triggers; row triggers (`FOR EACH ROW`) only as a PostgreSQL `BEFORE UPDATE` trigger |
| Transactions | Row-level locks cover `UPDATE` / `DELETE` by primary key and `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on one table; an `INSERT`, or a change of a table without a primary key or with a secondary `UNIQUE` or a `FOREIGN KEY`, still locks its whole table until `COMMIT`, so `SKIP LOCKED` inside `BEGIN` returns no rows (and `NOWAIT` fails) while another transaction holds that table that way, unless `kareladb serve --skip-locked-beside on`. `FOR SHARE`, `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` and `FOR KEY SHARE` take the same lock as `FOR UPDATE`: two sessions cannot share a row lock, the second one waits (stricter than PostgreSQL, never looser; see [FOR UPDATE](transactions.md#for-update)). |
| Text and JSON | regular expression back references and look-around, JSON path wildcards (`$.items[*]`), the `jsonb` operator `?` |
| Time | summer time in `ROUND ... TIME ZONE`, `time IN ... TIME ZONE` and the zone argument of `date_trunc` / `to_char` (fixed offsets only there) |
| Server | CORS, compressed replies, a Windows service mode; TLS certificates are read at start (restart after renewing one) |
| PostgreSQL port | pgAdmin's own catalog queries (psql `\d` and DBeaver work); API tokens as passwords |
| Users | `CALL` and triggers do not check table rights (rights per database, table, column and row work: [table rights](table-rights.md)); `kareladb sql` and `kareladb shell` never ask for a login |
| Other databases | writing into another database (`INSERT INTO otherdb.t` is refused; reading it works, see [queries across databases](cross-database-queries.md)) |

**Example: NATURAL JOIN is not there yet** (sample data: sample; shows an error)

```sql
SELECT * FROM brokers b NATURAL JOIN brokers c;
```

Result:

Error: `line 1, column 25: expected JOIN, LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN, FULL JOIN, ASOF JOIN, LT JOIN, SPLICE JOIN, CROSS JOIN, WHERE, LATEST ON, SAMPLE BY, GROUP BY, UNION ALL, ORDER BY, LIMIT, ';' or the end of the input but found 'NATURAL'`

<a id="safety"></a>

## Storage safety: crash, power cut, damage

These tests attack the part of a database that loses data: the moment a write is only half done.

| Test | What it does |
|---|---|
| `crash_test` | A child process writes (key-value work and bank transfers). The parent kills it at a random moment. Every confirmed change must be there, nothing unconfirmed, and the totals must be right. |
| `powercut_test` | A fake disk throws away every write that was not synced, as a power cut does, also during recovery. |
| `corrupt_test` | Flips bytes, cuts and deletes files. Damage must always be found and repaired from the previous version or the backup. |

Runs after the engine changes of 2026-09-23 (each change must pass both before it is merged):

| After | `crash_test` | `powercut_test` |
|---|---|---|
| keyless tables written as runs | pass (71 s) | pass (93 s) |
| table-level write locks and group commit | pass: 200 kills, 27,991 confirmed transfers; again on the merged master (90 s) | pass: 300 cuts; again on the merged master (236 s) |
| zone maps | pass | pass |
| indexes built at open, pinned queries | pass: 200 key-value kills, 200 bank kills, 11,128 confirmed transfers | pass: 300 cuts per mode; with batched syncs 45 torn log tails dropped, 0 repairs |

The long runs of 2026-09-12, 1,000 rounds each:

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| `crash_test 1000` | **pass**: 1,000 kills, 37,843 confirmed transfers, 987 unclean opens |
| `powercut_test 1000` | **pass**: 1,000 cuts, 72,555 confirmed operations, 89 cuts during recovery, 129 torn log tails dropped, 0 repairs |
| `corrupt_test 1000` | **pass**: 1,000 rounds, wrong data 0 (30 minutes) |

**One honest note on power cuts.** With `--sync-commits batch` (a flush every 10 ms) 135 of 300 cuts lost writes that had been confirmed to the client but not yet flushed. That is the trade batch mode makes for speed. `--sync-commits always` loses nothing, at about 4.8 ms per commit on this laptop's SSD. In both modes nothing was ever *wrong*: a write is either there or not, never half applied.

Source: reports/keyless-runs.md, reports/table-locks-merge.md, reports/zone-maps.md, reports/warm-at-open.md, reports/qa-tests.md.

<a id="disk-full"></a>

## A full disk

`test_disk_full` gives the database a fake disk that fills up after a random number of bytes (0 to 30,000), so the fault lands in a commit, a group flush, the start of a log file, a partition file or the manifest. It runs 24 rounds for each of 3 log modes and 2 places of the fault (at the write, or at the flush), about 40 seconds.

Each round: insert until the disk is full (never a crash), check that the count equals the confirmed rows, check that 3 more inserts and a checkpoint are refused and lose nothing, free the space, insert and checkpoint again, then close and reopen: no damage, no repair, the exact count, no abandoned file.

| Log mode | Writes resume without a reopen |
|---|---|
| one flush per commit | 24 of 24 rounds, both fault places |
| batched flushes, fault at the write | 24 of 24 |
| group commit (the default of `kareladb serve`) | 1 of 24: the database stops and must be reopened, by design for now |
| batched flushes, fault at the flush | a known limit: writes confirmed since the last flush are lost, a reopen recovers |

Over HTTP: `/write` answers 204, then 507 `{"code":"disk full"}`; an `INSERT` over `POST /exec` answers 507; a `SELECT` still answers 200 with the right rows; `/health` answers 200. The PostgreSQL port gives SQLSTATE `53100`.

The test found **5 faults**, all fixed: a full disk stopped the store until a restart; a failed start of a log file could leave a file the next open called corrupt; a failed manifest save stopped the store; a clean-shutdown mark was written after a failed flush; half-written partition files were left on the full disk. The real behaviour on a full disk is in [limits](limits.md#disk-memory).

Not done yet: a run on a real full volume (a small virtual disk), not only the fake one.

Source: reports/disk-full.md.

<a id="text-fuzz"></a>

## Dirty text and pattern attacks

`test_text_fuzz` puts junk into a table with a full-text index and searches it: NUL bytes, broken and overlong UTF-8, emoji, Devanagari joiners, 1 MB texts, 256 KB search texts, every query-syntax character. Half the rows go in as SQL text, half as parameters. A statement that reaches the 10 s timeout counts as a hang.

| What | Result |
|---|---|
| statements run | 12,132 |
| errors (all from `regexp_like` with a junk pattern, as expected) | 287 |
| crashes, hangs, timeouts | **0** |
| junk rows found by their clean word | 3,000 of 3,000, and 50 of 50 again after a reopen |
| `LIKE` checked against a simple second matcher | 300,000 random patterns, all agree |
| slowest statement | 3.1 s: `MATCH` with a 256 KB search text |

It also timed patterns that make other databases hang. `LIKE` stays at 1 to 7 µs per row whatever the pattern. The regular expression engine never backtracks, but costs 26 to 345 µs per row, so `regexp_like` over 200,000 rows takes 5 to 69 s.

It found one fault, fixed the same day: rows written since the last checkpoint were scanned without looking at the statement timeout. A 300 ms timeout let an 18.5 s scan run to its end; now the scan stops after 0.94 s.

Source: reports/text-fuzz.md.

<a id="unit-tests"></a>

## SQL and server tests

Each C++ test is its own program, registered in `CMakeLists.txt`: **56 programs**. Five of them are long (`crash_test`, `powercut_test`, `corrupt_test`, `fuzz_test`, `stress_test`), and `test_text_fuzz` takes about 7 minutes.

| Group | Test programs | What they check |
|---|---|---|
| Storage (12) | `test_env`, `test_allocator`, `test_crc32c`, `test_inflate`, `test_crypto`, `test_block_file`, `test_wal`, `test_manifest`, `test_store`, `test_backup`, `powercut_test`, `corrupt_test` | each part of the storage code alone |
| Database (30) | `test_sql_parser`, `test_catalog`, `test_database`, `test_tables`, `test_select`, `test_cross_database`, `test_vector`, `test_ingest`, `test_partition`, `test_windows`, `test_manager`, `test_procedures`, `test_txn_readers`, `test_table_locks`, `test_group_spill`, `test_param_pruning`, `test_symbol_pruning`, `test_zone_maps`, `test_view_pushdown`, `test_indexes`, `test_accounting`, `test_memory_budget`, `test_auto_ids`, `test_result_cache`, `test_analysis`, `test_pg_ddl`, `test_sql_features`, `test_mviews`, `crash_test`, `test_text_fuzz` | SQL, tables, queries, both engines, locks, transactions |
| Server (15) | `test_server`, `test_memory_limit`, `test_ilp`, `test_types`, `test_pg`, `test_users`, `test_protection`, `test_disk_full`, `test_pg_dml`, `test_versions`, `test_timers`, `test_activity`, `test_trigger_jobs`, `fuzz_test`, `stress_test` | the HTTP server, line protocol, PostgreSQL port, users, protection, the memory limit |

Tests that compare two ways of getting the same answer:

| Test | What it compares |
|---|---|
| `test_vector` | 437 queries through the column engine and the row engine, 1 to 8 threads, a tiny memory budget, 8 clients; the column engine ran 390 of them. The text of every value must be equal to 17 digits. |
| `test_zone_maps` | 102 queries with zone maps on and off; the rows must be equal to the last bit, and with maps on never more partitions read. Over the run: 13,390 partitions and 1,655 blocks skipped. |
| `test_indexes` | two databases, one with indexes and one without; every query equal, also after random changes, a replay and while indexes are built at open |
| `test_result_cache` | cached against fresh results after random changes; a pinned result kept and refreshed |
| `test_tables` ("keyless runs") | the same 10,000 rows through three write paths; equal after a power cut, a checkpoint, a restart and a `DELETE` |

**No single run of all 56 programs was recorded on 2026-09-23.** Each change ran the programs it touched (the reports list them), and all passed. Two tests were fixed on the way: `test_trigger_jobs` expected a lookup map that the faster duplicate check no longer needs, and `test_ingest` had a race where a background checkpoint left nothing to replay. The last full short-suite run is from 2026-09-12: 33 of 33 programs passed (there were 33 then).

Source: CMakeLists.txt, reports/zone-maps.md, reports/warm-at-open.md, reports/keyless-runs.md, TASKS.md "Done 2026-09-23 evening", bench/results/2026-09-12-ctest-short.txt.

<a id="fuzz-stress"></a>

## Fuzz and stress

**Fuzz test** (2026-09-12). Valid input is damaged at random and sent to the SQL engine, the line protocol, a running HTTP server and a running PostgreSQL port. Every 100 rounds the servers must still answer, and at the end the database is reopened and checked.

| Seeds | Rounds (SQL / line protocol / HTTP / PostgreSQL) | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1, 2, 3 | 4,000 / 4,000 / 2,000 / 2,000 | **pass**: no crash, no hang, slowest statement 142 ms |
| 4, 5 (lighter edits that reach the executor more often) | 4,000 / 4,000 / 2,000 / 2,000 | **pass** |

**Stress test** (2026-09-12). At the same time: 4 line-protocol writers, bank transfers over 4 PostgreSQL connections and 2 HTTP sessions with `CHECK (balance >= 0)`, 6 readers checking that the bank total never changes, a thread creating, altering and dropping tables, and 2 query threads.

| Run | Rows written | Transfers | Reads | Schema rounds | Queries | Failures |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 s | 357,500 | 1,064 | 5,692 | 56 | 3,086 | 0 |
| 5 min | 3,323,000 | 8,539 | 49,897 | 508 | 24,647 | 0 |

**Contention** (2026-09-23, before the table-locks merge): 4 line-protocol writers and 2 SQL writers flat out beside 16 query lanes: no row lost, 0 errors; reads slowed 2 to 3 times at the median, never starved. A 2.1 GB backup under 16 query lanes and 2 writers finished and verified in 7 s, 0 errors.

Source: reports/qa-tests.md, reports/table-locks-merge.md.

<a id="soak"></a>

## Soak

The owner asked for a 48-hour soak. **That has not been done.** Two shorter runs exist.

| | 2026-09-23 | 2026-09-12 |
|---|---|---|
| build | master after the table-locks merge | the code of that day |
| length | 1,826 s (about 30 minutes) | 2,046 s (34 minutes) |
| line-protocol rows written = stored | 19,895,600 = 19,895,600 | 8,738,400 = 8,738,400 |
| SQL rows inserted | 1,362,400 (1,348,540 left after 59 `DELETE` cycles, exact) | 479,350 (474,526 left, exact) |
| queries answered | 64,637 | 23,707 |
| `DELETE` cycles, checkpoints | 59 of 59, 14 of 14 | 67 of 67, 16 of 16 |
| errors | **0** | **0** |
| memory sampled | **no** | yes: 45.7 MB to 1,550 MB while the data grew; 158 to 190 MB per million rows in the second half; no sign of a leak |

The 2026-09-23 run shared the machine with a sanitizer build and a fuzz run. Its memory was not sampled, so the 34-minute run is still the only memory record.

| group commit on a full disk | stops the database until a reopen; changing that is the owner's decision |
| one run of all 56 C++ test programs on the same build | not recorded on 2026-09-23 |
| Linux and Docker runs of the 2026-09-23 code | not done |
| contention test on the merged table-locks build | not done yet (the run above is from before the merge) |
| a real isolation test (read a balance, decide, write) | not done; the balance check only proves the sum is kept |
| `psql \d <table>` from a real psql | not run (no psql on the test PC); every query psql 14 to 16 sends for `\d`, `\d+`, `\dt`, `\di` and `\dv` answers in `test_pg psql_describe` |
| the statement timeout inside one row | not checked: one 16 MB value in a slow regular expression runs to its end |
| more slow statements than HTTP workers | the others wait for a free worker (a `SELECT 1` waited 18.6 s behind 12 slow scans) |

Source: reports/soak.md, reports/disk-full.md, reports/text-fuzz.md, reports/table-locks-merge.md, reports/pg-copy-and-catalog.md, TASKS.md.

<!-- docs/benchmark-report.md -->

# Benchmark report

> How fast KarelaDB is against QuestDB and PostgreSQL on the same PC, and what each engine change of 2026-09-23 gave, including where KarelaDB is still slower and what is not measured.

- Category: Quality
- Keywords: benchmark report, benchmarks, speed, performance, how fast, QuestDB, PostgreSQL, KarelaDB vs QuestDB, KarelaDB vs PostgreSQL, rows per second, p50, latency, result cache, memory footprint, disk footprint, full-text search speed, news search, floor sheet, keyless, table locks, group commit, zone maps, saved stats, column mask, warm at open, A/B, index speed, slow parts, known slow, not measured
- See also: [About KarelaDB](about-kareladb.md), [Test report](test-report.md), [Performance tips](performance-tips.md), [Indexes](indexes.md), [Full-text search](full-text-search.md), [PostgreSQL protocol (port 8832)](postgres-protocol.md), [Limits](limits.md)

Every number on this page comes from a report or result file in the KarelaDB source folder, named under each section. Nothing is rounded beyond what those files say.

Two kinds of measurement are on this page:

- **Head-to-head**: KarelaDB and another database answer the same question on the same PC, and the answers are compared before the times.
- **KarelaDB-only A/B**: the same KarelaDB question before and after one change, the two builds interleaved in the same minutes. These say how much a change gave, not how KarelaDB stands against anyone.

<a id="setup"></a>

## Setup

| Benchmark | Kind | Date | Against | Data | Rounds | Noise |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Time-series](#vs-questdb) | head-to-head | 2026-09-12 | QuestDB 10.0.1, native | 1,000,000 rows, 527 symbols | p50 of many runs, cache off and on | clean machine, just restarted |
| [Time-series re-run](#vs-questdb-0923) | head-to-head | 2026-09-23 | QuestDB 10.0.1 in Docker | 100,000 to 2,000,000 rows | 1 run per size | other work on the PC |
| [Floor-sheet load](#floorsheet) | head-to-head | 2026-09-23 | QuestDB 10.0.1 in Docker | 814,535 real trades | 7 rounds, alternating, medians | 3 s quiet before each load |
| [Floor-sheet queries](#floorsheet) | head-to-head | 2026-09-22 | QuestDB of the 006 app | 1,530,394 real trades, 30 days | 9 runs, `cache=0` | quiet machine |
| [News search](#news-search) | head-to-head | 2026-09-23 | PostgreSQL 18.6 (GIN index) in Docker | 200,000 articles, 378 MB of text | 21 runs per query | a sanitizer build and a fuzz run for the phrase re-run |
| [App workload](#relational) | head-to-head | 2026-09-12 and 2026-09-23 | PostgreSQL 18.4 native; 18.6 in Docker | 20,000 users, accounts, posts; 8 clients | median of 9; 2 interleaved rounds | busy PC both days |
| [PostgreSQL wire](#pg-wire) | head-to-head | 2026-09-12 | QuestDB 10.0.1 | 50,000 rows, 8 clients | median of 9 | busy PC |
| [Indexes](#indexes) | head-to-head | 2026-09-12 | QuestDB 10.0.1 | 1,000,000 posts | 1 complete run | busy PC |
| [Memory and disk](#footprint) | head-to-head | 2026-09-12 | QuestDB 10.0.1 | 1,000,000 minute candles | median of 3 | busy PC |
| [Engine changes](#engine) | KarelaDB-only A/B | 2026-09-23 | the build before | 1,000,000 rows, one thread | 7-round medians, `cache=0` | agents on the PC |

- **Machine:** Intel Core i9-14900HX, 32 threads, 32 GB RAM, Windows 11, the same disk for both databases.
- **KarelaDB:** 0.2.0-dev, Release build, usually `--sync-commits batch` (QuestDB does not flush every commit either).
- **Fair rules:** the same client for both databases, every write timed until the rows can be read back, and row counts and checksums compared so both answered the same question. A benchmark checks `"truncated"`: `/exec` answers at most 10,000 rows unless `limit` is passed.
- **Docker:** on 2026-09-23 the opponents ran in throwaway Docker containers, so every request to them crossed Docker Desktop's network. Their single-request numbers are much lower than on 2026-09-12, when they ran natively. Compare within one day, not across days.

<a id="vs-questdb"></a>

## KarelaDB vs QuestDB: time-series, 2026-09-12

Head-to-head. **Writes** (rows per second, higher is better). The two QuestDB numbers are its results in the cache-off and the cache-on round.

| Test | QuestDB | KarelaDB (cache off) | KarelaDB (cache on) | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bulk load, 20,000 rows per request (line protocol) | 865k / 853k | 1.04M | 1.36M | KarelaDB 1.2-1.6x |
| SQL INSERT, 100 rows per request | 6.8k / 8.9k | 144k | 166k | KarelaDB 19-21x |
| One row per request (line protocol) | 10.6k / 11.1k | 11.8k | 13.7k | KarelaDB 1.1-1.2x |
| One row per request (SQL) | 3.3k / 3.2k | 9.4k | 11.6k | KarelaDB 2.9-3.7x |
| Replace 10% of the rows (dedup upsert) | 724k / 698k | 1.17M | 1.14M | KarelaDB 1.6x |
| Parallel load, 8 clients, 8 tables | 2.63M / 3.04M | 3.52M | 4.13M | KarelaDB 1.3x |
| Delete all rows of one symbol | not possible | 3.3 ms | 4.7 ms | KarelaDB only |

**Queries** (p50 milliseconds at the client, including HTTP and JSON; lower is better).

| Test | QuestDB | KarelaDB (cache off) | KarelaDB (cache on) |
|---|---|---|---|
| count + sum, all rows | 0.171 / 0.183 | 0.335 | 0.142 |
| 1 symbol, 1 day (218 rows) | 0.290 / 0.346 | 0.236 | 0.176 |
| 1 symbol, all days to 1h candles | 0.299 / 0.290 | 0.331 | 0.170 |
| All symbols, 1 day to daily candles (527) | 2.88 / 2.99 | 2.36 | 0.475 |
| Latest row per symbol, `LATEST ON` (527) | 0.271 / 0.240 | 0.416 | 0.239 (tie) |
| `GROUP BY symbol`, all rows (527) | 2.78 / 2.58 | 1.50 | 0.850 |
| `ORDER BY volume DESC LIMIT 10` | 0.746 / 1.10 | 0.321 | 0.122 |
| Parallel queries, 8 clients (queries per second) | 817 / 783 | 5,193 | 9,744 |

- **Writes:** KarelaDB won every test, from 1.1x to 21x, and it can delete rows, which QuestDB cannot.
- **Queries with the cache on** (the normal setting): KarelaDB won every test; `LATEST ON` is a tie. It answered 12x more parallel queries.
- **Queries with the cache off** (the engine alone): KarelaDB won 6 of 8. It was slower on `count + sum` over all rows and on `LATEST ON`. (`count + sum` of a whole table is now answered from [saved stats](#engine); not re-measured against QuestDB with the cache off.)
- **First run of a query:** QuestDB 1.0-7.6 ms, KarelaDB 0.43-4.7 ms.

Source: reports/benchmark-vs-questdb.md, bench/results/2026-09-12-clean-cache-off.json, bench/results/2026-09-12-clean-cache-on.json.

<a id="vs-questdb-0923"></a>

## KarelaDB vs QuestDB: time-series re-run, 2026-09-23

Head-to-head, one run per size, QuestDB in Docker, KarelaDB with `--memory 4096` and the harness's default result cache (on). Only the writes are shown: the query lines of these runs are cache hits on the KarelaDB side, and every QuestDB request paid Docker's network.

| Rows per second, 1,000,000 rows | QuestDB | KarelaDB |
|---|---|---|
| Bulk load, 20,000 rows per request (line protocol) | 726,048 | 1,370,726 |
| SQL INSERT, 100 rows per request | 6,830 | 120,228 |
| Replace 10% of the rows (line protocol upsert) | 610,207 | 866,090 |
| Parallel load, 8 clients, 8 tables (line protocol) | 1,598,723 | 4,054,938 |

At 100,000 and 2,000,000 rows the order is the same (bulk load 1,427,713 against 418,983, and 997,864 against 668,739 rows per second). Read this as "KarelaDB's writes did not get slower since 2026-09-12", not as a new margin.

Source: bench/results/2026-09-23-100k.json, bench/results/2026-09-23-1m.json, bench/results/2026-09-23-2m.json.

<a id="floorsheet"></a>

## Floor sheet: KarelaDB vs QuestDB

**Load**, head-to-head, 2026-09-23. 814,535 real trades (15 days), 8 columns with three `SYMBOL` columns, `PARTITION BY DAY`, 20,000 rows per `POST /write`, medians of 7 alternating rounds.

| | QuestDB | KarelaDB | |
|---|---|---|---|
| before: the floor sheet has no `DEDUP KEY`, so KarelaDB wrote it row by row | 686,476 rows/s | 438,373 rows/s | KarelaDB 36% slower |
| after: keyless tables written as runs, 3 s quiet before each load | 677,540 rows/s | **918,067 rows/s** | KarelaDB 35% faster, 6 of 7 rounds won |
| after, no pause between loads | 700,202 rows/s | 814,553 rows/s | KarelaDB 16% faster |
| the candle table (with a `DEDUP KEY`), same day | 726,048 rows/s | 1,370,726 rows/s | KarelaDB 1.9x |

**Queries**, head-to-head, 2026-09-22, in the container on real data (1,530,394 trades over 30 days), `cache=0`, every answer equal to QuestDB's:

| Query | KarelaDB engine | KarelaDB wall | QuestDB | Before (2026-09-18) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BUY by stock and broker | 11.9 ms | 19.2 ms | 23.9 ms | 20.0 / 29.0 ms |
| SELL by stock and broker | 13.3 ms | 21.0 ms | 24.1 ms | 19.3 / 28.0 ms |
| BUY + SELL in one (`UNION ALL`) | 118.6 ms | 129.7 ms | 243.9 ms | 1,337 ms against QuestDB's 365 ms |

The `UNION ALL` form went from 3.6x slower to 1.9x faster: each part is now grouped in the column engine before the parts are added up.

Found on the way: QuestDB 10.0.1 lost the first 20,000-row request after a `DROP TABLE` and `CREATE TABLE` of the same name, in 5 of 6 cycles, while answering 204 to it. Benchmarks now use a fresh table name per round.

Source: reports/keyless-runs.md, bench/results/2026-09-23-1m.json, reports/floorsheet-filter-speed.md.

<a id="news-search"></a>

## News search: KarelaDB vs PostgreSQL

Head-to-head, 2026-09-23. 200,000 articles (a title of 8 words, a body of 250 words, 378 MB of text), 21 runs per query. PostgreSQL 18.6 gets its best practice: a stored `tsvector` column with a GIN index, searched with the `simple` configuration (no stemming, like KarelaDB). KarelaDB gets `CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX` on title and body. Top-20 lists are ranked differently by design (BM25 against `ts_rank_cd`), so those are compared on row count only.

| Query | Rows | KarelaDB | PostgreSQL | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| load 200,000 articles | | 3.9 s (51,514/s) | 49.2 s (4,068/s) | KarelaDB 12.7x |
| build the full-text index | | 2.18 s | 9.07 s | KarelaDB 4.2x |
| common word, count | 182,571 | 3.6 ms | 250 ms | KarelaDB 69x |
| mid word, count | 40,255 | 0.66 ms | 82 ms | KarelaDB 124x |
| two words AND, count | 35,095 | 3.6 ms | 86 ms | KarelaDB 24x |
| prefix `hydro*`, count | 151,463 | 10 ms | 284 ms | KarelaDB 28x |
| rare word, ids | 218 | 0.36 ms | 0.64 ms | KarelaDB 1.8x |
| word + symbol + month | 9 | 0.54 ms | **0.48 ms** | PostgreSQL 1.1x |
| common word, top 20 by rank | 20 | 7.3 ms | 408 ms | KarelaDB 56x |
| mid word, top 20 by rank | 20 | 16.9 ms | 384 ms | KarelaDB 23x |
| two words, top 20 by rank | 20 | 5.5 ms | 364 ms | KarelaDB 66x |
| 8 clients, ranked search | | 348/s | 23/s | KarelaDB 15x |
| common word, all 182,571 ids | 182,571 | 188 ms | 636 ms | KarelaDB 3.4x |
| phrase "hydro power", count | about 2,376 | **9.7 ms** (was 2,347 ms) | 295 ms | KarelaDB 30x |

- Before the fixes of that day, on 20,000 shorter articles, a common-word count took 351 ms in KarelaDB against 2.5 ms in PostgreSQL. Three faults caused it (a planner that dropped the index for common words, `count(*)` fetching every row, `LIMIT` not reaching the index). All three are fixed.
- The phrase line: word positions were added to the index the same afternoon. The 9.7 ms was measured with a sanitizer build and a fuzz run on the PC; a quiet re-run is owed. The phrase counts differ by 3 rows (2,376 against 2,379) because PostgreSQL also finds a phrase across the end of the title and the start of the body.
- `word + symbol + month` is the one line PostgreSQL still wins. KarelaDB now lets the cheaper of the text index and the plain index go first; that is **not measured yet**.

Source: reports/news-search.md (with its addendum), bench/postgres/results/2026-09-23-search-200k-r1.json.

<a id="relational"></a>

## App workload: KarelaDB vs PostgreSQL

Head-to-head. Sign-ups, logins, transfers, forum posts, full-text search and a report join, 20,000 rows, 8 clients.

**2026-09-12**, PostgreSQL 18.4 native, median of 9 runs:

| Test | KarelaDB ops/s | PostgreSQL ops/s | KarelaDB won | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| sign-up (user and account, one transaction) | 3,203 | 943 | 9/9 | **KarelaDB faster** |
| login (lookup by unique login) | 11,858 | 10,367 | 5/9 | no clear difference |
| transfer (BEGIN, 3 statements, COMMIT) | 2,696 | 829 | 9/9 | **KarelaDB faster** |
| post a thread (5 posts, one transaction) | 1,322 | 694 | 8/8 | **KarelaDB faster** |
| 8 clients transferring | 1,343 | 4,661 | 0/8 | **PostgreSQL faster** |
| read a thread page (up to 50 posts) | 5,105 | 11,111 | 0/8 | **PostgreSQL faster** |
| forum full-text search (top 20) | 147 | 2,576 | 0/8 | **PostgreSQL faster** |
| report join (users, accounts, transfers) | 19 | 68 | 0/8 | **PostgreSQL faster** |

**2026-09-23**, PostgreSQL 18.6 in Docker, the build before and after the table-locks merge interleaved in the same minutes (master, merged, master, merged). A sanitizer build and a fuzz test ran on the PC throughout.

| Test | KarelaDB before the merge | KarelaDB after the merge | PostgreSQL, same runs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 clients transferring | 689 and 604/s | **1,821 and 1,981/s** | 861 to 988/s |
| 8 clients transferring, p50 | 11.7 and 13.5 ms | 4.4 and 4.0 ms | 8.6 and 8.7 ms |
| forum full-text search (top 20) | 2,846 and 2,840/s | 2,673 and 3,177/s | 834 to 923/s |
| read a thread page | 3,664 and 3,071/s | 3,166 and 3,847/s | 875 to 1,310/s |
| report join | 18 and 17/s | 16 and 18/s | 59 to 63/s |

- **Many writers:** table-level write locks and group commit took 8 clients transferring from 604 to 1,981 per second: 3x the build before, 2x PostgreSQL in the same minutes. Balances were conserved in every run.
- **Forum search:** it lost 17x on 2026-09-12. With `LIMIT` pushed into the index it went from 7.16 ms to 0.265 ms per search (PostgreSQL 0.843 ms), and wins about 3x now.
- **Read with care:** PostgreSQL in Docker did far fewer single-client operations than PostgreSQL native on 2026-09-12 (sign-up 123 to 408/s against 943/s). So the single-client lines of 2026-09-23 are left out here; they measure Docker's network as much as PostgreSQL.
- **Report join:** PostgreSQL is still 3.5x faster. That is the join engine (rows are copied three times on the way out).

Source: reports/benchmark-postgres.md, bench/results/2026-09-12-relational-medians.txt, reports/table-locks-merge.md, bench/postgres/results/2026-09-23-locks-master-r1.json, -r2.json, 2026-09-23-locks-merged-r1.json, -r2.json, reports/news-search.md.

<a id="pg-wire"></a>

## PostgreSQL wire protocol: KarelaDB vs QuestDB

Head-to-head, 2026-09-12. A Go client (pgx v5) over the PostgreSQL port, 50,000 rows, 8 clients, 9 runs. A winner is named only when the paired sign test gives p below 0.05 (8 or 9 wins out of 9).

| Test | KarelaDB ops/s | QuestDB ops/s | KarelaDB won | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| connect (fresh connection) | 1,431 | 1,583 | 3/9 | no clear difference |
| simple query `SELECT 1` | 14,917 | 12,000 | 5/9 | no clear difference |
| prepared query `id=$1` | 6,331 | 7,834 | 2/9 | no clear difference |
| INSERT 1 row | 12,368 | 13,293 | 4/9 | no clear difference |
| INSERT 1,000 rows in one statement | 104 | 62 | 9/9 | **KarelaDB faster** |
| SELECT 1 row | 6,417 | 6,903 | 2/9 | no clear difference |
| SELECT 500 rows | 3,511 | 3,193 | 5/9 | no clear difference |
| SELECT 50,000 rows | 66 | 79 | 3/9 | no clear difference |
| 8 clients, SELECT 500 | 12,788 | 12,043 | 6/9 | no clear difference |

Eight of nine tests are a tie. A 50,000-row `SELECT` ran at 66 per second over the PostgreSQL port against 25 over HTTP `/exec` (KarelaDB against itself, 9 of 9): the PostgreSQL port sends binary, HTTP builds JSON.

Source: reports/benchmark-postgres.md, bench/results/2026-09-12-pgwire-medians.txt.

<a id="indexes"></a>

## Indexes, and indexes built at open

Head-to-head, 2026-09-12, 1,000,000 forum posts, one complete run, p50 milliseconds. QuestDB has no full-text index, so it answers with `LIKE '%word%'`.

| Query | Rows | KarelaDB no index | KarelaDB with index | QuestDB | Against QuestDB |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| lookup `author = x` | 63 | 5.41 | 0.35 | 0.57 | KarelaDB 1.6x |
| range scan `status` + 1 month | 10,708 | 1.74 | 10.76 | 0.26 | QuestDB 42x |
| keyset page 1 | 20 | 1.81 | 281.93 | 12.74 | QuestDB 22x |
| `OFFSET` page 10,000 | 20 | 373.87 | 347.35 | 9.65 | QuestDB 36x |
| search a rare word, top 20 by rank | 20 | 15,091 | 0.49 | 27.35 (no rank) | KarelaDB 56x |
| phrase search | 28,101 | 7,603 | 3,721 | not possible | KarelaDB only |

The full-text lines of this table are from before the search fixes of 2026-09-23; see [news search](#news-search) for today's numbers.

**Indexes built at open**, KarelaDB-only A/B, 2026-09-23. Indexes live in memory and were built by the first query that needed them after a restart. Now `kareladb serve` builds them on a background thread right after the open. First request after a restart, 200,000 posts, 4 indexes, 9 rounds, cache off:

| First request after a restart | Built by the query | Built at open | Warm won |
|---|---|---|---|
| lookup `author = x` | 89.7 ms | 1.5 ms | 9/9 |
| range scan `status` + 1 month | 77.8 ms | 6.7 ms | 9/9 |
| common word, count | 774.4 ms | 3.1 ms | 9/9 |
| all indexes ready after the open | | 685 ms | |

The open itself did not get slower (274 against 291 ms, ranges overlap). One line got slower by direction only: keyset page 1, 23.0 against 26.4 ms, inside the round-to-round spread.

Source: reports/benchmark-indexes-and-footprint.md, bench/results/2026-09-12-indexes-1m-bench3-full.json, reports/warm-at-open.md, bench/results/2026-09-23-warm-restart-r1.json to -r9.json.

<a id="engine"></a>

## Engine changes of 2026-09-23

KarelaDB-only A/B. 1,000,000 rows, one thread, `?cache=0`, 7-round medians, before and after on the same build, unless the line says otherwise.

| Change | Query or load | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| a trigger on one table no longer slows loads into the others | 20,000-row load into a table without a trigger | 34 ms | 8 ms |
| the same trigger made `DEFERRED` (on the real floor sheet) | 20,000-row load | 103 ms | 9 ms |
| `LIKE` / `ILIKE` / `NOT LIKE` in the column engine | `sym LIKE 'S6%'` | 242 ms | 1.2 ms |
| | `NOT LIKE` | 243 ms | 3.3 ms |
| | `ILIKE` | 230 ms | 2.2 ms |
| `col = a OR col = b` as an IN list | `sum(qty) WHERE sym = 'S1' OR sym = 'S2'` | 151 ms | 0.30 ms |
| | `qty = 7 OR qty = 9` | 115 ms | 12 ms |
| branch-free filters in the column engine | random `LONG x > L` | 4.68 ms | 0.67 ms |
| | random `DOUBLE y > L` | 7.03 ms | 0.62 ms |
| | `b BETWEEN ...` | 8.77 ms | 0.84 ms |
| | `a > X AND b < Y`, on the thread pool | 1.17 ms | 0.49 ms |
| `count`, `sum`, `min`, `max` from saved stats | 4,000,000 rows in 200 day files, after a restart | 99.7 ms, 200 partition loads | 0.28 ms, 0 loads |
| the row path builds only the columns it reads (21-column table) | `count(*) WHERE a * 1 > X` | 460 ms | 210 ms |
| | `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10` | 554 ms | 268 ms |
| | `GROUP BY` | 549 ms | 242 ms |
| | `SELECT *` (must build every column) | 465 ms | 436 ms |
| manifest keys of dropped tables removed | 300 partitions, one table dropped: manifest size | 1,128 KB | 573 KB |
| | checkpoint | 24.6 ms | 14.7 ms |
| zone maps (814,535 floor-sheet trades, 15 day files, HTTP round trip) | `contract > p99`: 14 of 15 files skipped | 0.93 ms | 0.56 ms |
| | a value above every file: 15 of 15 skipped | 1.66 ms | 0.59 ms |
| | `rate > p99`: nothing skipped | 1.99 ms | 2.15 ms (noise) |
| stop flag read in the scan of unsaved rows (200,000 rows) | a 300 ms timeout | 308.8 s, never stopped | 0.94 s, stopped |
| keyless tables written as runs | floor-sheet load, rows/s | 438,373 | 918,067 |
| table-level write locks + group commit | 8 clients transferring | 604/s | 1,981/s |

Older engine A/Bs: window frames `corr(...) ROWS 199 PRECEDING` 9,536 to 431 ms (2026-09-12); `count(*), sum(volume)` after replaced rows 164 to 44 µs (2026-09-12); the `UNION ALL` buy-and-sell query 1,750 to 29.2 ms on synthetic data (2026-09-22).

Source: TASKS.md "Done 2026-09-23" and "Done 2026-09-23 evening", reports/zone-maps.md, reports/text-fuzz.md, reports/keyless-runs.md, reports/table-locks-merge.md, reports/window-frame-fast-path.md, reports/column-engine-speed.md, reports/floorsheet-filter-speed.md.

<a id="request-time"></a>

## Where the time of one request goes

KarelaDB-only, 2026-09-23 evening, the container on 9900 through Docker Desktop and a native build on Windows loopback, same minutes:

| Path | Round trip |
|---|---|
| the engine alone (server time of `SELECT 1`) | 8-10 µs |
| `/exec` through Docker Desktop | 448-800 µs |
| `/health` (does nothing) through Docker Desktop | 465-685 µs |
| `/exec` on Windows loopback | 48-103 µs |
| a bare Node server on Windows loopback | 49-80 µs |

So the socket path is under 2% of a request through Docker and under 15% on loopback. The rest is Docker Desktop's network and the `/exec` path itself.

Source: TASKS.md, "Re-judged 2026-09-23 evening, measured".

<a id="still-slow"></a>

## Where KarelaDB is still slower, or not measured

| Where | Measured | Source |
|---|---|---|
| joins with `GROUP BY` | report join 16-18/s against PostgreSQL's 59-63/s (2026-09-23) | reports/table-locks-merge.md |
| `SELECT 1` throughput | flat at about 3,000 requests/s with 8 clients (p50 469 to 2,071 µs), while `/health` does about 19,000/s: the ceiling is in the `/exec` path | TASKS.md, HFT item 1 |
| opening a big data folder | 124 to 233 s for 11,104 partitions (9.5 GB): one file open of 10 to 16 ms per partition | TASKS.md, item E |
| more slow statements than HTTP workers | a `SELECT 1` waited 18.6 s behind 12 slow scans on the 8 workers | reports/text-fuzz.md |
| `regexp_like` | 26 to 345 µs per row: 5 to 69 s over 200,000 rows | reports/text-fuzz.md |
| text + cheap filter | `word + symbol + month` 0.54 ms against PostgreSQL's 0.48 ms; the new plan is not measured | reports/news-search.md |
| zone maps on prices | `rate > p99` skips no file: every day holds the top prices | reports/zone-maps.md |
| index choice | an index used where a scan is faster: keyset page 1 1.81 ms without, 281.93 ms with (2026-09-12) | reports/benchmark-indexes-and-footprint.md |
| deep pages | `OFFSET` page 10,000: 347 ms against QuestDB's 9.65 ms (2026-09-12) | reports/benchmark-indexes-and-footprint.md |
| `ORDER BY` over many groups | 377-580 ms on 270,000+ groups against 44-54 ms without the `ORDER BY` | reports/floorsheet-filter-speed.md |
| the outer step of a `UNION ALL` grouping | about 90 ms of the 118.6 ms floor-sheet query runs on the row path | reports/floorsheet-filter-speed.md |
| commit with a flush | 4.8 ms per commit with `--sync-commits always`: the SSD's own flush | reports/performance-and-cache.md |
| not measured | a quiet re-run of the news search after the phrase and planner changes; the contention test on the merged table-locks build; any benchmark on Linux; the numbers on 9900 since the last image rebuild | TASKS.md, reports/news-search.md, reports/table-locks-merge.md |

What changed since the list of 2026-09-12: **many writers at once** (then 1,343 against PostgreSQL's 4,661 transfers/s) and **full-text search** (then 147 against 2,576 searches/s, and a common-word count 11.8x slower than QuestDB's scan) are now KarelaDB wins. They are not on this list any more.

Source: the files named in the table.

<!-- docs/data-formats.md -->

# How KarelaDB stores data

> A short tour of the files in a KarelaDB database folder - data files, blocks and checksums, the log, the manifest and backups.

- Category: Data formats
- Keywords: file format, on-disk format, files, folder, kdb.lock, \_manifest.a, \_manifest.b, manifest, wal, wal\_archive, \_trash, WAL, write-ahead log, log segment, LSN, checkpoint, block, CRC32C, checksum, digest, copy-on-write, version, partition file, column file, backup.kdb, .partial, timeline, FORMAT.md, little-endian, manifest keys, removed manifest keys, column stats
- See also: [Backup, check, repair and restore](backup-and-safety.md), [kareladb info, check, repair, dump-file](cli-maintenance.md), [Partitions, SORT BY and DEDUP KEY](partitions-and-dedup.md), [Limits (disk-memory)](limits.md#disk-memory)

This page explains, in simple words, what KarelaDB writes to the disk and why. You do not need it to use KarelaDB. It helps to understand `kareladb info`, `kareladb check` and the messages about damage.
The exact bytes, for developers, are in docs/FORMAT.md. When that file and the code disagree, the code is right.

**Do not change or delete files in a database folder by hand.** Use `kareladb` commands. To copy a database, stop every program that uses it, or better use [kareladb backup](backup-and-safety.md#kareladb-backup).

The format is the same on Windows, Linux and macOS, so a database folder can move between them.

<a id="folder"></a>

## The database folder

Syntax:

```sql
<database>/
  kdb.lock                   locked while a program has the database open
  _manifest.a  _manifest.b   the list of current files, saved twice
  files/                     data files: files/<name>.v<version>.kdb
  wal/                       the write-ahead log (the newest changes)
  wal_archive/               older log files, kept for backups and repairs
  _trash/                    files taken out of use, deleted after 24 hours
```

A database is one folder. In a data folder, each database is a sub-folder, plus `_trash` (dropped databases) and `_system` (the server's users).

| Name | What it is |
|---|---|
| `kdb.lock` | An empty file. While a program has the database open, the operating system **locks** it, so a second program gets `the database is open in another program`. Do not delete it: when no program runs, the lock is free anyway. |
| `_manifest.a`, `_manifest.b` | The **manifest**: the list of the current data files, their versions, sizes and checksums, and the log positions. Two copies (see [manifest](#manifest)). |
| `files/` | The **data files**: `files/catalog.v6.kdb` (the list of tables and columns) and `files/t/<table number>/<partition>.v<version>.kdb` (the rows of one partition). A table [split by symbol](partitions-and-dedup.md#partition-by-symbol) adds the symbol to the partition name, as hex: `2026-09/s-43495459` is month `2026-09`, symbol `CITY`. |
| `wal/` | The **write-ahead log** (WAL): every change is written here first (see [the log](#wal)). |
| `wal_archive/` | Old log files that the data files no longer need. Only backups and repairs use them. The oldest are deleted when this folder is over its limit: 1 GB by default, changed with [ALTER DATABASE ... SET WAL_ARCHIVE](databases.md#wal-archive) or on the [Settings page](console-settings.md#wal-archive). |
| `_trash/` | Files taken out of use: old versions, damaged files moved away by a repair, unknown files. Folders older than 24 hours are deleted when the database opens. |

**Command line: kareladb info lists what the manifest says** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb info market
```

Output:

```text
database        market
manifest        copy a, sequence 9
last shutdown   clean
log position    30 (saved in files up to 30)
newest change   2026-10-24 12:03:43
features        batched_log_sync, block_stats, compressed_log, partition_format_2
manifest keys   26

FILE                                      VERSION       SIZE          LSN  STATUS
catalog                                         6     2.1 KB           30  ok
t/1/all                                         7      777 B           30  ok
t/2/all                                         8      556 B           30  ok
t/3/2025                                        9     1.7 KB           30  ok
t/3/2026                                       10     3.6 KB           30  ok
t/4/2026-09                                    11    57.0 KB           30  ok
t/5/2026-09-09                                 12     1.4 KB           30  ok
t/5/2026-09-10                                 13     2.4 KB           30  ok
t/6/2026-09-10                                 14     2.7 KB           30  ok

9 files, 72.1 KB, 0 marked damaged
(STATUS is what the manifest records. To read every block and find new damage, run: kareladb check)
```

`t/4/2026-09` is table number 4 (tables are numbered in the order they were made; here `ochl_minutes`), partition `2026-09`. `all` is a table without partitions. `VERSION 11` is the file `files/t/4/2026-09.v11.kdb`.

<a id="data-files"></a>

## Data files are never changed

Syntax:

```sql
files/t/<table number>/<partition>.v<version>.kdb
```

A data file is written **once** and then never changed (this is called copy-on-write).

1. Changes first go into the log and into memory.
2. From time to time (a **checkpoint**), KarelaDB writes a **new version** of each changed partition: a new file with the next version number.
3. KarelaDB reads the new file back and checks it.
4. Only then it saves the manifest, which now names the new version.

- A crash at any moment leaves the old version complete. There is never a half-changed file.
- KarelaDB keeps the **2 previous versions** of every file, for the repair ladder. Older ones go to `_trash`.
- A checkpoint happens after about 1 million changes, every 5 minutes, when the changes use a quarter of `--memory`, about 2 seconds after the last write when at least 10,000 changes wait, when a database closes, before a backup or a schema change, and when you ask for one with [CHECKPOINT](backup-and-safety.md#checkpoint). On a busy database a write may leave its checkpoint to a background thread, but only until the changes use half of `--memory`, or for at most 5 seconds; after that the next write waits for the checkpoint, so unsaved changes cannot grow without limit. Rows a load (`POST /write`, `POST /imp`, `COPY`) keeps in column form count as 1/8 of a change, so a bulk load checkpoints about every 8 million rows (or at a quarter of `--memory`, whichever comes first) instead of every million: each checkpoint writes every partition it touched whole, and on a big load into a few partitions most of those bytes were rows already on disk (since 2026-10-02).
- One partition file holds all columns of that partition, column after column, with the number of rows, the smallest and biggest value and the sum of each column (the **column stats**).
- KarelaDB uses the column stats without reading the rows: a `WHERE` skips a partition in memory (or a block of 65,536 rows in it) whose values cannot match, and `count`, `min`, `max` and `sum` of a partition that is not in memory are answered from its file's stats, without loading the rows. [EXPLAIN](explain.md) shows both. This needed no change of the files: partition files have had the stats since 2026-09-12.

**Command line: One data file: the table securities** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb dump-file market/files/t/1/all.v7.kdb
```

Output:

```text
file         market/files/t/1/all.v7.kdb
type         data file
version      1
data         693 B
block size   65536
LSN          30
id           1
created      2026-10-24 12:03:43
blocks       1
digest       1d198644
OK: all blocks match their checksums
```

<a id="checksums"></a>

## Blocks and CRC32C checksums

Syntax:

```sql
[ header 64 bytes ][ block 1 ][ block 2 ] ... [ checksum table ][ trailer 16 bytes ]
```

Every KarelaDB file (data files, manifests, `backup.kdb`) is cut into **blocks** of 64 KB. Each block has a **CRC32C checksum**: a 4-byte number made from the bytes of the block.

- When KarelaDB reads a block, it computes the number again. If one bit on the disk has changed, the numbers differ, and KarelaDB says `block N (bytes ...) failed its checksum`. It **never** returns data from a bad block.
- The **header** (the first 64 bytes) says what the file is: its type, the format version, the block size, the data length, the log position, and when it was made. It has its own checksum.
- The **trailer** at the end holds the number of blocks and a checksum of the checksum table, so a file that was cut short is noticed.
- The **digest** is one checksum over the header and all block checksums. The manifest keeps it for each file, so KarelaDB also notices a whole file that was replaced by another one.
- The header is written **last**. A file that a crash interrupted has no valid header and is never used.
- `crc32c hardware: yes` in `kareladb version` means the CPU computes these checksums with fast special instructions.

**Command line: Check every block of one file** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb dump-file market/_manifest.a
```

Output:

```text
file         market/_manifest.a
type         manifest
version      1
data         2.3 KB
block size   65536
LSN          30
id           9
created      2026-10-24 12:03:43
blocks       1
digest       c9d2b3c1
OK: all blocks match their checksums
```

<a id="wal"></a>

## The write-ahead log (WAL)

Syntax:

```sql
wal/00000000000000000001.log      a log file (segment), named after its first LSN
record: length | checksum | LSN | transaction id | type (data or commit) | data
```

Every change is first written to the **log**, and the log is on the disk before KarelaDB says a statement is done.

- Each record in the log gets the next number: the **LSN** (log sequence number). `kareladb info` shows `log position` = the newest LSN.
- A transaction is its data records plus one **commit** record. The whole transaction is written in one piece and saved with **one** disk sync. Without its commit record, a transaction does not count.
- Every record has its own checksum.
- A log file (a **segment**) grows to 64 MB; then a new one starts. Log files that the data files no longer need move to `wal_archive/`.
- **After a crash**, KarelaDB reads the log from the position the data files have, and replays every committed transaction. `kareladb info` then shows `last shutdown: not clean`, which is normal.
- **A torn tail:** a power cut can leave the last, unconfirmed transaction half written at the end of the log. KarelaDB notices it and cuts it off (`dropped an unfinished write at the end of the log`). Nothing confirmed is lost.
- **Damage in the middle** of the log, in records that are still needed, is refused with a clear message. See [after damage](backup-and-safety.md#after-damage).
- With `--sync-commits batch`, several transactions share one disk sync every 10 ms.

<a id="manifest"></a>

## The manifest: two copies

Syntax:

```sql
_manifest.a   _manifest.b    the newer valid copy (highest sequence number) wins
```

The manifest is the list of what is current: every data file with its version, size, digest and log position, the previous versions, which files are marked damaged, and whether the last shutdown was clean.

- It is saved in two files. A save always writes over the **older** copy. So if a crash happens during a save, the other copy is still complete.
- When opening, KarelaDB reads both and uses the valid copy with the highest **sequence** number. `kareladb info` shows `manifest copy b, sequence 12`.
- If one copy is damaged, KarelaDB notes it and writes over it at the next save.
- It is saved at every checkpoint, after a recovery, and when the database closes (then with `clean shutdown`).

<a id="manifest-keys"></a>

### Manifest keys

Besides the file list, the manifest keeps small **keys** for the tables:

| Key | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `rows.<file>` | the row count of a partition file |
| `sym.<file>` | which symbols a partition file holds, so a `WHERE symbol = ...` skips files without opening them |
| `rowid.<table number>`, `auto.<table number>` | the next row id and the next `AUTO` value of a table |

- Every checkpoint rewrites the manifest with all its keys. Since 2026-09-23 the keys of a dropped table (and of partition files that are gone) are removed at the next checkpoint, and once when a database is opened for writing. Older builds left them behind for ever.
- The open then says `removed N manifest keys left behind by dropped tables`. `kareladb info` shows `manifest keys N`, and how many of them belong to files that are gone.
- This is no change of the format: an older KarelaDB opens such a manifest as before.

**Command line: Which copy is newest** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb info market
kareladb dump-file market/_manifest.b
```

Output:

In the header of a manifest, `id` is its sequence number. The copy that `kareladb info` names has the higher one; the other copy is one save older.

<a id="backups"></a>

## Backup folders

Syntax:

```sql
<backups-dir>/
  20260911-161530-123/          a backup; the name is the UTC time
    backup.kdb                  the list of the backup, written last
    files/<name>.v<N>.kdb       the current version of every data file
    wal/<first LSN>.log         the log files needed to replay from those files
  20260912-...-.partial/        an unfinished backup: never used, removed later
```

- A backup holds only the **current** version of each file, plus the log files needed. With `--hard-links`, the data files are hard links; log files are always copied.
- `backup.kdb` is a KarelaDB block file too (with checksums). It is written **last**, after every file was copied and synced. Then the whole backup is read again. Only then the folder gets its final name (without `.partial`).
- A backup knows which database it came from (a random id made when the database was created) and its log history. Repairs and `--logs-from` never use a backup or log of another database.
- **Restore** copies the files into a new folder, checks every copy, adds newer log files from `--logs-from`, cuts the log at `--until`, and writes a new manifest. The log is replayed when the new database is first opened. The restored database starts a new log **history** (timeline), so old log files of the abandoned history are never mixed in.

**Command line: A backup, and its list** (sample data: sample)

```bash
kareladb backup market backups
kareladb backups backups
```

Output:

`> kareladb backup market backups`

```text
backup created and verified: backups/20261024-061845-233
  9 files, 190.0 KB, log up to 30
```

`> kareladb backups backups`

```text
BACKUP                 CREATED               FILES       SIZE      LOG LSN
20261024-061845-233    2026-10-24 12:03:45       9   190.0 KB           30
1 backups
```

<a id="indexes"></a>

## Indexes are not stored

Syntax:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ...     only the definition is saved (in the catalog)
```

For `CREATE INDEX`, KarelaDB saves only the **definition** in the catalog. The index itself lives in memory. It is built from the rows after the database opens: `kareladb serve` builds every index on a background thread right after the open, and a query that needs one before that builds it itself.

- So `kareladb check`, `kareladb repair`, backups and restores have nothing to check for indexes, and an index can never be old or damaged after a crash.
- The cost: after a start, building a big index takes a while. A query that needs it early waits for it (see [indexes](indexes.md#warm)).

**Example: An index on a sample table: only its definition is saved** (sample data: sample)

```sql
CREATE INDEX trade_log_buyer ON trade_log (buyer);
SHOW INDEXES;
```

Result:

`CREATE INDEX trade_log_buyer ON trade_log (buyer)`

```text
index 'trade_log_buyer' created on table 'trade_log' (32 rows)
```

`SHOW INDEXES`

| name (STRING) | table (STRING) | kind (STRING) | columns (STRING) | built (BOOL) | rows (LONG) | memory_bytes (LONG) | create_sql (STRING) | building (BOOL) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| trade_log_buyer | trade_log | INDEX | buyer | true | 32 | 1777 | CREATE INDEX trade_log_buyer ON trade_log (buyer) | false |

(1 row)
